With this game Koei established itself as a studio specializing in historical simulations, and Nobunaga's Ambition became one of its most enduring brands. The series is named after Oda Nobunaga, one of the most significant figures in Japanese history, and the game thus gently acquainted players with genuine historical realities. For Western audiences it was a rare window into Japanese history wrapped in strategic entertainment.

The cultural significance here is twofold. On the one hand the game was among the pioneers of the strategy genre on consoles, where more action-oriented titles dominated, and on the other in Japan it built up an enormous fan base and became one of the defining series of its kind. Its turn-based system and emphasis on resource management made it a title over which players spent dozens of hours.

Today we regard Nobunaga's Ambition as an important milestone that proved even the limited NES hardware could run a complex strategy game with economics and diplomacy. The series continued with many further installments on newer platforms, and its legacy lives on among fans of historical strategy to this day.

**Why play:** A deep turn-based strategy set in Japan's warring states period, where you unite the country through economics, diplomacy, and military might, is a treat for patient strategists.

nes__romance-of-three-kingdoms.article:
Alongside Japanese history, the Koei studio also reached for one of the greatest epics of Chinese history and literature. **Romance of the Three Kingdoms** brought to the NES the saga of the Three Kingdoms period, the era of the Han dynasty's collapse, and wrapped it in an elaborate turn-based strategy of a kind that had few equals on an eight-bit console.

The game draws on the classic Chinese novel about the eponymous period, one of the most influential literary works of East Asia. The player takes on the role of one of many warlords and tries to gain control of fragmented China. Just as in the sister series Nobunaga's Ambition, it is not only about battles: you must manage your territories, look after the economy and supplies, hire and promote generals, form alliances, and conduct a diplomatic game with the other leaders. Each character has their own attributes, so choosing and nurturing capable commanders is the key to success.

Koei established itself as a master of historical simulations, and Romance of the Three Kingdoms is one of its cornerstone series. The studio managed to distill a dense historical source into playable form while acquainting players with the real figures and events of Chinese history. For many Western players this game was their very first encounter with the story of the Three Kingdoms, which is universally known in East Asia.

The game's cultural significance is considerable. It combined respect for its literary and historical source with an ambitious game system and became one of the defining strategies of its era. Its emphasis on long-term planning, resource management, and personnel policy made it a title for players seeking an intellectual challenge rather than fast action.

Today we see Romance of the Three Kingdoms as proof that even the NES hardware could bear an extensive strategic simulation with dozens of characters and provinces. The series received many sequels on newer platforms, and its name remains a byword among fans of historical strategy to this day.

**Why play:** An extensive turn-based strategy inspired by the famous Chinese epic of the Three Kingdoms period, where alongside battles the outcome is decided by economics, diplomacy, and the care of your generals.

nes__rampart.article:
What if a classic castle siege were combined with a puzzle game and cannon fire all at once? This crazy combination is exactly what stands behind **Rampart** by Atari Games, one of the most original arcade games of the turn of the 1980s and 1990s, which also found its way to the NES.

Rampart mixes genres in a way that is hard to file under a single label. The game unfolds in three recurring phases. First you enclose your castles with walls, which you lay down like Tetris pieces. Then comes the combat phase, when you fire from your positioned cannons at enemy ships and fortresses and try to smash them to bits. And finally, under the pressure of the ticking clock, you must frantically repair the damaged walls to protect your cannons. If you fail to enclose at least one castle with a wall, you are done for.

This loop between strategic planning, action shooting, and speed puzzling created incredible tension, especially in multiplayer, where players competed against each other for the same territory. Atari Games, the maker of many legendary arcade machines, came up with a concept here that had no equal and to this day counts as one of the most imaginative genre hybrids of its time.

In terms of development, the game was created at the beginning of the 1990s for arcades, and its success carried it to a range of home platforms including the NES. Porting the more complex controls, originally designed for a trackball, to a classic gamepad was a challenge, but the NES version preserved the essence of that frenzied game of building and demolishing.

Culturally, Rampart remains a textbook example of how mixing seemingly incompatible genres can result in something entirely fresh. The Tetris-like laying of walls under fire and against the clock makes it an unforgettable game, and its idea of defending and repairing a fortress influenced later tower defense titles.

**Why play:** An ingenious hybrid of strategy, artillery action, and Tetris-style wall building that in multiplayer unleashes properly heated battles for territory.

snes__super-mario-world.teaser: Perhaps the best 2D platformer ever; Yoshi's debut.
snes__super-mario-world.detail: A SNES launch title and, for many, the best 2D platformer ever. Yoshi's debut and a huge, interconnected world with 96 exits and secret paths (Star Road, Special World). It sold over 20 million copies. Miyamoto's team perfectly fine-tuned the controls and pacing.
snes__super-mario-world.article:
When the Super Nintendo console launched in Japan in 1990, it was accompanied by a title destined to become one of the most important platformers in history. Super Mario World by Nintendo EAD, led by Shigeru Miyamoto, was not merely the launch game of a new generation, but for many remains to this day the pinnacle of the entire genre of two-dimensional platformers.

The game introduced Yoshi, the friendly dinosaur who became an icon just like Mario himself. The ability to ride him, swallow enemies, and use his abilities added an entirely new dimension to the proven recipe. To that was added the famously fine-tuned handling and pacing, on which Miyamoto's team took exceptional care.

The real gem, however, is the structure of the world. Super Mario World offers a huge, interconnected map with 96 exits, secret paths, and hidden areas like Star Road or the legendary Special World. Discovering shortcuts and uncovering hidden passages turns playing into a little adventure, where the reward for curiosity is hidden literally around every corner.

Commercially it was an enormous success: the game sold more than twenty million copies and became one of the best-selling titles on the SNES ever. In doing so it helped define the success of the entire console and cemented Nintendo at the top of the gaming industry in the early 1990s.

Culturally, Super Mario World is a work that regularly appears in rankings of the best games of all time and became a benchmark against which other 2D platformers are measured. Its design, music, and atmosphere remain fresh and accessible to new generations of players to this day.

**Why play:** Perhaps the best 2D platformer ever, with Yoshi's debut and a huge world full of secrets, which still entertains decades later.

snes__super-metroid.teaser: The gold standard of the metroidvania genre; its atmosphere and design remain unsurpassed to this day.
snes__super-metroid.detail: The gold standard of the genre and a regular in the top 5 best games of all time. It masterfully guides the player without text, purely through environmental design; the atmosphere of loneliness on the planet Zebes is palpable. It introduced the moonwalk, weapon selection, and a map. To this day it is the foundation of the speedrunning community (sequence breaks). An unforgettable, emotional finale.
snes__super-metroid.article:
There are games that not only develop a genre but define it outright, and Super Metroid from 1994 is precisely such a case. This title by Nintendo R&D1 in collaboration with Intelligent Systems became the gold standard of the genre we now call metroidvania, and it regularly appears on the shortlists of the best games in history.

The genius of Super Metroid lies in how it guides the player through the environment almost without words. Instead of text instructions it relies on clever design, visual hints, and the gradual unlocking of abilities that open up previously inaccessible areas. The feeling that you are discovering the planet Zebes through your own effort is utterly exceptional and remains unsurpassed to this day.

The atmosphere of loneliness is meanwhile almost palpable. The bounty hunter Samus Aran explores the dark, organic corridors of an alien planet in complete isolation, and the game manages to build both tension and melancholy purely through environment, music, and pacing. To that it added mechanics like weapon selection, a clear map, and the famous moonwalk, which became a standard.

In development terms it was the culmination of what Nintendo R&D1 had achieved in the genre. The precise controls and interconnected world made the game a work whose influence is evident in dozens of later titles. It is no coincidence that one of the most active speedrunning communities still gathers around Super Metroid to this day, fascinated by so-called sequence breaks that make it possible to complete the game in an unexpected order.

Culturally, Super Metroid is a fixture in rankings of the best games of all time, and its emotional, unforgettable finale remains one of the most powerful moments of the SNES era. For anyone who wants to understand the roots of modern metroidvanias, it is a mandatory stop.

**Why play:** The gold standard of the metroidvania genre with unsurpassed atmosphere and a design that guides you through the world without words and entertains even after dozens of years.

snes__legend-of-zelda-link-to-past.teaser: For many the best 2D Zelda; perfect pacing and world.
snes__legend-of-zelda-link-to-past.detail: For many the best 2D Zelda. It introduced the mechanic of two parallel worlds (Light/Dark World) that influence each other, the Master Sword, and plenty of elements that became series staples. It sold over 4.6 million copies. It defined the shape of the top-down Zelda for decades.
snes__legend-of-zelda-link-to-past.article:
There are games that do not define a genre, and then there is **The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past** — a title that forged the top-down action adventure into a perfectly tuned machine and set a bar the series looked up to for many years to come. When Link first steps out into the rain on a stormy night to rescue Princess Zelda, you feel as though you are entering a living world, not a series of screens.

The ingenious idea on which the whole game rests is the coexistence of two parallel worlds. Alongside the Light World there exists a dark, warped Dark World, and the two influence each other: a rock you skirt around in one world turns into a platform in the other, and a chasm elsewhere becomes solid ground. This system turns both the dungeons and the overworld into ingenious spatial puzzles, where the solution often lies in switching between realities. The crown of the equipment is the legendary Master Sword, which you must first obtain — and that moment is one of the most iconic in the entire series.

**A Link to the Past** was created at Nintendo's internal EAD studio under the leadership of Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka, and it was released in 1991 in Japan, a year later in the West. After the experiment with a side view in Zelda II, the creators returned to the bird's-eye perspective of the first installment, but perfected it to a degree made possible by the power of the Super Nintendo. Koji Kondo's music gave the land of Hyrule melodies that now rank among the best known in gaming history.

The game's influence is enormous. Items like the hookshot, the boomerang, or bombs, the structure of gradually unlocking the world through newly acquired abilities, and the very pace of discovery — all of this became a series staple and a model for countless followers. The game sold more than 4.6 million copies and regularly appears at the top of rankings of the best games of all time. For many players and critics, **A Link to the Past** remains the pinnacle of two-dimensional Zelda.

Thanks to releases on the Game Boy Advance, the Virtual Console service, and as part of the Nintendo Switch Online subscription, the game is easily accessible today and ages remarkably well. The controls are brisk, the world clear, and every nook rewards curiosity. It is a textbook example of timeless design.

**Why play:** Because it is the essence of adventure — two intertwined worlds, perfect pacing, and a world you want to explore down to the last bush.

snes__chrono-trigger.teaser: Often called the best JRPG of all time; time travel, many endings.
snes__chrono-trigger.detail: It came about through the collaboration of the „Dream Team“ — Hironobu Sakaguchi (FF), Yuji Horii (Dragon Quest), and Akira Toriyama (characters). Time travel, where actions in the past change the future, battles without random encounters (you see enemies on the map), techniques that combine characters, and 13 different endings (New Game+). Music by Yasunori Mitsuda. Regularly voted the best JRPG ever.
snes__chrono-trigger.article:
When three legends of the Japanese gaming industry come together on a single project, expectations soar sky-high — and **Chrono Trigger** managed to exceed them outright. This game still regularly appears at the very top of rankings of the best JRPGs of all time, and it needs only a few hours to convince you why.

Behind the game stands the so-called „Dream Team“: Hironobu Sakaguchi, the father of Final Fantasy; Yuji Horii, the creator of Dragon Quest; and Akira Toriyama, whose unmistakable artistic hand you know from Dragon Ball. Together in 1995 at the Square studio they created a story about a band of heroes who accidentally tumble through time and discover that they can change the fate of the world. Time travel here is not just a backdrop — your actions in the past tangibly alter the future, which opens the door to one of the most inventive narratives of its time.

Mechanically, **Chrono Trigger** cast off a number of the genre's annoying conventions. No random encounters: you see enemies directly on the map, and battles flow seamlessly from exploration. The ATB combat system also allows so-called Techs — combined attacks, where two or three characters join forces into a spectacular shared skill. Add to that the beautiful music of Yasunori Mitsuda (with contributions from Nobuo Uematsu), which ranks among the finest ever to sound in the gaming medium.

The game's true pride, however, is its replayability. Thanks to the New Game+ mode and the possibility of facing the final enemy at various stages of the story, **Chrono Trigger** offers a total of thirteen different endings. That had no equal in 1995 and is to this day an example of how generously one can approach the player's freedom.

The game received a range of ports — from the PlayStation through the Nintendo DS to mobile devices and Steam — and the DS version is considered one of the best thanks to added content and a polished translation. Through all the reissues it retains its original magic completely.

Few games combine story, gameplay, music, and visuals into such a harmonious whole. **Chrono Trigger** is not merely an excellent JRPG — it is one of the few titles that can, without exaggeration, be spoken of as a perfectly balanced work of art.

**Why play:** A supreme JRPG where time travel truly changes the world, the battles are fun, and thirteen endings invite you back again and again.

snes__super-mario-world-2-yoshi-s-island.teaser: Artistically unique; a pastel style and inventive design.
snes__super-mario-world-2-yoshi-s-island.detail: Miyamoto insisted on a hand-drawn „crayon“ style despite pressure for pre-rendered graphics (like DKC) — the result is the most artistically unique Mario game. Yoshi carries baby Mario and protects him; a hit does not kill the child, you just have to catch him back in time. Inventive design, where every level brings a new idea.
snes__super-mario-world-2-yoshi-s-island.article:
Imagine stepping onto the most powerful console of its day with a game that looks as though a child drew it with crayons into a sketchbook. That is exactly what Shigeru Miyamoto did with Super Mario World 2: Yoshi's Island. At the moment when the competition bet everything on pre-rendered, technically polished graphics in the style of Donkey Kong Country, Miyamoto went against the current and, despite pressure from his own studio, pushed through a hand-drawn, pastel visual. The result is to this day one of the most distinctive and most beautiful games ever released on a 16-bit console.

But what sets Yoshi's Island apart is not only its look. It is a clever twist at the very heart of the gameplay. This time you do not play as Mario, but as Yoshi, who carries defenseless baby Mario on his back and must deliver him to safety. The key mechanic is ingeniously human: when an enemy hits you, the child does not die. He floats off your back in a bobbing bubble, and you have a few seconds of nervous countdown to catch him back before the Toadies enemies snatch him away. This little detail turns the entire rhythm of play into a tense dance between attack and protection.

Yoshi, meanwhile, was given a whole new arsenal of abilities. He swallows enemies and turns them into eggs, which he then uses as precise throwing ammunition. He can flutter in the air to prolong a jump for a moment, transforms into temporary vehicles, and solves spatial puzzles. Every level is designed as a self-contained idea — each time there comes a new mechanism, a new kind of environment, a new bit of level-design trickery. It is precisely this inexhaustible inventiveness that is why fans still call the game the pinnacle of Nintendo's 2D platforming school to this day.

The visual side is moreover helped by the special Super FX 2 chip in the cartridge, which enabled rotating and enlarging enemies and bosses on a scale the SNES itself otherwise could not handle. The bosses are one of the game's highlights — huge, artistically exuberant creatures that often combine a visual trick with an unconventional method of defeat.

Yoshi's Island became a cornerstone of Yoshi's entire standalone branch and kicked off a series of sequels and remakes (among others a version for the Game Boy Advance). It remains to this day a textbook example that the courage to follow your own artistic path can age far better than an attempt at a period technical show.

**Why play:** For the most artistically daring Mario game ever and for platforming design where every level surprises with a new idea — a joy that has not aged.

snes__donkey-kong-country-1-3.teaser: Pre-rendered graphics stunned the world; superb platformers.
snes__donkey-kong-country-1-3.detail: Rare used expensive SGI workstations to create pre-rendered 3D graphics that stunned the world in 1994 and helped the SNES fight back against 32-bit rivals (Rare showed the visuals to Nintendo, which at first didn't believe them). The first game alone sold over 9 million copies. Famous atmospheric music by David Wise (underwater and snow themes).
snes__donkey-kong-country-1-3.article:
When Rare showed Nintendo the first footage of Donkey Kong Country in 1994, the story goes that at first nobody believed such graphics were actually running on the SNES. And no wonder. The British studio reached for the then-astronomically expensive Silicon Graphics workstations and modeled its characters and environments in 3D, which it then pre-rendered into 2D sprites. The result was a look nobody expected on a 16-bit console — sculpted, glossy, almost tangible. For the aging SNES it was a weapon that helped it keep pace with the emerging 32-bit competition.

But Donkey Kong Country was never just a technical exercise. Beneath the flashy surface lay a first-rate platformer. You play as Donkey and the nimble Diddy Kong, switching between them on the fly, riding mine carts, blasting out of barrels, swimming through underwater caves and relying on animal buddies like Rambi the rhino or Expresso the ostrich. The second and third installments refined the formula further — the pirate-themed second game with the duo of Diddy and Dixie is, for many players, the absolute peak of the whole trilogy.

The first game alone sold over nine million copies, making it one of the most successful titles of the entire SNES era. The series helped cement Rare as one of the finest studios of the 1990s and gave the ape hero a pop-culture life of his own, well outside Mario's herd.

An inseparable part of the magic is David Wise's music. His atmospheric compositions — hypnotic underwater themes or melancholic snow passages like the legendary „Stickerbush Symphony“ from the second game — rank among the most acclaimed soundtracks of the 16-bit era and still appear on lists of the best video game music of all time.

The trilogy gradually saw ports to the Game Boy Advance and re-releases via virtual storefronts, and its legacy was later carried forward by Retro Studios in the Donkey Kong Country Returns series. Yet the 1990s originals remain the benchmark for just how great a classic platformer can look and play.

**Why play it:** For visuals that stunned the entire world in 1994, and for three beautifully tuned platformers with one of the finest game soundtracks ever made.

snes__final-fantasy-vi.teaser: For many the peak of the series; an epic story with an ensemble cast.
snes__final-fantasy-vi.detail: For many the peak of the series and one of the best stories in the medium. 14 playable characters without a single lead hero, a steampunk world and the mad clown Kefka who — rare for the genre — actually succeeds and destroys the world halfway through (you then explore the world in ruins). The opera scene is an iconic gaming moment.
snes__final-fantasy-vi.article:
The main villain genuinely succeeds midway through the game, destroys the world, and you then explore it in ruins. That single sentence about Final Fantasy VI is enough to explain why so many players consider it the peak of the entire series and one of the finest stories games have ever told. Square cast aside the genre clichés about chosen heroes and built an epic that dared to embrace both darkness and operatic pathos at once.

Unlike most RPGs, Final Fantasy VI has no single lead hero. You are guided by an ensemble of fourteen playable characters, each with their own past, motivation and moment to step into the spotlight — from the mysterious Terra with her magical genes, through the gambling adventurer Locke, to the forsaken knight Cyan. A steampunk world, half industrial and half magical, gives the whole thing a unique atmosphere you simply wouldn't find elsewhere in the genre at the time.

And then there's Kefka. A mad, cackling clown who works his way up from court jester to absolute power and becomes one of the most unforgettable villains in the history of the medium. The fact that the game lets him truly triumph and shatter the world to pieces halfway through the story was a bold narrative move at the time, one that still resonates today. The second half of the game, in which you gather your scattered companions across a devastated world, is among the most powerful things JRPGs have ever offered.

Combat rests on the proven ATB system with charging gauges, and every character brings their own gameplay layer to it — from Sabin's fighting-game-style command inputs to a magic system tied to the Esper beings. The game thus stays mechanically varied from start to finish.

The iconic moment is the opera scene, where your character dons the costume of a stage singer — a passage that showed just how far game storytelling and Nobuo Uematsu's music could reach. Final Fantasy VI originally launched in the West under the confusing title Final Fantasy III and has since seen a number of re-releases and remasters, but its heart remains untouched.

**Why play it:** For one of the most powerful stories in gaming history, an unforgettable villain, and a steampunk world that lodges itself in your memory.

snes__final-fantasy-iv-v.teaser: IV brought drama, V the best job system. Both classics.
snes__final-fantasy-iv-v.detail: The fourth game (originally released in the West as FF II) introduced the ATB system — real-time combat with a charging gauge that the series used for years — and serious dramatic storytelling. The fifth has the deepest job system of the classic FFs (you mix class abilities into your own combinations). Both classics, each in its own way.
snes__final-fantasy-iv-v.article:
Two games, two philosophies, one studio at the height of its powers. In the middle of the 16-bit era, Final Fantasy IV and V form a pair that showcased two faces of what a Japanese RPG can be — one bet on drama and storytelling, the other on the depth of its game systems. And both became classics.

Final Fantasy IV, originally released in the West as Final Fantasy II, was groundbreaking above all thanks to its ATB (Active Time Battle) combat system. Battles were no longer purely turn-based — every character and enemy had a charging gauge, so passivity was punished and tension returned to the fights. The series then used this system for years. Just as important was the shift in storytelling: the dark knight Cecil, his transformation into a paladin, the betrayals and sacrifices of his companions gave the genre a serious dramatic center of gravity that had largely been missing until then.

Final Fantasy V, on the other hand, became famous for the deepest job system of the classic installments. You freely assign classes to your characters — knight, black mage, blue mage, thief and many more — and, crucially, the abilities learned by each profession can then be mixed and combined across the board. This creates enormous room for experimentation and for building your own, often surprisingly powerful lineups. For players who love to bend and optimize systems, the fifth game is a little treasure.

Each of the games thus appeals to a slightly different type of player. The fourth leads you through a strong, emotional story with memorable characters. The fifth lets go of the reins and lets you build a party from your own imagination, while its story carries a lighter, more adventurous tone.

Both games came from Square's workshop at a time when the studio was defining what a JRPG should look like, and both have gradually seen a range of re-releases, remasters and ports to modern platforms, so they aren't lost to the past. Together they form the ideal double portrait of why Final Fantasy became the gold standard of the genre.

**Why play it:** For two classics in one — IV grabs you with its drama and the introduction of ATB combat, V with the deepest job system, which tempts you into endless experimentation.

snes__secret-of-mana.teaser: An action RPG with co-op for three; beautiful music.
snes__secret-of-mana.detail: The second game in the Mana series, famous for co-op with up to three players at once (a rarity) and the circular „Ring Command“ menu for selecting spells and items on the fly. It was originally meant to be a launch title for the Nintendo CD add-on that fell through, so it was trimmed down to fit a cartridge. Gorgeous music by Hiroki Kikuta.
snes__secret-of-mana.article:
Most RPGs send you off on your adventure alone. Secret of Mana said no — and sat up to three players at the screen at once. At a time when co-op in a sprawling action RPG was almost unheard of, this game from Square let you play through the entire campaign as a trio, and it's precisely because of this that it etched itself into the hearts of a whole generation who played it with friends on a single couch.

Secret of Mana is the second installment in the Mana series and bets on real-time action combat instead of turns. You slash into enemies live, charge up stronger blows and draw on spells based on your magic levels. The ingenious solution is the so-called Ring Command — a circular menu you summon on the fly and from which you quickly choose spells, items and equipment without ever leaving the action. This elegant idea significantly sped up play and became a hallmark of the series.

Behind the smooth gameplay, however, lies a troubled development history. The game was originally meant to launch as one of the flagship titles for the SNES's planned CD add-on. When that project fell through, the developers had to cut the game back and cram it onto a standard cartridge. Traces of the trims are visible here and there in the final version, yet the result remained extraordinarily charming.

An inseparable part of the magic is Hiroki Kikuta's music. His soundtrack ranks among the most beautiful and distinctive on the entire SNES — atmospheric, dreamlike and musically bold in a way that far exceeded the conventions of games at the time. Together with the colorful, almost fairy-tale visuals, it creates a world you want to keep returning to.

Secret of Mana remains one of the most beloved action RPGs of its era and later received a 3D remake that brought it to new players. But whether you play it solo or as a trio, its combination of fluid action, clever controls and fairy-tale atmosphere ages with grace.

**Why play it:** For the rare co-op of up to three players, the elegant Ring Command controls, and one of the most beautiful soundtracks of the SNES era.

snes__seiken-densetsu-3-trials-of-mana.teaser: Finally officially out; character choice and branching.
snes__seiken-densetsu-3-trials-of-mana.detail: The sequel to Secret of Mana, it only officially reached the West a decade later (for a long time it was only a fan translation). You pick three of six characters, changing the story, the available paths and the final boss — huge replayability. Beautiful pixel art and a day/night cycle. It received a 3D remake (2020).
snes__seiken-densetsu-3-trials-of-mana.article:
For a whole decade this game was the Holy Grail for Western players, one you could only taste thanks to a fan translation. Seiken Densetsu 3, officially released in the West only much later as Trials of Mana, is the sequel to the beloved Secret of Mana and long ranked among the most eagerly awaited imports of the entire SNES era.

Its biggest draw is a structure built on choice. From a sextet of heroes you pick three at the start — and that choice fundamentally transforms the whole game. It changes not only who you lead, but also the story line, the available paths and even who your final opponent will be. The result is enormous replayability: you can play through the game several times, assembling a different party each time and experiencing a different angle on the same world.

In terms of play it builds on the series' action roots — combat unfolds in real time and characters can also develop through a class system, where you choose a light or dark specialization and gradually unlock stronger classes and abilities. Added to this is a dynamic day and night cycle that affects the world around you and gives it a sense of life.

Visually it's one of the high points of pixel art on the console. Detailed character animations, richly colored environments and grandiose bosses show what Square's artists could squeeze out of 16-bit hardware when they were at the top of their craft.

Its long unavailability in the West turned the game into a semi-legend known mainly to the initiated. That has changed — Seiken Densetsu 3 was released officially as part of a collector's collection, and in 2020 it received a full-fledged 3D remake that finally introduced it to a wide audience. But the original remains a gem worth discovering even today.

**Why play it:** For character choice that changes the entire story and finale, huge replayability, and the gorgeous pixel art of one of Square's high points on the SNES.

snes__earthbound.teaser: A bizarre, funny, touching modern RPG; a cult with a huge following.
snes__earthbound.detail: By Shigesato Itoi; a bizarre, funny and touching RPG parodying modern America (instead of dragons you fight hippies, cultists and UFOs, instead of mana you have PSI and instead of taverns, hotels). It flopped commercially in the US (an expensive box with a game guide as an anti-piracy measure) and is a cult legend today. A „rolling HP“ system: health drains gradually, so you can save a character from death.
snes__earthbound.article:
Instead of dragons you fight enraged hippies, cultists and a hovering UFO. Instead of mana you crackle with the psychic power of PSI, and instead of a tavern you go rest at a hotel. Welcome to EarthBound, an RPG that took every convention of the genre and, with a smile, turned it inside out. Shigesato Itoi's bizarre, funny and unexpectedly touching game is a cult legend today, though the road to that status was anything but easy.

EarthBound takes place in no fantasy realm but in an ironically warped version of modern America. You play as a boy named Ness and his friends, wandering through suburbs, cities and shopping malls, while the tone of the storytelling constantly leaps between mocking parody and surprisingly sincere emotion. Beneath the humor lies a game that can be unexpectedly grown-up and touch you in a way you wouldn't expect from wacky satire.

Combat has its original ideas too. Famous is the so-called "rolling HP" system: after taking a hit, a character's health doesn't drop all at once but ticks down like a counter. When you take a fatal blow, you still have a few moments in which you can turn things around — defeat the enemy, heal up or flee before the counter reaches zero. This creates a tense race against the clock that lends the fights a surprising tactical layer.

Commercially, however, it was a flop in the US. The game was sold in an unusually large and expensive box that included a thick strategy guide — among other things as an anti-piracy measure. The high price and unconventional presentation put buyers off and the game sank without a trace. Only over the years, with the help of devoted fans, did it become one of the most cherished cult titles of all.

Today EarthBound is a symbol of the idea that a game need not take itself or its genre seriously to leave a deep mark. Its influence can be felt across a whole wave of independent games, and Ness became a fixture in the Super Smash Bros. fighting games, thanks to which his legacy lives on even among players who never touched the original.

**Why play it:** For unmistakable humor, a touching heart hidden beneath the parody, and an original combat system — a cult classic like no other.

snes__super-mario-rpg-legend-of-seven-st.detail: A rare collaboration between Square and Nintendo, the first Mario RPG and the forerunner of both Paper Mario and Mario & Luigi. Timing-based combat (a well-timed press strengthens your attack), isometric pre-rendered graphics and witty writing. Long unavailable due to the later Square/Nintendo rift; remake in 2023.
snes__super-mario-rpg-legend-of-seven-st.article:
What happens when two studios that otherwise defined mutually competing console worlds join forces? In 1996, Super Mario RPG: Legend of the Seven Stars was born — a rare and, at the time, almost unthinkable work sprung from the collaboration between Square, king of Japanese RPGs, and Nintendo, father of Mario. The result was the first Mario RPG game and, at the same time, a harbinger of two great series still to come.

Super Mario RPG took the familiar Mushroom Kingdom universe and smuggled full-fledged role-playing mechanics into it. The key novelty is timing-based combat actions: at the right moment you press a button and your attack grows stronger, or you soften a blow the enemy is preparing to land on you. What would otherwise be turn-based combat thus becomes a lively game of reflexes that fundamentally shaped every later Mario RPG.

Visually the game caught the eye with isometric, pre-rendered graphics in the spirit of the trend set at the time by Donkey Kong Country, which made it feel sculpted and fresh. Added to this is witty, warm-hearted writing and a gallery of fresh characters — including brand-new faces that players instantly took to. Here Mario stepped for the first time outside the box of the pure platformer, and it turned out role-playing suits him well.

The influence of this game is enormous. Without it, the Paper Mario and Mario & Luigi series would probably never have existed — both draw directly on the ideas that Legend of the Seven Stars first tried out. In a way, it laid the foundations for an entire branch of Mario's world.

Because of the later rift between Square and Nintendo, which arose after Square defected to a different console, the game remained hard to find for many years and a somewhat forgotten treasure. Fortunately that changed — in 2023 it received a full-fledged remake that introduced it to an entirely new generation of players.

**Why play it:** For the magical collaboration between Square and Nintendo, the witty writing, and the timing-based combat actions that kicked off the whole Mario RPG tradition.

snes__super-castlevania-iv.teaser: An audiovisual showcase; a whip in eight directions.
snes__super-castlevania-iv.detail: An SNES launch-window title; an audiovisual showcase using Mode 7 (rotating rooms) and multi-layer scrolling. The key novelty: a whip you can aim in **eight directions** and swing, which fundamentally made combat more accessible. Atmospheric music. One of the best classic Castlevanias.
snes__super-castlevania-iv.article:
At last, a whip that doesn't just crack straight ahead of you. When Super Castlevania IV arrived in the SNES's launch window, it was an audiovisual showcase that demonstrated what the new console could do — and, with one elegant idea, transformed how Castlevania is played at all.

The essential novelty is the controllable whip. The hero Simon Belmont can now swing it in eight directions and even flick it gently to control its reach. For a series famous for its stiff, almost tank-like controls, this was a small revolution. Combat became more accessible and supple without losing its characteristic tension and its emphasis on rhythm and timing.

Konami also made full use of the new hardware's possibilities. The game shows off the famous Mode 7 — rooms that rotate and tilt before you — and multi-layer scrolling that gives the gothic castle's environments depth and weight. You pass through halls, dungeons and towers whose atmosphere thickens with each new level, all the way to the final confrontation with Dracula.

An inseparable part of the experience is the music. The Super Castlevania IV soundtrack ranks among the most atmospheric ever heard on the console — dark, melodic and perfectly matched to the gloomy tone of the castle's recesses. Together with the precise level design, it completes the feeling that you are walking through a living, breathing manor of horror.

Super Castlevania IV is regularly ranked among the best classic installments of the series from the era before the arrival of the Metroidvania style. For many players it's the perfect demonstration of how a linear, action-packed Castlevania was meant to look, and it's worth discovering even today, whether you're a fan of the series or only just peering into it.

**Why play it:** For a whip you can aim in eight directions, a breathtaking atmosphere and Mode 7 effects — one of the very best classic Castlevanias.

snes__mega-man-x.teaser: A modernization of the series; faster, darker, addictive.
snes__mega-man-x.detail: A modernization of the series for the 16-bit era: faster pace, a dash, wall-climbing and collectible armor. The first game is famous for its hidden tutorial design — the first level teaches you everything without text, and a skilled player can beat the first „mid-boss“ in it, unlocking a secret ability. A darker tone and story.
snes__mega-man-x.article:
The first level teaches you absolutely everything without a single word of explanation — and if you can really play well, you can even defeat a mighty boss in it who would otherwise sweep you aside. It's precisely this hidden, brilliant tutorial that is the calling card of Mega Man X, the game with which Capcom modernized its legendary series for the 16-bit era and breathed a new, sharper life into it.

Classic Mega Man was great, but after dozens of installments it was starting to feel constrained. Mega Man X added speed and freedom of movement. The hero X can dash, climb walls and bounce off them, which sped the game up and gave it a fluidity its predecessors lacked. Added to this is a system of collectible armor — capsules with upgrades hidden throughout the levels that gradually strengthen X and open up new ways to overcome the environment.

Legendary is that subtle tutorial mastery of the opening stage. Instead of text instructions, the level design itself leads you to learn to jump, shoot, dash and climb — and the game rewards you for mastering it. A skilled player can take down a mid-boss right at the start and thus unlock a secret ability far earlier than expected. It's a textbook lesson in game design that people still reference today.

Visually and thematically the series grew markedly darker. The story of robots turning against humanity, of Mavericks and of the very nature of artificial intelligence gave the game a more serious, almost melancholic hue that contrasted with the colorfulness of the older installments. Together with addictive gameplay and a catchy soundtrack, the result is a game that's hard to put down.

Mega Man X became the start of its own successful sub-series that continued through a string of further installments, and it's still ranked among the best action platformers of the SNES era. For many players it's even the very best thing to ever emerge from the entire world of Mega Man.

**Why play it:** For fast, addictive action, the brilliantly hidden tutorial design of the first level, and a darker tone that reshaped the Mega Man series in a grown-up way.

snes__mega-man-x2-x3.article:
The blue bomber grew up, deepened into a darker blue and traded childlike innocence for the cool elegance of the future. After the revolutionary Mega Man X, with which Capcom recast an 8-bit series into nimble action featuring wall-running and dashing, came the pair of **X2** and **X3** as a fine-tuning of an already excellent formula. If you thought a faster and more fluid action platformer didn't exist on the SNES, this duo will prove you wrong.

At the core of the experience remains what made X so addictive: you control the cyber-hero X, who throws himself at a set of eight bosses (Mavericks) in any order, and after each defeated enemy you gain their weapon. This opens up a classic game of rock-paper-scissors, where the right order of fights changes the difficulty. Added to this are armor upgrades hidden in the levels, dashing on the ground and in the air, and wall-jumping that turns movement into something like a dance. **X2** added a trio of mysterious opponents, the X-Hunters, and the Japanese cartridge even included a special Cx4 chip for wireframe polygon effects. **X3** then introduced a playable Zero, the rideable Ride Armor mechs on a wider scale, and a greater emphasis on alternate paths.

Visually it's the peak of what the SNES could do in 2D: detailed backgrounds, multi-layer parallax, explosions and animations that still look fresh today. The soundtracks of both games bet on brisk, slightly melancholic melodies that perfectly match the aesthetic of the „Reploids“ and robots with a soul. The game runs at sixty frames per second, and every dash, every bounce off a wall feels precise and satisfying.

Among fans there's an eternal debate about which installment is better. **X2** tends to be praised for its polished design and fair difficulty curve, while **X3** is more ambitious but at times more chaotic. Together, however, they form the bridge between the brilliant first game and the series' later transition to the PlayStation. Both games were later revived in the Mega Man X Legacy Collection compilations, so a new generation can reach them too.

**Why play it:** They rank among the most fluid and stylish 2D action on the SNES — if you love precise movement, hunting for secret upgrades and boss battles, this pair will pull you in.

snes__contra-iii-alien-wars.teaser: The peak of run & gun on the SNES; intense.
snes__contra-iii-alien-wars.detail: The peak of run & gun on the SNES. You carry two weapons at once (switching between them), top-down levels using Mode 7 and giant bosses. Brutal pace and difficulty; best in co-op. A must for lovers of action.
snes__contra-iii-alien-wars.article:
Three, two, one — and the world around you crumbles in a fiery apocalypse. **Contra III: The Alien Wars** opens with a burning city, a helicopter and such a density of explosions that you immediately grasp why this game earned its reputation as the most intense run & gun ride on the Super Nintendo. In 1992 Konami didn't come out with a sequel, but with a manifesto of action.

Conceptually it's the pure essence of the genre: you run from left to right, jump and shoot at everything that moves, while enemy fire floods your screen. The novelty was carrying **two weapons at once** with the ability to switch instantly, so you could combine the iconic spread gun with a laser or homing shots. Added to the horizontal and vertical levels were also top-down sections, where the entire arena beneath you rotated thanks to the famous **Mode 7** effect — the console's technological trump card, serving here purely for spectacular mayhem.

The difficulty is notoriously infamous. Contra was always a series where a single hit means you're dead, and the third installment didn't disown that tradition. The bosses are huge, multi-phase and demand both the memorization of patterns and lightning-fast reflexes. That's precisely why the game still shines today in two-player co-op — the shared curses and triumphs, when you make it through a particularly hellish passage together, are among the best that retro multiplayer has to offer.

Konami was firing on all cylinders at the time, and Contra III is regularly ranked among the best action titles of the 16-bit era. It became the yardstick against which all later run & gun games are measured, and its DNA shines through in modern titles like Cuphead or Blazing Chrome. The series continued through many installments across generations, but for many players this one remains the peak.

**Why play it:** It's brutally fast, perfectly tuned action that tests your reflexes to the bone — and in co-op it offers one of the best shared experiences of the SNES era.

snes__super-mario-kart.teaser: The birth of the kart-racing genre; a legend.
snes__super-mario-kart.detail: The birth of an entire kart-racing genre. Mode 7 created a pseudo-3D track, items (shells, peels) added chaos and a two-player battle mode founded a tradition. It sold over 8 million copies. It laid the foundation for one of the most successful game series of all time.
snes__super-mario-kart.article:
Nobody back then suspected that sitting a plumber in a go-kart meant founding an entire game genre. **Super Mario Kart** from 1992 wasn't just another spin-off for Mario — it was the moment when something was born that dozens of games have imitated ever since, but few have surpassed. Nintendo EAD took racing and seasoned it with chaos, humor and a competitiveness that still wrecks friendships today.

The technical heart of the game was again **Mode 7**, thanks to which the flat track tilted and rotated into a pseudo-3D perspective, along which the karts zipped at a surprisingly brisk pace. The stroke of genius, however, lay in the items: shells, banana peels, lightning bolts and stars turned a straight race into an unpredictable battle where the leading driver could never rest easy. And then there was the **battle mode** for two players — a duel in an arena where you popped each other's balloons, which founded a separate tradition of multiplayer clashes.

The game ran on a split screen, where the bottom half served either the second player or the track map. The controls were subtle and demanded feel — drifting, collecting speed boosts and dodging obstacles formed a depth you discovered gradually. The characters differed in their attributes, so choosing Bowser, Toad or the Princess affected your driving style.

Commercially it was a huge success — it sold over **8 million copies**, placing the title among the console's best-selling games. More importantly, though, it laid the foundation for the Mario Kart series, today one of the most successful and most profitable gaming brands of all. Every later installment, from Mario Kart 64 to modern hits, grew out of the foundations laid right here.

**Why play it:** It's the historically first and still immensely fun kart racer — ideal for a nostalgic sit-down with a friend, where an entire genre was born.

snes__f-zero.teaser: Dizzying speed thanks to Mode 7; a futuristic classic.
snes__f-zero.detail: A SNES launch title showing off Mode 7 through the dizzying speed of futuristic hovercraft. No items — just pure racing, track memorization and reflexes. It introduced Captain Falcon (today a Smash Bros. star). A technical showcase for the console.
snes__f-zero.article:
Hit the throttle and the world blurs into a single streak of colour rushing toward you at a speed no console game had ever shown before. **F-Zero** was one of the launch titles for the Super Nintendo and served as a technological calling card — proof that the new Nintendo could conjure futuristic speed that the eight-bit generation could only dream of.

It all rested on the **Mode 7** effect, which allowed the background to be rotated and scaled so that the track beneath the player's craft felt three-dimensional and hurtled toward you at a dizzying pace. No items, no shells — just pure racing. F-Zero was about memorizing tracks, feeling out the braking point before a corner, and managing the energy of a vehicle you had to recharge in the pit lane and that could be damaged by slamming into a wall. It was a discipline for reflexes and concentration.

A choice of four craft with different characteristics added a tactical layer, and the difficulty ramped up fast — the higher leagues demanded almost surgical precision. The soundtrack, with its energetic, rock-flavoured melodies, became a cult favourite and remains one of the most memorable musical motifs of the era to this day.

The game also introduced **Captain Falcon**, a pilot who tended to stay in the background of his home series but who, thanks to the fighting game Super Smash Bros., became one of the most recognizable Nintendo icons ever, his „Falcon Punch“ passing into popular culture. F-Zero founded the genre of futuristic high-speed racing, later carried forward by titles such as WipEout and further sequels in the series.

**Why play it:** If you want to experience pure, adrenaline-fuelled speed with no crutches and see what Mode 7 could do right at the SNES launch, F-Zero is the perfect techno-demonstration that is still fun today.

snes__super-off-road.teaser: Top-down arcade off-road racing; fun for multiple players.
snes__super-off-road.detail: Arcade off-road racing from a bird's-eye view (the whole track on one screen), where you buy upgrades between rounds. Up to four players. Laid-back old-school multiplayer fun.
snes__super-off-road.article:
Sometimes you don't need photorealistic graphics or a simulation — all it takes is four little buggies on one screen, a heap of mud and a bunch of friends around a single TV. **Super Off Road** offers exactly that: honest old-school arcade off-road racing that originally conquered the arcades and arrived on the Super Nintendo in 1992.

The concept is instantly understandable. The entire track fits onto one bird's-eye screen, so you can see all your rivals and your own buggy at once as you race through several laps full of jumps, puddles and shortcuts. After each race you collect money to spend in the garage on upgrades — better tyres, engine, shocks or stocks of nitro for a quick burst of speed. This „race, earn, upgrade“ loop gives the game a surprisingly addictive rhythm.

The real strength of the title, however, lies in multiplayer. Thanks to the top-down view where everyone fits at once, the game is ideal for **up to four players** at the same time — no split screen, just shared chaos, overtaking and shoving in the corners. It's the kind of game where you laugh and shout more than you take the results seriously.

Super Off Road grows out of the arcade tradition, and its roots reach back to a racing-design legend tied to the monster trucks and off-road showdowns of the eighties. On the console it kept its immediate, undemanding fun — don't expect the depth of a simulation, expect pure party joy.

**Why play it:** It's uncomplicated, instantly graspable multiplayer fun for a group — the ideal retro showdown, all about laughter and competitiveness around a single screen.

snes__star-fox.teaser: The first 3D on the SNES (Super FX chip); a pioneer.
snes__star-fox.detail: The first 3D game on the SNES thanks to the **Super FX** chip built right into the cartridge (developed by Britain's Argonaut). A polygonal rail shooter with charismatic talking animals. „Do a barrel roll!“ comes from here. A pioneer that showed the future of 3D on consoles.
snes__star-fox.article:
„Do a barrel roll!“ Even someone who has never played Star Fox knows these four words — and this is exactly where they come from. In 1993 Nintendo did something on its purely 2D Super Nintendo that looked like magic: it got a genuine polygonal three-dimensional game running. The secret was hidden right inside the cartridge.

That secret was the **Super FX** chip, a co-processor developed by the British studio **Argonaut Software**, which was inserted into the game module and gave the console the computing power to render 3D polygons that the base hardware couldn't manage on its own. The result was a rail shooter in which you pilot the Arwing fighter of an animal squadron led by the fox Fox McCloud, flying through levels toward an enemy army. For most of the time the game guides you along a predefined path, but it gives you room to dodge, roll barrels (the famous „barrel roll“, which deflected shots) and choose between several difficulty routes through the galaxy.

By today's standards the graphics were blocky and short on detail, but in 1993 they felt like a glimpse of the future. The charismatic talking animals, the dramatic soundtrack and the sense of flying through real space created an experience no one had seen on consoles before. The character of Fox McCloud became a fixture of the Nintendo world and later a star of the Super Smash Bros. series.

The significance of Star Fox reaches beyond the game itself. It proved that a console could break past its limitations using add-on hardware in the cartridge, and it foreshadowed the era of 3D that the 32-bit and 64-bit consoles would fully open up a few years later. The series continued with the influential Star Fox 64 and further instalments, but that very first flight remains a historic milestone.

**Why play it:** It's a pioneering game that brought 3D to the SNES and is worth experiencing as both a technological and cultural landmark — plus it's the source of one of the most quoted lines in gaming history.

snes__kirby-super-star.teaser: Eight games in one + co-op; great value.
snes__kirby-super-star.detail: „8 games in one“ — a bundle of varied modes (a classic platformer, a race, a boss rush, sub-games) plus co-op, where the second player controls a Helper copied by Kirby. Great value and variety. Directed by Sakurai.
snes__kirby-super-star.article:
What if, instead of a single game, they gave you eight at once? **Kirby Super Star** proudly presented itself with the slogan „8 games in one“ — and it wasn't empty advertising: this 1996 cartridge was literally packed with content that made the pink puff called Kirby one of the most generous offerings at the end of the SNES life cycle.

Instead of a single linear adventure, it offers a bundle of separate modes each with their own structure: classic platforming quests, a combat race in which a rival stands against you, a boss rush that tests your skills, and several shorter sub-games. At the heart of it all remains Kirby's iconic mechanic — you inhale enemies and copy their ability, whether a sword, fire, hammer or dozens of others. Super Star deepened this system with rich move sets for each ability.

The most valuable new feature was co-op. A second player could take control of a **Helper** — a companion materialized from Kirby's copied ability — and go through the game side by side. That turned a traditionally solo series into a pleasant shared experience too. The graphics are fresh, colourful and rounded, the soundtrack catchy, and the whole thing breathes that unmistakable Kirby cosiness, beneath which, however, hides a surprisingly thoughtful design.

The game was directed by **Masahiro Sakurai**, the father of the Kirby series and later the creator of the Super Smash Bros. phenomenon. His signature — the joy of a game accessible to everyone, yet with depth for connoisseurs — is clearly felt here. The title later received a highly acclaimed remake, Kirby Super Star Ultra, on the Nintendo DS, which expanded the content even further.

**Why play it:** It offers exceptional value and variety in a single game, is accessible even for younger players, and in co-op it becomes great shared fun.

snes__kirby-s-dream-course.teaser: Mini golf with Kirby; unexpectedly deep.
snes__kirby-s-dream-course.detail: Mini golf where Kirby is the ball — you putt him across isometric fields, bounce him off walls and collect enemies. It looks like a cute detour, but it hides surprisingly tactical depth (calculating bounces, spin). Addictive.
snes__kirby-s-dream-course.article:
Imagine mini golf where, instead of a ball, you putt a cute pink sphere with eyes — one that can also get angry at enemies. **Kirby's Dream Course** is exactly the kind of unexpected genre detour no one would dare invent if it weren't for Kirby, and yet it works surprisingly well.

The principle is easy to grasp, hard to master. Kirby is the ball you putt across isometric, floating fields full of slopes, ramps, traps and enemies. Your goal is to collect all the enemies on the course — the last of them turns into the target hole. You have to aim, meter the power of your shot and use **spin** to curve the trajectory, calculate bounces off walls and predict where Kirby will come to rest. On top of that come copied abilities gained from defeated enemies, which change the ball's behaviour.

At first glance it looks like a sweet little thing for kids, but beneath the cute surface lies a tactical depth that hooks even hardened players. Calculating angles, reading the terrain and optimizing your moves for the fewest possible shots make it a game in which you can easily spend hours chasing the perfect score. And in a duel against a second player it takes on yet another dimension.

Behind the game stands the studio **HAL Laboratory**, Kirby's home, in cooperation with Nintendo. It's a demonstration of how willingly this brand experimented with genres — from platformers through racing to golf — without losing its unmistakable playfulness. The addictiveness here is high precisely because every shot is a little puzzle.

**Why play it:** Beneath the cute wrapping hides a surprisingly deep and addictive tactical game — ideal if you're looking for an original puzzle experience that's easy to learn and hard to put down.

snes__super-punch-out.detail: An improved SNES sequel to boxing as a puzzle of reflexes: you learn the patterns of colourful opponents and punish them with precise timing. Bigger, prettier sprites and smoother action than the NES version.
snes__super-punch-out.article:
Boxing as a puzzle for your reflexes — that's the recipe Nintendo brought to perfection. **Super Punch-Out!!** carried its iconic series to the Super Nintendo in 1994 and delivered a bigger, more colourful and smoother version of the formula players had already fallen in love with on the NES: it's not about strength, it's about reading your opponent.

Every opponent in the ring is essentially a living puzzle. They have their characteristic movement patterns, telegraphed punches and weak spots that you have to recognize and wait out. You won't win by frantic pummelling but by patient observation — you learn when an opponent telegraphs a punch, dodge or block it, and land a precise blow in the window of opportunity. Gradually you build up a meter for special punches that can break even the toughest fighters.

Compared to the NES version, the SNES release offers noticeably bigger and more detailed character sprites, smoother animation and generally snappier, more legible action. The gallery of opponents is full of colourful, often humorous caricatures with their own personalities, so every match has its own rhythm and character. The game moves fast, and every victory, once you've learned the right timing, is immensely satisfying.

The Punch-Out!! series is one of the Nintendo classics, and its roots reach all the way back to the arcade machines of the eighties. This „observe, learn, punish“ system became a model for a whole sub-genre of rhythm-and-reflex duels, and with its accessible depth it appealed to generations of players. Super Punch-Out!! is the polished peak of the sixteen-bit era.

**Why play it:** It's a fast, legible and exceptionally satisfying game about reflexes and pattern memorization — if you like fights decided by your head and your timing, this is a delight.

snes__super-ghouls-n-ghosts.teaser: Infamously demanding; a challenge for the hardened.
snes__super-ghouls-n-ghosts.detail: Infamous for its difficulty — for the true ending you must beat the game **twice** with a special weapon. Arthur in his armour (after a hit he's left in his underpants) against hordes of the undead. Mode 7 effects, beautiful gothic style. A challenge for the hardened; the satisfaction of finishing it is enormous.
snes__super-ghouls-n-ghosts.article:
There are hard games, and then there is **Super Ghouls 'n Ghosts** — a title whose very name can give veterans phantom thumb pain. In 1991 Capcom delivered not just a beautiful gothic platformer, but a ritual trial of patience that will teach you to swear in several languages at once.

You take on the role of the knight Arthur, who in full armour sets out against hordes of the undead, demons and flying monsters. The series' signature element is the damage system: after the first hit your armour falls off and you're left in just your underpants, and a second hit means death. On top of that you collect various weapons and new armour with magical abilities. The game uses **Mode 7** effects and gorgeous darkly fairy-tale graphics with graveyards, castle ruins and stormy skies, so despite the frustration it's a joy to look at.

Its most infamous feature is the ending. To reach the true finale and defeat the main villain, you have to complete the game **twice**, and the second time with a specific weapon, without which the final boss is invulnerable. It's a design that today feels almost sadistic, but it perfectly captures the ethos of the arcade era, when difficulty was worn as a badge of honour.

The Ghosts 'n Goblins series, to which this instalment belongs, is legendary precisely for its brutality and became a symbol of the hardcore challenge. Capcom was among the best action-game makers of the time, and Super Ghouls 'n Ghosts is still regarded as the benchmark of fair, if merciless, difficulty. Arthur later appeared in other games too, including the Marvel vs. Capcom series.

**Why play it:** If you're looking for an honest, uncompromising old-school challenge and a beautiful gothic platformer, this is the true test — and the satisfaction of finishing it is all the greater for how hard the road there is.

snes__actraiser.teaser: Action + city building; a unique mix and phenomenal music.
snes__actraiser.detail: A unique mix: you alternate a side-scrolling action platformer (as a god you descend into a statue and fight) with a city-building „god game“ part, where from above you develop human civilization and protect it. The phenomenal orchestral music of Yuzo Koshiro, some of the best on the SNES. A concept that was never quite repeated.
snes__actraiser.article:
Imagine you're not a hero with a sword but a god himself, descended to earth to wrest the world from the clutches of demons. This is exactly the audacious idea that ActRaiser, from the studio Quintet, brought — one of the most distinctive titles of the entire Super Nintendo era.

The genius of ActRaiser lies in the way it blends two seemingly incompatible genres. In the action part you enter the stone statue of a warrior and, in a classic side-scrolling platformer with a sword, clear the landscape of monsters and defeat the bosses who hold power over individual regions. Once the land is cleansed of evil, the game transforms into a city-building **god game**: from above you watch over the people, guide them in founding towns, drain swamps, burn forests and protect your charges from enemy raids using divine miracles. As civilization grows and offers sacrifices, your hero grows stronger for further action expeditions.

This alternation of pace is brilliant precisely because each part gives the other meaning. You fight so that people can live; and the better they thrive, the stronger you become. This creates the rare feeling that your deeds truly affect a world you watch grow from the first hut to a flourishing settlement.

An extraordinary chapter is the music of **Yuzo Koshiro**. His orchestral, monumental compositions rank among the absolute peak of the SNES sound chip and are still cited as an example of what the console was capable of in the hands of a brilliant composer. The soundtrack elevates ActRaiser from a good game into an unforgettable experience.

ActRaiser remains one of a kind, because no one ever managed to fully repeat its bold combination of action and building. The sequel, ActRaiser 2, dropped the building component entirely and bet solely on action, thereby paradoxically confirming how original the first instalment was. That is why the game holds cult status among connoisseurs.

**Why play it:** For an unusual, and today practically unrepeated, mix of action platformer and civilization building, crowned by one of the best orchestral soundtracks on the SNES.

snes__terranigma.teaser: Quintet's action RPG with melancholy; a cult favourite.
snes__terranigma.detail: An action RPG with melancholy themes of creation, life and death (Quintet, the authors of ActRaiser). Terranigma is especially prized — about bringing the world back to life — but in the West it was released only in Europe and Australia, never in the USA. Together with Soul Blazer it forms a loose „Quintet trilogy“. Deep and mature.
snes__terranigma.article:
Some games entertain you. Terranigma hits you. This action RPG from the studio Quintet is one of the most melancholy and mature stories ever released on the Super Nintendo.

Quintet, the people behind ActRaiser and Soul Blazer, here brought their favourite theme of creation, life and death to perfection. Terranigma tells of bringing the world back to life: you gradually awaken continents, plants, animals and humankind, and watch an empty planet turn into a living civilization. Together with Soul Blazer and Illusion of Gaia it forms a loosely connected „Quintet trilogy“, in which the motifs of renewal and the balance between creation and destruction recur.

In play terms it's a brisk action RPG with real-time combat, in which the hero Ark slashes enemies with a spear in isometric locations, gathers experience, upgrades his gear and solves logic puzzles. The gameplay is solid and enjoyable, but the game's real strength lies in its atmosphere and storytelling. The gradual flowering of the world gives every step weight, and the final twist ranks among the most emotionally powerful moments of its time.

Terranigma's fate is a story in itself. The game was released only in Europe and Australia, never received an official release in the United States, and so in the English-speaking world it long remained a half-forgotten treasure. It was precisely this unavailability that made it a sought-after cult title, spoken of with reverence among fans of Japanese RPGs.

Anyone looking only for quick entertainment may be confused by the slower start. But anyone who lets themselves be drawn in will find a work unafraid to speak of transience and of the price paid for the birth of the new. Terranigma is a game you never forget.

**Why play it:** For a mature, melancholy tale of creation and destruction, wrapped in a brisk action RPG and surrounded by the aura of a half-lost European treasure.

snes__illusion-of-gaia.article:
There are action RPGs that mainly want to entertain, and then there are those that also try to move you. Illusion of Gaia belongs to the second group and is still regarded as one of the most atmospheric titles of its kind on the Super Nintendo.

The game belongs to the loose „Quintet trilogy“ alongside Soul Blazer and Terranigma, and shares with them a characteristic tone: real themes of coming of age, of the journey and the search for meaning, interwoven with melancholy and a sense of the mysterious. Instead of a fantasy kingdom, you journey through locations inspired by real wonders of the world, which gives the game an unusual, almost adventurous-archaeological flavour.

In gameplay terms it's an action RPG with real-time combat in isometric environments. You slash enemies, solve logic puzzles and progress linearly through the story. A characteristic feature is the hero's transformation into two combat forms with different abilities, thanks to which both the combat and the puzzle-solving keep changing throughout. The pace is brisk, and the emphasis lies on the experience and the storytelling rather than on complex character building.

The game's strength is precisely its mood. Journeying through exotic places, the captivating music and the melancholy story of friendship, loss and growing up give Illusion of Gaia a tone that appears only rarely in the genre. It's an adventure that, beneath the surface of the action, deals with more serious questions.

Thanks to its membership in the Quintet trilogy, the game is today prized especially among fans of Japanese RPGs who appreciate its bolder storytelling and its connection to thematically kindred titles. For them it represents an essential piece of the puzzle.

**Why play it:** For an atmospheric action RPG with a more mature story and an exotic flavour, forming an important link in the cult Quintet trilogy.

snes__demon-s-crest.teaser: Dark action with Firebrand; an underrated gem.
snes__demon-s-crest.detail: The third and best Gargoyle's Quest game. You play the demon Firebrand, collect forms (each with different flight and attack abilities) and explore a dark, interconnected world with alternative endings. Atmospheric and underrated; one of the darkest Capcom titles of the era.
snes__demon-s-crest.article:
What if the main hero weren't a valiant knight, but the monster itself? Demon's Crest from Capcom casts you in the role of the demon Firebrand and is one of the darkest and at the same time most overlooked gems of the Super Nintendo.

It's the third and generally considered best instalment of the Gargoyle's Quest series, which itself grew out of the world of Ghosts 'n Goblins. This time you control a winged demon who collects magical forms (crests) that grant different abilities of flight, attack and movement. Switching between them is at the core of the gameplay: the fiery form burns enemies, another lets you swim or smash obstacles, and yet another opens previously inaccessible paths.

The game's structure is close to a Metroidvania. The world is interconnected and you return to it with new abilities to unlock hidden areas, secrets and alternative endings. Add to that the fluid flying, which gives movement a unique sense of freedom that wasn't common in platformers of the time. The boss fights are inventive and demanding, as befits the Ghosts 'n Goblins pedigree.

But Demon's Crest excels most in its atmosphere. The gloomy, gothic setting, the demonic music and the overall mood place it among the darkest titles Capcom released in that era. You play as a monster in a world of monsters, and the game holds this bleak tone from start to finish without compromise.

Even so, the title remained commercially overlooked and long lived in the shadow of more famous Capcom brands. Among connoisseurs, however, it earned a reputation as an underrated jewel that deserves far more attention than it ever received.

**Why play it:** For dark, atmospheric action in the role of a demon, an interconnected world with abilities in the spirit of Metroidvania, and a reputation as one of Capcom's best overlooked titles.

snes__tetris-attack-panel-de-pon.article:
Sometimes an unassuming little game turns out to be one of the best competitive puzzlers of all time. That's exactly what happened with Tetris Attack, which in the West hid the Japanese original Panel de Pon beneath a colourful Yoshi coat.

The principle is brilliantly simple. On the playing field you shift adjacent blocks horizontally, trying to line up three or more of the same colour in a row and clear them. The real fun, however, begins with chaining combos and so-called combos and chains: a cleverly set-up fall of blocks triggers a cascade of clearing that dumps a heap of unclearable rows onto your opponent's screen. On top of that the blocks keep rising from below, so you play under permanent time pressure.

Although the name refers to Tetris, the game has practically nothing in common with the traditional falling of tetrominoes. It's its own original system that emphasizes quick planning and anticipating cascades. That is precisely where its depth lies, which the simple rules don't reveal at first glance.

The absolute peak is the two-player duel. The versus mode against a live opponent is among the most thrilling things the puzzle genre has to offer: one well-executed chain can turn a seemingly lost match around, and the duels become an adrenaline-fuelled battle of nerves and reflexes. No wonder the game received a whole string of reincarnations and sequels in a series that later continued under the Puzzle League brand.

Recolouring it into the world of Yoshi from Panel de Pon made the title more accessible to a Western audience, but the gameplay core remained untouched and still ranks among the best in the genre.

**Why play it:** For one of the best competitive puzzlers ever, whose combo chaining and two-player duels offer surprising depth and adrenaline.

snes__wario-s-woods.teaser: Top-tier puzzle games for the console.
snes__wario-s-woods.detail: Tetris Attack (essentially Panel de Pon reskinned with a Yoshi theme) is one of the best competitive puzzlers ever made — you shift blocks, clear triples and up, and chain combos that attack your opponent. An outstanding two-player duel.
snes__wario-s-woods.article:
Wario's Woods holds one small place in history: it became the last officially released title for the classic NES, while also shining in its Super Nintendo version as a brisk and inventive puzzle game.

Unlike most logic games of the era, you aren't limited here to just shifting blocks around a static field. You directly control the character Toad, who runs across the playfield, picks up bombs and monsters, and arranges them so that bombs match colours with the creatures, clearing them in rows or columns. This more action-oriented layer gives the game a dynamism that classic falling-block puzzlers lack.

The design was handled by Intelligent Systems under Nintendo's wing, which shows in the thoughtful gameplay as well as in the signature villain Wario, who serves here as the main antagonist. The game combines quick decision-making with spatial planning: you have to track falling elements, manoeuvre Toad, and cleverly chain the elimination of enemies all at once.

Visually, the SNES version is colourful and fresh, the controls snappy, and the pace can ramp up considerably. Various modes are on offer, including a battle mode, so players looking for a competitive showdown on a single console will get their money's worth too.

Wario's Woods never reached the fame of Nintendo's biggest franchises, but among collectors and puzzle fans it holds its ground as a solid, original piece — and, on top of that, as a symbolic closing note to Nintendo's home 8-bit era.

**Why play it:** For its unusually action-driven take on the puzzle genre, where you directly control a character across the playfield, and for its reputation as the last official NES game with a well-crafted SNES variant.

snes__lost-vikings.teaser: A puzzle platformer with three characters; clever and funny.
snes__lost-vikings.detail: An early game by the studio that would later become Blizzard. You control three Vikings with different abilities (one fights, one runs/jumps, one shields) and have to get them all to the exit alive — it can't be done without teamwork. Funny and clever; a classic of cooperative puzzling.
snes__lost-vikings.article:
Three Vikings, one way out, and none of them can manage it alone. The Lost Vikings is a clever puzzle platformer that forces you to think in three bodies at once — and it carries a spicy pedigree to boot.

It is, after all, an early game by the studio Silicon & Synapse, which later renamed itself and became the legendary Blizzard. Long before Warcraft and Diablo, the creators here showed a knack for inventive design and humour. You control a trio of Vikings, each of whom can do something different: Erik can run and jump, Baleog fights with sword and bow, and Olaf shields himself — and can even glide with his shield. None of them is a complete hero; only their combination opens the way forward.

Each level is thus effectively a puzzle. You switch between characters, send them to different places, and coordinate their abilities to get all three to the exit alive. If even one of them dies, the level has to be solved again. The result is a clever game of interplay, where planning and observation matter more than reflexes.

And then there's the humour. The Vikings travel through time and bizarre settings during their adventure, commenting on events with a wry detachment that gives the game a light, entertaining tone that beautifully balances out the difficulty of the puzzles. The characters' banter remains charming to this day.
