Years later players still return to it, and it still sparks debate.

The success was staggering - over **14 million copies** were sold and Final Fantasy VII became one of the most important games ever made. It fundamentally helped make 3D graphics and the CD format the standard, and it helped the PlayStation win the console war of that generation. For many Western players it was their very first contact with the JRPG genre.

Today FF VII is an institution. It received an expansive remake that retold its story for a new generation, and its characters - especially the antagonist Sephiroth - rank among the most iconic in the entire medium. The original, however, remains the thing that started the legend.

**Why play it:** Because this is the game that popularized JRPGs in the West and to this day defines what grand game storytelling means - a cultural phenomenon you have to experience.

playstation__final-fantasy-ix.teaser: A return to fantasy roots; the favorite installment for many.
playstation__final-fantasy-ix.detail: Sakaguchi's favorite installment and a deliberate return to its medieval fantasy roots after the futuristic VII and VIII. A charismatic cast (the thief Zidane, the black mage Vivi and his emotional theme of mortality). Released at the end of the PS1's life, so technically polished. Considered by many the most „heartfelt“ installment.
playstation__final-fantasy-ix.article:
When most of the world expected another leap into the future, Squaresoft decided to go against the current and return home. Final Fantasy IX from 2000 is a deliberate return to the series' medieval fantasy roots - after the futuristic tones of installments VII and VIII, it is a loving tribute to what Final Fantasy once began as.

It is no coincidence that this particular installment is often named as the favorite of Hironobu Sakaguchi himself, the father of the entire series. Instead of technology and sci-fi, here it is knights, mages, airships and a fairy-tale atmosphere that reign. The hero is the likable thief **Zidane**, but the real heart of the game is, for many, the black mage **Vivi** - a small character whose story about mortality, identity and the meaning of existence ranks among the most touching things the series has ever offered. His theme resonates long after the game is over.

On the gameplay side, IX returns to time-tested principles: four-member parties, classic summoned beings and a system of abilities learned from equipment. The game came out at the very end of the PlayStation's life, and so it squeezed everything it could out of the console - the result is a technically polished, visually rich title full of both charming and grand moments. The characterful cast and warm tone make the journey an experience that is more of an embrace than a trial.

It is precisely this „heartfelt“ quality that earned IX a special place in the hearts of fans. While other installments dazzle with ambition or controversy, the ninth bets on the pure joy of storytelling and on emotions that need no grand gestures. Many therefore consider it the most „human“ and most tender installment of the whole series.

Today Final Fantasy IX is often remembered as one of the peaks of the PS1 era - a title that proved a step back toward tradition can also be a step forward in quality. For anyone who wants to know the soul of the series, it is an ideal starting point.

**Why play it:** For the most heartfelt and warm installment of the series - a return to fantasy roots with the unforgettable Vivi and a story that will not leave you for a long time.

playstation__final-fantasy-viii.teaser: Controversial but ambitious; the junction system and romance.
playstation__final-fantasy-viii.detail: The most controversial modern FF: realistically proportioned heroes, a strong romance and the unconventional „Junction“ system, where you draw power from summoned beings and absorb spells from enemies (you can easily break the balance). The Triple Triad card minigame is addictive in its own right. A massive sales success, but divisive in terms of gameplay.
playstation__final-fantasy-viii.article:
No other modern installment of the series divided players as thoroughly as this one. Final Fantasy VIII from 1999 is a bold, ambitious and to this day passionately discussed experiment that decided to break almost every rule its predecessor had set on the **PlayStation**.

This time Squaresoft bet on realism. The characters were given realistically proportioned bodies instead of the earlier stylized figures, the story revolves around a strong romantic thread between the withdrawn Squall and the spirited Rinoa, and the whole game breathes a more serious, more grown-up atmosphere. Visually it was a staggering leap - the sweeping cutscenes were among the best that the hardware of the time could offer.

The core of the controversy, however, is the **Junction system**. Instead of classic buying of spells, you literally absorb them from enemies and then „junction“ them onto your stats, while drawing power largely from summoned beings (Guardian Forces). It is an inventive and deep mechanism, but at the same time notorious for how easily it can be exploited - a clever player can smash the game's balance to smithereens and turn it into a walk in the park. Some love it for the freedom it gives, others cannot stand it for the lack of traditional structure.

Above all this floats one unexpected gem: the card minigame **Triple Triad**. This optional pastime became more addictive than the main story for a great many players and remains one of the best-designed minigames in the entire series. Collecting cards and the combat strategies around them easily swallow hours of your time.

In sales terms it was a huge success that confirmed the strength of the brand after the phenomenon of the seventh. In terms of gameplay, however, the eighth remains an installment that divides - for some it is a misunderstood gem full of courage, for others a misstep. And it is precisely this contradictory nature that makes it one of the most interesting titles worth forming your own opinion about.

**Why play it:** For an ambitious, controversial and unforgettable installment with the addictive Triple Triad - an experience you will either fall in love with or debate passionately.

playstation__final-fantasy-tactics.teaser: A deep tactical RPG; for many the best in the genre.
playstation__final-fantasy-tactics.detail: Matsuno's deep turn-based tactics set in the world of Ivalice, with a serious story of class struggle and manipulation by the church (inspired by the Wars of the Roses). A complex job system. The original translation was notoriously bad; the War of the Lions version (PSP) fixed it. For many the best tactical RPG ever.
playstation__final-fantasy-tactics.article:
Not every legend sounds its fanfares; some are born on chessboard battlefields, in quiet contemplation of the next move. Final Fantasy Tactics from 1998 is exactly such a game - a deep, serious and, for many players, still unsurpassed tactical RPG that had no equal on the **PlayStation**.

Behind the design stands Yasumi Matsuno, a master of elaborate worlds and mature storytelling. The story unfolds in the land of Ivalice and does not revolve around saving the world from cosmic evil but around far more earthly themes: class struggle, wars over the throne and cold-blooded manipulation on the part of the church. The inspiration of the English Wars of the Roses is felt at every step - it is a political thriller full of betrayal, intrigue and gray moral tones, where heroes and villains alike have their reasons.

In terms of gameplay it is turn-based tactics on isometric maps, where terrain height, unit positioning and turn order all matter. The heart of the system is the complex **job system**: characters change professions, learn abilities and combine them into countless variations. The depth is enormous and gives the player the freedom to build a unit exactly to their liking - from healers through knights to exotic combinations that change the course of battle.

An inseparable part of the game's history is its notorious original English translation, which was, to put it mildly, botched and at times confused more than it helped. Fortunately, along came the **War of the Lions** version for the PSP, which completely reworked the text into a form worthy of such an ambitious story and even added new content. Only thanks to it did many Western players appreciate just how sophisticated a narrative the game actually offers.

Today Final Fantasy Tactics is revered as one of the peaks of the genre and, for a large part of the community, simply the best tactical RPG ever made. For it combines intellectual challenge, depth of systems and a narrative that is not afraid to be dark and grown-up.

**Why play it:** For the deepest tactical RPG of its time with a mature story about power and betrayal - a must for anyone who loves thoughtful combat.

playstation__xenogears.teaser: A philosophical, ambitious JRPG with mechs; cult status.
playstation__xenogears.detail: A philosophically immensely ambitious JRPG with mechs (psychology, Gnosticism, religious symbolism). The second disc, due to a depleted budget, is told in abbreviated form (characters „sit and narrate“) - a notorious example of a truncated production that arguably added to the game's cult status. The team later made Xenosaga/Xenoblade.
playstation__xenogears.article:
There are JRPGs, and then there is **Xenogears** - a game that does not ask whether you will save the world, but why the world should even want to be saved. In 1998 Squaresoft released on the PlayStation a title so ambitious that its reach to this day extends beyond the boundaries of the genre. Gnosticism, Freudian and Jungian psychology, religious symbolism, collective consciousness, questions of identity and faith - all of it is woven here into a story about a pilot and his mech named Gear.

On the gameplay side it is a classic turn-based JRPG, but with its own piquant flavor. On-foot combat is built on the „Deathblows“ system, where you combine weak, medium and strong strikes into flashy combos. But once you climb into a Gear, the whole dynamic changes - you deal with fuel, the weight of attacks and an entirely different scale of damage. That contrast between the human and machine scale gives combat an unusual texture.

And then there is the notorious **second disc**. Due to a depleted budget and time, the second half of the game was cut down to a form in which the characters literally sit on a chair and narrate what happened, while the player merely watches a montage of scenes. For many it is a flaw on the beauty, for others paradoxically the strongest part - a concentrated dose of storytelling without filler. Either way, it became one of the most cited examples of „production hell“ in the history of the genre, one that arguably added to the game's cult status rather than diminished it.

Behind the scenario stood the team around Tetsuya Takahashi, who later founded the Monolith Soft studio and, in the spirit of Xenogears, developed the **Xenosaga** and **Xenoblade Chronicles** series. The line of ideas and themes stretches across decades and makes Xenogears a kind of origin point for an entire family branch of Japanese RPGs.

Xenogears is not a relaxing evening game. It is dense, at times overloaded with theology and philosophy, at times frustrating in its unfinished state. But it is precisely in that imperfection that it is more honest and more daring than a lot of more polished titles - it is a work of art that was not afraid to reach higher than it could grasp.

**Why play it:** If you want a JRPG that will haunt you long after the closing credits and force you to think, Xenogears is one of the most daring ever made.

playstation__chrono-cross.teaser: Visually and musically enchanting; dozens of characters.
playstation__chrono-cross.detail: An indirect sequel to Chrono Trigger with 40+ characters and parallel worlds. Visually and above all musically enchanting - Yasunori Mitsuda's soundtrack ranks among the best in the medium („Scars of Time“). A controversial relationship to Trigger, but a masterpiece in its own right.
playstation__chrono-cross.article:
When the opening tones of „Scars of Time“ ring out, the matter is settled - this game will get you before you even manage to pick up the controller. **Chrono Cross** from 2000 is an indirect sequel to the legendary Chrono Trigger and ranks among the most visually and musically enchanting titles ever released on the PlayStation.

At the heart of the game are two parallel worlds - Home and Another - between which you travel and watch how a small decision in the past branched reality into two different forms. You can recruit over **forty playable characters** into your party, each with their own personality, story hook and a way of being reached. It is a richness that no other game of the time offered on such a scale.

The combat system abandons classic MP and builds on the „Elements“ system - you slot spells and abilities into a grid and juggle stamina levels depending on how powerful the attacks you want to use are. Added to this is the colored battlefield, where advantages shift according to the elements. It is elegant, tactical and refreshingly different from most JRPGs of the time.

The music was handled by **Yasunori Mitsuda** and his soundtrack ranks among the absolute peaks of game music ever - from melancholic guitars to soaring orchestral motifs. It is precisely the music and the artistic conception that you carry away most deeply from Chrono Cross into your memory.

The relationship to Chrono Trigger remains to this day the subject of passionate debate. Some fans of the beloved predecessor took hard the way Cross handles its legacy and characters. But judged on its own it is a masterpiece with its own identity, atmosphere and sorrow over branched fates. In 2022 it moreover received a remaster in the form of Chrono Cross: The Radical Dreamers Edition.

**Why play it:** For one of the most beautiful soundtracks in the history of games and an ambitious story about parallel worlds that stands firm even without its famous forebear.

playstation__suikoden-i-and-ii.teaser: Collect 108 characters; the second game is often among the best JRPGs ever.
playstation__suikoden-i-and-ii.detail: A series about collecting 108 „Stars of Destiny“ into an army and building your own castle, which grows with recruitment. The second game is regularly among the best JRPGs ever thanks to its mature story of war and betrayal and one of the best villains of the genre (Luca Blight). Released in a small print run, it is rare and expensive.
playstation__suikoden-i-and-ii.article:
One hundred and eight heroes. One army. Your own castle that grows with every new ally. The **Suikoden** series from Konami stands on an idea so simple and yet so addictive that it became an obsession for an entire generation of JRPG fans - to recruit all **108 „Stars of Destiny“** and build a power of your own from them.

The inspiration comes from the classic Chinese novel Water Margin, and the scope matches. Your base gradually changes from an abandoned ruin into a living town full of merchants, blacksmiths, cooks, fortune-tellers and minigame attractions - each new character adds a function, decoration or simply a piece of soul. Battles take place in parties of six, joined by mass battles of armies and dramatic one-on-one duels.

The first installment from 1996 laid the foundations, but it is **Suikoden II** from 1998 that regularly appears in rankings of the best JRPGs of all time. The reason is a mature, surprisingly dark story about war, friendship and betrayal - and above all one of the best villains of the entire genre, **Luca Blight**. This character is pure hatred in human form, a general whose cruelty stays under your skin for a long time.

Both games are joined by the ability to transfer a saved position, so decisions from the first game have an echo in the second. This gives the series a continuity that few titles offered at the time, and rewards players who set out on the whole journey.

The sad irony is that **Suikoden II** came out in the West in a small print run and today ranks among the rarest and most expensive PlayStation games on the collector's market. Fortunately, both games received an official remaster in 2024, so the legend is no longer held hostage by inflated secondhand prices.

**Why play it:** For the unforgettable story of the second game, the joy of building your own army and Luca Blight - a villain you never forget.

playstation__legend-of-dragoon.teaser: Combat timing à la quick-time; an epic journey.
playstation__legend-of-dragoon.detail: Sony's own answer to Final Fantasy: a four-disc epic JRPG with timing-based combat („Additions“ - you press in rhythm with the animation for stronger combos) and transformations into dragon knights. A devoted fanbase still calls for a remake.
playstation__legend-of-dragoon.article:
In 2000 Sony decided it would not merely host other people's JRPG hits - it would build its own rival to Final Fantasy. The result was **The Legend of Dragoon**, a hefty four-disc epic adventure that to this day stirs passionate nostalgia and loud calls for a remake.

The most striking feature is the combat system built on **timing**. Instead of passively selecting attacks from a menu, you watch the animation and press the button at the precise moment - a system called „Additions“. Hit the rhythm and the combos continue and grow stronger; miss and the attack collapses. It is suspenseful, it demands concentration and it turns every ordinary battle into a small test of skill.

The second pillar is the **transformations into dragon knights** - Dragoons. At key moments your characters change into winged warriors with powerful spells and devastating attacks, which lends combat a fitting epic grandeur. The game does not skimp on animations or effects and for its time came across as a magnificent spectacle.

The story follows the hero Dart and his party across a vast world in a narrative that shamelessly draws on tried-and-tested genre schemes - a lost princess, an ancient prophecy, the threat of the world's demise. It is not the most original scenario of its time, but it is told with determination and heart across four discs that will keep you busy for dozens of hours.

Although the game lived in the shadow of colossi like Final Fantasy IX at the time of its release, it created a devoted fanbase that to this day tirelessly lobbies for a modern remake. That very loyalty is perhaps the most compelling proof that Sony did not build its own JRPG rival in vain.

**Why play it:** For active timing-based combat and grand dragon spectacle - a classic JRPG with a face of its own that deserves a second life.

playstation__vagrant-story.teaser: A deep combat/crafting system; storytelling like a film.
playstation__vagrant-story.detail: Another Matsuno work, with deep combat that targets body parts and extremely complex weapon crafting. Set in the cursed city of Leá Monde; direction on a cinematic level. No towns or shops - everything is one dungeon. Demanding and unique.
playstation__vagrant-story.article:
No towns. No shops. No world map. Just one cursed city and you in its bowels. **Vagrant Story** from Squaresoft in 2000 is one of the most daring and uncompromising works ever released on the PlayStation - an action RPG that looks and tells its story like a taut cinematic thriller.

Behind the game stands **Yasumi Matsuno**, a creator with a signature evident in every frame. The tale of the agent Ashley Riot, searching in the ruins of the city of Leá Monde, is delivered with cinematic direction, sophisticated dialogue and a dark, grown-up atmosphere that few dared attempt at the time. The locations flow one into another, so the whole game feels like a single enormous interwoven dungeon.

The combat system is a depth unto itself. In real time you target specific **parts of the enemy's body**, thereby influencing its movement and attacks, and chain combos with precise timing. Added to this is extremely complex **weapon crafting** - you combine blades, hilts, materials and properties effective against various types of enemies until you obtain an arsenal tailored to every situation.

This depth is at the same time the biggest barrier. Vagrant Story is a demanding, at times downright unfriendly game that requires the player to understand its systems and to have patience. The reward, however, is a sense of mastery that few titles offer - once you finally penetrate the logic of the combat and crafting, an extraordinarily satisfying tactical game opens up before you.

Visually the game still captivates with its unified, gloomy aesthetic and impressive camera work. It is a title that does not try to please everyone; it aims at players willing to learn and be rewarded with something truly unique.

**Why play it:** For a cinematically told story, intoxicatingly deep combat with body-part targeting and crafting like no other - if you can handle the difficulty.

playstation__threads-of-fate.detail: A charming action RPG with two playable characters each with a different story and style (Rue transforms into defeated enemies, Mint is a fast fighter). A lighter, charming tone. An underrated Square title.
playstation__threads-of-fate.article:
Two heroes, two completely different stories, one enchanting game. **Threads of Fate** (Dewprism in Japan) from Squaresoft in 2000 is one of those titles that never stirred up as much fuss as the studio's big series - and yet those who discovered it cherish it to this day like a little treasure.

The magic lies in the fact that at the start you choose between two playable characters, and each offers a different path, a different tone and a different style of play. **Rue** is a quiet young man searching for a lost girl, and his central ability is transformation - if he defeats an enemy, he can take on its form and use its strengths. **Mint**, by contrast, is an energetic, witty ex-princess longing to reclaim her throne, a fast fighter with a lighter and more playful tuning.

The gameplay is a brisk action RPG with an emphasis on real-time combat, platforming elements and exploration. It is not any sprawling colossus - rather a pleasantly shaped, charming journey that does not drag and bets on the distinctiveness of its characters and a colorful, fairy-tale world.

It is precisely that lighter, kinder tone that sets Threads of Fate apart from the darker and more serious titles for which Square was renowned at the time. After Xenogears or Vagrant Story, this game feels like a refreshing breath - sweet, witty and unburdened by cosmic tragedies.

Thanks to the pair of protagonists the game also has natural replayability: you finish Rue's story and immediately feel the urge to see the same events through Mint's eyes. It is an underrated piece from Squaresoft's rich catalog that deserves more attention than it ever received.

**Why play it:** For two distinct, mutually complementary campaigns, brisk action and a kind, playful tone - the ideal respite between more serious JRPGs.

playstation__castlevania-symphony-of-nig.article:
There is a game after which an entire genre was named - and **Castlevania: Symphony of the Night** is its second half. The term „Metroidvania“ would make no sense without this 1997 title. Here Konami took a long-running action series and transformed it into a sprawling, interwoven castle full of secret passages, abilities and treasures that unlocks gradually as your power grows.

Instead of linear progress through levels, you get one enormous, interconnected **Dracula's castle** to explore freely. New abilities - transformation into a bat, wolf or mist, a double jump - open up previously inaccessible areas, so you constantly return and discover more. Added to this were **RPG elements**: experience, levels, equipment and dozens of weapons that fundamentally change the style of play.

You play as **Alucard**, Dracula's son, an elegant vampire with both a katana and magic. The game became famous for its Gothic atmosphere, gorgeous hand-drawn 2D graphics and the music of Michiru Yamane, which to this day ranks among the best that game audio has offered. And then there is the notorious twist at the halfway point - the moment when you discover you have seen only half of what the game hides.

At the time of its release, when everything was rushing into 3D, the fully 2D Symphony of the Night came across almost as an act of defiance. Commercially it did not shine at first as it deserved to, but it gradually earned a reputation as a cult classic and one of the best titles of the entire PlayStation era.

Its influence is immeasurable. Together with Super Metroid it defined the template by which countless independent and major games are still built to this day. If you want to understand where half of the modern indie world came from, the path leads right here.

**Why play it:** For the founding work of an entire genre - Gothic atmosphere, addictive exploration and timeless 2D beauty that has not aged.

playstation__metal-gear-solid.article:
„Snake? Snake?! SNAAAKE!" Few lines have burned themselves into players' memories as deeply as this one. **Metal Gear Solid** from 1998, created by Hideo Kojima and Konami, was not merely a great game — it was proof that a video game could be a gripping thriller, a cinematic epic, and a bitter meditation on nuclear weapons and war all at once.

The game practically defined the modern **stealth genre**. As agent Solid Snake you infiltrate the Shadow Moses facility, where instead of trading fire you slip through the shadows, avoid the enemies' cones of vision, knock on walls to lure attention away, and hide beneath a cardboard box. The emphasis on avoiding combat, on patience and planning, was a revelation at the time and set the rules the genre still follows today.

But Kojima never spelled things out bluntly. **Metal Gear Solid** is famous for its cinematic storytelling, long, masterfully directed scenes, and characters who broke the fourth wall in unforgettable ways — the battle with Psycho Mantis, who „read" your memory card and controller, ranks among the most quoted moments in gaming history.

The atmosphere is equally captivating: a wind-battered Alaskan base, the voice on the codec radio, unforgettable bosses, and music that ratchets up the tension. The game managed to balance suspense, humor, and surprisingly serious themes of heredity, identity, and responsibility for weapons of mass destruction.

**Metal Gear Solid** became one of the most influential and commercially successful titles of the PlayStation era and launched a series that spent decades pushing the boundaries of what a video game can tell. To this day it remains the yardstick against which ambitious, story-driven action games are measured.

**Why play it:** For the founding work of modern stealth and a cinematic narrative that showed just how mature and intelligent a medium video games can be.

playstation__tenchu-stealth-assassins.article:
Before the world fell for ninjas in dozens of later games, there was **Tenchu: Stealth Assassins** from 1998 — a title that first truly cast players in the role of a ninja as fantasy imagined it: a silent shadow on the rooftops of feudal Japan, striking with a single blow and vanishing before anyone can cry out.

Tenchu arrived at a time when the stealth genre was still finding its shape, and it brought its own, distinctly different take. You play a ninja (Rikimaru or Ayame) in the service of a clan, and your task is to infiltrate fortified estates, avoid the guards, and eliminate targets. The key element is the „ki" meter, which warns you how close an enemy is and whether they have noticed you — nudging you to stay in the shadows and wait patiently.

The most delicious morsel is the **stealth kill** — when you creep up unseen on an unsuspecting guard and trigger a spectacular, brutal execution with a single strike. It is precisely the feeling of a perfectly performed silent kill that makes Tenchu an unforgettable experience, rewarding sneaking over direct combat, which is by contrast mercilessly harsh.

The game leaned on the atmosphere of feudal Japan, vertical exploration across rooftops, and the use of tools such as the grappling hook, shurikens, and smoke bombs. Through all of this it built a devoted following and the standing of one of the pioneering stealth titles of its day.

Tenchu became a respected brand that showed sneaking and patience could be just as thrilling as action — and that the role of a ninja in games is far more than merely a fighting style. For stealth fans it is an important, unforgettable chapter.

**Why play it:** For the authentic feeling of being a ninja in feudal Japan and satisfying silent takedowns — one of the pioneers of the stealth genre.

playstation__tenchu-2-birth-of-stealth-a.article:
A good stealth game calls for a sequel that expands the arsenal of shadows — and **Tenchu 2: Birth of the Stealth Assassins** from 2000 did exactly that. The second installment returns to feudal Japan, this time as a prequel that tells how young apprentices became the clan's deadly ninjas.

The core stays faithful to the first game: you sneak through fortified estates, watch the „ki" meter warning of nearby enemies, and strive for perfectly executed **silent takedowns**. Patience, reading the guards' movements, and exploiting verticality — moving across rooftops and from shadow to shadow — remain what separates a master from a dead ninja.

The sequel, however, adds more content and playable characters, including a new hero, thereby broadening the view of the world and the series' story. Each character offers their own perspective on the events, which adds variety and reasons to return to the game again.

The most notable new feature is the **level editor**, which let players build their own maps and share them — a remarkable step for its time that extended the game's lifespan far beyond the prepared missions. For the stealth genre it was an unusual openness toward the community and player creativity.

Tenchu 2 builds on its predecessor's solid foundations and polishes the formula that defined ninja stealth on the PlayStation. For fans of silent kills, feudal atmosphere, and sneaking across rooftops, it is a natural deepening of the experience the original Tenchu set in motion.

**Why play it:** For polished ninja stealth, a story about the birth of the assassins, and a level editor that put players' own shadows in their hands.

playstation__resident-evil-2.article:
The Raccoon City police station glows in the pinkish light of emergency lamps, the corridors are full of corpses that are not quite dead yet — and you have only a handful of bullets. Resident Evil 2 is, for many, the pinnacle of the classic survival horror era, a game that took everything good from the first installment and expanded it into a grander, more refined experience.

The key innovation was the so-called **zapping system**: you play the game once as rookie cop Leon S. Kennedy and a second time as Claire Redfield, searching for her brother. Each character has their own scenario (A and B), with your actions in the first playthrough shaping the world in the second — locked doors, collected items, enemy placement. Two discs, four variants of the playthrough, and a strong incentive to play again.

The gameplay rests on the genre's proven pillars: fixed cameras building tension through the framing of each shot, tank controls, a limited inventory, saving via typewriters and ink ribbons, and the constant pressure of scarce ammunition. The game masterfully alternates moments of calm with insidious scares, whether it is dogs crashing through corridor windows or the monstrous mutations of the **T-virus** experiment. The atmosphere of a city destroyed under the onslaught of the infection is among the best rendered in the entire medium.

Resident Evil 2 was created at **Capcom** and directed by Hideki Kamiya (later the creator of Devil May Cry and Bayonetta), with production overseen by Shinji Mikami, the father of the whole series. An interesting fact is that the original version of the game was roughly half finished, but the team scrapped it as inadequate — this discarded form is known to fans today as **Resident Evil 1.5**.

From both a commercial and critical standpoint it was an enormous success, one of the best-selling titles on the PlayStation and a work that defined what survival horror should look like. In 2019 an acclaimed remake on a modern engine was released, introducing the game to a new generation and earning enthusiastic reviews as well as game-of-the-year nominations.

**Why play it:** Because it is a textbook survival horror with a brilliant dual scenario and an atmosphere that weighs on you even decades later.

playstation__resident-evil-3-nemesis.article:
A single word can raise goosebumps even on seasoned players: STARS. That is what the giant bioweapon Nemesis roars at you before it starts chasing you through the streets of a dying Raccoon City. Resident Evil 3: Nemesis pushed the series toward a more action-oriented approach and introduced one of the most unforgettable pursuers in the history of the genre.

The plot largely unfolds in parallel with the events of the second game and returns **Jill Valentine**, one of the survivors from the original Spencer mansion, to the lead role. This time she tries to escape a city consumed by the infection while Nemesis is on her heels — an intelligent, relentless, and brutally powerful adversary who can appear practically anywhere and thereby keeps the game in constant tension.

The biggest mechanical innovation is precisely that pursuit system, complemented by **quick choices** (dodges and instant decisions in critical moments) that give the player a sense of control even in moments of panic. The ability to turn faster, dodge attacks, and mix gunpowder into your own ammunition was added. The environment of city streets, full of improvised barricades and burning cars, feels claustrophobic and open at the same time.

The game was developed by **Capcom** and released at the close of the nineties as the third pillar of the classic trilogy on the PlayStation. Compared to the second game it places greater emphasis on pace and action, thereby foreshadowing the direction the series would eventually take. At the same time it kept the characteristic predatory ammunition economy and puzzles linking the individual locations.

Nemesis became an iconic figure, and the game still ranks as one of the high points of the era. In 2020 its modern remake was released, reworking Jill's adventure into contemporary graphics and reminding everyone why that relentless, rocket-launcher-wielding colossus belongs among the most feared adversaries games have ever spawned.

**Why play it:** For Nemesis — a pursuer who turns fleeing a dead city into a nerve-shredding race for survival.

playstation__silent-hill.article:
Fog so thick you cannot see more than a few meters ahead, a pocket radio crackling with static every time something inhuman draws near, and a small American town that has sunk into a nightmare. Silent Hill did not come to frighten with blood and monsters around the corner — it came to frighten with silence, uncertainty, and whatever you imagine for yourself.

The player takes on the role of Harry Mason, who searches for his lost daughter Cheryl in the snowbound little town and gradually discovers that Silent Hill hides dark cults, a parallel reality, and horrors born of the human psyche. The game masterfully employs psychological horror: it is not about jump scares but about slowly mounting anxiety, an atmosphere of hopelessness, and symbolism that needles the subconscious.

The technical trick with **fog and darkness** was ingenious — the limited visibility on the console served to hide the short rendering range, but at the same time it became a defining stylistic weapon that keeps the player in permanent uncertainty. The crackling radio as a warning of enemies, the switching between the ordinary world and a rusted, blood-spattered alternate dimension, and several different endings make the game a tense, unforgettable experience.

Silent Hill was created by an internal team at **Konami**, later known as Team Silent. The music was composed by Akira Yamaoka, whose combination of industrial noise and mournful melodies became an inseparable part of the series' identity. The game set itself sharply apart from its rival Resident Evil precisely through its emphasis on atmosphere and psychology instead of action.

The title is today considered a founding work of psychological horror in games and one of the most influential creations of its genre altogether. It launched an entire series whose later installments (especially the second) rank among the most acclaimed horror games in history, and it continues to inspire creators around the world to this day.

**Why play it:** Because it will show you that the deepest dread is not conjured by a monster, but by silence, fog, and your own imagination.

playstation__dino-crisis.article:
What if Resident Evil, but instead of zombies you were hunted by dinosaurs? It was precisely from this heady idea that Dino Crisis arose — a game in which a team of special agents lands on a remote research island and, instead of an enemy of flesh, finds predators from the distant past that can smash through doors.

The gameplay rests on survival horror foundations: exploring interconnected locations, solving puzzles, managing a limited inventory and ammunition. Compared to the competition of the time, however, Dino Crisis brought a fundamental technical leap — environments rendered in real time in 3D instead of static pre-rendered backgrounds. Thanks to this the camera followed the action more fluidly and the world felt more tangible.

The protagonist Regina faces dinosaurs that are fast, aggressive, and clever — Velociraptors can attack from ambush, and the relentless **Tyrannosaurus** poses a threat from which there is often no choice but to flee. Mikami himself described the game's style as suspense more in the spirit of a thriller than of classic horror: the pressure evokes adrenaline and fear of a swift attack rather than slow dread. The emphasis on collecting keys, combining items, and managing resources nevertheless remains.

Dino Crisis comes from the workshop of **Capcom** and was directed by Shinji Mikami, the father of Resident Evil, which is evident in the game's DNA at every step. A new brand was thus born that filled the gap between horror and action thriller and won a devoted fan base.

The game is today among the beloved PlayStation classics, and a strong community still exists that calls for its return. The fusion of proven horror mechanics with an unexpected enemy in the form of dinosaurs makes it an unmistakable piece of gaming history.

**Why play it:** For the unique fusion of survival horror and prehistoric predators, where every opening of a door can mean a maw full of teeth.

playstation__dino-crisis-2.article:
If the first installment was a tense thriller, the sequel hit the gas and turned into an action ride full of gunfire, explosions, and hordes of dinosaurs. Dino Crisis 2 decided to swap cautious ammunition conservation for an adrenaline-fueled slaughter — and that transformation suited it splendidly.

Instead of slow exploration, the game pushes the player forward with a continuous stream of enemies. The key innovation is the **point/combo system**: for fast and spectacular dinosaur kills you earn points that serve as currency for buying weapons, ammunition, and upgrades. This motivates an aggressive, flowing playstyle where hesitation does not pay off, but pressing the attack does.

The player controls a pair of characters — the returning Regina and the soldier Dylan — and progresses through a lush prehistoric jungle as well as facilities struck by a time anomaly. The environment is more varied and colorful than the gloomy corridors of the first game, the pace is brisker, and the arsenal significantly richer. Even so, the game maintains its tension thanks to the sheer number of adversaries and several unforgettable boss battles.

Dino Crisis 2 was developed by **Capcom** as a sequel to the successful brand and deliberately shifted its genre center of gravity from survival horror to pure action. This decision divided the fans, but many players still consider the sequel more entertaining and playable than the original installment precisely because of its uncompromising pace.

Thanks to the combination of fast action, a rewarding point system, and a still-attractive premise with dinosaurs, the game earned the position of a cult PlayStation classic. For many it represents the peak of the series and one of the reasons fans still long for its revival.

**Why play it:** For an uncompromising action ride where you mow down dinosaurs in spectacular combos and every battle is an adrenaline spectacle.

playstation__parasite-eve.article:
An opera performance at Carnegie Hall turns into a nightmare when the audience begins to spontaneously combust and the soprano reveals her true, monstrous nature. With this scene Parasite Eve begins — a game that blended a Hollywood thriller, a Japanese RPG, and cosmic horror into a shape no one had seen before.

The player takes on New York police officer Aya Brea, whose own cells hold the key to the mystery. The combat system is hybrid and ingenious: you move around the battlefield in real time and dodge attacks, but once the action meter fills, the game pauses and you choose a shot or a supernatural ability. The result is a gripping combination of **action and turn-based strategy**, supported by upgrading weapons, armor, and parasitic abilities.

The game places emphasis on an unexpectedly scientific theme — mitochondria, the energy factories of cells, rebel against humanity. This biological horror lends the story an original flavor and sets it apart from typical fantasy. Cinematic interludes, quality music, and a serious, mature narrative made Parasite Eve an unusually cinematic experience for its time.

Behind the game stands the studio **Square**, then a powerhouse of the RPG genre and the force behind the Final Fantasy series. Square here experimented with a modern urban setting and a horror tone, and it was moreover one of the titles with which the company tried to break into the Western market with more mature content. The music was composed by Yoko Shimomura, and its dark, atmospheric soundtrack ranks among the most acclaimed elements of the game.

Parasite Eve is today valued as a bold genre crossbreed and a cult classic that proved an RPG need not mean only swords and dragons. It received a sequel, and its inventive combat system and raw atmosphere still fuel discussions among fans longing for the series' return.

**Why play it:** For an unconventional fusion of action, turn-based RPG, and biological horror that has no equal on the PlayStation.

playstation__medal-of-honor.article:
To step onto the beach of occupied Europe, take cover behind an anti-tank obstacle, and push forward under fire — war games have a thousand faces today, but this one stood at the birth of the genre. Medal of Honor brought the Second World War into the form of gripping action from the perspective of a single American soldier.

The player inhabits the role of an OSS secret service agent in the closing days of the war and carries out varied missions: sabotaging enemy facilities, stealing documents, infiltrating bases in disguise, and fighting through occupied fortresses. The game combined straightforward action with mild stealth and espionage elements, which gave it variety and the feeling that you are a genuine part of a covert operation, not just a pawn in the crowd.

For the console technology of the time it was an ambitious and atmospheric title. The **orchestral music** by Michael Giacchino, who later became famous as an Oscar-winning film composer, contributed significantly to this. His symphonic soundtrack gave the game a cinematic weight and dignity that shooters on consoles had not had until then.

**Steven Spielberg** played a fundamental part in the game's creation; his film Saving Private Ryan served as inspiration, and the project was made under the DreamWorks Interactive banner. It was precisely Spielberg's effort to create a respectful, authentic portrayal of the war that gave the series its characteristic tone — respect for the soldiers and an emphasis on the atmosphere of the period.

Medal of Honor laid the foundations of an entire subgenre of war shooters set in the Second World War and opened the way for later major series. From its creative circle later came people who stood behind other legendary brands of the genre. As a pioneer, the game belongs among the important milestones in the history of FPS on consoles.

**Why play it:** As a founding work of war shooters with unforgettable orchestral music and the spirit of Spielberg's films.

playstation__medal-of-honor-underground.article:
Heroes of war are not made only of soldiers in uniform — sometimes it is a young woman who risks her life in the streets of occupied Paris. Medal of Honor: Underground took the successful foundation of the first installment and moved it into a world of resistance, espionage, and guerrilla warfare behind enemy lines.

The player takes on Manon Batiste, a member of the French resistance movement whom players briefly met in the first game. Through her adventure you fight your way from the streets of Paris across North Africa to secret Nazi operations, carrying out sabotage, rescue missions, and infiltrations. The emphasis on disguises, sneaking, and improvisation gives the game a different charge than purely frontline action — you are a lone link in the resistance who must survive by cunning.

The gameplay rests on the series' proven pillars: varied missions with clear objectives, a combination of action and stealth elements, and period details carefully set into the Second World War. Underground expanded the arsenal and the environments and offered more varied situations than the original game. The bonus content reward in the form of unlockable extras also returned, motivating repeated play.

The game was once again backed by the studio **DreamWorks Interactive**, building on the concept at whose birth Steven Spielberg stood, and the characteristic orchestral music was again composed by **Michael Giacchino**. The continuity of the creative team ensured that the sequel kept the cinematic atmosphere and respectful tone toward the war theme that made the brand famous.

Underground confirmed that Medal of Honor was not a one-off success but a viable series with its own identity. By choosing a female resistance heroine it moreover offered an unusual and refreshing view of the war for its time, one that set the game apart from the flood of frontline shooters.

**Why play it:** For a view of war through the eyes of a resistance fighter — sneaking, sabotage, and espionage with cinematic music at your back.

playstation__spider-man.teaser: The defining superhero game of its era; freedom of movement.
playstation__spider-man.detail: The defining superhero game of its era: you swing across the city, climb walls, and fight villains from the comics. Stan Lee narrated the intro. The freedom of movement was intoxicating; it laid the template for later Spider-Man games.
playstation__spider-man.article:
To nimbly kick off a skyscraper, fire a web, and swing above the streets of New York in a red-and-blue suit — for every comics fan it is a dream come true, and this game was one of the first to fulfill it believably. Spider-Man from 2000 became the defining superhero game of its era.

The key to its charm was **freedom of movement**. Web-swinging, climbing the walls of buildings, and the seamless transition between combat and acrobatics gave the player the intoxicating feeling of truly being Spider-Man. The content was a mix of battles with villains from the comics, sneaking, completing objectives, and hunting for hidden bonuses, all interlaced with a story full of familiar names from the Marvel universe.

The game drew directly from its comic-book source and brimmed with references that delighted fans. The intro was personally narrated by **Stan Lee** himself, the legendary co-creator of the character, which gave the work a stamp of authenticity. The gallery of adversaries and allies, the ironic humor, and the comic-book styling made playing it a celebration of the entire brand.

Behind the development stood the studio **Neversoft**, famous for the Tony Hawk's Pro Skater series, and the game was published by **Activision**. Neversoft put its experience with fluid movement and trick physics to good use, thanks to which web-swinging felt unusually brisk and fun. The result was a title that critics and players alike received very warmly.

Spider-Man laid the template that later superhero games followed as well — the linking of free movement, combat, and comic-book storytelling became the standard. Its success opened the way for sequels and still ranks as one of the best works featuring the web-slinger on the classic consoles.

**Why play it:** For the unfettered feeling of swinging across the city and a comic-book celebration of Spider-Man blessed by Stan Lee himself.

playstation__tomb-raider.teaser: Lara Croft as a 90s icon; a pioneer of 3D adventures and spatial puzzles.
playstation__tomb-raider.detail: Lara Croft became one of the first iconic gaming heroines and a pop-culture star. A pioneer of the 3D action-adventure with an emphasis on spatial puzzles, leaps across chasms and solitary tomb exploration. The first two games are the purest; five installments in five years led to franchise burnout.
playstation__tomb-raider.article:
Out of the darkness of a forgotten tomb emerged a heroine who would forever change the face of the gaming industry — the archaeologist and adventurer Lara Croft. Tomb Raider turned her not only into a 90s icon, but also into a pioneer of the entire 3D action-adventure genre.

At the heart of the gameplay lies the solitary exploration of sprawling ancient temples and tombs. Lara climbs along ledges, leaps across chasms, swims through flooded halls and solves **spatial puzzles** built around moving stone blocks, levers and carefully timed jumps. The emphasis on three-dimensional orientation was revolutionary for its time and gave the adventure an intoxicating sense of discovering places no one had set foot in for ages.

The game masterfully alternates tense acrobatic sequences with quiet moments of solitude deep within crumbling ruins, punctuated by battles against wild beasts and supernatural threats. The atmosphere of abandonment, where you hear only Lara's footsteps and the distant drip of water, gave the series an unmistakable mood that set it apart from the more frenetic action games of the era.

Tomb Raider was created by the British studio **Core Design** and published by **Eidos**. Lara Croft quickly became a pop-culture star who transcended the boundaries of the gaming medium and appeared on magazine covers, in commercials and in films. The first two installments are regarded as the purest expression of the original vision. The series then churned out a new installment practically every year, which by the fifth game led to creative burnout and brand fatigue.

Even so, Tomb Raider remains one of the most influential works of its time and its heroine one of the first truly iconic gaming characters ever. It laid the foundations of the modern action-adventure and opened the way for later reboots that brought Lara Croft to new generations of players.

**Why play it:** For an encounter with the iconic Lara Croft and a pioneering 3D adventure full of spatial puzzles and solitary discovery.

playstation__tomb-raider-ii.article:
Lara Croft was no longer a hot new thing — she was a phenomenon, and Tomb Raider II knew it well. The sequel to the legendary 1997 adventure bet on the proven formula and added more of everything: more weapons, more enemies, more sprawling spaces and a markedly faster pace. The British studio Core Design took what worked in the first game and polished it into a form many remember as the peak of the series' classic era.

Where the first game focused on lonely wandering through silent tombs, the sequel widened the lens into a grand adventurous spectacle. Lara travels from a sunken Venetian lagoon through the Chinese highlands to a shipwreck on the ocean floor, accompanied throughout by considerably more aggressive opponents — instead of animals, there are armed gangs of human adversaries. The combat was given more room, and with it came an arsenal that delighted anyone longing for a more action-oriented approach.

The core gameplay, however, remained untouched: acrobatic leaps along ledges, searching for hidden levers, solving spatial puzzles and that characteristic feeling of standing on the edge of a chasm, gauging whether the jump will land. The grid-based movement controls and fixed camera demanded patience, but it was precisely this deliberateness that made every conquered section a small victory. The game also introduced an iconic element — the return to Lara's mansion, where you could roam the villa, train and, by tradition, lock the butler in the freezer.

Tomb Raider II became one of the best-selling titles on the PlayStation and definitively cemented Lara Croft as one of the first true icons of the gaming industry, a character who reached far beyond the gaming community. At a time when 3D adventures were still searching for their language, Core Design's series showed what cinematic action archaeology could look like.

Today the sequel is a window into an era when the 3D genre was only taking shape — and at the same time a surprisingly fun ride, if you accept its rules. The atmosphere of vast, abandoned places and the satisfaction of a well-timed jump still work today.

**Why play it:** The classic Lara Croft adventure in its most action-packed and grandest form, a 3D gaming milestone that shaped an entire genre.

playstation__tomb-raider-iii.article:
When a series reaches its third installment within three years, it is clear it is running at full throttle — and Tomb Raider III was exactly such a product of the feverish pace of the late nineties. Core Design churned out another helping of Lara Croft's adventures and bet on what fans knew and loved, only with a higher difficulty bar that became notorious for this installment.

The third game sends Lara after artifacts across four corners of the world — from the Indian jungle through icy Antarctica and Nevada to the streets of London. Structurally, the game offered greater freedom in choosing the order of locations, thereby trying to break the linear feel of the previous installments. Each environment had its own atmosphere and its own trap, which you usually fell for at least once.

The gameplay stayed faithful to the proven formula: precise jumping navigation, hunting for secret places, solving mechanical puzzles and gunfights. New moves and maneuvers were added, among them the famous crouching and sidestepping, along with vehicles that spiced up the pace. But the game is famous above all for its difficulty — Tomb Raider III is among the most demanding installments in the series, with mercilessly placed traps and sections that punished even the smallest mistake. For players of the time, who did not have today's flood of online tips at their disposal, it was often a test of patience as well as reflexes.

Visually, Core Design pushed the engine a little further — more colorful environments, weather effects and more elaborate locations showed just how far older technology could be driven. Meanwhile, Lara Croft had long outgrown the confines of games and become a pop-culture icon, the face of commercials and magazine covers, and each new installment was an event.

Today the third game is a fascinating testament to an era when franchises were released on a yearly rhythm and when difficulty was a badge of honor. For connoisseurs of the series it is a beloved, if uncompromising, notch in gaming history.

**Why play it:** The most demanding classic Tomb Raider with diverse worlds and a more open structure — a challenge for hardened fans of adventurous action.

playstation__tomb-raider-last-revelation.article:
After a series of yearly churned-out sequels, Core Design decided to send Lara Croft where an archaeologist really belongs most — to Egypt. Tomb Raider: The Last Revelation from 1999 set aside globe-trotting and focused on a single, tightly contained location full of tombs, temples and desert dust, and this very concentration served it well.

The installment delivered the most thematically cohesive adventure of the series so far. The story follows both a young and an adult Lara and begins with a tutorial set in Cambodia that elegantly eases the player in. Most of the game then unfolds in Egypt, where Lara inadvertently awakens the ancient god Seth and must set right what she has caused. The more linear, narratively connected structure gave the adventure a momentum and sense of purpose that the looser previous installments sometimes lacked.

The gameplay remained faithful to the proven foundation — acrobatic leaps, puzzles built on levers and mechanisms, exploration and combat. Core Design, however, enriched the mechanics: a more sophisticated item-combining system was added, new moves such as pole climbing and swinging, and the puzzles leaned more on environmental logic than on pure reflex-driven acrobatics. The Egyptian setting moreover provided a strong, unified atmosphere — sand, hieroglyphs, claustrophobic tombs and shadows that could pleasantly unnerve you.

The Last Revelation is often praised as one of the best classic installments precisely thanks to this focus and finely tuned puzzle design. It was also intended as a kind of farewell to the era — its famous ending left Lara's fate open and sparked much discussion among fans. For Core Design it was the pinnacle mastery of the formula they themselves had created.

Today the game holds up as one of the most atmospheric pieces of the classic era — a tight, thoughtful and stylistically unified experience that shows the series in fine form.

**Why play it:** The most thematically tight and, in terms of design, one of the most mature classic Tomb Raiders, a beloved Egyptian odyssey with outstanding puzzles.

playstation__tomb-raider-chronicles.article:
Every era eventually ends, and Tomb Raider Chronicles from 2000 was just such a full stop — the last installment of the classic series built on Core Design's original engine. Following the dramatic conclusion of the previous adventure, Chronicles took the form of a memorial anthology, a look back at Lara Croft's career through four separate stories.

The concept is unconventional: after Lara's disappearance, her friends gather and reminisce about her earlier adventures, which the player gradually experiences. These four episodes take Lara to Rome, to a submarine in the Black Sea, to a haunted Irish island from her childhood and into a modern skyscraper full of high-tech security systems. Each chapter has its own flavor — from adventurous classic through horror tones to a stealthier modern interlude — which gives the game a pleasant variety.

In terms of gameplay, Chronicles builds on the series' proven foundation: jumping navigation, puzzles, exploration and combat. It adds a few new moves and situations, including sneaking past guards and using hardware gadgets in the final episode. The individual stories are shorter and more contained, which gives the game more the character of a collection of short stories than a single grand adventure. After six years, however, the original engine and fixed camera were beginning to show their age, and this was one of the criticisms that accompanied the installment.

Chronicles closed the first chapter of the series on the PlayStation and became the last classically conceived installment before the brand set off in new directions. As an epilogue and tribute to the whole era, it has its charm, especially for players who accompanied Lara from the beginning.

Today Chronicles is more for devoted fans — an anthology that offers a dignified farewell to the classic form of one of gaming's most influential heroines.

**Why play it:** An anthological farewell to Lara Croft's classic era, diverse short stories and a nostalgic full stop to the original series.

playstation__crash-bandicoot-1-3.teaser: The unofficial PS1 mascot; brisk, demanding platformers.
playstation__crash-bandicoot-1-3.detail: The unofficial PS1 mascot (Naughty Dog before the Uncharted era). Brisk, demanding platformers with running „into the screen“ as well as sideways. The third game (Warped) added diverse level styles. In marketing, Crash mocked Mario right outside Nintendo's headquarters.
playstation__crash-bandicoot-1-3.article:
While Sega had Sonic and Nintendo had Mario, the PlayStation lacked a mascot face — until a bumbling marsupial in blue jeans escaped from the laboratory of a certain Doctor Cortex. Crash Bandicoot, the work of Naughty Dog from the years when it still made colorful platformers rather than the cinematic adventures of Uncharted, became the console's unofficial symbol and one of its most memorable heroes.

The trio of games gradually developed a clever idea. The first installment became famous for its unusual perspective — besides classic sideways movement, Crash also ran "into the screen," straight toward the player, often chased by a boulder, creating a tense, almost cinematic feeling of a hounded flight. The gameplay was brisk but, above all, demanding: precise jumps, smashing crates and collecting Wumpa fruit required a feel for timing and a hefty dose of patience.

The second installment refined the controls and level structure, while the third, subtitled Warped, added marked variety — levels set in various historical eras, motorcycle rides, flying and swimming broke up the established rhythm and gave the series a new lease of life. Naughty Dog moreover always bet on strong personality: Crash was an adorable clown without a single line of dialogue, full of grimaces and comic charm, and his world overflowed with color and humor.

One of the boldest marketing campaigns of the era erupted around Crash as well — the commercial in which the mascot mocked Mario right outside Nintendo's headquarters entered the history of the console wars as a symbol of the audacity with which the PlayStation fought for attention.

Today the trio ranks among the most beloved platformers of the PS1 era, and its popularity was confirmed by the modern remake N. Sane Trilogy, which made them accessible to a new generation. The difficulty remained, and so did the charm.

**Why play it:** An iconic and still demanding platforming trilogy, the unofficial PS1 mascot full of charm, humor and precise jumping design.

playstation__spyro-dragon-1-3.teaser: Colorful, smooth 3D platformers; charm and ease.
playstation__spyro-dragon-1-3.detail: Insomniac (before Ratchet & Clank and Spider-Man) created colorful, smooth 3D platformers about a purple dragon in open worlds. Relaxed pacing and excellent controls. The second great platforming icon of the PS1 alongside Crash; got the Reignited trilogy.
playstation__spyro-dragon-1-3.article:
Alongside the rugged marsupial Crash, the PlayStation also needed something warmer — and so a little purple dragon flew in, charming players with his laid-back ease and colorfulness. Spyro the Dragon, the work of Insomniac Games from long before Ratchet & Clank and Spider-Man, became the console's second great platforming icon and still brings a smile today.

Where Crash raced through narrow corridors, Spyro opened up sprawling, airy worlds full of gliding, flying and exploration. The trio of games bet on smooth, intuitive controls — Spyro charged with his horns, breathed fire, glided through the air and collected gems scattered across magical landscapes. The pace was pleasantly relaxed, the design welcoming, and the world simply invited carefree discovery. Therein lay the charm: Spyro was not about frustration, but about the joy of movement and exploring every nook.

Each installment expanded the foundation. The sequels added new abilities, side characters and minigames that varied the passage through worlds, and gradually one of the technically and content-wise most polished platforming series of the era took shape. Insomniac demonstrated a sense of fluidity and visual charm that made Spyro's worlds feel alive and colorful even on the hardware of the first PlayStation.

Alongside Crash, Spyro became a symbol that the PlayStation could also do playful, family-oriented games full of heart. The dragon built a devoted fanbase that never abandoned him — proof of which is the modern remake Reignited Trilogy, which captured the original trio in beautiful graphics and introduced it to new generations.

Today Spyro's games hold up as a textbook example of a relaxed, well-controlled 3D platformer. The charm, colors and calm they exude age only a little.

**Why play it:** A charming and smooth platforming trilogy about a purple dragon, a laid-back counterpart to Crash and one of the most beloved icons of the PS1.

playstation__rayman-2-great-escape.teaser: The transition to 3D handled brilliantly; a beautiful world.
playstation__rayman-2-great-escape.detail: A masterful transition of a 2D series into 3D — a beautiful world, smooth controls, inventive design. One of the best 3D platformers of the era, ranked alongside Mario 64 and Banjo. Ancel later made Beyond Good & Evil.
playstation__rayman-2-great-escape.article:
The transition of a beloved 2D series into three dimensions used to be a graveyard of good intentions around the turn of the millennium — many icons did not survive the leap. Rayman 2: The Great Escape from 1999 is, by contrast, a textbook example of how to do it right, and it still ranks among the best 3D platformers of its era.

Michel Ancel and the Ubisoft team took the armless and legless mascot and placed him in a beautiful, dreamlike three-dimensional world full of fantasy. The result was stunning: smooth and precise controls, inventive level design that constantly offered new ideas, and visually captivating environments that blended colorfulness with a gentle melancholy. Rayman runs, climbs, flies using his helicopter hairstyle and shoots energy orbs, with each ability woven into the game naturally and with a sense of pacing.

The Great Escape excels precisely in its balance. It never overloads the player with frustrating difficulty, yet it never slides into boredom — it constantly alternates action sequences, platforming challenges and calmer exploratory stretches. The atmosphere is meanwhile unique, imbued with a poetry few titles could boast, and the music and art direction complete the feeling of walking through a living, breathing dream.

It is no coincidence that the game is often ranked alongside such greats as Super Mario 64 and Banjo-Kazooie — it belongs to the golden canon of the three-dimensional platforming genre. Michel Ancel later proved his talent again when he created the cult Beyond Good & Evil, thereby taking his place among the most distinctive European game creators.

Today Rayman 2 holds up as a timeless piece of design. Its controls, inventiveness and visual poetry have not aged, and the game remains a joy for anyone who loves a well-crafted adventure.

**Why play it:** A masterfully handled transition to 3D, one of the best platformers of the era with a beautiful world and flawless controls.

playstation__tomba.teaser: A zany platformer-adventure; cult and rare.
playstation__tomba.detail: By Tokuro Fujiwara (creator of Ghosts 'n Goblins). A zany 2.5D platformer with a quest structure (over 100 tasks) and a hunt for devilish pigs. Energetic, colorful and original; rare and cult.
playstation__tomba.article:
There are games that defy all categories — and the pink-haired wild boy Tomba is one of them. This zany creation from 1998 combines platforming action with an extensive quest structure into such an original whole that it still holds cult status today and, among collectors, a reputation as a rare piece.

Behind the game stands Tokuro Fujiwara, creator of the legendary Ghosts 'n Goblins, and his signature can be felt in every detail — from the brisk, finely tuned gameplay to that characteristic blend of difficulty and playfulness. Tomba takes place in a colorful 2.5D world where the player, in the role of a wild little boy, chases devilish pigs that have cursed the land. What sets it apart from ordinary platformers, however, is its elaborate quest system: the game offers over a hundred quests that open up, branch and intertwine, so that instead of simply running left to right, a small open world lies before you to explore.

This combination makes Tomba a surprisingly rich experience. You jump, climb hand over hand, latch onto enemies and catch pigs in bags, with every pig you nab transforming part of the world and unlocking new paths and quests. The energetic, colorful and unrestrained presentation breathes with the joy of creation and fits into no period category — it is a game that does things its own way and delights precisely through its idiosyncrasy.

Commercially, Tomba remained rather outside the mainstream, which over time made it a sought-after and hard-to-find title that collectors and fans of unusual games still pursue today. It is precisely this rarity, together with its undeniable originality, that earned it a devoted, if small, fan community.

Today Tomba is a little treasure for anyone looking for something off the beaten path — proof that even a platformer can be an adventurous expedition full of discovery.

**Why play it:** An original and cult platformer-adventure from the creator of Ghosts 'n Goblins, full of quests, colors and unrestrained creativity.

playstation__ape-escape.teaser: The first game designed for dual-stick (analog sticks); catching monkeys is a joy.
playstation__ape-escape.detail: The first game designed around the DualShock's two analog sticks — you can't play without them (you catch monkeys with a net on the right stick). Inventive use of the new controller, wit and diverse gadgets. Technically pioneering.
playstation__ape-escape.article:
Some games could not exist at all without their controller — and Ape Escape from 1999 is a shining example. This inventive action platformer was, after all, the first game designed directly around the two analog sticks of the DualShock controller, and without them you simply cannot play it. It was a technically pioneering decision that today's players take for granted, but at the time it was a bold step into the unknown.

The principle is brilliantly simple: with the left stick you control the hero's movement, and with the right you catch scattered monkeys using a net and other ingenious gadgets. This two-handed choreography made monkey-catching a surprisingly addictive and satisfying activity — you had to learn to coordinate running and swinging the net, time your approach and outwit the clever evasive maneuvers of your furry targets. Sony's Japan Studio moreover loaded the game with an arsenal of varied gadgets, from a snapping short sword to a telescope or a water cyclone, so that each new toy changed the way you approached your prey.

Beyond its technical novelty, Ape Escape also captivated with its playful humor, colorfulness and unrestrained Japanese imagination. Monkeys with blinking helmets, time travel and a world full of wild ideas gave the game a distinctive charge that meshed wonderfully with the playful gameplay. The variety of environments and situations kept the pace fresh and constantly supplied you with new challenges.

Ape Escape wrote itself into history as proof that new hardware can give birth to entirely new game mechanics, not just prettier pictures. It demonstrated how fundamentally the method of control can transform an experience, and opened a path that many later games followed.

Today Ape Escape is a reminder of an era when people experimented with the controller as enthusiastically as with graphics — and at the same time a still fun, inventive game with infectious energy.

**Why play it:** A technically pioneering game designed around dual-stick controls, with infectious humor and unexpectedly addictive monkey hunting.

playstation__mega-man-x4-x5.teaser: X4 is the peak of 2D, Legends a bold 3D experiment.
playstation__mega-man-x4-x5.detail: X4 is the peak of the 2D X series with beautiful anime animation and a fully playable Zero. Legends is a bold and beloved 3D action/RPG experiment in a voxel world. Different flavors for fans of the blue bomber.
playstation__mega-man-x4-x5.article:
The blue bomber Mega Man has survived many eras, but on the PlayStation he experienced one of his most interesting chapters — and a few bold experiments as well. Capcom brought here both the peak 2D action of the X series and daring forays into the third dimension, thus offering fans a varied palette of flavors.

Mega Man X4 is, for many, the peak of the entire 2D branch of the X series. It offered gorgeous, hand-drawn anime animation, smooth action and, above all, the ability to play through the whole game as Zero — a charismatic swordsman whose combat style differed diametrically from classic shooting and gave the game a new dimension. The brisk pace, finely tuned controls and battles against varied bosses make X4 the essence of why fans grew so fond of the X series: speed, fluidity and a satisfying challenge in every level.

Alongside the action, a bolder face of the brand flourished on the PlayStation as well. The Mega Man Legends series abandoned the established 2D formula and thrust the blue hero into a full-fledged 3D world — an action RPG with exploration, dialogue and an adventurous structure, rendered in a distinctive voxel look. It was a bold experiment that, although it did not catch on commercially as it deserved, built a devoted fanbase that still ranks it among the most beloved and most daring works of the entire lineup.

This dual track captures well what made Mega Man interesting on the PlayStation: on one side perfectly honed classics, on the other the creative courage to seek new paths. Capcom proved here that it could honor its own heritage as well as risk something new.

Today both facets are worth getting to know — X4 as one of the most beautiful 2D action games of the era and Legends as a cult 3D experiment still spoken of with love among fans.

**Why play it:** The peak of the X series' 2D action together with a bold voxel 3D experiment — two faces of the blue bomber for every fan.

playstation__mega-man-legends.article:
When you picture Mega Man, you most likely think of lightning-fast 2D running and jumping with an arm transformed into a cannon. **Mega Man Legends**, however, boldly shattered that image and transplanted the entire brand into full-fledged 3D.

Instead of the classic platformer, Capcom offered an action RPG with a more open world. You play as a young archaeologist-adventurer named Mega Man Volnutt, who explores underground ruins, gathers treasures and ancient technology, and defends the inhabitants against pirate raids. The combat system uses targeting in three-dimensional space, various upgradable weapons and the classic arm cannon, while between the action you visit little towns, chat with the inhabitants and advance the story.

Visually, the game bet on a distinctive, cel-shading-adjacent, cartoonish style that to this day does not feel as dated as many more realistically intended 3D games of the era. The charismatic Bonne family of pirates, led by the unforgettable Tron Bonne, is among the best the series ever gave its characters — Tron even earned her own spin-off.

Legends never reached the sales marks of the big Mega Man installments, and commercially it was more of a cult affair than a hit. All the more ardent, though, is the fanbase the series won for itself. Notorious is the cancellation of the long-awaited third installment, which to this day accompanies this sub-series like a painful memory and a subject of petitions.

Today we look at Mega Man Legends as a bold experiment that showed even a traditional brand can leave the beaten track and find its own, distinctive voice. If you like 3D adventures with lightness, humor and heart, this is a treasure worth digging up.

**Why play it:** For the bold leap of a classic brand into 3D, likeable characters and a cartoonish charm that ages with grace.

playstation__klonoa-door-to-phantomile.teaser: An emotional puzzle-platformer; one of the console's most beautiful stories.
playstation__klonoa-door-to-phantomile.detail: A 2.5D puzzle-platformer where you inflate and hurl enemies. Beneath its adorable surface hides a surprisingly moving story with an unforgettable, sad ending. Technically gorgeous. One of the console's finest experiences; it got a remake.
playstation__klonoa-door-to-phantomile.article:
Sometimes a cute wrapper hides a story that hits you harder than you'd ever expect from a colorful platformer. **Klonoa: Door to Phantomile** is exactly that case — and perhaps one of the most beautiful experiences on the entire original PlayStation.

Mechanically it's a clever 2.5D puzzle-platformer: the characters and levels play out on a plane, but the game world is fully three-dimensional, which allowed Namco to craft gorgeous camera angles and depth of scene. Klonoa's Wind Ring lets you inflate enemies and then use them — fling them at another foe, or bounce off them for a double jump to reach higher. From this simple mechanic grows a surprisingly rich puzzle layer, where you work out whom to grab, when, and where to throw them.

Technically it was one of the most visually pleasing games on the console. The colorful, dreamlike environments of the land of Phantomile feel like a fairy tale you want to keep looking at, and the music completes an atmosphere of gentle, melancholic magic.

And then there's that story. Beneath the adorable surface lies a surprisingly touching tale that builds toward an unforgettable, sad ending — a moment players remember for many years afterward. It was precisely this emotional power that elevated Klonoa from a charming little diversion to a small gem.

That it was no fluke is confirmed by the fact that the game received a remake, bringing it to a new generation. Klonoa remains proof that a platformer doesn't have to be just about reflexes and collecting coins — it can also have a soul.

**Why play it:** For the clever throwing mechanics, dreamlike beauty, and a story whose ending will move you more than you'd ever guess from a platformer.

playstation__oddworld-abe-s-oddysee-exod.teaser: A dark puzzle-platformer with a conscience; wholly original.
playstation__oddworld-abe-s-oddysee-exod.detail: A dark puzzle-platformer with an anti-corporate undertone, where the slave Abe rescues his kind and can possess enemies or command them by voice (GameSpeak — you talk to NPCs using buttons). Atmospheric, funny, and unsettling; the vision of Lorne Lanning.
playstation__oddworld-abe-s-oddysee-exod.article:
Few platformers make you feel guilty for letting a companion die. **Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee** and its swift sequel **Exoddus** do exactly that — and they do it with a dark, satirical charm that had no equal on the console.
