The 3rd Birthday is a title that divided opinions — but few would deny it its boldness and visual machinery. For PSP owners looking for a dark, action-tinged ride with unusual combat mechanics and a strong atmosphere, it is a memorable stop.

**Why play it:** A dark action ride with the legendary Aya Brea and the unique mechanic of jumping into other bodies — a production-ambitious experience for action fans.

psp__silent-hill-origins.article:
Fog-shrouded alleys, a grinding siren, and the feeling that there is always something behind you in that darkness. Silent Hill: Origins brings one of the most famous horror brands into your pocket and proves that psychological terror does not need a big screen to get under your skin.

As a prequel to the legendary first installment, the game follows the story of truck driver Travis Grady, who gets stranded in the cursed town of Silent Hill. The gameplay honors traditional survival horror: you explore oppressive environments, solve logic puzzles, conserve ammunition, and fight for survival against disturbing monsters. This series was never about action as such — the fear stems from atmosphere, sound, and the uncertainty of what lurks around the corner.

The series was made famous by two key things, and Origins preserves them: the terrifying switching between the „normal" and the rusty, bloody „Otherworld," and the unforgettable sound design. Music and ambient sounds are a full-fledged part of the horror in Silent Hill — the crackle of the radio signaling the proximity of an enemy is among the most iconic audio moments in the history of horror games.

Bringing such an atmospheric experience to the PSP was not a self-evident task, and Origins shows that darkness, fog, and dread work even on a small display — perhaps all the more so when you play alone with headphones. The game offers a more compact but full-fledged Silent Hill experience with everything that belongs to it: a desperate sense of loneliness and confinement.

For survival horror fans as well as for those who want to know the roots of the Silent Hill story, this pocket chapter is an excellent choice. It is not a walk in the park — and that is exactly what you want from it.

**Why play it:** A full-fledged Silent Hill in your pocket — atmospheric survival horror with iconic sound and terrifying world-switching, ideal for playing in the dark with headphones.

psp__phantasy-star-portable-2.article:
Take the saga of an online action RPG, finely tuned co-op, and endless loot hunting — and cram it all into a handheld console. Phantasy Star Portable 2 is exactly that: a sprawling sci-fi action-RPG from Sega, built on the proven formula of the Phantasy Star Universe series, designed for playing on the go as well as in a shared party.

The gameplay rests on real-time action combat, where you hack through hordes of enemies using swords, guns, and magical techniques, collect ever-better gear, and gradually build and upgrade your character. This „go on a mission, get loot, upgrade, go on a harder mission" loop is the core of the genre, and Phantasy Star masters it with grace — the choice among various races and combat styles gives room to experiment and find your own playing signature.

But the heart of the experience is co-op. The game aims at shared multiplayer play, where you dive into dungeons with friends, coordinate attacks and healing, and hunt rare items together. It is precisely the social, multiplayer dimension that made Phantasy Star Portable 2 a phenomenon on the PSP, one the community grew fond of for long dozens of hours of joint grinding and character building.

Visually, the game bets on colorful sci-fi environments, snappy attack animations, and a clear interface adapted to handheld play. The scope of content — the number of missions, weapons, enemies, and customization — makes it a title where you can easily spend dozens of hours without coming close to the bottom of its possibilities.

For fans of action RPGs with an emphasis on loot and co-op, Phantasy Star Portable 2 represents one of the most loaded offerings the PSP had in the genre. It is a console-like experience squeezed into the palm of your hand — and that is precisely where its strength lies.

**Why play it:** A sprawling sci-fi action-RPG with addictive loot hunting and strong co-op — dozens of hours of joint character building right in your pocket.

psp__pursuit-force.article:
Leaping while driving from a police car straight onto the hood of a fleeing gangster and taking him down before he even rounds the corner — that is Pursuit Force in a nutshell. This action racing ride from London Studio takes B-movie police chases and pushes them to an absurd, adrenaline-fueled extreme in which physics is merely a vague suggestion.

The gameplay mixes two things that at first glance do not go together: fast arcade driving and shooting. Not only do you chase criminals through the streets, but at full speed you can jump out of your own vehicle, leap between the enemies' moving cars, shoot them down, and literally take over their vehicles. This „stunts-while-driving" mechanic is the absolute heart of the game and gives the chases a verve you will not experience in classic races.

The whole thing is styled as a tribute to over-the-top action films: gangs control the city, you are the elite unit that sets things straight, and every mission escalates into ever wilder stunt scenes. The pace is high, the presentation bombastic, and the game rewards you for boldness and risk — the crazier the maneuver, the better. It is pure, unabashed fun that does not take itself seriously.

On the PSP it was one of those titles that showed the handheld console could handle a really cranked-up, action-driven game with console pacing. The short, intense missions also fit the format of handheld play perfectly, letting you go to war in any free moment.

If you love arcade action without unnecessary fuss and dream of leaping between cars like an action hero, Pursuit Force fulfills that dream. It is a wild, energetic treat that is above all about fun.

**Why play it:** A crazy combination of racing and shooting where you leap between moving cars — adrenaline-fueled arcade action in cinematic style, right in your pocket.

psp__killzone-liberation.article:
When the Killzone brand arrived on the PSP, many expected a miniature copy of the console first-person shooter. Instead, Killzone: Liberation surprised with a bold move — it flipped the entire game into an isometric top-down view and thereby created tactical action that worked far better on a handheld console than uncomfortable FPS controls.

Instead of aiming through a sight, you tackle combat from above: you use cover, tactically maneuver your positions, throw grenades, and advance through war-torn terrain against the ruthless Helghast army. This change of perspective was not just a technical compromise — it turned Liberation into a distinctive tactical shooter where deliberation, movement, and using your surroundings matter, not just the speed of your reflexes.

The game retains the harsh, gloomy aesthetic of the Killzone series — war here is dirty, brutal, and bleak, far from the polished heroism of other shooters. Visually, Liberation was among the best the PSP offered; detailed environments and effects showed that the handheld console could conjure up an impressive war spectacle.

Beyond the campaign, the game also offered co-op and additional content that extended its longevity and made use of the PSP's multiplayer capabilities. Progressing through the missions rewards players for smart play and mastering the tactical battles, so a genuine sense of satisfaction lies behind clearing the harder sections.

Killzone: Liberation is a textbook example of how to cleverly adapt a big brand to a different platform — it does not pretend to be a console installment and instead plays to its own strengths. For PSP owners looking for mature, tactical action with a proper dose of atmosphere, it is one of the best shooting experiences on the console.

**Why play it:** Cleverly conceived tactical action from an isometric view that adapted the Killzone brand to a handheld console perfectly — gloomy, mature, and visually impressive.

psp__star-wars-battlefront-ii.article:
The great battle of Hoth, dogfights above the orbit, clones against separatists — and all of it in the palm of your hand. The pocket version of Star Wars Battlefront II brought sprawling battles from the star saga to the PSP and proved that epic warfare need not remain the privilege of big consoles.

The core of the gameplay is expansive battles where you, as a single soldier in the midst of chaos, capture strategic points, switch between various types of units, and gradually decide the fate of the entire map. Battlefront never aimed for a realistic simulation — it is about the feeling of being part of a huge battle from the films, where fighting rages around you on many fronts at once. This „large-scale" atmosphere is what made the series famous.

The variety is also enticing: you fight on the ground as well as in space, control infantry, vehicles, and iconic fighters, and in certain modes you even take a spin as heroes and villains from the Star Wars universe. The ability to sit in the cockpit of an X-wing or swing a lightsaber as a famous character adds spice and fan service to the battles, keeping you coming back to the game.

For the PSP it was an ambitious conversion that tried to preserve as much of the magic of the big versions as possible — from diverse maps across the saga to multiplayer support, thanks to which you could wage battles together with friends. It was precisely the multiplayer and the replayability of the individual clashes that made the title a great travel companion.

For every Star Wars fan as well as for lovers of action shooters with a team dimension, the pocket Battlefront II is a winning bet. It offers the right feeling of taking part in legendary battles — whenever and wherever you pull the console out of your pocket.

**Why play it:** Epic battles from the Star Wars world on the ground and in space, with playable heroes and multiplayer — large-scale action right in your pocket.

psp__star-wars-battlefront-renegade-squa.article:
What if you could build your Star Wars soldier from the ground up yourself? Star Wars Battlefront: Renegade Squadron took the proven formula of the series' large-scale battles and enriched it with depth that handheld shooters rarely offered back then — extensive character customization.

Instead of fixed soldier classes, you assemble your own unit here: you pick weapons, gear and abilities, tailoring your combat style to suit you. This freedom gives the Battlefront series a new dimension and rewards experimentation — one build works for defending points, another for aggressive incursions, yet another for supporting the team. It's a clever way to add depth to otherwise arcade-style team action.

Otherwise, Renegade Squadron builds on what made Battlefront famous: sprawling battles on the ground and in space, capturing strategic points, piloting vehicles and starfighters, and taking part in a war across iconic galactic locations. Story-wise, the game casts you as a covert commando unit fighting for the Rebellion, which gives the missions their own context and a reason to throw yourself into battle.

Multiplayer was essential for this kind of game — Renegade Squadron aimed for shared multiplayer battles where your hand-assembled unit faces off against others. It was precisely this combination of deep customization and competitive team combat that made the game a long-term companion for many PSP players, one they were happy to return to.

For Star Wars fans who want more than pre-made classes and long to fine-tune their hero exactly to their liking, Renegade Squadron is one of the series' most distinctive handheld offerings. It delivers large-scale action with a personal stamp.

**Why play:** Large-scale Star Wars battles with deep customization of your own soldier and an emphasis on multiplayer — team action you tailor precisely to your taste.

psp__star-wars-force-unleashed.article:
Pulling a Stormtrooper out of a Star Destroyer's window with a single flick of the hand — that's exactly the feeling *The Force Unleashed* wanted to offer, and on PSP it had to pull it off in your pocket. While the big consoles bet on flashy physics systems, the handheld version faced the task of translating the fantasy of an all-powerful Force-wielding apprentice onto hardware with a single analog stick. The result is an action game that strives to make you feel like an unstoppable weapon even on a small screen.

The story casts you as Starkiller, Darth Vader's secret apprentice in the period between *Revenge of the Sith* and *A New Hope*. This narrative gap was extraordinarily important for Star Wars canon at the time — the game was among the officially sanctioned titles of the Expanded Universe and was meant to fill the blank space between the trilogies. The release was conceived as a major multiplatform event, so the PSP version existed alongside variants for the big consoles and for the Nintendo DS, each tackling the same vision by different means.

The core of the fun rests on the combination of the lightsaber and Force abilities. Hurling enemies, lightning and telekinetic manipulation of objects form the foundation of combat, and the game encourages you to experiment and chain attacks into flashy combos. On PSP some of the physics play had to be simplified compared with its console cousins, but the core fantasy — being more powerful than a padawan ought to be — was preserved.

The environments take you through a range of locations across the galaxy, gradually unlocking new abilities and upgrades. The pace is brisk, the combat loud, and visually the game holds up bravely for its era and platform. It's a title that doesn't play to realistic difficulty but to the feeling of power — it wants you to enjoy how easily you scatter a superior force.

For Star Wars fans on the go, it was an enticing offer: a piece of official story that actually counted, plus action that let you behave like a dark apprentice. Even though the handheld version wasn't a technical showcase like the console one, it carried the same ambition and the same appetite to put the Force in the player's hands without compromise.

**Why play:** If you want handheld action in the Star Wars world where you feel like an unstoppable weapon of the Force, and you're curious about the narrative gap between the trilogies.

psp__star-wars-lethal-alliance.article:
A Twi'lek as the lead heroine and a combat droid at her side — *Lethal Alliance* bet on a pairing that isn't among the well-worn archetypes of the Star Wars world, and built an action game tailored to the handheld console around it. Instead of yet another Jedi with a saber, you get the mercenary Rianna Saren and her companion Zeeo, and the game makes this partnership its main mechanic.

The foundation is third-person action with an emphasis on combat, taking cover and using the droid as a partner. Zeeo can hack, reach places you can't, and generally open up paths you couldn't overcome on your own. This duo dynamic is what the title tries to distinguish itself with from an ordinary handheld shooter — you combine your own firepower with a helper and work your way through the levels bit by bit.

The plot sets the game in the era of the original trilogy and revolves around the Death Star plans, which ties it to one of the most iconic motifs of the entire saga. For the PSP it was an effort to offer a brisk, action-packed adventure of a kindly length for travel — nothing that dissolves into dozens of hours, but rather a tightly held experience.

On the small screen the game tackles the eternal problem of handheld action titles: how to manage aiming and movement on a single analog stick. It therefore opts for a design that leans on clear situations and use of the partner instead of tormenting you with demanding manual precision. Visually it sticks to the style of the era and tries to maintain a recognizable Star Wars atmosphere even at a limited scale.

Among the many Star Wars titles of that era, *Lethal Alliance* is interesting mainly for its choice of heroine and its buddy concept. It's not a grand flagship of the series, but honest handheld action that knows what platform it runs on and builds its pace and demands accordingly.

**Why play:** When you want brisk Star Wars action on PSP with an unconventional heroine and a droid partner around whom the whole gameplay revolves.

psp__field-commander.article:
Anyone who fell in love with turn-based war in the "just one more turn and then I'll sleep" style will find their pocket ally in *Field Commander* on PSP. This strategy game brings classic hex — or rather square — warfare to a handheld console and bets on the best the genre has to offer: clear rules, deep decision-making and the satisfying feeling of a well-planned strike.

The principle is purely turn-based. You command units on a map divided into tiles, capture strategic points, accumulate resources and send ground, air and naval forces into battle. Each unit type has its strengths and weaknesses, so it's not just about superior numbers but about deploying the right unit in the right place. Terrain matters, positioning decides, and a rash move can cost you the whole campaign.

For the PSP, turn-based strategy was a natural choice — it requires no fast reflexes or complicated controls, so it fits both short and longer sessions on the go beautifully. You can put a match on hold at any time and come back to it, which makes the title an ideal companion for the tram and for long waits.

Alongside the campaign, which gradually teaches you the mechanics and puts you in ever more demanding situations, there's usually room for battles against another player, where the depth of the system comes fully into play. It's precisely in a direct clash of two tacticians that it becomes clear how important it is to anticipate the opponent's moves and protect your own positions.

At a time when handheld consoles were starving for proper strategy games, *Field Commander* was a welcome addition for anyone who enjoys thoughtful war without the stress of a timer. It's not a flashy spectacle, but honest turn-based fare that rewards patience and clever planning.

**Why play:** For lovers of turn-based strategy who want clear hex warfare in their pocket with the addictive "just one more turn" effect.

psp__field-commander-theatre-of-war-warh.article:
A double serving of turn-based war in one — this pairing places an expansion of classic military strategy alongside a trip into the dark future of Warhammer 40,000. For fans of thoughtful battles on PSP, it meant several reasons to leave the console in sleep mode only rarely.

*Field Commander: Theatre of War* follows on from the turn-based war where you command units on a map divided into tiles, capture key positions and combine ground, air and naval forces. The emphasis lies on terrain, positioning and the right timing of a strike — that is, on everything that makes turn-based strategy so addictive. It's pocket entertainment cut for players who like to savor every move.

*Warhammer 40k: Squad Command* shifts the emphasis elsewhere: into a grim, war-torn future where you command a small squad of Space Marines against superior numbers. This game places greater emphasis on destructible environments and small-unit tactics — instead of large armies, you deal with the fight for cover, firing lines and the survival of a handful of elite soldiers. The atmosphere of desperate confrontation for which the 40K universe is renowned tries to assert itself even on the small screen.

Both games are united by a love of turn-based combat, but they differ in scale and mood. While strategy in the *Field Commander* style is about commanding an entire war machine, *Squad Command* is more intimate, harsher and more about the individual soldiers you don't want to lose. For PSP it was a welcome expansion of a genre that always worked splendidly on handhelds thanks to the ability to put a game on hold at any time.

Together they form an enticing offer for any tactician who wants more than just quick action on the go. Whether you prefer classic war over a map or brutal sci-fi survival combat, you'll find depth here that rewards clever planning.

**Why play:** For fans of turn-based tactics who want both classic war over a map and grim sci-fi combat of a small squad in the world of Warhammer 40K.

psp__r-type-command.article:
What happens when the legendary space shooter R-Type sheds its reflexes and dons turn-based strategy? *R-Type Command* is born (known in Japan as *R-Type Tactics*) — a bold experiment that takes one of the hardest and most revered series of classic shoot-'em-ups and dresses it in the garb of thoughtful tactics. For many players it was an utterly unexpected but fascinating turn.

Instead of dodging clouds of bullets in real time, you now command a fleet of ships on a turn-based map. You deploy units, plan their movement and attacks, and make use of the series' iconic gear — above all the legendary "Force," the detachable module that in the original games served as both shield and weapon at once. Here it becomes a tactical element you have to deploy cleverly.

The title's magic lies in how faithfully it carries R-Type's soul into an entirely different genre. You'll find familiar enemies, biomechanical aesthetics and that distinctive mood the series became famous for. At the same time it forces you to think completely differently than the original games — it's not about reflexes but about anticipation, positioning and managing your forces. Battles can be surprisingly merciless and demand patience.

For PSP it was an ideal platform: turn-based strategy plays comfortably on a handheld and the ability to put a match on hold at any time suits demanding battles. The game rewarded players willing to immerse themselves in its systems and repaid them with a depth that few would expect from a brand renowned for hardcore shooters.

It's precisely this genre bravery that makes *R-Type Command* an interesting piece for a collection. It's proof that even an established series can surprise when it's not afraid to reconsider its own foundations and try something entirely new.

**Why play:** For fans of turn-based strategy and of classic R-Type who want to experience how a legendary shooter works as thoughtful space tactics.

psp__star-trek-tactical-assault.article:
Slowly turning a heavy cruiser, maneuvering into firing range and watching the phasers charge — *Star Trek: Tactical Assault* promises fans one of the most enticing fantasies of the whole universe: commanding a starship in a tactical space battle. On PSP it delivers ship-versus-ship combat where reflexes don't matter but cold calculation and the right timing do.

The core is tactical management of the vessel. You have to watch the shields, distribute power among systems, choose weapons and maintain an advantageous position relative to the enemy. Starships don't turn on a dime — they have mass and inertia, so every maneuver is a decision that may pay off or land you in your opponent's firing line. This slower, more thoughtful form of combat is exactly what Star Trek fans expect from the captain's chair.

The game draws on Star Trek's rich world and builds on recognizable ships and factions, thanks to which every clash carries the mark of something more than generic space combat. Commanding a vessel you know from the series and sending it against traditional enemies has a special magic for connoisseurs of the universe.

For PSP it was a fitting choice of genre — tactical combat requires no frantic controls and suits both short and longer sessions well. The game gradually teaches you its systems and puts you in ever more demanding situations, where having a stronger ship is no longer enough and you also need to use it correctly.

For anyone who wished to sit in the commander's chair and experience a space clash on their own terms, this title represented a welcome offer for travel. It's not a grand space epic, but a focused tactical experience that honors the spirit of the source material.

**Why play:** For fans of Star Trek and tactical space battles who want to command a starship on PSP and win with their head, not their reflexes.

psp__grand-theft-auto-liberty-city-stori.article:
When **Grand Theft Auto: Liberty City Stories** came out in 2005, many doubted that an open world full of cars, gangs and chaos could fit into a handheld console. Rockstar Leeds (then still as Rockstar Leeds in collaboration with Rockstar North) showed that it could, and that it could be done surprisingly well. The game returns to the Liberty City known from GTA III, but three years earlier, in 1998, and casts you as the mobster Toni Cipriani.

Mechanically it's a classic sandbox in the spirit of the series: you drive, shoot, complete missions for various bosses, steal cars and wander among a trio of islands in between. The PSP retained the overwhelming majority of what made the big installments big. Freedom of movement, radio stations with licensed music and that trademark black humor. The controls were adapted to the console's single analog stick, which took getting used to when shooting, but the overall feeling of the open world remained untouched.

The development context is interesting in itself. Liberty City Stories was the first full-fledged, purely "big" GTA installment created primarily for a handheld, and it became proof that portable platforms could carry even the most ambitious brands. The success was so convincing that the game was later ported to the PlayStation 2 as well, and in modern times it even received mobile versions.

Culturally the title played the role of a bridge. For many players it was the chance to have the GTA world literally in their pocket for the first time, anywhere and anytime. In the mid-2000s that was no matter of course, and to a large extent it defined what was expected of the PSP as a "console for the road."

Thanks to the combination of a proven formula, a return to an iconic city and technical performance on a small screen, Liberty City Stories is among the titles that helped establish the PSP as a platform for big games, not just for lightweight experiences.

**Why play:** A full-fledged GTA in your pocket with a return to the iconic Liberty City. If you like open worlds and want them on the go too, this is a classic.

psp__grand-theft-auto-vice-city-stories.article:
Neon, palm trees, pastel suits and synthesizers. **Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories** from 2006 returns you to an artificially constructed version of 1980s Miami, this time in the role of the former soldier Vic Vance. Rockstar Leeds built on the success of the previous handheld installment and pushed handheld GTA a step further still.

In terms of gameplay it's again an open world full of missions, car theft, shootouts and free roaming. Vice City Stories, however, added an element that wasn't common in the series: empire building. The player could take over and manage their own businesses, defend them against the competition and expand their influence across the city. This gave the game an extra layer of strategic decision-making over the purely mission-based structure of its predecessor.

In development terms it was a display of the studio's confidence. Rockstar Leeds once again demonstrated that it could cram an extensive sandbox into the PSP hardware, and with its own plot, its own characters and an atmosphere faithful to the source Vice City. Just like Liberty City Stories, this title later made it to the PlayStation 2, thereby finding its way to players without a handheld as well.

Its cultural value lies in the atmosphere. Eighties Vice City is one of the most striking settings of the whole series, and its return, backed by a period soundtrack and visual style, is among the things fans remember most. Returning to this world on a small screen had its own inimitable magic.

Vice City Stories thus closes out a pair of handheld GTAs that together proved a portable console needn't mean compromise. On the contrary, these were full-fledged experiences with everything that belongs to the brand.

**Why play:** A return to the neon Vice City of the eighties plus running your own criminal empire. Great atmosphere and full-blooded GTA for the road.

psp__patapon.article:
Pata-pata-pata-pon! A few beats on the drums and suddenly you command an army of little one-eyed warriors. **Patapon** from 2007 is one of those games that could only have come about thanks to the courage to experiment, and the PSP gave it a perfect home. It came into being under Sony's wing, with Rolito contributing to the design along with the team around Pyramid, and the result was an utterly distinctive mix of rhythm game and strategy.

The principle is ingeniously simple and at the same time addictive. Using four buttons you enter rhythmic sequences that correspond to commands: march, attack, defend, retreat. When you keep the rhythm, your Patapons start moving like a well-oiled machine, and if you hit a series perfectly, they enter a feverish "fever" mode where they're stronger and faster. Here music and gameplay aren't separate layers but one and the same thing.

Visually Patapon is instantly recognizable. The flat, silhouette style with bold colors and cute yet warlike creatures creates an aesthetic that resembles nothing else. Together with the hypnotic rhythm it builds an atmosphere that draws the player in and won't let go.

In development terms it was one of the flagship experiments with which Sony showed on the PSP that the handheld was a platform for original, authored ideas too, not just for ports of big brands. Patapon became a cult affair and its success led to further installments of the series.

Culturally the title earned a reputation as one of the most imaginative games of its generation. To this day it's cited as an example of how a rhythm game can function as a full-fledged strategy and vice versa. It's quite simply an original worth getting to know.

**Why play:** An utterly original fusion of rhythm and strategy with an unmistakable look. If you want something you won't find elsewhere, this is it.

psp__patapon-2.article:
The drums thunder again, and this time even louder. **Patapon 2** from 2008 followed on from the cult first installment and took everything that worked to expand it into depth. Sony had clearly taken a liking to its idiosyncratic experiment with rhythm strategy, and fans got a sequel that bet on the familiar formula enriched with new possibilities.

The core remains the same and just as addictive. Using rhythmic sequences on four buttons you command your Patapons to march, attack and defend, and keeping a perfect rhythm again pays off in the form of a boosted "fever" state. The sequel, however, adds depth: expanded options for developing units, new types of warriors and more room for how you assemble and upgrade your little army.

The visual and audio identity remained faithful to the original. The silhouette style, bold colors and that hypnotic rhythm which fuses music with gameplay into a single whole. It's precisely this unmistakability that's the reason the series won a devoted audience and why the sequel didn't need to reinvent the wheel — it was enough to thoughtfully expand the good things.

In the context of the PSP it's a further confirmation that Sony saw its handheld as a space for authored, fresh titles too. Patapon 2 showed that the idea from the first installment had enough strength to carry a full-fledged sequel and didn't remain merely a one-off curiosity.

Anyone who took a liking to the first Patapon will find here everything they loved, only in a bigger and more elaborate package. And anyone just entering the series will get one of the most distinctive rhythm experiences on a handheld console.

**Why play:** A bigger and deeper sequel to the cult rhythm strategy. The same addictive drumming, just with more possibilities.

psp__locoroco.article:
Tilt the world to the left, tilt it to the right, and a round yellow creature rolls off toward adventure with a merry sing-song. **LocoRoco** from 2006 is one of the loveliest and most playful games ever to come out on PSP. Here Sony once again bet on an original idea instead of a safe sure thing, and it paid off.

What's ingenious above all are the controls. You don't move the character directly but tilt the whole world, using the shoulder buttons. LocoRoco then rolls along with gravity, gathers more pieces of itself and grows into a bigger blob, which a button can split into tiny individuals and then merge back together. From this simple principle arises a little game that is at once a platformer and a puzzle game — and above all incredibly accessible.

The visuals are pure joy. Richly colored, rounded shapes, cute creatures and a world that looks like a children's book come to life. To this belongs the catchy, sung soundtrack in an invented language that will probably lodge itself in your head for days. The atmosphere is carefree and infectiously cheerful.

In development terms it was another of the flagship authored titles with which Sony built the PSP's identity as a console not just for big licenses but also for imaginative, playful experiments. Alongside Patapon, LocoRoco became a symbol of the more original side of what the handheld offered.

Culturally the game earned a reputation as one of the most likable titles of its time. It's an experience that works across ages and gaming experience, because it builds on the simple joy of movement, colors and music. Few games can conjure a smile so easily.

**Why play:** A delightful, original platformer where you tilt the whole world. Colors, music and pure playfulness — ideal relaxation for everyone.

psp__wipeout-pure.article:
Antigravity machines slicing through neon tracks at breathtaking speed. **Wipeout Pure**, released in 2005, was one of the titles that accompanied the PSP launch and immediately showed what the handheld could do. Sony Liverpool, formerly known as Psygnosis, brought its iconic futuristic racing series to the handheld without compromise.

At its core it is a pure-blooded antigravity race. You pilot hovering craft, brake into tight corners with air brakes, pick up weapons and use boosts to overtake rivals. The pace is murderous and the controls demand precision. The Wipeout series always rested on a sense of speed married to tough, technical handling, and Pure carried that essence faithfully onto the smaller screen.

An inseparable part of it is the visual and audio side. Wipeout is famous for its clean, stylish design and electronic soundtrack that fuses with the polished aesthetic into a single whole. In this regard Pure fully lived up to the brand's reputation and delivered a PSP title that looked and sounded like something from the future.

In development and marketing terms, Wipeout Pure was important as a hardware showcase. It was among the games Sony used to demonstrate that the PSP could handle graphics and pacing previously unexpected from a handheld. In doing so it helped shape the first impression of the entire platform.

For series fans it was a joyful return to a beloved brand, and for newcomers a flashy entry into the world of futuristic racing. Wipeout Pure thus ranks among the titles that defined just how seriously you could play on the PSP.

**Why play:** A stylish, lightning-fast antigravity race with an iconic electronic soundtrack. A demonstration of what the PSP could do right from launch.

psp__ridge-racer.article:
Drift or lose. **Ridge Racer** for the PSP, released in 2004, was one of the console's launch titles and instantly reminded everyone why this Namco brand belongs among the legends of arcade racing. The series, whose roots reach back to the arcades and to the launch of the first PlayStation, felt right at home on the handheld.

The game's philosophy is purely arcade. No worrying about realistic physics; instead, a celebration of the drift. You enter a corner, kick the back end into a stylish slide and hold it, charging nitrous for a rocket boost on the straights. The controls are instantly graspable, but mastering the tracks perfectly takes practice and feel. It is exactly this blend of accessibility and depth that makes Ridge Racer an evergreen.

The PSP version offered a rich package of content that made use of the new hardware's power: plenty of tracks, cars and game modes. For a launch title it was a surprisingly generous offering that gave players reason to return again and again. The speed and smoothness confirmed that the PSP was well suited to racing games.

Culturally, Ridge Racer is firmly tied to the history of the PlayStation brand. The tradition of accompanying Sony console launches with a new entry stretches back to 1994, and the PSP version slotted naturally into that lineage. For many players this title was the first thing they put into their new handheld.

Anyone who enjoys clean arcade racing without needless complications will find exactly that in Ridge Racer. Speed, drift and the joy of driving in their most straightforward form.

**Why play:** Purely arcade racing built on drifting and nitrous. A great PSP launch title that is fun from the very first slide.

psp__gran-turismo.article:
Hundreds of cars, precise handling and an obsession with detail. **Gran Turismo** for the PSP, released in 2009, brought to the handheld a brand that made its name as "the real driving simulator." Polyphony Digital, led by Kazunori Yamauchi, spent a long time tuning the handheld version so it could carry the series' name, and the result was one of the most extensive racing titles on the platform.

Against arcade games like Ridge Racer, Gran Turismo stands at the opposite pole. The emphasis is on the faithful behavior of the cars, on the differences between individual vehicles and on honest handling that rewards feel and practice. The game offered an enormous car roster numbering hundreds of licensed automobiles and a range of real and fictional tracks, making it a genuine feast for car lovers on the go.

In development terms it was a demanding undertaking. Transferring the scope and reputation of Gran Turismo to the PSP was no trivial matter, which is why development took longer than originally expected. When the game finally released, it confirmed that the handheld could handle the ambition of simulator racing with plenty of content.

The series' cultural significance is unmistakable. Gran Turismo ranks among the most successful brands in PlayStation history and for many players represents a gateway into an interest in real cars. The PSP version thus brought a piece of that prestige into your pocket.

For players who prefer honest driving and the collector's joy of building a garage, this game was a wish come true to have Gran Turismo everywhere with them. It is a title for those who approach racing with respect and an appetite to polish every corner.

**Why play:** An extensive driving simulator with hundreds of cars right in your pocket. For fans of cars and honest driving fine-tuning, the ideal choice.

psp__resistance-retribution.article:
When Sony sent its handheld into battle against an alien threat in 2006, few expected it to become one of the most technically accomplished shooters on the small screen. Resistance: Retribution brought the atmosphere of an alternate history, where humanity faces an invasion of ruthless Chimera instead of the Second World War, into the palms of players who wanted a full-fledged action experience on the go.

Unlike its big brothers on the PlayStation 3, the handheld version bet on a third-person view, which proved a clever decision. Aiming and shooting on a console with a single analog stick was easier to manage precisely in this perspective, where the game automatically helped the player with targeting and thus freed up space for tactically minded progress. An arsenal full of inventive weapons that shot around corners or unleashed swarms of projectiles gave the battles with the Chimera a distinctive flavor.

The narrative followed Sergeant James Grayson, a British soldier driven by personal revenge across occupied Europe. The story tied into the events of the series' first entry and expanded the mythology that Insomniac Games had built as an alternative to the war shooters popular at the time. The game itself was developed to order by Bend Studio, the creators of the Syphon Filter series, who had rich experience with action on a handheld.

Culturally, Retribution fit into Sony's effort to prove that a handheld device could offer an experience close to home consoles and not remain merely a simpler spin-off. For PlayStation 3 owners the game also offered a link with the series' second entry, which brought small bonuses into the gameplay and strengthened the sense of one big world.

In a world where handheld shooters often settled for compromises, Retribution stood out with its ambition. It was a work that took its source material seriously and tried to carry as much as possible of the grand action onto a screen that fits in your pocket.

**Why play:** If you want to experience a full-fledged sci-fi shooter on a handheld with cleverly solved controls and the dark atmosphere of an alternate history, Retribution is one of the best candidates.

psp__dissidia-final-fantasy.article:
Imagine the heroes and villains from dozens of Final Fantasy entries suddenly finding themselves in a single arena and starting to duke it out in a battle of gods. This exact fan fantasy became reality when Square Enix, on the occasion of the twentieth anniversary of its legendary series, built a fighting game as a grand celebration of its own history.

Dissidia Final Fantasy was no ordinary brawler. The fights took place in freely explorable three-dimensional arenas where the heroes flew through the air, climbed walls and used the environment for flashy combos. The system rested on two types of attacks: one drained the opponent's bravery, the other only then converted the accumulated advantage into actual damage. From this arose a tense tug-of-war over the upper hand that set the game apart from ordinary fighters and gave it almost strategic depth.

Into the action stepped iconic heroes and unforgettable villains from the series' main entries, from the lonely Warrior of Light to the demonic Sephiroth. The game also offered a rich character-upgrade system with levels, abilities and equipment, so it was closer to an RPG than the genre would suggest. This mix of combat and character building gave players reason to spend dozens of hours with the console.

Development was in the hands of a team connected to the Kingdom Hearts series, which explains the fluid action and sense of grand staging. For fans it was a dream come true, and commercially the title became one of the most successful exclusive works on the handheld, earning itself a sequel and further adaptations.

Dissidia showed that a deep catalog of characters can be not only a nostalgic reminder but also the basis for entirely new gameplay. For anyone who grew up with the Final Fantasy epics, the chance to finally pit their favorites against one another was an irresistible lure.

**Why play:** It is a declaration of love for Final Fantasy in the form of an unexpectedly deep fighter, where heroes and villains from the whole series finally clash.

psp__metal-gear-solid-portable-ops.article:
Whoever says that great espionage epics cannot be squeezed into a pocket never infiltrated an enemy fortress with Metal Gear Solid: Portable Ops. This title was the first attempt to bring a full-fledged entry of the series to a handheld, one that would tie into the main storyline both in narrative and mechanics and push its mythology further.

The key novelty was the recruitment system. Instead of progressing alone, the player could drag off stunned enemies, persuade them to cooperate and gradually build their own squad of specialists. Each soldier brought different abilities, from medics through technicians to scouts, and the player switched between them according to the situation. In this way Portable Ops laid the foundation for the idea of building your own unit, which the series later developed into far greater breadth.

Story-wise the game took place after the events of the classic Metal Gear Solid 3 and followed a young Naked Snake as he faces betrayal from within his own ranks. The narrative, with full dialogue and comic-book-styled interludes, lent the plot an urgency that handheld games of the time often lacked. Stealth remained the heart of the gameplay: sneaking, drawing attention away and silently taking out guards worked even on the smaller screen.

Development proceeded under the baton of a team connected to the brand and under the supervision of Hideo Kojima, the series' creator. It was precisely his involvement that helped keep the handheld entry from being seen as a spin-off, and instead as part of the wider canon, something fans debated at length.

Portable Ops proved that stealth action with storytelling comparable to the big consoles had its place on the small screen. For players who wanted to continue Snake's saga on the go, it was an indispensable piece of the puzzle.

**Why play:** It offers a full-fledged stealth experience of the Metal Gear Solid series in your pocket, plus an innovative soldier recruitment system that foreshadowed the brand's future direction.

psp__syphon-filter-dark-mirror.article:
Secret agent Gabe Logan returns, and this time his shadow war fits right into the palm of your hand. Syphon Filter: Dark Mirror revived the series of espionage action games that originated back on the first PlayStation, and managed to bring it to the handheld in a way that left many home titles silent with shame.

The game masterfully balanced between silent progress and raw action. The player could sneak through the dark, use cover and quietly eliminate guards, or throw themselves into an open firefight with a varied arsenal. The taser remained a famous symbol of the series, a device that could literally roast enemies, along with the dark humor underscoring the otherwise serious espionage theme. An ingenious cover system and contextual controls helped bridge the limitation of a single analog stick.

Technically it was one of the most impressive works on the console. Detailed environments, dynamic lighting and shadows in the dark suggested the creators were pushing the hardware to the limit of its capabilities. A narrative about conspiracy, viruses and a global threat kept players on edge across diverse locations around the world.

Behind the game stood Bend Studio, the fathers of the whole series, who knew their brand well and understood how to adapt it to the handheld format. Dark Mirror met with a warm reception and was among the titles critics cited as proof that the handheld could handle mature action experiences too.

At a time when the stealth genre was only just establishing itself on the big consoles, Dark Mirror brought its full-fledged form into your pocket. For fans of covert operations and thrilling action it was one of the strongest offerings the console could provide.

**Why play:** A top-tier stealth-action experience on a handheld with a dark atmosphere, an inventive arsenal and technical brilliance that impresses to this day.

psp__lumines-ii.article:
Music, light and colors merging into a hypnotic rhythm - that is roughly how you could describe the magic that Lumines brought to the genre of falling blocks. Lumines II expanded this formula and confirmed that the union of a puzzle game with music can be just as addictive as any action hit.

The foundation remained ingeniously simple. Blocks made up of four squares in two colors fall from the top, and the task is to arrange them so that same-colored squares form. Crucial, however, was the so-called timeline, a line of light that swept across the playfield in time with the music and only erased the created shapes as it passed. In this way the game synchronized with its backing track and every clearing of blocks became part of the composition.

The sequel expanded the offering with licensed songs and music videos, so each environment, the so-called skin, had its own visual and audio identity. As the player progressed, the music and graphics changed and a stream of moods arose that resembled an interactive music album more than a classic puzzle game. This symbiosis of image and sound was absolutely defining for the series.

Behind the concept stood Tetsuya Mizuguchi, a creator known for combining gameplay with the synesthesia of sound and image, whose signature marked his other famous titles as well. Lumines was created as one of the flagship games for the handheld's launch and became one of its most characteristic representatives, which the sequel directly followed.

Lumines II showed that a puzzle game need not be merely a dry exercise for the brain but a full-fledged sensory experience. For anyone who wanted to play something on the go that is easy to learn and hard to put down, it was the ideal choice.

**Why play:** A hypnotic union of block stacking with music and light that turns a simple puzzle game into an unforgettable sensory experience.

psp__virtua-tennis-world-tour.article:
A serve, a dash to the net and a winning stroke into the empty court - **Virtua Tennis: World Tour** brought SEGA's famous tennis series into your pocket and proved that on the PSP a brisk and addictive sport can be just as fun as on the big screen. For fans of the white sport it was one of the best reasons to own a handheld at all.

The game principle rests on controls that are instantly comprehensible but gradually deepen. A few buttons suffice for different types of strokes - a flat topspin ball, a slice or a lob - and yet surprising tactical depth is born from that simplicity. The key is correct positioning, reading the opponent's movement and timing your stroke so as to chase your rival off the court and open the path to a winning ball. It is precisely this balance between accessibility and depth that made Virtua Tennis a phenomenon.

The **Virtua Tennis** series was first made famous by SEGA in the arcades, and its reputation rested on lightning-fast gameplay and a perfectly tuned feel. The World Tour version for the PSP was adapted for the portable console from the ground up and made use of its capabilities, including wireless linking of several consoles for player-versus-player duels. On top of basic matches it added a more extensive career mode and a set of minigames that turned training into fun in its own right.

At the time of its arrival, the PSP was a console that promised quality close to home systems right in the palm of your hand, and Virtua Tennis: World Tour was among the titles that fulfilled that promise. Fluid gameplay, fast matches ideal for short sessions and the multiplayer option made it a popular choice both for pick-up matches and for longer career campaigns.

Culturally, the Virtua Tennis series set the bar for what an accessible yet deep tennis game should look like and influenced the whole genre. The portable version expanded its reach and let players take their favorite sport with them anywhere, making it one of the perennially remembered titles of the PSP's early library.

**Why play:** For SEGA's perfectly tuned, instantly fun tennis gameplay, which thanks to the PSP and multiplayer you can enjoy anywhere.

psp__pro-evolution-soccer-2011.article:
There is a football rivalry that transcends the pitch itself, and in the first decade of the new millennium it played out between two brands: FIFA from Electronic Arts and Pro Evolution Soccer from Konami. PES long built a reputation as football for connoisseurs, football played not with the eyes but with the feet and a feel for pace. Pro Evolution Soccer 2011 in its handheld version for the PSP brought this legacy into your palm and promised full matches you could start on the tram, on a park bench or during a break at school.

Mechanically the PES series always rests on the feel of moving the ball. A pass is not just a button press but a matter of timing, weighting and anticipation; defending demands patience and reading the opponent rather than blind rushing in. It was precisely this depth that made PES a title rewarding players willing to invest dozens of hours into understanding the game's rhythm. On the PSP the development team naturally had to trim the demands on the portable hardware, yet it strove to preserve the essence of the brand, including various game modes, leagues and cups that gave players reason to return.

Konami developed the series at its Japanese football studio, and this brand was their flagship outside the Metal Gear series. PES was enormously popular in Europe and Latin America, and in some markets it long outweighed FIFA thanks precisely to its more authentic feel of on-pitch action. The series came out every year like a sports annual, so the number in the title denoted the season for which the game was updated. The mobile versions let fans take their favorite football everywhere with them, which in the era before full-fledged smartphones was no small luxury.

Culturally, PES embodied the idea that a football video game can be both a simulator and a toy at once. For many players, evenings at the neighbors', dorm tournaments and endless league battles were the duels that defined whole years. The rivalry between the PES and FIFA camps was almost religious, and everyone had clear arguments for why their series was the right one. The handheld release carried this passion into a lonelier but all the more accessible format, where you could raise your team anywhere.

The PSP was, at the same time, an exceptionally capable console that could render decent three-dimensional stadiums and animated players, impressive for its day. The widescreen display gave the on-pitch shots a cinematic touch and quality sound added the atmosphere of a packed stadium. Football titles belonged to the console's diligent repertoire, because the sport is ideal for the short, repeatable play sessions that handheld gaming demands, while at the same time offering almost endless replayability.

It is precisely in this union of depth and accessibility that the charm of the handheld PES lies. It offers serious, technical football in a form that requires neither a television nor a dedicated evening, just a moment of time and the urge to test your strength.

**Why play:** If football simulation is about the feel of the ball to you more than about polish, the handheld PES offers the brand's depth anywhere and anytime.

psp__fifa-street-2.article:
Forget offsides, corner kicks and the discipline of coaching whiteboards. FIFA Street 2 took football, stripped it down to a t-shirt, set it on a concrete pitch ringed by a fence and said: now show what you've got. Street football as a genre stands or falls on style, cheek and the ability to humiliate an opponent with a trick that on a professional pitch would be almost indecent.

The gameplay mechanics of the FIFA Street series revolved around flashy tricks and feints. The player chained together dribbles, flicked the ball over opponents, bounced it off walls and built a combo that translated into flashy gestures and so-called game breakers, special finishes. The goal was not just to score a goal but to do it with the maximum dose of style. Smaller pitches, smaller teams and an emphasis on individual skill made every match a fast, acrobatic show where creativity mattered as much as precision.

FIFA Street was developed by Electronic Arts as a lighter, more arcade-like alternative to its main football series. It was part of a wider wave of street sports games that at the time also included basketball and other titles built on the atmosphere of the street, music and visual style. This wave responded to the popularity of street culture and tried to bring its energy into video games. The handheld version on the PSP brought this concept into your palm, where it suited quick, informal sessions.

Culturally, FIFA Street captured the phenomenon of street football, which at the time was strongly present in advertisements and music videos. Football was presented as a form of self-expression, as a dance with the ball, and the game celebrated this aesthetic with colorful environments, urban backdrops and an emphatic soundtrack. Here players did not pretend to be professionals in jerseys but heroes of the street whose only measure was the respect won through flashy play.

The PSP suited this type of game splendidly. Its power was enough for the fluid animations of the tricks and the widescreen display gave the street environment the right atmosphere. Sports titles were among the popular choices on the portable console precisely because they offered fun in short doses without the need for a long campaign. It was enough to switch the console on, start a match and within a few minutes experience a portion of adrenaline and style.

FIFA Street 2 thus represented a counterweight to serious football simulation, a celebration of instant joy and glitter. Where the main series strove for credibility, FIFA Street exaggerated everything and made a virtue of it. Players did not seek realistic results but the flashiest moment, when they literally ridiculed an opponent with a trick and the crowd exploded.

It is precisely this self-confident cheek and emphasis on personal style that make FIFA Street 2 an interesting chapter of football games. Instead of imitating reality it offers a dreamlike, exaggerated version of it, in which the main goal is to look as good as possible. On the PSP this philosophy paired with the idea of playing anytime and anywhere, so flashy street football was always at hand.

**Why play:** When you tire of serious football simulation and just want flashy tricks and style, FIFA Street 2 is an arcade celebration of the street in your pocket.

n64__super-mario-64.teaser: Defined 3D platformers; a revolution in camera and movement controls.
n64__super-mario-64.detail: A launch title that defined 3D platformers and established how the camera and movement in 3D should work. The analog stick (a premiere on the N64 controller) gave Mario nuanced movement. Collecting 120 stars in open worlds became the genre's template. One of the most influential titles in history.
n64__super-mario-64.article:
When Mario first ran out of the doors of Peach's castle into the open courtyard, it was not just the start of one game - it was the moment video games learned to walk in three dimensions. *Super Mario 64* was not merely the launch title of the Nintendo 64; it was the textbook by which the entire industry learned, for the next decade, how to make a 3D platformer at all.

The secret was the new controller. The analog stick, which premiered on the N64, gave Mario something that had not been possible before: nuanced movement. He could sneak, walk, run and turn sharply depending on how far you pushed the stick. Jumps, backflips, the triple jump and the fabled "long jump" turned mere movement into a joy in its own right. Controlling Mario was fun before you even encountered an enemy.

The game's structure became the genre's template. Instead of linear levels you got open worlds hidden in paintings on the castle's walls, and in each of them lurked several stars you earned by completing various challenges. A total of 120 stars gave reason to explore every corner, experiment and return. This "collect and discover" model was adopted by countless games that came after it.

No less important was the camera control. *Super Mario 64* faced a problem no one had properly solved before - how to show 3D space so the player would not get lost in it. The solution with a camera you could rotate yourself was not perfect, but it established the basic language that 3D games speak to this day. Development under the baton of Nintendo EAD and Shigeru Miyamoto himself wrote the rules on the fly.

It is one of the most influential titles in the history of the medium - a game creators still reference today and whose DNA you will find in countless 3D adventures. It proved that the transition into the third dimension need not be a compromise but a leap forward that opens up entirely new possibilities for fun.

**Why play:** Because it is the cornerstone of 3D platformers and one of the most important titles in gaming history - Mario's movement is a joy to this day.

n64__legend-of-zelda-ocarina-of-time.teaser: Often hailed as the greatest game of all time; the benchmark for 3D adventures.
n64__legend-of-zelda-ocarina-of-time.detail: Regularly voted the greatest game of all time (holding one of the highest Metacritic scores ever). A 3D Zelda with its ingenious „Z-targeting" combat, time travel between childhood and adulthood, and unforgettable dungeons (the Water Temple is notorious for its difficulty). Still the yardstick for 3D adventures.
n64__legend-of-zelda-ocarina-of-time.article:
There is one game that critics and players alike have been proposing for decades whenever the question „what is the greatest game of all time?" comes up – and *The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time* has sat at the top of that debate practically since its release. It holds one of the highest Metacritic scores ever, and its influence on the entire action-adventure genre is hard to overstate.

The first great challenge was bringing Zelda into three dimensions, and Nintendo EAD solved it elegantly. The key was the „Z-targeting" system – a way of locking onto enemies that turned the dance of combat into a clear and intuitive affair. You could circle your opponent, keep them in your sights and focus on the rhythm of the fight instead of wrestling with the camera. This idea became the foundation for countless 3D action games that followed.

The story guides you through the life of the hero Link across time – you travel between childhood and adulthood and experience the same kingdom in different eras. This play with time was not merely a narrative backdrop but a mechanic too: some puzzles and paths open up only in one era. Hyrule felt like a living, cohesive world that was a joy to ride through on horseback at dusk.

The dungeons rank among the finest the genre has ever offered. Each one was a self-contained puzzle box with its own theme, item and boss. The infamous Water Temple etched itself into players' memories as a symbol of difficulty and complexity – cursed and admired in equal measure. And the ocarina that gave the game its name brought music into play as a tool: melodies could teleport you, change the weather and shape the world.

To this day *Ocarina of Time* is the yardstick against which 3D adventures are measured. It defined what exploration, combat and puzzle-solving should look like in an open three-dimensional world, and its solutions became so self-evident that we now take them for granted. That is perhaps the greatest proof of its greatness.

**Why play it:** Because it is the canonical benchmark for 3D adventures and one of the highest-rated games in history – an experience that shaped an entire genre.

n64__legend-of-zelda-majora-s-mask.teaser: Darker, experimental; a three-day cycle and melancholy. A cult classic.
n64__legend-of-zelda-majora-s-mask.detail: Created quickly by recycling the Ocarina engine, yet it is radically different: the world ends in three days and you keep resetting time with the ocarina, losing your progress except for the key things. A dark, melancholic atmosphere and an emphasis on the lives of the inhabitants. You transform using masks. Cult and experimental.
n64__legend-of-zelda-majora-s-mask.article:
What if a game told you right at the start that the world would end in three days – and there was nothing you could do about it until you learned to reset time? *The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask* is the darkest, strangest and boldest offshoot of the entire series, a game that took a well-known formula and turned it upside down.

It came together remarkably quickly by recycling the *Ocarina of Time* engine, and yet it turned that economy into a virtue. Instead of copying its famous predecessor, it struck out in a radically different direction. Above the land of Termina hangs a moon with a terrifying face, drawing relentlessly toward the earth, and you have just three days before it strikes. With the ocarina you send time back to the beginning – losing your accumulated progress along the way, except for key items and the knowledge you have gained.

This three-day cycle is ingenious and cruel at once. The people of Termina have their schedules, worries and fates, which play out again and again within those three days. You learn their lives by heart, intervene at just the right moment, and gradually assemble the mosaic of their stories. From this springs a deep melancholy rare in the gaming medium – a sense of transience and futility that lends the game an unexpected emotional weight.

With masks you transform into different beings and gain new abilities, opening up puzzles and a whole new approach to the world. This shifting of identity chimes with the game's overall mood, which is not afraid to be unsettling, dreamlike and at times downright oppressive. This is no fairy-tale adventure – it is a meditation on time, loss and repetition.

Nintendo EAD's work here showed that even within an established series there is room for an experiment that divides players into those who love it and those put off by its strangeness. That is precisely why *Majora's Mask* remains a cult item to this day – bold, different and unforgettable.

**Why play it:** For players who want a darker, experimental Zelda with an ingenious three-day cycle and a melancholic atmosphere unlike anything else in the series.

n64__goldeneye-007.article:
Four friends crammed around a single television, a split screen, one of them shouting „stop looking at my window!" – if you lived through the late nineties with a Nintendo 64, this scene is as inseparable from *GoldenEye 007* as Bond is from a martini. This first-person shooter went down in history not only as a surprisingly brilliant film adaptation, but as a title that rewrote the rules of the genre on consoles.

Until then, the accepted wisdom was that shooters belonged to the PC with its mouse and keyboard. *GoldenEye* proved that an FPS could not only work on a console but be superb. The single-player campaign, based on the Bond film, offered missions with clever structure – it wasn't just about running and gunning, but about completing objectives, using various tools and proceeding tactically. Stealth, sniping and loud action all had their place.

The real legend, though, was the four-player split-screen multiplayer. Arena battles with familiar weapons and characters from the Bond world became synonymous with the gaming parties of an entire generation. It wasn't about online connections or leaderboards – it was about people in one room, face-to-face rivalry and endless „just one more match". This form of shared fun is still praised today as one of the peaks of couch multiplayer.

The game also advanced how shooters handled aiming, hit zones and enemy behaviour. A headshot worked differently from a shot to the leg, enemies reacted more believably, and the overall feel of shooting had real weight. Many of these ideas later became a standard we now take for granted.

As a film licence that far exceeded expectations, *GoldenEye 007* is proof that an adaptation need not be a slapdash cash-in. Instead it became a milestone that entire generations of players remember fondly and that shaped the direction of console shooters for years to come.

**Why play it:** Because it is the iconic console shooter that defined the FPS on the Nintendo 64, and whose four-player split-screen multiplayer is still legendary at gaming parties.

n64__banjo-kazooie.teaser: The pinnacle of the „collect-a-thon" platformer from Rare; witty and rich.
n64__banjo-kazooie.detail: The pinnacle of the „collect-a-thon" platformer: a bear with a bird in his backpack explores rich, witty worlds full of collectibles and puzzles. Charismatic, technically advanced, brimming with humour. Tooie is even bigger and more interconnected. Rare at the height of its powers.
n64__banjo-kazooie.article:
A big-nosed bear whose backpack has room for a cheeky red bird — and suddenly you hold in your hands one of the most endearing duos a platformer ever produced. **Banjo-Kazooie** from **Rare** arrived in 1998 as an answer to **Super Mario 64**, and in many respects it pushed that formula to absolute perfection.

The game ranks among the peaks of the so-called „collect-a-thon" — a genre where your main task is to explore sprawling 3D worlds and gather all manner of curious items in them. Golden puzzle pieces (Jiggies), musical notes, red feathers, eggs for Kazooie's beak-cannon: every corner is stuffed with rewards and secrets that pull you onward. What's ingenious is how Banjo and Kazooie work together — the bird acts as Banjo's weapon, double jump, gliding flight and running turbo, so every new ability changes the way you perceive the world.

Rare was at the height of its powers at the time, and you feel that juice in every detail. Worlds like the marshy **Bubblegloop Swamp** or the frozen **Freezeezy Peak** have their own personality, **Grant Kirkhope's** music shifts dynamically depending on where you step, and the whole game overflows with British humour — the chatty witch Gruntilda speaks in rhyming verse and the characters comment on events with infectious cheek.

Technically it was one of the prettiest titles on the Nintendo 64; colourful, smooth and full of animation gags that made the console shine. And the characters' charisma wasn't merely cosmetic — Banjo and Kazooie quickly became one of the brand's iconic faces and later even earned a guest spot in the fighting game **Super Smash Bros. Ultimate**, which speaks clearly to their cult status.

The sequel **Banjo-Tooie** is even larger and more cleverly interconnected, but it's this first outing that has that unforgettable spark of discovery, where everything is new and every world surprises. If you want to understand why people remember the era of 3D platformers with such love, start here.

**Why play it:** A textbook collect-a-thon full of humour, inventive worlds and an unforgettable pair of heroes — Rare at its very best.

n64__banjo-tooie.article:
When you have one of the best platformers of your generation in your hands, how do you build a sequel? At **Rare** they chose the answer „more, bigger, more interconnected" — and **Banjo-Tooie** is exactly that. The bear Banjo and the bird Kazooie return in an adventure that takes everything good from the first game and stretches it to epic proportions.

The biggest change from the original **Banjo-Kazooie** is the very construction of the world. Whereas the first part offered neatly separated levels, here the individual worlds are huge, linked to one another by tunnels and passages, so you often have to carry an item or ability from one world into another. This shifts the game closer to an open adventure with an emphasis on puzzles spanning the entire map.

The duo have learned a host of new tricks — besides an expanded arsenal of abilities, Banjo and Kazooie can split up and be played separately, which opens up entirely new ways of solving obstacles. There are also more elaborate battles and, in some sections, even first-person shooting, giving the game a more grown-up, action-oriented tone than its predecessor.

Rare kept its trademark humour — chatty characters, self-deprecating quips and quirky ideas are everywhere, backed once more by superb music that breathes the distinctive atmosphere of each place. Visually it is one of the more ambitious Nintendo 64 titles, wringing everything it could out of the console.

That enormous scale is at once its greatest asset and its biggest demand on the player — anyone who prefers focused, compact levels can occasionally get lost in the intricate worlds. But anyone who loves the feeling of discovery and interconnected puzzles will find an exceptionally rich experience here, one that crowns the era of 3D collect-a-thons on Nintendo.

**Why play it:** A grand, interconnected sequel to a cult platformer — more worlds, more abilities and humour just as infectious as the first game's.

n64__mario-kart-64.teaser: A multiplayer classic; the battle mode is a party hit.
n64__mario-kart-64.detail: It brought kart racing into 3D and to four players on one screen. The battle mode (the Block Fort arena) became a party legend. It introduced iconic tracks (Rainbow Road). One of the most-played multiplayer games of the era.
n64__mario-kart-64.article:
Four friends, one screen split into quarters and a final round in the **Block Fort** arena — if you grew up in the nineties, you probably know exactly what's being talked about. **Mario Kart 64** from 1997 brought crazy kart racing into three dimensions and became one of the definitive reasons to buy a Nintendo 64.

Against the sixteen-bit original, the game from **Nintendo EAD** made a fundamental leap: the tracks were now genuinely three-dimensional, full of hills, drops, bridges and shortcuts. The classic driving formula with thrown shells, banana peels and the dreaded blue shell remained, but the new dimension added depth and the chance to drift through corners for dear life. And then there's **Rainbow Road** — a rainbow track set in space that became one of the most iconic racetracks in video game history.

The true heart of the game, though, is the multiplayer. The ability to play with four people on a single screen made it a party legend. The battle mode, where you chase each other with balloons in arenas like the aforementioned Block Fort, is to this day among the most fondly remembered multiplayer experiences of its time — the shouting, the betrayal of your best friend just before the finish and the instant rematches became a ritual.

The game also introduced elements the series carries to this day: the characters' distinctive voices, a set of proven items and the notion of tracks as small thematic experiences. The controls were nimble, accessible to newcomers, yet with enough depth for those who wanted to polish the ideal racing line and shortcuts.

Mario Kart 64 is among the best-selling and most-played titles of the whole console and did much to establish „mario kart" as a concept in its own right. Many still claim that this very instalment has the best atmosphere for local battle — no online, no excuses, just you and three enraged fellow players in one room.

**Why play it:** The founder of 3D kart racing and the eternal king of party multiplayer — Rainbow Road and Block Fort are immortal.

n64__star-fox-64.teaser: A rail shooter with the Rumble Pak; „Do a barrel roll!"
n64__star-fox-64.detail: A rail shooter with the debut of the Rumble Pak (vibration), charismatic characters and branching paths based on your performance. „Do a barrel roll!" comes from here. Zippy and still fun.
n64__star-fox-64.article:
„Do a barrel roll!" A single line known even to players who never once launched Star Fox — and it comes from right here. **Star Fox 64** from 1997 (released in Europe as **Lylat Wars**) is a zippy cosmic rail shooter in which you pilot the Arwing fighter of fox captain Fox McCloud's team and shoot your way through space battles.

The game from **Nintendo EAD** guides you along a predetermined path most of the time, but it gives you the freedom to dodge, weave and pull off acrobatic manoeuvres — including the famous barrel roll to the side, which deflects enemy fire. The great feel of the controls is complemented by the tension of boss battles and hectic firefights, where every downed ship is another point.

The cleverest idea is the branching progression. Depending on how well you do in a mission — who you save, which objectives you complete — different paths through the galaxy open up, so seeing everything requires playing through repeatedly along various routes. This gives it surprising replay value for a fairly short campaign.

Star Fox 64 also went down in history as the title that introduced the **Rumble Pak** — a controller accessory that added vibrations reacting to hits and impacts. It was one of the first widely adopted examples of haptic feedback in console games, something that is now an absolute given for every gamepad.

The characters and their constant chatter during flight are unforgettable too — teammates Falco, Peppy and Slippy give you advice, beg for help and comment on events, lending the battles a distinctive charge and humour. It was Peppy's call to barrel roll that became one of the most quoted video game lines of all.

**Why play it:** A still-fun rail shooter with the debut of the Rumble Pak, branching paths and a famous line the whole gaming world knows.

n64__paper-mario.teaser: A charming paper RPG; wit and style.
n64__paper-mario.detail: The successor to Super Mario RPG with a charming paper 2D-in-3D style, witty writing and clever timing-based combat. Charm at every turn. The start of a beloved series (its peak being the later Thousand-Year Door).
n64__paper-mario.article:
What if the whole world were cut out of paper? **Paper Mario** from 2001 took this playful idea and built on it one of the most charming RPGs on the Nintendo 64 — a game where the characters are as flat as cut-out figures, but the story and humour have a depth that keeps you glued to the screen.

Studio **Intelligent Systems** built on the spirit of **Super Mario RPG** and gave it its own artistic style: two-dimensional paper characters move through beautifully lit three-dimensional environments, so the whole world feels like a moving storybook or a children's puppet theatre. It's a visual that hasn't aged — it has its own, instantly recognisable charm.

The battles are turn-based, but don't be fooled: this isn't passive command entry. The key is the so-called action command — the correct timing of a button press during an attack or defence, which boosts damage or softens hits. This makes the battles active and demands attention, rather than degenerating into mindless button-mashing.

The real draw, though, is the writing. Paper Mario brims with wit, adorable characters and self-deprecating moments — even ordinary enemies and side characters have personality and lines that will make you laugh. The companions who join Mario each bring their own abilities, usable both in combat and in solving puzzles out in the world.

Paper Mario kicked off a beloved series whose peak, for many, is the later **Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door** on the GameCube. This first instalment, though, remains a superb and accessible entry point into the JRPG genre — light enough for newcomers, clever and funny enough to be enjoyed even by seasoned players.

**Why play it:** A charming paper RPG with clever turn-based combat and infectious humour — an enchanting start to one of Nintendo's most beloved series.

n64__f-zero-x.teaser: 30 ships, 60 fps, dizzying speed; a pure adrenaline ride.
n64__f-zero-x.detail: 30 ships on the track at an incredible 60 fps — Nintendo sacrificed graphical adornment for perfect smoothness and a sense of dizzying speed. No items, just pure driving and reflexes. Adrenaline for lovers of speed.
n64__f-zero-x.article:
