Devil's Crush built up a cult status and saw spiritual successors and ports, thanks to which its reputation survived decades. For the PC Engine it was proof that even a seemingly simple concept can, with brilliant execution, exceed all expectations.

**Why play:** Perhaps the best video game pinball ever — addictive, atmospheric and full of hidden objectives and bosses, one that draws in even opponents of the genre.

pc-engine__air-zonk.article:
Picture Bonk, the caveman prehistoric rascal from the legendary Bonk's Adventure series, trading the whack of his club for a futuristic blaster and setting off into a color-soaked future. That is exactly what **Air Zonk** is — a cyberpunk, cartoon spin-off of Hudson's mascot character that turned a platformer into a brisk shooter with horizontal scrolling.

On the PC Engine, which always prided itself on a rich palette and fast sprite processing, Air Zonk feels like a celebration of everything this console did best. The backgrounds glow with neon colors, the enemies are adorably wacky, and the whole thing breathes a downright playful, not-entirely-serious tone that set the **cute-em-up** subgenre apart from the gloomier cosmic battles of the competition.

In gameplay terms Air Zonk rests on the classic formula of the shmup genre: you fly from right to left, collect upgrades, dodge streams of shots and try to reach the sector boss. What sets the game apart is the buddy system and the charged shot — by holding the button you pump up a stronger shot, so you have to balance between aggressiveness and caution. The pace is fast, the controls are snappy, and each level adds a new visual idea.

For players who know Bonk's platformers, Air Zonk is a pleasant surprise — it shows how flexible Hudson's license could be and how cleverly a recognizable character could be transplanted into a completely different genre. For shooter fans, meanwhile, it is one of those titles that PC Engine connoisseurs mention with love, because it combines accessibility with visual charm.

If gloomy space epics have worn you out and you want a shmup that knows how to smile, Air Zonk is the ideal ticket. It's brisk, funny and exactly as colorful as a retro shooter should be.

**Why play:** A colorful, funny cute-em-up that takes Hudson's mascot and turns him into one of the most characterful shooters on the PC Engine.

pc-engine__neutopia-i-and-ii.teaser: Zelda clones, but very good ones.
pc-engine__neutopia-i-and-ii.detail: Zelda clones, but very well done: top-down exploration, dungeons and puzzles. If you've finished the Zeldas and want more of the same, this is a good choice.
pc-engine__neutopia-i-and-ii.article:
When a Japanese studio watches the success of The Legend of Zelda and says to itself „we can do this too", a pale copy usually comes out of it. **Neutopia** is the exception — and its sequel improves on it even further. Here Hudson created a pair of action adventures that, while they don't deny their inspiration, do it with such care that they deserve their own place in the sun.

Neutopia from 1989 takes over the proven skeleton: a top-down view, an open world divided into regions, hidden dungeons full of puzzles, enemies and treasures. The hero Jazeta fights his way across the landscape, collecting new equipment and gradually opening up the way to further areas. It's a **Zelda clone, but a very well-done one** — the map design is legible, the combat satisfying, and the puzzles exactly tricky enough to make you think, but not frustrate you.

The sequel **Neutopia II** from 1991 takes everything that worked and adds more content, more elaborate dungeons and an overall more polished presentation. The game draws on the colorful palette of the PC Engine and on how fluidly the console can render a top-down world. If you finished the first one and wanted to continue, the second is exactly that more of the same, only better.

Culturally the Neutopias are interesting precisely because they came about at a time when consoles were building their identity and every manufacturer needed a strong action adventure in its library. Here Hudson delivered a dignified alternative for PC Engine owners who didn't have access to Nintendo's exclusives, and today they rank among the titles that collectors and retro fans mention as hidden gems of the platform.

It's not a revolution of the genre, and it doesn't try to be one. Neutopia I & II are solid, honest craftsmanship — adventures that honor their model while offering dozens of hours of exploration. If you like classic top-down adventures and want more than the original Zelda offered, a double portion awaits you here.

**Why play:** If you've finished the Zeldas and want more of the same in an honest execution, the Neutopia pair offers dungeons, puzzles and exploration without empty filler.

pc-engine__military-madness.article:
A hexagonal grid, two armies and a planet where war is waged for survival — **Military Madness**, known in Japan as **Nectaris**, is proof that turn-based strategy doesn't have to be dry to be smart. On a console that most people associate with fast shooters and platformers, it feels like a surprisingly deep brain workout.

The story sets the conflict on the Moon, where an Earth alliance stands against the hostile Guni faction. But the plot here is more of a backdrop — the core is pure tactics. Across hexagonal maps you move units from infantry through tanks to aerial machines, using the terrain for cover and above all minding **zone support**: a unit surrounded by allies fights markedly stronger. This mechanic turns every battle into a small spatial puzzle.

What sets Military Madness apart from more cumbersome strategies is the elegance of its rules. It doesn't overwhelm you with hundreds of statistics or economy management — instead you mine factories for reinforcements and focus on maneuvering and anticipating your opponent's moves. It's accessible on the first playthrough, but deep enough that even after dozens of maps you'll be discovering new tricks.

For the PC Engine it was one of the few seriously intended strategy titles, and it built its reputation precisely for that reason. The game saw ports and remakes in various forms across generations, which testifies to the timelessness of its design — a good tactical system simply doesn't age as fast as graphics.

If you enjoy thinking your moves out in advance and searching for the one right sequence that crushes your opponent with minimal losses, Military Madness will hook you. It's calm, focused fun for those who give priority to the head over reflexes.

**Why play:** An elegant hexagonal turn-based strategy where position and the mutual support of units decide — smart strategy that hasn't aged.

pc-engine__dungeon-explorer.teaser: Action RPG for up to five players; early co-op.
pc-engine__dungeon-explorer.detail: An action RPG for up to five players at once (with a multitap) — an early cooperative hack & slash. You choose from classes and fight your way through dungeons. Old-school social fun; chaos in the party.
pc-engine__dungeon-explorer.article:
Sitting down at a single console as a foursome, plugging in the multitap and fighting your way together through hordes of monsters — in 1989 that sounded almost futuristic. **Dungeon Explorer** by Atlus and Hudson could do it, though, and even **for up to five players at once**, which placed it among the pioneers of console cooperative gaming.

The principle is beautifully simple and all the more addictive for it: you choose from several classes — a warrior, a wizard, an elf and others — each with its own abilities, and set off into underground labyrinths full of monsters, treasures and bosses. The game runs in real time, so it's a pure **hack & slash** where you bash, cast and collect whatever you can. Solo it's a decent action romp, but the real magic gets going only in a group.

It is precisely the multiplayer that makes Dungeon Explorer an old-school social experience. Five people on the screen means utter visual chaos, squabbles over potions, an accidentally taken hit from a friend, and a collective roar when a giant boss falls. It's the kind of fun you once went to a neighbor's with a whole gang for — cooperation and competition in one.

In the context of the era it was an important title, because it showed that a console didn't have to be just for one or two players. The PC Engine's multitap found here one of its best uses, and Dungeon Explorer became a kind of flagship of shared adventure on this platform, long before online co-op became a given.

Today it is a title best savored exactly the way it came about — with friends crammed around a single screen. Mechanically it may not be the deepest action RPG of its era, but in terms of party fun it has little competition from that time.

**Why play:** An early cooperative hack & slash for up to five players — chaotic, noisy and unforgettable party fun.

pc-engine__parasol-stars.article:
The bubble you fired in Bubble Bobble is gone — and an umbrella has replaced it. **Parasol Stars: The Story of Bubble Bobble III** closes out Taito's famous trilogy and sends the dragons Bubby and Bobby back into human form as the boys Bub and Bob, armed with a parasol they use to whack enemies, deflect projectiles and collect bonuses.

The umbrella mechanic is surprisingly rich. You can scoop up enemies with it as well as the elements — water, fire, lightning — and then hurl them at other opponents, creating flashy chain eliminations. Each screen is a self-contained room that you clear of all enemies in order to advance, which keeps the proven single-screen design that made the whole series famous.

Visually Parasol Stars is exactly the adorable, colorful game that made people fall in love with the PC Engine. Chubby little characters, exultant colors and catchy music create the atmosphere of a merry fairy tale, beneath whose surface, however, hides a surprisingly addictive arcade challenge — especially when you go after hidden bonuses and a high score.

As a cooperative game for two it blossoms the very most. Clearing screens together, competing for bonuses and coordinating at the tougher bosses make it an ideal title for two players who like accessible but not trivial action. It's that classic „one more screen" fun where you easily lose track of time.

For fans of Bubble Bobble and Rainbow Islands, Parasol Stars is a must, because it carries this series' hallmark through to playful perfection. And even without knowledge of the predecessors, it is one of the loveliest platformers you'll find on the PC Engine.

**Why play:** An adorable, addictive conclusion to the Bubble Bobble trilogy with an inventive umbrella mechanic and superb two-player co-op.

pc-engine__bomberman-93-94.article:
Few gaming concepts are as clean and perfect as Bomberman: a maze, bombs, and the last one standing wins. **Bomberman '93** and its successor **Bomberman '94** honed this formula on the PC Engine into one of its finest forms and defined what it means to be a truly great party game.

Just about everyone knows the basics: you move around a grid-based arena, plant bombs, blow up walls and opponents, and collect power-ups that extend blast range, increase your bomb count, or speed up your movement. The magic lies in the simplicity of the rules and the depth of the tactics — every match is a mix of foresight, trap-setting, and downright devious timing.

The key draw is **multiplayer**. With a multitap, a whole crew gathers around a single screen and pure chaos erupts, full of betrayals, bursts of laughter, and screaming when your own bomb corners you. Bomberman '94 also introduces the ridable Louie creatures (Rooey in Japan), which you ride around the arena to gain an edge — a small touch that broadens the variety of matches even further.

Beyond the battle arena, both games also offer a solid single-player campaign packed with mazes and bosses, so you won't be bored on your own either. Still, everyone knows that Bomberman's heart beats in multiplayer — it's one of the defining titles of the „party game“ genre long before that term became fashionable.

The series continued across every platform imaginable and became a Hudson icon, but the PC Engine versions are among those fans remember most fondly. If you're looking for a game that reliably fires up any gathering, this is exactly it.

**Why play:** The essence of party gaming — simple rules, endless tactics, and multiplayer that will shatter friendships and bring the group closer all at once.

pc-engine__cotton-fantastic-night-dreams.detail: A charming „cute-em-up“ about a little witch on a broomstick, with RPG elements (experience, level up). Stylish, colorful and playable; a cult classic of the genre that has received modern remasters.
pc-engine__cotton-fantastic-night-dreams.article:
A little witch on a broomstick, obsessed with sweets, soars through a magical landscape blasting spells all around her — **Cotton: Fantastic Night Dreams** is exactly the kind of game that gave rise to the term **cute-em-up**. In its 1993 CD version for the PC Engine, it dazzles with everything this powerful console could do.

Beneath the adorable exterior, however, hides a surprisingly thoughtful shooter. Cotton isn't just any shmup — it blends action with **RPG elements**, so you collect experience for defeated enemies and your witch grows stronger level by level. This progression gives the game a pleasant sense of momentum and sets Cotton apart from purely arcade rivals, where power is measured only by the power-ups you collect.

Visually and sonically, the CD version is a feast. Colorful, detailed backgrounds, striking bosses, and quality music and voice acting made possible by the CD medium create a stylish, fairy-tale world. This presentation is one of the reasons the game earned its cult status — it feels like an interactive anime from the early nineties.

Cotton gradually grew into an entire series and became one of the best-known faces of its subgenre. Its lasting popularity is proven by modern remasters and collections that have brought this classic to a new generation of players who never held the original hardware.

For shooter enthusiasts, Cotton is a mandatory stop — it combines accessible charm with enough depth to keep you entertained even after many playthroughs. And for anyone who thinks shmups have to be gloomy space battles, it's a welcome proof to the contrary.

**Why play:** A stylish, colorful cute-em-up with RPG progression and gorgeous CD presentation — a cult classic of the genre that still delivers.

pc-engine__dragon-spirit.article:
Instead of a spaceship, you pilot a dragon. **Dragon Spirit**, originally an arcade hit from Namco, transplants the vertical shooter into a fantasy world where instead of lasers you breathe fire and instead of soaring above planets you glide over lush jungles, deserts, and caves full of prehistoric monsters.

Mechanically it's a classic vertically scrolling shmup with one clever twist: it distinguishes between **aerial and ground** targets. Your fiery breath mows down flying enemies, while your dropping bombs destroy whatever crawls on the ground. This dual-layer mechanic forces the player to constantly switch focus and makes the game a slightly more tactical experience than the simpler shooters of the era offered.

You gain upgrades by collecting bonuses that grow extra heads on your dragon and multiply its firepower — the sight of a three-headed beast spewing beams of fire is one of the genre's iconic moments. The game doesn't skimp on difficulty, though; it's an honest old-school challenge where every advance is earned through diligence and memorizing enemy waves.

Namco was one of the most influential arcade studios of the eighties, and Dragon Spirit is a good example of their ability to take an established genre and give it a fresh theme. Its fantasy setting stood out in a sea of sci-fi shooters, and the game won a devoted audience that appreciated both the atmosphere and the uncompromising gameplay.

The PC Engine conversion brought this arcade experience into living rooms and remains one of the titles shmup fans seek out on the platform to this day. If you want a shooter with claws, scales, and fiery breath, Dragon Spirit is an obvious choice.

**Why play:** A fantasy vertical shooter where you pilot a fire-breathing dragon — with a tactical distinction between aerial and ground targets and an honest arcade challenge.

pc-engine__legendary-axe.article:
Some games etch themselves into memory with their very first impression, and **The Legendary Axe** is one of them — it was one of the titles that in the early days of the TurboGrafx showed this console could handle serious action. It's a rugged, muscular platformer in which the barbarian Gogan battles through a primeval wilderness armed only with his trusty axe.

Mechanically it's an action platformer where the timing of your strikes and cautious progress matter. The axe is your only tool of survival, and the game introduces a clever **charged-power** system — if you hold off attacking for a moment, a gauge fills and your next blow becomes significantly more destructive. This turns every fight into a small decision between careful waiting and quick aggression.

The difficulty here is honestly old-school: enemies attack from all sides, platforms demand precision, and every mistake hurts. Yet the game never feels unfair — progress is about learning the level layouts and about patience. This finely tuned difficulty, along with the dark, prehistoric atmosphere, earned it a reputation as one of the better action platformers of its era.

Visually, The Legendary Axe demonstrated what the PC Engine could do — detailed sprites, smooth movement, and elaborate backgrounds that rivaled even more powerful machines at the time. For many TurboGrafx owners it was one of the reasons they bought the console in the first place, and as such it's regarded today among the platform's important early titles.

If you like raw, challenge-packed platformers where mastering the mechanics is prized and every advance is earned, The Legendary Axe will delight you. It's a classic that flexes its muscles not just on its protagonist, but in its design too.

**Why play:** A raw, superbly tuned action platformer with an inventive charged-axe system — one of the platform's defining early titles.

pc-engine__ninja-spirit.article:
Moonlight, falling cherry blossoms, and a lone ninja with a katana — **Ninja Spirit** from studio Irem is an atmospheric action platformer that takes Japanese samurai romanticism and turns it into ruthless, stylish action. On the PC Engine, this arcade classic became one of the titles fans remember with reverence.

The hero Tsukikage fights through the levels armed with a whole arsenal of ninja tools — a katana, shuriken, kusarigama, and bombs, which you freely switch between depending on the situation. The action is fast and both vertical and horizontal, full of jumps, dodges, and slashing enemies from every direction. The controls are responsive and satisfying, which is absolutely essential for this type of game.

The most famous gimmick is the **shadow doubles** mechanic: at full equipment, two ghostly copies accompany you, mirroring your movements and attacks and tripling your firepower. It's not only flashy but strategically important — keeping the doubles alive means surviving tougher passages where enemies swarm in droves.

Irem was a master of uncompromising arcade design (recall R-Type), and Ninja Spirit bears the same signature — a beautiful but merciless challenge where every level must be conquered through diligence and knowledge. The atmosphere of feudal Japan, radiating from the backgrounds and music, gives the whole a distinction that elevates the game above ordinary hack-and-slash.

For lovers of demanding action platformers and ninja themes, Ninja Spirit is a small treasure. It combines stylish presentation with polished gameplay and belongs among the titles that prove why the PC Engine built such a strong reputation among connoisseurs.

**Why play:** Stylish, demanding ninja action from Irem with a shadow-doubles gimmick and a feudal Japan atmosphere that every fan of arcade platformers will love.

pc-engine__chew-man-fu.article:
Sometimes a simple idea taken to perfection is all it takes to turn a game into a little treasure. **Chew Man Fu** is exactly such a case — a wackily named puzzle-action game for the PC Engine where you zip around an arena with colored balls, trying to line them up so that three of the same color form a combination that clears the field. Beneath that adorable, slightly wacky shell hides a surprisingly addictive arcade puzzle.

The core mechanic is brilliantly simple: by kicking balls and bouncing them off the walls, you maneuver them around the screen and try to arrange fours of the same color. The ball picks up speed and ricochets, so you have to think ahead, calculate trajectories, and simultaneously watch the enemies who move around the arena complicating your plans. The game thus balances on the edge between tactical planning and quick reflexes — and it's exactly this mix that sets it apart from static puzzlers like Tetris.

Visually it's the typically colorful, clean presentation the PC Engine handled with ease. The screens are clear, the animations brisk, and the whole experience feels friendly, but as the difficulty rises it starts to push hard. A big asset is the **cooperative and competitive two-player mode** — the battle over who can clear the arena first, or solving the puzzles together, is among the most fun the title has to offer.

Chew Man Fu is a game that doesn't try to be epic or story-driven. It's pure arcade joy of play, ideal for short sessions as well as longer evenings with a friend on a single controller. It's this immediacy that ranks it among the small but honestly crafted pieces of the PC Engine library worth rediscovering.

Anyone who likes puzzle games with an action edge and is looking for something less well-worn than the big hits will find a pleasant surprise here. It's a title you'll learn quickly but struggle to put down.

**Why play:** An addictive blend of puzzle and arcade action that excels above all in fun for two players on one screen.

pc-engine__magical-chase.teaser: Notoriously rare and expensive shmup; beautiful.
pc-engine__magical-chase.detail: Notorious for its price — it shipped in a minuscule run and a complete copy is among the most expensive games ever (thousands of dollars). A beautiful, playable horizontal shmup with a cute aesthetic. Emulation is the only sensible way to get to know it.
pc-engine__magical-chase.article:
There are games that are legendary for their quality, and then those that became famous mainly for their price tag — **Magical Chase** curiously belongs to both categories at once. This horizontal shmup from 1991 by studio **Quest** (published by Palsoft) is today one of the most expensive and rarest games ever, with a complete copy in its original packaging selling for thousands of dollars. Its notoriety thus often outpaces the game itself.

And that's a shame, because beneath the collector's-relic label hides a truly beautiful and playable little gem. Magical Chase leans on a cute, fairy-tale aesthetic — you play as a little witch flying on a broomstick — and combines it with a smooth, pleasantly manageable shooter. Visually it's a feast for the eyes: colorful backgrounds, detailed sprites, and a soft, almost hand-drawn touch that sets the game apart from the harsh sci-fi shmups of the era.

The gameplay system is built around star companions that orbit your character and can be positioned as both defensive and offensive aid — you can use them to absorb enemy fire or send them out to attack. This mechanic gives the game tactical depth without feeling overwhelming, and keeps it in an accessible but still entertaining register. The music and overall tone underscore that light, playful mood.

The reason for its astronomical price is simple: it shipped in a minuscule run and collector demand drove it sky-high. For the average player, emulation is in practice the only sensible way to reach it. This in no way diminishes its gaming value — it merely separates the joy of play from the fetish of a rare medium.

Magical Chase is proof that a shmup doesn't have to be a harsh endurance test of reflexes to be fun. It's a graceful, artistically tuned title that deserves to be known more for how nicely it plays than for how much it costs.

**Why play:** A gorgeously crafted, accessible shooter with a fairy-tale atmosphere — a gaming experience that outshines even its notorious collector's price.

pc-engine__aero-blasters.article:
When you think of a flashy arcade shooter from the turn of the eighties and nineties, **Aero Blasters** is exactly what comes to mind — fast, loud, and beefed-up horizontal action where the screen lights up with explosions every few moments. On the PC Engine it delivered a portion of uncompromising shmup experience that genre fans love.

The game puts you in control of a fighter jet and drives you forward at a relentless pace, where waves of enemies alternate with mighty bosses that can fill half the screen. The tempo is brisk, the design isn't afraid of tough passages and emphasizes learning patterns and quick reactions — a typical trait of the arcade shooters of the era. Visually it leans on detailed sprite work and gorgeous boss battles, which are traditionally the highlight of every level.

An important plus is the option of **two-player cooperative play**, which makes Aero Blasters an ideal title for a session with two. Sharing the screen, covering your teammate, and coordinating fire add a layer of fun that single-player alone can't offer. It's in co-op that the game shows off its arcade pedigree the most.

From a genre standpoint, Aero Blasters is an honest representative of the classic horizontal shmup — no experiments, no fluff, just polished action, striking weapons, and an emphasis on drive. For players who like straightforward shooters without complex mechanics, it's a reliable choice that pleases immediately.

On a platform that was never afraid of shooters and had a whole array of top-tier ones, Aero Blasters holds its place as solid, energetic action. It may not be the most famous name in the catalog, but it's a title that knows exactly what it's doing and does it with grace.

**Why play:** A brisk, flashy horizontal shooter with gorgeous bosses and great two-player co-op — pure arcade joy.

pc-engine__snatcher.article:
Few games can evoke the atmosphere of cyberpunk noir detective fiction as faithfully as **Snatcher** — a visionary adventure from Hideo Kojima that, as early as the beginning of the nineties, showed where interactive storytelling could go. The CD version for the PC Engine is considered one of the definitive forms of the game, and thanks to a fan translation it became accessible to players outside Japan as well.

The story takes place in a dark future where humanity is threatened by mysterious android beings called Snatchers, who kill people and take over their identities. You step into the role of investigator Gillian Seed and journey through a world full of atmosphere, Blade Runner influences, and Kojima-esque intricate storytelling. The game is largely a command-menu-based adventure — you examine environments, interrogate characters, piece together clues, and gradually uncover a conspiracy.

For its time, Snatcher was extraordinarily ambitious: fully voiced dialogue on CD, a quality soundtrack, and cinematically directed scenes made it an experience closer to an interactive sci-fi film than to the games of the day. Kojima's signature is felt at every step — from the intricate characters through black humor to moments of tension and horror that can genuinely chill you.

Snatcher's cultural significance is enormous. It's one of the early milestones of Kojima's career, a foreshadowing of what he would later perfect in the Metal Gear series, and a cult favorite among adventure and cyberpunk fans to this day. The fan translation of the CD version was crucial for the Western community — without it, this icon would have remained locked behind a language barrier for most players.

Snatcher is a game you shouldn't miss if you're interested in the history of storytelling in games or have a soft spot for dark sci-fi. It's an atmospheric, cleverly written title that ages with unexpected grace.

**Why play:** Kojima's cyberpunk noir adventure with cinematic atmosphere and a powerful story — one of the milestones of interactive storytelling.

pc-engine__sapphire.article:
If there's a game that shows what the PC Engine hardware was capable of pushing to the very edge of its abilities, it's **Sapphire**. This CD shooter counts as one of the most technically polished demonstrations of the platform's capabilities — a showcase of just how far you could go with pre-rendered graphics and smooth animation on the Japanese hardware of the day.

Sapphire is a horizontal shmup that immediately captivates with its visual side: detailed, almost 3D-looking sprite graphics, elaborate backgrounds, and mighty bosses whose animations looked almost unheard-of for their time. The game boasts a flashy presentation, smooth scrolling, and an overall polish that made it something of a technological benchmark among shmups on the CD medium.

On the gameplay side it offers classic but polished shooter action — a choice of various companions and weapon systems, intense battles, and a pace that gives no rest. The emphasis here is on spectacle as much as on gameplay, which makes it a title worth experiencing fully, not just seeing in screenshots.

Sapphire is today a prized title among collectors and genre fans alike and is often mentioned in the context of the rarer and more sought-after pieces of the PC Engine CD library. It's a game that proves why the platform built such a strong reputation among enthusiasts as a paradise for shooter lovers.

For anyone interested in the peak technical achievements of the 2D era, Sapphire is a mandatory stop. It's a celebration of what the CD medium and skilled developers could conjure up before the polygon generation arrived.

**Why play:** A technically dazzling CD shooter that shows the PC Engine hardware at the peak of its abilities — spectacle and honest action in one.

pc-engine__cadash.article:
Combining a brisk platformer with RPG elements was hardly common at the end of the eighties — and that's exactly why **Cadash** stands out as a bold hybrid that retains its idiosyncratic charm to this day. This action game from Taito combines fantasy adventure, combat action, and light role-playing elements into a single accessible and enjoyable whole.

At its core it's an action platformer where you advance forward, hack down enemies, and defeat bosses, but Cadash also throws in an RPG layer: your character collects experience, levels up, gains new equipment and spells, and visits towns where you shop and talk to characters. This mix gives the game more depth and a sense of progression than the purely arcade action games of the era offered. There's also a choice of several character classes, which affects the play style.

Originally it was an arcade machine, and its strong point was **multiplayer cooperative play** — the shared adventure of fighting through a fantasy world with a friend is among the best Cadash has to offer. The home console versions then made this experience accessible outside the arcades too.

Cadash is interesting mainly as an early example of the genre blending that later became commonplace. Where many titles chose either pure action or full-blooded RPG, Cadash took the middle path and bet on immediately graspable fun with a light touch of adventure. It's this accessibility that makes it a pleasant title even for players who usually steer clear of big RPGs.

Today it's a lovely reminder of an era when arcades experimented with format and when the combination of sword, magic, and platform jumping felt fresh and exciting.

**Why play:** An enjoyable hybrid of action platformer and RPG with a choice of classes and great co-op — an accessible fantasy adventure with a sense of progression.

pc-engine__bloody-wolf.article:
When you want a proper dose of eighties Rambo-style action ride, **Bloody Wolf** won't let you down. This run & gun shooter from Data East is the polished essence of the action films of the era — a lone soldier (or two) against an army of enemies, explosions, prisoners to free, and endless waves of opponents.

Mechanically it's action seen mostly from above and the side, where you fight through the levels, mow down enemies with gunfire and grenades, and advance with an emphasis on quick reactions. Compared to purely vertical shooters like Commando, Bloody Wolf adds more varied situations — rescuing hostages, collecting new weapons and power-ups, riding vehicles, and boss battles that keep the pace fresh. There's a clear desire here to entertain the player with variety, not just endlessly churn out the same situations.

The big draw is again **two-player co-op**, which makes the game an ideal session for two. Fighting through enemy lines together, covering your partner, and coordinating attacks are exactly what this type of arcade action was made for, and the experience as a pair is significantly more intense than solo.

Bloody Wolf is a typical product of its time — loud, straightforward, and pumped full of the testosterone of B-grade action films. It doesn't aim for any depth or story beyond the necessary, but it knows exactly how to deliver the right portion of adrenaline-fueled fun. For fans of the run & gun genre, it's a reliable and enjoyable choice.

On the PC Engine, Bloody Wolf fits among the solid arcade conversions the platform managed to handle well. It's a game you come back to when you feel like simply switching off your brain and shooting.

**Why play:** Polished run & gun action in the style of eighties action films with varied situations and gorgeous two-player co-op.

pc-engine__dragon-s-curse.teaser: A port of Wonder Boy III; an excellent action RPG.
pc-engine__dragon-s-curse.detail: A port of Wonder Boy III: The Dragon's Trap (standalone version). An excellent action RPG with transformations into animal forms that open up new routes. Great even in this guise; another gem for fans of exploration.
pc-engine__dragon-s-curse.article:
Turning into a dragon, a mouse or a piranha and reshaping your path through the world accordingly - that was the wonderfully fresh idea brought by **Dragon's Curse**, the 1991 PC Engine port of the classic Wonder Boy III: The Dragon's Trap, made by Hudson and the developers at Westone. Under a different name and with a tweaked presentation, it is the very same superb action RPG that genre fans fell in love with.

At the heart of the game lies its ingenious transformation mechanic: after your hero is struck by a curse, he gradually shifts into various animal forms, each with its own abilities. The dragon form breathes fire, the mouse form squeezes into tiny cracks, the lizard can swim and climb - and it is precisely the switching between these abilities that unlocks new paths in the interconnected world. This structure, where you return to previously inaccessible places armed with a new ability, foreshadowed what we now call the metroidvania.

Beyond its inventive design, Dragon's Curse offers pleasant action gameplay, exploration of a sprawling world, gear collecting and battles against bosses who guard the transforming curses. Everything is delivered with the lightness and charm that made the Wonder Boy series famous - colorful graphics, catchy music and a sense of discovery that keeps pulling the player onward.

The PC Engine version ranks among the very accomplished conversions, and for owners of the platform it was a full-fledged way to enjoy this classic. To this day the game is considered one of the gems of the action RPG genre with platforming elements, and its legacy is confirmed by the fact that the original Wonder Boy III received an acclaimed remake in the modern era.

For anyone who loves exploration, the gradual unlocking of the world and cleverly designed abilities, Dragon's Curse is a must. It is timeless design that works just as well today as it did decades ago.

**Why play it:** An outstanding action RPG with an ingenious animal-transformation mechanic that opens up new paths - a timeless forerunner of the metroidvania.

pc-engine__soldier-blade-special-star-pa.article:
Hudson's Soldier line was a household name for PC Engine shmup fans, and **Soldier Blade Special** together with **Star Parodier** represent two idiosyncratic offshoots of that tradition. Both share the Star Soldier lineage, but each goes its own way - one down the path of polished hardcore action, the other down the path of playful parody.

Soldier Blade Special builds on one of the console's best vertical shmups. It is marked by brisk, smooth action, a distinctive weapon system and an emphasis on scoring - all with the refined presentation the series was renowned for. The special version aimed above all at players focused on the competitive caravan modes, that is, short timed challenges for the highest score, which were hugely popular in Japan around the Soldier games and built an entire competitive culture around them.

Star Parodier, by contrast, is a playful, self-mocking detour - a parody of the genre and of its own series. Instead of serious space fighters you pilot adorable characters, including the flying PC Engine itself, and the whole game is cast in cheerful, colorful and witty tones. Beneath the comedic shell, however, hides an honest, well-playing shooter, so even those who take the genre seriously will find plenty to enjoy.

Together this pair beautifully illustrates the breadth that shmups offered on the PC Engine - from adrenaline-fueled score chasing to good-natured parody unafraid to poke fun at itself. For a platform that was a veritable promised land among shooter fans, these are characteristic and cherished pieces.

Genre fans will appreciate both sides: the hardcore challenge and the light-hearted fun. It is a twofold look at why the PC Engine built such an exceptional standing among shmup lovers.

**Why play it:** Two offshoots of the famous Soldier series - a polished score chase and a playful parody - showcase the full spectrum of shmups on the PC Engine.

pc-engine__inscription-ish.article:
Think retro platforms retired long ago? This scene clearly disagrees - **Inscription -ish** is a homebrew title for the PC Engine, a game created by enthusiasts long after the console's commercial end. And that is exactly where its charm lies: it is living proof that the love for classic hardware never faded.

Homebrew development for older consoles is a distinct phenomenon today. Developers learn to work with period hardware, its limitations and its strengths, and create new games that could just as easily have come out decades ago. This scene is driven by pure passion, not commerce - it is about the joy of creation, experimentation and a tribute to a platform that holds cult status among fans. The results then often appear in limited physical editions as well as freely available ROM files.

With homebrew titles like this one, it is only fair to acknowledge that it is a product of the community scene, and it should be judged more by its ambitions and context than by the yardstick of major commercial releases. The value of such games lies largely in what they represent: the ability and desire of creators to expand the platform's library with new experiences and to keep it alive even in the modern era.

The PC Engine is a rewarding target for homebrew developers - it has devoted fans, intriguing hardware and a rich history to build upon. Every new title made for it is thus a small celebration of this community and its determination not to let the classics be forgotten.

For retro enthusiasts and collectors, homebrew games are an enticing chapter - a chance to experience something new on old iron and to support a scene that thrives on the pure joy of gaming. Inscription -ish is one such contribution.

**Why play it:** A contemporary homebrew title that keeps the PC Engine alive - proof that the retro community's passion for classic hardware never went to sleep.

pc-engine__lemmings.article:
Saving a horde of suicidally minded little creatures who, without your orders, cheerfully march straight into the abyss - Lemmings is proof that the best puzzle games arise from a simple yet irresistible idea. And on the PC Engine console, this classic found itself another home.

The game's premise is perfectly clear. A group of lemmings appears at the start and automatically begins walking forward regardless of danger. You assign them roles - diggers, stair builders, blockers, floaters, or those who sacrifice themselves in an explosion - and thereby carve out a safe path to the exit for the whole group. Each level is essentially a puzzle with limited resources, where you must precisely think through who gets which ability and at what moment. Gradually traps, time pressure and the intricacy of the solutions all pile up.

Lemmings is the work of the Scottish studio DMA Design, from whose ranks the creators of the Grand Theft Auto series later emerged, and it was published by Psygnosis in 1991. After enormous success on the Amiga came a wave of conversions to countless platforms. The PC Engine, a console popular especially in Japan and born from the collaboration between NEC and Hudson Soft, was one of them.

Culturally, Lemmings proved that a puzzle game could be a mass hit while still having its own distinctive humor. The helpless yet adorable lemmings etched themselves into memory, and their name became a metaphor for blindly following the crowd. To this day the game is considered one of the most influential titles of its genre.

The PC Engine version benefited from the console's ability to display colorful, legible graphics and to comfortably handle a multitude of tiny characters on screen. For players on that platform it was a pleasant way to savor one of the finest puzzle games of its time. The series then continued with many installments and remakes, but the original magic remains unsurpassed.

**Why play it:** For timeless, cleverly layered puzzles in which rescuing the last lemming brings true satisfaction.

pc-engine__blazing-lazers.article:
If you have ever wanted to know why the PC Engine had a reputation as a machine for lovers of shooting from right to left, just fire up Blazing Lazers. This vertical shooter is among the most distinctive shmups of the system's early era and to this day can get the blood pumping for anyone who loves a screen full of projectiles and explosions.

The game builds on the classic vertical shmup formula but stands out with a rich upgrade system. The player collects various types of main weapons plus support modules that change the behavior of the fire and add protective elements or firepower multipliers. The right combination of upgrades turns your ship into a maelstrom, but a single hit can strip you of the power you have gathered, so the tension grows with each successive level. The pace is brisk, there are plenty of enemies and the end-of-level bosses are among the most spectacular the genre had to offer.

For its time, Blazing Lazers dazzled with its smoothness and the amount of on-screen action. The PC Engine could throw around a large number of sprites without major slowdown, which gave the shooter a dynamism that home consoles of the day did not commonly offer. Visually the game bets on vivid cosmic scenery and striking enemy formations that make progressing a pleasantly chaotic spectacle.

In its North American release for the TurboGrafx-16, the game shone as one of the titles meant to show what the system could do against the competition. It helped build the PC Engine's reputation as a platform beloved by fans of action shooters, and in the retro community today it is regarded as one of its machine's leading shmups.

For players seeking a pure arcade shooter with an emphasis on upgrading and reflexes, Blazing Lazers is a great choice. It is accessible enough to draw you in and demanding enough to keep you at repeated attempts for a better result.

**Why play it:** A brisk vertical shooter that shows the PC Engine in its best shmup form, with an addictive weapon system and an avalanche of on-screen action.

pc-engine__neutopia.article:
When you want to experience a grand adventure in the spirit of classic action RPGs on the PC Engine, Neutopia is the right place to start. This action adventure makes no secret of its inspiration by early top-down titles and leads the player through a sprawling world full of dungeons, puzzles and enemies.

The gameplay rests on exploring a spherical fantasy world divided into several regions, each of which hides its own dungeon. A hero named Jazeta gradually collects better weapons, protective items and key artifacts that open the way onward. Combat unfolds in real time from a top-down view, complemented by solving spatial puzzles and searching for hidden passages. The gradual strengthening of the character and the uncovering of the map give the game a pleasant rhythm of discovery.

On the PC Engine, Neutopia looked colorful and clean. The world is varied, alternating between forests, caves and fortresses, and each dungeon has its own theme and a boss who guards an important item. The pace is balanced between action and exploration, so the game neither overwhelms with excessive complexity nor grows dull through directness. For owners of the system, it was one of the few larger adventure experiences the machine offered.

It was precisely the absence of similarly styled games on the platform that made Neutopia a significant title. It received a sequel and, within the PC Engine catalog, earned a reputation as a solid representative of the action-adventure genre. For fans who loved exploring dungeons and gradually acquiring new abilities, it was a welcome expansion of the library.

In the retro community, Neutopia is valued as an honest, well-playing adventure worth discovering even today. If you enjoy the slow unveiling of a world, solving puzzles and the classic sense of adventure, it is an ideal candidate for longer evenings.

**Why play it:** An honest top-down action adventure with dungeon exploration and a gradually strengthening hero, ranking among the best of its kind on the PC Engine.

pc-engine__fatal-fury-2.article:
When the fighting-game war raged in the mid-nineties, SNK with its Fatal Fury 2 showed that it had something to offer even beyond the hallowed Neo Geo arcade cabinets. And on the PC Engine, the darling of the hearts of all who swore by CD-ROM and juicy conversions in Japan, this game was a small miracle of both technology and ambition.

Fatal Fury 2 stands on what set the series apart from the competition: a two-plane combat system in which characters could move between the foreground and background of the arena. This gave matches a spatiality that few fighting games offered at the time. The player learned not only the timing of strikes and special moves but also when to dodge into the second plane and avoid a series of blows. The roster introduced new fighters such as Mai Shiranui, who over the years became one of the iconic characters of the entire fighting-game genre.

SNK was a studio that lived and breathed arcades and Neo Geo hardware, and Fatal Fury (Garou Densetsu in Japan) was its answer to the Street Fighter phenomenon. The second installment pushed everything further: more characters, more elaborate animations, a more distinctive soundtrack. For the PC Engine platform, adored in Japan for its ability to convert arcade hits for the home, this was a title that demonstrated just how far NEC's console could go.

Culturally, Fatal Fury was important because it built an extensive universe of characters whose fates intertwined across installments and the later King of Fighters series. Terry Bogard, the main hero in the red cap, became one of the most recognizable faces of SNK ever. What began as a story of the Bogard brothers' revenge grew into one of the backbone brands of Japanese fighting games.

Playing Fatal Fury 2 today means touching an era when the genre was still taking shape and every new installment moved the rules along. It is a rawer, tougher experience than the later polished series, but it is precisely in that directness that its charm lies. The two-plane combat remains pleasantly fresh even for players used to modern fighting games.

**Why play it:** For a taste of a classic SNK fighting game from the era when the genre was still defining itself, and for the unconventional combat system across two planes of the arena.

pc-engine__street-fighter-ii-champion-ed.article:
There are games that defined an entire era of the gaming industry, and Street Fighter II belongs among the very highest of them. Champion Edition was an enhanced version that opened the door to what players craved most: playing as the four bosses and pitting two identical fighters against each other. And the fact that it appeared on the PC Engine too is a small legend in itself.

The core of the game is a genre textbook to this day. Eight playable fighters (expanded in Champion Edition by the quartet of big bosses Balrog, Vega, Sagat and M. Bison) with distinct styles, sets of special moves and pacing. The Hadoken, Shoryuken and Tatsumaki of Ryu and Ken became part of gaming folklore, a combo known today even by someone who never held a controller. Champion Edition also fine-tuned the balance and enabled mirror matches of identical characters.

With Street Fighter II in 1991, Capcom created a phenomenon that literally jump-started the arcade industry and unleashed a wave of fighting games that flooded the entire nineties. The PC Engine conversion came out on a giant HuCard and was a prestige affair for NEC, proof that their console could handle even such a packed title. At a time when home ports of arcade hits were always a compromise, this was a respected piece of work.

The cultural impact of Street Fighter II is hard to overstate. The game stood at the birth of community competitive gaming, gave rise to tournaments from which the entire FGC scene later grew, and its characters penetrated films, comics and countless follow-up installments. In short, it became one of the pillars of the whole of modern gaming culture.

The strength of this game lies in its timelessness. The matches are readable, the controls precise and every victory is deserved. Champion Edition is one of the most valued versions precisely for its fine-tuned balance and the option of mirror duels, which became a given in every later fighting game.

**Why play it:** Because it is one of the most influential titles in history, and Champion Edition represents its classic, perfectly fine-tuned form.

pc-engine__final-lap-twin.article:
What happens when you cross a racing game with a Japanese RPG? Namco posed exactly this crazy question in the case of Final Lap Twin, and the result is one of the most unconventional titles on the PC Engine, where behind the wheel you live out a slice of adventure.

The game is split into two faces. The first is a classic racing mode derived from the arcade hit Final Lap, which is purely about speed and the fight for position on the track. The second, far stranger one, is the so-called Quest mode, in which the player, as a young racer, travels between towns, talks to characters, collects parts for their car and gradually works their way toward the top of the racing world. Instead of battles there are races, and instead of experience points there are upgrades to the machine.

Namco was one of the pillars of the Japanese arcade and console industry, and Final Lap was its respected racing brand. Combining it with RPG elements, a genre at the peak of its popularity in Japan, was a bold experiment that exploited the fact that the PC Engine held a strong position in the land of the rising sun and had an audience open to unconventional ideas.

It is precisely in this hybridity that the game's cultural significance lies. At a time when genres stuck to their pigeonholes, Final Lap Twin showed that a racing game could have narrative, progression and a sense of a journey. It was a harbinger of later titles that brought story and career elements into racing, even if at the time it was more of a fringe curiosity.

Today, Final Lap Twin is enticing above all for collectors and fans of unconventional concepts. The combination of straightforward racing and a slower quest mode offers an experience hard to find on other platforms of the era, and it is a fine showcase of the experimental spirit of the Japanese gaming scene.

**Why play it:** For the unusual fusion of racing and RPG progression that turns simple lapping of a track into a little adventure.

dreamcast__sonic-adventure.detail: Sonic's big leap into 3D and a launch flagship for the Dreamcast. The first game mixes fast Sonic stages with the slower styles of the other characters and had stunning graphics for its time. The sequel fine-tuned the pace (the beloved Sonic/Shadow stages vs. the less beloved treasure-hunting and mech levels) and added the Chao garden - virtual pets with VMU minigames. The defining 3D Sonic of the era.
dreamcast__sonic-adventure.article:
When the blue hedgehog first fully leapt into the third dimension in 1998, it was a moment Sega fans had awaited for years. **Sonic Adventure** became the flagship draw of the Dreamcast's Japanese launch, and its task was to convince the world that the legend of the 16-bit era could handle the transition to 3D without losing its pace. And to a large extent it succeeded.

At the core are the classic speed stages, where Sonic tears along loops, corkscrews and steep descents so briskly that the camera can barely keep up. To this the studio **Sonic Team** added a varied palette of playable characters, each offering a different style: Tails races, Knuckles hunts for shards of the Master Emerald, Amy flees and the robot E-102 Gamma shoots. Not every style was equally popular, but the variety kept the game fresh and gave it an unexpected breadth of content for its time.

Graphically it was a demonstration of the new console's power. The open hub zone of Station Square, the waterfalls, lava temples and the battle with the water god Chaos felt like sci-fi in 1998. The Dreamcast was flexing muscles the competition of the day did not have, and Sonic Adventure became one of the first calling cards of what the console could do.

Development continued with **Sonic Adventure 2**, which significantly fine-tuned the pace. It focused on the strongest element - the fast stages of Sonic and his dark counterpart Shadow - while the treasure-hunting and mech levels remained more of a supplement. The game also brought the **Chao garden**, where you raised virtual pets and, thanks to the VMU memory card, played minigames with them even away from the television. This combination of platforming and a tamagotchi element still has devoted fans to this day.

Both games defined the shape of 3D Sonic for years to come and received re-releases on later platforms, which introduced them to a new generation of players. Despite occasional technical quirks, they remain a symbol of Sega's ambitions at the twilight of the era of its own consoles.

**Why play it:** Because it is the defining leap of the iconic hedgehog into 3D - energetic, ambitious and full of ideas that shaped an entire era.

dreamcast__sonic-adventure-2.article:
If the question ever comes up of which 3D Sonic best nailed the pace, the name **Sonic Adventure 2** will ring out almost every time. This sequel to the Dreamcast's legendary launch title took the best of the first game and honed it into a form fans still remember with nostalgia today.

The game from **Sonic Team** split the story into two camps - the heroes around Sonic and the dark side led by the newly introduced Shadow. This structure gave the storytelling an edge while also underscoring what the game shines at most: pure speed. The running stages of Sonic and Shadow are among the most beloved moments of the entire series, where the camera, music and level design merge into an adrenaline-charged ride.

Alongside them you will find slower gameplay styles - mech battles with Tails and Eggman or treasure-hunting missions with Knuckles and Rouge. Not everyone loves them equally, but together they form a varied composition that keeps the player moving between the different genre modes.

The **Chao garden**, where you fed, trained and raised adorable creatures, became a cult component. Thanks to the link with the VMU memory card, you could care for them even away from the console, which turned a relatively fringe feature into a little obsession for many players.

Sonic Adventure 2 came out toward the end of the Dreamcast's life, so it was fully enjoyed only through a series of later re-releases on newer platforms. It was precisely thanks to them that the game was embraced even by a generation that never owned the original console, and its status as one of the most beloved 3D Sonics remains to this day.

**Why play it:** For the polished speed stages and the Chao garden - it is the peak of the blue hedgehog's classic 3D era.

dreamcast__soulcalibur.detail: A Dreamcast launch title and to this day cited as one of the best ports ever - it was graphically better than the arcade original and received a then-rare score of 10/10. A weapon-based 3D fighting game with an emphasis on sideways movement (8-way run) and beautiful animation. A showcase of the console's power right at launch.
dreamcast__soulcalibur.article:
There are ports, and then there is **Soulcalibur** on the Dreamcast - a home version that not only caught up with its arcade original but outright overtook it. In 1999 it was the moment when players understood that Sega's new console meant graphical superiority in absolute earnest.

This weapon-based 3D fighting game from **Namco** built on duels of swords, scythes and spears, where each character wielded a different weapon with its own reach and rhythm. The key innovation was the **8-way run** system, that is, free movement in eight directions, which gave the fights a spatiality and tactical depth that fighting games of the time rarely offered. Dodging to the sides, circling around the opponent and timing strikes elevated combat to an elegant fencing.

Visually it was the absolute top. The home version added sharper textures, smoother animations and richer environments than the coin-guzzling arcade had. Reviewers reacted with enthusiasm and the game gathered then wholly exceptional ratings on the edge of perfection, thereby ranking among the best-received titles of its time.

Beyond the combat core it offered rich accompanying content - unlockable characters, missions and challenges that extended the longevity far beyond the scope of a common arcade conversion. For Dreamcast owners it was the ideal title with which to show off the console's capabilities right at its launch.

The Soulcalibur series then continued with further installments on various platforms, but it is this Dreamcast first entry that tends to be remembered as the moment when everything came together perfectly - technology, gameplay and timing.

**Why play it:** It is cited to this day as one of the best ports and one of the most elegant weapon-based fighting games ever.

dreamcast__crazy-taxi.detail: An arcade hit brought home without compromise: you ferry customers around the city as fast and as wildly as possible for cash, all set to a punk-rock soundtrack (The Offspring, Bad Religion). Pure, addictive „just one more ride" fun. The definition of Sega's arcade style.
dreamcast__crazy-taxi.article:
A yellow cab hurtles against traffic, the passenger in the back seat shrieks with delight and punk rock blasts from the speakers — welcome to **Crazy Taxi**, the embodiment of pure arcade driving joy. A game that bothers with neither realism nor storytelling, only one question: how fast and how wildly can you get your fare to the destination?

The concept is brilliantly simple. You pick up customers, follow a big green arrow pointing to the goal and tear through the city at breakneck speed. Speed, drifts and daring maneuvers earn you money and time, while the clock ticks down relentlessly. This „just one more ride" loop is so addictive that it's hard to tear yourself away.

Originally an arcade hit from **Hitmaker** under the Sega banner, it made the jump to Dreamcast practically without compromise. The home version added extra modes and the miniature Crazy Box driving school, where you honed your drifts and tricks across a series of crazy challenges. The game thus offered far more than a mere copy of the cabinet.

An inseparable part of the experience was the licensed soundtrack featuring bands like **The Offspring** and **Bad Religion**, whose energy fit the frantic pace perfectly. Music and gameplay fused so completely that many players today can't even picture Crazy Taxi without those songs.

Crazy Taxi became one of the definitions of Sega's arcade style of that era — instantly graspable, always fun and ideal for short, intense sessions. It spawned numerous sequels and ports, but the spirit of that first wild ride remains unmatched.

**Why play it:** For instant, unadulterated arcade fun, where time and worries vanish the moment your first customer starts shrieking.

dreamcast__jet-set-radio.detail: A pioneer of **cel-shading** graphics (a comic-book look) that kicked off a whole wave of stylized games. You skate around Tokyo on inline skates, spray graffiti and evade the police, all set to an iconic funk/hip-hop/electronica soundtrack (Hideki Naganuma). A style icon of the era; a cult classic.
dreamcast__jet-set-radio.article:
Few games looked as different in 2000 as **Jet Set Radio**. While the rest of the industry chased ever more realistic polygons, Sega came out with a comic-book-stylized world that looked like a moving poster — and in doing so changed the very idea of what a video game could look like.

The game from **Smilebit** was one of the pioneers of **cel-shading**, a technique that makes 3D models look like hand-drawn artwork with bold outlines. That moment set off a whole wave of imitators and stylized games that abandoned the chase for photorealism in favor of artistic expression. Visually, Jet Set Radio still holds a freshness that realistic titles of the era lost long ago.

The gameplay is as rebellious as the look. You play as a crew of young inline skaters who cruise the streets of a stylized Tokyo, spray graffiti on walls and billboards and dodge the police and rival gangs all the while. The combination of smooth skating, tricks and spraying in the right rhythm gives the game its own, almost dance-like tempo.

The soundtrack by **Hideki Naganuma** plays an indispensable role, blending funk, hip-hop and electronica into a unique sonic collage. The music here is just as important as the controls — it sets the mood, the energy and the pace of the whole street, and became one of the most distinctive elements of the entire game.

Jet Set Radio became a style icon of the era and a cult title that transcended commercial success. Its influence on the visual language of games is felt to this day, and the game received re-releases that opened its doors to new players.

**Why play it:** For its unmistakable style, rebellious atmosphere and a soundtrack that turns skating around Tokyo into an unforgettable experience.

dreamcast__power-stone-1-and-2.detail: A 3D arena fighter where you move freely around the environment, collect items and gems to transform into a super form. The sequel added up to 4 players and chaotic, interactive arenas. Unique party fighters; rare and sought-after today.
dreamcast__power-stone-1-and-2.article:
Forget the static battlefield split into two halves — **Power Stone** throws you into a full-fledged 3D arena where the fight unfolds all around you. This zany series from **Capcom** took the fighting genre and spun it into a chaotic but incredibly fun party spectacle.

At its core is free movement around the environment. Instead of standing across from your opponent, you run around the arena, climb, throw objects and make use of everything within reach. Gems — Power Stones — roll around the battlefield, and whoever collects enough transforms into a devastating super form full of flashy attacks. The duel thus constantly flips and shifts dynamically.

The sequel pushed the concept even further. It added support for up to **four players** at once and arenas that were an enemy in themselves — shifting, collapsing, offering interactive traps and opportunities. What had been a relatively orderly brawler became a gloriously chaotic melee, ideal for playing with friends on one couch.

Working with items and the environment gave the fights a lightness and humor often missing from the genre. Power Stone never took itself deadly seriously, and that was precisely its charm — it was about the joy of play, not about memorizing complicated combos.

Because of their ties to the Dreamcast and its limited reach, both games remained something of a hidden treasure and today rank among the rare, collector-sought titles. For those who discover them, though, they're still one of the most refreshing takes on the fighter.

**Why play it:** For chaotic 3D arena fun for up to four players that still has few equals today.

dreamcast__marvel-vs-capcom-2.detail: An insane crossover with 56 characters and 3v3 teams in an explosion of effects and super attacks. Long considered the pinnacle of „team-based" fighters; the competitive scene still plays it today. The Dreamcast version was the best home port.
dreamcast__marvel-vs-capcom-2.article:
Fifty-six characters, three-on-three teams and a screen so crammed with effects that at times you can't tell where you're standing — **Marvel vs. Capcom 2** is a celebration of the unbridled madness a fighting game can allow itself. And yet beneath that explosion of color pulses a surprisingly deep and competitive system.

The game from **Capcom** united heroes from the Marvel comics with icons from the studio's own franchises into a single colossal crossover. The three-on-three format, letting you swap characters in a flash, call teammates in for assist attacks and chain combos, gave the game incredible speed and depth. The fights resemble a colorful storm more than a classic round of a fighter.

It's precisely this blend of spectacle and tactical depth that made it a long-standing pinnacle of „team-based" fighters. Players kept discovering new combos, character synergies and strategies for years after release, and the competitive scene returns to it to this day, making it one of the most enduring tournament titles of its kind.

The Dreamcast version was the best home port at the time — faithfully bringing the arcade experience, including its smoothness and vast roster, straight into living rooms. For console owners it was a ticket into a world that otherwise lived mainly in the arcades.

The combination of casual spectacle and enormous mechanical depth makes Marvel vs. Capcom 2 a one-of-a-kind — a game equally enjoyed by a random button-masher and a seasoned tournament fighter hunting for the perfect combo.

**Why play it:** For an insane crossover of dozens of characters and a timeless fighting system that the competitive scene still loves today.

dreamcast__shenmue.article:
Few games were as ambitious in their day as **Shenmue**. Sega didn't take the path of fast action with it, but instead tried to create a living, breathing world in which time flows, the weather changes and people live by their own schedules — a vision whose scope outran much of what only arrived years later.

The game combines adventure with action elements and places enormous emphasis on atmosphere and detail. You stroll the streets, talk to the residents, examine objects, follow clues and gradually uncover a story driven by the hero's personal motivation. The pace is deliberately slower, betting on immersion in the environment rather than nonstop action.

It's precisely this striving for a believable world that makes Shenmue a milestone. Characters have their own daily routines; you can drop into an arcade, go shopping or just watch the town's life flow by. Action sequences then spice up the storytelling with combat scenes and hectic moments that break the calmer rhythm of the investigation.

Shenmue became synonymous with ambitious, so-called „immersive" gaming, and its influence on genres focused on open, believable worlds is cited to this day. Many elements we now take for granted — living NPCs, day cycles, small interactive details — were introduced here in a form players of the time had never seen.

Still, it was a title tightly bound to the fate of the Dreamcast, so its vision was fully enjoyed by a devoted minority rather than the masses. That's exactly what turned it into a cult legend, still talked about today as a game ahead of its time.

**Why play it:** For an uncommon immersion in a living world and ambitions that foreshadowed the future of open-world gaming experiences.

dreamcast__skies-of-arcadia.detail: An optimistic JRPG about sky pirates in a floating world, with the discovery of new territories and airship battles. Charismatic characters and an adventurous tone (rare in a genre full of darkness). Highly acclaimed but, due to the Dreamcast's failure, little-played — cult status.
dreamcast__skies-of-arcadia.article:
In a genre that at the time so often bet on darkness and melancholy, **Skies of Arcadia** blew in like a gust of fresh wind beneath an airship's sails. This optimistic JRPG about sky pirates wagered on adventure, exploration and an indomitable zest for life — and won over the heart of everyone who gave it a chance.

The game from **Overworks** under Sega's wing takes you into a floating world divided into aerial continents, between which you travel aboard your own airship. Exploring uncharted territories, seeking hidden islands and uncovering treasures gives the game an air of pure exploration that many other JRPGs lacked. The world literally invites you to head over the horizon.

Battles take place on two levels. Classic turn-based fights with your characters are complemented by grand **airship** clashes, where entire flying vessels face off in a duel of cannons and maneuvers. This duality gives the combat system its edge and underlines the game's pirate theme.

Most of all, though, Skies of Arcadia lives through its characters and tone. A charismatic crew, adventurous humor and infectious optimism create an atmosphere rare in the genre. Instead of a brooding hero, you're pulling a story along with a crew you'll be delighted to spend dozens of hours with.

Critics prized the game highly, but due to the Dreamcast's commercial failure relatively few players got to try it. From that contradiction — high quality and small reach — grew its cult status as a game connoisseurs recommend as a hidden gem that deserves far more attention.

**Why play it:** For adventurous optimism, exploring a world in the clouds and airship battles — a JRPG that simply roots for the joy of the journey.

dreamcast__grandia-ii.detail: Famous for one of the best combat systems in the genre — a combination of turns and positioning on a timeline, where you can interrupt an enemy's attack (cancel/counter). Brisk and visually pleasing. A must for fans of JRPG combat.
dreamcast__grandia-ii.article:
If what you always loved most about JRPGs was the combat, **Grandia II** is a game that can grip you from the very first encounter. This sequel to a beloved series became famous for one of the best combat systems the genre has offered — so clever and dynamic that fans still point to it today.

The magic lies in linking turn-based strategy with positioning on a **timeline**. The actions of your characters and enemies advance along a gauge, so it's not just about which attack you choose, but also exactly when it lands. A key element is the ability to **interrupt** an enemy's attack the moment it's about to strike — a well-timed hit cancels the opponent's move, knocks them back down the gauge and turns the tide of battle in your favor.

This mechanic adds a layer of rhythm and anticipation to combat that static turn-based systems don't offer. You watch the gauge, plan your movement around the battlefield and the timing of spells and hits, so every fight turns into a little tactical puzzle where every moment matters.

Alongside its polished combat, Grandia II is also a visually pleasing and brisk game from **Game Arts**. The pace flows, the environments are varied and the overall experience doesn't hold the player up with needless delays, making the play a smooth and satisfying ride.

Grandia II may not have made a name for itself with mass sales, but among JRPG connoisseurs it earned a firm place thanks to the quality of its combat. It received re-releases on other platforms, so its combat system could be discovered by later generations of players looking for something more than plain hammering of the attack button.

**Why play it:** For one of the best and most tactical combat systems in JRPG history — a must for lovers of turn-based battles.

dreamcast__resident-evil-code-veronica.article:
When the Dreamcast received a major new Resident Evil chapter exclusively in 2000, it was a huge asset for Sega – the series that stood at the birth of the entire survival-horror genre abandoned fixed, pre-rendered backdrops for the first time and built its whole world from full-fledged 3D polygons. **Code Veronica** thus looked dramatically different from the previous PlayStation installments: the camera could move smoothly, the environments breathed with depth and, thanks to the Dreamcast's power, the game felt a generation ahead.

Storywise it follows on from the events of the first installments and tracks **Claire Redfield**, who's searching for her brother Chris. From a prison island controlled by the Umbrella corporation she makes her way to a snowbound Antarctic base, and later you take the controls of Chris himself. The storytelling here is more ambitious than before – the series fully develops the theme of the Ashford family and pits you face to face with one of the most theatrical villains of the entire franchise.

In gameplay it stays true to the proven recipe: limited ammunition and healing items, tank controls, puzzles involving the collection of keys and objects, and the permanent feeling that every bullet is precious. That very tension between exploration and fear of the next corner made Resident Evil such an addictive experience. The limited-capacity inventory forces you to think about what to carry and what to leave in the chest, and backtracking becomes a little logic game in itself.

The move to real 3D also brought new possibilities for horror direction. A freely tilting camera could reveal a threat at an unexpected moment, and the designers played with light and shadow in ways static backdrops didn't allow. The game was at the same time one of the flagship titles meant to demonstrate what the Dreamcast could do as hardware.

Today **Code Veronica** is remembered as one of the key installments of the series, which later came out in an expanded version and reached other platforms, so players outside the Dreamcast community got to enjoy it too. For fans of the franchise it represents an important link between the classic era and the later direction of Resident Evil.

**Why play it:** Classic survival horror at the moment the series fully transitioned to 3D for the first time – tense atmosphere, ammo conservation and a theatrical story that belongs in the Resident Evil canon.

dreamcast__ikaruga.detail: The spiritual successor to Radiant Silvergun and perhaps the most revered modern shmup. A brilliant polarity mechanic: you switch your ship between black and white, absorb bullets of your own color and destroy enemies with the opposite one — turning bullet-hell into almost a logic game. Treasure mastery.
dreamcast__ikaruga.article:
There's a handful of games that fans speak of in a hushed, almost sacred tone – and **Ikaruga** is one of them. This vertical shooter from the legendary **Treasure** studio is the spiritual successor to the revered Radiant Silvergun and to this day counts as one of the most respected modern shmups of all. It first appeared as an arcade game in 2001, then came to the Dreamcast in 2002.

At the core of the whole experience is a brilliant polarity mechanic. Your ship switches between two states – black and white – and this choice changes absolutely everything. Bullets of your own color don't harm you; on the contrary, you absorb them and charge up a powerful attack, while enemies of the opposite color take double damage. What would elsewhere be a chaotic bullet-hell thus becomes a game that resembles a logic puzzle in real time.

Each screen is a carefully designed sequence you learn to read, anticipate and master. The game also rewards chaining enemies in trios of the same color with bonus score, which turns the pursuit of a high score into a discipline of its own that players dig into for years. Ikaruga isn't so much about reflexes as about rhythm, planning and almost meditative focus.

Visually it's a clean, elegant game where the contrast of black and white isn't just aesthetics but the very game principle. Treasure was famous for building action around a single idea taken to perfection, and Ikaruga is perhaps the best proof of that approach – minimalist in its basic idea, infinitely deep in execution.

That's exactly why the game built a cult standing and over the years appeared on other platforms too, where a new generation of players found it. For the shmup community it remains a kind of benchmark against which other games of the genre are measured.

**Why play it:** A masterful shmup from Treasure, where the polarity mechanic transforms bullet-hell into an elegant puzzle – one of the deepest and most respected representatives of the genre.

dreamcast__bangai-o.detail: A Treasure action game where you pilot a mech firing in all directions and unleash giant „smart bomb" attacks (the more bullets around you, the stronger) — an explosion of hundreds of projectiles on screen. Chaotic, inventive, addictive.
dreamcast__bangai-o.article:
If you've ever wished to see hundreds of explosions on screen at once and still feel like it makes sense, **Bangai-O** from **Treasure** is exactly that experience. This action shooter for the Dreamcast from 1999 puts you in a robotic mech that spews bullets in every direction at once and fills the screen with such a density of projectiles that your eyes can barely keep up.

The heart of the game is a „smart bomb"-style mega-attack whose power depends on how many enemy bullets are around you at that moment. The greater the risk you take and the more you let yourself be surrounded by fire, the more devastating the salvo you can then unleash. This mechanic actively pushes you into danger and flips the usual logic of shooters on its head – instead of dodging, you actually want to throw yourself into the thickest fire.

The levels are sprawling and full of enemies, so the action constantly escalates into chaotic shootouts where the screen literally lights up with explosions.
