This component adds strategic depth to the racing, because a long stop costs you precious seconds, but worn tires or an empty tank end the race entirely. Thanks to this, the game felt unexpectedly realistic for its time.

The second big lure was the split screen for two players. Instead of taking turns at one monitor, two racers could drive simultaneously, each in their own half of the screen, and measure their strength directly against each other. This element made Pitstop II a great party game and pushed it ahead of a number of simpler racing titles of its day. The battle for a better time and for the right timing of the pit stop could keep a group of friends at the screen deep into the night.

The game was released in the mid-1980s and became one of the popular racing titles on the home computers of that generation. The combination of arcade driving with the managerial element of the pit stop was pioneering in its own way and foreshadowed the direction in which the racing genre gradually moved toward greater simulation. For many C64 players it was the first game in which they had to think about strategy even during the race.

**Why play:** A racing classic that, as one of the first, combined arcade speed with the tactics of pit stops and offered a great duel of two players on a split screen.

c64__sam-s-journey-ish.article:
When someone says a new game for the Commodore 64, most people imagine something from the 1980s. But the modern homebrew scene proves that this machine still has something to offer, and platformers in the spirit of Sam's Journey are the best proof of that. A few screens are enough and you see exactly what makes new C64 games so fascinating: technology that would have seemed impossible in the eighties, running on forty-year-old iron.

Platformers of this type bet on the brisk movement of the hero, smooth scrolling, and colorful, detailed worlds full of enemies and secret nooks. The player jumps through a series of levels, collects items, avoids traps, and searches for hidden paths. What distinguishes modern homebrew from period games is the degree of technical polish. Creators today know the C64 hardware far better than most of their predecessors and can squeeze effects out of the SID and VIC-II chips that the original developers never even dreamed of.

The modern C64 scene is interesting in its context too. It arises from pure passion for a machine that commercially retired long ago, and yet it keeps around it an active community of programmers, graphic artists, and musicians. These games often come out in physical form on cassettes or cartridges with printed covers, as a tribute to the original era, and their production quality tends to be comparable to or better than the commercial titles from the computer's heyday.

A platformer of this style is thus not only an entertaining game but also a small demonstration of how the retro scene lives in the twenty-first century. For a player who grew up on the Commodore, it is a homecoming with technology they would not have expected back then. And for a newcomer it is perfect proof that the magic of 8-bit graphics and music has not aged, it has just landed in the hands of more experienced creators.

**Why play:** A modern platformer that shows how far today's homebrew scene can push the old Commodore 64, with technique and polish worthy of the best classics of the genre.

c64__soul-force.article:
Run-and-gun action has one unwritten rule: it must be fast, loud, and must not let the player catch their breath. Soul Force, a game from the modern Commodore 64 homebrew scene, takes this genre seriously. From the moment the first level gets going, the screen is full of enemies, shots, and explosions, and you have only one duty: don't stop shooting and keep moving.

The run-and-gun genre is built on constant forward movement combined with fluid shooting in all directions. The player pushes through waves of opponents, dodges projectiles, and tries to stay alive long enough to reach the level's final boss. The emphasis is on reflexes, reading enemy patterns, and the ability to keep a cool head when the screen fills with chaos. It is a genre that was among the most popular on the arcade machines and home computers of the 1980s, and modern homebrew titles gladly carry it on.

On the old Commodore 64 hardware, creating a fluid action shooter is a technical challenge. The game must handle many moving objects at once, smooth scrolling, and at the same time distinctive music from the SID chip, which is to this day famous for its characteristic sound. That is exactly why modern run-and-gun titles for this platform are small technical showcases, where programming artistry blends with love for the classic arcades.

Games like Soul Force arise within a lively community of enthusiasts who continue to develop software for a machine introduced to the market back in 1982. This scene is proof that retro gaming is not only about rediscovering old titles, but also about new creation that expands the library of legendary computers with fresh pieces. For a player who likes straightforward action without unnecessary fuss, it is a welcome refreshment in a classic package.

**Why play:** Brisk run-and-gun action from the workshop of the modern C64 community, which bets on an uncompromising pace, distinctive music, and the joy of pure arcade shooting.

c64__briley-witch-chronicles-ish.article:
A JRPG on the Commodore 64 sounds like a contradiction. The genre of Japanese role-playing games surely belongs to consoles, not to an 8-bit home computer from the West. And yet it is precisely here that the modern homebrew scene shows its courage: games in the spirit of Briley Witch Chronicles bring to the C64 a world that this machine could scarcely have handled in the 1980s. Just immerse yourself in the first quest and you realize how much work and love hides behind such projects.

A JRPG is built on story, gradual character growth, and turn-based battles. The player travels through the world, talks to characters, completes quests, and gradually follows a narrative that unfolds over a longer time arc than in most arcade games. Battles take place on a separate screen, where decisions are made about attacks, spells, and tactics. For the Commodore 64 platform this means handling a large amount of text, music, maps, and game systems at once, which makes every such title an ambitious undertaking.

The modern homebrew approach to this genre is especially admirable because of its scope. Whereas an action game fits into a single load, an extensive role-playing game requires a well-thought-out data structure, a system for saving progress, and dozens of hours of content. The creators of the current C64 scene today know the machine's capabilities so well that they can carry such projects to a form that would have been hard to imagine in the days of the computer's commercial glory.

Such games often come out in a physical edition too, as a tribute to the classic era, complete with a manual and cover. They are proof that the community around the Commodore 64 is not only nostalgic, but also creative and ambitious. For a role-playing fan who likes pixel aesthetics and the sound of the SID chip, a JRPG on the C64 represents a unique experience on the border between retro and a new adventure.

**Why play:** An ambitious Japanese-flavored role-playing game that on the old Commodore proves the modern homebrew scene is not afraid even of the most demanding genres.

c64__l-abbaye-des-morts.article:
Some games win you over not with grandeur but with focused simplicity. L'Abbaye des Morts is exactly such a case. This platformer with captivating minimalist graphics and a dark atmosphere first appeared on other platforms and later found its way to the Commodore 64 thanks to enthusiasts of the homebrew scene. From the first screen it feels like a lost classic from the golden era of 8-bit computers.

In terms of gameplay, it is a classic platformer with exploration. You control a character who pushes through a sprawling monastery full of traps, chasms, and enemies, and your goal is to collect hidden items and find the way onward. The game bets on precise jumping, learning the layout of individual rooms, and on the atmosphere evoked by the sparse but distinctive graphics and gloomy setting. It is the type of game where every death teaches you and where progress is composed of patiently memorizing the safe paths.

The visual style of L'Abbaye des Morts is deliberately retro. The game imitates the look of computers that had a limited color palette and coarse resolution, and it makes a virtue of this limitation. The version for the Commodore 64 fits into this spirit perfectly, because the game's aesthetics and the machine's capabilities suit each other. The result is a title that looks as if it could have been released in the 1980s, and yet benefits from modern creators' feel for level design and atmosphere.

Such conversions show how interconnected today's retro community is. A game born in one environment travels thanks to fans to more and more platforms and lives on in the hands of new players. L'Abbaye des Morts is thus not only an interesting platformer but also a reminder that a good idea and honest design overcome the boundaries of individual machines and decades.

**Why play:** An atmospheric minimalist platformer with a dark touch, which comes alive on the Commodore 64 as a lost classic and rewards players with a feel for precise jumping and exploration.

c64__galencia.teaser: A modern Galaga clone; polished to the last detail.
c64__galencia.detail: A modern Galaga clone polished to the last detail (bonus phases, smoothness). One of the best new C64 shooters; popular as a physical cartridge too.
c64__galencia.article:
Some classics of the gaming world are so perfectly designed that it is enough to build on their foundations and add a modern shine to get a little treasure. That is exactly what Galencia did. This game for the Commodore 64 from 2017, from the workshop of Jason Aldred, is a tribute to the immortal arcade legend Galaga, and right from the first spaceship it is clear that this is no ordinary clone but a carefully polished piece.

The principle draws on the classic formation shooter. Your ship moves along the bottom edge of the screen and shoots down formations of alien attackers that descend in elegant curves. Galencia takes the proven core of Galaga, where enemies can capture your ship and you can win it back to double your firepower. To this it adds its own ideas, fluid movement, elaborate bonus phases, and an overall smoothness rarely seen on an 8-bit machine.

Technically, Galencia is one of the most admired modern C64 shooters precisely because of its smoothness and visual cleanliness. The game shows what an experienced programmer can pull out of forty-year-old hardware and radiates a shine that would hold up even among the best commercial titles of the golden era. The starry background, detailed sprites, and brisk pace make it an experience that is fun right away and where you want to improve your score.

Galencia also received a physical release in the form of a cartridge, which made it a favorite collector's piece among Commodore 64 fans. It is one of the flagship examples of how lively and high-quality today's homebrew scene around this machine is. For anyone who likes classic space shooters and wants to experience what a perfect Galaga on the C64 could look like, Galencia is a must.

**Why play:** A masterfully polished modern shooter in the spirit of Galaga, which ranks among the absolute top of new C64 games and entertains from the first minute with pure arcade action.

c64__hessian-mojon-twins-hry.article:
When someone says homebrew on the Commodore 64, most people imagine amateur attempts that are unplayable. The Mojon Twins are the exact opposite. This Spanish duo of developers proved that a retro platform from the 1980s is still alive to this day, and their titles often have a higher production level than many a period commercial game.

Hessian is one of their flagship projects, and it is an action platformer in the best sense of the word. The hero pushes through a labyrinth of hostile surroundings, collects equipment, searches for keys, and gradually opens up the way onward. The mechanics are built on the classic formula of exploration and combat, but with a feel for pacing and level design that forces the player to engage their head, not just their reflexes.

The strength of The Mojon Twins, however, does not lie in a single game. Their output is extensive and spans a range of 8-bit era platforms, from the ZX Spectrum through the Amstrad CPC to the Commodore 64 itself. Characteristic of them is a colorful, legible visual style and a sense of humor that seeps out of the titles and characters. Many of their games also come out under open licenses, so the community can further modify them and build upon them.

The cultural significance of this scene is enormous. It proves that retro hardware is not a museum exhibit but a living platform for which new, beatable, and often excellent games keep appearing. For C64 fans, discovering these titles is a little celebration, because they combine the nostalgia of a period look with a modern feel for playability.

With homebrew work it is always good to approach numbers with reserve, because verified data on sales or rankings usually does not exist for such projects. This, however, in no way diminishes the value of the games themselves, which is measured by playability, not marketing. And it is precisely here that The Mojon Twins excel.

**Why play:** If you want to see that the Commodore 64 is still alive and that contemporary homebrew can surpass many a period original, start here.

c64__star-wars.article:
Few licenses in the 1980s resonated as strongly as Star Wars, and when the vector arcade game from Atari appeared in arcades in 1983, it instantly became a legend. The home conversion for the Commodore 64, released around 1987, brought this experience right into players' living rooms and offered them the chance to sit in the cockpit of an X-wing fighter.

The game is a so-called rail shooter, that is, a shooter along a predetermined path. You see the world from a cockpit view and your task is to pass through iconic scenes from the first film, culminating in the attack on the Death Star and sending proton torpedoes into the fateful exhaust vent. The original arcade game was famous for its vector graphics made of lines, which the home versions had to imitate on hardware that was primarily built for raster graphics with sprites.

The development context is key here. Converting a vector arcade game to an 8-bit computer meant an enormous technical compromise, and the result naturally could not fully match the original. Even so, it was a valued effort to bring players at least a piece of the feeling that the big arcade machine offered. For many it was the first chance to experience the battle for the Death Star interactively.

Culturally, this game embodies an entire period when film licenses ruled the gaming market and when almost every major blockbuster was almost automatically converted into digital form. Star Wars was understandably one of the most sought-after brands among them, and its game adaptations became a phenomenon in their own right.

With the specific period figures and reviews of the home version, it is reasonable to remain cautious, because not everything is reliably documentable today. What is certain, however, is that the attack on the Death Star joined the ranks of the most memorable gaming moments of the early era and attracts players to this day.

**Why play:** For a nostalgic experience of the legendary attack on the Death Star and a taste of what film licenses looked like in the age of the 8-bits.

c64__empire-strikes-back.article:
A sequel must always live up to expectations, and with Star Wars this holds doubly true. The Empire Strikes Back on the Commodore 64 transports the player into one of the most iconic scenes of the entire saga, the icy battle on the planet Hoth, where the Rebellion stands against the giant walking machines of the Empire.

The core of the gameplay is an action shooter in which you control a nimble snowspeeder and try to stop the advancing AT-AT colossi. The key mechanic that every fan of the film remembers is wrapping the leg of the walking machine with a tow cable, which allows it to be knocked to the ground. This tactic carried into the game gives the battles a specific rhythm and forces the player to combine direct fire with clever maneuvering.

The game follows on from the previous arcade rendition of Star Wars and uses a similar visual language based on line-drawn, vector-flavored graphics. It was created at a time when film licenses were being turned into games as if on a conveyor belt and when players longed to relive the moments that had thrilled them in the cinema. The battle of Hoth was ideal material for this, visually striking and dramatically tense.

The cultural significance lies above all in how the game materialized one specific film sequence into an interactive form. Instead of diluting itself across the entire plot, it bet on a focused, intense experience of a single great battle, which was a clever approach given the technical possibilities of the time.

With detailed period data, such as exact ratings or sales figures of the home conversion, it is better to keep restraint, because reliable data has not been preserved for many titles of that era. What endures, however, is the memory of the feeling when you finally managed to knock down your first AT-AT.

**Why play:** For the chance to experience the legendary battle of Hoth firsthand and to try the iconic tactic with the tow cable against the walking colossi.

c64__star-trek-rebel-universe.article:
While most game adaptations of Star Trek bet on action, Star Trek: The Rebel Universe on the Commodore 64 took a different path. Instead of fast duels it offered strategy and simulation, in which the player takes command of the starship Enterprise and must think like a captain, not like a gunner.

The gameplay is built on managing the crew, exploring the galaxy, and making decisions that reach beyond a single shootout. The player distributes tasks among the familiar crew members, navigates between systems, and faces a threat that has engulfed an entire sector of the universe. The combination of a galaxy map, ship management, and tactical thinking gives the game the air of a captain's log, where every decision counts.

This concept fits well into the ethos of Star Trek itself, which was always more about exploration, diplomacy, and moral dilemmas than about pure gunfire. By placing emphasis on the strategic and simulation layer, the game tried to capture the spirit of the source material more faithfully than many a more action-oriented adaptation of the time.

It was created in a period when licensed games sought out all kinds of genre forms and when it was not unusual for a well-known brand to become more of a thoughtful simulation than an arcade game. For players who liked a slower pace and planning, it was a welcome refreshment in a sea of fast shooters.

With specific details about the development, sales, or period reception, it is appropriate to remain cautious, because there is not much verifiable data on this title. Its value lies mainly in the courage to conceive a famous license in an unconventional way and to bet on strategy instead of action.

**Why play:** If you enjoy commanding from the captain's chair and deciding the fate of an entire galaxy with reason rather than gunfire, this simulation is exactly for you.

c64__star-trek-strategic-operations-simu.article:
Sometimes the best way to enter the world of Star Trek isn't diplomacy, but a proper space battle. Star Trek: Strategic Operations Simulator offers exactly that, and on the Commodore 64 it delivers the experience of commanding a starship in direct combat with enemies among the stars.

The game is primarily a space-combat simulation. The player sits in the cockpit of the Enterprise, controls the phasers and photon torpedoes, and fends off waves of attackers, among which Klingon ships are not missing. The emphasis is on action and reflexes, but with that cosmic touch where you have to watch what's happening around you, aim, and time your fire in a space that feels three-dimensional.

The roots of this title reach back to an arcade machine that capitalized on the popularity of Star Trek, and the home version was meant to bring this experience into players' living rooms. Converting arcade action onto an eight-bit computer meant, as always, a number of compromises, but the goal was to preserve that addictive rhythm of repelling enemy attacks and piling up the score.

Culturally, the game represents an era when sci-fi brands and arcade machines fed off each other, and when every successful film or series tried to find its way into the games industry too. Star Trek was a constant among these licenses, and its action-oriented take appealed to players craving shootouts among the stars.

Because reliable period data about the home conversion for the C64 is fragmentary, it's reasonable not to overstate specific numbers or ratings. What does hold up, though, is the very essence of the game, namely brisk space action with a touch of one of the most famous sci-fi universes.

**Why play:** For straightforward space action at the controls of the Enterprise, ideal when you want mainly shootouts among the stars from Star Trek.

c64__silent-service.article:
The periscope breaks the surface, in the distance the silhouette of an enemy convoy takes shape, and you hold your breath. This scene played out in the minds of thousands of Commodore 64 owners in the eighties thanks to **Silent Service**, one of the titles that practically defined what a submarine simulator should look like.

Behind the game stand the legendary **MicroProse** and the name of **Sid Meier** himself, the designer who later became famous for the Civilization and Pirates! series. **Silent Service** puts you in the role of the commander of an American submarine operating in the Pacific during **World War II**. Your task is to hunt down Japanese ships, close in on convoys, and at the right moment launch torpedoes to send as much tonnage to the bottom as possible.

For its time, the game offered remarkable depth. The player switches between the **periscope, the map, depth and course control**, and the torpedo tube, calculates bearing and range, and decides when to attack and when to dive and escape the depth charges. All of this ran even on the modest C64 hardware, which was a technical feat in itself, because the game had to handle the simulation, the controls, and a clear presentation within limited memory.

What makes **Silent Service** stand out is the balance between accessibility and authenticity. It was neither a dry academic simulation nor a mindless shooter. It managed to evoke a sense of tension and command responsibility while remaining playable for the ordinary home computer owner. It was precisely this combination that made it an enormous success and one of the pillars on which MicroProse built its reputation as the king of simulators.

The game's cultural significance is hard to overstate. **Silent Service** ranks among the **founders of the genre** of submarine simulators and heralded a long line of successors as well as later sequels. It came out on a whole range of period platforms and for many players was their first contact with the idea that a computer game could credibly model a real machine and a real war. From today's perspective, it's a classic that stands at the beginning of an entire tradition.

**Why play:** A founding submarine simulator by Sid Meier and MicroProse that laid the foundations of the genre and can still evoke the tension of the hunt beneath the surface.

c64__prince-of-persia.article:
A slender figure breaks into a run, leaps across a chasm, and at the last moment catches the edge of a ledge — **Prince of Persia** on the Commodore 64 brings one of the smoothest and most realistic movement models of its time to an eight-bit computer. The game that changed the perception of what animation in a video game could look like tries, even in this version, to preserve the tension of a race against relentlessly ticking time.

At the core of the experience is the so-called cinematic platformer: the hero isn't controlled with arcade briskness but with realistic inertia, so that every jump and every duel demands deliberation. You claw your way through a labyrinth of palace dungeons full of traps — collapsing floors, spikes, and pits — and fight sword duels with guards. Above it all hangs a crushing one-hour limit within which you must rescue the princess from the power of the evil vizier Jaffar.

The original was created by Jordan Mechner and the game first came out on the Apple II in 1989. Mechner became renowned for using the rotoscoping technique, in which the character's animations were created based on filmed movements of a real person, which gave the game a hitherto unseen credibility. Conversions to a range of platforms including the Commodore 64 then carried this ambitious design onto weaker hardware, where fluid animation represented an exceptional challenge.

The cultural significance of Prince of Persia is fundamental. The game became a model for an entire genre, influenced later action-adventures, and its brand survived into the modern era, when the Ubisoft studio brought it back to life in a series of 3D games. Mechner's work with animation and storytelling foreshadowed the direction game design would take in the following decades.

On the Commodore 64, Prince of Persia is prized as a technically bold achievement and proof that even eight-bit hardware could carry a game built on detailed animation and atmosphere. For those who remember it, it's a return to a title that took your breath away; for newcomers, a glimpse of the roots of modern platforming.

**Why play:** For its pioneering realistic animation and a suspenseful race against time that laid the foundations of the entire cinematic-platformer genre.

c64__golden-axe.article:
A barbarian with a raised axe, an amazon with a sword, and a dwarf overflowing with rage — **Golden Axe** on the Commodore 64 throws players into a fantasy world where every step is paid for with the blood of enemies. This home conversion of Sega's legendary arcade brawler tries to bring the raw power and magical atmosphere of the original into the memory of the beloved eight-bit machine, and it's precisely this ambition that makes it an interesting part of gaming history.

The game mechanics honor the canon of the beat 'em up genre. You advance through the landscape, pummel waves of the villain Death Adder's minions, and choose from a trio of heroes with different strengths. Alongside ordinary blows and weapons, magic plays a key role, which you fill up by collecting vials of essence from stolen sprites — the more essence, the more devastating the spell. An unforgettable ingredient is the mountable beasts, which you can jump onto and turn their jaws and tails against your enemies.

Behind the original stands the Japanese company Sega, which brought Golden Axe into arcades in 1989 on the System 16 board. The game immediately captivated with its gritty fantasy aesthetic and cooperative two-player play. Conversions for home computers including the Commodore 64 were made in Europe, and programmers had to cram the grand source material into hardware that was never built for such an onslaught of characters and animations at once.

Culturally, Golden Axe ranked among the pillars of the genre and became one of Sega's enduring brands. It inspired a number of sequels and ports, and alongside titles like Double Dragon and Final Fight it defined what a party of heroes fighting through hordes of enemies should look like. Its fantasy world remained in players' memories as one of the most atmospheric in the entire genre.

On the Commodore 64, Golden Axe is necessarily a more modest echo of the dazzling arcade original, but as a historical document it has its value. It recalls a time when every big gaming hit had to find its way onto all home platforms, and when programmers wrestled with technical limits to preserve at least the spirit of the original.

**Why play:** For a fantasy slaughter with magic and mountable beasts, and a look at how the eight-bit Commodore struggled with porting an arcade legend.

c64__out-run.article:
Wind in your hair, a blonde in the passenger seat, and a red Ferrari Testarossa racing along a coastal road — that was the dream of the mid-eighties that Out Run brought straight from the arcade into the living rooms of Commodore 64 owners.

The original was created in 1986 for Sega by the legendary designer Yu Suzuki, and it was a revolution in several respects at once. Instead of a race for first place, it was about the pure joy of driving: the player fled against the clock from checkpoint to checkpoint, and at every fork chose for themselves which branch of the route to take next. This created five different endings and several distinct paths across the scenery — from desert through rocky canyons to snow-covered plains.

The arcade cabinet became famous for its moving cockpit, which tilted into the corners, and for its selection of music from the radio — tracks like Magical Sound Shower went down in the history of game soundtracks. The conversion to eight-bit computers including the Commodore 64 was released in Britain by U.S. Gold. The home versions necessarily had to sacrifice some of the smoothness and colorful splendor of the arcade, yet they tried to capture the true essence: the sense of speed, the branching tracks, and the iconic car.

On the modest C64 hardware, Out Run was a technical challenge, and the result was the subject of period debates about how much could be squeezed out of an eight-bit machine. Whether reviews praised or criticized the smoothness, the magic of the source material and the brand itself were enough for the game to find an enormous audience.

Out Run became one of the most influential racing titles of all time and kicked off a whole series of sequels and later remakes. Its DNA — arcade driving for pure joy, route selection, and a sunny atmosphere — still inspires developers around the world today.

**Why play:** For a nostalgic drive toward the sun that defined what the pure joy of speed should look like on an eight-bit computer.

c64__r-type.article:
A wall of enemy ships, giant organic bosses resembling a nightmare, and a single press that can change everything — R-Type is one of the hardest and most revered shoot 'em ups ever released, and its conversion to the Commodore 64 was a small miracle.

The original cabinet was released by the Japanese company Irem in 1987 and immediately set a new benchmark for the genre of horizontal shoot 'em up games. The key innovation was the so-called Force — a detachable satellite module that could be attached to the ship at the front or the back, served as both a shield and a weapon, and changed the entire tactics of flying through a level. The second iconic element was the beam charge: by holding down fire, the player charged a mighty blast capable of tearing through the enemies' defenses.

R-Type became famous for its uncompromising difficulty and design, in which the player had to learn the layout of each level almost by heart. The biomechanical visuals inspired by the work of H. R. Giger gave the game a dark, unsettling atmosphere, the kind that wasn't a given at the time.

The conversion for home computers was released in Europe by Electric Dreams, and the version for the Commodore 64 had to squeeze the extensive levels and elaborate mechanics into the bounds of an eight-bit machine. Even so, it preserved the essentials — the Force, the charged shot, and that characteristic feeling that every bit of progress is hard-earned.

R-Type became one of the longest-living brands of the genre, with a string of sequels across generations of consoles. For many players it remains the benchmark against which all other horizontal shooters are measured.

**Why play:** If you want to discover the roots of the modern shoot 'em up and test your nerves against one of the most demanding classics of the eight-bit era, R-Type is a must.

c64__rainbow-islands.article:
Rainbows instead of weapons, cute critters instead of enemies, and an all-pervading optimism — Rainbow Islands is a game that manages to be both sweet and surprisingly deep at the same time, and on the Commodore 64 it brought a hearty dose of colorful joy.

The arcade original was created by the Japanese company Taito in 1987 as a direct sequel to the Bubble Bobble phenomenon. The main hero Bub this time transformed from a little dragon into human form, and his main ability was creating rainbows. These served at once as stairs for climbing upward, as a bridge, and as a weapon — you just had to let the rainbow fall onto an enemy. The goal of each level was to climb upward as quickly as possible before the rising water level buried everything beneath it.

The game was famous for its hidden mechanics: collecting colored diamonds in the correct order, secret rooms, and an alternative ending that rewarded the most persistent players. So beneath the sugary shell lay surprisingly rich gameplay with room for mastery.

The conversion for home computers was released in Europe by Ocean, and the version for the Commodore 64 was among the well-done conversions of arcade hits of the time. The eight-bit machine couldn't fully capture the colorful splendor of the arcade, but the characteristic climbing design and the rainbow mechanic remained intact.

Rainbow Islands ranked among the beloved classics of the so-called Bubble Bobble series and is still remembered today as one of the most inventive platformer concepts of the eighties. Its lightness and colorfulness earned it a place in the hearts of an entire generation of players.

**Why play:** For an infectiously cheerful yet surprisingly thoughtful platformer, where every rainbow is at once a path upward and a tool of destruction.

c64__pac-man.article:
A yellow sphere with an insatiable appetite, four ghosts with their own personalities, and a maze that became an icon of pop culture — Pac-Man is perhaps the most famous video game in history, and on the Commodore 64 an entire generation of home players could play it.

The original was created for the Japanese company Namco by designer Toru Iwatani and arrived in arcades in 1980. Iwatani deliberately designed the game to appeal to female audiences too and to break free from the era's trend of space shooters. The principle was ingeniously simple: eat all the dots in the maze and avoid the quartet of ghosts, whereby after eating a large energizing pellet the roles reversed and the player could chase the ghosts themselves for a while.

Each of the four ghosts — Blinky, Pinky, Inky, and Clyde — had a different behavior pattern, which turned a game that at first glance seemed trivial into a surprisingly deep contest of reading the opponents' movements. Pac-Man became a worldwide phenomenon, gave birth to a mascot, an animated series, musical hits, and an endless number of imitators.

Several versions of Pac-Man and its variants came out on the Commodore 64, since the maze genre was extraordinarily popular on eight-bit machines. The home conversions brought the basic principle into living rooms and gave players the chance to chase the highest score without having to scrounge for coins for the arcade machine.

Pac-Man became a cultural symbol of the eighties and one of the few games recognized even by someone who never held a joystick. Its simplicity and addictiveness remain to this day a textbook example of perfect game design.

**Why play:** Because Pac-Man is a cornerstone of gaming history — a few seconds in the maze are enough to understand why the world fell in love with this yellow sphere.

c64__bard-s-tale.article:
Imagine the dark alleys of the medieval town of Skara Brae, held in the grip of the evil sorcerer Mangar, and a party of daredevils setting out into the freezing underground to stop the evil. Thus begins The Bard's Tale, one of the most influential dungeon RPGs of the eighties, which on home computers defined what a properly gloomy adventure should look like.

The game put you in the role of the leader of a party of up to six adventurers of various classes, whom you guided through labyrinths seen from a first-person perspective. It stood out for its scale, the number of enemies, and a combat system in which the composition of the party and the clever use of spells mattered. Unique was the bard character, whose songs could strengthen comrades or weaken enemies, which gave the game its unmistakable identity and its name.

The Bard's Tale was designed by Michael Cranford and published by Electronic Arts in the mid-eighties, at a time when the genre of computer RPGs was only just forming in the shadow of titles like Wizardry and Ultima. The game became an enormous success, gave rise to an entire series of sequels, and is among the titles that helped establish Electronic Arts as a significant player on the market.

The version for the Commodore 64, the best-selling home computer of all time, brought this gloomy world into countless households. The C64 was an ideal platform for RPGs thanks to its sufficient memory and popularity, and it was precisely on it that many players first savored the slow, atmospheric exploration of an underground full of traps and monsters.

Today The Bard's Tale is recognized as one of the cornerstones of the dungeon crawler genre, and its brand survived for many years, including a later comedically-tinged reboot and a modern return to the original style via crowdfunding. For anyone who wants to understand the roots of computer RPGs, it's an indispensable milestone.

**Why play:** It's an influential and atmospheric dungeon crawler that laid the foundations of an entire generation of computer RPGs, ideal for fans of slow, tactical adventure in the underground.

c64__ultima-iv-quest-of-avatar.article:
What if the goal of a game weren't to defeat an all-powerful villain, but to become a better person? This revolutionary idea stands behind Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar, a title that forever changed what we expect from games, and which to this day is considered one of the most significant RPGs of all time.

Unlike most adventures, here you're not supposed to save the world from a dark lord. Instead, you strive to become the Avatar, the embodiment of eight virtues, such as honor, compassion, humility, or justice. The game tracks your decisions and behavior, so if you lie, cheat, or rob the innocent, your path to virtue lengthens. This depth makes Ultima IV much more than just collecting experience and treasures; it's a philosophical pilgrimage through an open world full of towns, dialogue, and secrets.

Ultima IV is the work of Richard Garriott, the legendary designer performing under the name Lord British, and his studio Origin Systems. Garriott created the Ultima series as one of the flagship brands of the computer RPG, and the fourth installment in particular was his personal manifesto, a reaction to the criticism that games teach only violence. Thus a title with unprecedented moral reach came into being.

The version for the Commodore 64 made this vast world accessible to owners of the best-selling home computer of the eighties. The C64, with its memory and widespread adoption, was an ideal platform for a grand RPG, and Ultima IV offered on it a sprawling map that players could explore for dozens of hours.

Today Ultima IV is unreservedly ranked among the most important and influential games in history. Its system of virtues and its emphasis on moral decisions foreshadowed a whole decade of RPG development and inspired countless later titles. For anyone interested in how games matured and began to ask the big questions, it's an absolute classic.

**Why play:** It's a pioneering RPG that, instead of defeating a villain, explores morality and virtue, one of the most influential titles in history and a must for every fan of the genre.

c64__summer-games.article:
An Olympic fanfare, a crowd in the stands, and you with fingers sweaty from the joystick. That's what the pinnacle of sporting competition looked like on home computers of the eighties, and Summer Games from the California studio Epyx stood at the front line of it. This collection of summer disciplines became synonymous with what came to be called the "multi-event" sport, and for many Commodore 64 owners it was their first contact with what competing against friends at a single screen looks like.

The game's construction is ingeniously simple. You choose a country whose flag then flies over the stadium, and you gradually fight your way through a series of Olympic disciplines, from swimming through diving and gymnastics to sprints and other track-and-field events. Each discipline has its own controls, its own rhythm, and its own trick that needs to be mastered. Some require precise timing of a press, others frantic waggling of the joystick. It was precisely this variety that set Summer Games apart from the simpler titles of the time.

Epyx was in its day synonymous with quality action software for eight-bit machines, and Summer Games laid the foundation for an entire successful series. The game managed to extract unexpectedly colorful graphics and digitized sounds from the Commodore 64, and its ceremonial opening ceremony with the lighting of the flame and the flags was among the most spectacular opening scenes that home computers of the time offered.

The cultural footprint of this game is deep. Summer Games launched the genre of sports compilations, which was followed by a sequel as well as a winter variant and later countless imitators. For an entire generation of players it became the definition of what an "Olympics on the computer" looks like, and competing for the best time or the highest score in the living room with a bunch of friends became an unforgettable ritual.

Today Summer Games recalls how little it took to create a great social experience. No internet leaderboards, just you, a joystick, and the urge to beat the person next to you.

**Why play:** For nostalgia for an era when the Olympics were played at a single screen and the winner was decided by the calluses on your thumb, and to understand the roots of the entire sports-compilation genre.

c64__international-soccer.article:
Before the licensed mega-hits with real players and television cameras arrived, football existed in a simple but all the purer form. International Soccer for the Commodore 64 was one of the first titles that managed to capture the game on a home computer in a way that had real depth, and it became one of the most characteristic early sports experiences on this platform.

The game captivated above all with its presentation. The playing field was shown from a side, slightly angled view that gave the pitch perspective and depth, and the player figures were remarkably large and animated for their time. The controls rested on a single joystick button, but concealed surprising tactical variety, from passes and shots to defensive work. That made International Soccer a great game for two players at a single machine.

International Soccer was among the titles that Commodore distributed directly and that helped show what the eight-bit machine could do. At a time when the home computer was still seeking its identity as a gaming platform, this game served as a convincing calling card and long remained the reference football experience.

The cultural significance of the game lies in the fact that it set the bar. It showed that football could be conceived on a computer in an entertaining and addictive way, and it created a template from which later, more ambitious titles drew. For many players it was the very first football they played on a screen, and matches between friends dragged on late into the night.

Today International Soccer feels like a museum exhibit of its genre, but it still retains its immediate playability. It's a reminder of a time when one screen, one joystick, and an opponent at your side were enough.

**Why play:** For pure, immediately graspable football for two, and for a look at what football looked like at the dawn of home computers.

amiga__turrican-ii-final-fight.teaser: Peak of the series; huge levels and a cult soundtrack.
amiga__turrican-ii-final-fight.detail: The peak of the series on more powerful hardware: huge levels, secondary weapons and the cult soundtrack by Chris Hülsbeck, which ranks among the most famous game scores of all time. The essence of Amiga action.
amiga__turrican-ii-final-fight.article:
There are games that define an entire platform, and Turrican II: The Final Fight is exactly such a case for the Commodore Amiga. When the studio Factor 5 released the sequel to its cult action hit in 1991, it managed to make full use of the more powerful hardware and created what many consider the peak of the whole series.

At its core is run and gun action mixed with platforming and exploration. The player controls an armoured warrior armed with firepower that can be upgraded and switched between different types, fighting through huge, sprawling levels full of enemies and secret corners. The signature weapon is a laser whip that can be swung in all directions, and the ability to transform into an invulnerable spinning wheel is equally iconic. The combination of freedom of movement and non-stop action gives the game an unmistakable pace.

Visually and technically it was a demonstration of what the Amiga could do. The levels were enormous, full of detail and offered players room to explore that was not a given in the genre. Factor 5 built a reputation here as one of the most technically skilled studios on the European scene.

An inseparable part of the legend is the soundtrack by Chris Hülsbeck. His music for Turrican ranks among the most famous and acclaimed compositions in the history of game music, and to this day it is performed by symphony orchestras at concerts dedicated to video game soundtracks. For many players the opening theme of Turrican II is synonymous with the golden era of the Amiga.

The cultural significance of the series is undeniable. Turrican became one of the platform's icons and inspired generations of developers and players. The sequels and remasters that appeared in later years prove just how strong a mark the series left.

**Why play:** For the essence of Amiga action, huge levels to explore and one of the most legendary game soundtracks ever created.

amiga__another-world.teaser: Cinematic sci-fi adventure without text; an artistic milestone with influence to this day.
amiga__another-world.detail: An artistic milestone created almost single-handedly by one man (Éric Chahi) using vector (polygon) graphics. A cinematic sci-fi adventure without a single line of text or HUD — everything told through action and atmosphere. Huge influence on cinematic games to this day (Limbo, Inside).
amiga__another-world.article:
Occasionally a game appears that shifts our understanding of what the medium can do, and Another World from 1991 is one of them. This cinematic sci-fi adventure, also known abroad as Out of This World, was almost entirely the work of a single person, the French creator Éric Chahi, and became an artistic milestone whose influence we still feel today.

The story begins when a young scientist, during an experiment, is by unfortunate chance thrown into an alien, hostile world. From that moment the player fights through a mysterious environment, flees from predators, solves situations and gradually uncovers the unknown planet as well as an unexpected alliance. The gameplay mixes platforming, action and logic moments, but what sets it apart is the complete absence of text and a classic HUD. Everything is told exclusively through image, movement and atmosphere.

The technical heart of the game is its vector, polygon graphics. Instead of pixel sprites, Chahi relied on smooth outline animations that gave the characters and environment a cinematic, almost rotoscoped quality. The result was a visual style that felt like an interactive animated film and, at the time of its creation, looked utterly unlike anything on the market.

The cultural significance of Another World is enormous. It stood at the birth of the genre of so-called cinematic platformers, and its purely visual storytelling inspired entire generations of creators. Its legacy is evident in modern atmospheric games like Limbo or Inside, which rest on a similar principle of sparse, visual storytelling without unnecessary words.

The fact that such a complex and influential work came practically from the hands of a single person only underlines its exceptional nature. Another World gradually received a series of re-releases and remasters on the most varied platforms, which testifies to its timelessness.

**Why play:** For a timeless artistic experience that tells a breathtaking sci-fi story without words and stood at the birth of an entire genre of cinematic games.

amiga__flashback.article:
If you were enchanted by the atmosphere of games that feel like an interactive film, Flashback is another gem you must not miss. This French cinematic platformer built on the wave set by titles like Another World and pushed cinematic storytelling in game form a big step further.

The hero wakes up with no memory in an alien environment and gradually pieces together what happened to him and why enemies are after him. The gameplay combines platforming action, cautious exploration and puzzles, with a characteristic emphasis on realistic character movement. The hero does not climb or jump like a classic arcade figure but moves warily, grabs ledges, hesitates over chasms, and combat demands patience and timing.

Visually, Flashback became famous for its smooth, rotoscoped character animation, which gave movement an unprecedented believability. Between the individual acts, cinematic animated sequences were interspersed that advanced the story and gave it a pace reminiscent of a sci-fi film. This combination of movement realism and storytelling placed the game among the technically and artistically most advanced titles of its time.

Its cultural significance is considerable. Flashback belongs among the flagship representatives of the cinematic genre and helped establish a style of storytelling that built on atmosphere, plot and cinematic editing rather than pure arcade action. For many players it remains one of the strongest experiences on the Amiga and other period platforms.

The game was ported to a range of systems and, in later years, also saw attempts at sequels and modern re-releases, which shows how lasting a mark it left. Its confident fusion of gameplay and storytelling made it a lasting classic.

**Why play:** For a well-crafted sci-fi story, iconic rotoscoped animation and a cinematic experience that ranks among the very best of the cinematic genre.

amiga__shadow-of-beast.teaser: The Amiga's audiovisual showcase; parallax and music that amazed the world.
amiga__shadow-of-beast.detail: The Amiga's audiovisual showcase: up to 13 layers of parallax background and the hypnotic music of David Whittaker amazed the whole world with what a computer could do. Demanding and tough to play, but legendary as a technical demonstration.
amiga__shadow-of-beast.article:
There are games that are played, and games that are shown off. Shadow of the Beast from 1989 belongs to the latter group: when you first launched it on the Amiga, it was not so much about what you were doing as about what you were looking at and hearing. It was a stunning showcase of what the sixteen-bit machine of the day was capable of.

The game's most famous trick is its multi-layer parallax scrolling. The background unfolds into many planes that move at different speeds and create an impression of depth that no one had seen on home computers before. Added to this is the hypnotic, atmospheric music of David Whittaker, which to this day ranks among the most quoted work ever to come out of the Amiga. The audiovisual side was simply on a different level than the competition.

In gameplay terms it is an action platformer in which you travel through a bizarre, dreamlike world as a half-transformed hero and fight through hordes of enemies. And this is where the second side of the legend comes in: the game is notorious for its toughness and mercilessness. The battles are demanding, survival is short, and progress forward requires memorising and hard patience. Many players never reached the ending.

The studio Reflections, led by Martin Edmondson, created a title that was published by Liverpool's Psygnosis, famous for its lavish game covers. Shadow of the Beast became one of the brand's flagship titles and later saw sequels and a range of ports to other platforms, though not always in full Amiga glory.

Today the game is remembered above all as a technical demonstration and a symbol of an era. It is a work that showed how far computer graphics and sound could go, even at the cost of the game experience itself remaining frustrating. Even so, it earned a permanent place in the history of the Amiga.

**Why play:** For the unforgettable atmosphere, the legendary parallax and the music you will remember for a lifetime, even if the game may never let you go any further.

amiga__lemmings.teaser: The home platform of the phenomenon; brilliant logic.
amiga__lemmings.detail: The home platform of the phenomenon (see C64); on the Amiga in its full glory. Brilliant logic from the later creators of GTA.
amiga__lemmings.article:
Little green-haired creatures that march mindlessly toward certain doom unless you help them in time. Lemmings from 1991 ranks among the most brilliant logic games ever, and on the Amiga, its home platform, it showed itself off in full glory.

The principle is perfectly simple and at the same time inexhaustibly deep. A stream of lemmings pours from an opening, walking straight ahead, falling off cliffs and calmly striding into a chasm. Your task is to assign individual lemmings roles: diggers, bridge builders, blockers, floaters or, in extreme cases, the one who blows himself up. From the available abilities you must piece together a path that leads the required number of creatures to the exit.

The magic lies in how great depth arises from few rules. Each level is a puzzle that often has more than one solution, and the pressure grows with time and with the number of lemmings you are looking after. The game can be relaxed and insanely tense at the same moment.

Behind Lemmings stands the Scottish studio DMA Design, that is, the people who later created the Grand Theft Auto series. Even here you could see their sense for ideas, wit and gameplay. The title became an enormous commercial hit and was ported to just about everything that had a screen, from consoles to handheld devices.

Lemmings went down in history as one of the defining puzzle games of its time and still entertains today with its purity. It is proof that great game design does not need complexity, just a perfect idea taken to its logical conclusion.

**Why play:** A brilliantly simple idea with enormous depth; one of the best puzzles home computers ever received.

amiga__worms.teaser: Turn-based artillery with humour; immortal multiplayer fun.
amiga__worms.detail: Turn-based artillery with humour, where teams of worms bombard one another with crazy weapons (holy hand grenade sheep!) in destructible terrain. Immortal multiplayer fun on a single computer; the series lives on to this day. Team17 (now a publisher) started out with it.
amiga__worms.article:
Holy hand grenade sheep! If that sentence means something to you, you have probably spent more than one night with Worms, the turn-based artillery with humour where teams of little worms armed with the most absurd arsenal in the history of games face off against each other.

The basis of the game is actually the classic artillery scheme: you set the power and angle of your shot and try to hit your opponent across the rugged, fully destructible terrain, factoring in the wind as well. But Worms wrapped this old genre in crazy weapons, from the bazooka through exploding old ladies to the legendary sheep, and above all in an irresistible sense of humour. Every hit is a little comedic scene.

The absolute heart of the game beats in multiplayer on a single computer. You sit with friends at one machine, take turns and destroy each other's teams amid laughter and cursing. This form of fun turned Worms into a social phenomenon that works just as well today as in the mid-nineties.

Behind the game stands the studio Team17, for which Worms became such a fundamental brand that it develops it to this day, and it grew into a respected game publisher. Over the years the series expanded into dozens of instalments on the most varied platforms, but the core of the fun remains practically untouched.

Worms is today synonymous with witty turn-based strategy and one of the best examples of how fun is shared at a single screen. It is a title that does not age, because it is built on something timeless: on competitiveness and laughter.

**Why play:** An immortal multiplayer classic full of humour; ideal when you want to destroy each other's teams with friends at a single screen.

amiga__cannon-fodder.article:
War has never been so much fun, proclaimed the slogan, and yet Cannon Fodder ranks among the sharpest anti-war games of its time. This action strategy from the British studio Sensible Software managed to combine brisk, addictive gameplay with a surprisingly bitter subtext about the senselessness of war.

In gameplay terms it is a top-down action game where you control a small group of soldiers and send them with the mouse across jungles, snow and desert. By clicking you determine movement and fire, throw grenades and destroy buildings and vehicles. The missions are short, fast and devilishly catchy, but a single bullet means death, so you easily lose your men and every advance costs you something.

And this is precisely where that ingenious tension lies. The game is cheerful, colourful and playful, but at the same time it constantly reminds you of the cost of the fighting. Fallen soldiers get gravestones on the opening hill, and new recruits wait in line to replace them. That cold logic turns arcade fun into an unexpectedly powerful commentary.

Sensible Software, the authors of the famous Sensible Soccer, relied on their typical hallmark: tiny, cute little characters, clean design and instantly understandable controls. Together with the unforgettable opening song War, Cannon Fodder became one of the iconic Amiga brands of the first half of the nineties.

The game also stirred controversy over its use of poppy symbolism and its provocative tone, which only added to its reputation. To this day it stands as a great example of how a title can be entertaining and still have something to say.

**Why play:** Gripping top-down action with the mouse in hand and a bitter anti-war subtext; a catchy classic that entertains while making you think.

amiga__sensible-soccer.teaser: The definitive arcade football of the era; top-down view, pure fun.
amiga__sensible-soccer.detail: The definitive arcade football of the era: top-down view, tiny players, but surprisingly deep controls with ball "swerve". Fast, addictive, multiplayer king. It competed with Kick Off for the football throne.
amiga__sensible-soccer.article:
Before the realism of modern football simulations arrived, another king ruled the pitch: Sensible Soccer. This arcade football from 1992 deployed a bird's-eye view, tiny running players and, above all, such clean and immediate fun that it became the definitive form of the game of its era.

At first glance the game looks almost modest: tiny figures, a simple pitch, no grand graphics. But beneath that lies surprisingly deep control. The key is working with swerve, where after playing the ball you can, with a small movement, curve its trajectory and send brilliant crosses and uncatchable shots to the post. The controls are easy to grasp but take years to master.

The result is an incredibly fast, smooth and addictive game that excels above all in multiplayer. Matches against a friend were as fast as lightning and stirred the same passion as real football. It was precisely this immediacy that set Sensible Soccer apart from the competition.

And the competition was fierce. For the throne of the best football game on the Amiga, Sensible Soccer waged a bitter duel with the equally famous Kick Off. Players split into two camps, and debates about which title was better were part of the folklore of the community at the time. Behind the game stood the studio Sensible Software, masters of minimalist design and catchy gameplay.

Sensible Soccer gradually received a range of updated versions and sequels, and to this day it is remembered as one of the peaks of arcade sport. It is proof that fun does not need photorealistic lawns; a perfectly tuned game feel is enough.

**Why play:** Lightning-fast arcade football with a legendary ball swerve and great multiplayer; a classic that beats many a modern title on pure fun.

amiga__speedball-2-brutal-deluxe.teaser: Brutal futuristic sport; "Ice Cream! Ice Cream!"
amiga__speedball-2-brutal-deluxe.detail: A brutal futuristic metal sport (a mix of football and handball where you may injure your opponent). The stylish aesthetic of the Bitmap Brothers and the "Ice Cream! Ice Cream!" chant. Great multiplayer; an icon of the Amiga era.
amiga__speedball-2-brutal-deluxe.article:
Ice Cream! Ice Cream! Every Amiga player who ever tasted Speedball 2: Brutal Deluxe knows this chant from the fans in the stands. This brutal futuristic sport from 1990 took metal, violence and a stylish aesthetic and mixed them into one of the most muscular titles of its time.

Speedball is an invented sport somewhere between football and handball, played in a metal arena with a steel ball. The rules are simple: get the ball into the opponent's goal. The catch is that you may injure, knock down and send your opponents to the infirmary with impunity. Points are collected through goals as well as hard hits, so every match becomes an adrenaline-fuelled brawl in which both strength and tactics matter.

Visually it is a textbook example of the hallmark of the studio Bitmap Brothers. Their cool, metallic, almost industrial aesthetic with sheen and grey became their signature, and Speedball 2 is its peak. The game feels harsh, stylish and grown-up, which fit its theme exactly.

Besides the game on the field itself, the title also offers building your own team, buying players and upgrading their abilities, so it has strategic depth across a season. The absolute peak, however, is the multiplayer, in which two players batter each other for victory in a single arena, accompanied by that very famous chant.

Speedball 2 became one of the icons of the Amiga era and to this day stands as one of the best invented sports in the history of games. It even received later remakes, but the original retains its unmistakable charm.

**Why play:** A raw, stylish and addictive futuristic sport with the legendary atmosphere of the Bitmap Brothers; ideal when you want a metal brawl for two.

amiga__secret-of-monkey-island.article:
I always wanted to be a pirate. With this sentence begins the adventure of Guybrush Threepwood and one of the best adventure games ever made. The Secret of Monkey Island is a point-and-click gem from the studio LucasArts that shone on the Amiga with its humour, charm and cleverness.

The game takes you into a bizarre, funny world of Caribbean pirates, where the clumsy young man Guybrush tries to become a real sea dog. Gradually you must pass three trials, win the heart of governor Elaine and stand up to the evil ghost pirate LeChuck. The storytelling is brisk, full of puns and parody of the genre.

The gameplay is built on clicking the mouse: you combine verbs like take, use or talk with objects and characters and solve logic puzzles. Monkey Island became famous because, unlike many adventures of the time, you cannot die in the game or get stuck in an unsolvable state, which makes it a pleasantly welcoming experience. Absolutely cult is the insult sword fight, where it is not the sword but the sharp tongue that wins.

Behind the game stands Ron Gilbert together with Tim Schafer and Dave Grossman, and the whole series used the famous SCUMM engine. LucasArts defined the golden era of graphic adventures with this style, and Monkey Island became one of its most beloved brands.

The series continued with a number of sequels and, after decades, also received remastered editions with new graphics and voice acting. Even so, the original game holds its position as one of the peaks of the genre and a benchmark of game humour.

**Why play:** A funny, clever and ageless adventure with unforgettable characters and an insult sword fight; a must for every lover of point-and-click.

amiga__monkey-island-2-lechuck-s-revenge.article:
When you have one of the best adventures in history behind you, how do you surpass it? At LucasArts they answered in style: even bigger, even funnier and even more thoughtful. Monkey Island 2: LeChuck's Revenge is a sequel that took everything good from the first part and pushed it to a new level.

Guybrush Threepwood returns as a narrating braggart searching for the fabled treasure Big Whoop and once again gets tangled up in trouble with the zombie pirate LeChuck. The story is more extensive, leads across several islands and culminates in one of the most discussed and strangest endings in the history of games, which fans still debate to this day.

In gameplay terms it is a polished point-and-click in the SCUMM style. The puzzles are varied, funny and often very inventive, while the game again honours the rule that the player cannot die. The second part also introduced a choice of difficulty for newcomers as well as seasoned adventurers. Visually and aurally it was a big step forward, among other things thanks to the sophisticated dynamic music system iMUSE, which smoothly adapted the music to the action on screen.

The script was again worked on by Ron Gilbert, Tim Schafer and Dave Grossman, the trio that gave the genre of graphic adventures its golden standard. Their sense of humour, timing and absurdity made LeChuck's Revenge one of the most precious gems of the whole series.

Like the first part, the work later received a special edition with new graphics and full voice acting. For many players, however, the original Amiga and PC version remains the true one, and Monkey Island 2 one of the absolute peaks of the genre.

**Why play:** Even richer, funnier and more ambitious than the first part; a supreme LucasArts adventure with its notorious twist at the end.

amiga__indiana-jones-and-fate-of-atlanti.article:
There are a handful of moments when a game touches the legend of the silver screen and does not remain in its shadow. **Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis** is exactly such a case. Here LucasArts did not take the path of a mere adaptation but created an entirely new story that would stand without shame as the fourth part of the film series, which did not yet exist at the time. On the eve of the Second World War, Indy and the archaeologist Sophia Hapgood set off on the trail of the fabled Atlantis before it falls into the hands of the Nazis.

The game runs on the famous **SCUMM** engine and uses a point & click interface with a set of verb commands, at which LucasArts was a master. What sets Fate of Atlantis apart from most other adventures is the structure of progression: after the introduction, the player chooses one of **three paths** to the goal. The Team path (Wits, where Sophia accompanies you), the Fists path (with an emphasis on combat and action) and the solitary path (Team, where you solve everything yourself with ingenious puzzles). This choice fundamentally changes the playthrough and gives it a replayability that the genre at that time hardly knew.

The development context is key here. LucasArts, George Lucas's studio, had direct access to the Indiana Jones licence, and the team led by Hal Barwood and Noah Falstein managed to capture the spirit of the films, the light humour and the adventurous courage. It came out in 1992 first on PC, and the version for the Amiga followed and brought, on floppy disks, a somewhat more intimate but still impressive rendering of this extensive game.

Culturally it is one of the peaks of the golden era of adventures. Fate of Atlantis is to this day considered by many players and critics to be the **best game incarnation of Indiana Jones**, despite later 3D attempts. It became a benchmark for how a licensed game made with love and respect for the source material should look.

The magic lies in the dialogues, in the atmosphere of travelling around the world and in the ingenious puzzles, which are never so unfair as to spoil the enjoyment of the story. Sophia as a companion brings sparkling chemistry and humour, which LucasArts commanded like no one else.

**Why play:** A supreme adventure of the golden era that tells a story worthy of a film and, with three distinct paths, offers a replayability the genre rarely achieved.

amiga__beneath-steel-sky.teaser: The golden age of point & click adventures; humour, puzzles, story.
amiga__beneath-steel-sky.detail: The golden age of point & click adventures. Monkey Island (Ron Gilbert) is a witty pirate classic with legendary “insult sword fighting”. Fate of Atlantis is the best Indiana Jones game. Beneath a Steel Sky (Revolution) is a cyberpunk British gem (comic by Dave Gibbons). Humour, puzzles, story.
amiga__beneath-steel-sky.article:
From the parched Australian wasteland into the bowels of a dark metropolis where technology has swallowed humanity. **Beneath a Steel Sky** is a British cyberpunk adventure that managed to blend a bleak dystopia with typically island humour, becoming one of the jewels of the genre on the Amiga. The main hero Robert Foster is abducted from the wilderness into a city run by corporations and computer systems, where he must fight his way to the truth about his origins.

Development was handled by Charles Cecil's studio **Revolution Software** and the game was released in 1994. The comic artist **Dave Gibbons**, co-author of the legendary Watchmen, collaborated on the design, and his signature is evident both in the intro presented as a comic and in the overall visual style. This combination gave the game a unique aesthetic that set it apart from the competition.

In terms of gameplay it is a classic point & click adventure, but with its own control system and a faithful companion in the form of the robot Joey, whose personality chip can be transferred into various bodies. This mechanic brings an original dimension to the puzzles, and Joey is also a source of dry humour that lightens an otherwise oppressive world divided between the privileged upper floors and the desperate underclass.

The cultural significance of Beneath a Steel Sky is underlined by the fact that it became a cult classic, and Revolution later channelled its energy into the Broken Sword series. Moreover, in 2003 the studio **released the game for free** via ScummVM, giving it a second life among new generations of players. In 2019 a sequel titled Beyond a Steel Sky was also released.

On the Amiga the game demonstrated how a strong story and clever design can work even in a dystopian setting, which at the time was not very common in adventures. The atmosphere of a dirty futuristic city, corporate paranoia and questions about human freedom give the game a gravity that humour never overpowers, only pleasantly balances.

**Why play it:** A British cyberpunk adventure with the artistic signature of Dave Gibbons, clever puzzles and an atmosphere that holds up even after decades. And today it is legally free.

amiga__pinball-dreams-fantasies.teaser: The best video game pinball of its era; addictive.
amiga__pinball-dreams-fantasies.detail: The best video game pinball of its era, from the studio that later became DICE (Battlefield). Realistic physics and superb tables. Addictive; technically top-notch.
amiga__pinball-dreams-fantasies.article:
The click of a spring, a metal ball launched onto the playfield and hours that vanish before you know it. **Pinball Dreams** and its successor **Pinball Fantasies** showed that pinball on a computer need not be a poor substitute for a real machine, but a fully-fledged, addictive experience. On the Amiga they became a benchmark that no one could touch for a long time.

The games were made by the Swedish studio **Digital Illusions**, whose name later became famous as **DICE**, creators of the Battlefield series. Pinball Dreams was released in 1992 and Pinball Fantasies followed the same year with improved graphics, more elaborate tables and greater depth. Each of the titles offers several thematically distinct tables, from cosmic to sporting to musical.

The secret of the success was the **realistic physics** of the ball and brilliant technical execution. The game scrolled smoothly across long vertical playfields, the sounds of bounces and bumpers rang out convincingly and the overall feel of play came so close to a real machine that players lost track of time chasing a higher score. Score and the fight for the top spot are the very heart of the whole game.

Technically it was a showcase of what the Amiga could do when taken in hand by an experienced team. Smoothness, sound and controls were flawless and both games became a commercial and critical success. The series continued with Pinball Illusions and the concept was ported to a number of other platforms.

The beauty of these games lies in their immediate accessibility and at the same time in the endless drive to surpass oneself. You sit down for five minutes and get up an hour later. No complicated tutorials, no unnecessary fluff, just the pure joy of a well-crafted game mechanic.

**Why play it:** The best video game pinball of its era from the future creators of Battlefield, with realistic physics and an addictiveness that will glue you to your chair for hours.

amiga__superfrog.detail: Mascot platformers answering Sonic (the Amiga had no iconic platforming star of its own). Superfrog (Team17) is brisk and colourful, Zool (an alien ninja) became notorious for aggressive product placement (Chupa Chups). Brisk Amiga jumping.
amiga__superfrog.article:
When Sega had its Sonic and Nintendo its Mario, the Amiga desperately needed its platforming star. **Superfrog** applied for the role with all the energy a frog in a superhero cape can muster. This brisk and colourful platformer from the British **Team17** became one of the most enjoyable mascot platformers on Commodore computers.

The story is fairy-tale simple: a prince turned into a frog by a witch drinks a magical Lucozade potion (yes, it was also an advertising partnership) and gains superpowers to save his princess. The game was released in 1993 and offered sprawling, varied levels full of coin collecting, secret spots and bonus sections, among which even a shooter-style interlude is not missing.

In terms of gameplay Superfrog excels with **smooth movement** and responsive controls, which were considerable advantages on the Amiga, whose standard hardware was not ideal for fast scrolling. Team17, a studio later famous for the Worms series, put its sense for careful craftsmanship, animated intros and overall playfulness into it. The visuals are cheerful, the music catchy and the pace just brisk enough.

Culturally Superfrog fits into the period wave of efforts to give the Amiga a mascot that could compete with console stars. It shared this role with other titles, but thanks to the quality of its execution it stayed in players' memories as one of the best. Later years brought a remastered edition, Superfrog HD, which testifies to the enduring popularity of this frog.

At its core Superfrog is an honest platformer without grand ambitions to overturn the genre, but with perfectly tuned gameplay. It is the type of game one gladly returns to, because it simply fits the hand well and smiles at you from every screen.

**Why play it:** A brisk, colourful and perfectly controllable mascot platformer from the creators of Worms, which finally gave the Amiga a jumping star worthy of the console competition.

amiga__zool.article:
An alien ninja from the fifth dimension pushing his way through a world made of sweets. **Zool** was the Amiga's ambitious attempt to gain its own platforming icon that could rival Sega's Sonic. The acrobatic black ninja of gnome-like build became one of the most heavily promoted characters in computer gaming of the early nineties.

The game was released by **Gremlin Graphics** in 1992 and bet on **speed and acrobatics**. Zool can run on walls, climb and shoot, with the pace of the game markedly brisker than many contemporary competitors. The levels are packed with enemies and collectible items, and the first world, set in a landscape of candy and chocolate, became the visual calling card of the whole game.

Zool, however, went down in history not only for its gameplay but also as a textbook example of **aggressive product placement**. That sweet world was saturated with advertising for Chupa Chups lollipops, whose logo adorns the backgrounds and even the enemies. This commercial collaboration was remarkably conspicuous for its time and became one of the first striking cases of corporate advertising built directly into a game world.

In the context of the era, Zool was presented as a technological showcase of the Amiga's capabilities and the game enjoyed strong marketing support. It received a sequel, Zool 2, and ports to a number of other platforms, confirming its popularity across the gaming market of the early nineties.

Today Zool is interesting both as a solid fast platformer and as an artefact of a time when game makers were only just learning to work with advertising and mascots. That black ninja running across chocolate platforms remains an unmistakable symbol of the Amiga era.

**Why play it:** A fast, acrobatic platformer that wanted to be the Amiga's Sonic, plus a fascinating piece of gaming product placement history in the form of sweet Chupa Chups worlds.

amiga__project-x.teaser: Beautiful shmups; Apidya is a technical gem.
amiga__project-x.detail: Beautiful Amiga shmups. Apidya is a technical gem (insect theme, parallax, music), Agony a gorgeous owl shooter with painted backgrounds, Project-X a tough horizontal one. Showcases of the Amiga's graphical power.
amiga__project-x.article:
A wall of enemy bullets, the roar of the engine and decisions that must be made in a split second. **Project-X** from **Team17** is among the toughest that horizontal shooters offered on the Amiga. This technically polished shmup showed that the Commodore Amiga could spin the wheels of a genre otherwise built mainly by the Japanese on consoles and in arcades.

The game was released in 1992 and immediately earned a reputation as a **demanding** title. Project-X requires quick reflexes from the player, knowledge of enemy layouts and clever management of weapon upgrades, which gradually turn your craft into a flying arsenal.
