Retro enthusiasts appreciate Bomberman Max precisely for expanding the established concept without losing its brisk fun. It's one of those cases where the pocket version of a famous series didn't settle for copying the original and came up with an idea of its own.

game-boy-color__grand-theft-auto.article:
The notion that the entire original Grand Theft Auto could fit in the palm of your hand sounded almost absurd in 1999 — and yet **Grand Theft Auto (GBC)** exists and works. This cult curiosity brought the bird's-eye, top-down version of the controversial hit from DMA Design (later Rockstar North) to the Game Boy Color, and technically alone it's a remarkable piece.

The game preserves the original's core spirit: you move around open cities from above, steal cars, carry out missions for criminal bosses, and rack up points for the chaos you leave behind. Bringing it to such weak hardware naturally required concessions in the size of the cities and in the details, but the core of that anarchistic, sarcastic experience remained surprisingly legible. On a small console that most people associated with Mario and Pokémon, such a game felt almost provocative.

That's why the retro community keeps it in memory more as a fascinating rarity than as a full-fledged replacement for the PC version. It's a beloved proof of the developers' courage to attempt the impossible and an interesting coda to the era when GTA still ran in a bird's-eye view, before the series was reborn into three-dimensional form.

game-boy-color__perfect-dark.article:
When Rare conquered the Nintendo 64 with its spy shooter in 2000, it didn't forget the owners of the handheld console either — **Perfect Dark (GBC)** was created as a companion to the famous N64 version. It's not a mere port of the same game, but a standalone title that retold the story of agent Joanna Dark in a form suited to the capabilities of the Game Boy Color.

The gameplay mixes stealth action with a top-down view and rounds it out with a range of minigames and varied tasks, so the player isn't stuck with just one mechanic. Most interesting, however, is the link to the home version: via a link cable with the Nintendo 64, data could be transferred between the two games and bonuses unlocked, which at the time was an alluring way to tie the handheld and home experiences into one larger whole. With this, Rare demonstrated its traditional mastery of squeezing hardware to the max.

For retro gamers, the GBC version of Perfect Dark is more of an overlooked but likable little piece — solid pocket espionage with inventive elements. It's valued mainly as part of the broader Rare phenomenon and as a reminder of an era when a link cable between consoles promised small miracles.

game-boy-color__tony-hawk-s-pro-skater.article:
Few people in 2000 believed the famous skateboarding phenomenon could be crammed into an 8-bit handheld console — and yet **Tony Hawk's Pro Skater** on the Game Boy Color pulled off that near-impossible trick. While the big versions on the PlayStation set the tone for an entire generation, this miniature adaptation from studio Vicarious Visions took the heart of the game and translated it into an isometric 2D view that works surprisingly well on the small screen.

Here the player rides as real pros, led by Tony Hawk, completing objectives like collecting the letters S-K-A-T-E, reaching a score limit, or finding a hidden VHS tape, and above all chaining tricks into the longest possible combos. It's precisely the system of linking tricks, grinds, and manuals — which lets you sustain one huge combo across the entire map — that made the series famous, and Vicarious Visions got it onto the GBC in a surprisingly believable form. The controls are responsive, the pace brisk, and the urge for "just one more try for a better score" is just as addictive as on the big consoles.

For retro gamers, this port is small proof that limited hardware doesn't have to mean a stripped-down experience. It's one of those games that suit short sessions during a trip perfectly, yet you can easily spend hours polishing your personal records.

game-boy-color__croc.article:
The green little crocodile Croc was, at the end of the nineties, Argonaut's hope for a mascot that could rival Mario and Crash — and even though he never became a first-rate star, his pocket **Croc** on the Game Boy Color is a lovely reminder of that era. Studio Argonaut, which was also behind the technical side of the legendary Star Fox, took its original 3D platformer hit here and cleverly retold it in a classic 2D form suited to the small screen.

The player guides the adorable crocodile through colorful worlds full of jumping, collecting gems, and freeing furry creatures called Gobbos. The level design bets on classic platforming virtues — precise jumps, searching for hidden nooks, and simple but fun combat mechanics including Croc's characteristic tail whip. The graphics use the GBC's color capabilities to create a pleasantly cheerful visual that holds together even on the small display.

For collectors and fans of retro platformers, Croc on the GBC is a pleasant piece for the collection — no revolution, but an honest, accessible jumper with a charm of its own that's a good way to unwind. It recalls a time when every company had its cute animal hero and competed for the attention of young players.

game-boy-color__turok-2-seeds-of-evil.article:
When the brutal Nintendo 64 hit **Turok 2: Seeds of Evil** became a handheld game on the Game Boy Color in 1998, studio Bit Managers had to solve a fundamental problem: how to get a foggy first-person dinosaur shooter onto hardware that couldn't even dream of a 3D FPS. The solution was pragmatic and clever — instead of imitating the impossible, they bet on isometric top-down action that preserved the source's atmosphere and arsenal.

In the role of the hunter Turok, the player fights through exotic swamps and temples, wipes out dinosaurs and alien monsters, and collects the typically over-the-top weapons the series was famous for. It's precisely this transfer of that wild, somewhat pulpy aesthetic of prehistoric beasts and sci-fi cannons into two-dimensional action that makes this version an intriguing curious artifact. The game combines shooting, key hunting, and exploration of intricate levels.

Retro enthusiasts appreciate exactly this creative courage — instead of an embarrassing FPS substitute they got a distinctive action game that honors the spirit of the original. It's no unforgettable gem, but as an example of how licensed ports were approached in the days of strict hardware limits, Turok 2 on the GBC is definitely interesting.

game-boy-color__alone-in-dark-new-nightm.article:
Survival horror on the Game Boy Color? It sounds almost absurd, and yet in 2001 **Alone in the Dark: The New Nightmare** proved that fear can be evoked even on a handheld. While the big PlayStation and Dreamcast versions drew on pre-rendered backdrops and cinematic atmosphere, this GBC adaptation tried to carry the essence of the genre – dread, loneliness and tension – into an 8-bit world.

The player explores a dark house full of mysteries, solves logic puzzles, collects items and keys and faces monsters that a flashlight and light often defeat more effectively than brute force. The very interplay of light and darkness, the central mechanic of the whole New Nightmare brand, was carried into the handheld version with surprising ingenuity and gives the exploration the tension it needs. Firearms round out the combat, but the game relies on atmosphere and the gradual unfolding of its story more than on action.

For retro gamers this title is a fascinating showcase of ambition – an attempt to squeeze a grown-up, atmospheric genre into a format meant more for colourful platformers. It is not without flaws and technical compromises, but that very daring to attempt the impossible makes it a remarkable piece for collectors and lovers of unconventional retro experiments.

game-boy-color__disney-s-aladdin.article:
Disney's **Aladdin** is one of the most iconic licensed games of the nineties, and its 1999 Game Boy Color version carries a stamp of quality right on the box – development was overseen by Capcom, a master of the colourful action-platformer genre. That alone promised not a slapdash movie cash-in, but an honest platformer.

The player guides Aladdin through the alleys of Agrabah, across rooftops, the Cave of Wonders and even a flying carpet. Besides precise jumps he can throw apples as a weapon, slide down ropes and enjoy playful chutes that vary the pace. The GBC colour palette shines here – the sun-drenched desert scenery and the familiar characters from the film give the game an instantly recognisable Disney atmosphere. The levels are designed with a feel for fluid movement and offer a pleasant, accessible difficulty suitable even for younger players.

For fans of retro platformers and Disney classics, Aladdin on the GBC is a reliable choice – charming, colourful and solidly crafted. It may not rank among the toughest challenges, but its warm, fairy-tale tone still delights anyone who loves classic platformers based on animated films.

game-boy-color__tarzan.article:
When Disney released the animated **Tarzan** at the end of the nineties, a video game adaptation was inevitable – and on the Game Boy Color it was handled by Digital Eclipse, a studio known for its feel for craftsmanlike handheld games. The result is a colourful platformer that tries to capture the free, dynamic movement of the jungle hero.

The player leads Tarzan through dense jungle, swinging on vines, sliding along branches and trees and gliding through levels at a pace meant to evoke the film's action. Besides classic jumping and battling enemies, the game bets on that sense of fluid movement through the treetops – the swinging and sliding are its signature. The visuals make good use of the GBC's colour capabilities to render a richly green jungle environment and the well-known characters from the film.

As a licensed title aimed mainly at a younger audience, Tarzan offers no deep challenge, but it is conscientiously made, accessible fun. For retro gamers and collectors of Disney titles it makes for a pleasant piece in the collection – a solid handheld platformer that respectably carries the atmosphere of the animated original onto the small screen.

game-boy-color__legend-of-river-king-2.article:
Most RPGs send you off to hack monsters with a sword – **The Legend of the River King 2** instead puts a fishing rod in your hand. This unassuming gem on the Game Boy Color, from Natsume, the studio behind the beloved Harvest Moon, blends a calm fishing simulation with an adventurous quest to create one of the most unusual experiences on the console.

The story is touchingly simple: the hero sets out on a journey to save his sick sister, for which he must catch a legendary fish. As he wanders the countryside, the player explores rivers and lakes, lures fish with bait, wins the struggle against them through a line-tension system, and uses his catches to grow stronger and progress further. That mix of leisurely fishing, gentle RPG progression and map exploration creates a surprisingly addictive rhythm that soothes and at the same time tempts you into another cast.

It is precisely for this unhurried, meditative atmosphere that River King has won a devoted cult following. In an era ruled by action hits, it offered something different – a laid-back game about patience and communion with nature. For retro gamers looking for an unconventional, calm title outside the mainstream, it is a little treasure.

nds__999-nine-hours-nine-persons-nine-do.article:
Nine strangers wake up imprisoned on a sinking ship, numbers on their wrists and the only way out leading through doors marked with digits – that is how **999: Nine Hours, Nine Persons, Nine Doors** begins, one of the cleverest visual novels ever released. This 2009 title from Chunsoft became an icon of the genre and launched the beloved Zero Escape series.

The game ingeniously combines two layers: a gripping narrative full of psychological pressure and deadly dilemmas, and escape rooms in which the player searches the environment and solves elaborate puzzles to move forward. The true genius, however, lies in how 999 uses the two screens of the Nintendo DS – the split between the top and bottom display is not merely cosmetic but becomes a direct part of one of the cleverest plot twists in the history of the genre. Multiple endings compel you to replay the game and uncover further layers of the truth.

For retro gamers and fans of narrative games, 999 is a must. It is a tense thriller that plays with themes of faith, sacrifice and the human psyche, while perfectly exploiting the specifics of the hardware it launched on – something the remasters on other platforms could never fully replicate.

nds__dragon-quest-v-hand-of-heavenly-bri.article:
Few JRPGs dare to tell a story spanning three generations of one family – **Dragon Quest V: Hand of the Heavenly Bride** did it back in 1992, and its 2008 remake on the Nintendo DS finally brought this exceptional saga to the West in full glory. Many fans still regard it as the pinnacle of Square Enix's entire famous series.

The player lives through the hero's life journey from childhood through adulthood to the moment he becomes a father himself – and his children join the party. It is this cross-generational story arc, steeped in love, loss and fateful choices (including the unforgettable choice of bride referenced by the subtitle), that gives the game an emotional depth long unique in the genre. The battle system also lets you catch defeated monsters and recruit them into the party, making Dragon Quest V one of the forerunners of mechanics that Pokémon would later make famous.

The DS remake added more detailed graphics, new content and a long-awaited official translation. For retro gamers it is the ideal gateway into the world of Dragon Quest – a moving, timeless story combined with classic turn-based combat that ages with incredible grace.

3ds__legend-of-zelda-majora-s-mask-3d.article:
**The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask 3D** is a return to the strangest and darkest entry in the whole series — and at the same time proof that even after fifteen years Nintendo can carve a classic into a more perfect shape. The original game from 2000 was created in record time thanks to the Ocarina of Time engine and became famous for the oppressive atmosphere of a dying world: above the town of Clock Town hangs a giant, mocking moon that will fall in three days and destroy everything.

The whole game rests on a relentless cycle of time. You have only seventy-two in-game minutes before the world ends — then, using the Song of Time, you return to the start of the first day and everything begins anew. The characters live out their own schedules, keep appointments, go through small dramas, and you try to understand and save them. The masks are essential: by transforming into a Deku, a Goron or a Zora you gain entirely different abilities and views of the world. The 3DS version adds improved graphics, a reworked saving system, clearer time management through the Bombers' Notebook and gentler combat. Retro gamers love Majora precisely for that melancholy, existential weight and how boldly it breaks away from the rest of Zelda — it remains one of the most distinctive adventures Nintendo has ever released.

3ds__kirby-planet-robobot.article:
**Kirby: Planet Robobot** ranks among the very best that HAL Laboratory delivered on the Nintendo 3DS — it is a sharp, inventive and surprisingly polished 2D platforming gem that takes the proven formula of the pink glutton and gives it an entirely new dimension. This time the planet Popstar is invaded by the mechanized Haltmann Works Company, and Kirby confronts it at the wheel of a robotic suit.

The heart of the game is the Robobot Armor — a mech Kirby hops into and through which he copies the abilities not only of enemies but also of the machines around him. Scan mode turns the mech into, say, a power plant, a drill or a cannon, opening paths that an on-foot Kirby could not manage. The classic swallowing and copying of abilities remains, but the mech plays out combat and puzzle situations on a larger scale, including flashy camera rotations into 2.5D. The console's stereoscopic 3D effect is also put to use, lending the levels depth. Retro fans prize Planet Robobot for its perfectly tuned pacing, witty industrial style, catchy music and bonus modes like Meta Knightmare Returns. It is one of those Kirbys that even seasoned players put down with a smile and an appetite for another run.

nes__super-mario-bros-2.article:
**Super Mario Bros. 2** is the strangest and most magical black sheep of the whole series — a game Western players love precisely because it differs so conspicuously from the rest of Mario. Its secret is well known: the Japanese sequel was too cruel for Americans, so Nintendo repainted its game Doki Doki Panic in Mario garb and released it in 1988 in the West as a full-fledged sequel.

All the oddities spring from this. You do not jump on enemies' heads — instead you pull vegetables from the ground and throw them at foes, lift and carry objects and opponents, and fight your way through the dreamlike world of Subcon. For the first time you also choose from four characters: the balanced Mario, the high-jumping Luigi, the strong Toad and the floating Princess Peach, each with different abilities suited to different sections. Iconic enemies who later became fixtures of the whole series appear here — Shy Guy, Bob-omb, Birdo and Pokey. Even though it is really a repainted different game, retro gamers embrace it as a classic in its own right, full of imagination and colour. To this day it feels refreshing precisely because of how boldly it overturns the rules we are used to in Mario.

nes__teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-ii-arc.article:
**Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles II: The Arcade Game** is one of those rare cases where an entire arcade hall fit straight into the living room — and did so with admirable fidelity. Konami took its immensely popular 1989 arcade brawler and in 1990 brought it to the NES so successfully that it was one of the best licensed games of the whole console generation.

The gameplay is pure beat 'em up joy: you pick Leonardo, Michelangelo, Donatello or Raphael and fight through the streets of New York, burning buildings and sewers against endless waves of Foot Clan soldiers, all the way to bosses like Bebop, Rocksteady, Krang and, of course, Shredder. The character animations faithfully follow the cartoon series of the time, the colours are fresh and the hits have punch. The key to the fun is two-player cooperation — beating up enemies together on one screen is pure nostalgia. Konami also added two exclusive levels and bosses to the NES version that were not in the arcade. Retro gamers remember this game fondly precisely for that perfect harmony of licence, controls and co-op fun — it is a textbook example of how to make a good game based on a series.

nes__teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-iii-ma.article:
**Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles III: The Manhattan Project** is proof that Konami did not rest on its laurels with its turtle licence. While the second game was an arcade port, the 1992 third instalment was created directly for the NES as a standalone brawler tailored to the home console — and in many ways it surpasses its predecessor.

The foundation stays, but everything is richer. Shredder himself has lifted the island of Manhattan into the air, and the four turtles set out to save it across varied levels from beaches through trains to an airborne fortress. New attacks were added, including special moves and the ability to grab and throw an enemy, making combat swifter and more varied than in the second game. The game technically taps the NES to the full — large, detailed animated sprites, fluid movement and lots of enemies on screen at once. The excellent two-player cooperative mode, the soul of the whole series, still works too. Retro fans often rank the third game among the best beat 'em ups on the NES ever, because it offers more content and depth without losing that immediate fun of beating up the Foot Clan side by side with a friend.

nes__ice-climber.article:
**Ice Climber** is one of the cornerstones of the early NES era — one of those simple yet immensely characterful games that defined what fun looked like at the beginning of the eighties. The pair of mountaineers Popo and Nana climb ever higher up snowy mountains, floor by floor, toward the summit, where the flying bird Condor awaits them.

The gameplay is built on vertical progression: with a hammer you smash the icy ceilings above your head to break a way into the next floor, all while dodging polar bears, seals and falling ice blocks. The jumping is deliberately clumsy, and the precise timing of jumps onto disappearing platforms makes the game a real challenge — Ice Climber never spared the player's patience. There is also a two-player cooperative mode, which is as much about cooperation as about tripping each other up. Today the game is known mainly because Popo and Nana became fighters in the Super Smash Bros. series, winning over a whole new generation of fans. For retro gamers Ice Climber remains a fond reminder of a time when a simple idea and steep difficulty were enough to write a game into Nintendo's history.

nes__balloon-fight.article:
**Balloon Fight** is a small, timeless gem whose magic, as few people realize, owes much to none other than Nintendo's future president Satoru Iwata, who had a hand in programming it. At first glance it resembles the arcade hit Joust, but thanks to its refined physics and flawless controls it became a classic in its own right, one that ages with remarkable grace.

The concept is simply brilliant: your character floats on two balloons and rises by flapping its wings. The goal is to get above your opponents and pop their balloons before they pop yours. Whoever loses their balloons falls down, and beware of the water and the fish lurking at the surface. The charm of the game lies precisely in the momentum of movement: the character doesn't obey on command, it glides and drifts, so mastering its flight takes feel and practice. The simultaneous two-player mode is especially great, letting you cooperate as well as sabotage one another, and there's also the brisk bonus mode Balloon Trip. Retro gamers love Balloon Fight for that purity of design, a textbook example of how a simple mechanic taken to perfection holds up even after decades.

nes__duck-hunt.article:
**Duck Hunt** is one of the most iconic symbols of the entire NES era, a game recalled even by people who never owned a console. Its magic lay in the Zapper light gun, which turned the living room into a shooting range as the player aimed straight at the TV screen.

The concept was simple and addictive: ducks fly up out of the grass and you have to shoot them down before they escape off screen. Miss too many shots and you lose the round. Alongside the ducks, the game also offered a variant with clay-pigeon shooting. The most unforgettable element, though, became the hunting dog, that loyal four-legged companion who retrieves the ducks you shoot down, but when you miss, he pokes his head out of the grass and laughs at you mockingly. That dog earned a place in gaming history as one of the first video-game trolls. Technically the Zapper worked on a clever principle of sensing the screen's brightness, so the game could only be cheated on classic CRT televisions. Duck Hunt was often sold bundled together with Super Mario Bros. and thus became, for millions of people, their first encounter with Nintendo. For retro gamers it's pure nostalgia and an immortal piece of eighties pop culture.

nes__metal-gear.article:
**Metal Gear** is one of the most pivotal games in the history of the medium, this is where Hideo Kojima laid the foundations of the entire stealth genre and launched the legendary series that made him famous around the world. The original game from 1987 came out on the MSX2 computer, and its vision was revolutionary for its time: you're not meant to overpower the enemy by force, but to avoid him.

As soldier Solid Snake you infiltrate the fortress of Outer Heaven to destroy the walking war machine Metal Gear. Instead of shooting mindlessly, you sneak through the shadows, dodge the guards' lines of sight, hide behind walls and look for ways to slip past unnoticed. You collect weapons and equipment gradually and have to think about whether to get into a fight at all. This emphasis on stealth, tension and planning was utterly groundbreaking in an era of mindless action shootouts. The 1987 NES version reached the West as most players' first encounter with the series, but it was adapted without Kojima's oversight and carries its flaws: altered levels, a weakened finale and the infamous line about contacting your commander. Even so it remains historically hugely important: for retro gamers it's a fascinating look into the cradle of a genre from which one of the most acclaimed stories in gaming later grew.

nes__gradius.article:
Few shooters left as deep a mark on the genre as **Gradius**. In 1986 Konami brought to the NES a revolutionary idea that dozens of games still copy today: gradually upgrading the Vic Viper ship through your own choice. You collect orange capsules, which light up a bar at the bottom of the screen, and at the right moment you pick what you want to upgrade, speed, double shots, laser, Options (satellites that mirror your fire) or a shield. That freedom turns you into a strategist before you even fire a shot.

The game became famous for a difficulty that mercilessly punishes every mistake: lose your ship and you lose all your upgrades too, returning to a bare Vic Viper right into the ongoing chaos. That's exactly why Gradius is so inseparably linked to the legendary **Konami Code** (up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A), which hands you a full loadout at the start, players passed it around like a secret incantation.

Retro enthusiasts love Gradius for its clean, precise design and iconic bosses, including the pulsating brain Big Core. It's a game you learn by heart, level by level, and every successful run through a volcanic or organic stage is a small victory. A cornerstone of the whole series and of the entire genre of upgrade shmups.

nes__ghosts-n-goblins.article:
There are hard games, and then there's **Ghosts 'n Goblins**, a title whose name became a synonym for sheer gaming frustration. In 1986 Capcom sent knight Arthur onto the NES to rescue an abducted princess, and the very first enemy hit strips off his armor: Arthur finds himself in nothing but white underpants, and a second hit means death. This merciless two-hit logic sets the tone for the whole game.

You fight your way through graveyards, burning villages and icy caves full of zombies, demons and flying bird-monsters, throwing spears, daggers or torches. Enemies keep pouring in without pause, and precisely timed jumps across disappearing platforms will test even seasoned players. The peak of sadism is the ending: after finishing the game, it tells you it was all "a trap of the devil," and you have to play the whole run **again and harder** to reach the true ending.

And yet, or perhaps precisely because of that, retro gamers keep coming back to Ghosts 'n Goblins. The game has an irresistible gothic charm, a catchy soundtrack and that addictive "just one more try" loop. It spawned a famous series (Ghouls 'n Ghosts, Super Ghouls 'n Ghosts) and to this day remains a badge of honor for anyone who beats it.

snes__teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-iv-tu.article:
When people talk about the perfect arcade brawler, many think of **Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles IV: Turtles in Time**. Konami built this classic on its 1991 arcade cabinet and in 1992 brought it to the Super Nintendo in a form many fans consider even better than the original. You pick Leonardo, Michelangelo, Donatello or Raphael and set off through quadrants of spacetime to pacify Shredder and Krang's Foot Clan.

The game is packed with moments that stick in your memory. The most famous is throwing enemies "**into the screen**," you grab a Foot Clan soldier and hurl him straight toward the player until he shatters against the glass. Time travel takes you to pirates, to prehistory among the dinosaurs, to the Wild West and to a neon future, and each era has its own enemies and atmosphere. Two-player co-op is fun of exactly the kind that gave rise to the beat 'em up genre.

The retro community loves Turtles in Time for its snappy controls, excellent pixel art, catchy music and bosses like Metalhead or Super Shredder. The SNES version added exclusive levels and boss fights and became the benchmark against which other Turtle games are measured. It's pure gaming joy that anyone can pick up and no one tires of.

snes__final-fight.article:
**Final Fight** is one of the cornerstones on which the entire beat 'em up genre stands. Capcom conquered the arcades with it in 1989 and in 1991 brought it to the Super Nintendo as one of the console's flagship launch titles. The story is classically straightforward: mayor and former wrestler Mike Haggar, together with Cody and Guy, set out to clean up Metro City from the Mad Gear gang, which has kidnapped Haggar's daughter Jessica.

The game puts a trio of fighters with distinct styles in your hands, the hulking Haggar dishes out suplexes, the nimble ninja Guy lands quick combos, and the balanced Cody is the ideal starting point. You claw your way through streets, the subway and an elevator full of enemies, smashing barrels and phone booths for bonuses, and in the famous bonus round you demolish a car. The SNES conversion had its limitations (the character Guy and two-player co-op were missing, and some enemies were censored), yet it remained extraordinarily popular.

Final Fight's legacy is enormous: from here Guy moved permanently into the world of Street Fighter, and a number of characters and places became interwoven with the Capcom universe. Retro gamers appreciate the punchy feel of the blows, the iconic design of the Mad Gear gang and the raw atmosphere of a crumbling 1980s metropolis. A blueprint the genre learned to walk by.

snes__super-mario-all-stars.article:
**Super Mario All-Stars** is, for Nintendo fans, something like the holy grail of collector's care for one's own classics. In 1993 Nintendo released a collection on the Super Nintendo that reforged the plumber's entire golden era into 16-bit graphics and sound: Super Mario Bros., the lost and brutally hard Lost Levels (until then practically unknown in Europe and America as "the Japanese second game"), Super Mario Bros. 2 and the monumental Super Mario Bros. 3.

This is no mere port, the games got completely redrawn backgrounds, smoother animation, improved music and, above all, a **save system** that was missing in the original NES versions. Thanks to it you can enjoy even the most demanding sections without endlessly repeating from the start. All wrapped into a single cartridge, with a clear selection menu.

Retro enthusiasts love this compilation as the best way to play through Mario's history all in one place and in the best possible form. For many Europeans and Americans it was the very first chance to play the legendary Lost Levels. There's also a rarer variant with Super Mario World added, which collectors still crave to this day. All-Stars is a textbook example of how to care for a classic with respect.

snes__r-type-iii-third-lightning.article:
When someone in 1993 wanted to show what a 16-bit horizontal shooter could do, they reached for **R-Type III: The Third Lightning**. Irem, the fathers of the whole R-Type series, created exclusively for the Super Nintendo one of the most beautiful and demanding shooters of the time, visually rich, with detailed metallic ships, organic enemies and bosses half a screen in size.

At the heart of the game remains the iconic **Force** module, an indestructible orb you attach in front of or behind your ship, using it as both a shield and a weapon and juggling it strategically according to the situation. The third installment also adds three types of charged fire to switch between: the classic wave laser, the Bounce laser that ricochets off walls, and the deadly Shadow laser. It's precisely choosing the right weapon for a given stage that makes R-Type III a thinking affair, not just reflexive shooting.

Retro gamers value R-Type III for its relentless but fair difficulty, where death usually stems from your own mistake, not unfair design. The slower, deliberate pace forces you to learn the level layouts and bosses by heart. For connoisseurs of the shmup genre it's one of the pinnacles of the 16-bit era and one of the most sought-after SNES shooters of all.

snes__final-fantasy-mystic-quest.article:
**Final Fantasy: Mystic Quest** is a black sheep and a beloved underdog rolled into one. Squaresoft created it in 1992 as a deliberately simplified JRPG aimed at Western players who didn't yet know the genre well, it was meant to be a friendly entry gate into the world of turn-based battles, magic and heroic quests. Fans of the main series still argue to this day whether it was a step sideways or a clever move.

The game simplifies everything compared to a traditional Final Fantasy: the character moves along a clear world map between individual points, the battles are more direct, and there are convenient touches like visible enemies and the ability to use your weapons to break obstacles right in the environment. The battle system is lightweight but still offers tactical decisions with a choice of spells and attacks. On top of that, composer Ryuji Sasai's soundtrack is among the most energetic RPG music ever heard on the SNES.

The retro community takes a more conciliatory stance toward Mystic Quest than it once did. Yes, for a seasoned RPG player it's tame, but as an entry game for a beginner or for a relaxing afternoon it works splendidly. Its catchy music and stress-free pace make it a pleasant, undemanding gem of the 16-bit era.

mega-drive__splatterhouse-2.article:
On the SEGA Mega Drive, where colorful platformers and speedy hedgehogs reigned, **Splatterhouse 2** felt like a dark intruder from another world. In 1992 Namco brought out the sequel to its horror beat 'em up, in which the hero Rick dons the sinister **Terror Mask**, a talking mask that lends superhuman strength, and throws himself into a fight to rescue his girlfriend Jennifer from the realm of the dead.

You battle through walls of pulsating flesh, rotting corridors and hordes of monstrosities inspired by classic horror films. Rick dishes out blows with his fists and with improvised weapons, beams, cleavers, a shotgun, and the atmosphere is unusually brutal and disturbing for its time and platform. The bosses tend to be a grotesque parade of bodily horror, and the game prides itself on a gloomy, oppressive tone rarely seen on the Mega Drive.

Retro gamers love Splatterhouse 2 precisely for this courage to go against the current. It's a game that doesn't want to be cute, it wants to give you goosebumps and offer raw, dense action. Part of a cult series that horror and B-movie fans regard as a little treasure hidden in the library of an otherwise colorful 16-bit era.

mega-drive__splatterhouse-3.article:
**Splatterhouse 3** is the pinnacle of the horror trilogy and at the same time its most ambitious installment. In 1993 Namco pushed the series further: Rick, with the ill-omened **Terror Mask**, no longer defends only his girlfriend but also his own house and family, his son David, from a horde of monsters that have broken into his mansion. The combat shifted from linear progression to a more open, exploratory approach.

The most striking innovation is **branching based on time**: you move more freely through the levels, a clock ticks, and how fast and which way you progress affects the story's development and which ending you'll see, you even risk losing your loved ones if you don't make it in time. What's more, as Rick builds up strength he bursts into a monstrous berserker transformation in which he delivers devastating attacks. The graphics and animation are among the best the horror genre offered on the Mega Drive.

Retro enthusiasts value the third game for how it moves the formula from simple brawling toward tension and decision-making under pressure. The gloomy atmosphere, the chilling setting of your own cursed home and several endings give the game a replayability the earlier installments lacked. A dignified and unforgettable climax to one of the darkest series of the 16-bit era.

mega-drive__sonic-spinball.article:
**Sonic Spinball** is one of the blue hedgehog's most idiosyncratic detours away from the main series — a game that takes Sonic's timeless laws of physics (speed, bouncing, momentum) literally and turns him into a pinball. Developed under time pressure in 1993 as a quick filler between the big installments, it takes place across the vertical tables of Robotnik's fortress, Veg-O-Fortress, where the player uses flippers to bounce up and down through a tangle of pipes, valves and switches.

Instead of the classic side-scrolling run, this is about controlling chaos: you free captured animal friends, activate switches, open paths higher up and eventually topple the local boss. The controls combine pinball unpredictability with a touch of direct movement, which leads to moments both brilliant and frustrating — finding your way around the large tables is a challenge, and death lurks in the pits below.

Retro players forgive Spinball its rougher edges precisely because of that boldness: it's a bizarre, atmospherically dark and musically catchy experiment that shows Sega knew how to really experiment with its flagship brand. A cult classic for anyone who loves seeing a familiar face land in a completely different genre.

mega-drive__zero-wing.article:
**Zero Wing** looks at first glance like a solid but unremarkable horizontal shooter from the legendary Toaplan studio, masters of the shmup genre in the late '80s and early '90s. Originally a 1989 arcade game, it arrived on the Mega Drive in 1992 with an added intro — and it was that very intro that turned an ordinary shooter into an immortal internet legend.

The game itself offers the best of the Toaplan school: collecting weapon upgrades, helper „options“, swarms of enemies and a polished sense of ship movement. It's not the hardest or most famous Toaplan title, but it's honestly fun and today nicely represents the era when shmups were among the pillars of a console's lineup.

Zero Wing earned its fame above all through its grotesquely translated European intro — the line „All your base are belong to us“ became one of the first global internet memes at the turn of the millennium, circulating as remixes, images and videos. For the retro community, Zero Wing is doubly dear: partly as a piece of shmup history, partly as an artifact of early internet humor.

master-system__sonic-hedgehog-2.article:
**Sonic the Hedgehog 2** in its 8-bit form is a fascinating parallel universe to the famous 16-bit sequel — it shares the name and some ideas, but it's a completely different game. Developed at the Aspect studio for the Master System (and Game Gear) in 1992, it's one of the few chances to play a full-fledged Sonic adventure with Tails at your side on the 8-bit Sega.

The levels are designed differently from the ground up: the lower resolution demands a more careful, platform-focused approach rather than headlong dashing forward. You'll find your own zones, your own bosses and notoriously demanding passages — such as a rocket flight or minecart sections that raise the blood pressure of even seasoned players. And if you want the true ending, you have to collect all the Chaos Emeralds, otherwise a bitter, cut-short conclusion awaits.

It's precisely this distinctiveness and uncompromising difficulty that makes the 8-bit sequel a hidden treasure among retro fans. It's not just a shrunken version of the more famous release — it's a standalone, magical game with its own personality and atmosphere.

master-system__zillion.article:
**Zillion** is one of the smartest and most underrated titles in the entire Master System library. Sega built it in 1987 on the motifs of the Japanese anime series Zillion and, instead of straightforward action, offered something rare for the time: a sprawling enemy base to explore, full of locked doors, terminals and captured allies.

The gameplay resembles Metroid-like structures before the name for them had even caught on. As a member of the White Knights team, you infiltrate the complex, collect data disks, crack numeric codes to unlock doors and gradually free comrades who then help you themselves. That combination of shooting, puzzles and systematic exploration was unusually thoughtful on an 8-bit console and rewards patient players who keep the map in their heads.

The retro community loves Zillion precisely for this being ahead of its time — it's a game that bet on the brain as much as on reflexes. Anyone looking for a Master System treasure beyond the usual Sonic staples will find one of the most precious ones right here.

saturn__sonic-jam.article:
**Sonic Jam** is a dream come true for Sega Saturn owners: a complete collection of the classic blue-hedgehog platformers from the Mega Drive era on a single disc. Sonic Team released it in 1997, bringing together Sonic 1, 2, 3 and Sonic & Knuckles in faithful ports, supplemented with optional difficulty tweaks and small improvements for newcomers and veterans alike.

The collection's real gem, though, is „Sonic World“ — a fully 3D hub you can freely run around, a prototype of where the series would head a few years later with Sonic Adventure. Besides running around, there are mini challenges and, above all, a rich archive: concept art, manuals, videos, character histories and music. For a fan, it's a little museum of the brand right inside the game.

Among retro players, Sonic Jam has a reputation as the best way to enjoy the old Sonics on the Saturn — and, at the same time, a fascinating bridge between the series' 2D past and 3D future. The combination of honest ports and nostalgic bonus material makes it a collection that still delights today.

saturn__fighting-vipers.article:
**Fighting Vipers** is the energetic, slightly crazy cousin of Virtua Fighter — and that's exactly how the Sega AM2 studio intended it, the team that under Yu Suzuki's leadership defined 3D fighters. The 1995 arcade hit arrived on the Saturn in 1996 and, against VF's serious austerity, set a faster pace, more distinctive characters and one key idea: arenas bounded by walls.

Fighting in an enclosed cage changes the dynamics of the bouts — you can push an opponent into a wall, bounce them off it and launch aggressive attacks where there's nowhere to retreat. On top of that, the fighters wear armor that can be shattered by powerful hits, exposing the more vulnerable body beneath. All this gives Vipers a brisker, more action-packed charge compared with Virtua Fighter's chess-like rhythm.

Retro fans love Fighting Vipers precisely for that abandon: it shares AM2's technical foundation and precision, but isn't afraid to be more stylish and instantly fun. On the Saturn it's one of the pillars of the genre and remains a great choice for anyone who wants a 3D fighter with its own distinctive face.

playstation__wipeout-2097.article:
**Wipeout 2097** (released in North America as Wipeout XL) is the pure essence of the early PlayStation era's style — futuristic races of anti-gravity craft that hurtle down tracks at speeds held right on the edge of control. In 1996, Psygnosis took a good first installment and tuned it into a sharper, smoother and more addictive experience.

You race with weapons: along the way you collect rockets, mines and other gadgets to slow down rivals, while you yourself handle lightning-fast corners and hold the ideal racing line. The tracks are demanding and reward both memorization and precision, while the sense of speed was among the best on any console of the time. An integral part is also the visual design by The Designers Republic studio, which gave the game its iconically sharp, techno-club look.

Legendary above all, though, is the soundtrack — tracks by the Chemical Brothers, the Prodigy and others linked video games with '90s club culture like few other titles. That's why retro players love Wipeout 2097 not just as a great racing game, but as a cultural icon that defined just how cool the PlayStation could be.

playstation__wip3out.article:
When someone says futuristic racing on the PlayStation, many players think of **Wip3out** — the peak of the legendary anti-gravity series that Psygnosis launched at the very birth of the console. The third installment, from 1999, polishes the formula to perfection: cleaner controls, smoother driving and, above all, the iconic minimalist visuals by the British studio The Designers Republic, whose typography and sharp colors gave the game an unmistakable face.

The core of the experience is piloting craft that don't touch the ground — instead of brakes you learn to use airbrakes in corners and to tactically collect weapons and shields. The speed is dazzling and every mistake means slamming into a barrier. Wip3out also became famous for a soundtrack full of electronic music that perfectly matched the club aesthetics of the turn of the millennium.

For retro players it's a symbol of the era when the PlayStation grew up — the game combined artistic vision, difficulty and atmosphere in a way that has rarely been matched since. To this day it remains one of the most prized pieces in the PS1 library, and thanks to it the WipEout series kept its reputation as both a technical and a stylistic benchmark of the genre.

playstation__medievil.article:
Few heroes have as bitter a past as Sir Daniel Fortesque, the central figure of the cult **MediEvil** from 1998. A knight who once fell in the very first shot of a battle and was posthumously passed off as a hero, he gets a second chance: when the evil sorcerer Zarok reawakens an army of the undead, Dan too rises from his tomb to finally make amends for the old lie and win real glory.

Studio SCE Cambridge mixed a gothic atmosphere reminiscent of Tim Burton's films with light-hearted humor and solid action gameplay. The settings alternate between spooky graveyards, enchanted forests and misty swamps; along the way Dan collects ever better weapons and can even remove his own arm and use it as a projectile. Battles with skeletons and other monsters are accompanied by collecting chalices of souls, which unlock the Hall of Heroes.

Retro players love MediEvil precisely for that unique mood — it's funny and melancholy at the same time, and its half-there, mumbling hero became one of the PlayStation's unforgettable icons. No wonder it earned both a remake and a sequel; the PS1 original, however, still has its raw, unmistakable charm.

playstation__resident-evil-director-s-cu.article:
The survival horror genre has a clear starting point, and it bears the name **Resident Evil**. The 1997 Director's Cut is an expanded version of the original with which Capcom, in 1996, defined the rules that still hold today: an abandoned mansion full of zombies, a claustrophobic atmosphere, ingenious puzzles and a constant shortage of both ammunition and healing. Every bullet is precious, every opening of a door tense.

The player takes on one of the members of the S.T.A.R.S. team — Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine — trapped in a monstrous manor house near Raccoon City. Static cameras in the style of film direction, pre-rendered backgrounds and an unforgettable sense of helplessness create tension that mere action cannot replace. The Director's Cut added a reworked layout of enemies and items along with a new difficulty mode, so even veterans got a reason to return.

For collectors of retro games this is a foundation stone — the roots of the whole vast series, from which the beloved installments RE2 and RE3 also spring. Anyone who wants to understand where modern horror in games came from has to start right here, in the corridors where a zombie turns toward the sound of your footsteps.

playstation__grandia.article:
Among the legions of PlayStation JRPGs, **Grandia** from 1997 stands out with a single word: enthusiasm. Studio Game Arts crafted an optimistic story about a young man named Justin, driven by a pure desire to explore the world and unravel the secrets of an ancient civilization. Instead of gloomy fantasy, Grandia offers the joy of adventure, the magic of unknown lands, and a party you'll come to love.

The real star, though, is the battle system, still considered one of the finest in the entire genre. It combines free movement of characters across the battlefield with a timeline (the IP gauge) that shows you when each combatant will strike — and with clever timing you can interrupt an enemy's action before it lands. Battles are thus no passive wait for turns, but a lively, tactical spectacle full of decisions.

The way skills and magic improve through use gives the game a satisfying sense of growth. Retro gamers love Grandia precisely because it pairs mechanical brilliance with a warm, adventurous mood. It's a hidden gem worth discovering for anyone who loves classic JRPGs with a soul.

playstation__legend-of-mana.article:
The Mana series always aimed somewhere different from other action RPGs, and **Legend of Mana** from 1999 is its most beautiful proof. Squaresoft created a game that looks like a watercolor fairy tale come to life — every location is a hand-painted work of art, and the player literally assembles the whole world of Fa'Diel themselves by placing artifacts on an empty map that conjure up towns, forests, and dungeons out of nothing.

This nonlinear structure is the heart of the entire experience. There is no single fixed storyline; instead, you choose the order in which you unlock the three main narrative arcs and dozens of side stories. The action combat plays out in real time, and on top of that you can forge your own weapons, grow crops, raise pets, and experiment with a rich item system. The game doesn't hold your hand — it rewards curiosity.

It's precisely for this uniqueness and dreamlike atmosphere that Legend of Mana earned a devoted cult following. It's not a game for everyone seeking a straightforward narrative, but anyone who surrenders to its calm, meditative rhythm and the beauty of its hand-drawn worlds will find one of the most distinctive titles in the entire PS1 library.

playstation__rayman.article:
Amid the rise of 3D graphics, in 1995 Ubisoft played the opposite card — and won. **Rayman** is a gorgeous, hand-drawn 2D platformer whose colorful, picturesque worlds feel like a children's book brought to life. This is where the armless, legless mascot was born, a character who became one of the icons of the French studio and launched a long, beloved series.

Rayman saves the world by freeing the captive Electoons and facing the villainous Mr. Dark. Along the way he gains new abilities — from a punch he can fire off, to helicopter-like hovering using his own hair. But beauty comes at a price: the game became famous for its merciless difficulty, precise jump timing, and cunningly placed traps that test the patience of even the most hardened player.

Retro enthusiasts admire Rayman precisely for this contrast — a charming visual style hides one of the toughest platformers of its era. Finishing it is a badge of honor. To this day it remains one of the prettiest 2D games ever released on consoles, and a reminder of an age when hand-drawn animation could rival even fashionable polygonal 3D.

n64__turok-dinosaur-hunter.article:
When **Turok: Dinosaur Hunter** arrived in 1997, it proved that first-person shooters had a future on consoles. Studio Iguana, under the Acclaim banner, cast players as the Native American warrior Turok, who fights his way through the primeval jungles of the Lost Land, hunting not only enemy soldiers but entire herds of dinosaurs.

The game combined a freer, exploration-driven level design full of secret nooks with an impressive arsenal of weapons. The Cerebral Bore became legendary above all — a projectile that drills into an enemy's skull and explodes. The atmosphere was cult-classic material too: the thick fog on the horizon originally masked the technical limits of the Nintendo 64, but at the same time it gave the jungle an oppressive, mysterious air that is inseparable from Turok.

For retro gamers, Turok is a symbol of the bold N64 era, when console FPS were still learning to walk. It delivered raw action, exotic settings, and a sense of adventure the competition of the time couldn't offer. Even by today's standards it retains a distinctive charm and reminds us how thrilling it was to hunt dinosaurs long before it became commonplace.

n64__wwf-no-mercy.article:
Ask fans of wrestling games about their favorite, and surprisingly often you'll hear a single title: **WWF No Mercy**. This pinnacle of wrestling games from the Japanese studio AKI was released in 2000 under the THQ label, and many still consider it the best wrestling game of all time — more than a quarter century after its release.

The secret lies in the controls. The grapple system, where the same button triggers a different move depending on the situation and the opponent's damage, feels incredibly natural and yet holds enormous depth. On top of that, No Mercy offered an extensive career mode with branching storylines about championship belts, plus a character editor remarkably rich for its time, with which players created their own wrestlers and entire shows.

It's precisely this combination of superbly tuned gameplay, content, and an indestructible community that makes No Mercy an immortal classic. Fans still create modifications for it that update the rosters with current stars, so the game never fully aged. For retro gamers it's the gold standard of the genre — proof that well-designed controls outlive generations of consoles.

n64__ridge-racer-64.article:
Namco was already famous for its arcade racing series Ridge Racer on the PlayStation, but in 2000 a peculiar offshoot arrived on the Nintendo 64 — **Ridge Racer 64**, developed with Nintendo's involvement specifically for this console. It wasn't a mere port; the game combined tracks and driving feel from previous entries and tuned them for the N64's capabilities.

At the heart of the experience is pure arcade drift. Forget realistic simulation — here you enter corners in a slide, the driven wheels spin, and smooth, brisk driving rewards both boldness and precision. The game offered a decent selection of tracks, cars, and game modes, including the ability to win new cars, so it found something to offer both newcomers and series fans craving a drift on Nintendo's console.

For retro gamers, Ridge Racer 64 is a pleasant secret of an N64 library that wasn't exactly rich in classic arcade racing. Anyone who loves slides, bright colors, and uncomplicated joy of speed will find an honest helping of fun here that beautifully complements the platform's more famous racing names.

n64__harvest-moon-64.article:
**Harvest Moon 64** is, for many fans of the series, the very best the farming genre has ever offered. Beneath the calm pixel graphics of the Nintendo 64 hides a surprisingly deep game about patience: you inherit a rundown farm and have a precisely defined number of in-game years to turn it into a flourishing homestead. No enemies, no dying — just the flow of the seasons, work that means something, and a sense of home built day by day.

The core is the daily rhythm: you plant and water crops, milk cows, groom horses, cut grass for hay, and head into the mine for ore. But the key to success isn't just money — the game values relationships. Five girls live in the village, whom you court with gifts and conversation, and the courtship culminates in a wedding and, in time, a child. Natsume built on the SNES original here and added a warmer, more elaborate world with a firm bond to the surrounding community.

Retro gamers love Harvest Moon 64 precisely for that unhurried calm. In an age when the N64 was ruled by 3D action, it offered the opposite: a game where the reward is dusk over a field and the gratitude of neighbors. It's addictive in a quiet way — you sit down "just for a moment" and discover it's dawn outside. To this day it remains one of the hardest-to-find and most sought-after pieces in the console's library.

arcade__space-invaders.article:
**Space Invaders** isn't just a game — it's the moment video games became a cultural phenomenon. When Taito unleashed Tomohiro Nishikado's cabinet into arcades in 1978, no one suspected it would spark a mania. In Japan the game supposedly caused such a hunger for coins that the amount of hundred-yen coins in circulation had to be increased — a story perhaps embellished, but one that perfectly captures the frenzy that erupted at the time.

The principle is ingeniously simple: beneath rows of descending aliens you dodge behind four shields and pick off the attackers one by one. This is where the legendary mechanic was born — as the invaders dwindled, the hardware had fewer objects to render, so the remaining enemies sped up. Originally a technical limitation, it became one of the first true "difficulty curves" in history, and it still quickens players' pulses today. It's accompanied by that hypnotic, escalating "dun-dun-dun."

Space Invaders laid the foundation for the entire shooter genre and inspired countless followers. It established the high-score system as both a challenge and a social ritual. Retro gamers revere it as the forefather of everything — the invader silhouettes became a universal symbol of video games, recognizable even without playing a single round.

arcade__missile-command.article:
**Missile Command** is one of the most oppressive games Atari ever released — and its tension springs directly from the Cold War paranoia of 1980. With a trackball you aim a cursor across the sky and launch counter-missiles to intercept a rain of ballistic missiles hurtling toward six cities at the bottom of the screen. It's not a game about winning. It's a game about how long you can delay the inevitable end.

The game design is masterful in its cruelty. You have three batteries with a limited supply of missiles and must anticipate the trajectories of enemy rockets, MIRV warheads, bombers, and satellites. Each counter-missile explodes into a circle that has to catch as many of them at once as possible — so you're playing a game of timing and space. As the levels pile up, the sky fills and the decision of which city to sacrifice becomes chillingly personal. The famous ending "THE END" instead of the usual "GAME OVER" still sends shivers down players' spines.

The retro community reveres Missile Command as a rare case where an arcade game carries a real message. Its author, Dave Theurer, reportedly had nightmares about nuclear war because of the game. That atmosphere of helplessness, where you know you'll always lose in the end and it's only a matter of losing more slowly, makes it one of the most powerful experiences of the golden age of arcades.

arcade__xevious.article:
**Xevious**, from Namco and designer Masanobu Endo, is one of those games that quietly rewrote the rules of the genre. When it arrived in arcades in 1983, it offered something vertical shooters had never known before: two separate weapons. With the Vulcan you mow down aerial targets, and with the Blaster bomb you aim at ground units, forcing you to constantly switch between two planes of combat at once. This idea became a cornerstone of practically every later shmup.

But Xevious didn't captivate through mechanics alone. Namco created a mysterious, alien world inspired by the Nazca lines and ancient civilizations, with smooth scrolling over forests, rivers, and concrete fortresses. That atmosphere of mystery — the feeling of flying over an alien planet with its own history — was unheard of for its time. The game hid secrets quite literally too: legendary hidden bonuses like the Sol tower and the Special Flag rewarded curious players and fueled rumors around the world.

For retro gamers, Xevious is an icon not only because of its influence but also because of how well it ages. It's a clean, elegant, still-demanding game. In Japan it became a cultural symbol of the early arcade era and one of the first games to be granted the status of a true design classic.

arcade__dragon-s-lair.article:
**Dragon's Lair** was a 1983 revelation that literally stopped crowds in the arcades. While the competition ran on crude pixels, this game looked like a full-fledged animated film — because it essentially was one. Behind the animation stood Don Bluth, a former Disney master, and the picture played back from a laserdisc in a quality players of the time couldn't even imagine. The lines at the cabinet were as much about watching as about playing.

The gameplay, however, was completely different from what the looks suggested. The knight Dirk rescues Princess Daphne from a dragon's castle, but you don't control the movement freely — the game is a chain of scripted scenes where you have to press a direction or the sword at exactly the right split second. A wrong or late move means instant (and often comically brutal) death. It was essentially a visual memorization puzzle, a forerunner of what we now call quick time events.

Retro gamers love Dragon's Lair more as a phenomenon than as classic gameplay. It's a milestone that showed how far the gaming medium could reach for a cinematic experience, and it launched a short, wild era of laserdisc games. To this day it captivates with its animation — and it can also thoroughly infuriate with its ruthlessness.

arcade__marble-madness.article:
**Marble Madness** is one of those games where you immediately sense it was born from a pure desire to try something different. In 1984 Atari placed players before a series of isometric mazes through which you roll a glass marble to the finish — against a merciless time limit, over chasms, sloped surfaces, and strange enemies. The trackball controls give the marble physical inertia, so you feel it accelerate, slide, and topple over the edge when you overdo it.

The game was technically pioneering in several respects. Designer Mark Cerny used an isometric 3D perspective rendered so precisely that the levels looked like sculptural objects, and Marble Madness was among the very first cabinets with stereo music, composed by Brad Fuller on synthesizers. Six short but devilishly precise levels drive you ever onward, each introducing a new trick — from rubbery enemies to gravity reversals.

Retro gamers value Marble Madness for its unique identity. It's short, brutally demanding, and unlike anything else — a combination of a race against time, a game of dexterity, and a puzzle. The side-by-side two-player co-op mode adds chaos and fun on top. It remains an elegant reminder of an era when arcades could afford to be truly experimental.

arcade__paperboy.article:
**Paperboy** is proof that a cult game can grow out of the most mundane of chores. In 1985 Atari put players on the bike of a young paper carrier and sent them down a suburban street with a single task: deliver the morning press to subscribers. But what sounded like tedium turned, in the designers' hands, into a nerve-racking slalom full of absurd hazards — from barking dogs and runaway lawnmowers to toy cars and tornadoes.

The system of rewards and punishments is ingenious. You only deliver to subscribers' houses (you recognize them by color) and score by hitting the mailbox or landing the paper on the doorstep. A broken window at a non-subscriber's house, on the other hand, wins you a new customer — so vandalism paradoxically pays off. If you fail to deliver someone's paper or damage their house, you lose them, and with them a chunk of your delivery route. The cabinet became famous for its special handlebar-shaped controller, which pulled you perfectly into the role.

Retro players love Paperboy for its quirky personality and unexpected depth. It's a game full of black humor, precise timing, and ever-mounting chaos across the week you have to survive. Its bizarre premise and unmistakable style made it one of the most memorable oddities of the golden age of arcades.

arcade__contra.article:
**Contra** in its 1987 arcade original is the game where the legendary formula that Konami would later make famous the world over first appeared. Two muscle-bound commandos — clearly inspired by Rambo and the Terminator — fight their way through waves of an alien invasion and human mercenaries. It's a pure, adrenaline-fueled run & gun: you run to the right, shoot in every direction, and collect weapon upgrades, while a single hit means death.

The arcade version offered more detailed graphics and smoother animation than the later home ports, and became famous for its pseudo-3D levels, where the character heads into the depth of the screen against fortresses. But the heart of the experience is two-player co-op — Contra was built for playing together, where partners cover each other's backs, share power-ups, and jointly curse every cheap hit. The iconic Spread Gun is the weapon every player craves.

This arcade cabinet also gave rise to the fabled NES conversion, made famous by its infinite-lives code and its status as one of the hardest games ever made. Retro players revere arcade Contra as the very origin of this legend — rawer, tougher, and more uncompromising action that defined what a perfect run & gun should look like.

arcade__double-dragon.article:
**Double Dragon** is the game that in 1987 practically founded the modern beat 'em up as we know it. Technos sent the brothers Billy and Jimmy Lee out into the streets to fight their way through the urban underworld of the Black Warriors gang and rescue the kidnapped Marian. What we take for granted today — progressing from left to right, crowds of enemies, using weapons picked up off the ground — got its definitive, endlessly copied form right here.

The key innovation was the interplay of varied combat and cooperation. Beyond punches and kicks, you could grab enemies, use elbows, headbutts, and picked-up sticks, whips, and crates. Above all, though, it offered play for two people at once — two brothers side by side against the odds, which turned it into an arcade sensation. The mischievous cherry on top was the ending: after rescuing the girl, the two brothers had to fight each other over who would get her.

Retro players honor Double Dragon as the father of the genre on which Final Fight, Streets of Rage, and dozens of others were built. Its influence is immeasurable — it defined the visual language, the rhythm, and the cooperative spirit of brawlers. Even today it's a joy to walk its streets with a friend at your side and feel where it all began.

arcade__golden-axe.article:
Few arcades of the late eighties smelled of adventure quite like Sega's **Golden Axe** from 1989. This fantasy brawler pitted a trio of heroes against the evil Death Adder — the muscular barbarian Axe Battler, the axe-wielding dwarf Gilius Thunderhead, and the sword-armed amazon Tyris Flare. Each of them had different strength, reach, and magic, so choosing a character wasn't just cosmetic but a fundamental choice of playstyle.

The game's secret weapon was magic. Little gnomes with sacks scurried across the play areas, and when you kicked them, they dropped blue vials. Collected potions filled a magic meter and, at the right moment, unleashed a screen-filling spell — the more vials, the more devastating the effect. Unforgettable, too, were the rides on saddled monsters, whether a fire-spewing lizard or a pair of clawing creatures you could steal from an opponent.

Retro players adore Golden Axe above all for its two-player co-op and for the unmistakable sword-and-sorcery atmosphere the beat 'em up genre hardly knew back then. It received a host of ports — the most famous on the Sega Mega Drive — and became one of the pillars on which Sega built its reputation as the king of arcades.

neogeo__king-of-monsters.article:
When SNK unleashed **King of the Monsters** on the Neo Geo in 1991, it fulfilled the dream of everyone who grew up on Japanese films about rubber-suited monsters. Instead of a classic fighting game, it put you in the skin of a giant Godzilla-style kaiju and let you brawl with other monsters right in the middle of miniature Japanese cities — which literally crumbled beneath you.

At its core was a wrestling system: you grabbed opponents, threw them, pinned them to the ground, and tried to hold them down for three seconds like in a real match. There was a roster of iconic creatures to choose from — a fiery dinosaur, a giant octopus, a humanoid giant, and a robot — each with its own grapples and strikes. Wrecking the scenery wasn't just for show; stomped buildings, skyscrapers, and pylons were part of the fun.

Retro players prize King of the Monsters mainly for its bombastic two-player mode and its pure, dumb demolition fun. Compared to SNK's later fighters, it's a rougher, simpler piece, but it's precisely that raw, comic-book energy that keeps this early Neo Geo classic a rewarding pick for one wild evening for two.

neogeo__viewpoint.article:
**Viewpoint** from 1992 is one of those games the Neo Geo showed off to prove what its hardware could do. This isometric shooter from the Aicom studio, under the Sammy banner, looked like nothing else on the market — the world was tilted into a fascinating three-dimensional perspective where you had to gauge not only lateral movement but also the height and depth of space.

It was precisely that slanted projection that made Viewpoint so challenging and addictive at once. Enemy shots came along trajectories that read completely differently in isometry than in an ordinary vertical shooter, and precise dodging required reorienting your perception. Add to that a stylish acid-jazz soundtrack and smooth, technically advanced graphics with pre-rendered elements that keep the game looking fresh to this day.

Viewpoint has the reputation of being one of the most beautiful and, at the same time, hardest games on the Neo Geo. Its merciless difficulty made it an agonizing trial for shmup enthusiasts, but that's exactly why hardcore players still hold it up today. Anyone who once broke through into its strange perspective and rhythm finds it hard to forget this original.

neogeo__fatal-fury-3-road-to-final-victo.article:
With **Fatal Fury 3: Road to the Final Victory** from 1995, SNK pushed its flagship fighter a fundamental step further. The game abandoned the older two-line layout and introduced an improved three-lane system — characters could dodge into the foreground and background, giving the duels a tactical dimension that classic single-plane fighters didn't have.

The story again unfolded in the grim streets of Southtown, and around the Bogard brothers — Terry and Andy — gathered a gallery of distinctive fighters. Among the new faces were the Jin twins, whose subplot set in motion a story about mysterious scrolls. Visually it was a step forward, with larger, more detailed animated sprites and elaborate backgrounds that gave the game the series' typically gritty atmosphere.

For fans, Fatal Fury 3 is a key milestone: it was the direct predecessor of the legendary Garou: Mark of the Wolves, and many of its ideas later flowed into that game. Retro players love it for its bold combat system and for the unmistakable Southtown style that made the Fatal Fury series one of the pillar brands of the golden age of Neo Geo fighters.

cps__mega-man-power-battle.article:
**Mega Man: The Power Battle** from 1995 was a cleverly conceived arcade spin-off of the series by Capcom that took the best of the Blue Bomber and served it up in a concentrated gameplay dose. Forget long levels — here it's all about the pure essence of classic Mega Man: boss battles, one after another, no dawdling.

The game let you choose between Mega Man, Proto Man, and Bass and sent you into a series of battles against Robot Masters from the classic entries. In keeping with tradition, you gained the weapons of defeated enemies and could deploy them against the next bosses, so the order of the fights and your tactics always mattered. Two-player co-op worked great too, letting players pummel a boss together — something the home versions didn't offer.

Retro fans took to Power Battle precisely for that nostalgic concentration. Anyone who grew up on the NES entries met old, familiar enemies here in sharper CPS graphics and at a faster pace. Together with its sequel, The Power Fighters, it forms a duo that anyone wanting to enjoy the soul of Mega Man in brisk arcade form still reaches for today.

cps__mercs.article:
**Mercs** from 1990, known in Japan as Senjou no Ookami II, was Capcom's answer to the vertical commando-action fever that Commando and Ikari Warriors had whipped up back then. You step into the role of an elite mercenary whose task is to fight through enemy territory — jungle, bases, and military complexes — and free kidnapped hostages.

In gameplay terms it's a brisk top-down run & gun ride: you shoot in every direction, collect stronger weapons, and in a pinch trigger mighty bombs that sweep the whole screen. The arcade version could handle up to three players at once, so the screen ruled over a proper chaos of explosions, vehicles, and hordes of soldiers. Capcom's CPS hardware gave it all sharp colors and smooth action.

For retro players, Mercs is one of Capcom's unjustly overlooked gems. It doesn't have the fame of Final Fight or Ghouls 'n Ghosts, but with its explosive briskness and pure, no-frills action it still entertains today. The home port on the Sega Mega Drive also added an expanded story mode, which won its own circle of devoted fans.

cps__magic-sword.article:
**Magic Sword: Heroic Fantasy** from 1990 is among those Capcom gems unfairly forgotten, even though it offers one of the most magical fantasy action experiences of its time. The core idea is simple and catchy at once: you climb up a fifty-floor tower full of monsters, traps, and bosses, and with each floor you draw closer to a showdown with the evil Drokmar.

The ally system is ingenious. Along the way you come across imprisoned fighters — an archer, a mage, a knight, an amazon, a lizardman, and others — and when you free them, they join you and cover your back with their own firepower and abilities. Each helper has limited stamina and different strengths, so the choice of whom to take a floor higher gives the game a pleasant tactical flavor. Your hero, moreover, grows stronger by collecting items and upgrades his magic sword.

Retro players love Magic Sword for its beautiful pixel graphics, its medieval fantasy atmosphere, and its finely tuned two-player co-op. It's a game that combines platformer, action, and a pinch of strategy into an effortlessly entertaining whole — and that's precisely why it holds a loyal audience even after decades.

msx__goonies.article:
On MSX computers, Konami's **The Goonies** from 1986 holds an almost sacred standing. This platformer based on the film of the same name by Richard Donner put you in charge of the band of Goonies and sent them through a maze of underground caves after the pirate Willy's treasure and, above all, to rescue their captured friends.

The gameplay concept was cleverly intertwined for its time: you had to complete each of the eight levels by freeing a captured Goonie, which often required the coordination of two characters — one to hold a mechanism, the other to slip through. On top of that, you had to watch out for enemies like the Fratellis, collect keys, and uncover hidden passages. Konami spiced the game up with its trademark feel for melody and a resonant rendition of the film's theme, which just about everyone on MSX came to love.

Why do retro players still revere The Goonies today? It was one of the first games to bring a combination of action, puzzles, and a film license to the 8-bit MSX in such a polished form. In Japan it became such a hit that Konami even made an improved sequel, The Goonies II. For MSX owners it remains a symbol of the golden age of this often overlooked platform.

msx__zanac.article:
**Zanac** by the Compile studio from 1986 is one of those games that earned its reputation not through graphics or story, but through an ingenious idea hidden beneath the surface. At first glance it's a fast vertical shooter, of which there were dozens on the MSX — but in reality it was a pioneer of so-called adaptive difficulty, a system that quietly watched how well you played.

The game's artificial intelligence, which Compile called ALC (Automatic Level of Difficulty Control), reacted to your playstyle: how fast you shot, how you moved, how many enemies you destroyed. When you were doing well, the game cranked up the pressure and threw more opponents at you; when you were struggling, it eased off for a while. Thanks to that, every run was a little different and the game adapted to you personally. On top of that, Zanac offered a rich arsenal of secondary weapons, which you switched between on the fly depending on the situation.

For retro players, Zanac remains a textbook example of how Compile — later the creators of the legendary Aleste series — knew how to breathe depth into a shooter. Its briskness, clever design, and timeless adaptive-difficulty mechanic make it a title that holds up even next to far newer shmups.

msx__antarctic-adventure.article:
Few games capture the childlike innocence of the early eighties as perfectly as **Antarctic Adventure**. The adorable penguin Penta dashes across Antarctica's snowy plains, leaping over icy crevasses, dodging seals poking their heads out of holes, and hurrying from one research base to the next before time runs out. As early as 1983, Konami showed a knack for instantly graspable, catchy fun — a talent it would perfect a few years later.

The game runs in a pseudo-3D "into the distance" perspective — the track rises toward the horizon and the player really only accelerates, brakes, and jumps, yet a surprisingly addictive rhythm emerges from it. Each stretch ends at the flag of the next station, and the reward for speed is continuing the journey around the entire continent. The cheerful tune the penguin hums along to (an arrangement of Dvořák's "Humoresque") etched itself deep into the memory of MSX players.

Antarctic Adventure became one of the unofficial mascots of the MSX era, and the penguin Penta later appeared in other Konami titles as well. For retro gamers it's a pure, kind-hearted classic — a game that still brings a smile even four decades on.

c64__m-u-l-e.article:
When people today talk about games that were decades ahead of their time, **M.U.L.E.** ranks near the top of the list. This economic strategy game for up to four players from Ozark Softscape (led by Dan Bunten) was released in 1983 under the Electronic Arts banner and is still studied today as a textbook example of brilliant multiplayer design.
