Characters move along pre-set tracks, fire firearms, and the game distinguishes direct damage from so-called scratch damage, which needs to be confirmed with another hit or it regenerates on the enemy. The player spends hero points on acrobatic jumps during which time slows down and shots can be fired mid-air, and lining characters up into a triangle creates chain attacks across the whole arena. Weapons can literally be wrapped in components into grotesque shapes, and the game demands the player genuinely study its rules. World exploration additionally takes place on a hexagonal map that the player quite literally assembles from colored tiles to open up paths to further levels of the tower.

Technically it's a solid but not dazzling game whose strength lies in its environment design, in Basel's strange mechanical aesthetic, and in the unusually tasteful character costume work, which the player can change. Motoi Sakuraba's music leans into jazz, blues, and calmer melodies, and ranks among the most distinctive soundtracks of its generation. Contemporary reception was mixed, since the steep learning curve put many players off, but the game gradually built a solid circle of devotees. Today Resonance of Fate is a refreshing reminder of a time when Japanese studios allowed themselves to experiment even at the cost of accessibility.

ps3__nier.article:
**Nier** is an action RPG from studio Cavia that in 2010 fell behind in virtually every measurable respect except the most important one: how powerfully it can hit you. The main hero, in a decayed world of the far future, tries to save his sick daughter Yonah, and together with the talking book Grimoire Weiss, the tough Kainé, and the boy Emil, searches for a cure as well as for the true nature of the monsters called Shades. The Western release casts the hero as a father, while the Japanese version, Replicant, made him an older brother instead.

The gameplay is deliberately disjointed: the core is action combat with bladed weapons and magical projectiles, but the game shifts without warning into bullet hell, isometric dungeon crawling, a text adventure, or a fixed-camera platformer. On top of that come fishing, growing plants, and gathering materials to upgrade weapons — things that are deliberately tedious. The real core, though, lies in the structure of repeated playthroughs: a second run shows the same events from a different perspective and turns enemies from anonymous targets into beings with their own reasons, and further endings go even further, including one that has a lasting effect on the player's own save data. The combat itself isn't especially demanding, and the party members each have their own long side-stories, unlocked only later, which rank among the strongest parts of the whole.

Technically Nier was already lagging at the time of release — environments are empty and the image doesn't feel clean, which was the main target of contemporary reviews. All the more exceptional, then, is Keiichi Okabe's music, built on vocals in an invented language, which became one of the most acclaimed game soundtracks ever and can tell a story all on its own. Contemporary scores were average, but the cult around the game endured and eventually led to the sequel NieR: Automata, which turned Yoko Taro's name into a brand. Today Nier is played mainly for its story and the feeling it leaves behind.

ps3__dragon-s-crown.article:
**Dragon's Crown** is an action RPG from studio Vanillaware that combines a beat-'em-up in the style of classic arcade cabinets with a deep layer of loot collecting. The player picks from six archetypes, among them a fighter, an amazon, an elf, a dwarf, a wizard, and a sorceress, and with a party of up to four characters dives into labyrinths beneath the fantasy city of Hydeland, eventually reaching an artifact called the dragon's crown. The framing narrative is handled by a narrator whose fairy-tale tone gives the game the feel of an old adventure storybook.

Each expedition consists of short two-dimensional levels full of enemies, traps, and forks in the road, where the player chooses between two branches, and loot is split at the end. Weapons are found sealed and must be appraised in town, damaged gear gets repaired, and skill trees let each class be tuned quite differently. The game can be played solo with hired skeletons, in local co-op, or online, and higher difficulties unlock tougher variants of the same maps with new equipment. It's precisely these repeated runs for better items that make up the long-term content, and the game openly encourages them. Progress between expeditions is framed by a simple story with guild quests and visits to the tavern, chapel, and shop, where loot can be sold or upgraded.

The visual side is the major draw: hand-painted backgrounds, huge and fluidly animated characters, and richly decorated sets rank among the most beautiful two-dimensional games on PlayStation 3. The exaggerated proportions of some characters became the subject of considerable debate at the time. Hitoshi Sakimoto's music gives the whole thing an orchestral, almost cinematic feel. Reviews received it well, praising especially the graphics and co-op, with criticism aimed at repeating the same maps. Today Dragon's Crown remains one of the few games that managed to combine an arcade beat-'em-up with an RPG truly convincingly.

ps3__kingdom-hearts-hd-1-5-remix.article:
**Kingdom Hearts HD 1.5 ReMIX** is a collection that Square Enix released on PlayStation 3 in 2013, giving Western players for the first time the chance to play through the series' beginning in one package and at a higher resolution. It contains the fully playable Kingdom Hearts Final Mix, previously released only in Japan, plus Kingdom Hearts Re:Chain of Memories, along with a compilation of story scenes from 358/2 Days. The player, in the role of a boy named Sora, travels across worlds inspired by classic animated films, searches for lost friends, and is accompanied by a pair of well-known characters from animation classics — a pairing that sounded nonsensical on paper and yet worked.

The base game combines action combat with the key weapon called the Keyblade with a simple character progression system, spells, summoned helpers, and platforming exploration of the worlds. The Final Mix version adds new enemies, items, and an additional difficulty level, so even people who knew the original release have a reason to come back. Re:Chain of Memories takes an entirely different path, building combat around cards that determine which strikes and spells can be played and how an opponent's action can be countered — a system some players take quite a while to get used to. Controls and camera were adjusted for the collection and are noticeably more comfortable than in the original releases.

The move to high definition served the collection very well; character models got new textures, the image is clean and colorful, and the whole thing still feels fresh today, though the occasional plainness of the environments gives away its PlayStation 2 origins. Yoko Shimomura's music is one of the main reasons the series holds such a strong reputation, and it shines in the remaster. Reception was very good, especially because the collection finally made the series' tangled chronology clear. The collection also serves as an accessible overview of the series' mythology, since the bonus scene compilation explains the origin of the organization in black coats around which most of the later entries revolve. For a newcomer, it remains to this day the most logical way to get into Kingdom Hearts at all.

ps3__deus-ex-human-revolution.article:
**Deus Ex: Human Revolution** is an action RPG from Eidos Montréal that in 2011 revived the cult franchise and carried its cyberpunk vision into the near future of 2027. The player takes on the role of security chief Adam Jensen, who survives a brutal attack on the research firm Sarif Industries only thanks to extensive mechanical augmentations he never asked for. The investigation takes him from Detroit to Shanghai and beyond, confronting him with the question of who actually has the right to decide how far the enhancement of the human body should go.

The game consistently offers several ways through every situation: brute force, stealth, hacking, or persuasion in dialogues built like a minigame of reading an opponent's character. Augmentations are unlocked with praxis points and change what's even possible, from a safe landing from a great height to seeing through walls to silent movement. Levels are designed with several layers of access routes, ventilation shafts, offices overhead, and locked doors whose codes can be found in someone else's email. The game tracks whether the player kills, and offers a meaningful way to get through everything without a single casualty. It also strongly rewards exploration, since apartments, offices, and vent shafts hold not just supplies but entire side-stories the player would otherwise never learn about.

On PlayStation 3 the game runs well, if at a lower resolution and with a pronounced gold-black color filter that is both its greatest aesthetic asset and the target of jokes. Michael McCann's music is built on dark synthetic textures and ranks among the best soundtracks of its generation. Contemporary reception was very favorable, with criticism mainly aimed at the mandatory boss fights, which undercut the otherwise consistent freedom of approach. Human Revolution influenced an entire wave of so-called immersive sim games, and even today feels like an excellently designed game whose details have aged rather than its foundation.

ps3__diablo-iii.article:
**Diablo III** appeared on PlayStation 3 in 2013, a year after the PC version, and the console adaptation turned out surprisingly well, in many respects even a better way to play the game. The player chooses one of six classes, from the barbarian through the demon hunter to the wizard, and sets out into the world of Sanctuary, where a falling star heralds the return of hellish forces and where the path leads from the town of New Tristram all the way into hell itself. The core of the game is classic: cut a path through hordes of enemies, collect better gear, and go back for another run on a higher difficulty.

The console version scrapped the auction house that had long damaged the game on PC, adjusted loot drops to be more generous and meaningful for the chosen class, and above all added controller-based movement with a dodge roll, so combat feels much more physical. Co-op for up to four players on a single console works brilliantly, something the PC version never offered at all. Character progression is built around unlocking skills with runes that can be freely swapped, so experimenting with a build costs nothing, and after finishing the story it continues in the form of hunting for legendary items. Difficulty tiers open up gradually, and in the later stages it's mainly about putting together a build that lets you survive under the toughest conditions.

Technically the game holds up well on PS3, the image is clean, performance is stable, and the interface was rebuilt from the ground up for TV and gamepad. The atmosphere is darker than that of many imitators, with gothic cathedrals, desert tombs, and music that works more with mood and space than with a strong melody. Contemporary reviews praised the console version, and more than one critic called it the more enjoyable variant at the time. Today the PS3 release is interesting mainly as a game that can be played entirely offline and by two people on one couch, an experience the series' earlier entries on PC never offered.

ps3__call-of-duty-4-modern-warfare.article:
**Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare** cut the series loose from World War II in 2007 and moved it into the present day, setting the bar for an entire following generation of military shooters. The campaign alternates between the perspective of a British special forces soldier and an American marine, taking the player from a night raid on a cargo ship through street fighting all the way to a frozen Pripyat. It's the mission where you crawl in a ghillie suit through tall grass past enemy patrols, waiting for a single shot, that became one of the most-quoted sequences in the genre's history. The game also dared to include scenes nobody else touched at the time, including a moment where the player's character survives a nuclear blast only to die in the ruins of the city.

Even more significant than the campaign, though, was the multiplayer's impact. The developers built in an experience and rank system, gradual unlocking of weapons and attachments, a custom loadout editor, and so-called killstreaks, which rewarded a series of kills without dying with a recon plane, an airstrike, or an attack helicopter. The combination of perks, customizable weapons, and compact, clearly built maps created an addictive reward loop that dozens of competing games then copied in some form. Gunplay has real weight and readable feedback, match pacing is relentlessly brisk, and death arrives after a split second of inattention.

On PlayStation 3 the game was among the first titles to show the console in a better light: detailed weapon models, elaborate interior lighting, and sound design that still ranks among the best-executed in the genre. Reception was extraordinary, the game collected numerous awards, and for years it set the direction the action genre would follow. Today the campaign feels shorter and more straightforward than players remember it, but its direction, shifting perspectives, and ability to escalate a scene still hold up after all these years. Modern Warfare remains the moment when online shooters definitively turned into mass entertainment.

ps3__battlefield-bad-company-2.article:
**Battlefield: Bad Company 2** is the title with which the Battlefield series finally settled in on consoles, offering something the competition couldn't do at the time: a battlefield that literally falls apart under the players' hands. The Frostbite engine allowed shooting through house walls, knocking down fences, dismantling cover with rocket launchers, and, in extreme cases, leveling an entire building, so a dug-in machine gunner stopped being a problem the moment someone removed his house. The campaign follows a squad of soldiers from a notoriously disreputable unit, whose dark humor and constant friendly ribbing give an otherwise serious war setting a lighter tone rarely seen in the genre.

The real focus, however, is the multiplayer. Players choose from four classes with distinct roles, from an assault trooper resupplying ammo through a combat engineer with anti-tank weapons to a medic with a machine gun, and together fight over control points in Conquest mode or attack a series of objectives in the tense Rush mode, which tells each map as a gradual advance. Vehicles, helicopters, and other hardware get involved in the fighting, so it comes down to crew teamwork and whether the team can cover an advance. Long sightlines, ballistics, and sprawling maps create the feeling of a real battle rather than a match in an arena.

The PlayStation 3 version ran stably and looked technically impressive especially thanks to the destruction, dust effects, and gunfire sound, which still ranks among the best-executed in the genre. At the time the game was received very warmly as a counterweight to faster, more arcade-like shooters, and many players still consider it the peak of the whole franchise. The official servers no longer run, so the online portion is a thing of the past, but the campaign and overall design remain an excellent example of how a military shooter can be built around teamwork and a changeable environment instead of scripted set pieces. That's exactly why Bad Company 2 is still referenced as the benchmark against which players measure every new entry in the series, and nostalgia for its collapsible villages and snowy valleys remains a constant topic among the franchise's fans.

ps3__bioshock.article:
**BioShock** begins with a plane crashing into the Atlantic and a descent into Rapture, an underwater city built as a refuge for the best of the best, which instead of a utopia turned into a bloody labyrinth full of ruined inhabitants. The player moves through flooded art deco halls, listens to the recorded messages of long-dead residents, and gradually pieces together the story of what happened when an ideology of unlimited freedom collided with human nature. The narrative is almost entirely hidden in the environment and audio diaries, so Rapture feels like a place with its own history rather than mere backdrop for shooting.

The combat system is built on a combination of classic weapons and plasmids, genetically induced abilities that let the player electrify water, set enemies on fire, control swarms of bees, or hack automated turrets. Improvisation and use of the environment matter a great deal, since the game is by no means generous with ammunition. The Little Sisters, protected by hulking Big Daddies, play a key role: the player must decide whether to harvest them for resources or save them, one of the first genuinely weighty moral choices in shooters. The mid-game twist, which retroactively reframes the meaning of everything the player has been doing, remains to this day one of the most-quoted scenes in the medium.

The PlayStation 3 version arrived roughly a year after the original release and brought minor improvements as well as bonus content. Technically it held up well; the atmosphere is underscored by water effects, rusted metal interiors, and period music from the thirties and forties that sounds all the more unsettling in the empty halls. Critics received the game enthusiastically, considering it proof that a shooter could also be a thoughtful piece of writing. Even today BioShock is excellently playable, and its art direction and storytelling have aged better than most of its contemporaries. Rapture remains one of the best-conceived game settings ever, and it only takes a few minutes in its flooded corridors to see why.

ps3__borderlands-2.article:
**Borderlands 2** perfected the idea of combining an action shooter with loot-hoarding in the style of action RPGs and defined the shape of the whole subgenre for years to come. The planet Pandora is this time under the control of a corporation led by a charismatic villain who mocks the player over a public broadcast, insulting and praising him in the same breath, and who became, thanks to his writing, one of the best-remembered villains of his generation. The humor is harsh, cynical, and yet surprisingly well written, so even the side quests, of which there are dozens, have their own punchline.

At its core is an endless stream of weapons generated from predetermined parts, so two shotguns from the same manufacturer might differ in accuracy, rate of fire, elemental damage, and even whether they explode when thrown away. The player picks from several classes with distinct action skills, whether that's dual-wielding pistols, a decoy in the form of a digital duplicate, a flying combat robot, or a huntress using a telekinetic trap, and develops each of them across three skill trees. The game truly comes alive in co-op for up to four players, where abilities combine, difficulty scales, and arguments over loot splits are part of the experience.

The cel-shaded graphics with bold outlines work excellently even on PlayStation 3, where the game runs stably and manages to keep things readable even in firefights full of explosions and elemental effects, though split-screen play does take a toll on performance. Reception was excellent, and extensive add-ons, including some of the most highly rated, extended the game's life by dozens of hours. Today Borderlands 2 feels like one of the best-tuned loot shooters ever: it has pace, humor, an enormous amount of content, and it's still one of the most fun games to play with a group of friends. The addictive urge to see what dropped from the last crate or from a defeated boss works exactly the same after all these years, and few games can so reliably swallow up an entire evening.

ps3__dead-space.article:
**Dead Space** sends engineer Isaac Clarke aboard the mining ship USG Ishimura, which has stopped responding to hails, and what the crew found on the surface of a distant planet has since turned its members into necromorphs, disfigured organisms assembled from human bodies. The game builds on the claustrophobia of narrow corridors, cut power, and sounds that seem to come from somewhere in the ventilation, leaving the player practically no moment of calm. The narrative is restrained, and most of the horror comes from the environment, messages written in blood, and the logs of crew members who slowly slid into madness.

The key mechanic is dismembering limbs. You can't stop necromorphs by shooting them in the head — you have to cut off their arms and legs, primarily with a mining plasma cutter with a rotating beam. Added to that are stasis, which slows down both enemies and mechanisms, and kinesis for manipulating objects, so an improvised projectile can be anything lying around on deck. Another excellent idea is the fully diegetic interface: the health meter glows along the suit's spine, ammo counts are projected in mid-air, and the inventory opens as a hologram, so the game is never interrupted by a pause menu and the tension never lets up.

On PlayStation 3 the game felt technically advanced thanks to its handling of darkness, particle effects, and especially its outstanding sound design, which in vacuum sequences falls into total silence broken only by breathing inside the helmet. At the time it was very well received and quickly earned a reputation as one of the best horror games of its era, spawning an entire series. Even today it holds up without reservation: it has excellently measured pacing, can still surprise on a second playthrough, and its bleak, cosmic desolation has aged considerably better than most jump-scare horror. The Ishimura also functions as a single connected space the player returns to and gets to know, so by the end of the game the ship feels almost intimately familiar, even soaked in blood.

ps3__max-payne-3.article:
**Max Payne 3** moves the burned-out New York cop to São Paulo, where, as a washed-up bodyguard for a wealthy family, he gets tangled up in kidnappings, corruption, and a street war between gangs, militias, and police units. The snowy noir New York gives way to a dazzlingly sunlit Brazilian city, favelas, nightclubs, and port warehouses, and yet the game keeps the same weary, self-lacerating tone narrated in Max's voice. The character himself is the subject of irony here: shorn, drunk, and disgusted with himself, he comes across more as a wreck than an action hero, which gives the story surprising weight.

The gameplay is built on the series' famous bullet time and a sideways dive with slowed-down time, which this game embeds in unusually convincing physical animation. Max really does land wherever you send him during a dive, stays lying there, and has to fight back from a position on the ground; enemy hits visibly affect their movement, so firefights feel raw and unpredictable. Added to that are cover mechanics, elaborate weapon handling that Max visibly carries close to his body, and a final slow-motion shot at the gunman who killed him. The campaign was accompanied by a competitive multiplayer with its own modes and gradual loadout unlocking.

Technically it was one of the most visually polished titles of its generation on PlayStation 3, with striking lighting, cinematic color filters, and a seamless transition between cutscenes and gameplay, so the game never loads behind a black screen. Reception was very favorable, with criticism aimed mainly at its linearity and the amount of non-interactive footage. Today Max Payne 3 stands out precisely for its craftsmanship: the shooting, animation, and atmosphere of unbearable heat and hopelessness make it one of the best-aged action games of its era. The firefights still carry such weight and precision that many players return to them just for the feel of the guns and how convincingly enemies react to every hit.

ps3__vanquish.article:
**Vanquish** is PlatinumGames' answer to the cover-shooter craze: it took that genre's structure and injected it with a speed the genre had never seen before. The player controls a government agent in an ARS combat suit who can rocket-slide across the battlefield on his knees, dodge into slow motion, and flow seamlessly between cover, sliding, and shooting. The plot about a space station, an energy weapon, and a war with Russian robots is just an excuse, because the real subject is movement: standing still means dying, and survival depends on how long you can keep moving without overheating the suit.

The combat is a showcase of ingenuity. Enemy robots have exposed weak points, break apart piece by piece, and change behavior once you shoot off their head or limb. There are only a few weapons, but all of them upgrade by collecting duplicates and suit different situations. The game comes alive most in fights against giant opponents, where you need to alternate attacks, recharge the suit, and use the surrounding obstacles. The overheating system acts as a clever safeguard against abusing slow motion, forcing the player to judge when they can afford to risk it and when they need to pull back.

On PlayStation 3 the game runs briskly, and its metallic, blue-gray aesthetic focused on sparks, smoke, and explosions still feels very clean today. At the time it received enthusiastic reviews from critics but flopped commercially, a common fate back then for Japanese action games aimed at Western audiences. The campaign is short, playable in a single evening, but it's built for replaying, for refining your approach and chasing high scores. Vanquish still holds the reputation of one of the best-playing third-person shooters ever made, and its pace has few successors. Anyone who gets into its rhythm once and learns to chain slides, dodges, and precise shots will find that few action games offer a similar feeling of movement, regardless of generation.

ps3__spec-ops-line.article:
**Spec Ops: The Line** looks at first glance like another third-person military shooter, but it's actually the sharpest critique the genre ever received from a major publisher. A trio of American soldiers enters Dubai, buried under sand after devastating storms, to find a lost battalion and its commander. The story loosely draws on Heart of Darkness, and with each mission it shifts from a reconnaissance operation to the disintegration of Captain Walker, who gradually loses track of who he's actually saving and who he's killing, a shift the game signals through changing character lines and appearance.

The gameplay itself is deliberately conventional, meaning cover, moving between cover, and commands to two squadmates who can mark a target or throw a grenade. But the environment plays an active role: glass walls can be shot out to bury enemies under an avalanche of sand, and sandstorms reduce visibility and change the course of firefights. The game is strongest where it leads the player into decisions whose consequences can't be undone, then shows them without mercy. The white phosphorus sequence is one of the most discussed scenes in video games and remains a textbook example of turning the player's own routine against them.

On PlayStation 3 the production is solid, and what stands out most is the art direction of the buried luxury city, where skyscrapers, shopping malls, and swimming pools push up through the sand. At the time the game sold poorly, but critics praised its narrative and courage, and its reputation has grown considerably in the years since. Today Spec Ops: The Line is referenced as a key title in the debate over violence in games. The shooting has aged averagely, but as a statement the game remains uncomfortably effective. Its short length is actually an advantage here, because the whole holds together as one tight downward spiral you can't step out of before the final revelation.

ps3__resident-evil-5.article:
**Resident Evil 5** sends veteran Chris Redfield to a fictional African region, where investigating a bioweapon deal quickly turns into a fight for bare survival against infected locals. At his side stands local agent Sheva Alomar, and this duo is what defines the whole entry: the game was designed from the ground up for co-op, and a second player can join at any time, whether on split-screen at the same console or online. Sharing ammo and healing items and jointly opening doors or pulling each other up onto a ledge makes this one of the most thoughtfully designed cooperative action games of its time.

The gameplay follows on from the previous entry, meaning an over-the-shoulder view, an aiming mode, and a system of quick melee finishers on a staggered enemy. It was controversial at the time that the character couldn't walk while aiming, which led to deliberately tense situations where you had to judge whether you could still get a shot off or should instead dodge back. Enemies arrive in waves, flank, and use weapons, so the game becomes more of a tactical shooting gallery about managing space and resources than a horror game. Boss fights are spectacular, and the final act closes out one of the series' longest-running plotlines.

Technically the game was cutting-edge on PlayStation 3, mainly thanks to sharp daylight lighting, dusty effects, and detailed character models, a striking shift for a genre used to dark corridors. Reception was commercially extraordinary and critics praised the co-op, though there were also objections that the series had lost its horror identity, and the game also faced discussion over its depiction of the African setting. Today it's worth playing specifically as a pair: solo with the AI partner it loses its charm, but with a friend it's a brisk, well-paced action game. The offering is further expanded by bonus modes including a timed attack where you rack up score for quickly and precisely clearing waves of enemies, which is among the most addictive things the game offers.

ps3__mag.article:
**MAG** was one of the most ambitious attempts ever made in the shooter genre on consoles: it was a purely online title in which up to two hundred fifty-six players could take part in a single battle at once. The plot revolves around private military companies, and right at the start the player picks one of three factions, which differ not just in gear and weapon appearance but in overall tone, ranging from a well-equipped Western unit through a technologically advanced group to an improvised Eastern European army with battered equipment.

To keep such a huge number of players from collapsing into pure chaos, the developers built the game around a military hierarchy. Players formed squads, squads belonged to platoons, and above them stood commanders who issued orders, marked targets, and unlocked support abilities for their entire group. Anyone who followed orders earned more experience, which very cleverly motivated even random players to stick to a shared plan. Battles had phases: first break through the defense, then destroy inner objectives, and finally capture the base's core, so the map opened up and changed as the fight progressed.

Technically it was a remarkable feat, since keeping that many players on a single server was unheard of on console at the time; visually, though, the game sacrificed detail for it and looked rather plain. At the time it received a mixed reception, with critics praising the scale and team-based design but faulting a lackluster feel to the shooting and chaotic early matches. The servers were later shut down, so the game is unplayable today and remains mostly a historical footnote. That's exactly why it's worth remembering as one of the boldest experiments of its generation: it showed what an online shooter could look like when it doesn't try to be an arena for individuals but an actual battle with a front line, a chain of command, and the feeling that the player is just one small piece of a much larger clash. A similarly generous attempt hasn't been repeated on consoles for a long time.

ps3__far-cry-3.article:
**Far Cry 3** is the entry that gave the series the shape it still holds today: an open tropical island, a player with no combat experience, and a slow transformation into someone who gets a little too used to killing. Spoiled young Jason Brody falls, along with a group of friends, into the hands of pirates who control the archipelago and must free them one by one. But the real star is the unpredictable pirate leader, whose monologues about madness rank among the best-written passages in the entire series and were a major reason the game stuck in players' memory.

The world is densely packed with activities. The player takes over enemy camps, which can be cleared quietly with a bow and knife or blown apart, releasing caged animals onto the guards; once a camp is captured the surrounding area calms down and new tasks open up. Radio towers unlock parts of the map, hunting animals is used to craft bigger pouches and bags, gathering plants is used to brew potions, and earned experience unlocks skills recorded as tattoos on the hero's arm. The shooting is precise and satisfying, fire spreads across vegetation, and guard AI allows for improvisation, so every attack turns into a slightly different story.

On PlayStation 3 it's clear the game was pushing the hardware to its limit: the image is softer and the frame rate dips, yet the view of jungle, sea, and sunsets remains striking. At the time the title received very favorable reviews and became a commercial success that set the template for a number of later open-world games from the same publisher. Today Far Cry 3 is still a brisk and surprisingly free-form action game, whose main strength lies in how easily a planned strike turns into chaos you have to handle on the fly. A tiger appearing in the middle of a camp raid, burning grass changing the direction of the assault, or a badly aimed grenade can turn a careful plan into a desperate dash through the jungle, and it's exactly these moments that produce the best the game has to offer.

ps3__burnout-paradise.article:
**Burnout Paradise** turned an established arcade series on its head by ditching the menu of tracks and dropping the player into one continuous city. Paradise City is an open map laced with highways, shortcuts through construction sites, and ramps on rooftops, and every intersection in it functions as a starting line. A race begins with a simple stomp on the gas at a traffic light, the destination is marked only by a district's name, and finding the way there is entirely up to the player, since navigation practically doesn't exist and you have to build up your own sense of the city. Alongside standard races, the game offers modes like Road Rage, about knocking rivals off the road, or Marked Man, in which the player fights their way to the finish ahead of pursuers.

The core remains a contest for speed through risk: driving into oncoming traffic, close near-misses, and long drifts fill up a boost meter that can be burned instantly. Crashes aren't a punishment but a spectacle, since the camera slows down and the crumpled wreck keeps flying on through momentum, so even failure has its own rhythm. Technically it was an impressive piece of work; smooth loading of the sprawling city with no black loading screens was among the best on PlayStation 3, and the body-deformation system was remarkable for its time. The atmosphere is held together by a laid-back rock and electronic radio selection accompanied by a host's voice commenting on the player's progress and keeping up the impression that the city lives on even without them.

Reception was enthusiastic, though some fans of the earlier entries resented having to drive back to the start for the next race after a crash. Criterion supported the game for a long time with updates that added motorcycles, a day-night cycle, and an extra chunk of map, turning Paradise into one of the first great examples of a game growing after release. The influence is still felt today, since open cities without menus and with instant restarts have become the standard for arcade racers. Even years later the game handles beautifully, because it doesn't bet on simulation accuracy but on a pure sense of speed and the urge to drive through the city one more time, a different way.

ps3__need-for-speed-hot-pursuit.article:
**Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit** brought the brand back to what made it famous in the nineties, meaning police chases and fast road cars on long rural highways. After its Burnout experience, Criterion carried its sense of pace and impact over into the series, but instead of an urban jungle it offered Seacrest County, with mountain switchbacks, desert straights, and forest sections where the weather and time of day change from race to race. The player moves through two parallel careers: in one they sit behind the wheel of a supercar trying to escape, in the other they drive for the police and have to stop the fleeing car.

The contest between the two sides is built on a set of tools that get activated like weapons. The racer has access to radar jamming or vehicle repair, the cop deploys spike strips, calls in a helicopter, and unleashes an EMP burst. Because of this every chase has its own dramatic arc with several twists, ending either in an effective roadblock or a narrow escape. A major innovation was the Autolog system, which constantly compared times against a friends list and sent challenges straight to the menu, turning solo play into an ongoing competition. Technically the game made a clean, sharp impression on PlayStation 3, with convincing reflections on car bodies and rain sections that noticeably changed grip.

Reviews received the game very positively and often called it the best Need for Speed in a long time. Autolog became one of the most influential ideas of its time, and various other racing games adopted it in different forms, since it elegantly solved the question of how to keep players engaged through social motivation. Today the title still works mainly thanks to balanced handling that's direct enough for an inexperienced driver to enjoy while still rewarding precise braking before a turn. Its low barrier to entry and short, intense races make it an ideal game for a shorter evening session.

ps3__split-second.article:
**Split/Second** is a racing game that acts like a TV action show, and its central idea looks the part: the track falls apart right before the player's eyes. During a race a power meter fills up from drifting, jumping, and drafting in a rival's slipstream, and the accumulated power can be unleashed at precisely designated points. A weaker hit drops a bus onto the road or sets off an explosion by a wall, but the strongest one collapses an entire tower, brings down a plane onto the runway, or reroutes the track and opens up a completely new path to the finish. So a race never looks the same twice, and the last lap tends to be more dramatic than the first.

Against these tricks stands the need to anticipate: when a rival triggers a trap ahead of you, you have a split second to dodge, so the game demands both alertness and a steady hand. The controls are arcade-style, with long, controllable drifts and a simple model that pushes car tuning aside in favor of pure driving. Alongside standard races there are modes like a duel against a helicopter dropping rockets or a run among trucks releasing explosive barrels behind them. Technically it made for a very striking spectacle on PlayStation 3, full of particle effects, dust, and debris, accompanied by orchestral music in the style of action films.

Critics received the game warmly and praised its boldness and clean execution, but commercially it didn't reach the genre's big names, and studio Black Rock eventually closed down, so a sequel never happened. That's exactly why it now has the reputation of a forgotten gem, often brought up in discussions of which arcade racers deserve a comeback. Playing it today, it's surprising how well it holds its pace and how few unnecessary systems it contains; it's a direct, loud, and confident game built on a single strong idea that it sees all the way through. Part of the motivation to keep coming back is that the player gradually learns to read each track differently, knowing where a trap can be set up and where, conversely, there's a risk of getting caught by one. Split/Second simply belongs among the titles worth trying even for people who aren't normally drawn to racing games.

ps3__dirt-3.article:
**DiRT 3** is the peak of the period when Codemasters were looking for a balance between honest rally racing and a show for a broad audience. The career takes the player through classic special stages in Kenya, Finland, Norway, or Michigan, racing against the clock with a co-driver calling out the corners, and these alternate with rallycross, dirt ovals, and other disciplines with larger grids of cars. The car roster ranges from historic icons of the seventies and eighties to modern rally cars, so vehicles that handle completely differently in corners keep swapping in and out.

The handling model sits pleasantly between simulation and arcade. A car on gravel slides, left-foot braking and throttle work matter, but the game offers a range of assists and, above all, a flashback feature that rewinds the drive a few seconds after a crash, easing the frustration of a single mistake near the end of a long stage. The Gymkhana mode drew a great deal of attention at the time, meaning free-form acrobatic arenas full of ramps and containers, scored for drifts, spins, and passes through obstacles. Technically the game looked very good on PlayStation 3, especially thanks to striking lighting, dust kicked up behind the car, and changeable weather including snow and rain that noticeably altered grip.

Reception was strongly positive, and many players still consider it the best entry in the series, since it still contained a rich body of classic rally content that later entries partly abandoned in favor of a festival-style approach. The sound design ranks among the best the genre has offered, since engines, kicked-up stones, and the co-driver's voice create a convincing backdrop. Today DiRT 3 feels like a generous package: enough content for dozens of hours, handling that rewards patience, and at the same time a barrier to entry low enough for someone with no experience of gravel tracks to manage. Anyone who turns off the assists and the flashback gets a surprisingly demanding contest for tenths of a second, where a single missed braking point means the end of the stage. It's exactly this breadth of settings that makes DiRT 3 one of the few rally titles that a casual Sunday player and a dedicated fan can enjoy equally well.

ps3__ridge-racer-7.article:
**Ridge Racer 7** was one of the titles that accompanied the launch of PlayStation 3, and true to the series' tradition it served as a showcase for what the new console could do. It offered smooth, high-resolution visuals, rich colors, and a sense of speed that looked dazzling on TVs of the time. The series never promised realism; its signature is the drift: lifting off the throttle before a corner throws the back of the car into a long, theatrically held slide that the player maintains with gentle corrections while simultaneously filling a meter for a sharp burst of acceleration on the straight.

The seventh entry expanded this basic mechanic with a fairly deep layer of tuning. The player collects parts for the engine, transmission, and chassis, combines them according to their driving style, and tunes the car for tracks with long sweeping curves or, conversely, for tight urban sections. The career is split into a long series of events with rising difficulty, complemented by online play, which in 2006 was among the first such offerings on console. An integral part of the experience is the music, meaning the series' signature mix of drum and bass, techno, and electronic pop that has accompanied it since the nineties and contributes significantly to its recognizable mood.

Reviews received the game positively, but it was often seen as a respectful, rather conservative update of the previous entries rather than a genuinely new step. That paradoxically works in its favor today, since it's a distilled form of what Ridge Racer was: a clean, fast, instantly understandable arcade racer without unnecessary fuss. The tracks are designed to be learned by heart and reward repeated runs where a player shaves off tenths of a second. As a reminder of a style of Japanese arcade racing that's practically no longer made, it's a title that deserves attention. This is helped by the visual style, with bold colors, neon tunnels, and cars inspired by real sports cars but deliberately fictional, so the game never feels like a brand catalog. For PlayStation 3 owners it's also a pleasant reminder of what the console's first weeks looked like.

ps3__rock-band-3.article:
**Rock Band 3** is the culmination of an era when plastic guitars, drums, and microphones filled living rooms all over the world. The core remains playing a song together, where each player watches their own note highway, tries to hit the rhythm, and helps keep the band afloat together; mistakes drain energy, while correctly played passages let you trigger overdrive, which boosts the score and revives bandmates. The third entry added keyboards as a full instrument and expanded vocals to allow three simultaneous singers with harmonies, so more people than ever before could join in at once.

The most ambitious feature was Pro mode, meant to cross the line between game and real music. With a matching controller featuring real strings or a keyboard with a full octave, the game taught actual fingerings and chords, so the difficulty rose sharply, but the player learned something transferable beyond the screen along the way. Alongside this the game overhauled its song library management, which thanks to downloadable content numbered hundreds of songs across genres from classic rock to modern alternative, and offered a clearer way to quickly build a playlist without needless menu-clicking.

Critics received the game with great enthusiasm and often called it the peak of the entire genre, though commercially interest in music games with plastic instruments was already fading, and the market shut down almost entirely soon after. That's exactly why Rock Band 3 holds a special place today: it's the most complete form of an idea that briefly turned playing games into a social event. Anyone who can get hold of working instruments gets entertainment that still works great in a group, since it doesn't rely on story or graphics but on shared rhythm and the joy of an entire room nailing the chorus.

ps3__guitar-hero-iii-legends-of-rock.article:
**Guitar Hero III: Legends of Rock** is the entry that carried the brand to the absolute peak of its popularity and became the symbol of the entire wave of music games with a plastic guitar. The principle stayed simple: colored notes stream down the screen, the player holds the matching fret on the neck, and strums the pick at the right moment. Long note streaks without a miss raise a score multiplier, and when the Star Power meter fills up and the player triggers it by tilting the guitar or pressing a button, points double and the crowd erupts with excitement.

The third entry raised the difficulty and, above all, added guitar battles against legendary rockers, pitting the player against a rival in a duel where each side can send the other disruptive effects like a broken string or scrambled controls. Alongside these the game offered a two-player co-op career and an extensive tracklist made up of rock and metal classics as well as more modern cuts, for the first time largely in original recordings instead of studio re-recordings. The visual style is deliberately over the top, with cartoonish musicians, smoke, and a light show underscoring the feeling of a huge concert. The series' closing track became famous as one of the hardest challenges music games ever offered.

The reception was enormous, and the game became one of the best-selling titles of its generation, kicking off a flood of sequels and spin-offs that eventually wore the genre out. Today Guitar Hero III is interesting both as a perfect snapshot of its era and as a surprisingly honest rhythm challenge; on higher difficulties it demands real coordination and stamina. Without a working guitar peripheral it loses most of its point, but with one it delivers exactly what it promised: the instant, loud, and infectious feeling of standing on a stage in front of a sold-out arena.

ps-vita__uncharted-golden-abyss.article:
**Uncharted: Golden Abyss** was part of the PlayStation Vita's launch lineup, and it had one job — to prove that a big console-style action-adventure could be shrunk into a pocket without visible compromises. Nathan Drake gets tangled up in the search for a long-lost Spanish expedition, whose trail leads into a Central American jungle and to a discovery that was clearly meant to stay buried. The storytelling keeps the series' familiar face: buddy banter, ambiguous alliances, and temples that collapse just as the hero is climbing through them. The gameplay combines climbing weathered cliffs, cover-based shootouts, and exploration in which small finds gradually piece together the map of where to go next.

Development was handled by Bend Studio, and it clearly had fun with what the new console could do. Besides the classic dual-analog controls, the game offers touch input: you drag a finger across the screen to haul yourself onto a ledge, scrape charcoal across paper to reveal a hidden drawing, and use the Vita's camera to hunt for details in the surrounding landscape. Not all of these ideas have aged equally well, but most are optional or brief, so they don't disrupt the pacing of the action. Technically, it was one of the most impressive showcases of the hardware — jungle canopies letting light filter through, rain-soaked stones, and main-character animation that came close to the series' home-console entries.

The atmosphere is helped along by orchestral music in the spirit of adventure films and solid voice acting that makes the characters more than mere level guides. Contemporary reviews praised the title as proof that the Vita could handle a full-blown blockbuster, while also faulting it for not daring to diverge much from its predecessors. Today the game plays like an interesting stepping stone: it isn't the strongest Uncharted episode, but it's the best demonstration of what Sony hoped for from its second handheld. Anyone picking up a Vita today usually starts right here — it's a tight, well-crafted adventure that also holds up well played in short bursts.

ps-vita__gravity-rush.article:
**Gravity Rush** is the most distinctive thing the PlayStation Vita received in its first year. The heroine Kat wakes up in a strange floating city called Hekseville with no memories, a black cat at her side, and along with it the ability to switch which direction gravity pulls her. Instead of running, then, you fall — Kat pushes off, aims at the facade of a distant building, and lands on it as if it were the ground. This creates a kind of movement with few equivalents in the genre: exploring the city is itself the main attraction, and combat is its faster variant, where the heroine picks up speed and slams into enemies like a living projectile.

The game's structure is fairly traditional. Alongside story missions there are side quests, time trials, and gem collecting used to upgrade individual abilities. Kat gradually learns a gravity slide that sends her skimming across the ground as if on invisible skates, as well as a mighty gravity kick that flattens everything nearby, so there's plenty to choose from. Camera control can be supplemented with the gyroscope, so fine-tuning your flight direction is done by tilting the whole console. Visually, SCE Japan Studio went all in on a comic-book stylization with pastel colors, bold outlines, and cutscenes narrated like flipping through a European comic; the French inspiration shows in every corner. The music alternates jazz motifs with restless orchestral passages, and thanks to it, Hekseville feels like a place somewhere between a dream and a postwar European metropolis.

At the time, the game received a very favorable reception for its ideas and atmosphere, while criticism was aimed at repetitive side quests and boss fights that failed to fully exploit the gravity mechanics. The influence was nonetheless clear: a sequel came out on PlayStation 4, and the very concept of free-falling through a city became one of the icons of the entire Vita era. Today, Gravity Rush is worth playing mainly for the feel of movement. It hasn't aged one bit and can still deliver a light bout of vertigo after just a few minutes — something you rarely expect from a video game.

ps-vita__killzone-mercenary.article:
**Killzone: Mercenary** remains one of the best proofs that a first-person shooter can be played on a handheld without feeling like a compromise. Here the player doesn't side with the ISA or the Helghast, but hires out to whoever pays better — and money is also the game's central mechanic. Every hit, every silent takedown, and every completed objective brings in credits, which get spent between missions at a black-market dealer for weapons, shields, and combat drones. The campaign therefore offers several ways through each level: a loud firefight, careful stealth around guards, or a combination of both, depending on what pays off at the moment.

Guerrilla Cambridge built the controls around dual analog sticks and uses touch only where it genuinely helps — brutal close-quarters takedowns are finished with a finger swipe, and hacking terminals is a brief minigame. Technically it was a flagship of the hardware: wet streets, metallic interiors of Helghast ships, and the enemies' characteristic orange eyes glowing in the dark rank among the best things to appear on the Vita, and the game kept a smooth frame rate throughout. The sound is typically Killzone — heavy and loud, with music that underscores the industrial grime and hopelessness of war rather than any heroism.

It also included eight-player multiplayer, which kept a living community on the console for a long time and was one of the few handheld shooters that could be taken seriously. Beyond the campaign, the game also offered contract variants of already-completed missions, turning the same levels into purely stealthy or purely aggressive assignments, which significantly extended its lifespan. Reviews at the time praised it as the best shooter on the Vita while noting that the campaign is short and the story secondary. Today it's still worth booting up for how naturally it controls and how well its reward system works, pushing you to play aggressively and with style. It's a game where you forget after a while that you're holding a pocket console — something few games of its generation managed.

ps-vita__tearaway.article:
**Tearaway** is a game that never once tries to pretend it runs on anything other than what it actually runs on. Its entire world is made of paper, and the player doesn't enter it as an invisible camera but as a literally present character: there's a hole in the sky of this paper world, and your face, captured by the Vita's front camera, appears through it. The messenger Iota, or his counterpart Atoi, carries a message meant precisely for you, and the journey to deliver it winds through forests, mountains, and strange towns glued together from cardboard, corrugated paper, and colored construction paper.

Media Molecule built the gameplay on the idea that the player reaches into the world from the outside. Fingers push through the rear touch panel and appear in the level as giant fingertips, used to push aside an obstacle or launch an enemy into the air. Drums are set ringing with a tap, paper objects are cut out by tracing a finger along a drawn line, and your own drawings and photos then show up on characters and in the environment. The platforming portion is deliberately gentle and accessible, with the emphasis lying on exploration and on what the player themselves brings into the world. Creative tasks pile up gradually: the inhabitants ask for a crown, a squirrel-fur coat, or a butterfly, the player cuts it out of colored paper right on the touchscreen, and the creation then stays in the level, carrying the player's own handwriting.

Visually it's one of the most distinctive titles of its whole generation — everything has visible creases, folds, and paper fibers, shadows fall as if on a tabletop model, and music with folk instruments and hummed melodies holds it all together. At the time the game was received extremely well and was often cited as the best argument for buying a Vita, with its only real knock being its brevity. An expanded version later appeared for PlayStation 4, but it's the original that makes the most sense: without the Vita's touch panels, camera, and microphone, half its ideas couldn't exist at all. Today it feels like a small, personal gift rather than a technology demo, and that's rare.

ps-vita__littlebigplanet-ps-vita.article:
**LittleBigPlanet PS Vita** took the series about the sewn-together character Sackboy and brought it to hardware that, surprisingly, suits it even better than the home consoles. The foundation remains unchanged — a two-and-a-half-dimensional platformer where you run, jump, and grab onto objects in an environment stitched together from fabric, cardboard, zippers, and buttons. The campaign leads you through a colorful journey full of traps, carts, and whimsical machines, and as always offers material and sticker collecting that can then be used in your own level creations. Alongside the main campaign there's also a set of quick arcade minigames designed specifically for touch controls, perfect for a few minutes on the tram.

The novelty here is the use of touch. The front panel is used for pulling and squeezing rubbery blocks, the rear one for pushing platforms forward, and some levels are built entirely around the idea that the player interacts with the world using fingers instead of Sackboy. Tarsier Studios and Double Eleven didn't settle for a mere port, either: the level editor here is complete, and thanks to the touchscreen, drawing and placing objects in it is noticeably more pleasant than with a gamepad. A whole range of community-made minigames emerged as a result, sharing nothing at all with the classic platformer and exploiting the Vita's hardware in their own way. The editor also handles logic circuits and custom sounds, so the line between playing and creating is thinner here than elsewhere.

Technically, the game kept a clean look and smooth performance, albeit with fewer objects on screen than on PlayStation 3. Sound and music stayed true to the series' spirit — a mix of circus, world music, and electronic motifs layered according to wherever the player happens to be walking. Reception at the time was very good, and the title was often called the best entry in the series since the second installment. Today its value is mixed: the campaign itself works wonderfully and is still fun, but online sharing of user-made levels has since shut down, so the greatest strength of the whole brand is harder to access than it used to be.

ps-vita__soul-sacrifice.article:
**Soul Sacrifice** is a dark answer to the question of what a cooperative monster-hunting game might look like if, instead of cheerful fantasy, it drew on a cruel fairy tale. The player is a prisoner of a sorcerer named Magusar, and the only thing they have at hand is a living book that recounts past battles — each reading of it means another mission. The goal is to defeat a beast that used to be human, and then decide: save its soul, or sacrifice it. The choice isn't cosmetic; it changes the character's stats, available abilities, and the tone of the story, and the game never lets the player feel entirely clean about it.

Combat plays out in arenas against one or several large opponents and is built around spells with a limited number of uses. Before a mission, the player assembles six slots and burns through them in battle, so improvisation is necessary and hoarding doesn't pay off. Your own body can be sacrificed for a devastating attack at the cost of permanent weakening, which keeps the game under constant pressure. Cooperative play for up to four was the main draw at the time, and the sacrifice system took on new meaning within it: a fallen companion could be revived, or drained of their magical energy for yourself. Individual missions are short, usually ten to fifteen minutes, so the game's structure precisely matches how a handheld console is actually played.

Visually it's one of the rawest titles on the Vita — a pale palette, bloody motifs, monsters stitched together from human wreckage, and an interface presented as pages from an old book. The book itself serves as narrator, and its written commentary changes according to the player's decisions, so even repeated expeditions carry a different flavor each time. The music is orchestral and operatic, with female vocals that push the battles toward the register of a lament. Reviews praised the game for its ideas and dark tone, with reservations aimed at repetitive environments. The developers later released an expanded version, Soul Sacrifice Delta, and the brand built a devoted following that still remembers it as the most distinctive alternative to the monster-hunting genre. Today what holds it back most is that its multiplayer depends entirely on who you can scrounge up.

ps-vita__freedom-wars.article:
**Freedom Wars** is one of the strangest games Sony ever released for the PlayStation Vita. The player is born into a world where existence itself is a crime: at the start you're already carrying a sentence of a million years, and every completed mission, every task, and every resource gathered shortens it. The absurd bureaucracy reaches down to the most banal details — without logged work hours the character isn't allowed to lie down, run, have privacy, or move away from their supervising android, and unlocking these basic freedoms is a full-fledged part of progressing through the game.

The action itself is a cooperative hunting game for up to eight players built around one key tool: the Thorn, an energy tether that lets the player pull themselves toward a giant machine, climb up its side, and cut away its armor or limbs. Movement through the arenas feels noticeably more nimble than in the competition because of it, and combat has a distinctly vertical dimension. Alongside melee and ranged weapons, players can rely on fellow prisoners and accompanying androids; rescuing civilians is also important, since they serve as both the main currency and motivation in the conflict between city-states. Objectives range from pure machine destruction through defending a position to stealing prisoners from an enemy city, and the player enters them with a squad of AI-controlled fellow prisoners whenever they aren't teamed up with others.

Technically it was a solid performer — large enemy machines, plenty of objects on screen, and acceptable smoothness — and the visual style mixes stark dystopia with Japanese pop-culture stylization, including the ability to customize your own character and their android in detail. It also includes a surprisingly extensive crafting and weapon-upgrade system. The music is energetic electronica with orchestral surges. Reviews at the time praised the original framing and the Thorn-based combat, less so the confusing menus and long-winded rule explanations. Today, Freedom Wars is most interesting precisely for its world: few action games have built their progression on the idea that the player is literally serving out a sentence for the right to exist.

ps-vita__wipeout-2048.article:
**WipEout 2048** is the final installment of the legendary anti-gravity racing series, and also one of the best games the PlayStation Vita received right at the start of its life. Time-wise it goes back to the very beginning of the league, back when racing still happened directly through city streets between buildings — so the tracks feature concrete walls, ramps, and highway overpasses instead of the later, purely futuristic circuits. The campaign is arranged into three seasons by year and offers classic races, time trials, zone battles, and elimination runs where weapons are the whole point. Progression isn't strictly linear, either: every race offers several different objectives at once, and the player chooses which ones to pursue, so it's possible to move forward even without a perfect finish.

The controls remain brutally demanding on precision: the player has to master airbrakes for tight corners, manage energy that serves as both health and turbo fuel, and know when to use a weapon and when to scrap it for energy instead. Ships are divided by focus into speed, agility, and endurance types, and further split into performance classes, which changes track behavior far more fundamentally than it might first appear. Studio Liverpool also added the ability to race against PlayStation 3 owners on the same tracks, an unusual luxury at the time. Technically it's a showy display of the hardware — the game runs smoothly, sharply, with excellent reflections on the ships' bodies, and the series' clean typographic design still looks good years later.

Music is just as important here as the racing. The soundtrack leans on electronic acts and club rhythms, and together with engine noise and race-tower announcements it creates a feeling that has no equivalent elsewhere in the genre. Reviews at the time ranked it among the console's best titles, with the reservation of long loading times in early versions. Studio Liverpool was closed shortly after release, so 2048 ended up being its farewell — and, at the same time, the end of one of PlayStation's most important series. Today it's among the few games worth pulling the Vita out of the drawer for.

ps-vita__sly-cooper-thieves-in-time.article:
**Sly Cooper: Thieves in Time** brought back the master thief of the Cooper clan after a long break, and it arrived on PlayStation Vita alongside the PlayStation 3 version. The plot hinges on pages vanishing from the family book Thievius Raccoonus — someone in the past is rewriting the history of the entire Cooper line, so the old gang sets out to travel through time to feudal Japan, the wild west, medieval England, and even the ice age. Each episode has its own setting, its own villain, and its own forgotten Cooper ancestor who needs to be tracked down.

The gameplay stayed faithful to the original trilogy: sneaking along ledges and ropes, silently pickpocketing guards, switching between the three main characters, and missions that flow from freely explorable districts into a big heist at the end of each chapter. Sanzaru Games added costumes that change abilities — one lets you play a lute and summon allies, another lets you fly through the air or move through fire. This makes the structure more varied, though at the cost of occasional dead spots where the game sets its core thieving discipline aside. There are also minigames, in which Bentley hacks into security systems in the form of a retro arcade shooter, while Murray solves things with brute force.

The Vita version kept the cartoonish look with bold outlines and smooth motion, just with lower resolution and less detailed backgrounds than on the home console; it also supported cross-platform save transfers and touch inputs in several minigames. The music is playful, with jazz and ethnic motifs matching each era, and the voice acting still has the charm of classic animated series. Contemporary reviews received the title kindly as a decent comeback that nonetheless didn't surpass the second entry. Today it's the series' final chapter, and on Vita its mission-based structure makes it ideal for short play sessions. There are also plenty of collectibles, from bottles that unlock each episode's vault to masks, so anyone wanting to see everything will spend considerably more time in the game.

ps-vita__assassin-s-creed-iii-liberation.article:
**Assassin's Creed III: Liberation** was, in 2012, the main argument for why a PlayStation Vita owner should pick up a big licensed action-adventure game. The game runs parallel to the series' third entry, but instead of colonial New England, it takes place in 18th-century New Orleans, its surrounding swamps, and Mayan ruins. The lead character is Aveline de Grandpré, daughter of a French merchant and an African mother — an unusual perspective for the series, one the game manages to use not just in the story but directly in the gameplay.

The key mechanic is a set of three personas. In a lady's dress, Aveline doesn't arouse suspicion and can bribe people, but she can't climb; disguised as a slave, she blends in among laborers and moves unnoticed; in her assassin outfit she has full freedom of movement and her whole arsenal, but she instantly draws the guards' attention. The rest is classic Assassin's Creed of the era — rooftop parkour, combat counterattacks, silent kills from above, and an open city full of side quests, including a trading network and sending shipments by boat. The persona system comes with a suspicion meter that behaves differently for each disguise, so the player has to think not only about where to go but also how to look while doing it.

Technically, it was an impressive feat: on Vita, New Orleans has a dense crowd, a day-night cycle, and vegetation that wasn't common on a handheld at the time, though at the cost of minor hiccups and a shorter draw distance. Touch controls are used more out of obligation, for rowing or opening letters. Besides the city, the game also plays out in the open swamps of Louisiana, where the player moves along branches and treetops much like in the third game's colonial wilderness. The atmosphere is helped by music with Creole motifs and the sultry, damp swamp setting. Contemporary reviews praised the scope and the lead character while criticizing the simplified and poorly told story. Aveline later got a remaster for home consoles, but the original version remains a showcase of just how far portable gaming could be pushed at the time.

ps-vita__metal-gear-solid-hd-collection.article:
**Metal Gear Solid HD Collection** brought two of its era's most ambitious action-adventure games — Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty and Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater — to PlayStation Vita in reworked resolution and with all their bonus missions intact. For console owners, this meant getting games in their pocket that previously required a television and hours-long blocks of time, without losing anything essential. It was thus one of the most generous packages ever released on this platform. Both games also include extensive bonus and virtual missions, which push the total content into the dozens of hours.

Both games are built around stealth: the player skirts around guards, watches their fields of view and the sound of their own footsteps, and uses boxes, disguises, and a tranquilizer pistol, with direct combat generally being an admission of failure. The third game adds jungle terrain, camouflage matched to the environment, treating wounds, and managing your own food supply, making it one of the series' most detailed entries. The Vita lacked analog triggers and a second pair of shoulder buttons, so Armature Studio's port shifted part of the controls to the touch panels — aiming and certain actions are handled with your fingers, and it takes a while to get used to. The third game is also one of the few where a boss fight plays out as a long, silent wait in the grass, and on a small screen that feels surprisingly intimate.

Technically, the collection was one of the better ports on the console: the image is sharp, performance is mostly stable, and save transfers between Vita and PlayStation 3 worked. The audio remains extraordinary — cinematic orchestral themes, long codec conversations, and silence that works better during stealth than any music could. Contemporary reviews recommended the collection as one of the best reasons to own a Vita, with reservations about the controls. Today it's the most convenient way to play through Snake Eater on the go, a game that fundamentally shaped the entire stealth genre.

ps-vita__ninja-gaiden-sigma-2-plus.article:
**Ninja Gaiden Sigma 2 Plus** is a portable version of one of its generation's toughest action games, and on PlayStation Vita it kept everything that made the original an uncompromising experience. Ryu Hayabusa once again sets out against a demonic conspiracy, this time backed by several playable companions, and from the first minutes the game demands that the player learn its precise combat rhythm. This isn't a game you can button-mash your way through; every fight requires focus and a good knowledge of your own equipment. The series has a reputation as one of the genre's most demanding, and this version doesn't let up on that at all.

The combat system ranks among the most elaborate in the genre. Each of Ryu's weapons has its own strings of attacks, blocking, dodging, and counterattacks are essential, and once an enemy loses an arm or a leg, its behavior instantly changes — maimed opponents throw themselves into suicidal attacks. Battles pit the player against large numbers of enemies at once, mistakes are punished mercilessly, and the difficulty is high even on the base setting. The port added an easier mode for newcomers, reworked enemy placement, and missions that let you play as characters outside the main storyline. Alongside Ryu, you also get to play as Ayane, Rachel, and Momiji, each with her own arsenal and pace, which expands the game with several standalone segments.

Technically, this involved trade-offs: resolution and the number of enemies on screen had to be scaled back, and smoothness isn't always ideal — noticeable in a game built around reflexes. Still, the sense of power remains — the animation, weapon sounds, and movement speed are still exceptional, and the drum-and-orchestra soundtrack keeps pushing the pace forward. Contemporary reviews treated it as a decent but technically compromised port of a big action game; genre fans forgave it, since nothing else that demanding existed on the console. Besides the main storyline, there are also single-player challenge missions that make the whole package feel more like an arcade trainer than an adventure. Today it's mainly of interest to players who want portable action that forgives not a single mistake.

ps-vita__atelier-rorona-plus-alchemist-o.article:
**Atelier Rorona Plus: The Alchemist of Arland** brought the first entry in Gust's Arland trilogy to PlayStation Vita in a reworked form with new graphics and improved systems. The titular Rorona inherits an alchemy workshop from her teacher, only for the kingdom to immediately hand her an ultimatum: if she doesn't complete a series of assigned commissions within three years, the workshop will be shut down. So instead of saving the world, you handle fairly ordinary concerns — supplying the town with medicine, baking a cake for the queen, gathering materials, and trying not to go broke in the process.

The game is built on three interlinked activities. You gather materials at surrounding locations, synthesize items from them following recipes where the quality and properties of the ingredients genuinely matter, and all the while keep an eye on the calendar, since every action consumes days. Battles are turn-based and mainly serve as a way to get better materials. You recruit townsfolk into your party, and their goodwill grows depending on how you treat them and how much time you spend with them. There are several endings, and they hinge precisely on these relationships and on how well you handled your commissions. The workshop itself offers plenty of small optimizations, since a higher-quality intermediate product feeds into the final item's properties, and an experienced player can squeeze far more out of the same raw materials.

The Plus version added new characters, difficulty levels, costumes, and the option to keep playing after finishing the main story, and above all it adjusted the pacing, which felt rushed in the original release. The visuals are pastel, relaxed, and pleasantly unconfrontational, while the music leans on light acoustic and jazz motifs that make Atelier one of the most soothing series in the genre. Critics praised the depth of the alchemy system and the charming atmosphere, with reservations aimed at the time limit, which won't suit everyone. On Vita, it's a model game for evening play sessions when you don't want tension, just a well-designed system you can keep optimizing endlessly.

ps-vita__borderlands-2.article:
**Borderlands 2** ranks among the most ambitious ports ever to appear on PlayStation Vita, since it squeezed a full, sprawling shooter with dozens of hours of content and endless weapon generation into your pocket. The game takes place on the harsh planet Pandora, where four mercenary vault hunters fight against the corporate tyrant Handsome Jack, whose caustic commentary accompanies the whole journey. Its foundation blends shooter and RPG: characters level up, develop skill trees, and above all collect weapons that the game randomly assembles from different parts, so every chest might hide something slightly different. On top of that comes a comic-book art style with bold outlines that stays clear and colorful even on a smaller display.

The move to a handheld required compromises. The frame rate is lower than on home consoles, detail density in the open plains dropped, and co-op was limited to two players instead of four, turning the chaotic shared firefights into a more intimate experience. On the other hand, the release included the extra characters and part of the expansions, so the sheer volume of content remained staggering, and the touchscreen took over the map, inventory, and quick weapon swapping, which made managing the enormous collection much easier.

Contemporary reviews were split: critics praised the sheer nerve of bringing a game this big to a portable console, and the fact that the fun loop of collecting and shooting still worked here, but the technical side was frequently criticized. With hindsight, the Vita version is interesting mainly as proof that the looter shooter is a genre practically made for playing in short bursts: a few missions in the evening, an interesting new weapon part, and the urge to come back tomorrow. Anyone unfamiliar with Pandora gets one of the most wittily written shooters of its time, along with a distinctive soundscape full of one-liners and a desert guitar atmosphere. It was precisely that humor and stylization that set the series apart from the competition and helped define the whole loot-shooter genre that many later games built on.

ps-vita__legend-of-heroes-trails-of-cold.article:
