Critics received the game extremely well, and many reviewers called it one of the best arcade games of the digital era. Today it's an ideal fifteen-minute title that easily turns into two hours chasing a better score. It also nicely demonstrates that a cleverly reimagined classic can be more interesting than most new ideas, since it rests on rules proven by whole generations of arcade players.

ps3__ratchet-and-clank-future-crack-in-t.article:
**Ratchet & Clank Future: A Crack in Time** closes out the trilogy Insomniac Games launched on PlayStation 3, and it does so with an unexpectedly personal story. Ratchet finally catches up with the kidnapped Clank, while also learning more about the fate of his nearly extinct people, the Lombaxes. Clank, meanwhile, finds himself inside the Great Clock, a colossal machine at the center of the universe that keeps time running. This split is exactly what divides the game into two distinct halves. Ratchet's segments are classic action-platforming with a rich arsenal of bizarre weapons that improve on their own through use and can be further upgraded with the resource raritanium. Clank's segments, by contrast, are puzzle-based: on time-manipulation platforms, you record several copies of yourself who then act alongside you simultaneously, so you end up opening doors for yourself, holding down buttons, and assembling living gears out of your own repeated actions.

Free movement between planetoids is also new. Ratchet gets a small ship, and within a sector you can fly from one tiny body to another, collecting bonuses, completing side missions, and branching off the main line. On top of that come the hoverboots, which open up ground-level levels into fast, flowing runs. Technically, the game was among the best PS3 had to offer in the genre at the time: clean, colorful environments, plenty of objects and effects on screen without visible compromise, and animation on the level of animated feature-film production. Orchestral music and above-average voice acting complete the impression that you're playing an interactive animated movie.

Reviewers received the entry very warmly, and many still call it the peak of the entire series today. It's not just a technical showcase. It's an episode where humor partly gives way to melancholy, and where the final decision carries real weight. Today, A Crack in Time feels surprisingly fresh. The pace is fast, nothing bogs you down with unnecessary grinding, and combat still has plenty of drive thanks to the variety of weapons. If you missed Ratchet's cosmic escapades on PS3, this is exactly the entry to start with.

ps3__resistance-3.article:
**Resistance 3** is the final entry in the trilogy about the alien invasion of the Chimera, and at the same time the darkest game Insomniac Games made on PlayStation 3. Humanity has already lost the war. You play as Joseph Capelli, hiding underground with his family in a small American town, and when a chance appears to strike a decisive blow against the enemy, he sets out across a devastated America all the way to New York. The game's structure feels like a dark road movie: you make your way through flooded towns, mining tunnels, a river journey by boat, and abandoned industrial complexes, meeting a different group of survivors at every stop.

The gameplay deliberately returns to an older school of design. Health regeneration is gone, so you're back to collecting medkits, and above all, the weapon wheel is back, letting you carry your entire arsenal at once. This matters because Insomniac are masters of inventive weapons: shooting through walls, a trap that creates a gravity vortex, a freeze ray, or a shotgun with remotely detonated shells all form a set you genuinely want to switch between depending on the situation. Weapons also gain experience and turn into stronger versions with use. The campaign can be played in two-player co-op, and the game was among the titles that supported stereoscopic 3D on PS3.

Technically it was a solid performance: dense atmosphere, plenty of environmental detail, and impressive lighting work in the underground passages. The music and sound design push a hopeless mood, and the enemies genuinely feel hostile rather than just targets. Contemporary reviews were very good, though commercially the series could no longer compete with the genre's giants, and the third entry became its end. Today, Resistance 3 plays surprisingly well precisely because it doesn't chase the fashionable trends of its time. It's a straightforward, well-paced shooting journey with a strong identity, a properly long campaign, and one of the best-crafted endings of its era. For collectors of PlayStation 3 exclusives, it's also a mandatory stop, since you won't find the Resistance series anywhere else.

ps3__sound-shapes.article:
**Sound Shapes** blends platforming and a musical instrument into a single whole so elegantly that the boundary between them dissolves after just a while. The player controls a small sticky ball that clings to certain surfaces, crawls along walls and ceilings, and collects notes scattered throughout the level. Each collected note is instantly woven into the track playing in the background, so progressing through a level literally builds a song; the lethal elements have their own sound and rhythm, so even avoiding obstacles becomes part of the musical structure.

The campaign is divided into several albums, each with its own artist and musician and its own mood, ranging from lightly sketched worlds to strictly technical environments. Because of this, the game feels like a collection of short, heavily stylized pieces rather than one continuous adventure. The other half of the experience is an editor, in which the player can build their own level and their own track from the same building blocks and share it with others, turning the game into a kind of playful sequencer accessible even to people without any musical training. The PlayStation 3 version shared save progress with the handheld version, so you could continue on a second device.

Reviews praised especially the combination of ideas that on paper sound like an art experiment but end up playing pleasantly and clearly. The complexity of the platforming portion is modest, so the main campaign takes only a few hours, with the real value lying in replayability and community-made levels. Today, Sound Shapes stands as one of the best examples of what made the small digital scene on PlayStation 3 valuable: it offered games that didn't need a huge budget, because all they needed was one original idea carried through to completion with carefully executed craft.

ps3__skate-3.article:
**Skate 3** brought to its final form the control system that completely changed the way skateboarding games were viewed. Instead of a sequence of button presses, tricks are performed through movements of the right analog stick that mimic the actual motion of feet on a board; a different direction and a different speed of movement produce a different trick, so the player ends up learning timing and finesse rather than combinations. The result is a slower, more technical, and far more tangible experience than the arcade predecessors of the genre, where the point was mainly an endless combo.

The third entry shifted its focus toward building your own team and creating content. The player founds a brand, fulfills orders for photos and videos, and gradually builds a name for themselves in the city of Port Carverton, which is divided into districts with distinct characters, from smooth beaches to industrial zones. The park editor plays a big role, along with the ability to share your own spots and recordings from the built-in video editor, which let you cut together your own skate video with various camera angles. Cooperative play for several people in the same city was new to the series and fits well with the laid-back, unhurried atmosphere of the whole title.

The game was well received, though some players saw its lighter tone as a step back from the harsher realism of the first entry. It gained a peculiar second life thanks to its physics: a generous ragdoll mode, in which the character flies through the air and bounces off railings, became material for an enormous amount of videos, and the game earned a reputation as a source of absurd fun. Today it stands out mainly for controls that were never repeated anywhere else in such a pure form, and for its relaxed vibe backed by indie rock and hip hop music. It's a game that rewards patience, since the first hours can feel clumsy, but the movement, once learned, brings great satisfaction.

ps3__nba-2k11.article:
**NBA 2K11** is often regarded as the most significant basketball game of its generation, largely thanks to the mode dedicated to Michael Jordan, who returned to the series after years of absence. In it, players relive the famous games of his career under precisely defined conditions: to complete a challenge, they must match the statistics Jordan actually achieved at the time. The historical matches are also stylized visually to resemble period television broadcasts, complete with grain and period-accurate graphics, giving them a strong nostalgic charge.

The basketball on the court itself was among the most refined that simulations offered at the time. The game emphasizes spacing, timing, and physical contact under the basket; controlling the offense relies on managing tempo and on fine-tuned shot aiming with the right stick, rewarding patient play over quick shortcuts. There's also an extensive create-a-player mode starting from the draft, franchise management, and a wealth of tactical tuning options, making the game a title good for hundreds of hours. The presentation mimics a television broadcast, including commentary, instant replays, and music that accompanies the menus and breaks in play.

Reviews were exceptionally positive, and the game long remained part of debates about the best sports titles ever made. Its influence lies mainly in showing the value of historical content: a collection of licensed legendary teams and scenarios became a recurring feature of sports games. Today, NBA 2K11 is interesting mainly as a reminder of a time when annual sports series didn't yet rely primarily on microtransactions, and as a respectful tribute to one of the most famous athletes of all time. For basketball fans it remains an enjoyable game even years later, since the fundamentals of movement and battles under the basket age very slowly.

ps3__super-stardust-hd.article:
**Super Stardust HD** was one of the first titles to show that PlayStation 3's digital store could host games just as high-quality as boxed releases. It's a modern take on the classic asteroid-shooting concept, but instead of a flat screen, the action plays out on the surface of a round planet. The ship orbits the globe, the camera follows from above, and the player must constantly watch what's approaching from beyond the horizon, creating a peculiar tension that ordinary top-down shooters lack.

The core gameplay relies on three weapons that you switch between depending on the type of enemy: icy boulders, rocky asteroids, and golden fragments each require different ammunition, and anyone who doesn't learn to switch quickly will soon be swallowed by the debris. Added to this is a boost for quick escapes and a limited supply of bombs for emergencies. Each level ends with a boss fight, and the whole experience is built around repetition and improving your score, so a single run lasts tens of minutes, but return visits are frequent. Technically, it was excellent work, combining a fast, smooth picture with a huge number of particle effects and completely fluid performance even with hundreds of objects on screen, all accompanied by driving electronic music.

The reception was very positive, and the game became one of the flagship titles of the new service, often used to demonstrate the console's capabilities. Thanks to it, Housemarque earned a reputation as a studio specializing in modern arcade games and continued in this direction with further titles. Today, Super Stardust HD stands as a textbook example of a well-designed arcade game: the rules can be grasped within a minute, but mastery takes hours, and every failure has a clear cause that the player can see and correct on the next attempt.

ps3__pixeljunk-shooter.article:
**PixelJunk Shooter** belongs to a series of small digital games that studio Q-Games created for PlayStation 3, and of all its titles it's probably the best-balanced blend of action and thought. The player controls a rescue ship making its way into the depths of a planet, searching for trapped scientists. But the caves are full of fluids, and they are the true star of the game: water, lava, and gas behave according to their own physics, mixing and reacting with each other, so lava solidifies into rock upon contact with water, opening up a new path.

This gives rise to a peculiar hybrid gameplay style. Shooting mainly serves to break apart terrain and redirect flows, so most of the progress consists of finding a way to get water where it's hot, or to drain liquid from a sealed chamber. The ship overheats near lava and must be cooled in water, which puts a clear time pressure on every maneuver. Several special suits change the rules, for instance by allowing a dive into lava, and bosses close off individual sections. Visually the game is minimalist and cleanly drawn, the music is calm, electronic, and more atmospheric than action-oriented, which fits well with the pace of discovery.

Reviews were very warm and praised especially how gently the game teaches its mechanics without lengthy tutorials. The PixelJunk series became one of the symbols of an era when the console's digital store was discovering what smaller creators could achieve, and Shooter is probably the easiest of them to recommend. It's still enjoyable to play today, because its main strength, the fluid simulation, doesn't depend on powerful hardware or the trends of its time, and the playfulness of its individual puzzles is timeless.

ps3__braid.article:
**Braid** is a puzzle platformer that at first glance resembles classic jump-and-run games, but within a few minutes reveals that its true subject is time. The player can rewind events at any moment, without limitation, so death stops being a punishment and becomes an ordinary tool for experimentation. Each world then adds its own rule to this basic ability: in one, objects glowing gold are immune to the rewinding of time; in another, time flows according to the direction the character moves; and in yet another, the player is chased by their own shadow, which repeats the previous attempt.

The puzzles rely on the player working these rules through to their logical conclusion, and solving them often requires a shift in perspective rather than dexterity. Puzzle pieces collected by the player form images that close out each world, and the story, told through short texts at the start of each chapter, remains deliberately ambiguous; it speaks of searching, regret, and what a person considers their own. The visual style resembles a painting with soft colors, and the music, composed of existing acoustic and string pieces, gives the whole a melancholic, dreamlike tone.

The game was originally released on a competing platform and arrived on PlayStation 3 later, but its reception was strongly positive everywhere, and Braid became one of the titles that, at the start of this period, convinced the public that small independent games could have artistic ambitions. Its influence on the following wave of indie creation is hard to overlook. Today, Braid remains a surprisingly powerful experience: short, precisely measured, and free of unnecessary filler, with puzzles that haven't aged because they aren't built on trends but on a clean, well-constructed idea.

ps3__limbo.article:
**Limbo** begins without a single word of explanation: a boy wakes up in a forest and walks to the right. The whole game is black and white, rendered as silhouettes against a hazy depth of field and accompanied almost exclusively by ambient sounds, such as creaking wood, wind, and water. It's precisely this restraint that makes Limbo one of the most powerful atmospheric experiences of its time, since the player fills in most of the story themselves, and the game never tells them exactly what is happening or why.

The gameplay relies on physics-based puzzles and precise jumping. The player pulls crates, flips levers, swings on ropes, and uses gravity traps against enemies, among whom are other people and the famous giant spider from the opening sections. A significant portion of the puzzles are built around the player dying, which the game doesn't hide at all; the deaths are graphic and brutal, but checkpoints are generous and restarting is instant, so trial and error works as a natural way of learning. In the second half, the environment shifts from forest to industrial ruins, and the puzzles begin working with gravity and machinery, raising the pace.

The game was originally released elsewhere and arrived on PlayStation 3 in 2011 with solid technical execution. The reception was exceptionally praising, and Limbo, together with several other titles, became proof that the independent scene could produce games with their own clear authorial signature. Its visual style inspired numerous followers, and studio Playdead later followed it up with another, even more refined title. Today, Limbo can be completed in a single evening, and that's exactly its strength: it's a tight, evocative, and technically timeless game built on mood rather than effects.

ps3__bastion.article:
**Bastion** is an isometric action game that drew attention especially for its manner of storytelling. The world fell apart in a catastrophe called the Calamity, and the player, in the role of a silent boy, walks through its ruins to collect the cores needed to rebuild a refuge called the Bastion. Every one of his steps is commented on by a gravelly narrator who reacts to what the player actually does; when he falls, when he starts smashing crates, or when he chooses an unusual weapon, the narration adapts. This creates the impression that the story is being composed directly as you play.

Combat is fast and direct; the player carries two weapons at once from a fairly wide selection ranging from hammer and crossbow to rifle or throwing spear, plus a shield to deflect attacks and special abilities. Weapons are upgraded at a forge, and the player can adjust their own attributes using tonics, giving a decent amount of room for building a character to taste. Optional challenges, and above all a shrine that empowers enemies in exchange for better rewards, let experienced players fine-tune the difficulty themselves. The visual style is hand-painted and rich in color, and the environment assembles itself from pieces of terrain right under your feet, one of the most memorable visual ideas of its time.

The music, which blends acoustic guitar, American folk motifs, and electronics, is one of the most frequently praised elements, and together with the narration it sets the overall mood, which is melancholic but not hopeless. Reviews were very positive, and Bastion became one of the foundational titles of the new indie wave; studio Supergiant built further successful games on its foundation. Today it remains excellently playable, since it's short, fluid, and its main strengths, sound and atmosphere, don't depend on technical power.

ps3__rayman-origins.article:
**Rayman Origins** brought the well-known franchise back to two-dimensional platforming and did so with such care that the game quickly became one of the most praised titles of its genre on consoles of the time. Everything is hand-drawn and animated, environments move, breathe, and react to the music, so simply walking through a level feels like an animated film. At the same time, it's a game remarkably clean in terms of controls: the character accelerates, slides, glides, swims, and bounces off walls, and each of these movements has precisely calibrated momentum.

The structure is classic, meaning a world map with dozens of levels in which the player collects small creatures called Lums and frees captured friends, unlocking further content. The difficulty rises very gradually; the first worlds are friendly, but later sections demand precision at the level of experienced players, and several especially tough bonus levels rank among the hardest challenges platformers of that time offered. Chase sequences hold a special place, where the player flees a pursuer along a collapsing path in time with the music. Cooperative play for up to four players on a single screen is amusingly chaotic and suits shared laughter more than precise performance.

Music is one of the most striking elements, since the accompaniment changes with the action, and several levels are directly built around synchronizing jumps with the track. Reviews were enthusiastic, and the game helped spark a renewed interest in high-budget two-dimensional platformers, which Ubisoft followed up on with an even more refined sequel. Today, Rayman Origins has barely aged, since the hand-drawn style doesn't fall victim to fashion, and the controls rank among the best-tuned to be found in the genre.

ps4__uncharted-lost-legacy.article:
**Uncharted: The Lost Legacy** is a standalone adventure set in the world of the Uncharted series, in which Chloe Frazer takes the lead role for the first time, alongside Nadine Ross. The pair head into India's Western Ghats in search of a legendary artifact and must stay ahead of a ruthless local militia leader. The gameplay sticks to the tried-and-tested combination of climbing rock faces, cover-based shootouts, stealth takedowns of enemies, and the occasional puzzle, but this time players are given far more freedom. A sprawling chapter with an open valley offers off-road driving, optional tombs, and several paths to the same goal, a step toward a semi-open world previously unseen in the series.

Technically the game builds on the engine of the fourth installment, and on PlayStation 4 it ranked among the best-looking things the console could handle. Lush vegetation, dusty stone temples, and the detailed animation of both heroines still hold up very well even now, and on PlayStation 4 Pro it also gained higher resolution and smoother performance. The atmosphere is carried mainly by the relationship between two women who initially distrust each other and gradually find their way to one another; the dialogue during the car rides ranks among the best moments in the entire series. The music combines Indian instruments with an orchestral score, lending the expedition an exotic touch without slipping into cheap cliché.

Reception at the time was very favorable; critics praised the fact that what was originally intended as a piece of DLC turned into a full-fledged game, and that Naughty Dog managed to move the series forward even without Nathan Drake. Some critics also pointed out that it was a familiar formula in new clothing. Its influence on the genre lies mainly in how convincingly it showed that supporting characters can carry their own story and need not remain mere companions. Today it's the ideal entry point for newcomers: it's shorter, tighter, and requires no knowledge of the previous installments, yet it still delivers everything Uncharted became famous for, from collapsed temples to a spectacular escape from a rolling boulder.

ps4__last-guardian.article:
**The Last Guardian** is a game about a boy and a giant creature named Trico, who looks like a cross between a dog, a bird, and a cat. Narratively, it is a memory of a childhood spent in the ruins of a sprawling complex of towers and bridges, from which the pair try to escape. The gameplay is built on cooperation: the player alone can only climb, pull levers, and carry barrels, everything else has to be handled by Trico. The boy calls him, pets him, points the way, and waits for the animal to decide to listen. This unreliability is deliberate, because Trico behaves like a real animal: sometimes it lags behind, sometimes it gets spooked by the colored eyes depicted on the shields of the hostile guardian statues.

Development dragged on for years and the game was originally being made for the PlayStation 3; the resulting PlayStation 4 version carries traces of both. The textures and frame rate occasionally betray their older foundations, while the animation of Trico's body, feathers, and muscles ranks among the most impressive things the entire console generation offered. The environments are quiet, bare, and monumental, the music only comes in at key moments and hits all the harder for it. The atmosphere of melancholic abandonment directly continues the earlier work of the same creative team, namely Ico and Shadow of the Colossus, and shares with them a minimalist storytelling style with no wasted words.

The reception was mixed on essentially one single point: the camera and controls could really test a player's patience, and part of the audience never got used to Trico's stubbornness. Those who stuck with it, however, described one of the most powerful emotional experiences on the console. The game's influence is visible anywhere designers attempt a believable animal companion instead of an obedient helper that executes commands at the press of a button. Today it is a title that needs to be approached with patience and without haste. The reward is an ending that is unforgettable, and the feeling that you truly had to earn your relationship with Trico. Few games dare to be this slow and this consistent about their one single idea.

ps4__infamous-second-son.article:
**inFAMOUS Second Son** was one of the first games to show what the PlayStation 4 could really do. You play as Delsin Rowe, a young graffiti artist from an Indian reservation near Seattle, who discovers that by touch he can absorb the powers of other gifted people. He gradually gains control over smoke, neon, video, and concrete, each power having its own way of moving and fighting. Neon turns the city into a racetrack across illuminated billboards, smoke lets you slip through vents, video allows short bursts of flight. The open-world Seattle mainly serves as a playground for this movement, and the missions are rounded out by a fight against an occupying unit that hunts the gifted.

Technically, this was a genuine showpiece of the early generation. Wet asphalt reflecting neon lights, particle effects as the character dissolves into smoke, and detailed faces during dialogue made a strong impression on audiences at the time, and the game still looks decent today. Rain hammering against windows, gray skies, and music blending electronics with guitars create the atmosphere of a cold, watched northwestern city. The series also kept its system of moral choices, where the player decides between a heroic and a ruthless path, which changes both abilities and the ending of the story.

The contemporary reception was good, though reviews often mentioned that the missions themselves repeat fairly quickly and that the moral system is too black and white. What players remember, though, is the freedom of movement: few games managed to make simply traveling across a city this much fun. Its influence can be seen in later superhero titles that tried for the same fluid movement through a vertical city. Today it's a shorter, pleasantly straightforward adventure without filler, well suited as a breather between larger games, and it's rounded out by a standalone expansion, First Light. Also interesting is how the game handles the theme of surveillance and security measures that present themselves in the streets as protection for residents; at the time the setting felt like exaggeration, and today it sounds noticeably less distant.

ps4__killzone-shadow-fall.article:
**Killzone Shadow Fall** launched right alongside the PlayStation 4 and had the job of showing what a new generation of shooters would look like. The story takes place decades after the previous entries, when the Vektans and the surviving Helghast share a single planet split by a giant wall. The player takes on the role of a member of the special Shadow Marshal unit and moves between both sides of a conflict that has clear echoes of divided cities from our own history. Compared to earlier entries, the gameplay lightened up the controls, added bigger and more open maps, and above all introduced a small flying helper drone called OWL, capable of raising a shield, rappelling you down, hacking terminals, or providing covering fire.

Graphically, this was one of the best showcases of the first wave of PlayStation 4 titles. Sharp lighting, glass skyscrapers bathed in sunlight, dense vegetation in the jungle sections, and fine weapon detail were exceptional in 2013. The sound is typically harsh, and the music works with dark orchestral textures and industrial noise. The multiplayer offered classic classes with a great deal of rule customization and long retained a loyal community, and maps for it were also released without additional charge.

Reviews were more mixed than for previous entries in the series. Everyone praised the technical execution, but often criticized the unremarkable story, confusing navigation in the large levels, and uneven difficulty. Its influence on the genre was rather indirect; the main contribution is that it showed off the possibilities of the new console, and Guerrilla Games gained experience with more open design that it later put to use elsewhere. Today, Shadow Fall is interesting mainly as a period document of the start of the generation, but it still delivers solid action and several visually gorgeous missions. The zero-gravity section near a ruined station, or the descent into a contaminated zone, are among what players remember most strongly, and the series still hasn't received another major sequel since.

ps4__order-1886.article:
**The Order: 1886** takes the player to an alternate-history Victorian London, where an ancient order of knights has fought half-breed monsters for centuries while also facing a rebellion in its own streets. Thanks to a mysterious substance, the knights survive unusually long, and they wield inventions well ahead of their time, giving the game a strong steampunk flavor. The gameplay is built on cover-based shootouts featuring striking weapons, the standout being a thermite rifle that sprays flammable dust and then ignites it. Between fights, there's a lot of walking, listening to dialogue, and resolving small interactions, so the game leans closer to an interactive film than a classic shooter.

Technically, this was one of the most impressive titles of the early PlayStation 4 generation. The image is permanently cropped into a widescreen bar, runs in a distinctly cinematic style, with no visible seams between gameplay and cutscenes. The fabric textures, brass, leather, and wet cobblestones of gas-lamp-lit streets still look excellent today. The music is orchestral, restrained, and reinforces the somber mood of a city where disease and poverty are just as dangerous as the monsters.

The contemporary reception was quite mixed. Critics praised the visuals and atmosphere but were harsh about the short playtime, frequent linearity, and sections where the player just watches events unfold or presses an on-screen prompt. The debate the title sparked about the price-to-length ratio of games influenced the way people wrote about games at the time. Its influence on the genre is thus more polemical than direct. Today, The Order: 1886 plays surprisingly well precisely because it's short and tightly focused, and its world remains one of the most interesting to never get a sequel. The idea of blending Arthurian legend with the industrial revolution, airships, and wireless communication could have carried an entire series, but the studio never returned to it. What remains is a beautifully told glimpse of what could have been.

ps4__nioh-2.article:
**Nioh 2** is a prequel to the original Nioh, set during Japan's era of warring states, into which the player enters as their own created character, half human and half yokai. The combat ranks among the most technical the souls-like genre has to offer: every weapon has three stances with distinct attacks, plus a stamina-recovery system called ki pulse, blocking, dodging, and yokai abilities taken from defeated monsters. The result is action where every bit of timing matters, while also leaving enormous room for personal style. The missions take the form of enclosed maps full of shortcuts, hidden shrines, and demanding bosses inspired by Japanese mythology.

On PlayStation 4, the game ran in three optional modes depending on whether the player preferred resolution, smoothness, or a balanced compromise, and it held a brisk pace even on the base model. Visually, it rests on the contrast between realistic Japanese landscapes and wildly stylized demons, of which there is an enormous variety. The sound draws on traditional instruments, drums emphasize every heavy attack, and the music during boss fights takes on an almost ceremonial quality. The series has always also been about feverish gear collecting, and the second entry continues that, so alongside combat, players face plenty of work with inventory and the blacksmith.

Reviews were very favorable and often called the sequel a better version of everything the first game attempted. Criticism was aimed at reused environments and an overwhelming number of systems that can easily swamp a beginner. Its influence on the genre is clear in how it showed that a combat system can be deeper and faster than the one that inspired the series. Today it's one of the most substantial action games of its generation, capable of keeping a persistent player occupied for dozens of hours. Three expansions were also released for the base campaign, so anyone who finds their footing with the combat system has months of content ahead of them.

ps4__astro-bot-rescue-mission.article:
**Astro Bot Rescue Mission** is a platformer for the PlayStation VR headset, in which the player controls a tiny robot while also being physically present in the scene as a giant observer. This dual perspective is the whole joke of the game: you have to tilt your head, peek around corners, poke it into pipes, and search for hidden robots, while your fingers on the controller simultaneously handle jumping and attacking. The controller itself is also part of the world and transforms into a grappling hook, a water cannon, or a slingshot. The level wraps around the player in every direction, and battles against giant bosses play out literally in front of your face. The gameplay itself isn't complicated and rests on the classic platformer formula: jump, aim, dodge, find the secret spot. But the game is built so that players catch themselves crouching down or craning their neck to see around an obstacle, and this physical involvement in the play is exactly what makes it an experience that can't be replicated on a regular screen.

Technically, this was a showcase of how well the PlayStation 4 can handle virtual reality when a game is designed for it from the ground up. The image is clean, the frame rate stable, and above all it doesn't make anyone motion-sick, which was rare during the first wave of VR titles. The visual style is colorful, clean, and playful, full of small jokes and references to PlayStation history. The music is cheerful and catchy, and together with the little robots' sounds it creates a mood reminiscent of the best Nintendo platformers.

The reception was enthusiastic, and the game quickly became the most common answer to the question of why you'd actually want a PlayStation VR. Reviewers called it proof that virtual reality doesn't have to be just a brief novelty but can carry a full-fledged game with a well-thought-out difficulty curve. Its influence is clear in that this is where the direct line leads to the later, much better-known sequels featuring the robot Astro. Today it remains one of the best VR games ever made; you just need the old headset to play it the way it was intended.

ps4__tearaway-unfolded.article:
**Tearaway Unfolded** is a reworked version of the originally handheld game, in which the entire world is made of paper. The player accompanies a messenger named Iota or Atoi on a journey to deliver a message, while also being present within the world as a divine being watching events through a tear in the sky. This one idea holds the whole game together. Paper sheets can be folded, torn, and unfurled, the player blows away obstacles using the controller's touchpad, shines light into the scene with the controller's light bar, or uses the camera to insert their own face into the game, appearing as the sun.

The port to PlayStation 4 didn't stop at higher resolution. Levels were expanded, new abilities were added, and interactions were rewritten to use the speaker, touchpad, and light bar of the controller instead of the handheld console's rear touchpad. Visually, the game is unmistakable: everything is made of paper cutouts, including grass, water, and clouds, and once the player gets a pair of scissors, they can cut out their own decorations and place them into the world. The music is playful, featuring folk instruments and singing, and complements the crafted, handmade mood beautifully.

The contemporary reception was very warm, with reviewers praising its inventiveness and charm, though they often noted that part of the original version's magic was tied specifically to the handheld console and its rear touchpad. Its influence on the genre lies mainly in the courage to break the barrier between player and game in a way other than a witty one-liner. Today it's a sweet, undemanding adventure well suited even for younger players, and one that visually stands apart from the rest of the PlayStation 4 library at first glance. It isn't a difficult game, and an experienced player will breeze through it, but a challenge was never really the point. Tearaway Unfolded is above all a celebration of creation: every cut-out piece of paper the player designs themselves appears in the world and stays there, and this small feeling of co-authorship is exactly what one would expect from Media Molecule.

ps4__batman-arkham-knight.article:
**Batman: Arkham Knight** closes out Rocksteady's series about the caped crusader and, for the first time, opens up the whole of Gotham City as one continuous playable space. The city has been evacuated, Scarecrow has moved into the streets with his fear toxin, along with a mysterious enemy in powered armor who knows Batman uncomfortably well. The gameplay builds on the established rhythmic counter-based combat system and on silent takedowns from above, where the player gradually picks off guards and watches their panic grow. The new addition is the Batmobile, which serves as a vehicle, a combat tank, and a puzzle-solving tool, and a great many missions are built directly around it.

On PlayStation 4, this was one of the technically most impressive games of its time. Constant rain, reflections on wet pavement, smoke, and illuminated skyscrapers created visuals that put the series on an entirely different level than previous entries. The atmosphere is dark, comic-book exaggerated, and yet surprisingly heavy, since the story deals largely with what Batman's journey has done to him personally. The music is orchestral and menacing, and the main cast's voice acting ranks among the best the comic-book game genre ever had.

Reviews of the console version were very good, though critics often mentioned that the Batmobile is inserted too often and that the tank battles don't fit what the series originally started out as. The game is also dogged by the reputation of its exceptionally poor PC release, which had to be temporarily pulled from sale. Its influence on the genre is undeniable: the rhythmic combat of the Arkham games became the standard for the entire following decade. Today it remains a beautifully looking and substantial game, arguably the most convincing depiction of Gotham of them all. It also offers an extensive lineup of side cases featuring famous villains, riddle-collecting for the Riddler, and several missions where the player briefly takes control of Batman's allies, giving the game dozens of hours of content.

ps4__dishonored-2.article:
**Dishonored 2** moves the action to the southern city of Karnaca, where after a coup the player must choose whether to play as Empress Emily Kaldwin or her father Corvo Attano. Each character has her own set of supernatural powers, so Emily can bind enemies together with an invisible link or slip through shadows, while Corvo blinks short distances and can command rats. The gameplay lets the player decide completely freely whether to slip through a level unseen or leave it as a merciless killer, and the game remembers that choice and reflects it in the state of the city and in the ending.

The game's greatest strength is its level design. The Clockwork Mansion, with reconfigurable walls that pivot with the flip of a lever and open up entirely different paths, or the mission that travels between the past and the present, rank among the finest things the stealth genre has ever offered. On PlayStation 4 the game struggled a little with smoothness in larger scenes at launch, but later updates improved the situation. The visual style blends painterly stylization with Victorian technology powered by whale oil, and the music works with restless strings and a guitar that gives it a southern flavor.

Contemporary reception was very positive, and many reviewers called the levels a textbook example of how to design space for players with a mind of their own. Criticism was aimed at the technical state at launch and at a story that remained mostly a backdrop. The influence on the genre is noticeable everywhere so-called immersive sim games are discussed today. Today it's a title that deserves multiple playthroughs, because only the second or third reveals just how many paths each level actually offers. The game also offers a variant without supernatural powers, turning it into a pure stealth challenge, along with the standalone expansion Death of the Outsider, which brings the world's story to a close.

ps4__control.article:
**Control** sends the player into the building of the Federal Bureau of Control, a secret institution that studies objects and phenomena that defy the laws of nature. The main character, Jesse Faden, comes to the building looking for her lost brother, and within minutes becomes its new director, while the corridors have already been taken over by an alien entity called the Hiss. The gameplay combines shooting a weapon that shifts between several forms with supernatural powers. The player picks up pieces of furniture and hurls them at enemies, levitates, builds a shield out of debris, and at its best moments the whole fight turns into fireworks tearing the office apart.

The game's strongest asset is its environment. The Oldest House behaves like a living labyrinth, corridors rearrange themselves, brutalist concrete architecture turns into endless offices or into mine shafts, and the game wasn't afraid of bold narrative forms either, including a combination of live action and animation. On PlayStation 4 it was a technically demanding title that occasionally dipped noticeably on the base model during big firefights, but the atmosphere was strong enough that most players didn't mind. The sound design is unsettling, full of whispers and jarring tones.

Reviews were very complimentary, praising the environment, the sound design, and the courage to do something different from the usual action game. Criticism was aimed at navigating the building, at a map that's nearly unusable, and at the uneven difficulty of some bosses. The influence can be seen in how the game helped bring back interest in strange, unexplained worlds outside classic fantasy or sci-fi. Today it's one of the most original games of its generation, one that still feels like nothing else even years later. A large part of its charm comes from found documents, reports, and meeting recordings that describe the world of the Bureau in dry bureaucratic language, making it even more unsettling. Anyone who takes the time to read them will find a layer no fight can replace.

ps4__star-wars-jedi-fallen-order.article:
**Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order** takes place shortly after the extermination of the Jedi Order, and the player takes on the role of the padawan Cal Kestis, who has been hiding out on a ship graveyard and is forced to stand up and fight back once more. The gameplay combines several proven directions: lightsaber combat relies on blocking and parrying blows at the right moment, similar to soulslike games, movement through the world resembles a metroidvania, since new abilities open up previously inaccessible places, and along the way there's a lot of climbing, sliding, and jumping. The companion droid BD-1 serves as a med kit, a map, and a key to terminals, and quickly earns the player's affection.

The planets are designed as sprawling, interconnected maps with many shortcuts the player returns to with new abilities. On PlayStation 4 the game struggled at launch with texture pop-in and occasional stutters in smoothness, but later updates fixed most of the issues. Visually it holds to the classic look of the Star Wars universe, with emphasis on both inhabited and abandoned planets and lighting reminiscent of the original films. The music builds on familiar motifs without merely repeating them, and gains dramatic momentum in fights against the Inquisitors.

Reception was strongly positive, mainly because, after a long while, it was a big single-player Star Wars game without microtransactions and without requiring an online connection. Criticism mentioned technical issues and occasionally confusing orientation on the maps. The title's influence was clear in confirming audience interest in solid, story-driven single-player action games. Today it still plays very well, the combat is challenging in just the right way, and for fans of the series it's one of the best gaming trips into the era between the film trilogies. It's also worth appreciating that the game doesn't rely on familiar faces and instead builds its own cast of characters the player grows attached to along the way, and that the title's success led to a full-fledged sequel.

ps4__devil-may-cry-5.article:
**Devil May Cry 5** marks the series' return after a long pause, and at the same time shows exactly what a pure action game without unnecessary filler should look like. A demonic tree has grown through the city, and players alternately take control of three characters: Nero with his mechanical prosthetic arm that can be fired off like a rocket, the mysterious V, who doesn't fight himself but sends bound demons into battle, and the legendary Dante with four combat styles and an arsenal that fills the entire screen. The style rating during combat forces the player to vary attacks, avoid getting hit, and look flashy doing it, turning the combat system into something close to a musical instrument.

Technically the game runs on the RE Engine, and on PlayStation 4 it ranked among the cleanest-looking things the console had to offer. It runs smoothly, the characters were captured from real actors, and the game loves cinematic cutscenes that flow directly into gameplay. The music is typically over-the-top and excellent, blending metal and electronic sounds, and for some characters the track dynamically builds up during combat depending on how well the player is doing. The whole title maintains a self-aware sense of humor and never takes itself too seriously, even while saving the world.

Reviews were very positive and brought the series back to the top of the genre. Criticism aimed mainly at repetitive environments in the second half and at the fact that some players never quite warmed up to V's unconventional playstyle. Its influence on the genre is fundamental, since this series is the one that defined how style is measured in action games, and many later titles build on it. Today Devil May Cry 5 is an ideal choice for anyone who wants a game with a high skill ceiling that can be finished quickly but polished almost endlessly. It offers a wide range of difficulties, including ones that unlock only after finishing the game, so anyone who wants to can return to the same levels many times over and push themselves toward ever greater style and precision.

ps4__shadow-of-tomb-raider.article:
**Shadow of the Tomb Raider** closes out the trilogy about the young Lara Croft and sends her into the jungles of Central and South America, where her own rash act triggers a chain of natural disasters. Compared to previous entries, the game places less emphasis on shootouts and more on exploration, climbing, and quiet movement through the undergrowth. Lara can cover herself in mud, hide in dense foliage, and take out enemies from a rope hanging in a tree, making her feel much more like a huntress than a soldier. The tombs that gave the series its name are larger this time, and their mechanical puzzles involving water, counterweights, and fire rank among the best in the whole trilogy.

On PlayStation 4 the game looks excellent, mainly thanks to light filtering through the treetops, water, and detailed wet-terrain rendering. On the more powerful console model it offered a choice between higher resolution and smoother performance. The atmosphere is shaped mainly by the near-constant sound of the jungle and music that draws on local instruments and singing. The city of Paititi acts as a living hub with inhabitants, side quests, and merchants, and is one of the most memorable locations in the series. There are also underwater sections that combine limited air supply with narrow passages, ranking among the game's more tense moments.

Contemporary reception was good, though somewhat cooler than for the previous two entries. Reviewers praised the tombs, the exploration, and the visuals, but often noted that the main story and Lara's moral doubts weren't fully fleshed out. The influence on the genre lies mainly in how the trilogy as a whole redefined what a modern action-adventure with exploration looks like. Today it's a title best appreciated by players who want tombs and climbing from Tomb Raider more than shooting, since this entry returns closest to the series' original spirit. That's helped further by a wide range of difficulty settings, separately for combat, exploration, and puzzles, letting everyone tailor a playthrough exactly to what they enjoy about Tomb Raider.

ps4__metro-exodus.article:
**Metro Exodus** pulls the series out of the Moscow underground and up to the surface, sending players across a devastated Russia aboard a steam locomotive named Aurora. The game's structure changes with the season and the location: some chapters are narrow and claustrophobic like the earlier entries, others open up into vast regions where the player chooses the order of tasks and the timing of raids. Equipment care is essential. Weapons are cleaned and modified on the go from scavenged parts, gas mask filters run out, and the mask itself cracks and must be wiped by hand when rain or blood gets on it.

Atmosphere is the game's greatest weapon. Empty villages, a frozen harbor with a stranded ship, a desert landscape by a dried-up sea, and nights full of mutants create the feeling that the world is simply waiting for the player to stop disturbing it. On PlayStation 4 it was a technically very ambitious title that occasionally stumbled with larger open areas at launch, but the lighting and weather effects ranked among the best of the generation. The music is restrained, often giving way entirely to the sound of wind, footsteps in the snow, and breathing through the mask. Encounters with people are also more complex than before, since the game tracks how much blood the player leaves behind and reflects it in the ending of the whole journey.

Reception was very good, praising above all how the story connects with the more open structure, and the fact that the game didn't slide into the usual open-world collectible grind. Criticism was aimed at the dialogue, at a silent protagonist in a story-driven game, and at technical issues. The influence on the genre can be seen in how it showed a middle path between a linear shooter and an open world. Today it's one of the most atmospheric action games of its era, well worth playing on a higher difficulty with limited resources. The train crew deserves special mention: between chapters, players can walk through the cars, listen to conversations, and watch people gradually change, making Aurora one of the most enjoyable home bases in the whole genre.

ps4__yakuza-0.article:
**Yakuza 0** is a prequel to the whole series, set at the end of the 1980s during Japan's economic bubble. The player alternates between young Kazuma Kiryu in Tokyo's Kamurocho and Goro Majima in Osaka's Sotenbori, with each character working through their own plot that gradually intertwines. Fights take place right in the streets, and each character has three switchable combat styles, from a quick dancer's tempo to heavy, crushing blows. On top of that come flashy finishing moves the game displays with obvious delight in over-the-top spectacle.

Alongside the main story, which is surprisingly serious and well written, sits an enormous amount of side content. The player can run a real estate business or a cabaret club, sing karaoke, play period-appropriate arcade machines, go fishing, bet on horse races, and solve dozens of bizarre stories involving passersby, ranging from comedy to touching little dramas. It's precisely this contrast between the harsh underworld and utter silliness that's typical of the series. On PlayStation 4 the game came out first in Japan and reached the rest of the world two years later; technically it was a clean, smoothly running version with substantially reworked environments.

Western reviews were enthusiastic, and this entry is often cited as the title that opened the series up to a worldwide audience. Criticism mentioned a slower start and a large amount of reading. Its influence lies in showing just how well a smaller, densely packed urban space can work instead of a huge empty map. Today Yakuza 0 is the most frequently recommended entry point into the whole series and one of the most substantial games ever released on PlayStation 4. Anyone who lets themselves get pulled in will find that the main storyline is just a skeleton, onto which an entire city full of little stories is layered, and that people keep coming back to Kamurocho even after finishing the game, just to play a round of mahjong or sing a song at a bar.

ps4__dragon-quest-xi-echoes-of-elusive-a.article:
**Dragon Quest XI: Echoes of an Elusive Age** is a rare case of a game that doesn't try to turn the Japanese RPG genre upside down, but instead brings it to textbook perfection. A young, nameless hero learns on the day he comes of age that he's the reincarnation of an ancient Luminary, but instead of honors and glory he's met with accusation, flight, and a journey across the continent of Erdrea. Out of that grows a journey dozens of hours long, during which he's joined by a group of distinctive companions, from a thief with a good heart, through a mysterious warrior, to an absent-minded mage. Each of them has their own storyline that connects with the main plot at just the right moment.

The gameplay is built on classic turn-based combat, which the game presents clearly and without unnecessary complexity, yet with enough room for tactics. Characters unlock abilities on branching skill panels, change weapons and with them their entire fighting style, and later on combine attacks into shared team maneuvers. Alongside this, the game offers extensive blacksmithing in the form of a minigame, recipe collecting, riding saddled monsters, and a surprisingly large number of optional quests. Anyone wanting a challenge can turn on stricter rules at the start, which tighten up both the economy and combat.

Technically, on PlayStation 4 it's a clean, colorful, and smoothly running showcase. The art style draws on the iconic character designs of Akira Toriyama, so the world feels like a moving illustration, and Koichi Sugiyama's orchestral music lends even ordinary travel through the countryside a festive air. Critics received it very warmly, calling it the series' return to prominence and an ideal entry point for newcomers who had previously passed Dragon Quest by. The title's influence is more confirming than revolutionary, but it showed that an honest turn-based JRPG can hold its own even in an era of open worlds and action combat. Today Dragon Quest XI feels like a comforting, gentle game worth returning to precisely because it knows exactly what it wants to be.

ps4__divinity-original-sin-2-definitive-.article:
**Divinity: Original Sin 2** was one of the most ambitious attempts to bring the depth of a classic PC RPG to consoles, and the Definitive Edition for PlayStation 4 proved it could work better than expected. The player creates a character gifted with the dangerous power of source magic, which makes the whole world hunt them down, and sets out on a journey that ultimately asks who will become the new divinity. Alongside a fully custom hero, players can choose from pre-made origin characters with their own past and motivations, so the party isn't just a collection of combat roles but a group of people with conflicting interests.

The core of the game lies in turn-based, grid-based combat that works with clever environmental physics. Puddles can be frozen or electrified, oil set alight, poison turned into an explosion, and within a few turns the battlefield becomes a completely different place than it was at the start. Outside combat, the player enjoys unusual freedom: quests can be solved through negotiation, theft, persuasion, or brute force, characters can be talked to through the ability to understand animals, and many situations have more solutions than one would expect. Multiplayer co-op even lets fellow players openly turn on each other.

The Definitive Edition brought reworked controls adapted for the gamepad, an adjusted interface, and a range of balance changes that make the PlayStation 4 version fully viable, though the extensive menus and inventory remain demanding to navigate. The visuals rely on a detailed isometric view and a darkly fairy-tale atmosphere underscored by music with striking vocal themes. Critics received the game exceptionally well, ranking it among the highlights of the genre for that decade. Its influence is still visible today in how significantly it raised expectations for reactivity and freedom in RPGs. Today it remains one of the most expansive games playable on a console, easily lasting a hundred hours, and a second playthrough with a different character reveals entire chunks of story a player would never glimpse the first time around.

ps4__fallout-4.article:
**Fallout 4** drops the player into the post-nuclear ruins of Boston, where the sole survivor of a vault wakes up to find someone has kidnapped their child. The search for the lost son is the pretext that opens up the Commonwealth: a vast region full of ruined factories, radioactive swamps, settlements, raiders, and factions with very different ideas about what the world should look like after the catastrophe. The choice among them forms the backbone of the story and leads to markedly different endings.

Compared to previous entries in the series, the game shifted noticeably toward action. Shooting is snappier and more precise, but the tried-and-true system of slowed-down targeting of individual body parts remains, adding a tactical dimension to combat. A major new feature was extensive crafting: the player breaks down found junk into raw materials, uses them to build weapon and armor mods, and above all builds their own settlements, which must be supplied, defended, and managed. On top of that, players can upgrade power armor, gather companions with their own opinions on the player's actions, and lose hours to simple exploration, since almost every building hides its own small story told through the environment and found records.

On PlayStation 4 the game ran in an open world without loading breaks, though it paid for its scope with occasional frame-rate instability and technical quirks that have long been associated with the series. The atmosphere is held together by a retro-futuristic 1950s-style design and radio stations playing period swing songs whose cheerful mood forms a sharp contrast to the wasteland outside the window. Reception was very positive, though some players criticized the simplified dialogue and the reduced role of role-playing in favor of action and building. Today Fallout 4 is above all a giant toy in which you can vanish for hundreds of hours, and thanks to console mod support its content can be expanded even further. Anyone looking for carefully written roles and consequences of decisions should look elsewhere, but anyone who wants to explore every basement and build their own village will find a home here for many months.

ps4__dragon-age-inquisition.article:
**Dragon Age: Inquisition** was the series' first major entry into the PlayStation 4 generation and also its most expansive installment. A rift to a world of demons opens in the sky, the player's character is the only one able to seal these breaches, and an initially insignificant survivor thus becomes the leader of a restored Inquisition. The entire game revolves around this role: besides traveling and fighting, players decide on political alliances, the fates of entire orders, and who the Inquisition even lets close.

Combat combines real-time action control of one character with a tactical pause, during which orders can be given to the whole party and positioning on the battlefield resolved. Each of the three base classes has several specializations, so a mage can be a support or a destructive force, and a warrior a protector or a siege battering ram. The world is divided into vast regions each with their own character, from dry plains through swamps to snowy mountains, and alongside the main storyline it offers a large amount of side content, resource gathering, and fortress building. Back at their own keep, the player sends advisors on missions, talks to companions, and develops relationships, something the series has traditionally built on.

Technically it was a leap forward thanks to the Frostbite engine, which gave the landscapes scale, convincing lighting, and changeable weather. The sound and orchestral music work with strong themes, campfire scenes are accompanied by companion songs, and the whole thing feels very cinematic. Critics received the game enthusiastically and praised precisely its scope and return to epic fantasy, though with hindsight it's more often noted that some areas are filled with repetitive tasks. For the series it was an important milestone, as it showed how to combine character-focused storytelling with a large open space. Today Inquisition is a good entry point into the world of Thedas, provided the player accepts its slower, builder-like pace and isn't put off by the opening hours, which are among its least interesting. Once the political thread gets going and the companions start finding their voice, the game gains significant strength.

ps4__kingdom-hearts-iii.article:
**Kingdom Hearts III** closes out a long and famously convoluted story arc the series had been building for more than fifteen years. Sora, together with Donald and Goofy, once again sets out among the worlds to gather strength and allies before the final clash with darkness, visiting along the way a number of familiar places from animated films. It's precisely this blend of Disney settings with earnestly meant melodramatic fantasy that has always set the series apart, and in this entry it reaches its greatest scale.

The foundation of the gameplay is fast action combat with a key as a weapon, complemented by magic, summoning helpers, and flashy team-up attacks with the heroes of individual worlds. New features include transformations of the key into specialized forms with their own move sets, and so-called Attractions, giant carousels and roller coasters that briefly take over the whole screen. Between battles the game varies its pace: it offers ship sailing, cooking dishes as a mini-game, photography, and extensive exploration of individual worlds, which are noticeably larger than in previous entries.

On PlayStation 4 the game moved to Unreal Engine 4, and the result is a very clean image with impressive effects that make battles feel like fireworks. The worlds faithfully imitate the visual style of their film counterparts, which was especially praised, and the musical score maintains the series' emotional throughline. Reception was largely positive, with critics praising the action and visuals while pointing out that the story exposition is almost incomprehensible for a newcomer. The game's significance lies mainly in bringing an unusual collaboration of two very different worlds to a grand finale. Today it's a rewarding spectacle for fans, while a newcomer would do well to arrive with at least a rough knowledge of the previous entries, which the game assumes at nearly every turn. Whoever overcomes that hurdle gets a visually one of the richest adventures of its generation, full of moments no other series could afford to stage.

ps4__nier-replicant-ver-1-22474487139.article:
**NieR Replicant ver.1.22474487139...** is a modern remake of a game that fell through the cracks in its time and only received the second life it deserved after the success of its sequel. A young man cares for his sick sister Yonah, afflicted by a mysterious illness, and in a desperate attempt to find a cure sets out into a world thrown into disarray by the presence of creatures called Shades. He's accompanied by a talking book with a sharp tongue, a warrior woman who swears constantly, and a boy of uncertain origin. What begins as a simple fairy tale about saving a sister turns inside out over subsequent playthroughs.

The gameplay is deliberately variable. The core consists of melee action combat complemented by magic attacks, but the game shifts without warning into a top-down view, into platforming sections, into a bullet-hell shooter, and into passages told entirely through text. This very unwillingness to stick to one shape is the work's authorial signature. Crucially, the story doesn't close after the first completion: further playthroughs bring a new point of view, further explain the enemies' motivations, and gradually change the meaning of everything the player did the first time. The remake also added extra content and adjusted the pacing of the later parts.

On PlayStation 4 the game received a completely new combat system, significantly improved graphics, and smoother performance, shedding the original's main weakness. Its strongest point remains Keiichi Okabe's music, whose vocal tracks in an invented language rank among the best-reviewed video game soundtracks ever and carry most of the emotional weight. Reception was very warm, and many reviewers called the story one of the strongest the medium has to offer. The original's influence on the sequel and on the whole approach to repeat playthroughs is undeniable. Today it's a title worth the attention and the patience it demands from the player. Whoever gives it the time needed to complete all the playthroughs comes away with an experience that isn't forgotten.

ps4__ni-no-kuni-ii-revenant-kingdom.article:
**Ni no Kuni II: Revenant Kingdom** begins with the fall of a kingdom: young King Evan loses his throne to a coup, and instead of revenge decides to build a new land where all nations could live in peace. This unusually gentle premise sets the tone for the whole game. Joining him is a man from another world, a colorful group of allies, and a story unafraid to be plainly optimistic without giving up on dramatic moments.

The gameplay rests on three pillars. The first is real-time action combat, where the player switches between melee and ranged weapons, dodges, and gets help from small spirit companions who attack and boost abilities. The second is building your own kingdom, meaning constructing buildings, taking in citizens with various specialties, and allocating research, which amounts to an entire separate strategic layer with its own economy. The third is army battles on the world map, a simplified tactical game with units arranged in a circle around the ruler. The combination sounds scattered, but in practice the individual parts feed off each other, since developing the kingdom unlocks better equipment and new quests.

Visually it's one of the most beautiful games of its kind on PlayStation 4. The colorful, softly lit landscape and animated sequences draw on the tradition of hand-drawn Japanese animation, and Joe Hisaishi's music gives them cinematic grandeur. Critics received the game favorably, praising the visual side and inventive blend of mechanics, with complaints aimed mainly at the lower combat difficulty and the fact that the story doesn't reach the emotional depth of the first game. The title's influence lies in how confidently it merged a JRPG with a builder game. Today it's an ideal choice for players who want a sprawling adventure without dark tones and with a pleasantly kind mood. It's also one of the few big JRPGs that can safely be handed to younger players without boring an adult in the process.

ps4__dragon-s-dogma-dark-arisen.article:
**Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen** is one of the most distinctive action RPGs of its time, and on PlayStation 4 it took the form in which it shines best. A dragon tears out the player's heart, making them the Arisen, a person condemned to follow the dragon's trail. What follows is a journey through an open world inspired by western fantasy but seen through a Japanese lens, where night is truly dark, roads are dangerous, and a lantern in the backpack carries the same weight as a sword.

The heart of the game is a combat system that had no equal at the time of release. The player can literally climb onto giants and other colossi, cling to their fur, and stab at their weak points while the monster tries to shake them off. Nine vocations from warrior to archer to hybrid classes offer very different styles, with the mage in particular preparing devastating spells over long seconds and needing to be shielded by allies. Those are covered by Pawns, artificial companions the player raises themselves, teaching them tactics based on battles experienced and lending them out to other players over the network. The Dark Arisen expansion additionally adds the dark dungeon of Bitterblack Isle with tougher difficulty and better loot.

The console version for PlayStation 4 brought higher resolution and steadier performance than the original release, so today it feels brisk and legible. The atmosphere is held together mainly by restrained sound, the howl of wind across the wasteland, and sudden attacks out of the dark preceded only by the sound of footsteps. Original reception was mixed due to thinner side quests and inconvenient travel, but over time the game became a cult title referenced by other action RPGs and by its own sequel. Today it's an experience for players who appreciate roughness, tangible combat, and a world that doesn't hold their hand. Walking through a night forest with a torch, hearing nothing but your own breath and rustling in the bushes, ranks among the most tense things console fantasy has offered. The PlayStation 4 version also contains all the added content, so the player gets the game in its complete form and at a very fair price.

ps4__final-fantasy-xii-zodiac-age.article:
**Final Fantasy XII: The Zodiac Age** is a carefully prepared remaster of an entry that was, in its time, the series' boldest experiment. The story takes place in the world of Ivalice, where the small kingdom of Dalmasca falls under the rule of a powerful empire, and the fates of a street thief, a deposed princess, sky pirates, and imperial officers intertwine into a narrative that leans closer to political drama than to a typical Japanese save-the-world story. It's precisely this more sober, more mature tone that gives the entry its staying power.

Combat plays out seamlessly right in the environment without switching to a separate screen and is governed by the gambit system, meaning conditions of the type when an ally drops below half health, cast healing. The player essentially programs the whole party's behavior and during battle only oversees things, stepping in for exceptional moments. It sounded controversial, but it works remarkably well, since it's about deliberate planning rather than repeated command-mashing. The Zodiac Age additionally adds a system of twelve jobs, which prevents all the characters from ending up the same by the end of the game, and adds an optional speed-up for the game's pace, removing the original release's biggest source of drag.

On PlayStation 4 the game received higher resolution, adjusted textures, and above all a completely re-recorded orchestral score, letting Hitoshi Sakimoto's expansive composition shine. Ivalice remains one of the best-built worlds in the series, with its own architecture, peoples, and history, and its vast deserts and underground temples have appropriately grand scale. The original release divided players, but with hindsight and in this form the title received a markedly warmer reception. Its influence can be seen in how it steered the series toward smoother combat. Today it's among the classics worth discovering. It offers one of the most expansive worlds in the whole series and plenty of optional challenges in the form of hunts for giant beasts, which can easily occupy just as much time as the main story.

ps4__tales-of-berseria.article:
**Tales of Berseria** is unusually dark for the long-running Tales series, since it is narrated not by a noble hero but by a woman driven by revenge. Velvet Crowe loses everything dear to her because of one man's actions, and her quest for retribution casts her in a role the world regards as demonic. Around her gathers a crew of outcasts, pirates, and beings who belong nowhere, and the game takes care to make their conversations between battles just as important as the main plot. Whether the heroine's motives are justifiable remains an open question right up to the end.

Combat is action-based and plays out in real time. The player controls one character, chains attacks into long combos, and manages soul points that rise and fall depending on how well things are going. A high soul count unlocks stronger abilities, while losing them weakens the character, turning combat into a smooth flow of risk and reward. Added to this are Velvet's transformations into her demonic form, extensive cooking, gathering, and equipment-crafting options, and the series' traditional skill system tied to equipped items. World exploration is fairly straightforward but padded out with plenty of side quests and crew scenes.

Technically it isn't a showcase title for the generation on PlayStation 4, retaining a clean anime style with bold colors and fluid action, though the environments are rather plain. This is made up for by the music and excellent character writing and voice work. Critics received the game favorably and often called it one of the most interesting entries in the series precisely because of its atypical heroine and more serious tone. The title's influence shows in how it steered later Tales games toward more mature themes. Today it's a very good choice for players who want a story-driven JRPG with serious action and no rose-tinted glasses. Completing the main story takes dozens of hours, and the reward is one of the best-built character arcs the series has offered.

ps4__ys-viii-lacrimosa-of-dana.article:
**Ys VIII: Lacrimosa of Dana** is the entry that pushed the long-running Ys series into the spotlight with a wider audience beyond Japan. Eternal adventurer Adol Christin is shipwrecked on the forbidden island of Seiren, where instead of a quick escape he sets about building a castaway camp. He gradually finds other survivors, expands the settlement, maps the unexplored coastline, and discovers that the island hides the remnants of an ancient civilization along with creatures long thought extinct. Running alongside this is a second storyline in which the player relives the memories of a mysterious girl named Dana, and the two threads come together in a way that gives the game surprising narrative weight.

Gameplay is built on very fast action. Characters switch on the fly depending on which attack type is most effective against a given enemy, and a precisely timed dodge or block triggers a time slowdown or counterattack. Alongside combat, the game leans heavily on exploration, since new movement abilities gradually open up previously inaccessible spots, as well as on camp management, gathering resources, cooking, fishing, and defensive battles against waves of enemies. It's precisely this alternation between free exploration and piling up small tasks that keeps the game's pace brisk and addictive.

On PlayStation 4 the game looks rather modest technically, but it runs smoothly, which matters more for action this fast than detailed textures. A strong point is the music, made up of the distinctive rock and symphonic tracks from Falcom's house sound studio, capable of turning even an ordinary walk through a forest into an expedition. Reception was very positive, and the game is often cited as the best entry point into the series, though the first Western release was criticized for translation quality, which the publisher later fixed. Today Ys VIII is a great choice for anyone who wants an action RPG with an adventurous mood and no unnecessary grimness. The castaway theme also lends the whole thing an unusual sense of togetherness, since every person rescued shows up at the camp and starts being useful, which naturally pushes players to explore even the island's last corner.

ps4__kingdom-come-deliverance.article:
**Kingdom Come: Deliverance** is a historical RPG without dragons or magic, set in Bohemia at the start of the fifteenth century. The player takes on the role of Henry, a young blacksmith whose home village of Skalitz is burned down by Hungarian troops, and from there unfolds a story of revenge, coming of age, and what war looks like from an ordinary person's point of view. The plot is grounded in real events surrounding the dispute over the Bohemian crown and features historical figures, giving the game an unusually documentary flavor.

The focus is on believability. Melee combat works with several attack directions, blocks, feints, and considerable momentum, so fighting several opponents at once is genuinely dangerous and fleeing is often wiser than heroics. Henry starts out able to do almost nothing, he can't even properly read, and all skills from swordsmanship through alchemy to persuasion improve through use. The game wants the player to eat, sleep, keep their clothing clean, and mind their reputation in individual villages, and it only saves at a bed or with a rare potion, which gives every decision real weight.
