The side quests rank among the best written of their generation and often have several equally valid solutions, including ones that avoid violence entirely.

On PlayStation 4 the game had noticeable technical problems after launch, with long loading times and bugs the developers gradually fixed. The reward is a beautifully built Sázava region landscape with changing weather, misty mornings, and music that uses period instruments and choir. Reception was very good, and the game became the most successful Czech game project of its time. Its influence lies in demonstrating the viability of a realistic historical RPG without fantasy elements. Today Kingdom Come: Deliverance is slow, demanding, but immensely rewarding. The player has to learn just as much as their character does, and that's exactly where the unique feeling comes from when an incompetent village lad turns into a feared swordsman. For Czech players it also carries extra value thanks to familiar locations and Czech-language voice acting.

ps4__outer-worlds.article:
**The Outer Worlds** is a satirical sci-fi RPG set in the colonized Halcyon system, entirely controlled by corporations. The main character wakes up after decades in hibernation aboard a ship full of forgotten colonists and quickly discovers that this corner of the universe operates as one giant advertising brochure, beneath whose surface lie poverty, absurd bureaucracy, and deadly serious corporate power. The narrative tone is outright ironic, poking fun at corporate slogans and people's willingness to accept utterly nonsensical rules, all without losing seriousness where it's needed.

Gameplay combines first-person shooting with proper role-playing. The character is built through attributes and perks, and the game also offers so-called flaws, meaning voluntary weaknesses taken on in exchange for skill points. High values in persuasion, lying, or intimidation open up dialogue options that let players bypass most fights, and many quests can be resolved in several mutually exclusive ways, with corresponding consequences for entire settlements. Companions have their own quests and opinions, help out with special attacks in combat, and their reactions to the player's behavior are among the game's best parts. Combat can slow down time for more precise aimed shots.

On PlayStation 4 the game runs without issues and leans on a bold, colorful retro-futuristic look rather than technical cutting edge. Individual planets and stations are smaller, self-contained areas, which benefits the game since it's densely packed with content instead of empty stretches. Critics received it very favorably and called it a return to what the studio does best, namely reactive RPGs with well-written dialogue. Today The Outer Worlds is an ideal choice for players who want a rich RPG completable in a reasonable amount of time. The main campaign takes roughly twenty to thirty hours and offers plenty of reasons for replaying with a completely differently built character, since the persuasion path and the combat path lead to different endings.

ps4__yakuza-like-dragon.article:
**Yakuza: Like a Dragon** is a bold restart of the renowned series that replaced both its longtime hero and its entire combat system. The main character is Ichiban Kasuga, a good-hearted low-ranking gangster who serves eighteen years in prison for a crime he didn't commit, and upon release discovers that the organization he sacrificed his life for wants nothing to do with him. He ends up at rock bottom, penniless and homeless, and from there works his way back among people. The story mixes hard-edged crime drama with scenes that are completely absurd, and that range is typical of the series.

The major change is the shift from action-based street brawling to turn-based combat, which the game openly borrows from classic Japanese RPGs, since Ichiban loves them and imagines the fights as fantasy adventures. Party members have jobs that change at an employment agency, each with its own abilities, and the surroundings play a role in combat too, since characters pick up bicycles or trash cans and make use of the street layout. Alongside the main story, Yokohama is packed with side content: running a business as an economic minigame, cart races, karaoke, a movie theater, playing classic arcade cabinets, and dozens of small stories about passersby.

On PlayStation 4 the game runs very well, and its strong point is a densely populated, brightly lit city that's a joy to get lost in. The music alternates between dramatic orchestral themes and rock and pop depending on whether a funeral or a fight with a man in a diaper is currently underway. Critics received the game enthusiastically, praising above all Ichiban's party and the courage to switch genres. The influence is evident in how the series continues to build on this direction. Today it's one of the best entry points into the world of Yakuza. Anyone who's skipped the series so far because of its characters' complicated history can jump in here without any preparation at all. The game maintains a remarkable balance between sincere emotion and total absurdity, and that very range is what makes it such a distinctive experience.

ps4__tales-of-arise.article:
**Tales of Arise** is a modern reboot of the Tales series' look, leaning on markedly more advanced technical presentation and a tighter narrative. The story pits two planets against each other: the technologically advanced Rena has exploited its neighbor Dahna for three hundred years, keeping its people enslaved. A man with no memory and an iron mask over his face joins forces with a Renan noblewoman who cannot bear another person's touch, and together they spark a rebellion. The game moves through individual dominions one by one, and each opens up a different perspective on what oppression does to both the oppressed and the oppressors.

Combat remains action-based but is noticeably faster and clearer than before. The player chains ground and aerial attacks, manages points for special abilities, and at the right moment triggers devastating combo attacks with a specific party member, each with its own unique animation. Emphasis is placed on precisely timed dodges rewarded with a counterattack, making combat feel brisk and readable. Outside of battle, the game offers cooking, fishing, resource gathering, blacksmith upgrades, and extensive campfire conversations among the party, which traditionally deepen the relationships between characters.

Technically, the PlayStation 4 version is very well done. The game uses a distinctive rendering style that combines anime stylization with painterly environments, giving it its own easily recognizable look. The landscapes are varied, from parched plains to icy wastelands, and the music works with big orchestral themes. Critics received the game very favorably and called it the strongest entry in the series in years, precisely because of its balanced combination of pacing, visuals, and story, with reservations aimed at the occasional bluntness of the second half. Today Tales of Arise is the easiest recommendation for anyone who wants to try an action JRPG without needing to know anything about the previous entries. The PlayStation 4 version loses nothing essential compared to newer consoles and remains one of the most visually striking games on this platform.

ps4__titanfall-2.article:
**Titanfall 2** arrived on PlayStation 4 in the fall of 2016 and very quickly earned a reputation as one of the best-designed shooters of the entire generation. To the fast multiplayer action, where nimble, lightly armed pilots clash with giant combat mechs called Titans, developer Respawn Entertainment this time added a full single-player campaign, something the first game lacked entirely. The player leads pilot Jack Cooper and his Titan BT-7274, and it's the relationship between these two characters that forms the surprisingly tender, human core of an otherwise very loud and explosive game.

The campaign is still cited today as a textbook example of level design. Each mission introduces one new idea, follows it through to its full potential, and ends before it can wear thin, whether that idea is manipulating time, shifting gravity, or a modular factory that assembles its own rooms right before the player's eyes. The core of the experience, though, is movement: running along walls, sliding, and double jumps chain together into a fluid flow that gives combat unusual verticality. Titans act as a slower, heavier counterpart to pilot agility, offering several distinct chassis with their own loadouts and tactics, so even multiplayer has two clearly separate layers of play.

Technically, the title was one of the most polished games of its time on PS4. It held high smoothness even in dense firefights, had clean environmental readability, and remarkably strong sound design that gives every step a Titan takes real weight. Unfortunately the game launched into a crowded fall season among several major competitors and commercially fell well short of its potential, though critics received it very warmly. Over the years Titanfall 2 has become one of the most frequently recommended tips for PlayStation owners, and its movement system left its mark on a whole range of later action games. Even today the campaign feels fresh, keeps its pace from the first minute to the last, and a length of around six hours is a strength rather than a shortcoming.

ps4__battlefield-1.article:
**Battlefield 1** pulled the series out of the near future and deep back into the past, setting it during the First World War, a conflict big shooters had long avoided. It launched on PlayStation 4 in 2016, and the very opening scene, in which the player gradually dies in the role of various nameless soldiers while only their names and years appear on screen, made it clear right away that DICE this time didn't want to glorify, but to remember. The campaign takes the form of a collection of several separate stories from different fronts, from the Italian Alps through the Arabian desert to a tank battlefield in Western Europe.

The heart of the game, though, remained its multiplayer mode for several dozen players, in which sprawling maps combine infantry, cavalry, armored vehicles, aircraft, and heavy artillery. A new addition was the Operations mode, which linked several maps and phases into one long-running campaign of attack and defense and managed to convey the feeling of a genuinely fought-out offensive rather than an isolated skirmish. Early-twentieth-century weapons, meaning bolt-action rifles, early submachine guns, and unreliable machine guns, change the rhythm of combat: shooting is slower, every hit hurts, and a bayonet charge or a gas grenade can turn an entire line.

Technically the game ranked among the best-looking things running on PS4 at the time. Environmental destruction, changing weather, and sandstorms aren't just window dressing, since they directly affect how a battle unfolds, and the sound design, with the deep impacts of artillery and the whistle of shrapnel, was often called the pinnacle of the entire series. Contemporary reception was very positive, and Battlefield 1 became one of the best-reviewed entries in the franchise. Today it's remembered above all as the moment a big-budget shooter managed to be both a spectacular showpiece and, at least in hints, a serious statement about the futility of trench warfare. The collectible records and short profiles of real weapons also tie the game into history and have led more than a few players to go read up on the period. Even today Battlefield 1 remains among the best-looking shooters ever released on PlayStation 4.

ps4__wolfenstein-ii-new-colossus.article:
**Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus** built on the successful reboot of the series, moving the fight against the Nazi regime straight into occupied America of an alternate 1960s. The player once again takes on the role of B. J. Blazkowicz, this time a badly wounded and physically deteriorating hero who nonetheless sets out to spark a rebellion. Developer MachineGames leaned into contrast: between intensely brutal firefights come long, quiet, and surprisingly intimate scenes aboard a captured submarine, where a story unfolds about family, guilt, and the decision to fight.

The action itself is fast and aggressive. The game rewards constant movement, dual-wielding two weapons at once, and switching between open assault and quietly eliminating officers who would otherwise call in endless reinforcements. The arsenal ranges from classic automatic weapons to heavy energy cannons, and the player gradually unlocks abilities that change how levels can be tackled, such as squeezing through narrow gaps or smashing through walls. The levels are varied, from a devastated Manhattan to a flooded city, blending straightforward arenas with spaces that offer more than one way forward.

Technically, on PlayStation 4 the game leaned on high fluidity and striking interior lighting, and visually on a heavily stylized vision of America under the swastika that is strongest in the quiet moments between battles. The performances and dialogue rank among the best the genre has offered, and the score alternates between dark industrial soundscapes and period motifs. Critics received the game very well, praising the storytelling and pacing in particular, while some players complained about the high difficulty and the protagonist's fragility. Today, The New Colossus stands as proof that a classic shooter can carry a dark, satirical, and unexpectedly moving story. Alongside the main line, the game offers a set of side missions for supporting characters and the chance to return to already-visited areas, though the campaign itself is fairly short, dense, and deliberately free of padding.

ps4__alien-isolation.article:
**Alien: Isolation** is the game that finally gave fans of Ridley Scott's original film exactly what they had wanted for years: a slow, oppressive, and merciless horror built around a single alien. The player takes on the role of Amanda Ripley, daughter of Ellen Ripley, searching for her mother's fate aboard the decaying space station Sevastopol. The setting is a crucial part of the experience: the station is filled with flickering, blocky-graphic screens, cassette tapes, and cables, since the artists deliberately drew on the technical look of the late-1970s film rather than modern ideas of the future.

At the core of the gameplay is a single, essentially unkillable enemy that moves through the station according to its own logic rather than fixed patrol routes. It cannot be destroyed, only driven off with a flamethrower or confused with noise. The player creeps under tables and inside lockers, watches the famous motion tracker, which itself gives off sound, and crafts smoke bombs, jammers, and flash grenades from scavenged scrap. Tension is further heightened by hostile humans and malfunctioning androids, whose calm voices are among the most unsettling elements of the whole game.

On PlayStation 4 the game ran smoothly, and its power lay less in raw technical polish than in its handling of light, shadow, and sound. The soundtrack draws on themes from the original film, and silence broken by hissing ventilation ranks among the best the genre has offered. Contemporary reception was mixed, mainly over its length and difficulty, but critics and players alike came to appreciate how consistently the game refuses to let up. Looking back, Alien: Isolation has become the benchmark for how to make a licensed horror game, and one of the few titles where the fear truly lasts the entire playthrough. Beyond the main campaign, the game also includes standalone challenge missions and bonus scenarios set in the world of the original film, which will delight fans of the source material. Anyone looking for a horror game that forces them to sit quietly and just listen will hardly find a better choice on PlayStation 4.

ps4__evil-within-2.article:
**The Evil Within 2** is the sequel to the horror game from Tango Gameworks, the studio led by the creator of the original Resident Evil titles, and it feels significantly more balanced than the first installment. Detective Sebastian Castellanos once again dives into the shared mental network known as STEM, this time for a very personal reason: he is searching for his daughter, whom he had believed dead. The result is a horror game that, alongside its monsters, deals with guilt, loss, and parental failure, and it is this personal layer that holds the whole game together.

The major change is structural. Part of the game takes place in the semi-open town of Union, which collapses and rearranges itself, and the player chooses how much side content and exploration to indulge in. Resources are limited, so the player constantly weighs whether to craft shotgun shells or save components for traps and healing items. Combat is slow and unpleasant, sneaking up on enemies from behind is often preferable to a direct firefight, and some creatures cannot be defeated at all, only escaped. Upgrading the character and weapons lets the player steer the playthrough more toward stealth or toward open resistance.

On PlayStation 4 the game leaned on a dense atmosphere of a fog-shrouded small town, striking lighting, and unsettling enemy design, among which a photographer working with frozen tableaux stands out. The sound is restrained, the music arrives in precisely measured doses, and silence matters just as much as the jump scares. Critics welcomed the sequel warmly, praising in particular its improved pacing and clearer story, though some fans of the original mourned the loss of its raw, disjointed charm. Today it stands as one of the best-playing survival horror games of its generation, and one that will also serve players who never finished the first game. Toward the end, the game leans somewhat more toward open action and eases off on the oppressiveness, which suits some players and bothers others, though the overall pacing remains balanced. Anyone wanting a tougher ride can turn to the highest difficulty, where resources become even scarcer and mistakes are unforgiving.

ps4__outlast.article:
**Outlast** is one of the games that, in the middle of the last decade, brought horror back to its rawest form: complete helplessness. The player takes on the role of journalist Miles Upshur, who sets out to investigate events at the remote Mount Massive psychiatric hospital and almost immediately discovers there is no way back. On PlayStation 4 the game arrived in 2014 and quickly became one of the most popular titles among livestream audiences, since it offers exactly the kind of tension that shares well.

The core mechanic is the camera. The hospital's interior is mostly pitch black, and the only thing the player has is a handheld camcorder with night vision, whose batteries drain quickly and constantly need replacing. Switching on night vision turns the picture into grainy green noise in which distances are hard to judge, yet it remains the only way to see anything at all. There is no way to fight back at all, so the entire gameplay rests on fleeing, closing doors, hiding under beds and in cabinets, and quickly reading a room's layout under pressure. On top of that, the player collects documents and records key events, gradually piecing together the background of the whole case.

Technically it is a fairly modest title, but it squeezes the maximum out of its use of shadow, limited visibility, and sound, where distant footsteps and a pursuer's breathing create constant pressure. The game does not shy away from graphic imagery and is definitely not for the faint of heart. Contemporary reception was very favorable, and Outlast contributed significantly to the wave of combat-free horror games that a number of other titles later followed. Today it feels a bit more straightforward and its scares are easier to read, but as an intense five-hour experience for one evening it still works excellently. The base game was later followed by the Whistleblower expansion, which sheds light on the same events from the perspective of a hospital employee and is often described as even more brutal than the original campaign. For PlayStation 4 owners, it remains an easily accessible classic of modern horror.

ps4__soma.article:
**SOMA** is a game where the scariest thing is an idea, not a monster. Frictional Games, the studio known for the Amnesia series, this time set its story in the underwater research complex PATHOS-II, where the main character wakes up with no clear explanation of how he got there. The gradual unraveling of what happened at the station, and what happened to him personally, forms the backbone of the whole experience and leads to questions about what actually makes a person a person, and whether a copy of consciousness is identical to the original.

The gameplay is deliberately simple. The player moves through corridors, opens hatches, reroutes cables, reads logs, and listens to recordings, occasionally having to avoid disfigured creatures that cannot be fought. Sneaking and hiding in the dark is the studio's classic discipline, but here it serves more as a periodic heart-rate spike than as the main focus. The strongest moments come when the game confronts the player with a decision that has no good answer and leaves them to live with it afterward. The stretches along the ocean floor, where visibility extends only a few meters, rank among the best-constructed passages in the genre.

On PlayStation 4 the game leaned on a dense atmosphere of flooded interiors, excellent lighting, and sound design full of groaning metal and pressure impacts. Visually it isn't the technical pinnacle of its generation, but the art direction of the crumbling station works flawlessly. Contemporary reception was very positive, especially thanks to the storytelling and the philosophical dimension rarely found in horror games. A later update added a so-called safe mode, in which enemies do not attack, letting players focus purely on the story. Today SOMA ranks among the best-written science-fiction games ever made. Its ending is among the most frequently discussed conclusions in the medium and can occupy someone's thoughts long after the console is switched off. That is precisely why it is recommended to play it in one sitting, in the dark, with headphones on, since more than anything it works through silence and through what it chooses not to tell the player.

ps4__dying-light.article:
**Dying Light** combined two things that at first glance have nothing to do with each other, namely parkour and a zombie apocalypse, and squeezed exceptionally addictive gameplay out of that combination. Polish studio Techland set the game in the fictional city of Harran, where the player, an agent sent to retrieve a stolen document, gets caught up in fights between survivor communities and armed gangs. The story isn't what matters most, though, it's the feeling of movement: climbing along ledges, jumping between rooftops, and sliding evasions from a horde give the city a dynamic entirely different from typical action games.

The gameplay splits day and night into two different worlds. By day the infected are slow and can be avoided or dealt with using improvised weapons that wear out and must be crafted and upgraded from scavenged scrap. At night, fast and aggressive creatures wake up and chase the player across rooftops and alleyways alike, and the only solution is often to flee to the nearest safe house. This cycle creates tension that the player largely doses out themselves, since nighttime excursions bring significantly higher rewards. The entire campaign can also be played cooperatively with other players.

On PlayStation 4 the game felt generous thanks to a sprawling, vertically layered city, a smooth day-night transition, and convincing dusk lighting that alone stirs unease. Sound is one of the game's key tools, since the distant screams of nighttime creatures function as a merciless countdown. Contemporary reception was favorable, and thanks to long-term support and expansions Dying Light kept an active player base for many years after release. Today it is remembered as the title that defined the shape of parkour-driven action games and inspired numerous successors. The Following expansion additionally added a sprawling rural area and a modified buggy, pushing the gameplay another step further. Today Dying Light is easily accessible and remains one of the most enjoyable cooperative experiences on PlayStation 4.

ps4__prey.article:
**Prey** is a science-fiction game by Arkane Studios that, despite its name, makes no attempt to continue the earlier title of the same name and instead builds on the legacy of classic games about a lone person trapped on a closed-off space station. The player wakes aboard the orbital station Talos I as Morgan Yu and very quickly learns that the crew is dead and the station has been taken over by alien beings called the Typhon. The best known of them, the so-called mimics, can transform into any object, so an ordinary mug or chair can turn into an attacker at any moment.

The station is an interconnected whole that can be traversed in many ways, and the game almost never offers just one solution. A locked door can be bypassed through a maintenance shaft, opened with a code found elsewhere, shot open, or avoided entirely via a trip through open space outside the hull. A key tool is the GLOO cannon, whose substance hardens to create passable platforms as well as obstacles, and so-called neuromods, with which the player upgrades abilities, including alien ones, though at a cost. Materials are recycled and reprinted, so resource management is a constant part of play.

On PlayStation 4 the game stood out above all through its art direction, blending retro-futurism with Art Nouveau elements to give the station an unmistakable identity. The music, with its uneasy electronic textures, and sound design that lets players gauge approaching danger both support a persistent sense of threat. Contemporary reception was very good, though commercially the game did not achieve big numbers, and its slow start put off some players. Looking back, Prey is considered one of the best-designed immersive sims and a title that deserves far more attention than it originally received. The Mooncrash expansion later reshaped the same setting into repeatable runs with variable enemy and item placement, offering an entirely different rhythm of play. The base campaign, however, rests above all on the freedom with which every single situation can be solved.

ps4__resident-evil-3.article:
**Resident Evil 3** is a remake of the late-nineties classic and tells the story of Jill Valentine, who tries to escape Raccoon City just as the infection has completely overrun the city. Alongside her, mercenary Carlos Oliveira gets drawn into events, and in some sections the player takes control of him as well. The main antagonist is Nemesis, an extraordinarily resilient being sent to eliminate the surviving members of the S.T.A.R.S. unit, who pursues the heroine throughout the entire game and cannot be permanently stopped.

The gameplay follows the previous remake, meaning an over-the-shoulder camera, limited ammunition, oppressive interiors, and the need to weigh every shot. A new addition is a dodge maneuver that, when timed precisely, briefly slows time and rewards bold players, making the combat feel noticeably more action-oriented than before. The city feels more open than the police station of the previous installment, though the path through it is guided more firmly and the game pushes for pace. The package also included a standalone asymmetric multiplayer mode in which four survivors try to escape an area controlled by a fifth player.

Technically, on PlayStation 4 it was a very accomplished title. Lighting on rain-soaked streets, detailed character models, and convincing material work were among the generation's best, the game ran smoothly, and loading times were short. Sound is restrained, which makes Nemesis's thundering arrival stand out all the more. Contemporary reception was largely positive, though critics repeatedly noted the short playtime and the fact that, compared to the original, some locations and situations are missing. Today it is a fast-paced and very good-looking horror game that works best as an intense experience over two evenings and as a companion piece to the remake of the second installment. Nemesis himself is a chapter apart, changing form several times over the course of the game, and while most encounters follow a fixed script, each is staged differently. For players who never played the original late-nineties version, it offers an accessible and striking entry point into the series.

ps4__inside.article:
**Inside** is the second game from Danish studio Playdead and ranks among the most distinctive independent titles ever released on PlayStation 4. You control a nameless boy in a red shirt fleeing through a dark, industrial-looking world full of patrols, dogs, and a vaguely defined authority. The game contains not a single line of dialogue or explanatory text; all storytelling happens purely through imagery and the situations the player is dropped into. The foundation is classic platforming, meaning running, jumping, dragging crates, and swimming, but the real content lies in physics-based puzzles that must be solved before your pursuer catches up.

The design proceeds in small, carefully measured steps. Every new mechanic, whether it's controlling a procession of limp bodies, a submarine, or flipping gravity in a laboratory, is first introduced in a safe form before it becomes a trap. Death is frequent, yet checkpoints sit so close together that repetition never feels frustrating and instead gives the whole journey a rhythm. Progress is strictly linear, the game never stops to explain itself with a tutorial, and it relies on you working out the rules yourself. A playthrough takes only a few hours, but with virtually no dead spots, and a web of hidden secrets invites a second run.

Technically, it's a textbook example of how striking a game with a limited color palette can look. The environments rest on muted grays and browns, into which the boy's red shirt cuts sharply, and the camera holds a fixed side view with a great depth of field. The soundtrack is equally sparing, offering rumbles, static, and ticking instead of melodies, which in key scenes turns into an unsettling pressure. Critics welcomed the game exceptionally warmly upon release, and its stark ending in particular became the subject of endless interpretation. To this day, Inside is cited as proof that an independent platformer can be more narratively ambitious than most projects with a giant budget, and on PS4 it has aged practically without a single wrinkle.

ps4__little-nightmares.article:
**Little Nightmares** from Swedish studio Tarsier Studios places the player in the role of a tiny girl in a yellow raincoat who wakes up inside a giant vessel called The Maw and tries to escape it. The whole world is deliberately oversized, door handles sit at head height, chairs resemble towers, and the ship's inhabitants are grotesque caricatures of adults with unnaturally long limbs or masks instead of faces. The camera holds a side view, yet the space is fully three-dimensional, so you also move in depth and must judge distances when jumping and climbing.

The gameplay combines platforming sections, simple item-based puzzles, and above all stealth. Most enemies are unkillable, and the only defense is to hide under a bed, turn off a light, or squeeze through a gap the pursuer's body can't fit into. Tension builds during chases, where a slow, quiet game suddenly turns into a sprint for your life, and a single hesitation means a return to the checkpoint. The playthrough lasts around four hours, and the game never pads it out; every chapter brings a new type of threat as well as new spatial puzzles.

On PlayStation 4 the game benefits above all from its art direction. The ship is lit by warm, oily-looking light sources that contrast with the deep darkness of the corridors, and the materials feel convincingly grimy and greasy. The music works with detuned strings and winds, though elsewhere the soundtrack prefers to stay silent and let the creaking wood and footsteps overhead speak instead. Reviewers praised above all the atmosphere and the game's ability to evoke an unpleasant feeling without resorting to cheap jump scares. The title quickly became a brand and opened the way for a sequel as well as a host of imitators. Its handling of scale contributed to that too, since the game never explains who the giants are or why they behave as they do, and the player must infer everything important from what they glimpse in the background. Today it ranks among the best a PS4 owner can play if they want a one-evening experience, but one that's unforgettable, and together with its later sequel, Little Nightmares created one of the few genuinely new horror franchises of its time.

ps4__dead-cells.article:
**Dead Cells** is an action platformer from French studio Motion Twin that earned the label roguevania because it combines randomly generated levels and merciless death with the structure and abilities familiar from metroidvanias. The player controls a shapeless mass that comes to life inside the body of an executed prisoner and hacks its way again and again across an island full of mutated guards, dungeons, ramparts, and sewers. After every death you return to the start, losing the weapons and upgrades you gathered, and keep only the permanently unlocked abilities and items you managed to pay for.

Combat is the core of the game. Controls are exceptionally precise and fast, the dodge roll is safe within a precisely defined window, and every weapon has its own reach, speed, and side effect, from setting enemies alight through freezing to bleeding. You build your character out of whatever the game offers you, since the loadout is determined by chance and effective combinations emerge on the fly. The pace is unusually brisk, a run through a level takes tens of minutes, and the game rewards boldness, since the richest chests sit behind doors open only for a limited time. After completing the story, so-called boss cells accumulate, ramping up the difficulty into genuinely brutal territory.

Graphically the game combines hand-drawn-looking pixel characters with modern lighting and fluid animation, so on PS4 it runs perfectly smoothly and stays legible even when the screen is full of enemies. The electronically tinged music supports the pace and shifts mood with every biome. Reception was very favorable even during early access, and the game held onto players' attention thanks to years of free and paid expansions. Alongside new content, a range of options for adjusting the difficulty also arrived, so today the game can appeal even to players who would otherwise avoid the original's uncompromising form. Dead Cells today ranks among the most influential representatives of the genre, and many later action roguelikes openly acknowledge a debt to its combat system and its approach to unlocks. On PS4 it's an ideal title for both short and long play sessions, since a single run fits into a single evening.

ps4__stardew-valley.article:
**Stardew Valley** is a farming simulator essentially created single-handedly by Eric Barone under the ConcernedApe label, and it arrived on PlayStation 4 shortly after its success on PC. Your character inherits an overgrown plot of land from their grandfather, leaves a big-city office job, and starts from scratch with an old sickle, a hoe, and a handful of seeds. From there unfolds a game that seems calm on the surface but is in fact packed with content, since every in-game day has a limited number of hours and you're constantly choosing what to spend them on.

The activities split into several interconnected layers. In the field you plant crops according to the season, water them, harvest them, and process them into more valuable goods in a cellar full of barrels and preserves jars. In the mines beneath the town you fight monsters, extract ores, and search for rare minerals. Dozens of residents live in the village of Pelican Town, each with their own schedule, favorite gifts, and story scenes that unlock depending on how well you know them, and you can marry several of them. Hovering over all of this is the choice of whether to restore the local community center by completing collection tasks, or to side with a multinational retail chain instead.

Technically it's a modest pixel-art game that has no trouble at all running on PS4, while its music accompanying each season ranks among the most memorable in the genre. Reception was extraordinary, and the game became a symbol of what a single author with enough time and care can achieve. Cooperative play, where friends can farm together on one homestead, plays a key role. Years of free updates have added new areas, crops, and characters, so today's version is substantially richer than the original and easily swallows hundreds of hours. What's interesting is how the game handles pacing, since it never pushes at all and yet creates a quiet sense that one more thing could be squeezed in before the character collapses from exhaustion. That's exactly where its addictiveness comes from, and why people describe Stardew Valley as a game you can relax with while constantly planning at the same time. Its influence on the genre was enormous, and it spawned an entire wave of similarly styled farming and village life games in the years that followed.

ps4__what-remains-of-edith-finch.article:
**What Remains of Edith Finch** is a narrative adventure from Giant Sparrow in which a young woman returns to an abandoned family house on the northwestern coast of the United States and tries to understand why she's the only one left of a sprawling family. The house itself is the main character, a bizarre structure that generations of Finches extended upward and outward until it became a tower full of rooms sealed off after their occupants' deaths. The player gradually works through them via secret passageways, and in each one finds an object that triggers a memory of that family member's last day alive.

The game's strength lies in the fact that no two memories play the same way. In one you turn into a bird of prey hunting through treetops, in another you follow comic-book panels, elsewhere you balance on a swing, and the most famous sequence has you simultaneously gutting fish in a factory and dreaming of a fairy-tale kingdom, controlling both activities at once. Each segment lasts only a few minutes, has its own visual style and control scheme, and ends at precisely the moment the mechanic might start to wear thin. The full playthrough takes roughly two hours, and the game contains no failure states or combat of any kind.

On PlayStation 4 the game looks excellent above all thanks to its use of light and its immensely detailed, lived-in rooms, which tell more about their owners than any dialogue could. Text appears directly in space, floats in the air, and vanishes as you move forward, tying reading directly to movement. The music is intimate and lets the narrator's voice and the sounds of the old house come through. Critics received the game with enthusiasm, and the title won numerous awards for its storytelling. To this day it's cited as one of the most convincing proofs that games can handle the theme of death and family memory in a way no other medium can manage. Credit for that goes partly to the fact that the game never slides into cheap sentimentality and instead presents each fate with a strange, slightly bizarre tenderness. The title's influence can be seen across an entire wave of short narrative games that followed, adopting its idea of a set of standalone, mechanically distinct episodes within one framing story.

ps4__witness.article:
**The Witness** is a sprawling logic game made under studio Thekla by Jonathan Blow, creator of the platformer Braid. You wake up on an abandoned island with no explanation whatsoever, and the only thing guiding you forward are panels containing mazes, on which you trace a line from start to finish. It sounds trivial, yet the game builds several dozen entirely distinct rule sets on top of this single principle, none of which are ever explained in words. You recognize new rules by running into a panel that makes no sense and having to deduce how it differs from the ones before it.

The island is divided into areas, and each teaches a different logic, whether that's separating colored squares, the symmetry of two lines drawn at once, audio clues, or working with shadows. Nothing pushes the player anywhere in particular, the order is largely free, and if you get stuck somewhere you simply go elsewhere. The strongest moment arrives when you realize the puzzles aren't confined to the panels but exist in the landscape itself, since branches, clouds, and reflections can be traced with the eye into shapes that function exactly like a maze. From that moment on, the island can never be seen the same way again.

The graphics rely on flat, richly colored stylization with sharp outlines, so on PlayStation 4 the game runs smoothly and, crucially, stays perfectly legible, which is essential for this type of puzzle. Sound practically forgoes music altogether, working instead with waves, wind, and birds, which only deepens the concentration. Response was very strong, even though part of the audience bounced off the difficulty and the optional puzzles, which rank among the hardest in the genre. The scope is considerable, too; completing just the main path takes tens of hours, and fully exhausting the island takes far longer still. The Witness remains to this day the benchmark for logic games that teach without a single tutorial, and it's invariably mentioned whenever the conversation turns to guiding the player through environmental design instead of text. On PlayStation 4 it's a title best played in long sessions, since its greatest reward is that moment when you suddenly grasp a connection that had eluded you until then.

ps4__unravel.article:
**Unravel** is a physics-based platformer from Swedish studio Coldwood Interactive in which you control a tiny figure knitted out of red yarn named Yarny. Its body is itself a game mechanic, since the thread it's made of unravels as it walks, and once it runs out you can't go any further. You must therefore manage its length carefully, hunt for scattered extra skeins, and go back for thread you've left behind. The thread also serves as a rope, as a bridge between two hooks, and as a pulley with which you lift objects or lower yourself into depths.

The puzzles build on this single idea and develop it patiently throughout the whole game. You tie yourself to a nail, swing across a chasm, tie a knot, and create a trampoline. Elsewhere you need to drag an apple onto a scale, get past a flock of dangerous birds, or squeeze past a machine in a factory. Progression is linear, difficulty is gentle, and the game never punishes harshly, with checkpoints in abundance. The roughly six-to-eight-hour journey works as a parallel narrative about a family history, pieced together from photographs in an empty house and from vignettes playing out in the background of individual levels.

Visually it's one of the most beautiful titles of its kind on PlayStation 4. The settings draw on Nordic nature, meaning peat bogs, rocky coastlines, gardens, and snow-covered forests, and are shot with unusually soft light and a great depth of field, so the backgrounds resemble photographs. The music rests on accordion, violin, and piano, sustaining a melancholic, nostalgic mood. Critics praised above all the thread concept and the atmosphere, with reservations aimed at the way the puzzles start repeating toward the end. Today the game stands as an example of how a large-format publisher backed a small, personal project, and Yarny became an easily recognizable icon of the independent scene of its era. On PlayStation 4, Unravel ranks among titles that can be recommended even to players who otherwise avoid platformers, since the emphasis here lies not on reflexes but on finding solutions and on a calm pace.

ps4__guacamelee-super-turbo-championship.article:
**Guacamelee! Super Turbo Championship Edition** is an expanded version of the action metroidvania from Canadian studio DrinkBox Studios, and on PlayStation 4 it brought new areas, bosses, and abilities compared to the original release. The hero is Juan Aguacate, a simple farmer who, after encountering a magical mask, transforms into a luchador and sets out to rescue the mayor's kidnapped daughter from the clutches of a skeletal villain. The whole world draws on Mexican folklore, on Day of the Dead celebrations, on lucha libre, and on folk art traditions, lending the game a vividness you won't find elsewhere in the genre.

Gameplay is built around fistfighting combat that's unusually rich. You launch enemies into the air, juggle them, interweave strikes with throws and special moves unlocked progressively over time. Crucially, those same moves also serve as a means of movement across the world, since you use them to smash color-coded blocks, break through walls, and reach platforms otherwise out of reach. The second key mechanic is switching between the world of the living and the world of the dead, where platforms and enemies appear or vanish depending on which plane you're currently in. In later sections you need to switch mid-jump, which makes the game one of the most demanding platforming challenges of its time.

Graphically it's a hand-drawn two-dimensional game with rich colors and sharp outlines that look great on PS4 and run completely smoothly. The music blends Latin American motifs with electronica and actively drives the pace of the fights. The game earned a reputation for its humor, which pokes fun at gaming culture and internet jokes alike, though that same trait struck part of the audience as excessive. Co-op play for up to four players on one screen made it a favorite title for playing together, and it still ranks among the best-playing metroidvanias on the console today. Credit for that also goes to the pace, since a playthrough fits into roughly ten hours and the game never lingers on pointless wandering. DrinkBox's success opened the door to a sequel and at the same time proved that in a crowded genre it's possible to stand out through a distinctive artistic signature.

ps4__rayman-legends.article:
**Rayman Legends** is a two-dimensional platformer from Ubisoft Montpellier that arrived on PlayStation 4 in an expanded form and still ranks among the most polished games of its genre. Rayman and his friends make their way through a series of visually distinct worlds, from fairy-tale forests through medieval castles and underwater realms to settings inspired by Mexican festivities, and in each one they complete tasks built around running, jumping, swimming and freeing small trapped creatures called Teensies.

The controls are among the most precise you'll find in any platformer. The character accelerates smoothly, mid-air flight can be corrected with a helicopter spin, and punches and wall-sliding feel so intuitive that after a while the player stops thinking about buttons and focuses purely on the rhythm of the level. Alongside classic arenas, the game offers chases where you run from a threat with no way to stop, levels controlled by the helper Murfy who clears obstacles for you, and above all the musical finales of each world, where jumps and hits are precisely synced to cover versions of well-known melodies. Co-op for up to four players on one screen works brilliantly and turns the game into chaotic fun.

Technically, the game runs on the UbiArt Framework engine, which allows hand-drawn art at extraordinary resolution, so even years later it still looks sharp and colorful, and on PS4 it runs at a perfectly stable pace. The sound design is inventive and playful, with parodic bits alongside more earnest musical themes. The reception was enthusiastic, and critics repeatedly ranked the title among the best platformers of its generation. The scope is enormous, since besides its own levels it also includes reworked missions from the previous installment and daily challenges, giving it dozens of hours of content. The difficulty rises very gently, the main path is manageable even for less experienced players, while the hidden levels demand absolute precision. That's exactly why Rayman Legends is still recommended today as the first choice when someone is looking for a classic two-dimensional platformer on PS4, for themselves or for the whole family.

ps4__crash-bandicoot-n-sane-trilogy.article:
**Crash Bandicoot N. Sane Trilogy** brought a completely rebuilt trio of the original bandicoot Crash's adventures from the late nineties to PlayStation 4. Studio Vicarious Visions didn't just smooth out the textures; it rebuilt the games on a modern foundation while trying to preserve the level layouts and pacing of the originals. The result is a collection that looks like a current game but plays like a title from the first PlayStation era, demands included.

The gameplay sticks to the tried-and-true formula. Levels mostly lead forward into the depth of the screen, or from right to left, or take the form of chases toward the camera, and the player smashes crates, jumps on enemies' heads, and collects Wumpa fruit along the way. Landing precision is crucial, since the shadow beneath the character is often the only clue as to where you'll actually land. The second and third games add sliding, a double jump, and bonus levels on a motorbike, underwater, or riding a tiger. Collecting gems requires smashing every single crate in a level without losing a life, which turns what originally looked like a children's game into a tough challenge. The collection later added a playable Coco and several entirely new levels.

Visually, it's a very accomplished piece of work; environments are full of detail, characters have expressive faces, and enemy animations give the world a comedic edge. The music draws on the original scores and feels nostalgic without sounding dated. The reception was good, with the most common complaint being that the jump physics feel somewhat stricter than in the originals, which raises the difficulty especially in the first game. The collection was a huge commercial success and kickstarted a wave of returning classic platformer franchises that arrived on the same console in the following years. For old fans it's a nostalgic return to the games that once defined the first PlayStation, and for new players it's a solid, content-rich package offering dozens of hours of jumping. It's precisely this combination of faithfulness and a modern coat of paint that's why N. Sane Trilogy is still cited today as one of the better-executed attempts to revive an old franchise.

ps4__driveclub.article:
**Driveclub** was one of the first big racing titles for PlayStation 4 and was made by British studio Evolution Studios, previously known for the MotorStorm series. The game sits on the border between arcade and simulation; the cars feel notably heavy, braking points must be respected, and the handling model rewards a clean racing line, yet it never plays like a driving-school program or overwhelms the player with suspension settings. The car roster is made up mostly of road-going sports and supercar models, and the tracks run through real landscapes of Scotland, Norway, Chile, India and other countries.

The backbone of the game is the clubs, groups of players who accumulate experience together and complete club objectives. During every race, the game continuously issues small challenges, such as taking a corner faster than someone else or holding a longer continuous drift, and the points from these add up to overall progress. The challenge system, which lets you send challenges to specific players, was one of the most interesting ideas of its time and kept an ongoing indirect competition running among players. The game immediately penalizes dirty moves and track-cutting with a time penalty, so an aggressive style doesn't pay off.

The game's launch was very troubled, since the online services didn't work for weeks and part of the planned content was delayed. That's exactly what marred its reviews at the time. But once things settled down and a weather system with dynamic rain and snow was added, Driveclub proved to be a technically stunning piece of work, especially in terms of lighting, reflections on the bodywork, and the cockpit view. The music and engine sounds underline the sense of speed. Today the game is remembered as an underappreciated title that got ahead of its time visually, and driving in the rain at dusk remains one of the most impressive things PlayStation 4 offered in the genre. Studio Evolution Studios was later shut down, so no sequel ever followed, leaving the game as its final major work. For players looking for racing somewhere between arcade and simulation, it's still a very good choice.

ps4__dirt-rally.article:
**DiRT Rally** is Codemasters' return to hardcore rally simulation after previous entries in the series had drifted more and more toward arcade fun and festival atmosphere. On PlayStation 4 the game arrived after a period of tuning on PC, and it brought a handling model that mercilessly punishes any lapse in attention. Cars float on gravel, grip changes literally from corner to corner on asphalt, and any mistake in weight transfer ends in a guardrail or a tree, with the damage staying with you all the way to the service area.

The core of the game is made up of long special stages where it's just you, the car, and your co-driver's voice. Working with the pace notes is crucial, since you can't learn the track by heart, and the player has to trust what they hear and brake accordingly before they can even see the corner. Between stages you manage damaged parts with a limited number of mechanics and a limited amount of time, so a decision to sacrifice the gearbox in favor of the dampers can decide the whole rally. Besides classic rally, the game also offers rallycross on closed circuits and the famous Pikes Peak hill climb.

Technically it's a solid piece of work, at its strongest in the track surfaces, the dust kicked up behind the car, and the cockpit camera behavior, which conveys bumps and imperfections beautifully. Sound is one of its greatest strengths; engines sound raw, gravel rattles into the wheel arches, and the echo changes in enclosed spaces. Music is practically absent wherever it would be distracting, which only helps concentration. Critics received the game excellently precisely for its uncompromising approach, and many consider it the best rally game of its generation. The success of this approach led the series to later split into two branches, one staying with the more fun-oriented take and the other continuing this hardcore simulation line. Even today it's a title that demands patience from the player and a willingness to run the same stage ten times in a row, but it rewards you with a feeling you won't find anywhere else. It shines brightest with a wheel, though even on a standard controller you can get very far with a feel for the throttle.

ps4__wipeout-omega-collection.article:
**Wipeout Omega Collection** brings together on PlayStation 4 the best of the futuristic racing series, specifically the content of Wipeout HD, its Fury expansion, and the handheld Wipeout 2048. Everything was reworked into a higher resolution and, above all, a smooth frame rate, which is absolutely essential at these speeds. You race with anti-gravity craft that hover above the track, flying through tunnels, vertical loops, and steep drops, with the speed so high that the player has to rely more on learned reflexes than on looking ahead.

The controls combine classic steering with so-called air brakes on either side, which turn the craft and let you take a sharp corner without losing speed. On top of that sits a weapons system, where you pick up rockets, mines, shields, or homing missiles on the track, and the same pickups can be sacrificed for an instant energy top-up. Energy also serves as the craft's health, so every wall impact or weapon hit drains from the same gauge, and when it runs out, the craft explodes. This turns the game into a constant back-and-forth between attack and survival. Different teams have different characteristics, from nimble and fragile to slow and durable.

Visually, the collection is one of the sharpest-looking titles of its time, with clean surfaces, bold colors, and a graphic design rooted in the tradition the series has cultivated since its beginnings. Music is an essential part of the experience, since the series has always built on the electronic scene, and here too a brisk dance selection accompanies the races. The reception was very favorable, with players especially praising the amount of content and the technical level. The tracks from the handheld installment also deserve credit, since thanks to the higher resolution and smoother frame rate they feel completely different from their original form. Given that a proper new entry in the series hasn't arrived in a long time, this collection remains for many the definitive form of anti-gravity racing. Newcomers, meanwhile, face a steep learning curve, since mastering sharp corners at the highest speed classes takes dozens of attempts, but once you do, it's one of the most intense feelings of speed on any console.

ps4__burnout-paradise-remastered.article:
**Burnout Paradise Remastered** brought one of the most beloved arcade racing games ever back to PlayStation 4, this time with higher resolution, smoother frame rate, and all the expansions that were gradually released for the original. The foundation is the open city of Paradise City, which you can drive through freely with no menus or loading screens whatsoever. You start a race by braking at an intersection and hitting the gas, the finish line is always somewhere at the edge of the map, and how you get there is entirely up to you, since the game offers no set route.

The gameplay is uncompromisingly arcade. Nitro fills up through risky driving in oncoming traffic, jumps, drifts, and close near-misses, and the reward for boldness is even more speed. Alongside regular races, the game offers chases where you have to wreck an opponent's car, timed runs where you protect your own bodywork, and above all stunt runs, where you try to rack up the most points by smashing fences, billboards, and jumping across rooftops. A crash here is a spectacle, since the camera slows down and shows exactly how the car deforms, and you can still steer the wreck itself into rivals. The city is full of hidden shortcuts, breakable fences, and jump ramps, and finding them makes up a large part of the fun.

The remastered version also includes motorcycles and a winter makeover of the city. On PS4 it runs very smoothly, which matters most at these speeds. The soundtrack uses licensed rock and punk tracks that fit the carefree nature of the whole package perfectly. The original game was received enthusiastically at the time, and the remaster brought it back to the attention of players who'd missed it the first time around. Critics of the remaster only complained that it stuck too faithfully to the original and added practically nothing new, but otherwise it was honest, solid work. Open-world arcade racing isn't common these days, and that's exactly why Paradise City still feels fresh, especially compared to titles that lead the player from one point to the next. Crucially, the game barely interrupts the pace at all, since after finishing a race you can keep driving immediately, and the next competition can start at any intersection.

ps4__tony-hawk-s-pro-skater-1-2.article:
**Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 1 + 2** is a remake of two skateboarding classics from the turn of the millennium, made by studio Vicarious Visions, and it arrived on PlayStation 4 as one of the best-executed returns of an old franchise ever. All the levels from both games were rebuilt from scratch, but with the layout preserved with pinpoint accuracy, so a player who remembers where the rope hangs in the hall or where the hidden ramp leads will get their bearings within seconds.

The gameplay stays faithful to the originals and is built around two-minute runs, during which you complete a set of tasks: collecting letters, finding the secret tape, breaking records, and fulfilling passersby's requests. The trick system combines jumps, spins, rail grinds, and manuals, which let you link individual tricks into a single endless combo across the whole level. It's precisely this loop, where the player gradually discovers how to connect distant parts of the map, that's the reason the series hasn't aged in twenty years. The remake also adds later tricks like the revert to both games, so it plays somewhat more smoothly than the originals, and it adds an extensive skatepark editor and custom characters.

Technically it's an accomplished piece of work; environments are full of detail, the skaters' animations feel believable, and the game keeps a very brisk pace that's essential for precise trick timing. The music selection is a key part of its identity, since it contains a large portion of the original punk and hip-hop tracks alongside new additions. The reception was very favorable, and many reviewers called the game an example of how a remake should be done. The title's success also had an impact beyond the game itself, since it once again drew attention to nineties skateboarding culture and the music tied to it. For players who never experienced the originals, it's a surprisingly demanding but extremely addictive arcade game, where you play the same level over and over until you beat your personal record. On PlayStation 4 the game runs smoothly and the controls are readable enough that the basics can be learned within a few minutes, while true mastery takes dozens of hours.

ps4__steep.article:
**Steep** is an open winter-sports game from studio Ubisoft Annecy that drops the player into a vast Alpine landscape and lets them choose for themselves where and how to ride down. Snowboard, skis, wingsuit, and paraglider are all available, and you can switch between them practically at any time, so a single run might start as a descent through the woods, continue with a cliff jump in a wingsuit, and end with soaring above the valley. The mountains aren't divided into separate tracks; it's one continuous world that unlocks as you climb or fly to new starting points.

The structure is deliberately loose. Challenges of various kinds are scattered across the map, from time-based races through trick contests to precise landings inside a target circle, and completing them gradually unlocks further areas and gear. The game places heavy emphasis on sharing, since every run can be recorded, viewed from different cameras, and sent to others as a challenge, and while moving freely you'll encounter other players' ghosts. The physics sits somewhere between realism and arcade; falls look dramatic and painful, but getting back on the slope is instant.

On PlayStation 4 the game feels strongest thanks to the sheer size of the terrain and its handling of weather and fog, when peaks disappear into the clouds and a descent into the valley brings a gradual change of surroundings. Snow reacts to your riding, tracks form in it, and avalanches are among the most striking moments. The sound design works with silence and the rush of wind, which is the only accompaniment during fast riding, with music kicking in more during free roaming. Reviews praised the atmosphere and the sense of freedom, with criticism aimed at repetitive tasks. Later expansions added further areas as well as an Olympic-discipline layer, so there ends up being considerably more content than at launch. To this day it's one of the few games that convincingly conveys the calm and scale of high mountains, and many players come back to it more for the free riding than for completing challenges. Steep also pointed the way other open-world sports games would later follow, an emphasis on freedom of movement rather than fixed set tracks.

xbox-one__ryse-son-of-rome.article:
**Ryse: Son of Rome** was one of the first games meant to show what the new Xbox could do, and in that respect it delivered without compromise. You play as the Roman soldier Marius Titus, whose family is slaughtered by a conspiracy at the very heart of the empire, and the story of revenge unfolds through flashbacks interspersed with battles in Britain and in the streets of Rome. It's a fairly straightforward, corridor-led action-adventure that doesn't bet on freedom but on direction — the camera constantly hunts for a cinematic angle, crowd scenes are packed with extras, and individual missions try to alternate between sieges, arena duels, and quieter passages.

Combat rests on a simple foundation: attack, block, dodge, and interrupt the enemy's action. Once you've weakened an opponent enough, an execution triggers where you just need to press the button matching the color the enemy flashes. The system is deliberately undemanding and rewards rhythm and smooth chaining rather than mechanical precision, which drew criticism for being too simple. On the other hand, throwing weapons, shield formations, and javelin-volley commands give the fights at least a hint of tactics and remind you that Marius commands a unit. Alongside the campaign, the game also offers an arena mode where you complete varying tasks in the Colosseum, with rules and conditions that change and points awarded for style of killing; played with a partner, it's a surprisingly addictive diversion.

Technically, at the time of release this was one of the best-looking console games period — detailed faces, elaborate armor materials, and lighting that made Ryse a convincing showcase for the new generation. The sound design is equally lavish, with an orchestral score and an atmosphere steeped in antiquity. Reviews were mixed: the game was criticized for repetitive content and a shallow combat system, while its presentation and direction were praised. Today Ryse plays like a brisk, shorter spectacle, and what's most interesting about it is how confidently it played the Hollywood blockbuster at the very start of the generation — and how well that look has held up.

xbox-one__dead-rising-3.article:
**Dead Rising 3** brought the zombie apocalypse series to Xbox One and immediately threw out a number of old rules along the way. The city of Los Perdidos is open, without walls or loading screens, and swarms with hundreds of undead at once — that very crowd was the main argument for why the game launched as a new-console exclusive. You play as mechanic Nick Ramos, who has a few days to get out of quarantine before the army clears the area. The time limit remains, but it's far more forgiving than before, and in an alternative mode it can be turned off entirely, making the game welcoming even to players whom earlier entries put off with their stressful clocks.

The core is still just as gloriously silly: anything lying around is a weapon, and combining items produces absurd tools of destruction. New this time are combined vehicles, so a cross between a steamroller and a motorcycle now rolls through the streets. Alongside the main storyline run side missions rescuing survivors and boss fights against psychopaths who embody individual human vices. The character improves through experience, collects blueprints, and unlocks further madness, keeping the loop of exploring and slaughtering fresh even after many hours. The game also offers two-player co-op across the entire open city, so the campaign can be played start to finish together.

Technically the game chose a compromise: a sharper, grittier, less colorful palette than its predecessors, along with variable frame rate during the biggest hordes. Reviews of the time praised the scale and freedom, while reservations targeted the story and the fact that a more serious tone doesn't entirely suit the series. Even so, it remains one of the Xbox One's most distinctive launch titles and, to this day, an entertaining toy for anyone who wants to try how many zombies can be mowed down at once with a homemade contraption. An interesting extra was the use of the console's companion features of the time, letting you call in an airstrike via a mobile app or follow the map on a second screen.

xbox-one__halo-wars-2.article:
**Halo Wars 2** is a rare specimen — a real-time strategy game designed primarily for a controller, and one that genuinely works. It continues the story of the crew of the Spirit of Fire, who wake after a long sleep near a giant installation called the Ark and run into a new threat in the form of the brutal warlord Atriox and his renegade faction, the Banished. The campaign is told through impressive cinematics and missions that alternate classic base-building with tasks where you're given only a handful of units and have to make it through to the end with them.

The controls rely on clever shortcuts: a radial menu for construction, buttons to select all units or all army groups, and a cursor with automatic target snapping. The base expands across predefined slots, which simplifies the economy to two resources and leaves room for decisions about how much to invest in supplies, research, and population. Alongside classic deathmatch and a tug-of-war over control points, the game brings the Blitz mode, where the army is built from cards and combat focuses purely on capturing points — a brisk variant that makes strategy a surprisingly accessible affair. The campaign can also be played entirely in two-player co-op, which is far from common for strategy games.

Visually, Halo Wars 2 is above average for the genre: legible units, well-differentiated factions, and flashy orbital-bombardment and airstrike abilities. The music works with motifs typical of the series and lends the battles appropriate weight even though you're watching the action from a distance. Reception was warm; the game was criticized for a shorter campaign and less content for long-term play, while its accessibility and how well it translates strategy to console were praised. Today it stands as one of the best proofs that real-time strategy can indeed work on a gamepad, and for Halo fans it's also an important piece of the series' mythology. After release the game received the Awakening the Nightmare expansion, which added a new campaign and the playable Flood faction.

xbox-one__halo-infinite.article:
**Halo Infinite** was meant to be both a restart and a return to roots at once, and in many ways it succeeded. Master Chief wakes up in space above the shattered Zeta Halo ring, where the remnants of human forces are now ruled over by the Banished faction. For the first time in the series, the campaign takes place in a semi-open world — you move freely across the ring's surface, liberate outposts, take down commanders, and thereby unlock reinforcements and fast travel. Crucially, the rhythm of classic Halo hasn't been lost in the process: firefights still play out in spacious arenas where weapon choice, grenades, and shield management matter.

The biggest new addition is the grappleshot, which lets you pull yourself to a ledge, yank a weapon out of an enemy's hand, or catapult yourself straight into a fight. It has changed movement so much that combat has opened up into the vertical plane, and the player is suddenly far more aggressive than before. Other tools are added on top, such as a portable shield or an area scanner. Multiplayer launched as a standalone free-to-play component and returned to a fair foundation where everyone starts equal and better weapons are picked up on the map. The campaign can also be played in co-op, which the developers added after launch, and a Forge mode is available for building custom maps.

Technically, the game also came out on Xbox One and holds up decently smooth even there, at the cost of lower resolution and sparser vegetation. Sound and music are excellent across all versions, though — the return of the iconic choral theme ranks among the strongest moments in the whole series. Reception was largely very positive; reservations targeted the repetitive nature of open-world side activities and how slowly multiplayer content filled out after launch. As a campaign, though, Infinite still plays today as the best Halo in years and a great point to return to the series. Collecting the audio logs scattered across the ring further fills in the story behind the human forces' defeat and the fate of characters the Chief never meets.

xbox-one__forza-horizon-5.article:
**Forza Horizon 5** moved the traveling music festival to Mexico and offered perhaps the most varied map the series has ever had. Within a few minutes you can drive from a tropical beach through jungle and desert up the slopes of a volcano where snow falls — and all these biomes are handled so that each has its own weather and its own mood. The structure remains pleasantly unconstraining: you earn points for all sorts of things, unlock new festival hubs, and between races you simply drive around discovering billboards to smash, jumps, and speed-trap sections.

The driving model keeps the series' famous compromise between simulation and arcade. Cars have noticeably different weight and behavior on tarmac, gravel, and off-road, yet the game is also packed with assists including time rewind, so it's completable even for a complete beginner. The huge roster of cars can be tuned in detail, and setups and custom liveries can be shared with others. A key component is the online layer — players continually cross paths in the open world, trigger shared events, and take part in large co-op events that the series has gradually honed to perfection. Story-driven jobs with their own rules form a separate chapter, ranging from stunt driving to shooting commercials, spicing up the otherwise racing-focused routine.

Visually it's one of the best-looking games of its generation; even the Xbox One version retains impressive lighting and dense environmental detail, just with a lower resolution and a less stable frame rate than on newer hardware. The radio stations cover a wide musical range from electronic to Latin American styles, making the drive a pleasant backdrop even for long evenings. The game was received very well and is often called the peak of open-world racing titles. Today it can be recommended to practically anyone — as a relaxing drive or as an in-depth tuning project. The game also offers extensive controller-customization options and aids for players with hearing or vision impairments, something rarely seen in racing titles.

xbox-one__gears-of-war-ultimate-edition.article:
**Gears of War: Ultimate Edition** is a complete rebuild of the first installment, which in 2006 redefined third-person, cover-based action. The story follows Marcus Fenix, released from prison into a desperate war against the Locust, an underground race that has driven humanity from the surface. The campaign holds to a tight, corridor-based rhythm: darting between cover, laying down suppressive fire, and flanking to force the enemy out of position. The firefights carry their characteristic weight — the characters are armored colossi, every movement has inertia, and the Lancer rifle with its chainsaw bayonet remains one of the most iconic weapons of its era.

The remake didn't stop at higher resolution. Models, textures, and lighting were rebuilt from scratch, cinematics were reshot, and most importantly, chapters that had originally appeared only in the PC version — and which console players had never seen — made it into the game. Multiplayer was rebuilt on a more modern network foundation and offers the classic modes with the slower, more deliberate pace that the first game specifically had — that is, without the acrobatics later sequels introduced. The entire campaign can be played in two-player co-op, whether on a single console or online, and it's precisely that pairing of two players that remains what makes Gears, Gears.

Technically it's very clean work — the game runs smoothly, noticeably sharper than the original, while still keeping the grim, gray-and-brown-toned atmosphere of the pseudo-ancient ruined cities. The music and weapon sound design rank among the best the genre has offered. Reception was very good, and Ultimate Edition became the standard for what a remaster should look like: preserve the feel of the original while not hiding that it's a game from a different era. Today it plays noticeably slower than later entries, but that's exactly what shows why Gears scored so well back then and why cover-based action became the norm for years. It also served as a bridge to the next installment — anyone who bought the game back then also got access to the series' older Xbox 360 entries, playable thanks to backward compatibility.

xbox-one__gears-tactics.article:
**Gears Tactics** took the brutal universe of the series and translated it into turn-based tactics — and against expectations, it clicked. The story takes place twelve years before the first game, shortly after the event known as Emergence Day, and follows the rebellious Gabe Diaz, whom command sends to eliminate the scientist responsible for the worst Locust experiments. Instead of base management and a global map, as you'd know from other tactics games, this is a more briskly paced, mission-structured campaign, where gear and squad abilities are upgraded between operations.

Combat runs on action points — each character has three, and can spend them on movement, shooting, reloading, or a special ability, so a single turn can accomplish considerably more than in classic genre entries. The system also rewards aggression: finishing off an enemy in one go grants an extra turn, and knocking an opponent down lets you execute them in a brutal animation that boosts the whole squad's morale. Classes such as support, sniper, or heavy complement one another, and the upgrade tree offers plenty of specializations. At the end of each act awaits a fight against a giant creature that must be taken down piece by piece. Soldiers can also be dressed in scavenged gear that isn't just cosmetic but changes stats, turning loot collection into a motivation of its own.

Visually, the game looks exceptionally good for a tactics title — the camera zooms in on gunfire, the environment is full of rubble and smoke, and even on Xbox One it holds a decent frame rate. Sound and music carry over the main series' oppressive tone and land well during fights with larger creatures. Reviews were favorable, praising the dynamism and presentation, with criticism aimed at repetitive side missions. Today it's an excellent pick for anyone who wants to enjoy turn-based tactics without the lengthy strategic layering and resource management between individual battles. Optional missions help restore squad condition, since wounded soldiers heal over several turns, and at higher difficulty losses are counted as permanent.

xbox-one__psychonauts-2.article:
**Psychonauts 2** came out sixteen years after the original, and it's almost startling how naturally it picks up the thread.
