Raz Aquato finally arrives at the headquarters of the secret psychic-agent organization, only to find, instead of a celebrated welcome, an internship, cleaning duty, and a conspiracy reaching deep into the founders' past. The core remains a platformer built around exploration and collecting, but the real attraction is the levels set inside human minds — each with its own visual language derived from what that particular person suffers from or is trying to suppress. The game loosely continues on from a short episode released between the two main entries, though newcomers won't miss anything essential.

Gameplay combines platforming movement with an arsenal of psychic abilities: telekinesis, pyrokinesis, time slow, a ball form for quick movement, or a mental link that pulls Raz along a thread of thought. The abilities can be chained together, and the game uses them both in combat and in puzzles. What matters most, though, is the tone — the story deals seriously and sensitively with anxiety, addiction, and trauma, while never ceasing to be funny and playful, a combination few games manage. The game is also unusually accommodating — it offers optional simplification of both combat and platforming sections, so it's reachable even for someone mainly interested in the story.

Visually it's one of the most imaginative games of its time; every world has its own palette and its own logic, from a cooking competition to a hospital environment assembled from fragments of memory. The music shifts just as much as the worlds do and, at key moments, brilliantly underscores the emotion. Reception was excellent; the game collected awards and is often mentioned among the best releases of its year. Today it can be recommended even to people who never played the first game — the story is sufficiently explained, and the craftsmanship is generations ahead of its predecessor. The voice acting is top-notch, and the dialogue often changes depending on who happens to be in your team.

xbox-one__grounded.article:
**Grounded** builds on a simple yet remarkably rich idea: a group of kids is shrunk down to the size of an ant and must survive in a backyard garden. What was once mundane scenery suddenly turns into a dangerous wilderness — a dewdrop becomes a water source, a blade of grass a building material, and an ordinary spider a nightmare you can only run from. It's precisely this change of scale that turns an otherwise familiar survival loop into something distinctive and surprisingly creepy. You can play as any of four characters, and the game keeps a light, adventurous tone despite how merciless the environment is described to be.

The foundation is classic: you gather resources, build a base, cook, upgrade your gear, and gradually venture into more dangerous parts of the yard. But the game also offers a solid story thread — underground labs, scientists' logs, and an explanation for why the shrinking happened in the first place. Combat requires reading your opponent's movements, blocking, and dodging, so a clash with a beetle plays out more like a duel than mindless clicking. Co-op for up to four players is clearly what the game was designed for, and building a nest together high in the grass is one of the best experiences the genre offers. Besides classic survival, it also offers calmer modes where hunger and thirst are no threat, so you can explore the garden purely for the building and discovery.

Visually it leans on stylization with bold colors and soft shapes, which let it run even on Xbox One and also suits its lightly comic-book storytelling. Sound is essential — buzzing, crackling, and the distant footsteps of arthropods make every night a tense affair, and for players with arachnophobia the game offers a slider that reduces spider detail. Grounded spent a long time in early access and grew stronger with every update; in its final form it's one of the most approachable and best-written survival games out there. Special mention goes to the garden map, which unlocks through journal entries and turns gradual wandering into systematic exploration.

xbox-one__pentiment.article:
**Pentiment** is a game that, in a major publisher's catalog, shouldn't have had a chance to exist at all — and yet it did. It's set in a Bavarian abbey and the surrounding village in the first half of the sixteenth century, and its protagonist is Andreas Maler, a painter finishing a commission in the monastery scriptorium. When a murder occurs, he finds himself thrust into the role of a reluctant investigator and must, within limited time, gather testimonies, compare versions of events, and ultimately point to a culprit without ever gaining absolute certainty. The choices are never simply good or bad.

The gameplay largely consists of conversations, reading, and deciding whom and what to spend your limited time on. At the start you choose Andreas's education and background, which opens up different sets of topics — you talk to a monk differently if you studied theology than if you wandered through Italy. Choices carry long-term consequences, the game unfolds across three time blocks spanning years, and the village changes along with the era's upheavals. This isn't a detective story with a single correct solution, but a tale of how a truth that a community accepts as its own comes into being. Part of daily life includes small vignettes of village life — a shared meal, fieldwork, or book printing — that carry no gameplay reward but flesh out the world.

Visually, Pentiment is utterly distinctive — the whole game looks like an illuminated manuscript and woodcut, text appears via pen strokes, and individual characters have handwriting matching their education and status. The music works with period instruments, and the sound of writing and footsteps on stone floors rounds out the cloister's silence. Critics received the game enthusiastically, praising its boldness and historical care. Today it's one of the strongest proofs that a publisher's portfolio can withstand a quiet, text-based, historical experiment without a single shot fired. The game runs without trouble even on older hardware, since its demands lie purely in reading, not in computation.

xbox-one__minecraft-dungeons.article:
**Minecraft Dungeons** took the blocky aesthetic of the world's best-selling game and transplanted it into the top-down action dungeon crawler genre. No digging, no building — instead you move through generated levels, cut down hordes of enemies, collect better gear, and work your way toward a fight with the main villain, the Arch-Illager, a small forgotten creature who found an artifact and turned it into a tool of revenge against a world that cast him aside. The story is told through comic-style cutscenes with a narrator and fits into just a few hours.

The game is deliberately simple to control: one attack button, a bow, three artifact ability slots, and no classic classes. Your role is determined by your gear, so within one mission you might become a fast archer and in the next a heavily armored hammer-wielder. Items can be upgraded with enchantment points, and the best pieces have unique properties, which drives the collecting loop. Difficulty levels escalate and unlock better loot, so missions are worth replaying. Four-player co-op works both online and on a single screen, and that's exactly what made Dungeons a beloved family title. Beyond the main campaign, paid expansions were released over time, adding new settings from deserts to the underworld along with more item sets.

Technically it's a game designed to run everywhere — smoothly and without issues on Xbox One, with pleasant lighting and effects that surprisingly suit the blocky world. The music continues Minecraft's calm, ambient tradition, supplemented with more forceful battle themes. Reviews were kind, with reservations about lesser depth compared to genre classics and repetitive content, but praise for its accessibility. Today, Dungeons is an ideal entry point into the genre for younger players and for couch co-op sessions. The controls are tailored even for the youngest players — you can't fall into lava, and death only means losing part of your collected emeralds, so the game never truly punishes you.

xbox-one__rise-of-tomb-raider.article:
**Rise of the Tomb Raider** arrived on Xbox One as a timed exclusive and was the console's biggest trump card at the end of 2015. Lara Croft continues in her father's footsteps, searching for a lost city somewhere in the Siberian wilderness, with the Trinity organization on her heels. Compared to the series reboot, the game is considerably more open — instead of corridors you get sprawling areas worth exploring for supplies, skills, and above all optional tombs full of puzzles. The previous entry made Lara a vulnerable beginner; here she's already an experienced adventurer.

The tombs are the best thing the game offers: each is a self-contained mechanical puzzle about water, wind, fire, or pulleys, solved spatially and rewarded with a new skill. The main content remains a mix of climbing, stealth, and shootouts. Lara can be played quietly — a bow, poisoned arrows, and luring away guards work surprisingly well — or loudly, with crafted explosives. Crafting happens on the fly, so combat is never interrupted by menu digging, and the skill system allows specialization in hunting, combat, or surviving the cold. Alongside the campaign, the game offers an expeditions mode where modified sections are replayed with card-based modifiers, a popular way at the time to extend playtime.

The Siberian landscape is one of the visually most striking environments of its era — snow reacts to movement, ice caves are lit with care, and the shift from a blizzard into a heated Soviet base has real punch. The music works with choral motifs, lending the expedition a mystical edge. Reception was very good, the game was praised for its pacing and especially for the tombs, with reservations aimed at the story and somewhat cardboard villains. Today it still holds up wonderfully, and many consider it the most balanced entry in the modern trilogy — action-packed enough, but still genuinely about discovery. On Xbox One the game was first released in its base form and later in an expanded edition that added extra content, including a chapter set at the Croft family estate.

xbox-one__tell-me-why.article:
**Tell Me Why** is a story-driven adventure about twins Tyler and Alyson Ronan, who return to their family home in the Alaskan town of Delos Crossing after ten years apart. They're there to sell the house and close the book on the past — but their memories of the night their mother died differ from one another. The game is split into three episodes, and its core mechanic is exactly this negotiation over memory: the siblings can replay scenes from childhood, and the player must choose which version to believe. The choice isn't just for dramatic effect — it gradually changes the twins' relationship and how they perceive their family. Neither version is ever marked as the one and only truth.

Beyond the memories, the game also works with a book of fairy tales their mother wrote — the individual stories function both as keys to puzzles and as a picture of how a child processes things it doesn't understand. The pace is calm, with a lot of walking, listening, and talking; there's practically no action to speak of. The title also drew attention because Tyler is a transgender man, and the game portrays him as an ordinary character with his own life, not as a topic for debate. The game was released episode by episode, and each one takes roughly three hours to complete, so the whole doesn't exceed the length of a single movie marathon.

The Alaskan setting is rendered with great care — snowy forests, a small harbor, wooden houses, and winter light that lends everything a melancholic quality. The sound design features a subdued, mostly acoustic soundtrack that keeps the game in the register of an intimate drama. Reviews were favorable, praising the sensitivity of the storytelling and the atmosphere, with reservations about the weaker detective core and the limited scope of actual decision-making. Today, Tell Me Why is a quiet but powerful experience for one long afternoon, one that feels unusually personal within a major publisher's catalog. Consultants from an organization focused on transgender rights collaborated on the development, and the creators made no secret of it.

xbox-one__battletoads.article:
**Battletoads** returned in 2020 after a long hiatus, in a form nobody quite expected — a cartoonish, visually exaggerated brawler with a heavy dose of humor at the expense of its own past. Rash, Zitz, and Pimple wake up after years spent in a simulation and discover that nobody has cared about them for a long time. From that grows a story about chasing lost glory, one that pokes fun both at nostalgia and at how much games have changed over the years. The trio then tries to make their way back into a world that has since been taken over by someone else entirely.

At its core is a three-player co-op beat 'em up that tries to have a deeper combat system than is typical: each toad has a different reach, tempo, and set of attacks, enemies have color-coded defenses that require the right type of attack, and deflecting projectiles is a given. Between brawls, the game keeps breaking into other genres — puzzles, arcade sections, a hoverbike ride that's a tribute to the notoriously infamous level from the original, and utterly absurd minigames. This constant switching is both the game's main asset and its biggest weakness, since not all the interludes are equally well made. Difficulty can be adjusted, and the game even offers a mode in which you can practically not lose, which, given the franchise's reputation, is almost ironic.

The visuals are entirely hand-drawn and animated in the spirit of modern TV cartoons, which makes the game a great spectacle and also contrasts noticeably with the original's rougher style. The music is energetic, and scenes are full of voiced humor. Reception was mixed — the game was criticized for inconsistency and reduced difficulty compared to the legendarily brutal original, while its look and co-op were praised. Today it's an enjoyable short game for one evening with three players, and also an interesting attempt at reviving a brand that survived mostly on its reputation. The game was also released straight into a subscription service, so it reached far more people than would be typical for reviving such an old brand.

xbox-one__as-dusk-falls.article:
**As Dusk Falls** is an interactive drama following two families bound together by a single unfortunate night at an Arizona motel in the late nineties. One thread belongs to Vince, a man who has just lost his job and is moving his family across the country; the other to Jay, the youngest of three brothers who decide to pull off a robbery that immediately goes wrong. The hostage situation at the motel grows into a story spanning decades, and the player makes decisions for both sides, gradually coming to understand the motivations of people standing against one another. The two threads keep intertwining throughout, and what you do for one side lands on the other.

The game doesn't work with classic gameplay — it's a sequence of decisions, quick reactions, and exploration of static scenes. Decisions converge into a branching tree you can view at any time, seeing which paths you took and how many remain unexplored. Playing together is essential: up to eight people can join in using their phone as a controller and vote on the next step, which makes the game a surprisingly good social experience even for people who otherwise don't play games at all. Mastering quick reactions isn't a requirement for progress, either — failure just pushes the scene in a different direction, so the story never gets stuck.

Visually it's an unusual hybrid — actors were filmed and their performances converted into stylized, seemingly painted images, between which movement plays out in soft transitions. At first it feels unusual, but after a few minutes the style works and lets the game maintain a high quality of expression even on older hardware, including Xbox One. The music is restrained, with American guitar-driven motifs. Reviews were favorable and praised mainly the script and the acting performances. Today it's an ideal title for a shared evening where, instead of playing, you mostly discuss what to do next. The whole is split into two books of several chapters each, and one complete playthrough takes roughly six to eight hours.

xbox-one__ashen.article:
**Ashen** is an action RPG set in a world without a sun, where the only light comes from a giant creature whose awakening means both hope and ruin for the land. Playing as a wanderer, you try to found a settlement, bring craftsmen into it, and gradually turn the ruins into a place worth coming back to. Building the community is exactly what sets the game apart from its otherwise obvious inspirations — every rescued character brings a new function to the village, whether upgrading weapons, cooking, or crafting protective items, and the village visibly changes before your eyes. The world is also one connected whole with no loading screens.

Combat-wise, it belongs to the so-called soulslike school: it depends on stamina, dodge timing, and reading the enemy, death means losing collected currency and having to return for it. The system is somewhat more forgiving than its models, though, and above all you're never truly alone — another character continuously accompanies you through the world, either controlled by artificial intelligence or, without warning, taken over by another player joining in their place. This quiet, understated cooperative connection was, at the time of release, one of the most interesting ideas the genre had brought forth. Weapons are divided into fast one-handed weapons, heavy two-handed weapons, and spear-and-shield combos, and each category changes the pace of combat enough that the game plays differently after a gear swap.

Visually the game leans on stylization with plain, smooth faces and strong use of light and shadow, which let it look striking even on a small budget. Ashen landscapes, underground passages, and glowing horizons form a bleak yet beautiful atmosphere, underscored by restrained music. Reception was good, with praise for the atmosphere and the co-op idea, while reservations targeted the technical state at launch and occasionally confusing navigation. Today, Ashen is a recommendation for anyone wanting a soulslike in a more intimate and less exhausting package. In the end, the settlement also serves as a measure of progress — the further you get, the more it lights up, talks, and works.

xbox-one__batman-arkham-knight.article:
**Batman: Arkham Knight** concluded Rocksteady's trilogy and was the first entry in the series built exclusively for the Xbox One generation. Gotham has been evacuated, Scarecrow is threatening the city with toxin, and a mysterious Arkham Knight enters the fray, someone who knows Batman's methods uncomfortably well. For the first time, the entire city is available in one seamless piece, with no loading between districts, and players traverse it by gliding, grapple hook, and above all the Batmobile. It isn't just a vehicle but also a combat machine, a puzzle tool, and a component of almost every major mission, so the driving and on-foot sections constantly intertwine.

Combat builds on the proven freeflow system, where the rhythm of strikes, counters, and dodges becomes an almost musical affair. New additions include combined takedowns with allies, smarter enemies with different armor types, and expanded predator rooms where Batman hangs from gargoyles and picks off armed guards one by one. Side plots with the Riddler, Two-Face, or Firefly offer dozens of extra hours of content, and the puzzles rank among the toughest in the series. The heavy presence of tank battles against drones sparked debate, as some players found them too frequent and repetitive, even though they gradually grow more complex with new enemy types.

Technically, this was a very convincing showcase on console: rainy streets mirror neon signs, and particles, smoke, and volumetric lighting give Gotham a dense noir atmosphere. The music works with dark string sections and helps build the feeling that the city is collapsing and that this time things might not turn out well. While the PC version launched with a reputation for significant technical problems, the console release was received very well and reviews were high. Today, Arkham Knight remains one of the best-looking and smoothest superhero games ever made, and its take on Gotham has inspired the entire genre. Anyone who finished the previous entries gets a dignified, grim send-off here.

xbox-one__middle-earth-shadow-of-mordor.article:
**Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor** was one of the first titles to show what the new console generation, including Xbox One, could actually do extra. The player controls the ranger Talion, whose family falls at the hands of Sauron's servants and who, instead of dying, awakens bound to the spirit of an elven smith. That pair shares one body and one vengeance and sets out into Mordor to unravel the orc army from within. The narrative borrows names and motifs from Tolkien's world but takes its own, harsher path and doesn't try to be a reverent adaptation.

The real star is the Nemesis system. Every orc captain has a name, a rank, strengths and weaknesses, and their own memory. When they kill the player, they get promoted, gain scars, and mock him at their next encounter. When they survive fire, they start to fear it. Talion can kill the captains or use the wraith's abilities to dominate them, pit them against each other in an arena, and gradually build his own puppet army. Combat draws on the freeflow school of the Arkham games, supplemented with slow-motion archery and stealthy movement across rooftops and ruins. Gradually unlocked abilities turn the vulnerable ranger into the terror of the entire region, capable of turning an entire garrison against its commander during a single fortress assault.

Technically, this was a smoothly running game with large open areas, crowds of enemies on screen, and solid draw distance; visually it sticks to Mordor's grey-brown palette, which some criticized as monotonous. The music leans on drums and low strings, and when dozens of orcs pile onto the player, it works exactly as it should. Reception was strongly positive, and the Nemesis system collected innovation awards; its influence can be seen in many later games that attempted similarly personalized enemies. Today, Shadow of Mordor remains an example of how a single well-conceived system can overshadow a conventional story and the repetitive clearing of forward camps.

xbox-one__dragon-age-inquisition.article:
**Dragon Age: Inquisition** was a huge bet for BioWare: after a chamber-scale second entry marked by rushed development came a sprawling fantasy RPG built on the Frostbite engine and designed primarily for the new consoles, including Xbox One. A massive rift into the demon realm tears open the world of Thedas, the hero survives the catastrophe as the sole survivor, and with a strange mark on their hand becomes the face of the newly forming Inquisition. From there, the story branches into political drama, dealing with faith, the power of the nobility, and the question of whether the organization the player is building isn't itself dangerous. Decisions are made at the judgment table as well as on the battlefield, and they have visible consequences.

The game moves between sprawling regions, from swamps through deserts to snowy mountains, each with its own quests, camps, and fortresses to conquer. Combat can be played directly in real-time action, or via a tactical top-down view where time stops and the player issues orders to the whole party. A key innovation is the war table, where advisors and passing time are used to resolve diplomatic, espionage, and military operations off-screen. A strong point remains the companions and their personal storylines, romances, and bickering by the campfire, which give the Inquisition a human dimension and often reveal more than the main plot.

On Xbox One, this was a visually generous game with beautiful lighting, vegetation, and lacquered armor, albeit at the cost of occasional framerate dips in the busiest battles and longer loading times between areas. The music works with choir and chamber motifs, and the tavern songs became a beloved part of the series. Contemporary reception was very good, and the game won several major game-of-the-year awards, though some players criticized the excessive amount of collectible busywork in the open zones. Today, Inquisition reads as a transitional title between the classic BioWare RPG and the modern open world: whoever accepts its pace and focuses on the main story and companions gets one of the most expansive fantasy adventures of its generation.

xbox-one__final-fantasy-xv.article:
**Final Fantasy XV** had one of the longest and most closely watched development journeys in the genre's history, and on Xbox One it finally arrived as the main series' first truly open-world adventure. Prince Noctis sets out with three friends on a journey to his wedding, but in the meantime the empire of Niflheim occupies his homeland, and the wedding trip turns into a quest to reclaim the kingdom. The narrative is uneven, and some twists assume familiarity with the accompanying film and animated episodes, but the friendship of the foursome holds the whole experience together and gives it an unexpected melancholy.

The player drives across a sprawling landscape in the car Regalia, camps under the stars, fishes, hunts, and takes photographs, and the gathered ingredients are cooked into meals granting temporary bonuses. Combat takes place in real time and is built around holding down the attack and guard buttons, warp-strike (teleporting to a target or a high point), and cooperating with companions on combined attacks. Spells are crafted from elemental sources scattered across the terrain and also have consequences for your own team, so they must be aimed with care. Side activities, monster hunts, and giant dungeons last for dozens of hours beyond the main story, and some of them rank among the toughest content the series has offered.

On Xbox One, the game earned admiration for its magnificent visual style, elaborate lighting, and the scale of some bosses, who literally exceed the horizon; in towns and busy battles, though, the framerate sometimes wavered. The music was composed by Yoko Shimomura and ranks among the game's strongest points, as does the option to listen to tracks from earlier entries in the series while driving. Reception was positive with reservations about the story structure, which developers subsequently expanded through updates and episodes devoted to individual characters. Today, Final Fantasy XV feels like an imperfect but unforgettable road trip, whose best moments are the quiet ones: four friends by the fire when something big rustles in the forest.

xbox-one__divinity-original-sin-2-defini.article:
**Divinity: Original Sin 2 - Definitive Edition** brought to Xbox One one of the most ambitious classic RPGs of the past decade, in a reworked form with rebuilt combat, adjusted storytelling, and controls designed specifically for a gamepad. The player begins as a Sourcerer, a user of forbidden magic, whom the Order of Magisters transports to a prison colony, and from there unfolds a story about gods, immortality, and who has the right to decide for the entire world of Rivellon. The character can be created from scratch or chosen from among origin characters with a ready-made past and their own agenda, which fundamentally changes the dialogue and the reactions of those around you.

Combat is turn-based, built on action points and, above all, on environmental interaction. Oil can be set alight, water electrified, smoke used to block a shot, poison detonated. Every encounter is thus a small physics exercise, in which a creative solution often beats brute force. Freedom outside combat is unusually strong as well: most quests can be completed in several ways, important characters can be killed, robbed, persuaded, or bypassed entirely, and the game accepts this without complaint. The whole story is also playable in co-op with up to four players, who need not share the same goals and can cross each other's plans, which turns a single campaign into a different story every time.

The console version deserves praise for its interface: radial menus, a clear inventory system, and split-screen support for co-op play make sense even without a mouse. The price paid is longer loading times and occasional framerate drops in the biggest battles. Visually it's a colorful, detailed isometric world, the music works with violins and ethnic motifs, and each race has its own version of the main theme. Reception was extremely positive, and the game quickly took its place among modern classics of the genre; Larian later built their subsequent, even bigger project on its foundations. Today it remains one of the deepest and most generous RPGs playable on a console.

xbox-one__kingdom-come-deliverance.article:
**Kingdom Come: Deliverance** is a realistic medieval RPG without dragons or magic, set in Bohemia in the year 1403, during the conflict between Wenceslaus IV and Sigismund of Luxembourg. The player takes on the role of Henry, a blacksmith's son who, after his home village of Skalitz is burned down, has no training, money, or social standing, and must learn everything from scratch. This is also the main driving principle of the whole game: at the start you can't properly read, hold a sword, or speak with nobility, and each of these skills improves solely through use. Progress thus feels like genuine growing up, not like collecting points.

The combat system works with five directions of attack, with blocks, feints, and the weight of armor, so a clash with a trained knight is at first almost a certain defeat. The rest of the world is just as honest: characters have daily schedules, armor gets dirty and damaged, food spoils, stolen goods can only be sold to fences, and sleep and hunger have real effects. Quests often offer an investigative approach with interrogations, tailing, and the option to reach the goal through diplomacy, alcohol, or quietly at night. Saving is limited and forces the player to bear the consequences of their own decisions, which part of the audience loved and part condemned as needless harshness.

On Xbox One, this was a technically demanding title built on CryEngine; the Posázaví landscape, forests, and towns like Rataje or Sázava feel remarkably believable, though the game suffered at launch from long loading times and bugs that developers addressed with a series of updates. The music draws on period motifs and orchestra, and together with the Czech voice acting creates an atmosphere unlike any other game offers. Contemporary reception was mixed in the details but very welcoming overall, and it was a major commercial success that opened the door to a sequel for the Czech studio. Today, Kingdom Come remains the most convincing playable reconstruction of medieval everyday life you can find on a console.

xbox-one__outer-worlds.article:
**The Outer Worlds** is a satirical sci-fi RPG in which the player wakes from hibernation aboard a lost colonization ship and finds themselves in the Halcyon system, entirely in the hands of corporations. Their advertising language, absurd employment contracts, and perfectly calm announcements that an employee is also company property make up the game's humor. Obsidian continues its tradition of RPGs with consequences here: practically every major conflict can be resolved in several ways, and the main factions can be supported, betrayed, or wiped out without the game punishing the player for taking an unexpected path.

Gameplay combines first-person shooting with an extensive skill system that affects not just combat but especially dialogue and the possibilities of trading, persuasion, lying, or intimidation. Special attention deserves the flaw mechanic: when the player is repeatedly hurt by a specific danger, the game offers them a permanent drawback in exchange for a skill point. Also available is time slowdown while aiming, along with a party of companions with their own quests and combat abilities that can be unleashed on the enemy at the right moment. The world isn't one big continent but several smaller, dense locations connected by your own ship, so travel happens across planets as well as orbital stations.

On Xbox One, the game runs without major issues and relies on a distinctive art style with venomously colorful vegetation and retro-futuristic equipment design that conceals a technologically more modest foundation. The music is understated but underscores the colonial kitsch of the advertising announcements well. Reception was very good, with a shorter length compared to big open-world RPGs and a lesser degree of adventurous exploration being frequent criticisms. But that tightness is a strength today: the game respects the player's time, has a high density of well-written dialogue, and can be completed several times with a completely different approach and ending.

xbox-one__star-wars-jedi-fallen-order.article:
**Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order** brought back to the Star Wars brand a big single-player story game, and it did so surprisingly confidently. The player takes on the role of Cal Kestis, one of the few padawans who survived Order 66, and together with the crew of the ship Mantis and the droid BD-1, searches for a holocron containing a list of children sensitive to the Force. Opposing him are the Inquisitors, dark Force users trained to hunt down surviving Jedi, and above all his own trauma from the moment the Order collapsed. The narrative is serious but doesn't forget the adventurous tone that belongs to this brand.

The game's structure blends two influences. Exploring planets like Zeffo, Kashyyyk, or Dathomir works in metroidvania style: sprawling interconnected maps, shortcuts, and new abilities that let the player reach previously inaccessible areas. Combat, on the other hand, draws on the soulslike school of games, where the key is reading enemies, correctly timed blocks, and stamina management; the lightsaber is deadly, but the player is just as vulnerable, and resting at a meditation point respawns enemies. There's also climbing, sliding, and simple physics puzzles using the Force. Collectible extras are purely cosmetic, so the reward for a detour is a lightsaber or poncho appearance, not better stats.

On Xbox One, this was a good-looking game with convincing vistas and carefully crafted design that respects the films' visual tradition; at launch there were glitches with texture pop-in and framerate that later updates alleviated. The music sticks to the series' orchestral language but doesn't try to be a mere imitation of familiar themes. Reception was very good, and the game proved there's demand for a proper single-player Star Wars title. Today it feels like a solid foundation for the later series: smaller and tighter than its sequel, but with a strong pace and several fights players still remember today. It's helped by the fact that it doesn't try to be an open world and treats each planet as a clearly bounded, hand-designed playground full of shortcuts.

xbox-one__control.article:
**Control** is the strangest and yet most self-assured game Remedy Entertainment has made to date. Jesse Faden arrives at the headquarters of the Federal Bureau of Control, a secret agency investigating objects and phenomena that break the laws of physics, and within minutes the search for her missing brother turns into the job of director. The building itself, known as the Oldest House, behaves like a living place: corridors rearrange themselves, rooms lead to places that weren't there before, and the agency has been overrun by an entity called the Hiss, which turns employees into muttering attackers hovering near the ceiling.

Combat combines the Service Weapon, a shapeshifting sidearm that changes form depending on the chosen mode, with telekinesis. The player rips chunks of concrete, office desks and forklifts off the walls and hurls them at enemies; levitation and mind control are added later. The environment is largely destructible, so after any major clash an open-plan office is left in ruins, full of drifting paper. The structure is metroidvania-style: new powers open up further sectors, alongside side quests, cryptic documents, live-action footage and puppet-show training films that flesh out the world and give it its dry bureaucratic humour.

Visually the game rests on brutalist architecture, red light and the tilting of ordinary office spaces into nightmare territory; combined with sound design full of whispers and rhythmic music, it creates an unusually dense atmosphere. The high point is the Ashtray Maze sequence set to music, one of the most frequently mentioned moments of the entire generation. On Xbox One the game occasionally loses smoothness during big fights, but otherwise holds its quality and offers a sharp image. Reception was very good, and the title picked up numerous awards for its art direction and sound design. Today Control stands as proof that even a big budget can accommodate an unusual, almost literary idea, and that a mystery doesn't have to be explained away completely by the end.

xbox-one__dishonored-2.article:
**Dishonored 2** pushes immersive-sim design a generation forward and adds one of the most cleverly built sets of levels in the genre's history. After a coup in Dunwall, the player chooses to play as Empress Emily Kaldwin or her father Corvo Attano, and travels to the southern city of Karnaca, where the threads of the conspiracy converge. Each character has their own set of supernatural powers: Corvo relies on the tried-and-tested Blink and time-stopping, while Emily has a reach that pulls enemies toward her or a power that links several victims to a single fate. The game can also be completed entirely without powers, a recognised challenge for veterans.

Freedom of approach remains the core of the game. Every mission can be played out quietly and without a single casualty, or as an all-out massacre, and the game responds with a chaos system that changes the city's mood, guard behaviour and the ending. The most frequently mentioned level is the Clockwork Mansion, a residence whose rooms mechanically rearrange at the flip of a lever, and the mission A Crack in the Slab, where the player switches between past and present and a single change in time transforms the whole house. Ideas like these raise the bar for mission design well above average and are still referenced today as textbook examples.

Karnaca is visually distinctive: Mediterranean light, dust, windmills and Art Nouveau metal details give the world a shape all its own, different from the gloom of Dunwall. The sound design works with creaking mechanisms and low tones that instantly reveal when the player has been spotted. On Xbox One the game runs decently, though the most open parts of the city occasionally strain the frame rate. Reception was very good, though sales fell short of expectations, often cited as the genre's sad fate as a whole. Today Dishonored 2 is a mandatory stop for anyone who loves games that reward patience, observation and their own ideas over a prescribed path.

xbox-one__prey.article:
**Prey** is a sci-fi immersive sim set aboard the space station Talos I in an alternate history where the space program never let up. Morgan Yu wakes up into a day already lived several times over and quickly discovers the station has been taken over by the Typhon, faceless alien organisms with no comprehensible motive, understood only through what they do. The best known of them, the mimic, can transform into any object, so over time the player starts suspecting every chair and coffee mug in the room, and before entering an office would rather throw a key inside first.

Gameplay is built around free exploration of one large, interconnected station with no artificial division into levels. Every problem has multiple solutions: a door can be opened with a password found in an email, shot open, bypassed through a vent, or a path can be built up a wall with the GLOO cannon. Neuromods grant human and alien abilities, though using them has consequences for the station's defence systems, which start to treat the player as a target. Materials are recycled and printed at fabrication stations, so managing resources matters as much as shooting. Combat is deliberately tense, and a weaker player is often better off running.

Talos I is one of the best-designed game locations of its era: art deco office interiors, laboratories, an arboretum, and a free excursion into the vacuum around the station form a place the player remembers by heart after a few hours and can navigate even without a map. The sound design works with silence and sudden shocks, and the music blends synthesizers with restless motifs. On Xbox One the game holds a solid pace, though loading accompanies transitions between decks. Reception was very good, sales more middling, yet Prey built a strong reputation among genre fans. Today it stands as one of the best-written and most free-form sci-fi games there is, and its ending, which retroactively reframes everything before it, remains one of the most discussed in the genre.

xbox-one__devil-may-cry-5.article:
**Devil May Cry 5** is the classic action series returning in full force, and a showcase of just how well Capcom's RE Engine serves them. The demonic tree Qliphoth has grown through Red Grave City, its roots draining blood from people, with the mysterious Urizen behind it all. Three playable characters take him on in turn: the young hunter Nero with his prosthetic arm, the mysterious and physically weak V, and finally Dante with his full arsenal. The campaign is split into short missions that can be replayed for a better rank, a model typical of the series and still effective today.

Each character plays completely differently, which is the game's greatest strength. Nero uses interchangeable Devil Breakers, single-use prosthetics with special effects, and his style is built around pulling enemies in and sustaining combos. V never fights personally; instead he sends a panther, a bird and a giant golem into battle and only finishes off weakened opponents himself. Dante switches between four combat styles and a whole range of weapons in real time, the most demanding but also the most rewarding way to play. The style rating at the end of every encounter pushes the player toward variety and against repetition, since mashing the same attack over and over stops adding points.

Technically this was one of the smoothest, cleanest action games of the generation: photorealistic characters, detailed effects and the tight control response that matters so much in this genre. The music mixes metal and electronica, with character themes dynamically kicking in when the player holds a high style rating, one of the best-conceived musical ideas in action games. Reception was excellent, and the game brought the series back to the top after a long pause. Today Devil May Cry 5 is a textbook example of the genre: simply accessible on lower difficulties and nearly bottomlessly deep for anyone who decides to truly master the combat system.

xbox-one__nier-automata-become-as-gods-e.article:
**NieR: Automata Become as Gods Edition** brought to Xbox One a cult action RPG that combined PlatinumGames' combat craftsmanship with unusual storytelling and extraordinary music. Humanity has been driven from Earth by alien machines, and androids fight the war in its place. The player takes control of combat unit 2B and her recon companion 9S, who descend to the ravaged planet and gradually discover that the hostile machines are behaving more and more like thinking beings. The game asks questions about consciousness, purpose and death without ever ceasing to be brisk, enjoyable action.

The combat system is fast, fluid and supported by a Pod that fires shots and offers special abilities. What's most striking, though, is the game's willingness to shift genre: the camera cuts without warning to a side view, a top-down view, a classic shoot-'em-up, or a text passage, and everything works as part of a single whole. Upgrading is done through chips slotted into limited memory, so the player trades away interface elements, for instance, in exchange for combat advantages. Crucially, a single playthrough doesn't end the game; further runs offer a different perspective and different abilities, gradually completing the full picture, with an ending that ranks among the most discussed in video games.

On Xbox One the game shipped in an edition containing downloadable content and runs at a solid pace, though visually it leans on atmosphere rather than technical horsepower; abandoned cities overgrown with greenery carry a peculiar melancholic calm. Keiichi Okabe's music is one of the most frequently praised soundtracks of the last decade, and the vocal tracks became a hallmark of the series. Reception was extraordinary, and the game built a strong fanbase far beyond Japan. Today it remains one of the most original big-budget games of its generation, and an example of form itself carrying part of the message.

xbox-one__assassin-s-creed-valhalla.article:
**Assassin's Creed Valhalla** closes out the series' RPG trilogy and moves it into the age of Viking raids on the British Isles. The player takes on the role of Eivor, playable as either a man or a woman, who leaves Norway and founds the settlement of Ravensthorpe in England. From there the story branches out into individual counties, where alliances are forged with Saxon lords, intrigues are resolved, and occasionally the stakes rise to who will rule the whole land. Throughout, the conflict between the Order and the Hidden Ones, the series' long-standing legacy, keeps returning, along with a modern-day storyline outside the Animus.

Compared to earlier entries, classic gear upgrading has been reduced in favour of hunting for unique pieces of armour scattered across the world. Combat is harder, noisier and built around chipping away at stamina, dual-wielding weapons, and finishing moves. New raids on monasteries and settlements let the longship's crew seize supplies needed to grow the player's own village, which gradually expands with a forge, a fishery or a hall for allies. Besides the main storyline, the world offers Viking games, flyting duels, cairns, and dozens of small vignettes that stand in for classic side quests and can be finished within minutes.

England, Norway and the additional regions look lavish on Xbox One: mist over the marshes, deciduous forests and Roman ruins form one of the series' most beautiful landscapes, though older consoles must compromise on draw distance, and the game shipped with more bugs than usual. The music draws on Nordic motifs, and the rowing chants are among the details players remember fondly years later. Reception was good, with reservations about the sheer scale, which can wear a player down. Today Valhalla is a title for players who want dozens of hours of unhurried wandering and don't mind that the assassin roots stay somewhat in the background. Anyone who paces it out county by county, rather than trying to finish it in one go, gets one of the most expansive historical adventures of its generation.

xbox-one__yakuza-0.article:
**Yakuza 0** is a prequel to the entire series and also the best possible entry point for newcomers, which only reached Xbox One in 2020, straight into a subscription service. The story takes place in Japan at the end of the 1980s, during the real-estate bubble, and follows two heroes: young Kazuma Kiryu in Tokyo's Kamurocho, accused of a murder he didn't commit, and Goro Majima in Osaka's Sotenbori, who runs a cabaret club and dreams of returning to the clan. Both storylines revolve around a single empty lot on which enormous sums of money depend.

Combat is arcade-style, punchy, and built on switching between three fighting styles for each character, from quick strikes to heavy swings with a bicycle wheel or a traffic cone. Upgrades are paid for literally in cash, which pours in from every direction in the bubble economy. Alongside the main story, the game offers a huge amount of side content: real-estate management with Kiryu, running a cabaret club with Majima, karaoke, phone dating services, bowling, disco, arcade cabinets with old Sega games, and dozens of bizarre encounters with passers-by that swing between humour and touching endings. That mix of serious gangster drama and outright absurdity is exactly what defines the series.

Technically this is a game originally from the previous generation, which runs on Xbox One without a hitch and leans on density of detail within small but intricately crafted city districts; neon streets in the rain rank among the best the series has offered. The music mixes funk, rock and eighties synth-pop, and shifts into driving guitar action during boss fights. Reception was excellent, and this very entry helped the series break through in the West. Today Yakuza 0 is recommended as an introduction to the whole world of the clans and as an example of a game that can be gravely dramatic one moment and completely off the wall the next. Anyone who gives it a few hours usually ends up hooked on the whole series, and Kamurocho becomes as familiar a place to them as maps from their favourite shooters.

xbox-one__battlefield-4.article:
**Battlefield 4** was among the big shooters that accompanied the Xbox One launch, meant to show what the new generation would do with massive online battles. The single-player campaign follows a squad of American soldiers caught up in a conflict between the United States, Russia and China, and serves mainly as a slick, cinematically staged ride full of scripted disasters. The game's real center of gravity lies elsewhere, though: in the sixty-four-player multiplayer, where infantry, tanks, helicopters and jets meet on huge maps, and where a single well-coordinated squad can turn the whole match around.

The foundation is four classes with different loadouts, a squad system whose members revive each other and share ammunition, and the famous environmental destruction that gradually reduces concrete cover to rubble. DICE added so-called Levolution on top, big scripted twists where a skyscraper collapses or a dam bursts and the map transforms from the ground up. A Commander mode let one player watch the battlefield from above, mark targets and call in support, turning multiplayer into a game even for those who didn't want to pull the trigger. The Xbox One version ran at a lower resolution than full HD, but in exchange kept a brisk pace and doubled the number of players per server compared to the Xbox 360 generation.

The atmosphere rests above all on sound: the booming echo of gunfire between buildings, the whistle of shrapnel and the roar of engines were among the best things shooters of the time had to offer. Reception was initially mixed, as the game suffered from crashes, lost progress and server problems after launch, leading to a long string of fixes and delays to the studio's other projects. Once the technical state settled down, Battlefield 4 earned a reputation as one of the best-tuned online shooters of its time, and the community stuck with it for years. Even today it plays as a textbook example of large-scale team chaos with rules, where teamwork wins out over pure aim.

xbox-one__call-of-duty-black-ops-iii.article:
**Call of Duty: Black Ops III** pushed the series forward to 2065, when soldiers are fitted with cybernetic implants and the battlefield belongs to drones, robots and linked minds. The campaign follows a maimed operative whose life is saved by new technology, which simultaneously starts blurring the line between reality and simulation, so the military action gradually turns into a dark story about who actually owns your own memories. A key novelty was that the entire campaign can be played in co-op by up to four players, which made it a much looser, arena-like experience than previous entries.

Movement gained a new dimension thanks to a jump-jet pack, wall-running and swimming, so fights play out across three dimensions and maps are built around constant repositioning. Multiplayer introduced a system of specialists, heroes with their own ability or unique weapon that can be charged once during a match and used as a trump card. The famous Zombies mode also returns, this time with its own storyline set in a stylized 1930s city, and it ranks among the most elaborate variants of the mode ever made. On Xbox One the game ran smoothly and leaned technically on density of effects, neon colors and readability rather than photorealism.

The music and sound design support a cold cyberpunk edge, the campaign frequently dives into hallucinatory passages, and Zombies instead rides on pulpy B-movie atmosphere with theatrically exaggerated characters. Contemporary reception was mostly positive, praising both the scope of the package and the movement mechanics, with criticism aimed mainly at the confusing campaign story. Its influence on the genre showed in how long character abilities and vertical movement stuck around in the series and among competitors. Today it stands as an interesting document of an era when shooters tried to be action, sci-fi and heroically colorful all at once, and Zombies remains a reason to return. Anyone looking for a campaign for a group of friends will find one of the few big shooters that offers it from start to finish without compromise.

xbox-one__call-of-duty-modern-warfare.article:
**Call of Duty: Modern Warfare** from 2019 is a reboot of the series' most famous branch and a deliberate return to a realistic, raw depiction of modern war. The campaign takes the player through London streets, a fictional Middle Eastern country and special forces operations, repeatedly pausing on civilians caught up in the conflict. Missions often play out at night, with night-vision goggles and an emphasis on verifying the target first, so the pace is slower and tenser than in previous entries.

Mechanically, the novelty rests on the studio's new technology, which brought elaborate weapon physics, the ability to lean a weapon against a corner, careful door-opening and an overall heavier, weightier feel to shooting. The Gunsmith system lets you fit dozens of attachments to every weapon, changing aiming behavior, stability and range, turning customization into a hobby of its own. Multiplayer offered classic modes alongside sprawling battles with dozens of players and cooperative operations, and above all it was the first in the series to open full cross-platform play. On Xbox One the game looks exceptionally good thanks to its work with light and shadow, though the highest effect settings are reserved for stronger hardware.

The atmosphere is carried by subdued, anxious music and sound that literally hurts in confined spaces. Contemporary reception was very strong on the gameplay side, while the narrative sparked debate over how it handles real historical motifs and civilian suffering. The title fundamentally shaped the brand's future direction, since it spawned a follow-up free battle royale that became a phenomenon in its own right. Today the game is worth playing mainly for its campaign and gunplay feel, which rank among the best console shooters offer. Missions built around night vision, silent movement and slowly clearing a house rank among the strongest scenes the series has ever produced and are still often remembered fondly. Thanks to them the game feels more like a tense thriller than the usual military spectacle.

xbox-one__wolfenstein-new-order.article:
**Wolfenstein: The New Order** revived the legendary franchise in an alternate history where Nazi Germany won the war and by the 1960s rules the world with giant robots and concrete monuments. The player returns to the role of B.J. Blazkowicz, who wakes from years of unconsciousness into a world where the resistance survives in sewers and basements, and launches a one-man campaign against the occupation. Surprisingly, the game doesn't rely solely on action, spending plenty of time on quiet scenes in the resistance hideout, where the supporting cast becomes genuine characters.

Combat blends an old-school approach with modern comfort: the hero can carry an entire arsenal, collects health packs and armor, can dual-wield two weapons at once and reloads mid-firefight like in the nineties. Alongside that, the game also offers a stealth approach, where it pays off to find and eliminate the commander before he calls in reinforcements, so many levels can be completed in two very different ways. The structure is linear yet richly packed with secret nooks and collectibles, and one early decision also changes part of the story and available abilities. On Xbox One the game runs smoothly and stands out especially for its art design of retro-futuristic machines and architecture.

The atmosphere is remarkably heavy, the music alternates industrial beats with reworked period pop songs in German, which makes the whole world all the more sinister. Critics and players alike welcomed the return very well, praising above all that a purely action-driven franchise was turned into a game with real storytelling and emotion. The title proved that a single-player shooter without multiplayer can be both commercially and artistically successful. Today it ranks among the best-aging action games of its generation. Credit goes not only to the brisk gameplay but also to the fact that the game never treats its theme as mere scenery for entertainment. Anyone wanting to find out why MachineGames earned such a reputation should start right here, because no other entry in the series balances action and storytelling so well.

xbox-one__wolfenstein-ii-new-colossus.article:
**Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus** moves the resistance against Nazi occupation straight to America and is even more unhinged and darker than its predecessor. Blazkowicz starts the game physically shattered, spending the first hour in a wheelchair, an unusual and paradoxically very effective opening for a shooter. From there the journey winds through flooded New Orleans, a small Roswell town whose residents calmly look the other way, all the way to actions meant to awaken resistance across the whole country, and the game isn't afraid to switch between raw grotesque and honestly painful scenes.

Gameplay is built on dual-wielding weapons, the ability to combine practically any pieces of the arsenal, and a trio of technical upgrades that let the hero squeeze through narrow vents, smash through walls or pull himself up to greater heights. Enemies hit harder and the hero takes fewer hits, pushing the game toward constant movement, stealth takedowns of commanders and improvisation mid-firefight. Alongside the main line, it also offers a set of optional missions where the player returns to already-visited locations to hunt down high-ranking officers. On Xbox One the game keeps its smoothness even during dense firefights and visually stands out with the dirty, raw palette of occupied America.

The soundtrack again mixes industrial motifs with twisted period hits, and the sound design significantly adds weight to the whole world. Reviews praised especially the boldness of the storytelling, the strong supporting cast and how the game can make you laugh in one scene and chill you in the next; criticism targeted the difficulty and the fragmented structure of the second half. The title confirmed that story-driven shooters still have a place in the modern age. Today it stands as one of the most distinctive auteur-driven action games of its generation. Anyone looking for a shooter unafraid of grotesque exaggeration while still having something to say will find it here. Recordings, notes and interviews with the crew below deck of a submarine also generously reward players who take their time and let the story unfold between firefights.

xbox-one__alien-isolation.article:
**Alien: Isolation** is a horror game that, as one of the few, tried to faithfully follow the atmosphere of the original 1979 film, and it succeeded better than anyone expected. The player takes on the role of Amanda Ripley, daughter of the film's main heroine, and heads to a remote space station to investigate her mother's fate. Instead of the expected action, however, a decaying, dark complex awaits, patrolled by a single alien creature that cannot be killed, along with terrified people and glitchy androids with an unpleasantly calm voice.

The entire game rests on hiding, eavesdropping and improvisation. The motion tracker only shows an approximate direction, so the player constantly hesitates over whether to peek out or stay under the desk; the alien also reacts to sound and light and gradually learns from the player's tricks, so the same hiding spot stops working. Scavenged parts can be used to craft smoke bombs, noisemakers or flares that temporarily lure the creature away, but never get rid of it. Saving is done at terminals and takes a moment, turning every trip to a save station into a small drama. On Xbox One the game leans on darkness, smoke and flickering screens with the roughly styled graphics of seventies sci-fi, which makes it look very believable.

Sound is the strongest weapon here: hissing ventilation, distant footsteps and orchestral motifs from the film keep tension high even when absolutely nothing is happening. Contemporary reception was mixed mainly due to length and difficulty, but many quickly labeled it one of the best horror adaptations ever made. Its influence can be seen in many later games featuring a single indestructible pursuer. Today Alien: Isolation is considered a classic that players return to even years later. Anyone who enjoys slow, oppressive horror built on patience will find one of the genre's peaks here; anyone expecting an action-packed slaughter against overwhelming odds will be disappointed. Playtime runs well above the horror-genre norm, and the game genuinely earns it.

xbox-one__outlast.article:
**Outlast** is a pure-blooded horror experience in which the player, as a journalist, infiltrates a remote psychiatric asylum on an anonymous tip and very quickly learns something terrible happened inside. There's no weapon, no help, and the only advantage is a camera with night vision, without which the dark corridors would be completely invisible. The game is thus built on one simple equation: find a way forward, gather batteries, and run when someone spots you before you spot them.

Gameplay rests on running, vaulting over obstacles, squeezing through windows and hiding in closets or under beds. The camera also doubles as a recorder, turning the filming of key scenes into a ritual that forces the player to stay put a few seconds longer than they'd like. Batteries are scarce, so night vision has to be rationed and a lot of the fumbling happens in the dark, keeping the game in a state of constant discomfort. Progression is linear and rather short, yet dense, and the Xbox One version handles chases in tight spaces smoothly, where the picture judders and blurs.

The atmosphere is carried above all by sound. The player's own breathing, distant footsteps, door thuds and buzzing electricity work better than most of what's visible on screen, and the music comes in more as a warning signal than an accompaniment. The game reaches for cheap jump scares more often than necessary, but at its best it can create genuine panic. Contemporary reception was very favorable, and Outlast helped kick off a wave of weapon-free horror games that also grew popular thanks to videos of players reacting to jump scares. Today it feels raw and concise, which is more a strength than a flaw. The game can be finished in one long evening, and that suits it well, since the tension has no time to grow stale or dilute. The follow-up expansion offers a standalone story in a different setting that many players find even more unsettling than the original asylum. On Xbox One it remains one of the most effective horror games you can start up without lengthy preparation.

xbox-one__evil-within.article:
**The Evil Within** is a return to classic third-person survival horror as defined long ago by the earlier Resident Evil games, made under the direction of Shinji Mikami. Detective Sebastian Castellanos goes out to investigate a massacre at a city hospital and soon plunges into a world where the environment reshapes itself before your eyes, corridors lead somewhere different than a moment ago, and reality dissolves into bloody visions. The storytelling is deliberately fragmented and leaves plenty of questions open, something some players held against it and others considered its greatest strength.

Gameplay is deliberately uncomfortable: ammo is scarce, the hero quickly runs out of breath, many enemies are better avoided than killed, and fallen foes must be burned with a match or they'll get back up. A crossbow with special bolts lets you electrify, blind or freeze groups of enemies, turning encounters into small puzzles about using the environment, traps and mines. Character and weapon upgrades are bought with green gel at a safe haven the player regularly returns to. The Xbox One version runs in a persistent cinematic aspect ratio with black bars top and bottom, giving the game a specific edge, though this became a target of criticism.

The atmosphere is dense, grimy and full of unsettling imagery, the music works with silence and sudden bursts, and the main grim motif lingers in the memory for a long time. Contemporary reviews were more mixed than the studio expected, praising the tension and inventiveness while criticism targeted the controls and inconsistency. The title nevertheless helped revive interest in classic survival horror at a time when the genre leaned mainly on action. Today it's appreciated as a tough, distinctive game for patient players. Anyone willing to accept that the title deliberately withholds comfort and certainty gets one of the last great representatives of the classic survival horror school. The boss fights are inventive and force you to look for a weakness instead of burning through supplies, ranking among the very best the game has to offer.

xbox-one__dead-by-daylight.article:
**Dead by Daylight** is an asymmetric online horror game pitting four survivors against a single killer. Survivors play from a third-person view, tasked with repairing scattered generators, opening the exit gate and escaping the foggy arena, while the killer, in first-person view, roams the map, listens for the sounds of work and tries to catch them one by one and hang them on a hook. The whole concept draws on classic slasher films and the game makes that clear from the very first moment, including tense music that swells as the killer draws near.

The charm lies in the constant tension between selfishness and cooperation. Survivors can heal each other and pull each other off hooks, but every attempt costs time and carries risk, so the last surviving player often has to choose between saving a teammate and escaping themselves. Killers differ enough in abilities to genuinely change the game, and players build loadouts of perks that alter repair speed, trail visibility or ability range. The game has gradually absorbed a range of licensed characters from famous horror films, becoming an unusual shared playground for genre icons. On Xbox One it's technically rather modest, but pace and readability are sufficient.

Sound is a core game mechanic, since heartbeats, the moans of the wounded and the terror radius all help estimate the killer's distance. Reception was cautious at first due to technical state and balance, but the game built a massive and very persistent community and still receives new content today. Its success kicked off an entire wave of asymmetric horror games. Today it stands as one of the longest-lived multiplayer titles of its generation. Newcomers don't have it easy at first, since they must learn to recognize the abilities of dozens of killers and their habits, but that's exactly where its long-term appeal lies. The game works best in a group of friends, where desperate escapes and sacrificing yourself for a teammate turn into stories for long evenings.

xbox-one__dying-light.article:
**Dying Light** combines an open world overrun by the infected with parkour that turns rooftop running into the core mechanic. The player lands as an agent in the sealed-off city of Harran, where surviving residents fight over supplies and medicine, and quickly discovers that the assignment is more complicated than it looked. Movement is a joy in itself: the character vaults over ledges, jumps gaps, runs along walls, and bounces off enemies' heads, so fleeing a horde is just as fun as fighting it.

Combat relies on melee weapons that wear down and need repairing or upgrading using found blueprints, so the loadout is constantly changing. The day-night cycle plays a crucial role. By day the infected are slow and the player has the advantage, but after dark fast and extremely dangerous predators appear, chasing their prey across entire districts, and the only salvation is light, shelter, or a desperate sprint. Night runs reward experience generously, creating great tension between caution and greed. The campaign can be played in co-op with up to four players, and a special mode lets another player invade your game as a night creature. On Xbox One the world runs smoothly and expansively, with impressive lighting.

The atmosphere is held together by sound and electronically tinged music that turns into raw, pulsing tension at night. Contemporary reception was very good, praising mainly the movement and the fear of darkness, with criticism aimed at the story and repetitive tasks. The game received long-term support and a large expansion with a vehicle and countryside setting. Today it's considered one of the best zombie action games ever made. The combination of free movement, tangible combat, and genuine fear of the dark has rarely been matched since. Anyone wanting a taste of an open world built around running and climbing will still find a model example here, and playing with friends adds dozens more hours to it.

xbox-one__tom-clancy-s-rainbow-six-siege.article:
**Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Siege** abandoned the traditional campaign and bet everything on a single idea: five attackers versus five defenders in an enclosed building, with no respawns, where a single mistake means the end of the round. Attackers must find and secure the objective, while defenders get time to prepare, barricading doors, reinforcing walls, and placing barbed wire and traps. The result is a game that plays more like chess with a rifle in hand than a classic shooter, since the outcome is often decided by information, not reflexes.

Destruction is key. Most walls, floors, and ceilings can be shot or blown through, so a room can't be defended just by watching the doors, and an attack can come from above, below, or through a wall the defender never suspected. Every operator has unique gadgets, from breaching charges to drones, cameras, shields, and electronics jammers, and their combinations create an enormous range of situations. The reconnaissance drone at the start of the round and cameras scattered across the map make observation a discipline of its own. On Xbox One the game runs smoothly, relying on readable environments and precise sound design that lets you gauge floor and direction of footsteps.

The launch was rocky due to technical issues, harsh difficulty, and limited content, but Ubisoft supported it for years, adding operators, reworking maps, and gradually turning it into one of the most respected competitive titles of its era. Its influence on the genre is huge, proving that a high-skill tactical shooter can work on consoles and sustain a long-term competitive scene. Today Siege is still alive, though it can give newcomers a rough time at first. Learning map layouts, defender habits, and dozens of operators' abilities takes a lot of hours, but the reward is an experience with no equal in the console lineup. Every round is short, tense, and decided by seconds, so even a loss usually carries a clear lesson.

xbox-one__destiny.article:
**Destiny** was Bungie's first major game after leaving the Halo series behind, and it arrived with the ambition of merging a console shooter with a shared online world full of loot. The player takes on the role of a Guardian, a revived warrior protecting the last human city, and travels to Earth, the Moon, Venus, and Mars, encountering missions, public events, and hostile factions with distinct behavior. Along the way they choose between three classes with their own super ability, grenades, and movement style, though the differences become most noticeable later in the game.

The core is a loop of shooting and gear collection. The gunplay was among the best in the entire genre, with every weapon having its own rate of fire, recoil, and personality, and hunting for better pieces can keep players engaged for dozens of hours. Alongside story missions, the game offers cooperative strikes for three players, demanding raids for six coordinated teammates requiring communication and role assignments, and competitive player-versus-player modes. The raids in particular became the highlight of the entire game, and their puzzle-like mechanics are still remembered as some of the best cooperative content of their time. On Xbox One the game ran smoothly and excelled in its depiction of abandoned landscapes.

The music is monumental and melancholic, and together with the art direction it creates the feeling of a vast, silent universe after civilization's fall. Contemporary reception was mixed, since the story felt fragmented and there was less content at launch than players expected, while the gameplay earned praise. Expansions gradually improved the situation, and the game laid the foundations for the entire shared looter-shooter genre. Today Destiny is seen as an important, if imperfect, pioneer. Anyone wanting to play this specific version will especially appreciate the excellent shooting and cooperative raids, which still have few equals. For everyone else, it remains a fascinating record of how console shooters first tried to transform into a long-running live service.

xbox-one__apex-legends.article:
**Apex Legends** appeared with virtually no announcement and became one of the most-played console titles within days. It's a free-to-play battle royale set in the world of the Titanfall series, where sixty players drop onto a map divided into three-person squads, and the last surviving squad wins. It stands apart from the competition mainly because each player picks one of several Legends with their own passive, tactical, and ultimate abilities, turning a purely shooting-based competition into a game about combining roles, mobility, and information.

Respawn brought several solutions to the genre that competitors quickly adopted. The ping system lets players share found gear, enemy direction, or a suggested objective with a single button, making it possible to play effectively even without a microphone. Fallen teammates can also be picked up and revived at special beacons, so death doesn't mean an immediate end of the match for the whole team. Movement is fast, featuring hill slides, climbing, and zipline traversal, drawing directly from Titanfall's legacy. Weapons have tangible feedback and a clearly readable hierarchy of attachments. On Xbox One the game ran smoothly and was tuned more for fluidity than maximum visual effects.

The atmosphere is colorful and comic-book-inspired, carried mainly by a roster of distinctive characters with their own humor and one-liners. Contemporary reception was extremely favorable, with particular praise for voiceless communication and team-based gameplay. The game strongly influenced the entire genre, as target pinging and teammate revival became standard features. Today Apex Legends is still running and ranks among the most playable shooters ever released on Xbox One. Entry is free and the core gameplay isn't stripped down in any way, so the game also works as an ideal gateway into the whole genre. Anyone looking for fast-paced action full of running, sliding, and improvisation, where even a lost match usually has its own point, won't need to look far.

xbox-one__playerunknown-s-battlegrounds.article:
**PlayerUnknown's Battlegrounds** is the title that made the battle royale genre famous worldwide, and it first arrived on Xbox One through the Game Preview program. A hundred players jump from a plane over a vast island, land without a single weapon, and must find everything in abandoned houses, warehouses, and military bases. The playable area then gradually shrinks under a relentless circle that forces survivors into an ever-smaller space, until the final minutes play out as a tense showdown between a few remaining players within a few dozen meters.

The game leans into a more realistic approach than its competitors. Shooting accounts for ballistics and bullet drop, sprinting exhausts the character, the loudness of footsteps gives away position, and getting into a car is a loud decision the whole area notices immediately. A huge part of the tension comes from long minutes where nothing happens at all, and the player just listens, watches the horizon, and guesses where others will move. It can be played solo, in duos, or in squads of four, with team play adding a system for reviving wounded teammates. The Xbox One version long struggled with smoothness and detail pop-in, though gradual updates improved it significantly.

Compared to its more colorful competitors, the atmosphere is stark, almost cold; music is virtually absent, and the main role is played by silence broken by distant gunfire. Contemporary reception was enthusiastic, mainly because of the concept's originality and the unpredictability of matches, with criticism aimed at the technical state. The game's influence is unmistakable, since practically every major shooter of the following years got its own battle royale mode. Today it's a title that plays slower and rougher than its successors. But that patience is its main asset, because a won match carries a weight you won't find elsewhere. Anyone wanting to try where the whole genre began has no other choice, and playing a squad of four with friends remains one of the most tense multiplayer experiences around.

xbox-one__metro-exodus.article:
**Metro Exodus** took the series out of the Moscow metro for the first time and turned it into a journey across a devastated Russia. Artyom and his companions acquire an old locomotive and set out to find a place where life might be possible again, with each stop corresponding to a season and a major setting, from the dried-up Caspian Sea to a forested taiga. The game thus alternates between vast areas where the player chooses the order of objectives themselves, and classically tight, dark sections familiar to fans from earlier entries.
