The fourth entry added a grenadier class capable of indirect fire and a reserve-summoning system usable at certain moments in battle.

On Switch the game runs smoothly, and its art style — where everything looks like pencil and watercolor drawing with heightened outlines — is a huge advantage over more technically demanding titles: it doesn't age and reads well on a small screen. The music is orchestral, with marching motifs and mournful themes, and the scenes between battles get plenty of room to breathe. Reception was good, seen as a return to form after the series' mixed attempts on other platforms. Today it's one of the most distinctive strategy games you can play on a console, and a title that keeps its own shape even years later. The combination of carefully planned tactics and moments where the player aims and goes all in has few equals in the genre, which is exactly why people keep coming back to the series. The campaign runs roughly thirty hours.

switch__divinity-original-sin-2-definiti.article:
**Divinity: Original Sin 2 - Definitive Edition** is one of the most ambitious classic RPGs of the last decade, and its port to Switch was among the platform's biggest technical surprises. The player creates a character, or picks one of the pre-made heroes with their own story and their own secrets, and sets out into the world of Rivellon, where a magic called Source has been outlawed and where one of the heroes is on the verge of becoming a new god. The storytelling is unusually open: almost every problem has multiple solutions, many characters can be killed, persuaded, robbed or bypassed, and the game reacts to this without ever complaining.

Combat is turn-based and rests on the interaction of elements and surfaces. Rain wets enemies and a subsequent bolt of lightning stuns them, oil slows them down and fire turns it into a blaze, frost turns a puddle to ice that's slippery underfoot. On top of this comes a two-layer defense system — physical and magic shields that must be knocked down first before stun or binding effects can land — so battles resemble a logical puzzle with many variables. The whole campaign can be played in co-op with up to four players, and fellow players can have conflicting goals and betray each other along the way.

The Switch version brings the whole Definitive Edition, including the rewritten ending and an interface adapted for controller play. It runs at a lower resolution and loading times are longer, but the gameplay remains untouched, and being able to carry hundreds of hours of content around is a major advantage. The music combines violins, choral singing and folk motifs, and each race has its own variant of the main theme. Reception was outstanding, and the game is often cited as one of the main reasons for the renewed interest in turn-based RPGs. Today it still feels fresh — it demands patience but rewards it with a freedom few other games offer. The first act on Fort Joy island is, moreover, a textbook example of how to teach a player complex rules without a single boring lecture.

switch__ys-viii-lacrimosa-of-dana.article:
**Ys VIII: Lacrimosa of Dana** is the high point of the long-running series about the red-haired adventurer Adol Christin, and at the same time the best place to jump in, since the previous entries aren't needed to understand the story. This time Adol is shipwrecked on the cursed island of Seiren, from which, according to legend, no one has ever sailed away. He gradually gathers other castaways, together they build a village, repair the fence against nightly attacks, and above all explore jungles, caves and ruins full of creatures that should have gone extinct long ago. In parallel, a second thread unfolds about a girl named Dana, who lives in the same places, only in the distant past.

Combat takes place in real time and is unusually fast: the player controls one of three characters in the active party, switches between them on the fly and uses three types of attack — crushing, slashing and piercing — against the corresponding enemy types. The key is dodging and blocking at precisely the right moment, which, when performed perfectly, slows down time or boosts your attack. On top of this comes gathering materials, fishing, village building, and defense battles where waves of enemies attack the camp and the player builds barricades. Exploration is rewarded with a generous number of secret paths, and the game maps them clearly.

On Switch the game runs smoothly, and the speed of the combat system makes it an ideal handheld title, since it reads well even on a small screen. The music by Falcom's in-house sound team is a typical rock storm of guitars and keyboards and ranks among the best soundtracks of its time in the genre. Reception was very good, even though the English localization of the original release on other platforms had to be entirely redone due to criticism; the Switch version already includes the fixed translation. Today it's one of the best action RPGs on console, and a surprisingly moving survival story. Anyone expecting a mindless hack-and-slash will be surprised by how powerfully the game's second half deals with the theme of entire civilizations' collapse.

switch__tales-of-vesperia-definitive-edi.article:
**Tales of Vesperia: Definitive Edition** brings to Switch an entry long considered by Tales series fans to be one of the best, mainly thanks to its protagonist. Yuri Lowell isn't a typical virtuous young man but a former knight who has given up on organized justice and has no problem handling things his own way, including decisions other games wouldn't forgive their hero for. The world of Terca Lumireis rests on a technology called blastia, which protects cities from monsters but also creates a gulf between the wealthy center and the poor lower quarter — and it's exactly this inequality the game draws its main tension from.

Combat takes place in real time in what's called a linear motion battle system: the character moves along an axis toward and away from the enemy, chains basic attacks into skills, and the player controls one character while the rest of the party follows preset strategies. The key is a system of equipment-bound skills gradually learned permanently, and so-called Overlimit modes, in which attacks can be chained without interruption. Definitive Edition adds two playable characters originally available only in the Japanese version, additional missions, costumes and fuller voice acting.

Technically it's an older game from the Xbox 360 era, which shows in the character models, though its anime-style cel-shading ages slowly, and on Switch the game runs smoothly and in nicely sharp image. The music is melodic and at times almost cinematically pathos-laden, with a striking opening theme. Reception of the Definitive Edition was good, mainly because Western players finally got access to the full content. Today it's roughly a fifty-hour adventure of classic cut, one that stands out mainly for its cast of characters — their short side conversations rank among the most entertaining things the Tales series has to offer. For someone just entering the series, it's, along with its clear combat system, the best possible starting point.

switch__trials-of-mana.article:
**Trials of Mana** is a complete three-dimensional remake of Seiken Densetsu 3, which came out in Japan on the Super Famicom in 1995 and only officially reached the West decades later. The foundation remains: at the start the player picks three heroes out of six possible ones — among them a princess, a wolf-girl, a thief or an armored warrior — and this choice determines not only the party's makeup but also which of the three main villains becomes your true antagonist and how the entire story unfolds. Replaying the game therefore opens up completely different chapters, which was an extraordinarily bold design in the 1990s.

Combat has changed from the original's semi-turn-based template into full-blooded action: the player moves freely around the arena, combines weak and strong attacks, dodges bosses' telegraphed attack zones, and charges a gauge for special techniques. But the legendary class-change system remains, where each character switches to a more advanced class twice over the course of the game and the player chooses between a light and a dark path, changing both their skills and their appearance. A new skill grid with passive bonuses was added, along with the ability to switch between party members at any time during battle.

Visually the game goes for a colorful, almost fairy-tale look with big eyes and glowing meadows, which looks charming on Switch, even though the resolution is lower than on other platforms and some players minded the simpler textures. The music is a newly recorded arrangement of the original songs, and you can switch to the original Super Famicom version at any time. Reception was welcoming, with reservations about the simplicity of combat in the first half. Today it's a pleasant, clear and not too long action RPG that also suits younger players. The real value, though, only shows on a second playthrough with a different trio of heroes, when new chapters and a different villain open up — and in that regard the game remains unusual even after thirty years.

switch__disgaea-5-complete.article:
**Disgaea 5 Complete** was one of the first major games to arrive on Switch in its launch year, and for fans of tactical RPGs it was an ideal showcase of what the hybrid console could do. The Disgaea series is famous for pushing the genre to absolute extremes: the story of the demon Killia and his rebellion against an overwhelmingly powerful overlord is told as a parody of heroic epics, full of exaggerated characters, absurd one-liners, and constant self-irony, yet underneath it hides one of the deepest character-building systems ever created.

Battles play out on a grid and look like classic tactics at first glance, except the rules are wild. Characters can pick each other up and throw one another across the entire map, stack into towers and attack together, carry and rotate colored blocks that change the rules of the whole battle, and in the so-called Item World you can literally step inside your own equipment and level it up floor by floor. Damage numbers climb into the millions and beyond, and the game openly assumes that its most demanding content only begins long after the main story is finished — anyone who dives into maximizing characters can lose hundreds of hours here.

The Complete label means the package bundles all the expansions from the original PlayStation 4 release, including additional playable characters, scenarios, and costumes. Technically the game runs without a hitch, the visuals are a simple combination of pixel characters and three-dimensional maps, and it suits portable play down to the ground, since a single battle can be finished in a few minutes. The music is energetic and over the top, just like the rest of the game. Reception was good, and the title was frequently recommended as one of the first games worth picking up on Switch. Today it remains the best entry point into the series and an endless time sink for anyone who loves crunching numbers. The main story can be finished without digging deep into the systems in roughly thirty hours, but anyone who gets pulled in never quite finishes for good.

switch__sea-of-stars.article:
**Sea of Stars** is a modern tribute to Super Nintendo-era Japanese RPGs that doesn't just copy the look, but also the pacing and mood of games like Chrono Trigger. The player leads a duo of Children of the Solstice — Valere, who wields the power of the moon, and Zale, who commands the power of the sun — who have been training since childhood to fight the creations of an evil alchemist. They're joined by a childhood friend who can cook, and gradually by more companions with pasts of their own. The story starts out as a classic tale of chosen heroes, but surprisingly turns in its second half, raising questions about the price such a destiny demands.

Combat is turn-based and built on two key ideas. The first is timed hits: pressing a button at the exact right moment increases damage dealt or reduces damage taken, so the player stays alert even during the enemy's turns. The second is the lock system — before an enemy unleashes a big attack, elemental symbols appear above it, and the party has a few turns to knock them down with matching attack types, weakening or fully canceling the attack. The result is a turn-based system that plays actively and never slides into mashing a single command. Exploration matters just as much: characters climb ledges, swim, swing on ropes, and the maps are built with real verticality.

Visually it's one of the most beautiful pixel-art games ever made, with dynamic lighting, a day-night cycle, and gorgeous ocean views. It runs completely smoothly on Switch and belongs among the titles that look flawless on the small screen. Alongside the in-house composer, Yasunori Mitsuda, one of the names associated with the genre's classics, contributed to the soundtrack, and it shows in the result. Reception was excellent, and the game earned wide acclaim as proof that a retro format can carry fresh content. Today it's a great and fairly approachable entry point into the genre. The game never punishes players with pointless grinding, sticks to roughly thirty hours, and its pacing is tuned so it never drags.

switch__unicorn-overlord.article:
**Unicorn Overlord** is a sprawling tactics game from Vanillaware that combines a classic fantasy tale of an exiled prince's return with an unusually clever command system. Prince Alain, the sole surviving heir of a toppled kingdom, gradually frees the continent of Fevrith from the grip of an enemy empire, and his army grows to include dozens of named characters with their own motivations. The story is deliberately straightforward and heroic, but it works thanks to the sheer number of people you can befriend — feasts and shared conversations deepen relationships and unlock better cooperation in battle.

The heart of the game is military organization. The player doesn't command individuals, but small squads of a few members each, where it matters who stands in front and who stands behind, how archers, cavalry, and shield-bearers complement each other, and what synergies they share. The actual clash between two squads plays out automatically, but the player sets conditional orders in advance: who to heal and when, who to attack first, whether to save an ability for flying targets. Preparation thus replaces micromanagement, and the result is a game where you build a machine and then watch to see if it works. Meanwhile everything on the map runs in real time with the option to pause, so it also matters where you send your squads and when you let them rest.

Visually it's classic Vanillaware: hand-drawn, richly decorated two-dimensional characters with fluid animation and detailed backgrounds that look like illustrations from a storybook. On Switch the game runs smoothly, and thanks to its pausable pacing it also suits short sessions. The music is broadly orchestral and celebratory. Reception was excellent, with the game praised for both the depth of its systems and the sheer amount of content, which easily exceeds fifty hours. Today it's one of the most remarkable strategy games in recent memory, even for someone who's afraid they don't have a head for tactics — the game handles the details itself and leaves the interesting part to the player.

switch__mario-rabbids-sparks-of-hope.article:
**Mario + Rabbids Sparks of Hope** is the sequel to the surprising crossover between the world of Mario and the Rabbids series with turn-based tactics, and in many ways it's a bolder game than its predecessor. The team of heroes, which alongside Mario, Luigi, and Peach includes their Rabbid counterparts, this time leaves the Mushroom Kingdom and travels by spaceship between several planets, each with its own theme, inhabitants, and pile of side quests. A new threat named Cursa is destroying light itself, and the heroes collect Sparks, small creatures born from the fusion of a Luma and a Rabbid.

The key change from the first game is the abandonment of the square grid. During their turn, characters move freely within a range circle, can dash toward an enemy, knock them down with a slide, bounce off a teammate to gain height, and only then fire — and if they haven't fired yet, they can keep repositioning. Combat gains a fluidity and improvisation that grid-based games usually lack. Sparks function as equipment granting elemental effects or defensive traits, and swapping them between characters is the main source of tactical combinations. Outside of battle, players explore colorful worlds full of puzzles and hidden items.

On Switch the game runs steadily and looks noticeably richer than the first entry, albeit at the cost of occasional frame drops in denser scenes. The humor stays scattered and zany, yet the game also maintains a surprisingly serious tone in its main storyline. The music blends orchestral motifs with playful themes, and the soundtrack features well-known composers tied to the games industry. Reception was good, although commercially the game didn't reach the success of its predecessor. Today it's one of the most approachable tactics games on the platform, one that even someone afraid of the genre can handle. Adjustable difficulty, the option to skip battles, and a generous helping of side content make it an ideal family title that still has plenty to offer an experienced strategist.

switch__monster-hunter-stories-2-wings-o.article:
**Monster Hunter Stories 2: Wings of Ruin** takes the world of the Monster Hunter series and turns it inside out: here the player isn't a hunter, but a Rider, someone who doesn't fight monsters but raises them from eggs and rides them. The story follows the descendant of a legendary Rider who takes in a mysterious egg and, together with a girl named Ena, faces a prophecy of ruin tied to Rathalos dragons. The narrative is noticeably friendlier and more colorful than in the main series, has a clear adventurous throughline, and suits younger players well without feeling childish.

Battles are turn-based and rest on a simple yet surprisingly deep foundation: three attack types — power, technical, and speed — beat each other like rock, paper, and scissors, and the player has to guess what type the monster will choose that round. Guessing correctly triggers an advantage and greater damage. On top of that comes the management of your own monsters, which inherit genes determining elemental affinity and abilities, plus an intricate breeding system inside the so-called Ritual Chamber. Outside of combat, players explore sprawling areas, search for nests full of eggs, and complete hunting quests, with monsters also serving as a means of movement — some swim, others climb walls or fly.

On Switch the game runs reasonably well, even though it isn't a technical showcase for the platform; resolution is lower and loading times occasionally longer, but gameplay doesn't suffer for it, and the monsters are modeled with great care and instantly recognizable. The music picks up the main series' celebratory orchestral tone, and the battle themes are memorable. Reception was good, and the game earned a reputation as a surprisingly substantial title that offers an extensive postgame after completion. Today it's an excellent bridge between the world of Monster Hunter and classic Japanese creature-collecting RPGs. Anyone who's always wanted to saddle up a dragon but was put off by the main series' difficulty will find exactly what they're looking for here — and it'll keep them busy for dozens of hours.

switch__sonic-mania.article:
**Sonic Mania** is a rare case of a game made for a major publisher by people who came up through the fan romhacking scene, and the result ended up outshining most official attempts to bring the blue hedgehog back to his roots. Sega gave the creators free rein, and they built a platformer that picks up exactly where the Mega Drive-era games left off. The player rockets through loops, bounces off springs, collects rings, and searches for hidden paths in multi-layered zones that reward knowledge of the terrain more than fast reflexes. Alongside reworked classic zones like Green Hill or Chemical Plant, the game also offers entirely new settings, including the media-themed metropolis of Studiopolis, and each zone has its own set of ideas, gimmicks, and boss fight.

On Switch the game runs in high resolution and completely stable, with pixel art that's been redrawn from scratch rather than simply scaled up. Portable mode suits it exceptionally well, since individual acts can be cleared in just a few minutes and the game offers an instant restart. Three playable characters are available: Sonic gets a new drop dash, Tails can fly, and Knuckles climbs walls, which fundamentally changes how the same levels play out. Bonus stages chasing after Chaos Emeralds draw on the 3D sequences known from Sonic CD and offer a pleasant change of pace.

Tee Lopes's music combines chiptune sound with funk and jazz motifs and ranks among the best-received soundtracks in the whole series. Critics welcomed the game as the best Sonic in years, and among players it earned a reputation as a title proving that the classic 2D formula never went stale, it was just forgotten. A later expanded version, Sonic Mania Plus, added further characters and an Encore mode with rearranged levels. Today the game plays like a perfectly tuned essence of the genre: short, dense, full of hidden shortcuts, and built for repeat playthroughs. For Switch owners, it's one of the easiest retro experiences to recommend, period.

switch__cuphead.article:
**Cuphead** arrived on Switch in 2019 as one of the first major acquisitions outside its original platforms, and instantly became a flagship example of what the independent scene can achieve in hand-drawn animation. The game builds on the visual language of American cartoon grotesques from the 1930s — rubber-hose animation, grainy film texture, and watercolor backgrounds — with every single frame genuinely drawn by hand. The story of two brothers who lost a bet to the devil and must collect debts from other debtors is just an excuse for a series of boss fights. Those fights are the game's core: every opponent moves through multiple phases, changes shape and attack patterns, and forces the player to memorize the rhythm of the entire encounter.

Mechanically it's a run-and-gun with beautifully tuned controls. The character shoots finger bullets from their hand, can dash-roll out of the way, lock their firing direction, switch between purchased weapons, and parry pink-colored objects to charge a super attack. Alongside the boss fights there are also classic side-scrolling platforming levels and a few aerial sections in the style of vertical shoot-'em-ups. Difficulty is high and uncompromising, yet the game never feels unfair, since death is always the result of a specific mistake, and restarting is instant.

On Switch the game runs smoothly even in portable mode, and the smaller screen doesn't hurt it in the slightest, since the readability of enemy attacks was designed very carefully. The game also includes two-player co-op on a single console, making it a wonderful couch title. The soundtrack, recorded live by a big band with ragtime and jazz, is just as striking as the visuals and helps create the impression that the player is controlling a forgotten animated film. Critics praised its unrivaled craftsmanship above all, and the game became one of the symbols of independent game-making for its decade. Today it still feels fresh, and the later expansion The Delicious Last Course added another set of boss fights along with a new playable character.

switch__shovel-knight-treasure-trove.article:
**Shovel Knight: Treasure Trove** is a combined edition of one of the most influential independent platformers of recent years, and it arrived on Switch practically alongside the console's launch. The base campaign, Shovel of Hope, is built on a very thoughtful tribute to the 8-bit era: an armored hero wielding a shovel makes his way across a world map divided into individual levels, knocks down enemies with a shovel-point-down jump, and in each level searches for treasure, secret rooms, and relics with their own abilities. Controls are precise, and the game prides itself on every death being a readable mistake, while checkpoints can be voluntarily broken in exchange for treasure — an elegant way to set your own difficulty.

The package's strength lies in the fact that it doesn't stop at a single campaign. Plague of Shadows is built around an alchemist with explosive potions and a different kind of movement, Specter of Torment offers a darker story and much snappier acrobatics with wall-climbing and airborne enemy attacks, and King of Cards adds another campaign along with a card-based minigame. Each variant uses the same levels differently, so returning to familiar places never feels like recycling, but rather like a fresh perspective on the same game.

Technically, this is a title that suits Switch well. The pixel art draws on the limitations of period consoles, but works with smooth scrolling, widescreen visuals, and effects the hardware of the time couldn't have handled. Jake Kaufman's chiptune music ranks among the most memorable soundtracks of the indie scene and manages to swing between marching heroism and melancholy. The game grew out of a successful Kickstarter campaign and became a textbook example of how to deliver on promises to backers, since every promised expansion was delivered for free. Today Treasure Trove remains one of the best entry points into the genre for newcomers and veterans alike, and on Switch it works perfectly as a game for short returns.

switch__undertale.article:
**Undertale** arrived on Switch in 2018, bringing to the console a game that had already built a reputation as a cult phenomenon in the meantime. It looks like a modest pixel-art RPG about a child who falls into an underground world inhabited by monsters, but it actually dismantles the very foundations of the genre. Battles combine a classic turn-based menu with dexterity: when it's the opponent's turn, the player controls a small heart within a bounded field and dodges patterns of projectiles like in a bullet hell shooter. Every enemy also has, alongside its attack, an alternative way to end the encounter peacefully, whether through conversation, dancing, complimenting, or simply fleeing.

This very choice forms the core of the entire game. Undertale remembers how the player behaved, and depending on the level of violence, changes the dialogue, the characters' fates, and the endings. There is a playthrough where no one dies, as well as a considerably darker variant that the game itself comments on with displeasure. This creates an unusual sense of responsibility, because the death of a side character here is not routine game economy but a permanent decision. The humor and dialogue writing are exceptionally distinctive, alternating absurd jokes with moments of genuine melancholy, and the game is not afraid of the fourth wall.

Technically it's an undemanding title, well suited to the Switch's portable mode, since it's a game for one longer sitting or a few evenings. The graphics are deliberately spare, but the soundtrack, written by the author himself, is all the more striking and has become one of the most cited in independent game-making. The melodies return throughout the game in transformed arrangements, functioning as the story's emotional memory. Critics embraced the game enthusiastically upon its original release, and since then it has influenced an entire wave of games built on choice, metanarrative, and compassion instead of accumulating experience points. Today Undertale still feels surprising, especially for a player who can keep their expectations unspoiled.

switch__ori-and-blind-forest-definitive-.article:
**Ori and the Blind Forest: Definitive Edition** is one of the most notable arrivals of an earlier exclusive title on Switch, and technically it's a surprisingly clean conversion. The game tells the story of a small being of light trying to save a dying forest, and it does so with almost no spoken word, relying instead on imagery, narration, and music. Visually it's a hand-painted environment with several layers of parallax, luminous mists, and soft particle effects that, even years later, rank among the most beautiful in the genre, and on the Switch's small screen they may stand out even more than on a television.

The gameplay is built on a classic metroidvania structure. The interconnected world gradually opens up new abilities, from a double jump through wall-climbing to the bash, a rebound off enemy projectiles and fireflies that serves both for movement and for deflecting attacks. It's the bash that turns the game into an acrobatic exercise, where the player quite literally flies between dangers. Combat is present, but the core of the difficulty lies in movement and precision, culminating in the famous escape sequences where water or lava surges after the player and a single mistake means starting over. The game also uses a manual save system powered by energy, so the player decides for themselves when to secure a return point.

Compared to the original release, the Definitive Edition adds further areas, abilities, and a choice of difficulty, making the whole more accessible even to less patient players. Gareth Coker's orchestral soundtrack is an integral part of the experience, sustaining tension and emotion in places where other games would reach for dialogue. Critics especially praised the combination of audiovisual craft with precise controls, and the game became proof that a metroidvania can also be an intimate emotional narrative. Today it stands as a modern classic of the genre, and on Switch it's one of the best ways to experience it.

switch__messenger.article:
**The Messenger** starts out as a straightforward tribute to eight-bit ninja platformers in the style of Ninja Gaiden, but after a few hours it pulls off a twist that made it one of the most talked-about independent titles of its time. The player first moves through linear levels, slashing with a sword, climbing walls, and using the magical cloudstep, a second jump in mid-air that resets every time the blade strikes an enemy, a lantern, or a projectile. This single mechanic turns progression into a swift chain of jumps, where a skilled player practically never touches the ground, and it's the main reason the game controls so well.

Halfway through, however, the structure opens up, and the linear platformer becomes an interconnected world in the spirit of metroidvania, where the player returns to earlier levels to find paths that were previously impassable. At the same time, the game switches between an eight-bit and a sixteen-bit visual layer, and this change is not merely cosmetic, since the terrain looks different in each era and some passages exist only in one of them. The switching happens seamlessly in real time and is one of the most imaginative ideas the genre has received in recent years.

On Switch the game runs without issues, the controls are responsive, and the short stretches between checkpoints suit it well in portable mode. The writing is strongly comedic, largely thanks to a talkative merchant who comments on the player's progress, though it occasionally slips into longer monologues. The music employs chiptune sound in two versions matching both graphical eras, switching along with the visuals, a detail that shows just how much care went into the game. Critics especially praised the boldness of changing its own genre mid-playthrough, and the game earned a strong reputation among players who grew up on NES platformers. Today it remains one of the best-playing titles of its kind, able to both entertain and surprise.

switch__katana-zero.article:
**Katana ZERO** is a short, brutal, and remarkably stylish action game in which the player controls a katana-wielding hitman in a neon-lit metropolis reminiscent of eighties film noir. The basic rule is merciless: one hit means death, for enemies and the player alike. Every room is therefore a short puzzle about the correct sequence of moves, requiring the player to deflect a bullet back at the shooter, dodge-roll, throw an object as a distraction, and only then strike. Death carries no punishment beyond an instant restart, so playing becomes a rhythmic loop of attempts until the whole room can be cleared in one fluid pass.

The game cleverly wraps this mechanic into its narrative. The protagonist replays the future in his head in advance, so a failed attempt is, within the story, merely imagined, and a successful run is replayed at the end of the mission as a continuous, uninterrupted film clip. Added to this is a time-slowing ability that can be activated for a limited duration, and a dialogue system in which the player can interrupt their conversation partner, changing the tone and content of scenes. The story of trauma, drug addiction, and manipulation is dark and at times unsettling, making this definitely not a game for the youngest players.

On Switch it's an ideal title for portable mode, since individual missions last only a few minutes and the game runs perfectly smoothly, which is crucial for such reflex-demanding action. The pixel-art graphics rely on a saturated palette, striking lighting, and cinematic cuts, while the soundtrack leans on dark synthwave and drum and bass motifs that precisely match the game's pace. Critics received the game very well, praising above all the combination of hard-edged gameplay with a bold narrative. Today Katana ZERO stands as one of the sharpest representatives of its wave of independent action, and as proof that a short game can be more memorable than much longer competitors.

switch__blasphemous.article:
**Blasphemous** is a dark pixel-art metroidvania that builds its world on baroque religiosity, penitent processions, and the painful iconography of southern Spain. The player takes on the role of the silent Penitent One, wearing a helmet of thorns, who travels through a land struck by a miracle that turns suffering into a grotesque form of holiness. This aesthetic is the main reason the game stands out: the environment is full of statues, altars, bell towers, and deformed bodies, with every enemy and boss looking like a scene torn from a religious painting that has spiraled out of control.

The gameplay combines exploration of an interconnected world with a combat system derived from soulslike games. The character attacks with a sword, can guard and deflect with a precisely timed parry, and gains new moves and abilities that gradually open up previously inaccessible areas. Upgrades come through rosary beads, hearts, and prayers, passive and active items that leave the player fairly free to decide whether to invest in endurance, damage, or spells. Death leaves behind a guilt stain that reduces maximum mana reserves until the player retrieves it, a variation on the familiar lost-souls mechanic. Boss fights are among the most demanding parts and require learning attack patterns.

On Switch the game runs well, and portable mode suits it, since the stretches between prayer pews, which serve as checkpoints, aren't overly long. The detailed pixel-art graphics, with large, hand-animated bosses, remain legible even on a smaller screen, and the audio, featuring flamenco guitar and choral motifs, rounds out the oppressive atmosphere. Critics especially praised the unmistakable visual style and the boldness of building an entire game around a single cultural context, with reservations aimed more at platforming precision. The developers kept improving the game long after release, adding free new content, so today it feels considerably more balanced than at launch.

switch__axiom-verge.article:
**Axiom Verge** is a tribute to the classic Metroid games, created almost entirely by a single person, and that is precisely the source of its almost obsessive coherence. Scientist Trace wakes up after a lab accident in an alien biomechanical world full of decaying machines, speaking entities, and organic structures that appear to be the remnants of an ancient civilization. The game sends him to explore a sprawling interconnected map, where new areas are gated by abilities found along the way, and where careful exploration is rewarded with further weapons and health upgrades.

The most interesting aspect is how the game engages with the theme of a glitch in the system. The key tool is a device that literally corrupts the game's reality: aimed at a wall or an enemy, it starts generating graphical artifacts, alters object behavior, and opens passages that otherwise don't exist. What would be a technical malfunction in other games becomes here a legitimate mechanic and part of the storytelling. The arsenal is also remarkably wide, containing dozens of very different weapons, from spray beams to tools that shoot around corners, and the player is encouraged to switch between them depending on the situation.

On Switch it's an ideal title for both short and longer sessions, since the map is clearly laid out and the game runs entirely smoothly. The visuals deliberately imitate the limited palette of eight-bit consoles, including flickering sprites and rough textures, but they use these with a modern sense of composition and atmosphere. The soundtrack, also written by the author himself, relies on heavy industrial and darkly ambient layers, helping maintain the impression of a foreign, unsettling place. Critics received the game as one of the best modern attempts to capture the feel of the original Metroid without being mere imitation. Today Axiom Verge feels somewhat rougher and less welcoming than newer entries in the genre, but that isolated, oppressive mood is precisely its greatest strength.

switch__steamworld-dig-2.article:
**SteamWorld Dig 2** was among the first notable independent titles to launch on Switch before other platforms, and for many console owners it became one of the first games to show just how well the Switch suits shorter, densely designed experiences. The player takes control of the steam-powered robot Dorothy, who searches for a friend who went missing in the first game, and to that end digs ever deeper beneath a desert town. The core loop is simple and addictive: dig downward, collect ore, return to the surface, sell the haul, upgrade equipment, and push a little further.

The second installment, however, significantly strengthens the platforming and exploration side. The underground is no longer just randomly generated earth but a hand-designed world with clear biomes, hidden chambers, and puzzles built around new abilities. Dorothy gradually gains a grappling hook, jet propulsion, the ability to break through walls, or to change direction mid-air, turning what was once cumbersome digging into surprisingly nimble acrobatics. Alongside the main path, optional chambers with isolated puzzles are scattered throughout, arguably the best part of the game, since each one teaches one specific use of the tools. The upgrade system is open and allows specialization in combat, mining, or mobility.

Technically it's a very polished title that runs smoothly on Switch and stands out in portable mode thanks to clear, hand-drawn graphics in rich colors. The transition from the sunlit surface into the dark depths is supported by lighting and sound that gradually thicken, giving the descent a genuine sense of escalation. The music alternates western motifs with mechanical rhythms, subtly reinforcing the pace of the digging. Critics received the game very positively and considered it a significant improvement over the first installment in every respect. Today it stands as a textbook example of a game that knows exactly how long it should be, never overstays its welcome, and ends right when the player still wants more.

switch__hyper-light-drifter-special-edit.article:
**Hyper Light Drifter: Special Edition** is a top-down action game that tells its entire story without a single word. The player controls a wandering figure suffering from an illness, traveling through the remnants of a civilization destroyed by an ancient catastrophe, searching for a way to reverse their condition. The narrative unfolds through visual sequences, environmental clues, and silent characters who communicate in pictures, so the player must piece together most of the connections themselves. The result is a peculiar blend of melancholy and uncertainty rarely found in the genre.

Combat is fast, precise, and merciless. The character wields an energy sword, a ranged weapon with limited ammunition recharged by melee hits, and, above all, a dash that serves both for movement and for slipping between attacks. Health is scarce, healing is limited, and enemies can kill within a few hits, so every encounter demands full concentration. The world is divided into four main regions that can be visited in any order, each offering a different environment, a different set of enemies, and a demanding boss. Beyond that, the game is riddled with hidden rooms, secret passages, and modules that unlock new moves, none of which is marked by an arrow or a quest log.

The Special Edition for Switch adds a further region, new equipment, and several control adjustments, and the console's hardware suits it well, since the pixel-art graphics with their striking palette of purple, cyan, and crimson look exceptionally good on a smaller screen. Disasterpeace's audio accompaniment relies on dark ambience and low synthetic tones that often weigh down the mood rather than accompany the action, further intensifying the atmosphere of decay. Critics praised the game for its visual style and sense of movement, with reservations aimed at occasionally unclear navigation. Today Hyper Light Drifter is regarded as one of the formative games of its era's independent scene, and its aesthetic has been imitated by numerous later titles.

switch__gris.article:
**GRIS** is a short platformer that builds its entire experience on visuals, music and feeling rather than challenge. The player guides a young girl through a world that has collapsed along with her, moving through a landscape that begins almost colourless and gains a new part of its palette with each new area. The game uses no dialogue, no text and no quest markers, relying entirely on the player understanding where to go and what is happening from the composition of the scene itself. The theme is clearly about coping with loss, yet the game never states this directly and leaves the interpretation open.

The gameplay is deliberately non-confrontational. There is no way to die, no enemies in the usual sense and no time limits; instead the player jumps, climbs, swims and solves undemanding environmental puzzles. Along the way she gains new abilities, such as turning into a heavy stone block that withstands gale winds and breaks through fragile surfaces, or the ability to swim and later move through currents. Each ability opens up a different kind of environment, and the game introduces it, develops it and lets it fade away within a few minutes, so the pacing is always in motion.

The audiovisual presentation is the main reason the game earned so much attention. Hand-painted watercolour visuals combine flat colour fields with delicate animation and sweeping panoramas, where the character is often a tiny speck within an enormous vista. On Switch the game looks great both handheld and on the TV, and the smooth performance reinforces the sense of a painted film. The music by the Catalan group Berlinist, with piano, strings and a female vocal, is timed to the scenes so closely that it often shifts mood at the exact moment of transition between screens. Critics praised the game especially for its aesthetics and its sensitive way of guiding the player, while more critical voices took issue with its low difficulty. Today GRIS is one of the most frequently cited examples of a game experienced as an artistic work, one that can be finished in a single evening and yet stays in memory much longer.

switch__rayman-legends-definitive-editio.article:
**Rayman Legends Definitive Edition** brought to Switch, shortly after the console's launch, one of the best-reviewed 2D platformers of the modern era, and it still ranks among the best the genre has to offer on the console. The game is built on very fluid movement, with the hero running, sliding, gliding on his hair, punching enemies and bouncing off walls, and the levels are designed so that a skilled player can clear most of them without ever stopping. The structure is split into worlds with distinct themes, ranging from fairy-tale groves through medieval castles to underwater and oriental settings.

The standout feature is the musical levels that form the finale of each world. The entire progression, jumps, enemies and environmental movement are precisely synced to the rhythm of a well-known song, turning the platformer into a rhythm game for a few minutes. Alongside the main campaign, the Switch version also includes reworked levels from the previous game, Rayman Origins, daily and weekly challenges, and extensive collecting of small Teensies that unlock further content. Local four-player co-op works excellently and is one of the main reasons to bring the game out for a group evening.

Technically it's a showcase of what the UbiArt Framework engine can do. The visuals look like a moving illustration, with hand-drawn characters, delicate animation and richly decorated backgrounds, all while running perfectly smoothly in both handheld and TV mode. The Switch version also adds touch controls for the Murfy sections and a few small extras, including local races. Critics received the original release extremely warmly, praising above all the amount of content, the variety of ideas and the precision of the controls. Today the game hasn't aged a bit, because its visual style doesn't rely on technical specs, and for Switch owners it's one of the easiest platformers to recommend outright.

switch__hat-in-time.article:
**A Hat in Time** is an independent 3D platformer that openly embraces the legacy of games like Super Mario Sunshine and Banjo-Kazooie, aiming to revive the collect-a-thon adventures of the turn of the millennium. The player controls a small girl with a hat whose spaceship has lost its fuel in the form of scattered hourglasses, forcing her to explore the planet below. Each world is a self-contained chapter with its own tone, ranging from a mafia-run port town through a film studio of rival directors to a haunted forest, and individual goals within the same map vary widely enough that repeated returns never grow stale.

Movement is the core, and the game leans heavily on it. The character jumps, performs a roll into a follow-up leap, uses an umbrella both as a weapon and as a way to grapple onto ropes, and collects hats with different abilities, such as summoning an arrow pointing to the next objective, an explosive, or the ability to slow down time. Badges add further passive upgrades, letting the player build their own personal movement style. Chapters are divided into full-fledged levels and shorter tasks, and the game also offers time trials for those who want to fully master the controls.

On Switch the game arrived later than on other platforms, and handheld mode suits it well, since individual missions typically last around ten to twenty minutes. The visuals go for a soft, cartoonish style with bold colours and exaggerated character expressions, while the music leans on playful orchestral and jazz motifs that shift with each chapter. The project came about thanks to a successful Kickstarter campaign, and critics and players alike praised how it managed to capture the mood of classic platformers without being mere nostalgia. Occasional technical rough edges and an imperfect camera are the main complaints, but overall it's one of the few modern games that truly deliver on this nearly extinct genre.

switch__cave-story.article:
**Cave Story+** is the console incarnation of one of the most important independent games ever made, a project that a single author developed over several years in his spare time and released for free in 2004. The game tells the story of a memoryless robot who wakes up in the caves of a floating island inhabited by the peaceful Mimigas, gradually uncovering why the entire island is in danger. The storytelling is surprisingly elaborate, with side characters the player will remember, and several endings, the best of which requires meeting non-obvious conditions and skipping one seemingly tempting item.

Gameplay-wise it blends platforming with shooting in the spirit of classics like Metroid or Blaster Master. Weapons level up by collecting energy triangles, but getting hit costs the character her progress, which pushes the player to play cleanly. The arsenal is varied, and some weapons change how the character moves, such as a rocket launcher that lets her launch herself upward with her own explosion. The final stretches rank among the harder parts of the game and also offer optional tough levels for those who want to see the game truly through to the end.

The Plus version adds improved graphics, new modes and the option to switch back to the original look and original music, which matters a great deal to longtime fans. On Switch the game runs perfectly smoothly, supports two-player play, and handheld mode suits it well thanks to short stretches between saves. The chiptune soundtrack, which the author also composed himself, ranks among the most memorable in all of independent gaming and can shift within a single hour from a carefree melody to a thoroughly oppressive theme. The game's influence is hard to overstate, since it showed that a single individual could create a title comparable to professional production, opening the way for an entire wave of later independent projects. Today it still plays excellently and belongs on the genre's required reading list.

switch__owlboy.article:
**Owlboy** is a pixel-art platformer about a mute owl boy named Otus, who struggles to hold his own in a world of floating islands while constantly falling short of what those around him expect. The main thing that sets it apart from most games in the genre is movement: Otus can fly almost anytime and without restriction, so the game doesn't take place on platforms but in the air. The environments are shaped accordingly, with caves and temples built vertically, full of shafts, draughts and narrow passages, and the player moves through them more like through open water than across solid ground.

Combat is handled cleverly. Otus himself has essentially no attack of his own; instead he can pick up one of his companions and use their weapon, whether a gunner with a ranged shot or a character able to break through solid surfaces. Switching between companions mid-flight is the basis of both combat and puzzles, since each one opens up different paths. The game constantly combines exploration, simple puzzles and firefights against pirates threatening the islands. The structure is fairly linear and story-driven rather than open, which actually suits it, since it lets the game focus on its narrative.

Visually it's one of the most striking pixel-art games ever made. Development took nearly ten years, and it shows in the sheer number of hand-animated details, the colour gradients of the sky and the large panoramas built from several layers of background. On Switch the game runs without a hitch, and handheld mode really highlights the care put into the scenery. The music works with orchestral and chamber motifs and carries most of the emotional weight in key scenes, since the game barely uses spoken dialogue at all. The story of feeling inadequate and searching for one's own place among others is unexpectedly melancholic, and it ends more powerfully than the setting of floating islands might suggest. Critics received the game warmly, and it's still cited today as an example of just how far pixel art can be pushed.

switch__crash-team-racing-nitro-fueled.article:
**Crash Team Racing Nitro-Fueled** is a complete rebuild of the kart-racing classic from the late nineties, prepared for modern consoles by Beenox. The core remains untouched: tracks full of shortcuts, beach curves, volcanic caves and futuristic highways, raced by characters from Crash the wombat's world. The main draw, though, is a driving model built around chaining boosts. The player charges boost by drifting and must release it with precisely timed hops to keep the acceleration going, and anyone who nails the rhythm can drive an entire lap essentially without ever slowing down. This one mechanic alone makes the game something more than relaxed family fun, splitting players into those who simply enjoy the colourful spectacle and those who hone the ideal racing line as a technical discipline.

There's an unusually large amount of content here. Alongside the tracks from the original, courses from the sequel Crash Nitro Kart were added, and there's a classic story mode with bosses and relic collecting, time trials, battle arenas and online matches. The developers also kept adding further tracks, karts and costumes in seasonal waves for months after release, so the offering grew far beyond the source material. On Switch the game runs at a lower resolution and with more noticeable compromises in detail than on more powerful consoles, but the smoothness of the driving remains intact, and in handheld mode it's one of the best-looking racers of its generation. The preserved local split-screen also makes the console an ideal machine for couch gaming.

The atmosphere is held together by cartoonish visuals with a bold palette and music that plays with the original themes in modern arrangements. Reception was very favourable, with reviewers praising above all the amount of content and the fidelity of the demanding driving model, while criticism was mainly aimed at unpolished online services in the first weeks after launch. Today it's the strongest competitor to Mario Kart on Nintendo's platform, a game that relies not on chaos and luck but on genuine driving skill and knowing the tracks down to the last corner.

switch__team-sonic-racing.article:
**Team Sonic Racing** is an attempt to bring the idea of a team-based game into the kart-racing genre, and it does so quite thoroughly. The player doesn't race alone but as part of a three-member team that shares a combined finishing result. When a teammate is out in front, they leave behind a yellow trail that others can ride to pick up extra speed, while whoever is lagging behind receives items from the team and can, in turn, send their own items forward to whoever needs them more. Filling the team gauge unlocks a shared ultimate manoeuvre that pits the whole trio against their rivals for a few seconds. The result is a racer where it pays to watch the others and share, rather than focusing solely on your own line.

Mechanically it's a classic kart racer with drifting, jump boosts and items built around the Wisps from the main series. Three car types, speed, technique and power, differ in how they handle shortcuts and collisions with obstacles, which forces the player to think when assembling a team. The Team Adventure campaign leads the player through dozens of tasks that, besides regular racing, add slaloms, target-destruction runs or time-limited driving, and unlock parts for kart customisation. The Switch version is the most technically scaled-back of the whole release, with lower resolution and less smoothness than the other consoles, but handheld mode works well, and local four-player split-screen has been kept intact.

The visuals lean on the colourful environments typical of the newer Sonic games, while the music draws on rock and electronic motifs characteristic of the series. Reception was fairly good: reviewers praised the team system as a fresh idea, but criticised the smaller variety of tracks and characters compared to the same studio's earlier Sonic and All-Stars Racing Transformed. Today, Team Sonic Racing is an interesting alternative for group play, since it forces even people who otherwise just stay quiet and floor the gas in races to actually communicate.

switch__burnout-paradise-remastered.article:
**Burnout Paradise Remastered** brings to Switch one of the most free-roaming racing games ever made. Paradise City isn't a set of separate circuits but an open city with no loading screens, where the player simply drives off and the game itself offers up races, time trials, chases or tasks in which a hulking car has to be delivered across town without a scratch. Routes aren't marked with arrows on the ground, only by the finishing intersection, so the player chooses their own path. That's exactly why it pays to learn the city, searching for shortcuts through construction sites, ramps on rooftops and shortcuts through narrow alleys.

The driving model is built on aggression. Driving into oncoming traffic, close near-misses with other vehicles and drifting all fill the boost gauge, so the game practically punishes caution. The series' signature feature remains takedowns, ramming an opponent into a wall or guardrail, accompanied by a slow-motion shot of the bodywork tearing apart. Crashes are part of the fun, not a failure state, and a standalone mode centred on finding the most efficient way to cause a pile-up was one of the most popular parts of the original release. The remaster includes all the later expansions, including an island with rough off-road driving and motorbikes, and the Switch version sacrifices resolution and some effects to keep things smooth. In handheld mode it's a surprisingly well-executed port of a game from 2008.

The atmosphere is recognisable at first glance: a sun-soaked city, a radio host commenting on the player's exploits, and a soundtrack made up of rock and punk tracks. The original Burnout Paradise was very well received at launch and is considered one of the high points of arcade racing, since it convincingly dissolved the boundary between menu and driving by opening up the city. Today the game feels remarkably fresh precisely because it explains nothing and simply lets the player drive, and on a handheld console it becomes an ideal title for short bursts of play, since one great chase lasts just a few minutes and can start anywhere on the map.

switch__grid-autosport.article:
**GRID Autosport** is one of the most ambitious ports on Switch ever: a full-fledged circuit racer from Codemasters, brought to the handheld by Feral Interactive. It's neither arcade nor a hardcore simulator, but a middle ground between the two. The cars have noticeable weight, tires lose grip when the player pushes too hard into a corner, and damage affects handling. At the same time, the game offers so many assists that it can be tuned from a relaxed ride to a mode where every mistake is final.

The career consists of five disciplines that play completely differently. Touring cars are overtaken through nudging and body contact, GT cars demand a smooth racing line, single-seaters tolerate no contact at all, drift events score angle and fluidity, and endurance races force the player to watch tire wear over long distances. The player races under a team's colors alongside a teammate who can be sent ahead or ordered to drive safely via radio. Feral split the game into smaller data chunks and lowered the resolution, yet still managed to keep the full grid of rivals and stable smoothness. Wheel support, a touch menu, and later added online multiplayer made it a complete release rather than a stripped-down demo.

The visuals rely on clean lighting and honest car models, and engine sound plus crowd noise do more for the atmosphere than the music, which mostly plays in the menus. The original 2014 release was well received as the series' return to racing without unnecessary spectacle, and the Switch port earned admiring reactions precisely because of its technical achievement. Today it remains one of the few racing titles on the platform that offer serious circuit racing, and for players who want something other than go-karts on the go, it's practically a mandatory choice. At the same time, it's a showcase of how much can be squeezed out of the Switch hardware when a studio that knows exactly what to sacrifice and what to keep handles the port.

switch__fast-rmx.article:
**Fast RMX** was one of the first games Switch owners downloaded right after turning on the console, and for a long time it stood as the platform's best technical showcase. It's an anti-gravity racer in the style Nintendo's own F-Zero series once represented: vehicles hover above the track, race at several hundred kilometers per hour, and colliding with a wall means an instant loss of momentum. The tracks run through deserts, frozen canyons, futuristic cities, and orbital structures, and include loops, jumps, and sections where the player clings to a tunnel wall.

The whole game is defined by a single mechanic: phase switching. Boost panels on the track glow either orange or blue and only work when the vehicle is set to the matching color. Switching is done with a single button and must be timed mid-race, so besides holding the ideal line, the player is constantly reading the colors ahead. On top of that, energy is collected into a separate turbo boost, which is also consumed when returning to the track after a crash, forcing a choice between risk and reserve. The mode selection is modest, there are championships, time trials, local split-screen for up to four players, and online races, but the quality of the driving itself carries it a long way.

Technically it was something of a minor sensation: the game ran smoothly at high resolution docked and without any visible drop in handheld mode, which was surprising for a launch title from a small German studio. The audio consists of a hard electronic soundtrack that matches the speed on screen precisely. Reviews were largely favorable, praising the speed, visuals, and price, while mainly criticizing the limited mode selection and the high difficulty at higher speed classes. Today Fast RMX is a reminder that the anti-gravity racing genre didn't die, it just moved to smaller developers who keep it alive. For Switch owners it remains the fastest thing you can launch on the console, and for newcomers a decent lesson in what it means to drive with precision.

switch__doom-eternal.article:
**DOOM Eternal** is the sequel to the rebooted series that pushed first-person shooting into the form of a fast action game about resource management. The player once again takes on the role of the Doom Slayer, blasting through hordes of demons on Earth and beyond, but this time it's not just about aiming. Every weapon and ability gives something different: the chainsaw restocks ammo, the flamethrower knocks armor off hit enemies, and brutal melee finishers restore health. If the player stops or starts holding back, resources run out and death follows, so the only way forward is to keep attacking and switch tools according to what's needed at that moment.

Compared to its predecessor, mobility is far more pronounced. A double jump, air dash, grappling hook, and monkey bars turn arena fights into a three-dimensional dance where the player is constantly moving above enemies' heads. Stronger demons have weak points that can be shot off, giving combat a logic of priorities: disable the healer first, then the one shooting from range. Between arenas, the game weaves in platforming sections and searches for hidden upgrades. The Switch port was handled by Panic Button, and the result is a remarkable compromise, that is, lower resolution scaled to the load and a lower frame rate than on other platforms, but combat readability and the full campaign content are preserved.

The atmosphere is built from a combination of raw metal music, metallic environments, and a story that deliberately takes itself with comic-book seriousness. Reception was strongly positive, the game was called one of the best action titles of its generation, though some players had reservations about the sheer number of mechanics piled on top of each other and the platforming inserts. Today Eternal stands as the peak of one approach to shooters: no cover, no rest, just constant motion. On Switch, it's also one of the most demanding titles ever gotten running on the console, and for that alone it deserves attention even from people who already know it from elsewhere.

switch__wolfenstein-ii-new-colossus.article:
**Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus** continues B. J. Blazkowicz's story in an alternate history where Nazi Germany won the Second World War and occupies the United States. The player joins the resistance and pushes through devastated cities, secret bases, and bizarre locations that couldn't exist in a more realistic game. The story is told far more cinematically than in most shooters: long dialogue scenes, dark satire, and characters with their own arcs alternate with extremely brutal action. It's precisely that contrast between quiet interludes at the base and the massacre in the following mission that gives the game its distinctive tone.

Gameplay is built on the choice between stealth and open combat. Officers patrol every larger map and can be eliminated with a knife or a silenced weapon. Whoever kills them in time prevents reinforcements from being called in; whoever fails faces an endless wave of enemies. Dual-wielding weapons, reloading on the move, and extensive weapon upgrades allow for very aggressive play, yet the game doesn't tolerate reckless charging, since the health pool doesn't refill above its base level on its own. In the second half, the player gains special equipment that opens up alternative routes and retroactively changes how earlier locations can be traversed. The Switch version by Panic Button lowers resolution and effect detail and is noticeably softer visually, but keeps a stable pace and even offers motion controls for aiming.

The audio is one of the game's most distinctive elements: period-styled German-language cover songs, heavy industrial motifs, and loud weapon sound. Reviews were very favorable, praising above all the boldness of the storytelling and the quality of the shooting, with unbalanced difficulty and a short campaign length as the most common complaints. Today it stands as one of the few big shooters on the platform bold enough to be both a brutal spectacle and a politically outspoken game, and it definitely doesn't belong in the hands of the youngest players.

switch__elder-scrolls-v-skyrim.article:
**The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim** arrived on Switch as one of the first big third-party ports and proved that a sprawling open-world RPG could work on a handheld console. The player wakes up as a condemned prisoner on the chopping block in a northern province, only to discover they carry a dragon's soul and the ability to use the dragon tongue as magic. What follows, though, is mainly freedom: the main quest can be shelved for dozens of hours in favor of joining the thieves' guild, the college of magic, the war between the empire and the rebels, or simply wandering mountain trails and digging up old tombs.

The character system has no classic classes. The player improves at whatever they actually do, meaning whoever shoots a bow gets better with a bow, whoever steals gets better at sneaking, and on top of that they pick perks from skill constellations. Combat is simple but has weight: blocks, power attacks, and spells in both hands, plus dragon shouts that can knock an opponent off a cliff or slow down time. The Switch version includes all three major expansions, motion control support for sword swings and bow aiming, and bonus content tied to Zelda in the form of Link-inspired gear. Technically it's a compromise, meaning lower resolution and simpler effects than on other consoles, but it's a fully playable version in your hands, which changes how a player returns to a game of this scope.

The atmosphere rests on the Nordic landscape, mist between the mountains, and music with sweeping choirs that even someone who's never launched the game remembers. The original 2011 release ranks among the most influential RPGs ever, since it opened the genre to a wide audience, and its modding scene keeps the game alive to this day. The Switch version's reception was favorable, with complaints about the price and the aging technical side. Today it's the easiest way to carry the entire province of Skyrim in your bag, and the game keeps its main strength: the player decides for themselves what actually matters in it.

switch__diablo-iii-eternal-collection.article:
**Diablo III: Eternal Collection** is the complete edition of the action RPG about hacking through hordes of demons and collecting ever more absurd gear, and it works surprisingly naturally on Switch. The player chooses from several classes, from the barbarian and monk to the wizard and necromancer, each with its own set of abilities that can be further customized with runes. The core loop is simple: run through a location, cut down everything that moves, pick up better gear, and move on. But the game tunes this loop for so long that it becomes an extraordinarily satisfying rhythm, where picking up a new pair of gloves can change a character's entire build.

Once the campaign is finished, the main content opens up: an endless scaling of difficulty. Rifts generate randomly assembled levels with a boss at the end, higher tiers punish the player with steadily rising enemy stats, and the seasonal system regularly resets progress so players start fresh under new rules. The Switch release includes both the Reaper of Souls expansion and the later-added necromancer class, and above all local four-player co-op on a single screen. Just plug in controllers and you're playing instantly. Technically it's a well-executed conversion that keeps smooth performance even in the densest fights, topped off with a handful of cosmetic items referencing Nintendo brands.

The atmosphere is dark, gothic, and quite loud: blood, torches, cathedrals, and the roar of dying monsters accompanied by orchestral music that pulls back into quiet motifs during calmer moments. The original Diablo III had a troubled reception at its 2012 launch because of the auction house and mandatory internet connection, but after being reworked and expanded, it became the genre's benchmark on consoles. Today the Switch version is the most convenient way to get a short dose of this loop, even though a short evening threatens to turn into an all-nighter. For playing together on a single console, it also has few competitors on the platform, since the co-op here works without a single compromise.

switch__streets-of-rage-4.article:
**Streets of Rage 4** is the sequel to the legendary Sega Mega Drive beat-'em-up, arriving decades after the last installment, yet most players still embraced it as a true successor. The setting stays the same: a city under the control of a criminal organization, streets, subway, galleries, and rooftops through which a group of heroes moves, solving problems with their fists. Axel and Blaze return to the roster, joined by new characters, each with their own speed, reach, and special attacks, so the choice of fighter significantly changes the play style.

The combat system runs deeper than it first appears. Special attacks drain health, which can be earned back by hitting enemies without taking a hit yourself, creating a risky bet on how long to stay on the offensive. Combos are tracked, and a scoring system rewards keeping a chain going, throwing enemies into each other, and bouncing them off walls, turning an ordinary playthrough into a game about clean execution. Two-player local co-op is preserved, and there's also an online mode, a single-life arcade run, and a battle arena. Character versions from the classic games can also be unlocked, complete with their original pixel art and behavior, which follow their own rules. On Switch, the game runs without a hitch, and the sharp hand-drawn art gets along well with handheld mode.

The visuals from Lizardcube rank among the most striking in the genre, since the drawn backgrounds look like an illustration brought to life. The music was led by Olivier Deriviere, with contributions from composers tied to the original series, so the soundtrack alternates modern electronica with nods to nineties sound. Reviews were very favorable, and the game is considered proof that the classic beat-'em-up still has a place today. Today it's the ideal game for an evening with friends: short, tough, and the kind players return to for a better score. On Switch, it's enough to unplug the Joy-Cons and a second player joins within seconds.

switch__teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-shr.article:
**Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Shredder's Revenge** is a beat-'em-up that deliberately returns to the arcade and console takes on the Turtles from the turn of the eighties and nineties. The player chooses from a roster of characters, that is, all four turtles, Splinter, April, and others, and fights through the streets of New York, sewers, construction sites, and a TV studio against members of the Foot clan and familiar villains from the animated series. Each character has a different reach and speed, so the choice isn't purely cosmetic: whoever plays as Donatello keeps enemies at range, whoever plays as Raphael has to go in for close contact.

Combat is simply readable but has enough depth to hold up over repeated playthroughs. Besides basic combos, there are dodges, deflecting projectiles back at the shooter, throws, and a chargeable special attack that briefly makes the player invulnerable. The game comes most alive in co-op, which supports up to six players at once, both locally and online, including the ability to revive each other and pull off joint moves. Alongside the arcade run, there's a story mode with a map, character quests, and gradual fighter leveling, giving a reason to return to individual missions. On Switch, it's a completely trouble-free title that looks just as good handheld as on a TV.

The pixel art nails the style of the original cartoon, including its animations and color palette, the music was composed by Tee Lopes and alternates funky and synth sounds with loud drums. Reception was very favorable, reviewers called it one of the best licensed beat-'em-ups ever and praised above all the co-op and the precision of the controls, with criticism aimed at its short length. Today Shredder's Revenge shows what a genre tribute should look like, one that doesn't rely solely on nostalgia but on genuinely well-designed combat. In a group of four or six, it ranks among the safest bets you can boot up on Switch, since everyone grasps the rules instantly.

switch__overcooked-2.article:
**Overcooked! 2** is a cooperative cooking game that really tests your ability to communicate under pressure. Two to four players run a shared kitchen where orders keep coming in on one side while the clock runs down on the other. Every dish demands a sequence of steps: chop, cook, plate, serve, and finally wash the dishes that keep piling up. Nobody has enough hands to manage alone, so everything depends on splitting roles and shouting instructions like who grabs the rice and who puts out the burning pan.

The series' main joke is that the kitchens themselves work against the player. The floor moves on drifting ice floes, tables ride conveyor belts, the path between the stove and the serving hatch splits apart over a chasm, or the whole room rotates. The second game added the ability to throw ingredients across a distance, which fundamentally changes tactics in split kitchens, and crucially it added online multiplayer, which the first game lacked. Alongside a campaign with levels that unlock progressively, there's also a scoring mode where players return to individual kitchens trying to earn three stars. On Switch the game works exactly as it should, since two people can split a pair of Joy-Cons and start playing instantly, with no setup and no extra hardware.

The visuals are deliberately cute, with a colorful cartoon world and characters scurrying around each other in a panic, while the music keeps a light, quick rhythm that pushes players forward as time runs out. Reception was very positive, and the series became one of the most common answers to the question of what to play with a partner or with kids. At the same time it has a reputation as a game that can make even well-matched couples argue, and that's exactly why people keep coming back to it. Difficulty ramps up gradually, and the final kitchens demand a rehearsed routine, so what started as easygoing fun can easily turn into a multi-hour session repeating the same level until that third star finally drops. For Switch it's one of the best party titles around, and proof that a cooperative game doesn't have to be a stripped-down version of something bigger.

switch__puyo-puyo-tetris.article:
**Puyo Puyo Tetris** is an unusual crossbreed of two completely different puzzle classics, released on Switch in the console's very first year and becoming one of its best titles for a train ride. On one side stands Tetris with its four-piece blocks and line clears, on the other Puyo Puyo, where colorful blobby drops fall and the player must link them in groups of four or more. The two games run on completely different logic: Tetris is about space and speed, Puyo is about setting up chain reactions, where one well-placed piece triggers a cascade.

The game finds its true purpose in versus play. Every successful move sends obstacles to the opponent, so the match becomes a question of who can keep up the pace longer. The mode selection is broad: there's a classic duel within the same game, but also one where one player plays Tetris and the other Puyo simultaneously on a single screen, plus Swap, which regularly switches between the two games, and Fusion, where blocks and drops fall onto one shared field together. The story mode, with voiced anime cutscenes, mainly serves as a tutorial that gradually teaches players advanced techniques. On Switch there's the option to play two players on one console with detached Joy-Cons, plus a snappy online mode, which keeps the game a reliable pick for a group.

The visuals are loud and colorful, full of animated characters commenting on the match as it unfolds, and the music adapts to how close a player is to losing. Reception was very positive, with reviewers especially praising the sheer number of modes and the quality of both base games, while frequent criticism was aimed at the price and having to sit through a repeated story thread. Today Puyo Puyo Tetris ranks among the best things you can play on a handheld console in short bursts, and at the same time among the toughest competitive puzzle games out there. Anyone who gets used to both rulesets at once ends up with a game that can be played for years while there's still room to improve. For newcomers, it's also nice that either half can be played entirely on its own.

switch__super-bomberman-r.article:
