**Super Bomberman R** was one of the first games available on Switch and marked the return of a franchise that had essentially been dormant for several years. The principle hasn't changed since the eighties: the player moves across a grid, plants bombs that explode into a cross shape after a moment, and tries to catch opponents in the blast before ending up caught in their own trap. Destroying blocks unlocks upgrades, meaning more bombs at once, longer blast range, faster movement speed, or the ability to kick and throw bombs, and gathering that loadout from every match creates an escalating race for the advantage.

The core of the game is battles for up to eight players, playable both locally and online, and this is where the game truly shines. The arenas have their own obstacles, conveyor belts, or teleporters, a round lasts roughly a minute, and once eliminated a player becomes a ghost who can still shoot into the field and return to the game, so nobody just stares at the screen for nothing. Alongside that there's a story campaign with its own bosses and voiced cutscenes, playable in two-player co-op as well, though its difficulty was a frequent target of criticism at launch. Single Joy-Con controls mean that all it takes for a group game is one console and a handful of controllers, which is exactly the scenario Bomberman suits best.

The visuals are clean and colorful, with three-dimensional arenas viewed from above, while the music leans on upbeat, fast-paced tunes including rearranged classic themes from the series. Reception at launch was mixed, with reviewers criticizing the price, the unpolished online mode, and a dull campaign, but Konami kept patching the game long after release and adding characters and modes for free, which noticeably raised its standing. Today Super Bomberman R is a simple but reliable pick when a group gets together and nobody wants to read rules. It also remains one of the few games on the platform where eight people can gather around a single console, and that quality keeps it in the library to this day.

switch__rocket-league.article:
**Rocket League** is a game whose description sounds like a joke, and yet it's one of the most precisely tuned competitive titles of the last decade: soccer played with rocket-powered cars in an enclosed arena. The rules are trivial, namely get the giant ball into the opponent's goal, and anyone can learn the controls within a minute. Underneath that, though, is a physics model that players spend years learning. The cars can jump, spin in mid-air, bounce off walls and the ceiling, and use collected boost fuel to launch upward and strike the ball out of the air, so the gap between a beginner and an experienced player is enormous, and the game is effectively played in three dimensions.

Matches last five minutes, played in lineups from one-on-one up to three-on-three, and every duel for the ball is also a duel for position, since whoever launches badly leaves their goal empty. Around that core sits extensive car customization, seasonal content, and ranked ladders. The Switch version launched in the console's first year and kept the smoothness that's essential for this game, albeit at the cost of lower resolution and simpler effects. It supports cross-play with other platforms, which significantly extends the lifespan of a competitive title on less powerful hardware, and local multiplayer on a single screen is also included.

The atmosphere rests on simple, clean graphics, explosions on impact, and an electronic soundtrack that keeps the tempo without becoming distracting. After launching in 2015, the game became a phenomenon, moved to a free-to-play model, and built a strong competitive scene with its own tournaments. Today it remains one of the few titles that work just as well as fifteen minutes of couch fun as they do as a discipline you can devote hundreds of hours to, and on Switch it's still always within reach. Crucially, the game has no purchasable content that grants any advantage, so the outcome depends solely on how well someone flies and reads the ball. Landing that first aerial hit, meanwhile, is a moment most players remember.

switch__it-takes-two.article:
**It Takes Two** is a game that can't be played alone, and that's the entire point of it. A couple of parents on the verge of divorce are turned into rag dolls and must fight their way back together, with every step requiring the other player's cooperation. It's played exclusively by two people, either on one screen in split windows or online, and the game shows both halves at all times, so players can see exactly what the other one is doing and when they need to pull a lever or jump.

What makes It Takes Two exceptional is the pace at which it discards old mechanics and introduces new ones. Players have barely gotten used to a pair of abilities before the chapter ends and the next one starts with something entirely different, whether that's a nail and hammer, a magnet and attraction, time manipulation, or flight. Almost every section is built so that one player has the tool and the other has the target, so neither can progress alone. Scattered throughout are dozens of small competitive minigames, from tug-of-war to hockey, serving as a breather. The Switch version arrived later and is technically among the more modest, with lower resolution and softer visuals, but it's content-complete and split-screen works even in handheld mode.

Visually it's a colorful fairy-tale world seen from the perspective of shrunken characters, where a shed or a garden becomes a giant adventure, and the music gives it a cinematic touch. Reception was extremely positive, with the game collecting numerous awards including Game of the Year, and it's often cited as proof that co-op doesn't have to be a mere add-on to a single-player game. The story about a relationship falling apart never feels like an excuse for a string of minigames, since every chapter comments in some way on what's happening between the two leads. Critics especially praised the inventiveness of individual levels and the fact that the game never lets itself repeat the same trick twice. Today it's the most common recommendation for a pair who want to play together, whether that's a couple, friends, or a parent and child, and the second player doesn't even need to own the game.

pc-dos__jazz-jackrabbit.article:
**Jazz Jackrabbit** was the PC's answer to fast console platformers and still ranks among the most polished action games ever released for DOS. The hero is a green rabbit armed with an oversized weapon, setting out to rescue a princess kidnapped by the turtle Devan Shell, journeying across planets with wildly different looks, from jungles through icy slopes to mechanical mazes. Unlike most platformers of its time, the game isn't just about jumping between platforms but mainly about shooting: Jazz has several types of ammo, can run at tremendous speed, slide through narrow tunnels, and collect gems that unlock bonus levels. Each episode ends with a boss fight, and the world map between levels gives the whole game a pleasant sense of rhythm.

Technically, the game was a showcase of what a 386 processor with VGA graphics could do. It runs at a smooth pace, uses multi-layered parallax-scrolling backgrounds, large colorful sprites, and a number of effects that had until then been rare on PC. Smooth screen scrolling in particular was the biggest surprise for players of the time, since it was a discipline where home computers had long lagged behind game consoles. The music uses module tracks played through a sound card, mixing energetic, fast themes that suit the breakneck pace perfectly, and even the gunfire sounds carry a pleasantly arcade-like sharpness.

At the time, Jazz Jackrabbit was very well received precisely because it filled a long-empty niche: the PC had shooters and strategy games, but hardly any quality fast platformer. Shareware distribution made it widely known, and a sequel later followed that pushed the whole genre line even further. Today the game feels charmingly over-the-top and colorful; the difficulty at times rests on reflexes and knowledge of level layouts, but the core remains fun and the controls are surprisingly precise. Anyone who wants to see that DOS could do snappy platformers too, and not just dark corridors, should start right here.

pc-dos__jill-of-jungle.article:
**Jill of the Jungle** is a platformer in which the heroine fights her way through intricate jungle levels full of lizards, bats, and spikes, wielding a throwing knife as her main weapon. The game was released as a trilogy of episodes, and its most interesting idea lies in transformation: at certain points, Jill can turn into a frog, a bird, or a fish, and with each form the way she moves changes too. Jumping in frog form, gliding through the air, or swimming underwater isn't just a cosmetic variation — it completely redraws the possibilities for getting through a level. Besides combat, the levels also feature simple puzzles with keys, switches, and moving platforms, so the pace regularly alternates between action and unhurried exploration.

Technically, the game left a pleasantly clean impression. The graphics use bright, richly saturated colors and clearly readable backgrounds, the levels are large enough that you can get lost in them for a while, and the screen scrolling is decently smooth for the standards of the time. The music is simple but catchy and contributes significantly to a slightly fairy-tale atmosphere that sets the game apart from darker action titles of the era. The controls are straightforward and the game doesn't tend to punish the player excessively, though some jumps over spikes require patience and a few extra attempts before you get used to the character's momentum.

Jill of the Jungle was one of the titles with which Epic MegaGames built its reputation on the shareware scene in the first half of the nineties. The first episode circulated freely and served as a hook for the remaining two, a model that worked brilliantly on PC at the time. The reception was warm, mainly thanks to the unconventional heroine and the transformation mechanic, which elevated the game above the average attempts to imitate console platformers. Today it's more of a short nostalgic experience that you'll get through quickly, offering less depth than the publisher's later platformers, but the transformations and the calm jungle mood are exactly what make it a title people remember fondly.

pc-dos__cosmo-s-cosmic-adventure.article:
**Cosmo's Cosmic Adventure** tells the story of a small alien whose family ship crash-lands on an unknown planet, and when his parents go missing, Cosmo must find them on his own. The core mechanic is suction cups on his hands: Cosmo can cling to vertical walls and climb up them, turning ordinary jumping into a much more interesting spatial puzzle. Enemies are dispatched by jumping on their heads, levels are full of bonuses, hidden rooms, and explosive crates that reveal secret areas. The game is split into three episodes, and its design consistently alternates safer passages with more demanding sections where you need to carefully plan how to actually get upward.

Graphically, this was one of the more attractive titles of its time on PC. The sprites are large, rounded, and expressively animated, the environments burst with saturated colors, and the game noticeably goes beyond what players were used to from DOS platformers. Smooth screen scrolling and carefully drawn backgrounds give the world a pleasant sense of depth, and yet the whole thing runs briskly even on modest hardware. Sound through an Ad Lib card accompanies the adventure with light, almost cartoonish melodies that underscore the game's childlike, gentle tone, even though some levels can be surprisingly tricky and demand good jump timing.

Apogee distributed this game in the usual shareware fashion, with a freely available first episode and paid sequels, and Cosmo became one of its signature titles alongside the publisher's other platformers. At the time it was praised mainly for its graphics and for the wall-climbing idea that set it apart from the rest of the field. Today it's a pleasantly short adventure good for one or two afternoons, delighting mainly with how clean and readable its gameplay is. Anyone who enjoys classic platformers with an emphasis on exploration and finding secret nooks will find exactly what they're looking for here. The short runtime is, if anything, an advantage, since the game never loses pace anywhere.

pc-dos__crystal-caves.article:
**Crystal Caves** is a classic cave platformer in which the hero Mylo Steamwitz descends beneath the surface of alien planets to collect precious crystals to fund his own business. Each level has a clear goal: collect all the crystals and find the exit, with the path leading through moving platforms, laser traps, poisonous plants, and alien vermin. Mylo is no warrior — he only carries a simple weapon with limited ammo, so it often pays to go around enemies or use the environment against them instead. Between levels the player moves across a clear map with entrances to individual mines, which gives freedom in choosing the order and a pleasant sense of progress.

Technically the game runs on sixteen-color EGA graphics, which look sharp and contrasty today but were entirely standard at the time and, above all, ran smoothly even on very modest hardware. The screens don't scroll continuously but switch whole-screen by whole-screen, and the level design cleverly uses this so that each screen functions as a small standalone puzzle. The sound is limited to internal-speaker beeps and simple effects, so the atmosphere is carried mainly by the visual style of underground corridors, pipes, and machinery. This very austerity contributes to the game feeling focused and never wasting your time.

Crystal Caves belonged to Apogee's early wave of shareware titles that showed the PC could have its own platformer scene even without game-console hardware. The game was well received mainly thanks to its balanced difficulty and the careful design of individual screens, which rewards thoughtfulness more than fast reflexes. Its influence came especially from being part of the family of games that made Apogee a major publisher of action titles for DOS. Playing it today is a pleasantly old-fashioned yet honest experience: short, clear, and at times surprisingly demanding, especially if you want to collect absolutely everything.

pc-dos__bio-menace.article:
**Bio Menace** puts the player in the boots of agent Snake Logan, who is shot down over a city overrun by mutated monsters and must fight his way out while figuring out who's behind the whole chaos. Compared to most platformers of the era, there's a much heavier emphasis on shooting here: the hero starts with a submachine gun, gradually finds stronger weapons and grenades, and the environment is full of enemies who walk, jump, and attack from range. Besides combat, the levels also involve finding hostages who need to be freed, as well as keys or switches that open further paths. The levels are large and intricate, so exploration plays just as big a role as accurate aim and knowing when it's better to retreat instead.

The game runs on an engine derived from Apogee's earlier platformers, which shows in the smooth scrolling, precise controls, and carefully built levels. Visually, though, it's much grittier than most colorful platformers of the time: the environments are dark, full of green slime and crumbling city sets, and the enemies are drawn with a relish for disgustingly gruesome detail. The Ad Lib or Sound Blaster soundtrack leans into tension and pace, so the overall impression is closer to an action movie than a children's adventure. This gave the game its own niche among PC platformers aimed at an older audience.

Bio Menace came out late in the life cycle of this type of game, at a time when players' attention was already being pulled toward first-person shooters, so its reception wasn't as strong as it deserved. Even so, it's one of the technically best and most enjoyable shooting-focused DOS platformers, and it kept a good reputation within the community. The authors later released it as freeware, which extended its lifespan even further. Today it delights mainly with its large levels, the pleasant weight of its weapons, and a raw atmosphere that feels refreshingly different from most modern platformers. Anyone who enjoys fast side-view shooting won't find a much better choice on DOS.

pc-dos__hocus-pocus.article:
**Hocus Pocus** sends into action an apprentice of a sorcerers' order who must pass a series of trials to be accepted among true masters. The player thus goes through four episodes full of castles, caves, temples, and fantasy landscapes, dispatching skeletons, giant spiders, and other vermin with magic bolts. The core of the gameplay rests on searching: each level requires collecting a certain number of items or finding all the crystals and keys that unlock the exit. Potions, teleport pads, invisibility, and temporary weapon upgrades help along the way, turning the ordinary progression into a pleasant change of pace and rewarding players who search every corner of the map.

Graphically, this is one of the most colorful DOS platformers of its time. The game uses the VGA palette to the full, the backgrounds are detailed and built from several layers, the sprites are cleanly animated, and the whole visual side feels more mature than most cartoonish platformers. The music rests on module tracks with striking fantasy themes that fit the theme of masters and sorcerous trials well and noticeably help the atmosphere. The controls are simple; the hero isn't a particularly acrobatic character, so the game relies more on thoughtfulness and orientation within a level than on demanding jumps over chasms.

The title was released under the Apogee label at a time when the PC platformer market was already saturated and attention was shifting to other genres, yet it found a decent following and is still mentioned among the finer shareware games today. At the time, the graphics and music were praised most, while criticism pointed to the level structure repeating itself over time. Today it's a pleasantly extensive game that lasts several evenings and has a surprisingly good rhythm if you enjoy hunting for collectibles. Anyone who likes fantasy settings and a calmer platformer pace gets exactly what they wish for. Collecting every item and searching for hidden rooms also gives good reason to revisit earlier levels.

pc-dos__monster-bash.article:
**Monster Bash** is a horror-themed platformer in which young Johnny Dash falls asleep, wakes up in a realm of monsters, and sets out to rescue kidnapped puppies and kittens. The enemies form a whole classic gallery of spooks, from skeletons through mummies and zombies to bats, and the player fends them off with a slingshot whose shots can be upgraded. Besides combat, the game is above all about exploration: the levels hide secret rooms, locked cages with animals, and bonuses tucked behind walls, so thoroughly searching the map matters just as much as reflexes. The layout of graveyards, cellars, and castle corridors is intricate, and the game happily rewards those who try even unconventional paths.

The game uses the same technological lineage as Apogee's other platformers of the time, so it runs smoothly and controls precisely. Visually, though, it stands apart with its dark palette, moonlight, cobwebs, and a wealth of small details that make it one of the most atmospheric DOS platformers. The horror charge is playful rather than truly scary, more in the style of childhood spooky tales. The soundtrack through a sound card uses gloomy themes with a dash of humor, and it's one of the reasons players remember this game so fondly. The slingshot can even fire diagonally upward, which is often the difference between surviving and a sudden end.

Monster Bash came out at a time when other genres were already gaining the upper hand on PC, so it didn't leave as strong a mark in the press of the day as the publisher's more famous titles, but it earned a solid place among shareware fans. Today it's a short yet very distinctive experience whose mood evokes an animated spooky fairy tale more than an action game. The difficulty is pleasantly balanced, the levels can be replayed, and the effort to rescue absolutely every animal gives a reason to come back. For fans of retro platformers, it's one of the best-aged pieces in the genre. Revisiting it, meanwhile, won't take more than one evening.

pc-dos__another-world.article:
**Another World** begins unusually: a young scientist is struck by lightning during a nighttime particle accelerator experiment and finds himself in a foreign world full of hostile creatures and unknown machines. The game has no introductory text, no tutorial, no indicators — all the storytelling happens through imagery, and the player learns through his own death. The core of the gameplay consists of running, jumping, kicking, and later an energy weapon that can shoot, build a protective barrier, and blast obstacles, turning every encounter into a small tactical puzzle. Progress happens through trial and error, with the player repeating a short section until they understand its correct solution and can execute it precisely.

Visually, this was an utterly exceptional title. Instead of the usual sprites, the game uses vector polygons, so characters and environments are made of shapes that can be smoothly animated and resized. The result feels like a moving comic-book illustration, and despite a very limited color count it manages to convey space, depth, and mood. The animation of the main character is remarkably convincing, and cinematic cuts flow seamlessly into playable sections without any pause. The sound is sparse, often leaving nothing but silence broken by footsteps or a distant roar, which only amplifies the foreignness of the whole world.

Contemporary critics received the game as proof that a video game could tell a mature story without a single word, and its influence is visible throughout the entire line of so-called cinematic platformers, as well as in later games built on atmosphere and wordless storytelling. It's also a title that essentially originated as the work of a single author, which made it a frequently cited example of an auteur game. Today it can be finished within a few hours, and its harsh trial-and-error schooling will put plenty of players off, but its visual power and the boldness of telling a story entirely without dialogue remain extraordinary even decades later. That's exactly why it still appears in surveys of games that pushed the medium forward, and its newer remakes keep arriving on further platforms even after all these years.

pc-dos__flashback-quest-for-identity.article:
**Flashback: The Quest for Identity** opens with a hovercraft crash in the jungles of Titan, where the hero Conrad wakes up with no memory, his only clue a recording of his own voice leaving him a message. The game blends precise platforming action with exploration, dialogue, and simple tasks the player completes in cities and laboratories alike. Conrad moves slower and more deliberately than the heroes of arcade jumpers: he crouches, grabs ledges, carefully swings across gaps, draws his pistol, and takes cover behind force fields. It's exactly this weight of movement that creates tension, since every misjudged distance or mistimed jump hurts, and fights are won more often through positioning and anticipation than quick fingers.

Technically, the game builds on the rotoscoped animation the studio was already known for, so every character movement looks remarkably natural. The environments are drawn in fine detail, backgrounds carry their own layers with numerous small animations, and comic-book-style cutscenes tie the individual chapters into a coherent story. On PC the game uses a VGA palette, and later releases add CD audio, though even the floppy disk version holds onto a strong mood thanks to ambient melodies and economical sound effects. The structure is chapter-based, and each part has a different focus, from arena combat to infiltrating an enemy complex.

Flashback was very well received in its time and became one of the most acclaimed European titles of the early nineties, seeing ports to numerous platforms. Its influence can be seen everywhere games lean on realistic character movement, atmospheric sci-fi, and environmental storytelling. Today it demands patience, since the controls are deliberately slower and several passages can prove tricky, but the story of searching for one's own identity, along with the extraordinary animation, still ranks among the best DOS has to offer. It works best when the player takes their time and treats each screen as a small situation to solve.

pc-dos__rise-of-triad-dark-war.article:
**Rise of the Triad: Dark War** sends five agents of a secret unit to an island where a cult is preparing an attack on the surrounding city, and before starting the player picks one of the characters, each differing in speed and stamina. The game originally began life as a sequel to an older shooter from the same publisher and grew technically beyond it too, which shows in the level design. The weapons are utterly over the top: alongside pistols and a submachine gun there are rocket launchers, homing missiles, and magical items that temporarily turn the hero into a god or a dog. On top of that come bounce pads, narrow walkways over chasms, moving platforms, and a wealth of traps, making the levels feel far more vertical and playful than the flat corridors of the previous generation.

The engine is an extended version of older technology, but with a host of additions that mask its age: characters move at different heights, there are jump pads, walls of fire, and breakable windows. What stands out most, though, is the gore, since a rocket hit turns an enemy into a shower of flying body parts, and the game clearly plays this for laughs. Digitized guard barks and exaggerated death sounds underline the overall comic-book tone. The title also offered a multiplayer mode with its own rules and modifications, which considerably extended its lifespan among players.

Rise of the Triad arrived at a time when it was already competing against far more modern shooters, so technologically it felt a bit behind, but its sheer inventiveness and over-the-top attitude won it a loyal following that has stuck with it to this day. At the time, reviewers praised the wealth of ideas in the levels and the playful weapons, while criticizing the aging graphics. Today it's one of the most fun old shooters around, because unlike serious modern shooters it never once tries to be realistic, and its chaos is exactly what keeps it alive. Thanks also to a community that still builds custom levels for it, this game hasn't been forgotten in retro circles.

pc-dos__raptor-call-of-shadows.article:
**Raptor: Call of the Shadows** is a vertically scrolling air shooter in which the player, a mercenary pilot, takes on jobs against corporations and spends the earned cash between missions on new weapons and upgrades for their ship. It's exactly this shopping element that makes the game more than a classic arcade shooter: the player has to weigh whether to invest in a stronger main weapon, a shield, or homing missiles, and every decision shows up in the next mission. The campaign is split into several sectors, each with its own set of levels capped off by a battle against a giant ship or a ground base. Downed enemy craft drop crates with bonuses and cash, so it pays to risk flying into heavier fire.

Technically, this was a very accomplished piece of work. The game runs in VGA mode with a huge number of colorful sprites, the explosions are unusually detailed, and the backgrounds shift from deserts through cities to factory complexes without the pace ever dropping. Sound Blaster audio accompanies the action with fast music and punchy explosion effects that give impacts real weight. At the time of release the game felt like proof that a PC could hold a first-class shooter of this type, a domain that until then had belonged to consoles and arcade cabinets, and it remained one of the few genre representatives to truly succeed on DOS.

Released under the Apogee label with the usual shareware model and a freely available first episode, the game was very well received by players, mainly for combining arcade action with the gradual buildup of one's own ship. It's exactly this purchasing system that gives it a structure keeping players glued to the screen longer than pure arcade action, which is why it's still mentioned among the best PC shooters of its kind. Today it delights with its straightforwardness: you take off, you fly, you shoot, and between missions you treat yourself to the joy of buying stronger gear. The difficulty rises smoothly and the game stays readable and fair. This clarity, plus the pleasure of gradually upgrading your own ship, is exactly why players keep coming back to it even after all these years.

pc-dos__halloween-harry.article:
**Halloween Harry** is an action platformer about a mercenary called into an underground complex after aliens start turning people into zombies. His main tool is a flamethrower, later joined by other weapons, and above all a jetpack that lets the hero fly for short bursts. It's exactly this flying that changes the whole rhythm of the game: instead of precisely judging jumps, the player hovers above enemies, hunts for a good position, and strafes hordes of zombies from above. The main objective of each level is to find and free captured scientists and lead them to the exit, so besides combat there's also plenty of thorough exploring of sprawling bases full of elevators, pipes, and hidden nooks.

Technically the game ranks among the best of DOS platformers. It runs in a VGA palette, the screen scrolls smoothly, the sprites are large and well animated, and the game uses digitized voice lines and sound effects that give it a peculiar cinematic flair. The environments mix sterile laboratories, frozen storage areas, and organically infested sections, and the flames and explosions rank among the most impressive things the genre had to show on PC. The soundtrack goes for fast, slightly horror-flavored themes that complement the game's crazy tone well, where a serious sci-fi premise meets total over-the-top absurdity.

The game was released under the Apogee label and later also sold under the title Alien Carnage, the name by which many players know it. Reception was very positive, praising in particular the technical execution and the idea of the jetpack, which set it apart from an otherwise similar crowd of platformers. The authors later released it for free, which helped it keep a steady circle of fans. Today it's one of the most enjoyable old DOS action games around, one that requires no compromises: the pace is brisk, the controls are comfortable, and the pleasure of torching zombies with a flamethrower hasn't aged a bit. At the same time it's a good example of where DOS platformers were heading just before the shift to a three-dimensional viewpoint pushed them aside.

pc-dos__disney-s-aladdin.article:
**Disney's Aladdin** is a platformer based on the animated film of the same name and ranks among the best-looking games ever released for DOS. The player moves through the marketplace of Agrabah, the Cave of Wonders, the Sultan's dungeon, and the final palace, using a scimitar for close combat and apples as a throwing weapon. Besides regular jumping, Aladdin swings on ropes, slides down stall awnings, climbs poles, and in one section flees on a magic carpet ahead of rising lava. The levels are full of small secrets, hidden gems, and bonus items, so it pays to move through them more slowly than the pace of the game might suggest.

The main draw is the graphics. The characters are animated using a hand-drawn technique close to film animation, so Aladdin runs, dodges, and fights across hundreds of smoothly connected frames, and the whole thing feels like an interactive cartoon. The backgrounds are colorful and full of detail, from crackling fires to moving crowds, and the PC version makes full use of a VGA palette. The audio side borrows familiar melodies from the film and plays them through a sound card, backed by pronounced sound effects. The game demanded a fairly capable computer by the standards of its time, but the reward was a visual experience the likes of which had barely been seen on PC before.

The title originally started life on consoles and arrived on PC as a port, and for many European players this version became their first encounter with the game. At the time, reviewers praised the graphics and animation, while criticism centered on its relatively short length and on difficulty that was gentler compared to other platformers. Today it holds a reputation as one of the finest movie tie-ins in gaming history, mainly because it didn't settle for simply retelling the plot but offered its own carefully designed action game with immediately readable controls. Visually it remains one of the most charming games to appear on computer screens of its era, and many players remember it exactly for that reason.

pc-dos__titus-fox-to-marrakech-and-back.article:
**Titus the Fox: To Marrakech and Back** is a platformer about a fox who sets off across Europe and North Africa to rescue his kidnapped girlfriend. The gameplay rests on one distinctive feature: the hero can't defeat enemies by jumping on their heads or shooting them, but he can pick up crates, barrels, and all sorts of objects to throw at foes or use as stepping stones. Most levels are therefore, in a sense, spatial puzzles where you need to carry the right object to the right place to reach an otherwise unreachable platform. Add flying enemies, chasms, and time pressure, and the game constantly alternates between thinking and pure action.

Technically it's a typical representative of French production of the era. The graphics are colorful and stylized in a slightly comic-book manner, the settings shift from city streets through desert landscapes to strange dreamlike levels, and the screen scrolls smoothly. The sound is sparser, the game leaning more on effects than a rich musical score, and the controls have noticeable momentum that takes a while to get used to. It's exactly this control responsiveness combined with strict enemy placement that makes Titus the Fox one of the toughest platformers available on DOS.

The game was released on numerous platforms and became one of the signature titles of its European publisher, known for churning out colorful, demanding action games for home computers. At the time it was received with mixed feelings: praised for its inventive object-carrying system, criticized for its unforgiving difficulty and unpleasant enemy placement. Today it's a title for patient players who enjoy old European platformers with a distinctive personality of their own. Anyone who chews through the first levels will find surprisingly cleverly built environments and a game that forces more thought than it seems at first glance. It's exactly this combination of charm and toughness that makes it a title still remembered in Europe with decidedly mixed feelings.

pc-dos__prehistorik-2.article:
**Prehistorik 2** is a colorful platformer about a prehistoric hunter armed with a club whose only real goal is to eat his fill. The player moves through levels full of dinosaurs, mammoths, insects, and other prehistoric inhabitants, clubbing them and collecting everything edible along the way, from roast chickens to giant cakes. Collecting food isn't just decoration, since it's exactly what makes up the score and the bonuses that decide your progress. Besides regular combat, there are hidden rooms, platforms over chasms, and enemies that need several hits, so the game gradually ramps up and can challenge even experienced players in the later levels.

Visually it's a very pleasant title. The graphics are drawn in a bold cartoonish style with strong colors, the characters are large and easy to read, and the individual worlds are clearly distinct from one another, from green prehistoric plains to caves and snowy regions. The screen scrolls smoothly and the game ran well even on more modest computers, which was an important selling point at a time when more demanding titles kept requiring ever stronger hardware. The soundtrack is simple but infectiously cheerful, and together with the hero's exaggerated animation it rounds out the light-hearted mood typical of the whole game.

Prehistorik 2 became one of the most widespread titles on computers in schools and homes across Central Europe, played by entire generations of kids, often without knowing who actually published it. At the time it wasn't a genre-defining breakthrough so much as a solid, skillfully made platformer that delivered exactly what was expected of it. Today it stands as a showcase of the European platforming school: straightforward, fast, tough in its second half, and free of any unnecessary padding. For many players it remains a strong memory of their first encounter with PC gaming. Playing it today means returning to the simple joy of moving, jumping, and swinging a club, a joy that later, more complicated games often lack. Getting through it takes barely a few hours.

pc-dos__wolfenstein-3d.article:
**Wolfenstein 3D** is the title that, in 1992, practically defined the shape of first-person shooters on PC. The player takes on the role of American agent B. J. Blazkowicz, who fights his way out of a cell in a Nazi fortress and steadily pushes deeper into the heart of the enemy empire. The structure remains a model of simplicity to this day: each floor is a maze of corridors, secret doors, and patrols, through which the player collects keys, ammo, gold treasure, and medkits in order to finally reach the elevator to the next level. There are no scripted sequences or branching quests, just the pure rhythm of opening doors, shooting, and feeling along walls in search of hidden stashes.

Technically, it was a revelation. The chosen method of rendering space allowed textured walls to move smoothly and quickly on the computers of the time, something the competition couldn't match for a long while. Viewed today, the execution feels archaic — aiming is purely horizontal, all walls are perpendicular, and each floor sits on a single flat plane — yet it's exactly this economy that kept the pace up. Digitized guard screams, barking dogs, and an energetic soundtrack courtesy of Ad Lib and Sound Blaster cards gave the game a raw, comic-book-exaggerated aggression that etched itself into memory just as strongly as the visuals.

The game spread through the shareware model, with the first episode circulating freely while the rest was ordered separately, which opened its way onto BBSes, floppy disk collections, and school computers around the world. It sparked the first great wave of imitators, and for years the whole genre measured itself against it. Today Wolfenstein 3D plays surprisingly briskly: the levels are short, the pace is fast, and hunting for secret walls still has its charm, even if navigating the repetitive corridors can grow tiring. Its main value, though, lies in the experience itself — you get to feel firsthand the moment PC games first properly stepped into three-dimensional space. It helps that the game never tries to be anything other than what it is. Anyone wanting to understand why an entire branch of the games industry headed in this direction should play through the whole first episode.

pc-dos__doom.article:
**Doom** arrived at the end of 1993 and pushed everything its own creators had established a year earlier. The player is a nameless space marine at the bases on Phobos and Deimos, where teleporter experiments tore open a passage to hell. The narrative unfolds across a few lines between episodes; all the attention goes to the level-by-level progression itself: hunting for colored keycards, opening elevators and platforms, dodging traps filled with toxic sludge, and above all fighting hordes of demons whose behavior and strength combine differently in every room. The arsenal, from the shotgun through the chainsaw to the plasma rifle and the BFG, remains one of the best balanced in the genre's history.

The engine represented a huge leap over its predecessor. Levels were no longer a grid of perpendicular walls; they could have varying floor and ceiling heights, slanted walls, staircases, changing lighting, and flickering lights, turning the environments into real places rather than mere corridors. The game also supported multiplayer combat over a network, and it's from here that the term deathmatch spread. Equally crucial was the openness of the data format: the community soon began creating its own levels and modifications, giving rise to a creative scene that still functions today. Oppressive sound effects, demons roaring out of the dark, and rhythmic music completed an atmosphere somewhere between an action film and a horror movie.

At the time it was an enormous phenomenon that spread through shareware channels as fast as gossip and became an argument for buying a more powerful computer and sound card. At the same time, due to its bloodiness and hellish iconography, it became a target of criticism outside gaming media. Today Doom has aged remarkably well: movement is fast, levels are clear and legible, and combat is built on movement and spatial judgment rather than cover and waiting. It's one of the few games from the early nineties recommendable even without a nostalgia surcharge. Its influence doesn't end with the genre either — thanks to countless later ports to all sorts of devices, it became something of a benchmark for what a computer can run, and it remains one of the best-documented titles in the medium's history.

pc-dos__doom-ii-hell-on-earth.article:
**Doom II: Hell on Earth** came out in 1994 as a full-fledged sequel that doesn't bet on a technical revolution but on expanding and refining what already worked. This time hell has spilled over onto Earth, and the player fights through devastated cities, industrial complexes, and finally hell itself across thirty consecutive levels with no division into episodes. The map design is noticeably more generous and intricate than in the first game, with sprawling outdoor spaces, tougher jumps, and trickier enemy placement that forces the player to plan movement ahead of time.

The most visible addition is the double-barreled shotgun, a weapon with a slow reload and a devastating blast at close range that fundamentally changed the rhythm of combat and remains one of the best-designed pieces of the genre's arsenal to this day. A whole range of new opponents also arrived, including an enemy capable of reviving fallen foes and others that fire homing projectiles or summon reinforcements, turning fights into more complex situations where the order in which you eliminate targets — and who you turn against whom — really matters. The engine stayed the same, but the designers squeezed more out of it, and some levels play out like open arenas.

Reception was very strong, and the game sold through traditional retail rather than shareware, making it one of the commercial pillars of its era. Even more important was its impact on the community: it was precisely the Doom II dataset that became the standard for which thousands of amateur maps and extensive campaigns were built, and the creation of new content for it hasn't stopped to this day. It plays practically as well as the first game, just with higher difficulty and more chaotic firefights. For a newcomer it makes sense to start with the first game; for anyone it clicked with, the sequel is an obvious next step. It's worth adding that it was here that id Software's design took on the shape community creators still return to today, and many now-acclaimed amateur campaigns rank among the best the genre has to offer. The sequel is thus not just a continuation, but above all a foundation for decades of further creation.

pc-dos__system-shock.article:
**System Shock** from 1994 combined a first-person perspective with a depth that shooters of the time simply didn't have. The player wakes from a medically induced sleep aboard the orbital station Citadel and discovers that the artificial intelligence SHODAN has taken control of everything that moves, turning the crew into cyborgs and corpses. Progress isn't linear: each deck is an interwoven complex of laboratories, storage areas, and maintenance shafts where you look for access codes, switch systems, hack electronics, and gradually piece together what happened aboard the station. The story is carried through a network of found audio logs and emails, an approach that would go on to settle into the genre for decades.

Technically the game was staggering for its time. The environment is fully three-dimensional; you can look up and down, lean, crouch, jump, and move in zero gravity. The interface covered a large part of the screen and offered management of inventory, implants, and cybernetic upgrades, letting the player tailor the character to their own style. Also included is cyberspace, an abstract wireframe flight sequence where you break through data locks. The sound is claustrophobic, the music shifts with the situation, and SHODAN, with her decaying, digitally glitching voice, ranks among the truly unforgettable villains.

Critics welcomed the game very warmly at the time, but commercially it never reached the popularity of purely action-oriented titles, partly due to its complex controls, which demanded patience and a great many keys. A later CD release added voiced dialogue and made the game significantly more accessible. Its influence, though, is enormous: the whole line of immersive sims, where the player deals with space and systems rather than simply pulling a trigger, traces back to here. Today the entry barrier is tough because of the controls, but anyone who pushes through finds a surprisingly modern-feeling game. What stands out most is how little it holds the player's hand: the station opens up gradually, and plenty of connections stay hidden from anyone who doesn't read the logs and explore the corners. It's from exactly that that the feeling of genuine discovery arises, one that's hard to find in later games.

pc-dos__ultima-underworld-stygian-abyss.article:
**Ultima Underworld: The Stygian Abyss** came out in 1992 and was the first major proof that a real world, not just a maze, could exist in first-person view. The hero is accused of a kidnapping and thrown into a giant underground complex, from which he must find a way out while rescuing the abducted girl. The eight sprawling levels aren't a collection of random corridors but an inhabited environment with its own logic: clans of dwarves, wanderers, merchants, and whole cultures of monsters live here, and you can talk to them, trade with them, and complete tasks for them. Violence is just one of several ways to get further.

The technical execution was extraordinary for the early nineties. Space is textured in every direction, floors slope, there are bridges, chasms, swimming in water, and the ability to look up and down. On top of that comes an extensive simulation: the player cooks food, repairs weapons, splits items, collects runestones and assembles them into spells, reads scrolls and notes, and keeps a journal. Lighting plays a role, so without a torch or a light spell it's practically impossible to find your way deep in the Abyss. The sound is restrained, which makes the echo of footsteps and the oppressive silence of the underground work all the better.

Critics received the game enthusiastically, calling it a technical and design breakthrough, though commercially it stood in the shadow of simpler, faster action games that followed shortly after. Its true legacy showed only with time: the idea of a continuous, physically and socially believable space viewed through your own eyes became the foundation of an entire development lineage. Today, playing it is demanding mainly because of the mouse-driven interface and the lack of modern mapping conveniences, but the feeling of discovering the depths remains powerful and, in many ways, more authentic than in more modern games. It works especially well how the player gradually learns to read the Abyss — learning shortcuts, remembering where a merchant lives, and turning hostility into truce. The underground thus turns from a threat into a place you make your own.

pc-dos__ultima-underworld-ii-labyrinth-o.article:
**Ultima Underworld II: Labyrinth of Worlds** followed up the breakthrough first game in 1993 and expanded its concept from a single underground to a whole set of distinct worlds. The hero, along with other guests, is trapped in Lord British's castle, which has been encased in a giant crystal of black rock. The only way out leads through portals hidden inside that very crystal, and each one opens onto a different area with its own rules, inhabitants, and atmosphere — from a flooded prison through an icy wasteland to environments where the player must contend with a deeply hostile setting and society alike. The castle serves as a permanent home base to return to, where you talk with fellow prisoners and push the story forward.

Gameplay-wise it's an expansion of the tried and tested. Once again you look up and down, swim, climb, assemble spells from runes, cook, repair equipment, and above all talk a great deal, because many obstacles have diplomatic or logical solutions. The engine got minor improvements in richer rendering and the ability to display more varied environments, which came in handy since the visual diversity of the individual worlds is the main draw. The scope is noticeably larger than the first game's, and the game is also more merciless in how easily you can get lost or miss an important item.

Contemporary reviews were favorable, though there were complaints that the rapid switching between worlds disrupted the cohesion that the first game's continuous underground had. Commercially it was a solid rather than a breakthrough success, and the series never got another sequel. Even so, it remains one of the most ambitious RPGs of its time, and for anyone the first game clicked with, it's the logical next step. It plays similarly today: the controls and inventory management demand patience, but exploring the worlds still holds strong appeal, and the maps rank among the most thoughtfully designed the genre has produced. Anyone willing to take their own notes and experiment with spells and conversation will find surprisingly much freedom in how to solve individual obstacles. It's precisely this trust in the player that makes people return to both games after all these years.

pc-dos__spear-of-destiny.article:
**Spear of Destiny** is a standalone episode from 1992 that sends B.J. Blazkowicz on a mission preceding the events of the main game. The goal is to recover a spear the Nazi leadership credits with supernatural power, and the player fights through twenty-one levels in one continuous run with no division into episodes. The core mechanics remain unchanged: a maze of corridors and halls, keys opening locked doors, secret walls hiding treasure and health kits, guards reacting to gunfire, and an escalating stream of enemies with every floor.

The additions are mostly cosmetic, but noticeable. The environments got new texture sets, giving the game a distinct look from the original campaign; new collectible items were added, and above all a series of original boss fights against supernatural opponents with behavior patterns different from regular guards, forcing the player to conserve ammunition. Difficulty is higher from the start, since the title assumed players had already mastered the base game. Technically it runs on exactly the same foundation, so you get the same smooth movement, digitized voice lines, and driving sound-card music.

Unlike the original game, Spear of Destiny wasn't sold as shareware but through traditional boxed retail, which made it something of a bonus, yet full-fledged, addition to the catalog. At the time it was received warmly, albeit with the note that it's more of the same and that the technology was aging fast in the meantime. Today it plays exactly like the original Wolfenstein 3D: fast, straightforward, with a pleasant dose of secret-room hunting. It's the ideal choice for anyone who finished the main game and wants one more dose of the same rhythm, just a bit sharper. Its shorter length is actually an advantage: the game doesn't overstay its welcome, and the final escalation arrives exactly when it should. It's also worth noting that this was the first time B.J. Blazkowicz's world took on an openly supernatural dimension, one that later sequels would build on.

pc-dos__catacomb-3-d.article:
**Catacomb 3-D** is, from today's perspective, the missing link between early action games and the rise of first-person shooters on PC. It came out in 1991, and the player takes on the role of a wizard descending into catacombs full of skeletons, monsters, and the undead in order to stop a dark threat. Instead of a gun, magic bolts shoot from the hand; scrolls, potions, and keys are collected, and progress moves through a series of levels made up of corridors, secret passages, and rooms hiding secret treasure. Walls can be broken by spell in certain spots, creating the pleasant sense that space isn't untouchable.

The technical side is what matters most. It was one of the first titles where the player moved through a textured three-dimensional space from their own perspective, and in the sixteen-color EGA mode at that. Visible on screen is the character's outstretched hand, an unusual and very striking detail at the time that strengthened identification with the hero. There's no looking up or down, floors are flat and walls perpendicular, but movement was smooth on the hardware of the era. The sound design is restrained, and the atmosphere is carried more by the dread of dark corridors and unexpected encounters than by a musical score.

The game came out outside its era's main distribution channels and never reached mass popularity, so for a long time it was known mainly by collectors and enthusiasts of the genre's history. Its significance, however, is undeniable, because the technology tested here led directly to what followed over the next two years and made an entire studio famous. Today it's a short, raw, and surprisingly focused affair that can be finished in a single afternoon. This wizard's take on what soon became the standard also carries a distinctive flavor that later military and sci-fi shooters would lose. It's also interesting how well the simple idea of controlling a wizard instead of a soldier works — the magic bolts have a different rhythm than firearms, and undead enemies force the player to back off and keep their distance. For understanding the genre's development, it's a couple of hours well spent.

pc-dos__heretic.article:
**Heretic** arrived at the tail end of 1994 and showed that the technology behind Doom also works in fantasy dress. The player takes on an elven hero whose people have been wiped out and who sets off for revenge against the first of three brothers who have seized control of his world. Instead of shotguns and plasma rifles, the arsenal holds a staff, a crossbow spewing bolts, the dragon claw, and other magic weapons, each of which can be powered up by a collected artifact and temporarily turned into a much more devastating variant. The settings are gothic cathedrals, ramparts, swamps, and underground temples soaked in damp and mysticism.

Compared to its template, Heretic brought several substantial changes. Most visible is the ability to look up and down, which helps in the more vertically layered levels. Equally crucial is the inventory, where you store potions, scrolls, an hourglass that slows time, or feathers that let you fly, letting the player choose exactly when to use them; that adds a tactical layer purely action-driven predecessors didn't have. Moving environmental elements and wind that carries the hero also arrived. The sound design leans on booming footsteps, hoarse enemy roars, and darkly orchestral music that stands well apart from Doom's industrial rhythm.

At the time the game was well received and confirmed that licensed technology can carry its own distinctive work. It also opened the way to a sequel that pushed the fantasy action concept even further. Today Heretic is a great addition for anyone who's finished the classic id Software shooters and wants a similar rhythm in a different setting. It plays fast, the levels are clear, and the artifact system keeps things interesting even after several hours. A newcomer just needs to expect that the weapons feel a bit softer than the iconic shotgun they're used to. Also worth mentioning is a small detail players quickly grew fond of: enemies hit by stronger weapons literally vanish in spectacular disintegrations, and the whole world feels more tangible than in its template. The fantasy setting also still stands out among action games of this type today, which helps the game age better than one might expect.

pc-dos__shadowcaster.article:
**ShadowCaster** from 1993 is one of the most fascinating detours in the early era of first-person games. The player takes on the role of a young man who discovers he carries the legacy of an ancient line of shapeshifters, gradually gaining the ability to transform into six different forms. Each one has its own speed, stamina, attack, and special ability: one swims effortlessly, another withstands heat, while others excel in close combat or can cast spells. Progressing through the levels isn't just about shooting — it's about figuring out which form suits the situation, since each shape's energy drains as it's used.

Technically, the game builds on the lineage started by Wolfenstein 3D, but pushes it further — it features floors and ceilings of varying heights, transparent surfaces, a textured sky, and impressive transformation animations that take up a large part of the screen. The environments are varied, ranging from underground temples through lava caverns to flooded areas, and rely heavily on colorful palettes and atmospheric lighting. The music and sound design work with a dark, adventurous tone, and each transformation is backed by a sound that gives it weight. The story is carried through cutscenes between chapters.

Reception was warm, though the game fell between genres: too slow and intricate for a purely action-focused audience, yet too shallow in character development for RPG fans. As a result, it's remembered today by a smaller circle of people than it deserves. Still, the idea of changing your body to suit an obstacle anticipates later games where the player chooses an approach rather than a single path. Today, ShadowCaster comes across as an endearingly inventive stepping stone — shorter, but imaginative, with good pacing and a visual style that keeps its own identity. Its sensible length also helps, letting the game introduce all the forms and give the player time to play with them without becoming repetitive. Anyone looking for something other than yet another military shooter in the genre's history will find it here.

pc-dos__cyclones.article:
**CyClones** launched in 1994 as a sci-fi shooter that tried to offer something its contemporaries lacked: independent hand aiming via the mouse. Where other games had the player turn their whole body while the projectile always flew toward the center of the screen, here movement is handled by the keyboard while the mouse independently moves a crosshair across the screen, letting you shoot sideways, up, or down without changing your walking direction. The story is built around an invasion of cybernetic machines, and the player fights through a series of complexes and bases, eliminating enemies, collecting new weapons and upgrades, and unlocking sealed sections.

Besides the aiming, the handling of equipment is also interesting. Weapons and their upgrades can be combined, and there are also gadgets that change your approach to combat, so the player doesn't just get progressively stronger rifles but also reasons to think about what to carry. Technically, the game combines a textured 3D backdrop with digitized, strikingly rendered enemy characters, whose hits land with satisfying, explicit impact. The setting is industrially cold, full of metal, pipes, and blinking panels, accompanied by grim sound design that underscores the feeling of a lone fight inside an enemy machine.

Contemporary reception was mixed. Reviewers praised the independent aiming as a clever idea, but also criticized it as unintuitive to control and more of a hindrance in fast firefights, so the game stayed in the shadow of the more popular titles of its era. In hindsight, though, it's interesting precisely for how close it came to the solution that would become standard mouse-and-keyboard control just a few years later. Today it's played more as a curiosity for genre-history enthusiasts than as fully rounded entertainment, but that curiosity is worth trying. It's fascinating to see how the developers searched for an answer to the limitations of controls at the time, and how close they got to something that became commonplace within a few years. The studio also used this project to try out ideas it would later put to good use in its much more famous fantasy action games.

pc-dos__blake-stone-aliens-of-gold.article:
**Blake Stone: Aliens of Gold** is a 1993 shooter in which the player, as a secret agent, infiltrates the complexes of mad scientist Dr. Pyra Goldfire and foils his plan to conquer the world with an army of genetically engineered creatures. The campaign is split into six episodes, and progress takes you through laboratories, mines, and research stations, opening doors, finding elevators, and clearing floor after floor. The foundation is clearly inspired by id Software's earlier hit, whose technology the game uses, but the additions on top are its own and often surprisingly well thought out.

The most interesting element is how the base's civilian population is handled. The scientists and technicians the player encounters aren't just scenery — some act as informants and offer useful hints about how to proceed, while others immediately raise the alarm or attack outright, so pulling the trigger after every encounter doesn't pay off. On top of that come an automap that greatly helps with orientation, access cards, vending machines dispensing food and extra health, and recharge stations for energy weapons. Visually, the game leans on richly colored, technical-looking environments and digitized characters with a period B-movie sci-fi flavor.

The timing, however, wasn't kind to it. It came out just a few weeks before Doom arrived and instantly pushed it into the technological past, so it received less attention than it deserved. Still, it retained a loyal following, and a sequel wasn't long in coming. Today it's a very pleasant classic for anyone who enjoys the rhythm of Wolfenstein 3D but appreciates the automap, more varied environments, and the idea of characters you can talk to instead of shoot. Its length is generous, so the game lasts longer than most of its contemporaries. In the end, it's one of the few imitators that actually added something to the formula it borrowed, rather than just swapping textures. Players who appreciate a calmer pace and floor-by-floor exploration will find a surprisingly cohesive and well-paced campaign here.

pc-dos__alone-in-dark.article:
**Alone in the Dark** from 1992 is usually cited as the first true survival horror and as one of the earliest titles to combine polygonal characters with hand-drawn backgrounds. The player chooses between a private detective and the niece of the deceased owner, entering the Louisiana mansion of Derceto to investigate the circumstances of a strange death. Within minutes it becomes clear that the house is steeped in something that has nothing to do with a rational explanation, and the game turns into a careful crawl through hallways, the attic, the cellar, and a library full of danger.

The gameplay rests on a combination of exploration, puzzles, and very sparing combat. The player searches furniture, reads diaries and books whose contents provide clues on how to defeat individual threats, moves wardrobes in front of doors to keep monsters out, and conserves ammunition, since it's desperately scarce and direct confrontation often means death. The camera sits fixed in the corners of rooms and switches on transitions, letting the developers deliberately play with what the player can't see. The low polygon count looks blocky today, but the rough shapes and dark backgrounds paradoxically strengthen the sense of something unnamable. The sound is sparse, which makes a creak or a sudden musical stinger all the more jarring.

At the time it was a sensation, praised by critics for both its technology and its courage in building a game around fear rather than action. Its influence on the genre is major: the scheme of fixed cameras, limited ammunition, and the house itself as a central character was adopted by the most famous horror series of the following generation. Today, the main obstacles are the controls, with the character turning on the spot and moving stiffly, plus merciless deaths. Anyone who can stomach these hurdles gets a short, dense, and still unpleasantly oppressive Lovecraftian night. Restraint is the game's greatest strength: there are few monsters, even less action, and the tension is sustained more by silence and anticipation. If you set your patience accordingly and accept the rules the house operates by, you get one of the best-aged horror experiences of its time.

pc-dos__magic-carpet.article:
**Magic Carpet** came out at the end of 1994 and still feels like one of the most original experiments in what can be done with a first-person view. The player is a wizard on a flying carpet, soaring over an open landscape, casting spells and trying to collect magical energy scattered across the world after a botched spell released it. But the energy isn't gathered directly — first you must slay monsters that drop it, then have it carried off by flying helpers to your own castle, which grows larger with every delivery while also needing to be defended against rival wizards.

It's precisely this fusion of action and building that makes the game exceptional. The magical arsenal ranges from simple bolts through lightning and fireballs all the way to spells that literally reshape the terrain, trigger earthquakes, or summon your own creatures. The landscape isn't just scenery: hills can be leveled, seas can be raised, and the marks of battles remain in it. Technically, it was a flagship title of its time, with sloped terrain, smooth flight, a day sky, and effects not seen elsewhere at the time; the game could even handle the experimental stereoscopic 3D displays of the era. The sound and Middle Eastern-flavored music round out the exotic mood.

Reviewers were enthusiastic above all about the technical side and the unusual combination of genres, though it was noted that the fifty levels start to repeat after a while and that orientation in open space without fixed landmarks is demanding. The concept barely got any direct successors, which makes Magic Carpet a distinctive island in the genre's history. Today it's still a fresh experience: the sense of flight is excellent, and the territorial struggle against opponents has a surprising drive, though you should expect a dense interface and the need to learn the rules. The sense of rivalry also works beautifully: an opponent's structures on the horizon grow just as yours do, giving each match a natural momentum and a clearly readable plot without a single word of story. Few games from the mid-1990s still look this distinctive today.

pc-dos__elder-scrolls-arena.article:
**The Elder Scrolls: Arena** launched in 1994 a series that, at the time, no one suspected would grow so long and so high. The player wakes up in a dungeon after the emperor is overthrown and replaced by a double, and the only path to setting things right leads through collecting eight pieces of a shattered staff scattered across the continent of Tamriel. The game is staggering in scope from the very start: it offers dozens of towns and villages traveled between on a map, each with its own shops, temples, inns, guilds, and, at night, thieves lurking in the streets. Besides the main storyline, you can endlessly take small contracts and clear randomly generated dungeons.

Combat takes place in real time from a first-person perspective and is controlled by dragging the mouse, so the direction of movement determines the type of slash or thrust. Alongside swordplay there's rich magic with the ability to compose your own spells, sneaking, lockpicking, various races with different traits, and professions ranging from warrior to mage. Technically, it's a textured 3D space with digitized enemies and impressive weather effects along with a day-night cycle, which at the time contributed significantly to the feeling of a living world. The music varies by environment and carries the atmosphere of towns and catacombs very well.

The game's launch was rough due to bugs and unfortunate release timing, and only later patches and decent reviews helped it find an audience. Its scope, freedom of movement, and near-endless playability made it a blueprint for everything that followed. Today, Arena is the most demanding entry in the series: the dungeons are long, maze-like, and merciless without a proper map, the difficulty fluctuates, and some quests are repetitive. For players interested in the series' roots, though, it's a valuable and surprisingly sprawling adventure. It's fascinating to see how many elements of later entries were already present here in basic form — from guilds to custom spellcrafting to freely roaming the countryside. Anyone who calibrates their expectations to the year of release can spend dozens of hours here.

pc-dos__maniac-mansion.article:
**Maniac Mansion** stands at the start of the modern history of point-and-click adventures. A group of high schoolers led by Dave head to a decrepit mansion on a hill, where the mad scientist Dr. Fred is holding the kidnapped girl Sandy, and for the first time the player doesn't have to guess which verb a text parser will understand. Everything is controlled with the cursor: the bottom of the screen lists commands like Open, Push, Use, or Walk to, with an inventory beside them, and sentences are built simply by clicking. It was specifically for this game that the SCUMM scripting system was created, which Lucasfilm Games and later LucasArts would then use for the entire following decade.

The second major innovation is character selection. Besides Dave, the player picks two of six friends before starting, and each one is good at something different — one is a hacker, another types, another plays keyboards — opening up different paths to a solution and giving the game several different endings. The mansion itself is one big interconnected puzzle full of secret doors, a pool of radioactive water, and family members who wander the halls and can catch the player. Characters are switched on the fly and often need to cooperate remotely, which was an unusually bold design for the time of release.

On PC, the game ran in EGA graphics with a striking cartoonish art style and PC speaker sound, later supplemented with sound card support; the atmosphere of 1950s B-movie horror shows through on every screen, from a guardian tentacle to a meteor in the basement. Contemporarily, the game also became known for the fact that you could fail irreversibly or kill a character, which was common at the time but feels harsh today. Even so, it remains readable and funny: the humor is built on absurd situations, and the reward for experimenting arrives instantly. The mansion also remembers what the player did, and the same scene can play out quite differently on a second playthrough — which is exactly what enticed players to replay the game with a different pair of friends. Maniac Mansion's influence is hard to overstate — it defined what a classic adventure game looks like, and its legacy is carried by a whole line of games that came after it.

pc-dos__zak-mckracken-and-alien-mindbend.article:
**Zak McKracken and the Alien Mindbenders** casts the player as a tabloid journalist who works his way up from writing nonsense about two-headed squirrels to uncovering a genuine alien conspiracy. Aliens are controlling humanity through a telephone switchboard and gradually dulling the intelligence of the entire planet; Zak, together with student Annie and two girls imprisoned on Mars, tries to piece together an ancient artifact that can stop the conspiracy. The game runs on an improved SCUMM engine and is controlled the same way as Maniac Mansion — by clicking verbs and objects in the bottom bar.

The key difference is in scale. Zak travels by plane across the entire globe, from San Francisco through Cairo and Kathmandu to Mexico, with Mars and sunken Atlantis added on top, and the player freely switches between four characters, passing items between them. The openness is enormous, but also demanding: money for plane tickets is limited, maps and codes had to be looked up in the accompanying printed materials, and some item combinations are quite far-fetched. That's exactly why the game has a reputation as one of the hardest adventures of its time, one that's tough to get through without your own notes.

Technically, it was a showcase DOS title of the late 1980s: an EGA palette, static screens packed with detail, and music that gained noticeably fuller sound on a better sound card than on the PC speaker. The mood is a mix of conspiracy theories, ufology, and gentle parody of tabloid journalism, giving the game its own oddly melancholic tone. It gained a cult following at the time, especially in Europe, where it's remembered more fondly today than in America. Today, Zak is interesting mainly as evidence of how ambitious adventure games could be before the studio smoothed them into a friendlier and fairer form. Anyone who enjoys adventures with a lot of travel and a bit of getting lost will find here one of the most sprawling game worlds the PC of that era offered — and, at the same time, a reminder of a time when a computer game inseparably came with a notebook full of your own notes.

pc-dos__indiana-jones-and-last-crusade-g.article:
**Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade: The Graphic Adventure** is a graphic adventure adaptation of the third film, though it doesn't settle for simply retelling the screenplay. The game follows the search for the Holy Grail from Venice through an Austrian castle to a desert temple, but adds its own locations, alternative solutions, and an IQ point system that tallies the player's score based on how elegantly they got through each problem. Controls are classic SCUMM: verbs at the bottom, inventory next to them, and sentences built with the cursor.

The most interesting part is precisely that variability. Many situations have more than one solution — some can be reached through trickery, others through persuasion, and others simply with your fists — and the game even includes simple close-quarters combat, where the player defends against an opponent's attacks. Anyone who plays it a second time via a different path gets a different score, which was by no means common at the time. Part of the experience is also Henry Jones's Grail Diary, a printed booklet with notes and sketches, without which the final puzzles involving the catacombs and markings are hard to solve; the period copy protection genuinely served the atmosphere here, for once.

On DOS the game was released in EGA graphics with backgrounds that surprisingly well captured the film's composition, and with music based on the well-known themes of the source material. A sound card made it a considerably more cinematic experience than the PC speaker. At the time it was received as proof that a licensed game didn't have to be a cash-in, and a few years later LucasArts followed it up with the even better Fate of Atlantis. Today Last Crusade is somewhat harsher and less forgiving than the studio's later titles — you can die and get stuck here — but its emphasis on player choice and multiple paths to the same goal reads surprisingly modern. Also interesting is how the game handles pacing: calm investigation in libraries and archives alternates with escapes from guards, so the player never lingers anywhere long enough to get bored. Among licensed adventure games of its era, it still ranks among the best.

pc-dos__loom.article:
**Loom** is the most unusual adventure game Lucasfilm Games ever released. The player takes on the role of Bobbin, a young man from the Weaver's Guild, whose people have vanished without a trace, and travels through a world divided among the Glassmakers', Blacksmiths', Shepherds', and other guilds. Instead of an inventory and verbs, he has a single tool at his disposal — a magical distaff on which four-note melodies are played. Every spell is a note sequence the player learns by ear, straight from the world around them: greening from a budding sprout, opening from an opened chest, and the same melody played backwards does the exact opposite.

This single mechanic carries the entire game and makes it feel more meditative than puzzle-driven. Loom is short, playable in a single long afternoon, and deliberately avoids frustration — it's practically impossible to die, and the game never hides its solutions behind an absurd combination of items. The optional difficulty setting even determines whether the player sees the notes displayed on screen or has to recognize them by ear alone, which turns the harder mode into a genuine exercise in listening and memory.

Technically, on DOS it was an EGA game with unusually soft, painted backgrounds and music built on themes from Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake, which fit the story of fate and woven threads perfectly. A later CD release brought 256 colors and spoken dialogue. At the time, Loom was received with respect, though commercially it never reached Monkey Island's numbers, and the planned sequel was never made. That's exactly why it's such a legend today: it's an elegant, quiet, and unusually mature work that showed an adventure game didn't have to be just item collecting and joking around, and that it could be built on a single strong idea carried through to the end. For today's player, it's also an ideal entry point into the genre: it never gets stuck, the game never punishes you for anything, and you can experience the whole world before you'd even have time to get tired of it. What lingers afterward, above all, is the melody you'll remember long after finishing it.

pc-dos__secret-of-monkey-island.article:
**The Secret of Monkey Island** is the game against which good adventure design is still measured today. Guybrush Threepwood arrives on Mêlée Island with a single goal — to become a pirate — and before he knows it, he must pass three pirate trials, fall in love with Governor Elaine Marley, and stand up to the undead Captain LeChuck.
