The marine creeps through dark corridors with a flashlight and a motion tracker whose beeping ranks among the most nerve-wracking sounds in the genre's history. The Xenomorph runs across walls and ceilings, attacks up close, and navigates by feel in the dark, so the player has to master a disorienting freedom of movement. The Predator hunts from a distance, switches vision modes, uses cloaking, and collects trophies.

The three perspectives on the same environment work brilliantly, since a place you crept through in terror as a marine you later occupy from the predator's position. The original release was also notorious for its harsh difficulty, since you couldn't save at will and a mission had to be completed in one go, turning every advance into a tense gamble. Later releases eased the rules. Technically the game relied on colorful dynamic lighting, translucent effects, and smooth performance on the accelerators of the time, and although the environments are mostly metal corridors, the handling of darkness and sound holds the horror atmosphere together far better than texture detail ever could.

Contemporary reception was largely very favorable, and the game kept a strong multiplayer community, since asymmetric combat between three different species was something unique at the time. It's still considered one of the finest adaptations of both film franchises and a template that later attempts drew on as well. Today it's strongest as a horror experience: the marine campaign can still get you out of your chair, and the Xenomorph's movement hasn't lost its strangeness. Somewhat sparse levels and raw storytelling, though, give away its release year.

pc-9x__soldier-of-fortune.article:
**Soldier of Fortune** sends the player into the role of a mercenary chasing stolen nuclear weapons around the world, from the New York subway through Siberian complexes to locations in Africa and Asia. The structure is classically mission-based, meaning progress through corridors, objective completion, and firefights against huge numbers of armed enemies, but the game stands out for its weapons. The arsenal is largely based on real-world models, each weapon has a secondary fire mode and distinct behavior, so a shotgun, a sniper rifle, and a flamethrower all really handle differently. Good pacing helps too, alternating open firefights with quieter stretches and squadmate escorts.

What people talked about most was the localized-damage system, which could tell exactly where a bullet landed and change both the enemy's reaction and its model accordingly. The result was an extreme level of brutality for its time, which got the game released in trimmed versions in some countries and made it a fixture in debates about violence in games. The developers aimed for a realistic touch too, working with an expert with real combat deployment experience on mission design. Technically the game was built on modified Quake II technology, so it ran smoothly even on weaker rigs of the day, with hardware acceleration support and quality weapon sound.

Contemporary reviews praised the gameplay and weapon handling, with criticism aimed at the repetitive environments and the fact that the story is little more than an excuse. Even so, the game found a large audience and got a sequel. Its influence is mainly technical, since it showed that more precise hit reactions could dramatically change the feel of shooting, and similar systems later showed up elsewhere. Today Soldier of Fortune is a legible period action title with excellently tuned shooting, but it lacks variety, and its portrayal of violence may be uncomfortable for some players.

pc-9x__operative-no-one-lives-forever.article:
**The Operative: No One Lives Forever** is a spy action game that pokes fun at the sixties and secret-agent movies without ever ceasing to be a good game in its own right. The player takes on agent Cate Archer, who works her way up from a rank-and-file employee of a secret organization to uncovering a conspiracy, visiting Morocco, Germany, a sinking ship, a Siberian base, and even an orbital station along the way. Missions combine stealth, firefights, and objective completion, and the game never forces the player into a single solution: you can sneak past guards, eavesdrop on conversations, pick locks, or simply pull out a gun and go loud.

The game's character comes from its gadgets: a listening device hidden in a powder compact, a hairpin for picking locks, perfume that works as a sleeping gas, or a lighter that doubles as a welding torch. The enemy guards' dialogue ranks among the funniest ever written in the genre, since it's scripted as little comic sketches that the player only hears by taking the trouble to move quietly. Technically the game was built on the LithTech engine, which handled sprawling outdoor scenes, colorful environments, and decent character animation, and although it could be demanding on period computers, its visual style with bold colors and period-poster-inspired graphic design has aged well. The music, with its spy jazz and beat-driven themes, ties the whole thing together.

Critics received the game enthusiastically and ranked it among the best titles of its year, though commercial results fell far short of the acclaim. Even so, it earned a devoted following, got a sequel, and still comes up today in discussions of games that deserve a comeback. Its influence shows up in action titles that mix humor, style, and freedom of approach instead of stark realism. Today it's one of the most charismatic shooters of its era, marred only by period quirks like occasionally punishing difficulty or missions where a single mistake means it's over.

pc-9x__counter-strike.article:
**Counter-Strike** began as a community modification of Half-Life and received a standalone release in 2000 without losing any of its rawness. The rules remain the same to this day: two teams, terrorists and a counter-terrorist unit, clash in short rounds with no respawning. Whoever falls watches the rest of the round as a spectator, which turns every duel into a decision with consequences. The objectives are simple and clear, whether planting and defusing a bomb or freeing hostages, and between rounds players buy equipment with money earned from performance, so even the team's economy becomes a tactical layer.

It was precisely this combination of simple rules and enormous depth that made Counter-Strike a phenomenon. The weapons have a realistic feel, pronounced recoil, and distinct spray patterns that players learn by heart; movement is slower and louder than in arena shooters, so listening for footsteps is a fully-fledged skill. Maps like a dusty desert alley or a small Italian town became as familiar to a whole generation of players as real places. Technically the game ran on the GoldSrc engine, meaning it was undemanding even on weaker computers, which was a crucial reason for its spread during the heyday of internet cafés and local networks.

The reception at the time was enormous, and Counter-Strike became the most-played online action game of its era, with later versions keeping the community together for years. It practically founded the modern competitive scene, since leagues, tournaments, and professional teams grew up around it before the term "esports" was in common use. Every later round-based shooter with equipment purchasing carries its influence. It can still be played today and feels surprisingly current, since its essence has barely changed in later installments. Anyone who wants to touch the roots of the genre starts right here.

pc-9x__blood.article:
**Blood** is the maddest and bloodiest of the great shooters built on the Build engine, and it still plays like a carnival horror ride today. The player takes on the role of the resurrected gunslinger Caleb, betrayed by a cult of a dark deity, and sets out on a path of revenge through graveyards, abandoned hotels, carnivals, trains, and frozen fortresses. The basics are classic: finding keys, secret rooms, switches, and hordes of enemies, but the arsenal is unmistakable. A pitchfork, dynamite, a lighter-spray combo, a double-barreled shotgun, a voodoo doll, and a magical fire item together form an arsenal that is equal parts weapon and toy.

The enemies are merciless, and the game prides itself on the fact that cultists carry weapons just as deadly as the player's and use them from a distance and from ambush, so the difficulty is high and rewards caution as well as knowledge of the levels. The level design is one of the highlights of its era, since the environments feel like places with purpose, full of small scenes, traps, and horror set pieces. The atmosphere is held together by a dark palette, film references scattered throughout the levels, and the black humor of the protagonist, who comments on events with one-liners. Technically it's a software-rendered game that handled environmental destruction, sloped floors, water, and shooting in every direction, but it did not make use of hardware acceleration.

At the time, Blood was received very well, though it was somewhat overshadowed amid the deafening competition of the emerging fully three-dimensional shooters. Its cult following endured, however, and the game is now considered one of the peaks of the so-called Build era, alongside other classics from the late nineties. Thanks to modern ports and community engines, it runs without trouble on today's computers too. It feels raw, fast, and hard, with a difficulty that forgives no one, but its inventiveness with weapons and levels outshines many a newer action game.

pc-9x__turok-dinosaur-hunter.article:
**Turok: Dinosaur Hunter** brought to PC a jungle full of dinosaurs, alien technology, and enemies charging out of thick fog. The player takes on the role of a Native American warrior guarding the border between worlds and fights their way through the Lost Land, where prehistoric creatures mix with armed soldiers and cyborgs. The structure is episodic: each level is a sprawling maze of platforms, caves, temples, and rivers in which the player collects keys, seeks out secrets, and gathers pieces of a powerful artifact needed for the final battle. Alongside shooting there's a lot of jumping and climbing, which was not common in the genre at the time.

The arsenal is among the best the game has to offer, combining a bow with silent shots, classic pistols and shotguns, and heavy sci-fi tech that literally tears opponents apart. Fights with dinosaurs feel different from firefights with humans, since the animals attack up close, quickly, and in packs. The PC version used hardware acceleration and offered higher resolution and a cleaner picture than players knew from the console, but the thick fog around the player remained a signature feature here too, since it masked the draw distance while also lending the environment a sense of unease. The sound works with distant roars, drums, and the hum of the jungle, holding the atmosphere together very well.

The original console version was a huge success at the time, and the brand followed up with further installments. The PC release met with a somewhat more mixed reception, since by 1997 it was competing on computers against the genre's cutting edge, but the visual work and the sheer size of the levels were praised. Today Turok is interesting mainly as an intersection of console and PC shooter design schools, with an emphasis on exploration and platforming sections. First-person jumping and easy disorientation are its biggest weaknesses, but modern remastered releases have significantly improved both visibility and controls.

pc-9x__diablo-ii.article:
**Diablo II** arrived in 2000 as the sequel to a game that had defined the action RPG four years earlier, and it turned that recipe into a genre standard for years to come. The player chooses one of five characters, each with its own combat style, and moves through four acts that lead from desert towns through the jungle all the way to hell itself. Control is purely mouse-driven: you click on enemies, gather piles of randomly generated loot, and put points into extensive skill trees whose combinations make each character play almost like a different game. Randomly assembled levels and endless item variations meant the world changed with every new character, and that's exactly what kept players glued to the screen for hundreds of hours.

Technically, Diablo II was built on a classic two-dimensional isometric engine with hand-drawn sprites, which could optionally be accelerated via Direct3D or Glide. On the 3D cards of the time, dynamic lighting and transparency effects were added, which suited the dark dungeons and rainy nights very well, while in software mode the game ran without trouble even on weaker Pentiums. A resolution of 800x600 counted as a pleasant step up, and the whole visual design was crafted to stay readable even with dozens of enemies on screen. The atmosphere is held together by Matt Uelmen's music, whose acoustic guitar from the Rogue encampment is among the most memorable themes of its era, along with sound design full of grinding metal, distant screams, and hollow underground echoes.

At the time it was a massive success, and the Battle.net service turned the game into a social affair where items were traded and characters built according to shared guides. Its influence on the genre is hard to overstate, since an entire generation of later loot games builds on the structure that Diablo II honed to perfection. Today it still feels surprisingly fresh: the controls are instantly understandable, the pace is fast, and the loop of hunting for better gear works just as well as it did twenty years ago. Its age mainly shows in the narrow inventory and the lack of modern conveniences, though a wide range of community support exists to address that.

pc-9x__baldur-s-gate-ii-shadows-of-amn.article:
**Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn** was released in 2000 and still stands as one of the pinnacles of the classic computer RPG. The story follows on from the fate of the descendant of the god of murder, who wakes up in the torture chamber of the wizard Irenicus and then sets out into the wealthy and corrupt city of Athkatla in the land of Amn. The player leads a party of up to six characters; combat plays out in real time with the option to pause at any moment and issue orders, and the entire system is built on the rules of Advanced Dungeons and Dragons. Alongside the main storyline, the game offers a huge number of side quests, companions' personal stories, romances, and even the chance to build your own stronghold based on your chosen profession.

The game runs on the Infinity Engine, meaning two-dimensional, hand-painted backgrounds with an isometric view and characters rendered as sprites. The result ages remarkably well, since the backdrops of Athkatla, the underground passages, or the elven city are essentially paintings that don't depend on graphics chip performance. On the Pentium-based systems of the time with a few dozen megabytes of memory, the game ran smoothly; only the installation took up a lot of space by the standards of the day. The sound design pairs orchestral themes with an extremely extensive voice cast, which gives the companions a strong personality and noticeably contributes to players still remembering them years later.

Critics received the game exceptionally warmly, praising above all its scope, the quality of its writing, and the freedom with which one can proceed. The Throne of Bhaal expansion brought the story to its conclusion, and the whole became the yardstick by which new party-based RPGs are still judged today. Its influence can be seen across a whole range of later games that adopted the combination of pausable tactical combat with a heavily narrated campaign. Today it requires a bit of patience, since the rules of the second edition are occasionally unintuitive and the player has to learn to read the combat system, but the reward is one of the densest fantasy adventures ever released on PC. Modern re-releases also address resolution and controls, making entry considerably easier.

pc-9x__fallout-2.article:
**Fallout 2** expanded the post-apocalyptic vision of the first game in 1998 to a scale few expected at the time. The player begins as the Chosen One, descendant of the hero from the first game, and sets out from the impoverished village of Arroyo to find a device that can save their tribe. The journey leads through the casinos of New Reno, cities ruled by criminal families, all the way to a secret organization with its own vision for humanity's future. The game uses the SPECIAL system, meaning seven basic attributes complemented by skills and special traits that fundamentally change the style of play. Combat is turn-based and works with action points and aimed shots at individual body parts, so even an ordinary skirmish demands careful thought.

Technically, it's an isometric two-dimensional engine with pre-rendered graphics that ran reliably on an ordinary Windows 95 or 98 setup and did not require 3D acceleration. The world is divided into locations connected by a wasteland map, across which travel carries the risk of random encounters. The visuals lean on dirty browns and grays, a retro-futuristic design straight out of the 1950s, and black humor hidden in item descriptions. Mark Morgan's music works with ambient soundscapes and dark synthetic themes that underscore the wasteland with silence rather than melody, and the result counts among the best-realized atmospheres of its time.

Reviews praised above all its freedom: almost any task can be solved through violence, persuasion, stealth, or circumvention, and the game rarely tells the player they're not allowed to do something. At the same time, it was known at release for a considerable number of bugs, which were addressed through patches and later community fixes. Its influence on the genre was significant, since Fallout 2 showed how an RPG could combine moral grayness, satire, and open-ended problem solving. Today entry is harder due to an unfriendly interface and a tough start where the character is very weak, but anyone who pushes through will find a game that, in freedom of decision-making, still outdoes most new titles.

pc-9x__icewind-dale.article:
**Icewind Dale** arrived in 2000 as the tougher, more combat-focused cousin of the great narrative RPGs of the time. It takes place in the frozen north of Faerûn, in the region of Icewind Dale, where a group of adventurers sets out to investigate strange events around remote settlements and gradually gets caught up in a much larger conflict. The key difference from its competitors is that the player creates the entire party themselves, from race and class to portrait, so instead of ready-made companions with their own stories you get a lineup exactly to your own liking. The game is built on the rules of Advanced Dungeons and Dragons, and real-time combat with pause makes up most of the playtime.

Under the hood runs the same Infinity Engine as other titles of its generation, but with noticeably richer artwork. The hand-painted backgrounds of snowy plains, ice caves, and dwarven halls are among the most beautiful that two-dimensional isometric RPGs ever offered, and thanks to the static graphics they still look good on today's monitors. Demands on period computers were modest, since the engine didn't need 3D acceleration and relied on the processor and memory. Jeremy Soule's music lends the whole thing an epic, cold edge and is one of the reasons players remember the game above all as a mood piece, carrying a sense of wintry isolation.

Reception at the time was welcoming, although reviewers noted that the story was simpler and more linear than in related games and that the focus lay on a continuous chain of battles. But that's exactly what earned the game its own audience, which appreciates tactical party planning, spell management, and gradually building a lineup from scratch. The Heart of Winter expansion further expanded the difficulty and scope. Today Icewind Dale is an ideal choice for a player who wants a classic isometric RPG without dozens of hours of dialogue, but with honest tactics and a strong atmosphere of wintry wilderness. It demands patience with the rules, but the reward is a very clean and clear gameplay loop.

pc-9x__might-and-magic-vi-mandate-of-hea.article:
**Might and Magic VI: The Mandate of Heaven** brought the old and respected RPG series into fully three-dimensional worlds in 1998, without sacrificing what made it distinctive. The player assembles a four-member party, which is then controlled as a single unit while traversing the open continent of Enroth. Exploration is completely free, so right from the start you can wander into an area where the enemies are several orders of magnitude stronger. Combat has a clever dual mode: it runs in real time, but can be switched to turn-based mode at any moment, allowing precise timing of spells and attacks even amid a rush of large monster groups.

Technically, the game used an engine with three-dimensional terrain and buildings, but with enemies and items rendered as sprites, which was a sensible choice in 1998 for computers without a powerful 3D card. The result ran on ordinary Windows 95 setups and offered huge, continuous maps with time of day, weather, and dungeons that often stretch on for hours. Visually it's a colorful, at times almost fairy-tale fantasy that isn't afraid of sci-fi elements hidden beneath the world's surface. The music works with melodic themes for individual regions and temples and noticeably helps distinguish areas from one another, so players remember the map partly by sound.

Reception at the time was very warm, since the game offered a scope that was hard to find elsewhere then, along with the classic feeling of discovery without guiding arrows. Critics pointed out the repetitive design of some dungeons and the fact that the final sections feel excessively long, but admiration for the freedom of movement prevailed. The series followed up its success with further installments and cemented its place alongside other major franchises of the eighties and nineties. Today it's a game for the patient: it demands mapping, notes, and a willingness to get lost, but in return offers a sense of genuine adventure without a hand guiding the player along.

pc-9x__ultima-online.article:
**Ultima Online** opened the gates to a persistent online world back in 1997, at a time when most players were still connecting through a modem. Thousands of people simultaneously inhabited the continent of Britannia, where there were no classic character levels, only a skill system that grew through whatever the player actually did. It was possible to live as a blacksmith, fisherman, tailor, miner, or healer, build your own house on free land, and trade with other players. It was precisely this effort to simulate a functioning society, complete with an economy and the risk of another player stripping you of all your belongings, that made the game more than just a combat adventure against monsters.

Technically it was a two-dimensional isometric client that deliberately kept its requirements modest so that anyone with an ordinary Pentium and a slow connection could play. The world was, at the same time, remarkably interactive: items could be placed on the ground, combined, crafted into other things, and left lying wherever the player forgot them. Visually it has a warm, hand-drawn style that has aged better than the early three-dimensional attempts at the same thing. The sound is restrained, but this only makes the melodies borrowed and expanded from the Ultima series tradition stand out more, giving the world a sense of home and tying it to the older entries.

At the time it was a breakthrough, since the game showed that a subscription for access to a shared world could work as a business model. It also became a textbook of the problems online worlds bring, from player-killing through economic inflation to the necessity of administrator intervention. Later titles drew from it directly and indirectly, and many of their solutions arose as a reaction to what had gone wrong in Britannia. Today Ultima Online is interesting mainly as a historical document and as a game for those who want freedom without quest arrows. What's more, the official servers still run today, and the community remains surprisingly alive.

pc-9x__ultima-ix-ascension.article:
**Ultima IX: Ascension** closed out one of the longest and most influential RPG series in history in 1999, making the transition to a fully three-dimensional world. The player once again takes on the role of the Avatar and returns to Britannia, which is gripped by the influence of an ancient enemy and giant columns that have corrupted the lands tied to the series' virtues. Progress is organized around a journey between individual regions, purifying shrines and solving local problems, while the game combines exploration, simple real-time combat, and the classic item and inventory handling the series was always proud of.

Technically it was a very ambitious project: a seamless open world with no loading screens between areas, a day-night cycle, weather, and fully three-dimensional cities were extraordinarily demanding for 1999. This is precisely what became its main weakness, since the game required a powerful computer with a 3D accelerator on release and still suffered from performance drops and bugs. Visually, though, it offered regions that looked picturesque and inviting to explore, and the orchestral music ranks among the best the series ever had. Voiced dialogue and the ability to search houses, pick up items, and fiddle with small details kept the spirit of the older entries alive even in a new coat.

Contemporary reception was mixed. Some players and reviewers criticized the technical state, the simplifications compared to previous entries, and a story treatment that did not always respect the rules of the world, while other voices praised the atmosphere and the boldness of translating such a vast franchise into three dimensions. The series effectively ended with this entry, and the game became a symbol of an entire era's transition from two-dimensional worlds to three-dimensional ones. Today it is a title mainly for fans and genre historians: with patches and modern fixes it runs more stably than it once did, offering one last look at the Britannia the Ultima series built over almost two decades.

pc-9x__nox.article:
**Nox** arrived in 2000 with an idea unusual for action RPGs of the time: the game can be completed with three classes, each with its own campaign featuring different locations, a different order of events, and a different style of play. The main hero is an ordinary person pulled into a fantasy world, where he becomes a warrior relying on precisely timed strikes, a wizard building on ranged spells, or a conjurer who controls monsters and sets traps. Controls are fast and action-oriented, spells can be pre-learned into quick slots, and combat demands movement, dodging, and careful management of mana.

Technically, the game ran on the studio's own engine with an isometric view and very carefully handled lighting and line of sight. One of its most interesting features was a system that only showed the player what they could actually see: darkness lurked around corners and behind walls, which changes tactical thinking especially in narrow corridors and in player-versus-player combat. On 2000-era rigs the game ran briskly and looked clean and colorful even without the latest graphics card. Artistically it blends fantasy with a lightly comic-book exaggeration, and the music accompanies each region with both dark and heroic motifs that give combat its momentum.

Contemporary reviews praised the game especially for its trio of campaigns, which increased replayability, and for its very well-made multiplayer with duels and team modes. It nonetheless stayed in the shadow of bigger genre names and did not commercially reach the top, over time becoming a title passed among enthusiasts. Its influence shows up more in details, for instance precisely in how it handles line of sight and in how one game can be designed as three different experiences. Today Nox feels brisk and clear, gets going quickly, and suits shorter sessions too, making it a pleasant discovery for anyone who only knows the genre's biggest names from its era and wants to add a lesser-known but inventive companion to them.

pc-9x__darkstone.article:
**Darkstone** was released in 1999 as one of the first notable attempts to bring the point-and-click, loot-collecting action RPG into three-dimensional graphics. The player picks from four classes, and unlike most of the competition, leads two characters at once, switching between them with a single button, allowing for combinations like a strong warrior paired with a wizard supporting him from a distance. The task is to gather seven stones, defeat a dragon, and free the land, but the path there leads through randomly generated dungeons, towns full of merchants, and side quests that get shuffled with every new campaign.

Technically it was a genuinely three-dimensional engine with a freely rotating camera, which was a welcome refresher at a time when most similar games still relied on two-dimensional sprites. The game required a 3D accelerator and, on the cards of the era, offered lighting effects, fog, and smooth transitions between open areas and dungeons. An interesting feature was a day-night cycle that changed enemy behavior and the appearance of towns, giving the world a rhythm. The atmosphere rests on gothic fantasy with dark castles, graveyards, and caves, accompanied by music that is more of a backdrop, letting the sounds of combat and footsteps in empty corridors stand out.

Contemporary reception was lukewarm to favorable: reviewers praised the three-dimensional treatment, the pair of characters, and the replayability, but faulted a shallower character system and a simpler story compared to the genre's biggest names. The game still found an audience and even received a console release, which was not common among similar titles. From today's perspective it is a pleasant, shorter action RPG that plays briskly and doesn't demand dozens of hours of preparation. The graphics naturally show their age, but the two-hero switching mechanic remains a fresh idea, and the whole title is an interesting reminder of how the genre searched for its way into three dimensions.

pc-9x__vampire-masquerade-redemption.article:
**Vampire: The Masquerade - Redemption** brought the famous tabletop system of vampire clans to computer screens in 2000. The story follows the crusader Christof, who is turned into a vampire in medieval Bohemia and then, after centuries, awakens in the modern world, where he must face the consequences of his curse as well as the search for a lost love. The game takes the player through four cities, two historical and two contemporary, combining real-time action combat with RPG management of attributes, disciplines, and blood, which serves as fuel for vampiric powers. The player leads a group of companions and can switch between them depending on the situation and the demands of combat.

Technically the game relied on its own three-dimensional engine with dynamic lighting and detailed models, which in 2000 made it one of the genre's more visually demanding titles. It required a 3D accelerator and a decent processor, but the reward was city streets, catacombs, and cathedrals that felt dense and dark. Special attention deserves the depiction of medieval Prague and Vienna, whose narrow alleys rank among the most memorable settings of their time. The music combines choral and orchestral motifs with dark electronica, and the main character's voice acting lends the narrative a pathos that suits gothic horror well.

The game also offered an unusual multiplayer mode in which one player acts as a storyteller, crafting a story for the others in real time, an attempt to emulate tabletop play. Reviews praised the atmosphere, visuals, and narrative boldness, but criticized the linearity and the fact that combat becomes repetitive over time and is needlessly stiff in some passages. A later game set in the same world leaned more toward roleplaying and achieved greater cult fame, but Redemption remains an interesting and atmospheric title with an unrepeatable mood. Today it will especially please those who enjoy gothic horror and long stories and don't mind older controls.

pc-9x__jagged-alliance-2.article:
**Jagged Alliance 2** put the player in 1999 in the role of a commander tasked with using the resistance's funds to liberate the fictional country of Arulco from a ruler who relies on an army and fear. The game begins at a computer: the player browses a roster of mercenaries, reads their biographies, compares prices, and hires a team through an in-game internet agency. Every mercenary has their own personality, opinions about their colleagues, and lines of dialogue, so putting together a squad is also a personnel job. What follows is turn-based combat on isometric maps with cover, aimed shots at body parts, night-time stealth, and careful management of action points, where a single mistake costs a life.

Between battles the game works as a strategy layer: the country is divided into sectors that are captured, defended, and administered, local inhabitants can be trained as militia, mines bring in money for further wages, and the enemy tries to retake lost territory. Technically it was a two-dimensional engine that needed no 3D acceleration and ran on ordinary Windows 95 and 98 rigs, yet it offered a surprisingly rich simulation: range, light, noise, individual limb injuries, and gear wear and tear. The audio stands out for its wealth of voiced lines, which give the team personality, and for mood music alternating tension with calm.

Reviews were very positive, and the game quickly built a devoted community that keeps it alive to this day with extensive mods and resolution fixes. Its influence can be seen across a whole wave of later tactical games that adopted the combination of turn-based combat and territory management in between. Today Jagged Alliance 2 is still one of the best-designed tactical games ever made, it just requires a willingness to learn: the interface is dense, the start slow, and the game has no mercy for an unprepared player. Whoever sticks with it gets a campaign of dozens of hours with enormous freedom of approach and stories the player creates themselves.

pc-9x__final-fantasy-vii.article:
**Final Fantasy VII** arrived on PC in 1998, opening the door for European and American computer owners to a Japanese RPG that until then had mostly been known to console owners. The story begins in the industrial city of Midgar, where a group of rebels fights against a corporation draining the planet's life energy, and gradually expands into a journey across the whole world after an enemy who ranks among the most famous villains in the history of games. Combat runs on a turn-based system with a gauge that measures when a character can act, and the main depth lies in the Materia system, spheres of spells and abilities that are slotted into weapons and equipment and can be freely combined.

The PC version used the same structure as the original: pre-rendered backgrounds over which three-dimensional characters move, and cinematic sequences that were extraordinarily impressive for their time. On Windows 95 and 98 it was a demanding title due to its data volume, and the game supported the 3D accelerators of the era, though compatibility varied greatly between cards and later required community fixes. Nobuo Uematsu's music ranks among the most famous game soundtracks ever, and even in the PC version, which played the original tracks in a different format, it holds the entire atmosphere together and carries the story's strongest moments.

At the time it was a major event, since the game significantly boosted the popularity of Japanese RPGs outside Japan and showed that storytelling in games could work with grand emotions. Reviews of the PC version praised the content but pointed out the technical shortcomings of the conversion. Its influence on the genre is undeniable, from structured storytelling through character work to an emphasis on cinematic sequences. Today the game shows its age visually, especially the character models in the field, which look rough, yet the story, music, and Materia system still work, and new releases and mods make the experience accessible on modern systems.

pc-9x__total-annihilation.article:
**Total Annihilation** arrived in 1997 as an answer to the question of what a real-time strategy game would look like if it weren't tied down by flat two-dimensional maps. The conflict between the Arm and Core factions is told as the tail end of a millennium-long war between two civilizations that have long forgotten why they're even fighting: one side replaced human bodies with machines, the other went its own way, and the planets between them have been burned to bare rock. The player doesn't start with a handful of villagers but with a commander mech capable of building an entire base from scratch, and the campaign gradually opens up dozens of missions on both sides of the front.

The economy rests on two continuously flowing resources, metal and energy. Instead of counting up batches, you track a balance of income and expenditure, so construction is more a question of throughput than stockpile, and wreckage of destroyed units can be recycled back into metal, turning the battlefield into a resource itself. Units are polygonal models moving across a heightmap, projectiles have real ballistics that can miss, ricochet, or hit something else entirely, and a hill in front of artillery isn't just cosmetic but an actual obstacle. On top of that come order queues, patrolling, automatic repairs, and radar coverage, tools the competition of the time was only just discovering.

Technically it was one of the first titles in the genre where you could comfortably command hundreds of units at once, and the orchestral, dynamic soundtrack lent the mass battles an unexpectedly grave, almost documentary war tone. Contemporary critics received the game very well, placing it alongside the genre's biggest names, even though it never commercially reached their scale. Its influence, though, is felt to this day: streamed economy, build queues, smart orders, and an emphasis on terrain all became standard, and a direct line runs from it to the later Supreme Commander series. The game is also kept alive by its community, unofficial patches, and open engines inspired by its design, so anyone who likes strategy games about logistics and masses of steel will still find a remarkably modern experience here.

pc-9x__warcraft-ii-tides-of-darkness.article:
**Warcraft II: Tides of Darkness** is a game that in 1995 turned real-time strategy into mass entertainment. The sequel to the first clash between humans and orcs expanded the war for Azeroth across an entire continent, added elves, trolls, dwarves, goblins, and dragons, and split the story into two parallel campaigns that can be played from either side of the conflict. Every mission has a clear objective, a short briefing, and brisk pacing, so the game works equally well as a series of short challenges and as a continuously told campaign that decides the fate of the entire world.

The core is simple and still easy to grasp today: gathering gold and wood, building a base, working through a tech tree of buildings, and producing an army. New compared to the first game were naval and aerial units, so maps suddenly offered islands, harbors, transport ships, and battles for control of the water. Real fog of war was added too, obscuring previously explored territory, turning scouting into a constant necessity. Spellcasters on both sides have their own set of abilities, from invisibility through lightning to raising the dead, and well-used magic can decide a battle that sheer numbers would have lost.

Technically the game benefited from higher resolution and more colorful, detailed graphics than was then customary, and added narrated cutscenes, a dark fantasy atmosphere, and orchestral-leaning music that became one of the brand's hallmarks. The units' quotes are legendary too, responding to repeated clicking with increasingly annoyed remarks. Multiplayer over networks and modems drew enormous acclaim; it was Warcraft II that taught entire generations of players what it means to share a map with someone who builds faster than you. A later Windows release added internet play and kept the game current well past the turn of the millennium. Today it still feels surprisingly brisk, if limited by how many units a single order can cover, and remains the shortest path to understanding where the entire Warcraft universe came from.

pc-9x__sid-meier-s-civilization-ii.article:
**Sid Meier's Civilization II** came out in 1996 and for a great many people is still the game where they first realized it was already morning. The premise remains grand: lead your own nation from a handful of settlers in the fourth millennium BC through the whole of history to a space flight to Alpha Centauri, or at least to the point where the other civilizations cease to exist. Victory can come through conquering the world or winning the science race, but the real substitute for storytelling here is the run of history itself, which the player assembles differently every time.

Compared to the first game, the view of the world changed to isometric, and above all most systems were deepened. Cities deal with citizen happiness, pollution, famine, and corruption, units now have three basic combat values instead of one, zones of control were added, and the game distinguishes between forms of government from despotism to democracy, where waging war regardless of the voters' mood is no longer possible. Wonders of the world remain the main reward for research, their completion accompanied by short cinematic sequences, the advisors in the main menu are live actors, and the Civilopedia encyclopedia turns the whole game into a history textbook in its own right.

The game shipped natively for Windows 95, so it ran in a window, supported higher resolutions, and offered comfortable mouse control, making it an ideal title for long evenings at an office computer. Critics at the time received it exceptionally well, and many outlets called it one of the best games ever. Expansions with new scenarios followed, along with a later release with multiplayer. Its influence on the genre is hard to overstate: most later turn-based strategy games work with a tech tree, wonders of the world, and city happiness exactly in the spirit that the second installment set. It's still easily playable today, though you should expect the interface to demand patient reading, and a single game can easily swallow an entire weekend.

pc-9x__sid-meier-s-alpha-centauri.article:
**Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri** begins right where Civilization left off: a colonization ship arrives at the Alpha Centauri system, the crew falls into disagreement, and seven ideological factions disembark onto an alien planet, each with its own idea of what humanity is actually for. Instead of nations, the game pits believers, ecologists, technocrats, soldiers, or merchants against one another, and their leaders have distinctive enough voices to be remembered long after the game is finished. The planet itself is hostile, full of red fungus and strange life.

The basic turn-based framework is related to Civilization, but almost everything is pushed a step further. Units aren't picked from a list but assembled in a workshop from chassis, weapon, armor, and special equipment, so technological progress is immediately reflected in what the player's army can do. Society is tuned through social engineering, where choices of economy, values, and politics directly change how one's own cities behave. The environment isn't passive scenery either: pollution and terraforming wake native mind worms, and the more the player damages the landscape, the harder it strikes back. Secret Projects, the equivalent of wonders of the world, are accompanied by short sequences and quotations that turn technologies into philosophical statements.

Atmosphere is the main asset. Text logs, leader voices, and datalinks create a coherent vision of the future that reads almost like a good science-fiction novel, while the music and sounds of the planet reinforce the feeling that man is only a visitor here. Contemporary critics received the game excellently and often ranked it among the best turn-based strategies ever, even though visually it already looked austere in 1999 against colorful competition. An expansion, Alien Crossfire, followed later with more factions and new technologies. Today Alpha Centauri is still held in extraordinarily high regard, because no one has really repeated its ideas on unit design and social tuning.

pc-9x__master-of-orion-ii-battle-at-anta.article:
**Master of Orion II: Battle at Antares** is a textbook space 4X strategy game in which a single home planet grows into an interstellar empire. The player explores neighboring systems, colonizes planets with varying gravity, atmosphere, and mineral wealth, develops technologies, signs and breaks treaties in the galactic senate, and ultimately decides whether diplomacy is enough for victory or whether a fleet will be needed. Several races with distinctive traits are available, but the real draw is the option to build your own race from a point budget and decide whether it should be scientific, warlike, telepathic, or simply incredibly rich.

At the game's heart are two interlinked systems. The first is colony management, where the population is divided among farms, factories, and laboratories, and where building construction means a long-term decision about the whole empire's direction. The second is the ship designer: each hull can be armed however you see fit, and the turn-based tactical combat then reveals whether betting on shields, missiles, or a boarding party was the right call. Heroes hired in bars, espionage, alien technology recovered from wrecks, and random events keep every playthrough different, which is why players keep coming back even after dozens of galaxies played.

Visually it was a pleasingly detailed two-dimensional production with illustrated races and clear icons that still read well after all these years, and calm space music supports the feeling of long-term building. The game came out for both DOS and Windows, and reviewers of the time received it very warmly, above all for its depth and replayability. Its influence on the genre is fundamental: the combination of building your own race, modular ship design, and turn-based space battles became a template for many later games, and fans still return to it today, often with community patches. Anyone who enjoys planning dozens of hours ahead will struggle to find a better starting point.

pc-9x__homeworld.article:
**Homeworld** is a story about coming home that begins in the worst possible way. The inhabitants of the desert planet Kharak discover in the wreck of an ancient ship proof that they are not the original inhabitants of their world, build a giant mothership, and set out to find a long-lost homeland. It's clear from the very start that there's no going back, and this loss gives the campaign an unusually quiet, melancholic tone that real-time strategy games of the era otherwise lacked. The narration is held together by the calm commentary of the ship's AI and by animated cutscenes.

In gameplay terms it was a breakthrough: Homeworld was the first major representative of the genre set entirely in full three-dimensional space. The fleet moves up and down as well as sideways, attacking from above or from behind makes real sense, and the player has to learn to control the camera as well as the ships themselves. There's no base-building in the usual sense; everything stems from the mothership, specialized vessels harvest resources from asteroids and wrecks, and enemy ships can be captured with boarding frigates. Crucially, the fleet carries over from mission to mission. Losses aren't reset, so every lost battle still hurts hours later, and careful conduct of the war is itself a strategy. Formations, tactics, and the specialization of fighters, corvettes, and capital ships form a clear rock-paper-scissors system.

Visually the game still holds up today thanks to its clean design, wide space panoramas, and pleasantly restrained interface. The music blends ambient textures with serious orchestral music, and one of the campaign's most powerful moments uses a well-known orchestral piece in a way that people still remember. Contemporary critics received Homeworld enthusiastically, and many outlets named it one of the best games of the year. Its influence is visible in every later space strategy game, and the series went on to sequels and modern remasters that make the original campaign accessible on today's computers.

pc-9x__myth-fallen-lords.article:
**Myth: The Fallen Lords** arrived in 1997 with an idea that sounded almost heretical at the time: a real-time strategy game with no resource gathering and no base building. The player is given a fixed squad at the start of each mission and has to make do with it, because no reinforcements are coming. The dark fantasy premise, about a world already losing its war against undead lords, is told mostly through the terse notes of an ordinary soldier between missions, and that restraint works better than a lavish cutscene ever could.

The battlefield is a fully three-dimensional terrain over which detailed two-dimensional characters move, and terrain is what decides everything. Archers on high ground shoot farther, aiming is harder down in a valley, rain reduces the effectiveness of firebombs, and snow slows down marching. On top of that, physics governs everything: a dwarf's explosive charge can be thrown downhill and it really does roll down, explosions throw around bodies and severed limbs, and shooting into the middle of a melee genuinely kills your own men. Orders work with formations, retreat, and unit facing, so one well-executed flanking maneuver is worth more than twice the numbers. The campaign is unforgiving, because every fallen veteran is irreplaceable and the next mission simply does without them.

The atmosphere is raw, filthy, and dark. The combination of muddy battlefields, fog, and muted music makes Myth one of the least romantic fantasy games of its time, underlined further by the sheer amount of blood on screen. At the time it was a critically acclaimed title, and its internet multiplayer resonated even more strongly, played competitively for years after release. Its influence is felt anywhere strategy gives up economy in favor of pure tactics. Today the game is kept alive by community projects and open-source versions of the engine, which keep it playable, and its emphasis on terrain and physics feels fresher than more than a few newer titles. Anyone who can get used to treating soldiers as a scarce resource will get one of the most tense campaigns of its era.

pc-9x__dark-reign-future-of-war.article:
**Dark Reign: The Future of War** bet in 1997 that players were already used to real-time strategy games and wanted to think harder about them. The sci-fi conflict between the authoritarian Imperium and the guerrilla Freedom Guard plays out on arid planets where water is the key resource, and both campaigns offer several dozen missions with their own units and tactical flavor. While the Imperium relies on heavy machinery and sheer firepower, the Freedom Guard leans on mobility, sabotage, and fighting in confusing terrain.

The main contribution lies in unit control. Every unit has its own behavior settings: the player determines whether it should attack, retreat, hold position, or simply report and vanish upon contact with the enemy, how far it may pursue, and how it reacts to damage. Added to that are order queues, patrol routes, ongoing use of special abilities, and detailed handling of sight, since scouts see further and snipers can shoot beyond their own line of sight. The result is a game where the army can be set up to largely take care of itself on the map, which was unusual at the time and still feels elegant today.

Technically it was a solid two-dimensional production with clear isometric graphics and decent performance even on then-typical machines, complemented by a strong map editor and network play. Reviews praised the title specifically for its unit AI and tactical options, though it ultimately stayed in the commercial shadow of the genre's biggest names. Still, a direct line runs from here to later strategy games that give units behavior modes and automated orders. Today Dark Reign is interesting above all for players who want to see how the genre was already trying to handle micromanagement by the end of the nineties, and for anyone who finds classic strategy games needlessly chatty with clicking.

pc-9x__ground-control.article:
**Ground Control** closed out the nineties with a genuine technical showcase of where real-time strategy could go once stripped of resource gathering. In a distant future, the Crayven Corporation clashes with the religious Order of the New Dawn over colonies, and the player doesn't command an economy but a landing force. Before each mission you assemble several squads from the available unit types, choose their equipment and specialization, and whatever lands on the surface is everything you have to win the mission with. Reinforcements arrive only when the scenario allows it, so losses are real losses.

In gameplay terms this is pure tactics. Units have behavior modes, formations, and abilities, terrain elevation affects both range and sight, forests and rocks provide cover, and artillery without scouting eyes fires blind. Battles between infantry squads, armored vehicles, and aircraft form a clear system of counters, where correctly deploying one squad against an exposed weakness decides an engagement faster than any reserve force could. The campaign is complemented by narration with voiced characters, and the game also offered multiplayer, where the same squad-building system proved surprisingly balanced.

What drew the most attention at the time, however, was the presentation. A fully three-dimensional engine allowed the camera to freely rotate and zoom in all the way to individual soldiers, maps felt sprawling and cinematic, and the lighting effects and explosions ranked among the best available on graphics accelerators in the year 2000. Reviewers praised the game for its looks as well as its nerve in dropping base-building, though some players sorely missed the usual construction layer. A sequel followed later, and the game was also distributed for free, which keeps it an easily accessible showcase of the genre's tactical branch. Today it's mainly a pleasantly short, tight campaign without wasted menu-clicking, one that shows that stripping strategy of its economy doesn't impoverish it, but instead shifts attention to decision-making on the battlefield.

pc-9x__shogun-total-war.article:
**Shogun: Total War** founded one of the most important strategy series ever in 2000, and it did so by fusing two games into one. On a turn-based map of Japan during the Sengoku period, the player leads one of the rival clans, manages provinces, collects taxes, builds temples and training grounds, arranges marriages, and works toward the title of shogun. Once two armies meet, the game switches to a real-time battle where thousands of soldiers face off on three-dimensional terrain, and the player is no longer deciding economics but formation, timing, and nerve.

The battles are why people remember this game. Units have morale, fatigue, and facing direction; spearmen hold off cavalry, archers suffer in the rain, arquebuses need time to reload, and attacking downhill or into a flank has a dramatically different effect than a frontal clash. Morale collapse spreads like a contagion: one broken unit is enough for an entire wing to rout before the player can react. On the campaign map this is joined by agents, namely ninjas, spies, and emissaries who can solve a problem before it ever comes to blows. The result is a game where you lose more from bad planning than from slow clicking.

The atmosphere rests on restrained Japanese aesthetics: calm music with traditional instruments, opening quotes from Sun Tzu's Art of War, and dry commentary from advisors. Technically it was a demanding title, yet on the accelerators of the day it managed to show huge masses of soldiers in motion, something nobody had offered before. Critics received the game very well precisely for combining strategy with mass battles, and later an expansion about the Mongol invasion followed. The influence is obvious: the entire modern Total War series, including its two-layer structure, begins right here. It still plays well today, only the campaign map is markedly simpler than in later entries and there are fewer unit types. But that very simplicity serves the battles well: the player watches rows of spearmen and archers and decides based on what they see, not on tables of numbers.

pc-9x__settlers-iii.article:
**The Settlers III** is a game about the idea that wars are won by whoever keeps their production in order. Three gods send their peoples, the Romans, the Egyptians, and the Asians, to a contested territory, and the player builds a settlement for one of the cultures that must produce everything itself, from bread to swords. The third installment dropped the road system from the previous game and let settlers walk freely, which sped things up and simplified them, but the foundation stayed the same: nothing gets made without raw materials, and nothing moves without someone to carry it.

The heart of the game is the production chain. A woodcutter fells trees, a sawmill processes the logs, a stonemason quarries rock, farms grow grain, a mill and bakery turn it into bread that feeds the miners in the pits; ore and coal become metal at the smelter, from which a forge makes weapons, and only then can a barracks train a soldier. Every broken link shows up elsewhere immediately, and the player spends most of the time solving bottlenecks, surpluses, and building placement so settlers don't walk needlessly far. The military side is more straightforward: guard towers are occupied to expand your territory's borders, and combat is decided by the number and level of soldiers plus support from spells, which priests must save up for by sacrificing resources.

Visually it's one of the most beautiful 2D games of its time, full of finely animated little figures that are fun to just watch, accompanied by calm, almost lulling music. It's precisely this contrast between peaceful building and eventually quite fierce war that makes the series something distinctive. Commercially it was a very successful title, especially in Europe where the brand had a strong following, and the game got an expansion adding a fourth nation. Today it's easy to pick up, it just takes patience: the first hour is about logs and bread, and only then comes the army, giving a reason for all that logistics that was built up. The series' influence shows in every later building game that relies on production chains instead of simply subtracting resources from a stockpile.

pc-9x__populous-beginning.article:
**Populous: The Beginning** took the old god-game brand and moved it into a fully three-dimensional world that is, quite literally, round. Each level takes place on a small planet you can rotate all the way around, and the goal is usually to conquer it entirely and move on to the next. This time the player isn't just an invisible deity but commands a specific shaman who walks the surface, casts spells, and whose loss is a real problem, so the game sits somewhere between strategy and directly controlling one hero character.

A tribe grows by having somewhere to live, so the first concern is always flat terrain and building huts. Trained braves, warriors, fire warriors, and spies then fill their roles, ships and balloons can be built, and distant islets can be occupied. But the most fun comes from spells: earthquakes, volcanoes, mudslides, or a massive wave that sweeps an entire enemy village into the sea. The terrain is fully shapeable, it can be raised or lowered, which makes the landscape both a weapon and a building material at once. Enemy tribes are led by their own shamans and do exactly the same thing, so matches often end as a duel of two divine powers over a broken planet.

Technically, in 1998 this was an impressive affair with hardware acceleration, smooth terrain deformation, and an enjoyable view whether close up or from a distance; the atmosphere is held together by tribal, drum-driven music and a ceremonial pace between disasters. Critics of the time received it warmly and praised especially the courage of bringing the familiar gameplay into three dimensions, even though some missed the playful simplicity of earlier entries. Today it's a pleasantly distinctive title with few real successors, which is exactly why it's worth trying; anyone who wants to see what the British game-design school looked like at the end of the nineties is in the right place. The campaign also keeps a decent pace, and individual planets can be finished in one sitting.

pc-9x__dungeon-keeper.article:
**Dungeon Keeper** turned fantasy clichés upside down: the player isn't the hero descending into the dungeon for treasure, but the owner of that dungeon, whose job is to kill the heroes at the threshold of their own treasure room. Every mission starts with bare rock, into which imps gradually dig tunnels and rooms, and it usually ends with the surrounding kingdoms no longer taking the victory of good for granted. The whole game is carried by black humor, from a sardonic narrator through the advisor to the very descriptions of what each room is for.

Gameplay-wise, it's a mix of building and managing a strange household. Rooms have clear functions: a hatchery that lures monsters in, a dining hall that feeds them, a treasury to pay wages from, a library for researching spells, a training hall for leveling up, and a torture chamber that turns enemies into new members of the household. Monsters show up on their own based on what the player builds, but they aren't obedient. If they don't get paid, sleep badly, or have a falling-out with someone, they might start wrecking the furniture or simply walk out. On top of that come traps, doors, spells, and above all the ability to take direct control of a specific monster and see the dungeon through its eyes in first person, an impressive idea for its time.

Technically the game combined a three-dimensional dungeon with a clear top-down view, ran under both DOS and Windows, and felt surprisingly smooth given the number of creatures roaming the tunnels. The atmosphere is held together by dim lighting, rumbling sounds, and music that moves between horror and parody. Critics of the era received the game excellently and highlighted exactly this humor and the originality of the premise. The influence shows up in every later game where the player builds a dungeon and defends it against heroes; the series itself got sequels and spiritual successors, and the original is still easy to play today and still amusingly wicked. It's also worth noting how well the game teaches you to play without a single on-screen tutorial, just through the narrator's commentary.

pc-9x__grim-fandango.article:
**Grim Fandango** came out in 1998 as LucasArts' last major adventure game, and at the same time as its first to drop hand-drawn characters in favor of polygonal models moving across pre-rendered backdrops. The player takes on Manny Calavera, a clerk at a travel agency in the Land of the Dead who sells his clients tickets for a four-year journey to eternal rest. When he discovers someone is systematically stealing the best souls and sentencing them to a walk across the wasteland instead, he sets off after a fraud that reaches all the way to the top of that world. The story unfolds across four acts, with a full year passing between each, and with every jump the setting, Manny's standing, and the cast of characters around him all change.

Control dropped the cursor in favor of directly controlling the character from the keyboard: Manny turns his head toward whatever can be interacted with, and the player confirms the action. Solving puzzles relies on combining items in the inventory, carefully examining locations, and conversations with branching responses, and several puzzles rank among the toughest that nineties adventure games ever offered. Technically this was the debut of the GrimE engine, which allowed changing camera angles and lighting scenes so they felt cinematic. The game ran under Windows and could take advantage of the emerging 3D acceleration of the time, although the control scheme itself became the most frequent target of contemporary criticism.

Visually it's a blend of the Mexican Día de los Muertos holiday, art deco architecture, and film noir, accompanied by jazz and orchestral music that changes with each city along with the story's mood. The dialogue ranks among the best-written in the genre's entire history, and the humor never overpowers the melancholy tone of a story about a journey with no way back. Critics received the game enthusiastically and ranked it among the year's finest, but sales fell short and, together with other titles, contributed to the decline of classic adventure games. Today Grim Fandango plays without a hitch thanks to a later remastered version, and its storytelling and visual style have aged only minimally.

pc-9x__longest-journey.article:
**The Longest Journey** arrived on PC at the turn of the millennium as one of the last great classic adventure games before the genre stepped back for several years. The main heroine is April Ryan, a student at an art school in the city of Newport, which comes across as an ordinary near future full of levitating vending machines, corporate towers, and grimy districts on the edge of town. April starts having dreams that spill over into reality, and she gradually discovers she can cross between two parallel worlds: the technological Stark and the magical Arcadia. The balance between them is collapsing, and she is one of the few people who can do anything about it.

The game is controlled with a classic point-and-click interface with a small set of actions and an inventory, but it puts storytelling front and center. The dialogue is extensive and branching, side characters have their own backstories, and the player often just talks to them because it's interesting, not for another item. Most of the puzzles grow out of the situation and the logic of that world's rules, although a few of them are still remembered today as needlessly convoluted. Technically it used pre-rendered two-dimensional backgrounds combined with three-dimensional characters, which on the Windows PCs of the day allowed for very detailed artwork without requiring a 3D accelerator, though at the cost of a game that spanned several discs.

The atmosphere rests on the contrast between the cold, urban Stark and the colorful, at times almost fairy-tale-like Arcadia, each with its own music and narrative pace. The voice acting was unusually extensive for its time, and April ranks among the best-written game heroines of the nineties: ironic, uncertain, and never coming across as a mere plot device. Critics praised especially the story and its length, which for most players ran to dozens of hours. The game quickly earned cult status, got a sequel in Dreamfall, and is still recommended today as a showcase of what adventure games can achieve when they don't try to be just a collection of puzzles.

pc-9x__broken-sword-shadow-of-templars.article:
**Broken Sword: The Shadow of the Templars** opens with one of the best-remembered introductory scenes in adventure game history: American tourist George Stobbart is sitting outside a Paris café when a clown with an accordion walks in and leaves behind a briefcase ticking with a bomb. From an accidental witness he becomes an investigator who, together with journalist Nicole Collard, unravels a trail leading through medieval history, lost manuscripts, and a secret society tied to the Knights Templar. The story takes the player from Paris to Ireland, Spain, Syria, and Scotland, and play alternates between the two heroes, so the same plot gets uncovered from two sides.

Control is classic point-and-click with a simple interface where the cursor itself hints at what can be interacted with. The puzzles are mostly logical and grounded in the situation, so the player advances more through conversation and observation than by blindly trying every item in the inventory; the game does contain a few traps that can kill you, though, so it's worth saving regularly. Technically it was a two-dimensional game with hand-drawn backgrounds and fully animated characters, released in both DOS and Windows versions, and on the Pentiums of the day it ran smoothly straight off the CD, complete with full voice acting and animated cutscenes.

The artwork is the main reason the game has aged so well: the backgrounds have a watercolor palette, the character animation draws on traditional cartoon filmmaking, and the orchestral score with a hint of ethnic instruments keeps the tone of an adventure film rather than a detective story. The humor is dry and British, the dialogue is well written, and violence stays in the background. Critics of the time ranked the game among the best the genre produced in the mid-nineties, and the series carried on thanks to it with further installments continuing to this day. Today Broken Sword is often recommended as an entry point into classic adventure games, because it's accessible, well told, and doesn't demand patience with nonsensical puzzles.

pc-9x__blade-runner.article:
**Blade Runner** ranks among the most ambitious adventure games of the nineties and, at the same time, among the most successful game adaptations of a film source. The player takes on detective Ray McCoy, who in rainy Los Angeles in 2019 gets assigned a case involving a group of replicants. The plot runs parallel to the film rather than replacing it, so familiar locations and motifs appear from a different angle while the well-known storyline remains untouched. McCoy walks crime scenes, collects clues, analyzes photographs, and interrogates suspects, while gradually starting to doubt which side he's actually on himself.

The most interesting part is the structure: the suspects aren't fixed, the game decides at each playthrough who among the characters is a replicant, and side characters move through the world on their own schedule even when the player isn't around to see it. The investigation can be conducted harshly or leniently, and the game has several different endings depending on who McCoy kills, who he lets live, and how he treats his companion. Technically it was Westwood's own solution combining pre-rendered backgrounds with characters built from voxels, so everything ran in real time without needing a 3D accelerator; in exchange for a soft, at times blurry image, the game gained smoothness and the freedom to move about the streets.

Atmosphere is the game's main asset. Neon signs, endless rain, industrial smog, and music drawing on the original film's themes create a setting the player remembers longer than the individual puzzles. The voice acting is extensive and the game shipped on several discs, which back then was a sign of a genuinely major production. Critics praised especially the variability of the case and its mood, while criticizing the occasional lack of clarity about where to go next. Today Blade Runner is available in a restored version and stands as an early showcase of how an adventure game can be built on investigation and moral ambiguity instead of item collecting.

pc-9x__curse-of-monkey-island.article:
**The Curse of Monkey Island** is the third instalment of the pirate saga and the high point of how far a classic two-dimensional adventure could go in terms of art design. Guybrush Threepwood meets his Elaine again, slips a ring stolen from a treasure hoard onto her finger, and discovers he has just turned her into a golden statue. The rest of the game is a quest to lift the curse, taking him across Caribbean islands, through ship battles, a carnival-style attraction and the innards of a giant volcano, and of course through repeated run-ins with the zombie pirate LeChuck, whose intentions this time are rather more romantic than conquering.

The game runs on the final version of the SCUMM engine and is controlled through a circular menu with three basic actions, which streamlines and speeds up the whole process. The puzzles are typically LucasArts-style — based on absurd but retrospectively understandable logic — and the game cannot be lost or become permanently unwinnable. The insult-swordfighting returns, this time in a version for naval battles, and the game offers two difficulty settings, the easier of which drops some of the more elaborately chained tasks. Technically it was a title for Windows and DOS with high-resolution hand-drawn backgrounds, full voice acting across two discs, and animation approaching the quality of television cartoons.

It's precisely the art direction that explains why the game has aged so remarkably well: the artwork has a distinctive cartoonish style, the colours are vivid, and every location has its own handwriting. The music works with Caribbean motifs, and in one scene it even turns into a song the characters sing. Voice acting was used across the series in full for the first time here, and the hero's voice became part of the brand for the next decade. Reviews were highly favourable, and the game still ranks among the most beloved entries in the series, even though it was made without the original creators of the first two parts. Anyone who wants to see what a classic adventure game looked like at its artistic peak should start right here.

pc-9x__riven-sequel-to-myst.article:
**Riven: The Sequel to Myst** followed one of the best-selling titles of the mid-1990s and, instead of expanding the formula, distilled it into an almost perfect form. The player is sent into the world of Riven to free Catherine and resolve the situation surrounding Gehn, a man who has built himself the standing of a god on a crumbling archipelago. None of this is explained up front: the story unfolds purely through the environment, notes, the constructions of the natives and a handful of encounters with people, so for a long time the player has no idea who to actually trust.

The gameplay is built around moving between static pre-rendered shots and around observation. The puzzles aren't separate tasks with levers but part of a functioning world: the player must understand how the archipelago draws its power, how the individual islands relate to one another, how the local numeral system works, or why a particular animal reacts to a particular sound. Notes on paper are practically a necessity while playing, and many players keep their own maps and sketches of symbols. Technically it was cutting-edge for its time: the game shipped on several discs for Windows, the shots were rendered at a quality unthinkable in real time, and they were accompanied by live-action video sequences inserted directly into the image.

The atmosphere is remarkably quiet and lonely. The sound design works more with ambient noise, wind and creaking mechanisms than with music, and it's precisely that silence that gives the world its weight. Riven was very well received and sold strongly, though some critics faulted the harsh difficulty and the frequent disc swapping. The influence of both games on the genre was enormous: a whole wave of first-person adventures with pre-rendered graphics followed, one that lasted until the end of the decade and fed an entire segment of the CD-title market. Today both a modern remake and the original version exist, and thanks above all to how tightly its puzzles are woven into the environment, Riven is commonly cited among the best-designed logic games of all time.

pc-9x__last-express.article:
**The Last Express** is an adventure game from the creator of Prince of Persia and one of the most original titles released in the 1990s. It is July 1914, and American doctor Robert Cath boards the Orient Express bound from Paris to Constantinople, only to find his friend dead right at the start. Instead of investigating as a free agent, Cath must assume his identity, survive the journey, and at the same time get his bearings amid intrigues involving weapons, gold and an approaching war that still only hangs in the air.

The whole game runs in real time. The train follows its timetable, passengers have their own schedules, go to dinner, argue in their compartments and vanish from the corridor regardless of whether the player happens to be watching them. Whoever arrives late misses a conversation; whoever is caught in someone else's compartment has a problem. The player can speed up time and, in case of failure, rewind a few minutes, which turns the playthrough into a gradual refinement of one long journey. Technically it was a Windows title with hand-drawn rotoscoped animation that turned filmed live-action footage into a style close to an Art Nouveau poster; instead of smooth animation it uses a sparser frame rate, giving the game a distinctive theatrical rhythm.

The atmosphere of the train is built with precision, from the noise of the wheels through multiple languages in the dialogue to music that only plays where it belongs. Passengers speak their own languages, and the player often understands only from context, which underscores the sense of a foreign environment and uncertainty. The game came out at a time when the market was dominated by three-dimensional action titles and flopped commercially, even though critics praised it. Over the years it became a textbook example of bold game design, one referenced even by much newer titles built around repeatedly experiencing one contained situation, and thanks to later re-releases it is easily available. Anyone looking for an adventure that doesn't bet on puzzles but on time, places and people will find it right here.

pc-9x__sanitarium.article:
**Sanitarium** is a psychological horror game in the form of an isometric adventure and one of the darkest titles released on Windows PC in 1998. The player wakes up in an asylum for the mentally ill with a bandaged head, no memory and no certainty whether what he sees is even real. Escaping the cell is only the beginning of a journey through several entirely different chapters: a village inhabited by deformed children, a town under the rule of insects, an alien wasteland, or a comic-book city with a superhero. Each functions as a self-contained world with its own rules, characters and its own logic of horror.

The gameplay is classic adventure fare: the player walks through locations in an isometric view, talks to characters, collects items and solves puzzles that mostly grow out of that chapter's own logic.
