Between battles the game offers platforming sections, secret areas, and challenges that stretch its length well beyond the campaign itself. It also included an asymmetric multiplayer mode and, later, an extensive story expansion.

Technically, it's a very finely tuned title: the id Tech 7 engine handles enormous, visually striking spaces at high frame rates, and the game keeps excellent readability even in the middle of chaos. The visual style moved away from grey industrial aesthetics toward saturated colors and comic-book exaggeration, and the music once again builds on hard electronic metal. Reviews were very favorable, though some players objected that the game is more demanding and less relaxing than its predecessor. It's precisely that demanding edge, however, that makes it one of the best-designed action games on PC today, one worth trying again on a higher difficulty. Anyone who learns to switch weapons without thinking gets an experience found nowhere else in the genre: combat turns into fluid motion in which every button press has its exact reason.

pc-modern__crysis.article:
**Crysis** etched itself into players' memory twice over: as an excellent open-ended shooter and as the benchmark against which new graphics cards were tested for years. The story sends a squad of American soldiers to a tropical island in the South China Sea, where something considerably older and stranger lurks alongside the North Korean army. The player commands a character in a nanosuit that allows switching between enhanced strength, speed, armor, and cloaking. This single mechanic reshapes the whole structure of the game, because there's always more than one way to attack a base, and the player chooses whether to shoot their way in, sneak through, or drive around the enemy along the beach in a vehicle.

The environment is varied and open, with tall grass, dense jungle, and buildings that can be shot to pieces. Enemy AI tries to flank, shouts to warn each other, and falls back, so even repeated attempts on the same objective play out differently each time. In the second half the game transforms, the pace speeds up, and the tropical island gives way to frozen interiors and weightless gravity; some players welcomed the change, others mourned the loss of the early missions' freedom.

The technical side was utterly exceptional in 2007. The CryEngine 2 engine offered dynamic lighting, light filtering through foliage, convincing water, and extensive vegetation destruction. The game managed to bring even the most expensive rigs to their knees, and the phrase "can it run Crysis" became a permanent fixture of gamer vocabulary. The sound design underlines the tension with jungle ambience and an orchestral motif that surfaces at key moments. Critics praised the freedom of approach and the visual execution above all. Today the game runs without a hitch, still looks good, and its system of tactical choices anticipated many later shooters with more open design. Anyone who wants to remember the era when a single game measured a whole computer's performance has an extra reason to install it again.

pc-modern__call-of-duty-4-modern-warfare.article:
**Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare** moved the series from the Second World War into the present day, and in doing so reshaped what action games would look like for years afterward. The campaign alternates between two storylines, the British SAS and American Marines, taking the player from a night-time boarding of a ship in a storm through the streets of a Middle Eastern city to a nuclear catastrophe that ranks among the genre's most powerful moments. The narrative is tight, cinematic, and unafraid to briefly strip away the player's agency to underscore the impact of events.

In terms of gameplay it's a brisk, corridor-based shooter that still puts weight on precise weapon handling, aiming down sights, suppressive fire, and cooperation with squadmates. The iconic mission "All Ghillied Up," in which the player creeps through a contaminated zone in a ghillie suit, shows that the developers also knew how to turn the pace down. The real revolution, though, was the multiplayer. Its system of levels, weapon unlocks, perks, and kill-streak rewards created an addictive progression loop that virtually the entire competition has copied ever since.

On PC the game ran beautifully even on the mid-range hardware of the time, offering sharp visuals with elaborate lighting and very good weapon sound design that still ranks among the best the series has ever produced. Music and sound design build tension without ever drowning out the action. Critics received the title enthusiastically, and it became one of the most successful games of its generation, kicking off the franchise's yearly release rhythm. Today the campaign is still excellent to play, though it's on the shorter side and some of its scripted moments read as predictable after all these years. Compared to later entries in the series it feels surprisingly restrained, since it doesn't yet chase endless effect escalation and instead relies on pacing and precisely timed twists. As a historical milestone that shaped the direction of modern military shooters and the shape of online progression in dozens of other games, it's impossible to overlook.

pc-modern__battlefield-3.article:
**Battlefield 3** was a major technical and marketing comeback for the series, and on PC it became one of the best-looking titles of its time. Its center of gravity is the multiplayer mode, where two teams clash over control points on sprawling maps, with infantry supported by tanks, armored transports, helicopters, and fighter jets. It's precisely this combination of infantry combat with vehicles and air support that gives its matches a scale the competition couldn't offer; a single map can contain dozens of simultaneous engagements that feed into each other.

The game is built on a system of four classes: the assault trooper with healing gear, the engineer with anti-armor equipment, support with a machine gun and ammo, and the recon soldier with a sniper rifle and target marking. Progression unlocks scopes, attachments, and new weapons, giving the player a reason to keep coming back. Environmental destruction plays a crucial role, changing available cover as the match unfolds, toppling walls, and erasing entire floors of buildings. The single-player campaign is shorter and more cinematic, complemented by a cooperative mode.

Technically, the game ran on the Frostbite 2 engine, which delivered quality lighting, dusty interiors, convincing explosions, and sound design that ranks among the genre's finest. Gunfire in enclosed spaces sounds completely different from an open field, and the echo of shots can give away an enemy's direction. The PC version supported more players than the console release, making it the reference platform. Reviews were very favorable, with criticism aimed mainly at the external game launcher of the time. Today Battlefield 3 still delivers the unique feeling of a large-scale battle, and its sound design and destruction remain a benchmark against which later entries are measured. For anyone who wants to experience what a shooter feels like when a single soldier is just a small part of a much bigger battle, this is one of the best opportunities available, and at the same time a reminder of an era when big online shooters bet on scale instead of seasonal content.

pc-modern__battlefield-bad-company-2.article:
**Battlefield: Bad Company 2** is, for many players, the high point of the entire series, because it managed to combine a relaxed tone with very well-balanced combat across sprawling maps. The campaign follows a squad of soldiers whose humor and friendly ribbing lighten an otherwise serious story about a secret weapon, taking the player from snowy mountains through jungle to desert cities. It's entertaining and well put together on its own, but the main reason to install the game always was, and still is, its multiplayer.

The key innovation was environmental destruction, which here made full tactical sense for the first time. Building walls can be shot through, blown apart with explosives, or leveled by artillery support, so a team defending a house can never feel truly safe, and attackers can always create their own entrance. The Rush mode, in which one side defends pairs of objectives while the other destroys them, became iconic precisely because of how the map gradually turns into ruins over the course of a match. Four classes with their own gear, plus vehicles and helicopters, round out a rich variety of situations, and the unlock system keeps players engaged for dozens of hours.

On PC it was a good-looking title with engaging lighting and dust effects, though it wasn't as demanding as later entries. Weapon and explosion sound design was top-notch, and the game could convey through audio alone that a battle was raging somewhere the player couldn't see. Reviews were very positive, and many looking back highlight precisely the balance, in which no single weapon or vehicle dominated. Today Bad Company 2 mainly serves as a reminder of how well a shooter works when built on simple rules and a changeable environment; its pace is slower and easier to read than that of many current competitors. The player has time to decide, read the map, and coordinate with the team, instead of just reacting to blinking icons. That's exactly why many people return to it even years later, and its name still comes up regularly whenever the best entries in the series are discussed.

pc-modern__f-e-r.article:
**F.E.A.R.** combined two things that don't seem related at first glance: the best-crafted firefights of its time and a Japanese-flavored horror story centered on a girl in a red dress. The player takes on the role of an unnamed member of a special unit investigating an incident at a corporate compound, where something far worse than an armed uprising has been unleashed. Moving through the buildings alternates between sharp confrontations with cloned soldiers and quiet passages in which reality falls apart, corridors fill with blood, and the player is never quite sure what was real.

Combat is the heart of the game. The enemy AI ranks among the most highly praised in the genre's history: soldiers inform each other, flank the player through a side corridor, flip tables to create cover, and retreat once they lose the upper hand. The player can compete with them thanks to a time-slowing ability that turns a brief firefight into a choreography full of sparks, dust clouds, and flying chunks of plaster. There aren't many weapons, but each has clear weight, especially the shotgun and the rail gun, after whose hit practically nothing remains of an opponent.

Technically, the game relied on very good dynamic shadows and particle effects that turned every post-fight room into a demolished ruin. That came at a cost to performance, making it one of 2005's more demanding titles. Sound and music work with silence and sudden jolts, keeping the horror alive even between fights, though the repetitive office corridors are among its most common criticisms. Critics praised the game especially for its combat and atmosphere. Today F.E.A.R. feels surprisingly modern precisely because of its enemy behavior, which plenty of newer shooters still can't replicate. On a modern computer the game runs without a hitch, and its firefights in office spaces retain a raw dynamism that's hard to find elsewhere. The horror has lost some of its surprise over the years, but the feel of combat remains first-rate, and many still consider it an unmatched peak of the genre.

pc-modern__far-cry.article:
**Far Cry** was a revelation in 2004, because it showed that a shooter didn't have to be just a series of corridors. Playing former sailor Jack Carver, the player ends up on a tropical archipelago where he was originally only supposed to ferry a journalist, and soon discovers that mercenaries working for a dubious scientist have taken over the islands. The environment is open and readable over long distances, and the game cleverly makes use of that: through binoculars the player can mark patrols, plan a route, and decide whether to break into a camp at night, arrive by boat, or go around it through the jungle.

Combat is merciless and fast. Enemies aim well, call in reinforcements, and behave aggressively, so a direct assault against superior numbers usually ends badly. The game therefore rewards patience, use of elevation, and vehicles ranging from a buggy to a boat with a mounted machine gun. Later sections introduce mutated enemies who pick up the pace and shift the action into laboratory interiors; this change remains a subject of debate to this day, since it takes away the game's greatest strength, namely freedom.

Technically, it was a showcase for the first CryEngine. Sweeping views of the sea, dense vegetation, quality water reflections, and sharp long-distance visibility weren't common in games at the time, and Far Cry quickly became a standard fixture of graphics card benchmarks. The sound of the jungle, the distant calls of patrols, and tense music round out the feeling of isolation in a foreign environment. Reviews were very favorable, and the game's success led both to further entries under the Ubisoft banner and, indirectly, to the creation of Crysis. Today Far Cry is still interesting as a blueprint for open-world shooters, though it's noticeably harsher and less forgiving than its more modern successors. Saving is limited, enemies don't forgive mistakes, and the player has to reckon with the fact that many a plan will fall apart in the very first minute. For anyone who enjoys tactical planning and freedom of approach, though, it remains a valuable experience and, at the same time, an important milestone in the genre's history.

pc-modern__titanfall-2.article:
**Titanfall 2** ranks among the best-designed shooters of the last decade, even though it didn't get the attention it deserved at launch. The game builds on two layers: on the ground, the player controls a nimble pilot who wall-runs, slides, chains jumps and uses a grappling hook, while at any moment they can call in a giant combat robot called a Titan and hop inside it. The transition between light acrobatics and the machine's heavy power is seamless, giving the combat a rhythm that's hard to find elsewhere in the genre.

The single-player campaign was surprisingly strong. The relationship between the pilot and his Titan forms a surprisingly touching duo, and individual missions build on standout ideas, including the famous level where the player switches between two timelines of the same building and has to connect them mentally to progress. It's exactly this inventiveness that keeps the campaign moving from start to finish. The multiplayer mode then carries the acrobatic movement into fast matches where teams face infantry, robots, and Titans all at once.

On PC the game runs very smoothly, the controls are precise, and movement feels completely natural, which is crucial for this kind of design. Visually it's a clean sci-fi aesthetic without unnecessary visual noise, the music is orchestral and gains power exactly when a Titan drops onto the battlefield. Critics praised the game extremely warmly, but its release timing among other big titles hurt its sales. Today, Titanfall 2 is often recommended precisely because of its campaign, which can be finished over a few evenings while offering more ideas than many titles twice its length. Its pace never stalls, every mission arrives with its own idea, and the game never tries to pad its content through repetition. The influence of its movement system is also visible across a whole range of later action games that adopted wall-running and fluid jump-chaining as a given. Few, however, manage to combine it with such a well-crafted battle of giant machines.

pc-modern__wolfenstein-new-order.article:
**Wolfenstein: The New Order** took one of the genre's oldest franchises and turned it into a surprisingly serious story about a world where Nazi Germany won the war thanks to advanced technology. The player once again takes on the role of B.J. Blazkowicz, who after years wakes up into a gray 1960s Europe, where the occupying regime controls the cities with concrete fortresses and giant robots. The game surprisingly works as a story of resistance, loss, and defiance, and between missions it gives room to the characters hiding in the resistance's shelter, so the action has someone to fight for.

Gameplay-wise it's a hybrid of old and new school. The player carries a large arsenal at once, collects health packs, and can dual-wield weapons, while the game also offers stealth, silent takedowns of commanders who otherwise call in endless reinforcements, and classic secret-room hunting. The levels are more spacious than is typical for corridor shooters and often allow a choice between a fast or a quiet approach. Collecting upgrades and gold items encourages exploration.

Technically the game runs on the id Tech 5 engine and offers very well-lit environments ranging from foggy fortresses to a moon base; on PC the release was initially criticized for compressed textures, but performance was excellent. The sound design relies on oppressive electronic music and period-style songs rewritten into the occupiers' language, creating an unpleasantly convincing atmosphere of alternate history. Reviews were very positive, and the game revived interest in the whole franchise. Today The New Order stands as one of the few big shooters that can alternate brutal action with quiet, purely human scenes without losing pace. On a modern computer it runs without issues, and its length of around fifteen hours is above average for the genre. For players looking for action with a real story and the courage not to treat their own world merely as a backdrop for shooting, it's one of the best choices of recent years.

pc-modern__bioshock.article:
**BioShock** begins with a plane crash in the middle of the Atlantic and a descent into Rapture, an underwater city built as a refuge for the most capable individuals who refused to submit to any government or morality. By the time the player arrives, the utopia is a ruin inhabited by mutated wrecks of people, and all that remains of the original vision are advertising signs and residents' voice recordings. It's these audio diaries that carry most of the story, letting the player piece the city's history together through exploration.

Combat combines classic weapons with Plasmids, genetic abilities that let you hurl lightning, set enemies on fire, or throw them through the air. The environment can be drawn into the fight: water conducts electricity, spilled oil burns, and automated turrets can be hacked to your side. Alongside regular enemies, the game is defined by Big Daddies, hulking guardians of little girls whose defeat is always the player's own choice and opens up a moral decision that affects the ending. An economy of ammo, health kits, and upgrades forces careful management.

Technically the game was built on the Unreal engine and excelled especially in its art direction: art deco interiors, leaking water, flickering neon, and diving suits pressed against glass form one of the most memorable worlds in gaming history. The music alternates between period swing recordings and unsettling string motifs, and the sound of water is present almost constantly. Critics received the game exceptionally well, and discussions about its plot twist and about how freely the player actually acts were among the most cited of its time. Today BioShock requires a bit of patience with its older combat, but as an atmospheric journey through a strange world it remains extraordinary. Rapture has become one of the few gaming locations remembered as well as any film setting, and the game's influence is visible wherever creators let the environment tell the story instead of dialogue. Anyone wanting to experience the classic that changed what a shooter could narrate should start right here.

pc-modern__s-t-l-k-e-r-shadow-of-chernob.article:
**S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl** takes the player into a fictional Zone around the Chernobyl power plant, which after a second disaster has been overrun by anomalies, mutants, and rival groups of armed outcasts. The player begins as a man with no memory and a single entry in his PDA, gradually pushing deeper into the exclusion area, taking on jobs, trading, and deciding which factions to help. The structure is semi-open world: individual large areas are connected by passages and can be explored freely, whether hunting artifacts or simply trying to survive the night.

Combat is merciless. Weapons have wide spread until the player acquires a better one, enemies aim well, and a few hits mean the end, so it pays to use cover, a scope, and a cautious approach. Survival is complicated by hunger, radiation, a damaged suit, and limited carry weight, forcing every kilogram of ammunition to be weighed carefully. Anomalies, invisible traps that burn or crush anything that enters them, are located by throwing bolts, and they keep the journey through the landscape in constant tension.

Technically the game ran on its own X-Ray engine, whose lighting, dynamic weather, and sweeping views of abandoned settlements were among the best 2007 had to offer, though at the cost of occasional bugs. Sound is the atmosphere's main weapon: the crackle of a Geiger counter, distant barking dogs, a guitar by a stalker campfire, and silence broken only by the wind. Reviews were positive, with reservations about the technical state at launch. Today the game is kept alive by its exceptionally strong atmosphere and huge modding scene, thanks to which S.T.A.L.K.E.R. can be played in dozens of forms and still ranks among the most distinctive shooters on PC. Mods fix bugs, expand the world, add weather and new weapons, and often change the whole game beyond recognition. Anyone looking for a harsh, lonely trek without markers and without hand-holding will find here an experience that big commercial series don't offer.

pc-modern__left-4-dead-2.article:
**Left 4 Dead 2** is a purely cooperative shooter in which a quartet of survivors makes its way across the infected American South from one shelter to the next, while hordes of infected pour down on them. The structure is simple and brilliant: each campaign has several maps, at the end of which rescue awaits, and in between the game combines exploration, weapon collecting, and sudden surges of hundreds of enemies. You won't get far without cooperation, because a downed player needs help, and a lone player is almost always a dead player.

A central role is played by the so-called AI Director, a system that tracks how the team is doing and places enemies, health kits, and ammo accordingly. Thanks to it, every playthrough of the same map is different, and the game never slides into pure memorization. Alongside regular infected lurk special types, from the choking Smoker to the roaring Tank, which force the team to instantly change tactics. The second installment added melee weapons, new campaigns, daylight, and a mode where human-controlled survivors face off against human-controlled infected.

Technically the game runs on the well-optimized Source engine, so it runs on practically anything and can put a large number of characters on screen without slowdown. Visually it leans on the cinematic stylization of B-movie horror, including posters introducing each campaign. Sound is a core gameplay mechanic: the distinctive sounds of individual special infected let the team know what's coming before they even see it. Critics received the game excellently, and the community still keeps it alive with its own campaigns. Thanks to them and its flawless playability, Left 4 Dead 2 still ranks among the best choices for an evening with three friends. The game requires no learning of complex systems—everyone understands the rules within a few minutes, yet it still offers plenty of room for tactics and personal heroic moments. Its influence is visible across a whole wave of later cooperative shooters that borrowed its campaign structure and the idea of a director controlling the pace.

pc-modern__gothic-ii.article:
**Gothic II** sends the nameless hero from the first game into the province of Khorinis, where after the fall of the magic barrier the existing order is collapsing and the land is threatened by dragons with their hordes. The world is one continuous piece of land without dividing loading screens: a walled city, farmsteads in the valley, forests, mountains, coastline, and old mines all connect the way they would in reality. Every character has their own daily routine, going to work, to the tavern in the evening, and sleeping at night, so the world feels like it exists even without the player. The beginning is famously harsh, since the hero loses all his abilities and can initially be killed even by an ordinary wolf.

Progress isn't unlocked just by gathering experience, but by learning from specific masters, who accept the hero only once he's made a name for himself with them. Learning points are spent on strength, dexterity, handling one-handed and two-handed weapons, bows, crossbows, magic circles, or crafts like blacksmithing and alchemy. Combat relies on timing, blocking, and rhythm rather than button-mashing, and choosing the wrong moment means a quick death. Choosing a faction is crucial, since joining the city militia, the fire mages, or the mercenaries transforms your approach to quests, dialogue, and equipment. The expansion Night of the Raven adds another island, a new story thread, and even more content.

Technically the game runs on its own engine, which was demanding at the time of release but today runs on any modern computer and, thanks to community fixes and system packages, works reliably even on current graphics cards. The atmosphere is held together by subdued acoustic music that changes with the environment and the unmistakable gravelly voice acting of the characters. Reception was strongest in Central Europe, where Gothic became a phenomenon with a large modding scene and its own Czech translation. Today the game feels harsh and unforgiving of mistakes, yet players still seek it out precisely for the feeling that the world wasn't built for them and that they have to earn their place in it.

pc-modern__star-wars-knights-of-old-repu.article:
**Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic** shifts Star Wars four thousand years before the film saga, to a time when the Jedi and the Sith were numerous and the galaxy shook under war. The player begins as an insignificant crew member on a ship that is attacked right at the start, and gradually works their way toward their own lightsaber and an answer to the question of who they really are. The journey leads across several planets, from the urban levels of Taris through the Jedi academy to places the player wouldn't expect at the outset. The narrative has a clear core but also leaves plenty of room for the side stories of companions.

The rules system draws on the Star Wars tabletop role-playing game and translates dice rolls into a combat model that runs in real time but can be paused at any moment to plan the whole party's actions. The player chooses a class, distributes attributes, skills, and possibly Force powers, learns to wield both a lightsaber and a blaster, and decides whether to rely on diplomacy, hacking a droid, or brute force. Decisions accumulate on a light-side/dark-side axis, which affects the price of Force powers, the reactions of species, and the ending of the game. A party of up to three characters in the field forms the core of the game, and the conversations with companions rank among the best the studio had written at the time.

Technically the game was built on a modified Neverwinter Nights engine and looked solid on period computers; today it runs without problems, and the community has prepared bug-fix and texture packs that address the resolution and errors of the original release. The music sticks to the orchestral language of Star Wars but has its own motifs that don't directly compete with the film scores. Critical reception was very strong, and the game quickly became the benchmark for licensed RPGs. Its influence can be seen in how companion conversations and moral choices were later built in the studio's other games. Even today it stands as one of the best-told adventures set in the Star Wars universe, even if the combat system feels slower than we're used to now.

pc-modern__neverwinter-nights.article:
**Neverwinter Nights** brought the rules of Dungeons and Dragons third edition into a fully three-dimensional world while also giving players the tools to build their own adventures. The base campaign takes the hero into the city of Neverwinter, stricken by a plague, where they must gather the cure's ingredients, uncover a conspiracy, and finally confront the force behind the outbreak. The story is accompanied by a single hired companion, a more intimate approach compared to the studio's later games. Two official expansions, Shadows of Undrentide and Hordes of the Underdark, then offered noticeably stronger storytelling and higher character levels.

The heart of the game is its faithful translation of the rules: the player chooses race, class, attributes, skills, and special abilities, tracks armor class, saving throws, and multiclass combinations, and in combat, rounds play out in real time but can be broken down into individual actions with a pause. True longevity, though, came from the included Aurora Toolset editor, in which anyone could build maps, script characters, and release their own module. A huge community grew around it, with thousands of modules and persistent multiplayer servers where a dungeon master leads a group of players much like at a tabletop. Many of today's creators took their first stab at level design right here.

The engine was technically ambitious for its release year, with dynamic lighting and a fully rotatable camera, though at the cost of higher requirements and interiors built from repeating tiles. Today the game runs without issues and has also received an enhanced edition with higher resolution and better support for modern screens. The music works with a classic fantasy orchestral sound and supports the slower pace of exploration well. Reception was very good, though some reviewers considered the base campaign the weaker part of the package. The game's influence is undeniable especially in the field of player-made content, since it showed that an editor bundled with a game can keep a title alive for years after release.

pc-modern__vampire-masquerade-bloodlines.article:
**Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines** drops players into a nocturnal Los Angeles, where vampire clans coexist under the rules of the Masquerade — the strict ban on revealing their existence to humans. A freshly turned vampire gets tangled up in a dispute over a mysterious sarcophagus and gradually makes their way through the districts of Santa Monica, Hollywood, Chinatown, and Downtown, each with its own atmosphere, characters, and smaller stories. The game is played from both first- and third-person perspective and alternates between conversation, stealth, hacking, melee, and firearms.

The choice of clan is crucial, because it determines not just abilities but also how the world reacts to the player. An elegant Toreador can talk their way through most of the city, a Nosferatu must stick to the sewers because of their appearance to avoid breaking the Masquerade, and a Malkavian has their entire dialogue tree rewritten into fractured, hard-to-parse speech. On top of that comes managing blood thirst, disciplines like invisibility or mind control, and classic skill-point allocation. The game is at its strongest in the places where it steps back from combat, such as the famous haunted hotel, which gets by without a single enemy and still ranks among the best-built horror sequences in the genre.

The game ran on the then-new Source engine, which gave it convincing faces and facial animation in conversations, but the release was plagued by a host of bugs and unfinished elements that only unofficial community patches would later fix. It's precisely those patches that make it a playable and stable title today, one that runs on practically anything. The music mixes rock and electronic tracks with oppressive ambient textures, and together with excellent voice acting it holds the overall mood together. Commercially the game underperformed and the studio closed shortly after release, yet the game has gradually earned a reputation as a cult classic. Today it stands out chiefly for its writing, its atmosphere, and how seriously it takes roleplaying, even though the combat-heavy final stretch is noticeably weaker than the brilliantly written opening.

pc-modern__fallout-3.article:
**Fallout 3** brought the post-apocalyptic series from an isometric viewpoint into a fully three-dimensional open world, setting it amid the ruins of Washington, D.C., known as the Capital Wasteland. The player begins as a resident of an underground vault who, after their father's escape, emerges onto the surface and searches for him across a landscape full of radiation, mutants, slavers, and the remnants of human civilization. The opening sequence inside the vault doubles as character creation, since the player shapes their attributes and skill focus throughout childhood and adolescence.

The world is open practically from the moment the player steps outside, and it rewards curiosity. Collapsed subway stations, abandoned schools, laboratories, and small towns hide their own little stories told through terminals, logs, and the arrangement of objects, often entirely without dialogue. The combat system combines direct shooting with the tactical VATS mode, which stops time and lets the player spend action points on an aimed hit to a specific body part. Add to that ammunition management, weapon wear, radiation, the hunt for clean water, and moral choices that build karma, changing how factions react and who will join the player as a companion.

Technically the game built on the engine previously used in The Elder Scrolls series, and on the computers of the day it offered a large, continuous world at the cost of occasionally stiff animation and bugs that over time became part of the studio's reputation. On modern rigs a few community fixes are needed to make everything run smoothly, but otherwise the game still looks solid today thanks to its distinctive greenish color grading. Much of the atmosphere is carried by radio stations that play old American swing tunes across the devastated landscape, creating a contrast that became typical of the series. Reception was very strong, though part of the fanbase of the older entries criticized the shift toward action. Today it remains one of the best-built open worlds of its era.

pc-modern__dragon-age-origins.article:
**Dragon Age: Origins** is a dark fantasy RPG set in the kingdom of Ferelden, which faces a catastrophe called the Blight — an invasion of corrupted creatures led by an archdemon. The player becomes one of the Grey Wardens, the order that alone is capable of stopping the threat, and must gather allies from among humans, elves, dwarves, and mages just to be able to raise an army at all. The title refers to six different opening chapters based on the character's race and background, which differ not just in setting but also in how others perceive the player later on. As a result, replayability is unusually high.

The game deliberately builds on classic computer RPGs. Combat runs in real time with the option to pause, the camera can be pulled up into a tactical overhead view, and the player commands a four-member party whose composition decides whether a fight goes smoothly or grinds to a halt. This is complemented by a tactics system that lets companions be given simple conditional behaviors in advance. Above all of this stand the conversations and relationships with companions, who have their own opinions, can leave the player or even turn against them, and the game's final decisions rank among the best-written dilemmas in the genre.

Technically it was the studio's own engine, which on computers offered higher detail and a tactical camera absent from the console versions, so the PC release was long considered the definitive one. Visually the game bets on grime and blood that stays on characters even after a fight ends, reinforcing its grim tone. The music works with dark orchestral motifs and a sung theme that players still remember today. Reception was very good, and the game became one of the pillars of modern fantasy RPGs. Today it feels slow-paced and some locations repeat, but the strength of the writing, the party, and the consistency with which the game carries the consequences of decisions keep it at the top of recommended titles.

pc-modern__fallout-new-vegas.article:
**Fallout: New Vegas** opens with the player getting shot in the head and buried in a grave in the desert near the small town of Goodsprings. The courier who survives sets out to track down a stolen package and along the way gets caught up in a power struggle over the Hoover Dam — that is, over the source of energy and water for the entire region. Facing off against each other are the New California Republic, the slave-holding Caesar's Legion, and the mysterious owner of the New Vegas casinos, and the player may join any side or carve out their own path to power.

The game uses the previous entry's foundation but rebuilds it in favor of roleplaying. Skill checks returned to dialogues, so a player gifted in speech or technically skilled can resolve entire blocks of content without firing a single shot. The key new feature is reputation with individual factions, tracked separately and determining who welcomes the player and who opens fire on sight. Also added were weapon modifications, custom ammunition crafting, a harder mode with hunger, thirst, and sleep, and companions with their own quests, whose resolution ranks among the best content in the game. There are also noticeably more weapons, each with its own personality.

The release was plagued by serious technical issues and crashes, a reputation the game carried for a long time, but community fixes and unofficial patches now ensure stable performance even on modern computers. Visually it's weaker than the top titles of its time, but it has a strong identity built on the contrast between the scorched Mojave desert and the neon lights of the New Vegas Strip. The music again works with period radio songs, this time with a greater emphasis on country and western tones. Reception at launch was more divided, but with the passage of time the game is considered the peak of the series thanks to its writing and the sheer number of ways to solve the same problem. Today it still remains among the most common recommendations for anyone looking for an RPG with genuine freedom.

pc-modern__deus-ex-human-revolution.article:
**Deus Ex: Human Revolution** is a prequel to the original Deus Ex, set in the near future, when humanity splits between those who can afford mechanical body augmentations and those who reject them or can't afford them. The player takes on the role of Adam Jensen, head of security at a biotech company, who survives a brutal attack on the lab only thanks to extensive implants and sets out to find who was behind it. The path leads through Detroit, Shanghai, and other locations that serve as small open cities full of side quests.

The core of the game is the ability to solve every situation in more than one way. A building can be entered through the front door after a conversation, through a rooftop vent, through the sewers, or by force through security. The player spends Praxis points on augmentations that unlock silent falls from height, seeing through walls, hacking better terminals, greater carrying capacity, or a social module that gives an edge in conversations. Combat works with cover and a shift to third person, but stealth is often more advantageous and the game rewards it with both experience and content. Verbal duels with key characters are a self-contained minigame, all about reading the other person and picking the right tone.

Visually the game bet on a striking gold-and-black color scheme with nods to Renaissance painting, which still gives it a distinctive look today despite its older engine. On computers it offered higher-resolution textures and better controls than the console versions, and today it runs on practically anything. The music rests on subdued electronic textures that reinforce the feeling of an alienated, corporate world. Reception was very good, and the game is considered a successful revival of the franchise, though the boss battles against major antagonists were often criticized and the studio later reworked them. Today it stands as one of the cleanest fusions of RPG, stealth, and storytelling, one that also laid out themes that haven't lost any relevance.

pc-modern__dark-souls-prepare-to-die-edi.article:
**Dark Souls: Prepare to Die Edition** brought to computers a dark fantasy adventure set in the cursed kingdom of Lordran, where the player, as an undead, searches for a way to stop the fading of the fire that holds the world together. The story isn't told through cutscenes but through item descriptions, architecture, and terse character lines, so the player pieces it together themselves and much of it remains open to interpretation. The game's strength lies in how interconnected its world is, since the entire map forms one linked whole, where an unlocked shortcut surprisingly leads back to a place the player passed through hours earlier.

Combat is slow, deliberate, and built around managing stamina. Every dodge, block, and attack costs stamina, and a mistake means death, after which the player loses the souls they've collected, which serve as both currency and experience. Getting them back is possible only by returning to the place of death, which creates tension with every step forward. The character can be built in vastly different ways, from a heavily armored fighter with a large shield to a swift swordsman, a sorcerer, or a faithful wielding miracles, and equipment is upgraded at blacksmiths using rare materials. Multiplayer is handled unconventionally, through other players' accumulating messages, summoning help, and invading other players' worlds.

The computer release was originally a weak port with a locked resolution and a low frame count, which community fixes quickly resolved, and a reworked version was released later. Visually the game feels subdued and grimy; music appears almost exclusively during fights against major bosses, so exploration is accompanied only by environmental sounds, which considerably heightens the tension. Reception was very strong, and the game popularized difficulty as part of the experience rather than an obstacle. Its influence is enormous, having spawned an entire wave of imitators that adopted its bonfires, the loss of currency upon death, and storytelling through the environment. Today it remains harsh, but fair.

pc-modern__pillars-of-eternity.article:
**Pillars of Eternity** is a conscious return to the isometric RPGs of the nineties, but built on an entirely new world and a modern technical foundation. The player arrives as a settler in the land of Dyrwood, witnesses a strange ritual, and gains the ability to see souls and the past lives of anyone they touch. Around this unfolds an investigation into the mystery of why children in the region are being born without souls, and through it the game reaches questions of faith, power, and what gods who may not always have been gods do to a person.

The combat system runs in real time with pause and demands attention, since it depends on positioning, on who's holding an enemy's attention, and on combining abilities. The party can hold up to six members, and the player chooses from eleven classes, including unconventional ones like the Chanter, who recites long incantations, or the Cipher, who works directly with souls. Alongside combat, the game engages with exploration, resting, limited supplies, and extensive dialogues where not just skills but also personality traits gathered from previous decisions often come into play. Managing your own stronghold and an extensive dungeon are also part of it, serving as an optional trial for a well-prepared party. The expansion then pushes the whole story toward a much harsher conclusion.

Technically the game combines pre-rendered painted backgrounds with three-dimensional characters, which lets it still look detailed after years and run smoothly on practically any computer. The music is intimate and slightly melancholic, with a pronounced use of strings and winds, and together with the painted locations it creates a calm, bookish atmosphere. Reception was very good; the game was praised for its writing, its world, and for not blindly copying the classic form but rather smoothing out its most tedious spots. Its influence lay chiefly in confirming the viability of this entire type of game and paving the way for further titles.

pc-modern__kingdom-come-deliverance.article:
**Kingdom Come: Deliverance** is an RPG without dragons or magic, set in Bohemia at the start of the fifteenth century, during the conflict between Wenceslaus and Sigismund. The player takes on Henry, the son of a blacksmith from Skalitz, whose village is burned down by soldiers, and follows his journey from an inexperienced young man to someone who can hold a sword and deal with nobility. The world is a scaled-down but fairly faithful reconstruction of the actual Sázava region, including the Sázava Monastery, Talmberg, and the town of Kutná Hora with its surrounding mines and villages.

The game pushes for authenticity in nearly everything. Henry can't read at first, shoots poorly with a bow, and quickly runs out of breath in combat. Swordplay works with attack directions, blocks, feints, and combos, and against multiple opponents, defeat is real and frequent. Add to that managing hunger, sleep, the cleanliness and damage of clothing, armor repairs at craftsmen's shops, alchemy where potions are genuinely mixed according to a recipe at a brewing stand, and lockpicking and pickpocketing. Investigating the main storyline often proceeds through conversations, following clues, and persuasion, where eloquence, reputation, and how the player looks all matter. Quests have a time limit, so delay can change how they play out or close them off entirely.

Technically the game runs on CryEngine and, at release, offered very convincing nature, lighting, and draw distance at the cost of high hardware demands and a number of bugs that subsequent patches addressed. Today it still looks great and runs noticeably better than at launch. Its sound is carried by Czech folk and period music arranged in orchestral form, along with voice acting that comes across especially well in the local release. Reception was strong, especially in the Czech Republic, where it represented an exceptionally large domestic project. Its influence lies chiefly in showing that there's a market for historical RPGs without fantasy elements, and that such a premise can carry a game even outside major publishers. Today it's a demanding, slow game that rewards patience and a player willing to accept its rules.

pc-modern__disco-elysium.article:
**Disco Elysium** is an isometric RPG that almost entirely drops combat and instead builds the whole game around conversation, investigation, and the inner life of its main character. The player wakes up as a detective with total amnesia in a wrecked hotel room in the city of Revachol, a place that has never recovered from a lost revolution and occupation. There's a hanged man in the courtyard, and somebody has to solve the case. Over the course of a few days, the game follows not just the investigation but also how the detective pieces together his own identity and worldview.

Instead of classic skills, the game has twenty-four inner voices that act as independent characters in the dialogue. Logic offers conclusions, Empathy reads other people's feelings, Electrochemistry pushes for one more drink, Inland Empire makes things up, and Authority urges the player to slam a fist on the table. Dice are rolled, and both success and failure move the story forward — failure often opens a more interesting path than winning would. On top of that sits the Thought Cabinet system, where the player lets opinions and beliefs mature in the detective's head, permanently changing his stats. Health and Morale function as life bars, so the detective can die even from a memory he can't bear to face.

Visually, the game uses painted locations that resemble oil paintings, with characters stylized into blurred, almost sketch-like shapes. It runs smoothly practically everywhere, and text is its main content, which makes computers its natural home. The music is subdued, atmospheric, and sometimes melancholic, with a strong presence of guitars and horns. Reception was extraordinarily strong, the game won a string of awards, and it was praised above all for writing that is unusually literary and funny at the same time. An expanded version with full voice acting followed later. Today it stands as proof that an RPG doesn't need combat to have momentum and tension, and it remains one of the strongest pieces of writing the medium has produced.

pc-modern__cyberpunk-2077.article:
**Cyberpunk 2077** is a first-person action RPG set in Night City, a huge American metropolis run by corporations, gangs, and technology that reaches directly into the human body. The player takes on the role of a mercenary known as V, who ends up with someone else's personality recorded in their head after a job gone wrong, and with time running out. From there the story unfolds around identity, dying, and what's left of a person afterward, filled out by extensive side stories that often outshine the main plot.

Character building rests on five attributes, each tied to skill trees for shooting, melee combat, stealth, technical skills, and hacking. Cybernetic implants form a separate layer of equipment and fundamentally change how you play, from slowed-down time and hidden blades to quickhacks that let you disable enemy weapons or turn enemies against each other. Night City is densely built and vertical, with distinct districts that differ in architecture and residents alike, and driving, racing, and exploration hold it all together. Decisions in quests often carry delayed consequences, and the game has several markedly different endings.

The launch was troubled, as the game shipped in a state that didn't match expectations, especially on older consoles, and even on PC it was plagued by bugs. A long series of patches followed, along with a major update that overhauled skills, police behavior, and enemy AI, so today's version is a substantially different game from the original release. Technically it ranks among the best, especially thanks to its lighting, reflections, and neon night-time atmosphere, but it demands serious hardware. The music blends electronic sounds, rock, and fictional radio stations with their own in-game bands. Today, Cyberpunk 2077 is seen as an example of a game that repaired its reputation only after years of work, and as an open world it stands among the best-built cities in the genre.

pc-modern__elden-ring.article:
**ELDEN RING** combines the demanding combat system the studio is known for with a sprawling open world called the Lands Between. As the Tarnished, the player searches for shards of a shattered ring and becomes a rival to the demigods who divided its fragments among themselves. The storytelling stays sparse and unforgiving toward a careless player, since essential information hides in item descriptions and conversations that are easy to miss entirely. The world is split into six large above-ground regions and an extensive underground that forms a second map almost as large as the first.

The open world changed the pacing. The player almost always has a choice of where to go, and if something stops them, they can leave, grow stronger elsewhere, and come back later. Helping with this is a horse capable of a double jump and quick movement, along with a huge number of smaller dungeons, castles, and catacombs scattered across the land. Combat relies on stamina, dodging, and attack timing, but adds Ashes of War — interchangeable special weapon skills — and the ability to summon allies. Character building is quite open, ranging from heavy weapons through sorceries and incantations to bows, and stat points can be reallocated at will at the appropriate NPC. Multiplayer again rests on messages, summoning, and invasions into other players' worlds.

Technically, the game suffered from frame-rate stutters on PC at launch, which later patches addressed; today it runs considerably better, though it remains demanding. Visually it relies on muted, golden, misty vistas that lure the player toward the next destination from a distance, which is one of the main reasons exploration works so well. The music again mostly appears during fights against major bosses and ranks among the best in its category. Reception was extraordinary, and the game won numerous awards, including several Game of the Year titles. The later expansion Shadow of the Erdtree added another large region. Today it serves as the foundation of the genre and, at the same time, as the most accessible entry point into the studio's games.

pc-modern__baldur-s-gate-3.article:
**Baldur's Gate 3** continues the classic series but rebuilds it on the rules of fifth-edition Dungeons and Dragons and a turn-based combat system. The player begins as a captive aboard a ship belonging to an alien race whose members have implanted a parasite in their head meant to turn them into one of their own. After the ship crashes, a group of survivors sets out to find a cure, and the road takes them through a coastline, cursed lands, and finally into the city of Baldur's Gate itself, where it's revealed who is really behind the infection. The main storyline branches depending on whom the player chooses to trust.

The game offers an unusual amount of freedom. Nearly every problem can be solved in more than one way — through conversation, a dice roll to persuade someone, sneaking around a cliff edge, shapeshifting into an animal, talking to the dead, or simply setting the whole room on fire. Combat is turn-based and makes use of elevation, reach, patches of fire and poison, shoving enemies off ledges, and combinations of spells. The party can hold up to four members, and companions have their own storylines, opinions, and endings. The entire campaign can be played together with other players, with each person controlling their own character and free to split off from the group at any time to go their own way.

Technically the game looks exceptional thanks to full motion-capture performances, meaning even side conversations are fully directed instead of relying on static text screens. Performance on modern PCs is good, though the final act grows more demanding due to the sheer number of characters present in the city. The music draws on both orchestral and period instruments and features original songs performed directly within the world. Reception was extremely strong, and the game took home the industry's top awards. Its influence lies mainly in raising the bar for how many consequences an RPG can accommodate, since it accounts even for very unusual player behavior. Today it's one of the most expansive games in the genre and can easily run past a hundred hours without losing pace.

pc-modern__warcraft-iii-reign-of-chaos.article:
**Warcraft III: Reign of Chaos** brought the famous fantasy series into full 3D while also pushing real-time strategy further toward role-playing elements. Alongside the four warring factions — the Human Alliance, the Orcish Horde, the Undead Scourge, and the Night Elves — the center of the action belongs to heroes: characters who gain experience, learn new abilities, carry items, and gradually become the backbone of the entire army. A unit cap and an upkeep system that penalizes overly large armies with higher costs push players toward smaller, more carefully assembled forces. Fights over neutral creature camps, which guard treasure and experience, turn every map into a space full of secondary objectives worth fighting for before ever reaching the enemy base.

The campaign takes players through all four factions and tells a continuous story about the fall of Prince Arthas and the arrival of the Burning Legion. Missions often skip base-building entirely and turn into small tactical expeditions with a handful of units, where managing potions and abilities matters most. Technically, in 2002 this was a remarkably clean engine that kept a smooth frame rate even on weaker hardware, and its art style, with saturated colors and bold silhouettes, has aged considerably better than the more realistic competition of its time. The music alternates orchestral themes with drums and choir depending on which faction you're playing, and together with directed cutscenes it holds the storytelling together.

Contemporary reception was enthusiastic among both critics and players, and the game quickly became a pillar of the competitive scene of its time. Its true legacy, however, was born outside the main game mode: the included World Editor allowed players to build custom maps and scenarios, and it was from these that Defense of the Ancients emerged, the forerunner of the entire MOBA genre. The expansion The Frozen Throne then added further heroes, campaigns, and neutral units available for hire. Today, Warcraft III still reads like a textbook example of giving strategy a face and a story. The pace is slower than modern titles, but every unit and every hero carries a weight that's hard to find in later games.

pc-modern__age-of-mythology.article:
**Age of Mythology** is a spin-off from the historical Age of Empires line, set instead in a world of gods, heroes, and mythical creatures. Instead of real nations, you choose between the Greeks, the Egyptians, and the Norse, and right at the start you also pick a major god who determines which bonuses, units, and abilities will be available to you for the rest of the match. With every advance to a new age you then choose a minor god, so no two matches with the same civilization ever play out quite the same. Alongside the usual three resources comes favor, which each culture earns differently, and it's favor that's spent to recruit mythical units and cast divine powers ranging from earthquakes to plagues.

The basic construction and economy remain recognizable to anyone who has played Age of Empires II, but the move to 3D allowed for things the two-dimensional predecessor couldn't manage: centaurs, colossi, and giant serpents move across the battlefield with real weight, units collide physically, and divine powers can reshape an entire hillside of the map. The campaign follows the Atlantean hero Arkantos across the Mediterranean and the north, framed as a classic adventurous journey with story twists rather than a string of isolated battles. The sound design relies on deep drums, horns, and choral themes that reinforce the mythological atmosphere well.

The game was received very favorably and remains among the studio's most beloved titles to this day, partly thanks to its scenario editor, in which the community created a huge number of custom maps and campaigns. The expansion The Titans added the Atlantean civilization and giant Titans as the climax of a match. A modern release under the name Extended Edition brought the game to current systems and resolutions. Today, Age of Mythology is a pleasantly accessible strategy game with a brisker pace than contemporary war simulations, built on an idea nobody has quite repeated since: turning religion and mythology into a playable system of decisions that shapes your style of play from the very first minute all the way to the final assault.

pc-modern__rise-of-nations.article:
**Rise of Nations** attempts to combine the speed of real-time strategy with the sweeping scope of turn-based games like Civilization, and it pulls it off surprisingly well. A single match carries a nation from antiquity all the way to the information age, and advancing through eight eras doesn't just mean better units — it also brings new buildings, new resources, and new ways to win. Alongside food and timber, players manage wealth, metal, oil, and above all knowledge, which is generated in universities and unlocks research across four fields. There's also a military and economic cap that prevents every match from degenerating into simply churning out armies.

The key innovation was national borders. Territory expands around cities and buildings; inside your own borders your units fight better, while in enemy territory they suffer reduced strength, so conquest isn't a matter of one long march across the whole map but a gradual shifting of the front line and securing your rear. Victory can be achieved through conquest, territorial dominance, accumulating wonders of the world, or racing ahead in technology. The Conquer the World campaign additionally adds a turn-based map on which you move armies, collect bonus cards, and then resolve individual clashes in real time. Visually it's a clean, legible, unadorned style that has aged well precisely because it prioritizes clarity.

The game earned strong reviews, and many players still consider it one of the best-balanced real-time strategy games ever made. The expansion Thrones and Patriots added further nations and government forms, and the later Extended Edition release brought the game to modern PCs along with online play. Today, Rise of Nations feels unusually welcoming: much of the micromanagement is automated, the economy runs itself, and the player can focus on the big decisions. For anyone who wants to experience the rise of their own civilization over the course of one evening instead of fifty hours, it remains one of the best options available.

pc-modern__homeworld-2.article:
**Homeworld 2** is one of the few strategy games to genuinely pull off combat in three full dimensions. The fleet moves through open space where there is no up or down, and the player has to think about attacks from above, flanking from behind, and which direction the guns of large ships are actually facing. The camera can be freely rotated around the entire battle, a tactical map reduces the whole engagement to a legible grid of icons, and a special formation-spacing system lets you move even large fleets while keeping them in fixed formations. Controls that could easily have become a nightmare instead remain surprisingly manageable.

The campaign continues the story of the Hiigaran people, who face an invasion by the Vaygr fleet, carried in a similarly grave, almost meditative tone as the first game. Crucially, your ships carry over from mission to mission: whatever you lose stays lost, and whatever you preserve, you bring into the next engagement. Every battle therefore carries a double cost, since winning at a heavy price means fighting the next fight with half-empty hangars. New here are the subsystems of large ships, which can be targeted and destroyed individually, so instead of a long, grinding bombardment, a giant cruiser can be blinded by knocking out its sensors or slowed by disabling its engines. Visually it's an impressive study in light, nebulae, and scale: tiny fighters vanish against the flanks of mothership hulls like insects.

The music, combining ambient textures, choral themes, and silence in between, ranks among the best space games have ever offered, and together with hand-drawn interludes it creates an unmistakable mood of a lonely journey. Reviews were very positive, though some players regretted the shorter campaign compared to the first game. Relic later released modding tools that spawned extensive mods, including ones set in other science-fiction universes, and the game also received a modern remastered version. Today, Homeworld 2 remains the best argument that a space strategy game doesn't have to be just a chessboard laid flat.

pc-modern__warhammer-40-000-dawn-of-war.article:
**Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War** took the brutal world of the tabletop game and turned it into a real-time strategy focused on combat rather than woodcutting. The core resource is requisition, earned from strategic points scattered across the map, so hiding behind walls makes no sense: whoever doesn't hold territory has nothing to pay their soldiers with. The army is also built not from individuals but from squads, which get reinforced with new men in the field, equipped with heavy weapons, and strengthened by a commander. Add morale, cover, and the ability to capture buildings, and every clash becomes a fight for position, not just numbers.

At the heart of the experience are truly brutal melee clashes. When two squads collide, the game switches to animations where units grab, stab, and throw each other around, and commanders have their own devastating attacks. The launch lineup featured four factions - Space Marines, Orks, Eldar, and Chaos Space Marines - each with a different rhythm of play, from the unsubtle Ork hordes to the fragile but fast Eldar formations. The campaign follows the Space Marines' crusade on the planet Tartarus and serves more as a guide to the mechanics than a complex story. Technically, the game impressed with detailed models that could be zoomed in on down to the individual soldier, and sound full of roars, prayers, and gunfire.

Reception was very good, as the game managed to appeal both to fans of the source material and to players who knew nothing about the 41st millennium. A string of expansions followed, adding new factions and a campaign map system, and the series continued with sequels that moved even further from base-building toward purely tactical combat. Today, Dawn of War remains the easiest way to experience the atmosphere of this dark future, and a reminder of a time when strategy games could still be loud, dirty, and straightforward.

pc-modern__supreme-commander.article:
**Supreme Commander** is a strategy game about scale. While most games in the genre work with dozens of units, here you routinely command hundreds on maps so vast that a bomber's flight across the battlefield can take a full minute. The key to making sense of it all is the famous seamless strategic zoom: a single scroll of the mouse wheel takes you from a view of a single robot to an abstract map of an entire continent, where armies are just icons. The economy runs continuously, managing mass and energy, and building can't be rushed with a single click, since a lack of income simply slows production down rather than stopping it.

Every match is led by a commander mech, a giant amphibious machine that builds structures, defends itself, and whose loss usually means the end of the game. The three factions in the conflict - UEF, Cybran, and Aeon - share a basic skeleton but differ in detail and in the appearance of their massive experimental units, which battles often culminate around. These are what make the late game a spectacle: spider-like colossi, flying fortresses, or a cannon that can shell the opposite end of the map. The game can even be played across two monitors, with one serving as the battlefield and the other as a permanently displayed tactical map - an unheard-of feature back in 2007.

Reviews were very favorable, though there was talk of steep demands on period computers, since simulating thousands of projectiles and units taxed the processor heavily. The game is a spiritual successor to Total Annihilation and, like it, cultivated a devoted community that kept it alive for years with its own balance mods and tournaments. The expansion subtitled Forged Alliance also refined the balance so much that for many players it became the only version they return to. Today, Supreme Commander offers something rare even in modern lineups: the feeling of true command, where you're not thinking about individual clicks but about supply lines, logistics, and where your army will be five minutes from now. It's a strategy game that rewards planning ahead more than fast fingers.

pc-modern__starcraft-ii-wings-of-liberty.article:
**StarCraft II: Wings of Liberty** arrived after a long wait, carrying the weight of one of the most respected titles in the genre's history. Even so, it chose a path of careful modernization: the three factions - Terrans, Zerg, and Protoss - remained unmistakably distinct, the mineral-and-gas economy stayed unchanged, and the emphasis is still on precise unit control, map awareness, and attack timing. New units, however, shook up established habits, whether it's Terran mechs transforming into siege tanks or the Protoss ability to warp entire squads in from a distance.

The campaign offers something rare in the genre. Between missions you walk around the ship Hyperion, talk to the crew, spend rewards on unit upgrades, and choose which contract to take, giving a sense of agency even off the battlefield. Individual missions almost never repeat themselves: one moment you're fleeing rising lava, the next you're gathering resources only at night, when the hordes retreat. Technically it's an exceptionally polished game that ran smoothly even on then-average machines, and its interface is among the clearest in the entire genre. The music mixes western guitars with orchestral and cold electronic motifs depending on whether you're in a story segment or in combat.

The game immediately became a pillar of competitive play and, together with the elaborate Battle.net ladder, redefined what an online strategy game should look like: automatic matchmaking by skill level, leagues, and broadcasts of tournament matches. The story continued in the expansions Heart of the Swarm and Legacy of the Void, which finished telling the fates of the remaining races. Today the base game is available for free and remains perhaps the best entry point into classic real-time strategy: tough, fast, and unforgiving, but with superbly guided training and a campaign forgiving enough for beginners.

pc-modern__xcom-enemy-unknown.article:
**XCOM: Enemy Unknown** revived the legacy of the old classic UFO: Enemy Unknown and translated it into the language of modern games without losing what mattered most: the feeling that every decision has a cost. The game operates on two levels. On the strategic level, you manage an underground base shown as a cross-section like an ant farm, build laboratories and workshops, launch interceptors against unidentified objects, and above all try to keep the world's nervous nations within the coalition, since every country that leaves cuts into your budget. On the tactical level, you command a handful of soldiers in turn-based firefights, where movement and action fit into two moves per turn.

The magic lies in how the two layers connect. Soldiers gain ranks, specializations, and abilities, and the longer they survive, the more valuable they become. But the aliens have better weapons, panic reduces accuracy, and a single misjudged position can cost the life of a veteran you've led through ten missions. In Ironman mode, the game only saves once, so no mistake can be undone. That's exactly what turns an ordinary skirmish into a drama players still talk about long afterward, and it's why the habit arose of naming soldiers after friends and acquaintances.

Technically, the game relies on tight, clear maps and a dynamic camera that swoops in on a soldier for key hits, giving combat a cinematic pace without unnecessary delay. The sound plays with silence and nervous droning interrupted by shouts and enemy hisses. Reception was very strong, and the game is often cited as an example of how to revive an old concept without betraying its original idea. The expansion Enemy Within added genetic modifications for soldiers, mechanical suits, and a new human threat. It was followed by the sequel XCOM 2, which sped up the pace and moved players into the role of the resistance. Today, Enemy Unknown is still a great place to start with turn-based tactics: the rules are few, they're easy to understand, and yet they generate tension that more complex games often can't produce even with a manual ten times as long.

pc-modern__europa-universalis-iv.article:
**Europa Universalis IV** is a game about running a state in the period from the late Middle Ages to the Napoleonic Wars, played out on a map of the entire world divided into thousands of provinces. It doesn't run in turns but in flowing time that can be paused and resumed at any moment, which is necessary since so much happens at once: diplomatic negotiations are underway, manufactories are being built, a distant colony is asking for money, and a neighbor has just laid claim to your border province. The player leads any existing state, from France to small Italian city-republics, and essentially sets their own goals.

At the heart of the system are three types of monarch points - administrative, diplomatic, and military - which accumulate according to the current ruler's abilities and are spent on technologies, on absorbing conquered territories, and on national ideas that determine the country's long-term focus. Alongside this, the game tracks stability, inflation, religious unity, and above all aggressive expansion, which causes surrounding powers to unite into a coalition against a state that has grown too greedy. War is therefore never just a matter of a bigger army, but also of whether you can politically afford it. The interface is dense, full of numbers and options, and the first hours can be tough despite the built-in advice and tutorials.

The game has been shaped over the long term by an endless string of expansions and free updates that gradually reworked trade, the navy, government forms, and the behavior of individual regions, so today's version differs substantially from the one from 2013. Reception was very favorable, and the title became the backbone of the entire grand-strategy genre as well as a source of countless player stories about improbable empires. Today, Europa Universalis IV is above all a giant story-generating machine that rewards patience: once you understand why your neighbor behaves the way they do, it's hard to tear yourself away from the map. Getting used to the sheer number of menus takes a while, but the reward is a game you can spend a hundred hours on and still keep discovering corners of the world you haven't visited yet.

pc-modern__stellaris.article:
**Stellaris** took the proven skeleton of grand strategy games and moved it into space, where the player first builds their own civilization: choosing the species' appearance and traits, its ethics, form of government, and method of interstellar travel. The game then begins with a single planet and a handful of ships, and the first dozens of hours belong to exploration. Survey ships fly from system to system, stumbling upon anomalies, the wreckage of long-dead empires, and strange phenomena that trigger short story events. This phase, when the map is still dark and every jump might bring anything, is among the best the game has to offer.

Gradually, though, a second face opens up: managing a growing empire. Colonies need resources and labor, the population has opinions of its own and can rebel, neighbors form federations, and the galactic community votes on laws you might not like. Alongside ordinary wars lurk crises that can upend an entire game, whether awakened ancient empires or a threat arriving from outside the galaxy in the late game. The military side relies on designing your own ships, assembling weapons, shields, and engines based on what you know about the enemy.

The game has undergone an extraordinarily extensive transformation since release. Several major free updates fundamentally rewrote the way of interstellar travel and planet management, while paid expansions added entirely new ways to play, from machine civilizations to a focus on trade or espionage. Reception was very good, and Stellaris quickly became its studio's most approachable title, since it requires no knowledge of history, just a willingness to experiment. Today it's the best game for anyone who wants to experience a sci-fi story of their own civilization, from the first jump to the stars all the way to galactic politics, and doesn't mind that the most interesting things often happen off the battlefield. The slower mid-game stretch is often criticized, but the early exploration and the late crises rank among the strongest experiences the genre offers.

pc-modern__rimworld.article:
**RimWorld** is a colony simulation set on a remote planet, where a handful of crash-landed survivors gradually builds an entire settlement with fields, workshops, a hospital, and defensive positions. The game looks down on a simple two-dimensional map with figures that look almost like paper cutouts, but underneath runs an unusually deep simulation. Each colonist has their own skills, personality traits, relationships with others, illnesses, scars, and moods affected by everything from lack of sleep to an ugly dining room. The player doesn't issue commands directly, only sets work priorities and lets the colonists figure out what needs doing.

The plot isn't driven by a script but by the so-called Storyteller, an AI that sends events to the colony based on the chosen style. One time a trade caravan arrives, another time it's a raid by raiders, a plague, a lightning-caused fire, or a refugee begging for asylum. This is where the stories arise that players tell each other: the tale of a colonist who went mad in winter, or of a doctor who botched a single operation and thereby sealed the fate of the whole settlement. The game doesn't shy away from dark themes either, from organ trading to drug addiction, leaving it up to the player how far they go.

Technically, RimWorld is undemanding and runs almost anywhere, which, combined with exceptionally open mod support, has given it a huge and still-active community; thousands of mods exist, changing the game from minor tweaks to entirely different settings. The music relies on calm guitar that lets the sounds of work and combat stand out. Reception was very good, the game launched after a lengthy early-access period, and it has received several substantial expansions. Today it ranks among the best building simulations of all, because at its core it's not about building a base but about the people who live in it. The simple graphics even work as an advantage: they leave room for the imagination to fill in scenes that realistic visuals could never convey so powerfully.

pc-modern__frostpunk.article:
**Frostpunk** is a city-building game that deals with survival instead of prosperity. The world has frozen over, the last people have gathered around a giant coal generator, and the player's job is to make sure the fire doesn't go out. The city grows in concentric rings around the heat source, so the very first decision - what to build closer and what farther away - determines who freezes at night. On top of that, you manage coal, wood, steel, and above all people, who need food, medical care, and hope.
