Scouting expeditions head out into the snowy wasteland to look for supplies and other survivors, who will nonetheless bring new mouths to feed.

At the heart of the game is the Book of Laws. You gradually pass rules that govern the settlement, and almost every one has a dark side. You can allow child labor, or instead set up shelters; you can introduce forced shifts that save the economy but exhaust the people. Over time, the paths split into Faith and Order, and both lead to the leader, in trying to save the city, becoming someone they would have condemned at the start. The game never moralizes, it just shows the consequences and lets them hang in the air.

Technically, it's a very impressive piece of work: snow builds up in layers, the generator's sirens echo between the houses, and the moment a great blizzard hits, the screen turns into a gray wall pierced only by red boilers. The music relies on solo strings and silence, and together with the visuals creates one of the tightest atmospheres in the genre. Reception was very favorable, especially for how the game combined city-building with moral dilemmas, and the developers went on to expand it with further scenarios. The campaign isn't long, but every playthrough raises uncomfortable questions. Today, Frostpunk is proof that a city-builder can be tense without an enemy army on the horizon; all it takes is a thermometer that drops a few degrees lower every day, and people watching to see what you'll do. The sequel then took the idea and expanded it to the scale of an entire city.

pc-modern__anno-1800.article:
**Anno 1800** brings the city-building series into the nineteenth century, the age of the Industrial Revolution, steam engines, and overseas trade. It starts modestly, with a handful of fishing huts and lumberjacks, but once the first settlers are promoted to craftsmen, the production chains that define the game start turning. Work clothes need wool and dye, canned goods need meat and tin, and every satisfied tier of population unlocks another level of needs. Watching a fishing village grow into a harbor full of chimneys and cranes is unusually satisfying.

The game doesn't stick to a single map. Alongside your home archipelago in the Old World, you colonize the New World, where crops grow that can't be cultivated back home, and shipping routes must be maintained between the two regions. On top of that come expeditions for rare goods resolved through text-based decisions, an arctic region with its own rules, and tourism. There are also rivals to trade with, sign treaties with, or wage war on, but the game's center of gravity clearly lies in logistics and planning. That's exactly why it plays well even at a calm pace without any pressure toward conflict.

Visually, it's one of the most beautiful city builders ever made. The cities are packed with tiny animations, people walk the streets, smoke rises from factories, and the harbor lives in constant motion, with individual pedestrians visible up close when you zoom in. The music alternates parlor waltzes with sweeping orchestral pieces and captures the era's mood of enthusiasm for progress very well. Reception was very good, and the game is generally considered the best entry in the series; it was supported by a long line of expansions that added new regions and mechanics. Today, Anno 1800 is the right choice for a player who wants to spend hours tuning a perfectly functioning industrial organism while looking at something beautiful. It's more demanding on your PC than most of the competition, since large cities with tens of thousands of inhabitants can strain even a modern rig.

pc-modern__crusader-kings-iii.article:
**Crusader Kings III** is a grand strategy game in which you don't play as a state, but as a person. You pick a specific medieval ruler, from an Irish count to a Byzantine emperor, and play as them until death; then you take over their heir and continue on, with the main concern usually being keeping power within your family. This flips the genre's usual logic on its head. Conquered land is worthless if inheritance law splits it among three sons, and your most dangerous enemy is often your own brother.

Every character has traits, skills, secrets, and a stress level that rises when they act against their nature. Relationships are built from concrete memories of what you did to whom, so when a vassal refuses to send troops, it's usually obvious why. Outside the battlefield, the game is played through intrigue: you can plot against a rival, gain allies through marriage, raise a foreign heir at your own court, or simply focus on longevity. Alongside this runs a religious layer, where you can modify or even found your own faith, and a system of lifestyle paths that gradually turns a ruler into a scholar, a warrior, or a scheming courtier.

Compared to the previous entry, the game has worked hard on clarity: the interface explains where every number comes from, character portraits are fully three-dimensional and change with age and personality, and there's an extensive guide for newcomers. Reception was excellent, and the title is often cited as the most accessible gateway into the world of grand strategy. It was followed by expansions focused on Norse cultures, court life, royal residences, or religious power. Today, Crusader Kings III is played mainly for its stories: far more than the optimal move, you'll remember the moment your closest friend betrayed you at your own wedding. The military side is deliberately simpler by comparison, and the game doesn't try to be a precise historical simulation, but rather a machine for dynastic drama that you can't stop playing.

pc-modern__satisfactory.article:
**Satisfactory** is a factory-building game that, unlike most of the genre, you experience from a first-person view, standing right in the middle of your own machines. A giant corporation drops you on an alien planet with a single task: get industry running. You start with hand-mining ore and a portable smelter, and end up with multi-story complexes where dozens of kinds of parts roll along conveyor belts, freight trains run on rails, and a tangle of pipes carrying molten material stretches overhead. Progress is governed by a research tree tied to a giant space elevator, into which you send ever more complex products.

The game's charm lies in the fact that you actually walk through the factory on foot. A poorly planned layout isn't an abstract number in a spreadsheet, but a confusing tangle you have to physically crawl through to find out where the supply chain got stuck. At the same time, this gives building an architectural dimension: players construct halls, ramps, and elevated viaducts, fine-tuning symmetry and color schemes even though a pile of machines in a field would do just fine. The planet itself is a hand-designed world with biomes ranging from grassy plains to caves and swamps, full of hostile fauna and nooks with upgrades, so exploration works as the other half of the game.

The title spent several years in early access and reached its full release in 2024, when it also received a proper ending to its story line. Technically, it benefits from a modern engine: sweeping vistas, time of day, fog over the hills, and the hum of machinery that blends into a surprisingly soothing soundscape. The game can be played cooperatively with other players in one world, which makes it one of the best co-op projects for long evenings. Reception was very favorable, and Satisfactory today stands as the clearest proof that optimizing production can be just as addictive as any action game. It's demanding mainly on your patience, since rebuilding a working line can eat up an entire evening — but for many players, that's exactly the best part.

pc-modern__super-meat-boy.article:
**Super Meat Boy** is pure distilled essence of the tough platformer: you play a cube of raw meat fighting its way through hundreds of short, lethally dangerous levels to rescue its girlfriend Bandage Girl from the evil Dr. Fetus. Individual levels take only a few seconds on a good run, but you'll die a hundred times before you get there. The game doesn't hide this fact at all — quite the opposite: after completing a level, it plays back a replay showing all your previous attempts pouring across the screen at once, turning mass death into both a joke and a reward.

The controls are precise to a surgical degree. Meat Boy bounces off walls, slides along them, accelerates while sprinting, and everything responds instantly. When you die, the restart comes in a flash with no loading, which keeps up the pace of constant retrying. This very loop of attempt, death, and instant restart became the template for an entire later wave of tough platformers. The level design progresses from simple jumps to contraptions made of circular saws, rocket missiles, and crumbling platforms, and the game regularly introduces new elements without ever resorting to a lengthy tutorial. Bonus worlds and unlockable characters from other independent games were also a nice tribute to the indie scene of the time.

On PC, the title runs smoothly even on very weak machines and offers crisp control with both keyboard and gamepad, though the gamepad turns out to be the most comfortable choice. Visually, the game relies on roughly drawn, comic-book-dark humor, and the music accompanies the action with an energetic rock backdrop that manages to keep the mood up even after your fiftieth failed attempt. After release, Super Meat Boy became one of the symbols of independent game development, and thanks to the documentary Indie Game: The Movie, plenty of people who never played it still know about it. Today it still feels fresh: it's short, tough, fair, and remains one of the best examples of what a platformer built purely on the quality of movement should look like.

pc-modern__cuphead.article:
**Cuphead** looks like a lost cartoon from the 1930s and plays like a merciless shooter. The title hero, whose head is shaped like a mug, loses a bet with the devil and has to collect debts from an entire gallery of debtors in his place, which in practice means one boss fight after another. Most of the game takes place in these very encounters: each boss has several phases, changes shape and attack patterns, and defeating them takes a combination of patience, good memory, and precise reactions. Between fights, the game intersperses classic run-and-gun levels that serve both as a breather and as a source of currency for buying new weapons and abilities.

The gameplay rests on simple but well-tuned foundations. You shoot in eight directions, dash, glide through the air, and parry pink-colored objects to charge your special attack. The choice of weapons and so-called charms then significantly changes your approach to individual bosses, so even after several failures you have ways to tackle the fight differently. The difficulty is high, but attempts are short and the game always drops you right back at the start of the encounter, which keeps you wanting to try again.

Technically, it's an extraordinary piece of work. The animations are hand-drawn, the backgrounds painted in watercolor, and the whole picture is finished off with subtle grain and slight flicker that mimic old film stock. On PC, the game runs smoothly, supports high resolutions, and offers local co-op for two players. The music is live-recorded jazz and big band, which fits the visuals perfectly and contributes decisively to the sense that you're watching an animated cartoon come to life. Cuphead was praised after release primarily for its audiovisual execution and became one of the most distinctive independent titles of its time. The expansion The Delicious Last Course later added a new character and further bosses. Today the game is just as impressive as ever and remains a mandatory stop for anyone who enjoys demanding fights. For less experienced players, there's an easier difficulty setting, which, however, won't let you finish the story — a fitting reminder that this title is meant to be played the hard way.

pc-modern__ori-and-blind-forest.article:
**Ori and the Blind Forest** is a platformer about a small creature of light trying to save the dying forest of Nibel. The story opens with a quiet, purely visual prologue about loss, and from that moment the game regularly alternates calm, melancholic passages with action sequences in which you flee from rising water or a raging inferno. The structure follows the metroidvania genre: the world is interconnected, many paths are initially closed off and only open once you gain a new ability, whether that's a double jump, the ability to bounce off enemy projectiles, or the power to break through walls.

The heart of the gameplay is movement. Ori is remarkably agile, and the core ability, which lets you bounce off a flying projectile or enemy while launching it in the opposite direction, turns both combat and platforming sections into one continuous, fluid dance. The combat system is more of a side feature; the real focus lies in precise jumps and in searching for hidden nooks containing upgrades. The game also uses an interesting save system where you create your own recovery points from limited energy, forcing you to choose between safety and pressing forward. The difficulty is fair but can get genuinely tough during the escape sequences.

Technically, it's one of the most beautiful 2D games of its generation. Hand-painted backgrounds, layered scene depth, and subtle lighting effects shine on PC at high resolution, and the game runs smoothly even on weaker hardware. The orchestral music is an integral part of the experience and carries most of the emotion that the narrative only hints at. The release was praised for its audiovisual craft as well as for its sensitive storytelling without unnecessary words. The Definitive Edition later added new areas and abilities. Today, Ori and the Blind Forest stands as proof that an independent game can offer production values on par with big studios while keeping its own intimate tone. It's best played with a gamepad, since the precise bounces in the escape sequences require very sensitive directional control, and the reward is one of the best-tuned movement systems in 2D gaming.

pc-modern__ori-and-will-of-wisps.article:
**Ori and the Will of the Wisps** continues the story of the light spirit Ori and sends him beyond the boundaries of the familiar forest into a vaster and more hostile land. The narrative is again carried mainly by imagery and music, but this time with greater emphasis on the fates of supporting characters and on a settlement that acts as the world's hub, gradually growing thanks to the tasks you complete for its inhabitants. The structure remains faithful to the metroidvania genre: an interconnected map, gradually unlocked abilities, and plenty of detours that reward curiosity.

Compared to the first game, combat has changed significantly. Ori no longer has just an automatic attack, but a full set of weapons and abilities that you freely assign to buttons, letting you build your own fighting style out of a sword, bow, hammer, and various traps. Full-fledged boss fights were also added, and the escape sequences the predecessor was famous for haven't disappeared either. Movement is even freer than before, and once you gain the advanced abilities, the game turns into an almost continuous flight across the landscape. The save system was changed to automatic checkpoints, which made the game more accessible to a wider audience.

Technically, it's once again top-tier 2D craftsmanship: hand-painted environments, rich lighting effects, and smooth animation, on PC at crisp resolution and with support for high refresh rates. After release, the game suffered performance issues on some setups, which the developers gradually addressed through updates. The orchestral music is once again among the best independent gaming has to offer, and at key moments it carries the full emotional weight of the story. Reception was very warm, and many players consider the sequel better than the original thanks to its richer combat system. Today, the two games form a pair worth playing back to back. Alongside the main story, it also offers optional challenges, races, and hunting quests, so anyone wanting to see absolutely everything will spend roughly twice as much time in the world as with a straight run through the story.

pc-modern__dead-cells.article:
**Dead Cells** combines the interconnected world of a metroidvania with the randomly generated runs of roguelike games, and the result is one of the best-playing action platformers of recent years. You control a shapeless mass of cells that operates a headless body, waking up again and again in the dungeon of an infested island. Each attempt produces a different combination of levels, each death sends you back to the start, but at the same time you permanently unlock new weapons, abilities, and shortcuts, so progress is measured less by how far you've gotten than by everything you're now capable of.

Combat is fast and tactical at once. You carry two main weapons and two skills, and each item has its own behavior, speed, and special traits that can be combined into surprisingly different build strategies. The dodge roll, precisely timed blocks, and knowledge of enemy attack patterns matter more than raw stats. The game also rewards speed: a faster run unlocks hidden rewards, creating tension between caution and greed. Choosing your route between biomes then lets you trade off difficulty against better loot.

Visually, it's an interesting hybrid, with characters modeled in 3D and then converted into pixel form, giving the animation unusual fluidity. On PC, the game runs great even on older hardware, offers high frame rates, and very fast loading, which suits a title built around repetition. The music blends electronic sounds with darker melodies, complementing well the grim yet ironic tone of the writing. Dead Cells launched after a longer stretch in early access, and its creators kept supporting it for years afterward with major free updates as well as paid expansions. Today it ranks among the best entry points into the roguelite genre. Players wanting even more of a challenge can gradually unlock higher difficulty tiers that change enemy placement and healing rules, turning a well-known route into a completely different experience.

pc-modern__shovel-knight.article:
**Shovel Knight** is a tribute to eight-bit platformers that doesn't stop at nostalgia and in many ways surpasses its inspirations. You play a knight armed with a shovel, setting out across the land to defeat an order of evil knights and rescue his lost companion. The structure is classic: a world map, an optional order of several levels, treasures hidden in side paths, and a fight against a distinctive boss at the end of each stage. The shovel serves as both weapon and tool, since a downward pogo-jump lets you bounce off enemies and obstacles much like in the legendary games that inspired it.

The level design is remarkably careful. Every stage introduces its own idea, whether shifting gravity, moving platforms, or an environment that changes shape, and before a motif has a chance to wear thin, the game exhausts it and moves on. Alongside your basic gear you collect relics with secondary abilities and upgrade your armor, so you can choose to be tougher, more mobile, or better armed. The difficulty is well balanced, and the game offers an interesting compromise: checkpoints can be smashed in exchange for treasure, letting you fine-tune the challenge yourself.

The audiovisual side faithfully imitates the NES era, but with larger palettes, smoother scrolling, and effects the hardware of the time could never have handled. On PC the game runs on virtually anything, supports both gamepad and keyboard, and offers display options including aspect ratio. The chiptune music ranks among the most quoted independent soundtracks ever, and many of its tracks hold up well as standalone listening. The project came to life through a successful Kickstarter campaign, and the creators gradually delivered on their promises with sprawling campaigns for each of the evil knights, which together form the Treasure Trove collection. Today Shovel Knight is the standard other retro platformers are measured against. Anyone wanting to see it all faces several full-fledged campaigns, each of which changes movement and combat enough that it feels more like a separate game than a mere expansion.

pc-modern__fez.article:
**Fez** looks at first glance like a charming pixel-art platformer, yet its central idea is far cleverer. Little Gomez receives a magic hat that lets him realize his flat world actually has three dimensions, and from that moment on he can rotate the entire scene in quarter turns around a vertical axis. You still only control a two-dimensional character, but by changing the viewpoint, platforms that seemingly don't connect suddenly join up and open a path to places you couldn't otherwise reach. A simple idea thus becomes a full-fledged space for puzzles.

The game emphasizes discovery rather than skill. Enemies are practically absent, falling won't kill you, and there's nowhere to rush to, so all the tension comes from the question of where to go next and what the strange symbols scattered across the world mean. Besides collecting cubes that unlock further areas, Fez contains a second, much deeper layer of puzzles built around its own alphabet, number system, and ciphers hidden directly in the background. Many players never finish this part alone, and solving it became the subject of a massive collective hunt by the player community at launch.

Technically it's a combination of pixel art with three-dimensional space, and the scene's rotation is accompanied by pleasant animation that explains the whole trick without a single word. On PC the game runs undemanding, offers higher resolution than the original console version, and plays comfortably with a gamepad. The atmosphere owes a great deal to ambient electronic music, dreamy and slightly hazy, which underscores the feeling of wandering through a half-forgotten dream about old games. Fez launched first on console, and its long development became part of the story of the independent scene. Today it remains one of the most original games to ever come out of indie development. Anyone content with the main collectible track will finish the game in a few hours; anyone who dives into decoding the hidden ciphers will spend many times longer with it and will eventually reach for a notepad all the same.

pc-modern__inside.article:
**Inside** is a dark platform adventure in which you control a boy in a red shirt fleeing through a landscape that gradually shifts from forest through research complexes to places that are hard to describe without spoiling them. The game doesn't use a single word, no dialogue or text of any kind, and yet its storytelling is surprisingly clear. Everything is conveyed through the environment, the behavior of background characters, and scenes glimpsed out of the corner of your eye as you keep running. This trust in imagery alone makes Inside one of the strongest examples of wordless storytelling in the entire medium.

The gameplay is deliberately simple. You run, jump, swim, drag crates, and solve physics puzzles that are never there for their own sake and almost always fit into the events around you. The game regularly introduces a new idea, whether controlling other characters, working with a shockwave, or diving into the depths, and each motif is used only as long as it's needed. Tension arises because death comes quickly and often unpleasantly graphically, so even a mundane obstacle carries weight. The whole playthrough lasts roughly four hours, and the game keeps its pace from start to finish.

The visuals rely on a muted palette, strong silhouettes, and lighting that turns every shot into a deliberate composition; the camera stays at a distance, letting the scale of the environment stand out. On PC the game runs smoothly and is technically among the cleanest titles of its kind. Sound matters just as much as image; the music is more a muted pulse than a melody, and in key scenes it works with silence instead. The title followed the same studio's previous game, and its reception was exceptionally warm, especially for its atmosphere and its ambiguous ending, still debated today. Inside still feels perfectly tight today and ranks among the best the independent scene has offered. It works especially well played through in a single sitting, since the pacing of the story is built to let tension grow steadily toward the final stretch.

pc-modern__undertale.article:
**Undertale** starts out as an unassuming retro RPG about a child who falls into an underground realm full of monsters, and it very quickly turns out to be playing with genre conventions on purpose, and cleverly. The core idea is simple: you don't have to kill anyone. Every fight can also be resolved peacefully if you figure out what the monster in question needs, whether that's a compliment, a dance, or simply being left alone. The choice between fighting and mercy affects not only the ending but also the tone of the whole journey and the behavior of characters, who remember your decisions more than you'd expect.

Battles combine a classic turn-based menu with short sequences in which you control a heart and dodge enemy attacks like in a bullet-hell shooter. Every opponent has their own pattern and their own sense of humor, so even repeated encounters never turn into routine. Outside of combat, the game interweaves puzzles, absurd dialogue, and phone calls that make up a large part of its charm. A basic playthrough runs around six to seven hours, but the game expects you to go through it multiple times and in different ways, and it's precisely the repeat playthroughs that reveal its most interesting layers.

The graphics are deliberately modest, pixelated, and at times almost clumsily plain, which sharply contrasts with the confidence of the storytelling. On PC the game runs on anything and has practically no requirements. Music plays a crucial role; its motifs return, transform, and carry most of the emotion at key moments, and quite a few tracks became hugely popular even outside the game itself. Undertale came about after a successful Kickstarter campaign, and after release it became a phenomenon with a huge community of creators and fans. Today it's clear that its influence on independent RPGs and on storytelling that plays with player expectations was enormous. The game also copes very well with players who decide to work around its rules, and it's precisely this readiness for unexpected behavior that makes it a title people still talk about a great deal today.

pc-modern__terraria.article:
**Terraria** is a two-dimensional world you can dig up, rebuild, and refill with your own constructions entirely. You start with a pickaxe, an axe, and a sword in the middle of a randomly generated landscape, where the first night mostly means building yourself some kind of shelter. From there the game unfolds into a remarkably vast adventure: you dig deep for better ores, discover underground temples, deserts, jungles, and strange corrupted regions, and each better piece of gear opens up the next tier of danger. Unlike purely building-focused games, Terraria has a clearly marked path forward, whose milestones are boss fights.

The core of the gameplay is a loop of exploration, mining, crafting, and combat. Equipment recipes are interconnected so that almost every material you find is good for something, and the arsenal ranges from swords and bows through magic staffs to summoned minions, allowing very different playstyles. Settlers gradually move into your world, requiring built houses and offering goods or services in return. After defeating a key boss, the world transforms and offers tougher enemies and better loot, so the second half of the game feels almost like a new campaign.

Technically it's an undemanding title with pixel art graphics that runs on virtually any PC and has always offered comfortable multiplayer, including your own servers. Cooperation is one of its strongest points, since building and expeditions into the depths both work noticeably better in a group. The music is calm and melodic, with distinctive motifs for each biome, and holds the relaxed mood well even during tough fights. Terraria became one of the most successful independent titles ever, and its creators supported it with enormous free updates for many years. Today it offers so much content that a single world can easily keep you busy for dozens of hours. The start can feel confusing, since the game explains very little, but after the first few hours its interconnectedness pays off and you start setting your own goals.

pc-modern__spelunky.article:
**Spelunky** looks like a classic adventure about a treasure hunter in caves, but it's actually a precisely designed game in which every run is generated anew and death means a complete return to the start. You control an explorer equipped with a whip, bombs, and ropes, descending ever deeper while trying to gather as much gold as possible, rescue trapped dogs, and survive encounters with snakes, bats, spiders, and much nastier denizens of the underground. A full run takes only a few dozen minutes at a good pace, but it takes a long time before you're capable of that pace.

The game's strength lies in how honestly all its elements interact with each other. A bomb meant to clear a path can wake a shopkeeper, whose wrath then follows you through the rest of the run. Enemies kill each other, a trap snaps shut on someone other than you, and random confluences of events create stories players still tell to this day. None of it is unfair, because the rules are simple and consistent; the hard part is only keeping a cool head. Progress isn't measured by unlocked gear but by what you've learned, and the game also holds a surprisingly large amount of content in reserve for those who get further than it looks possible at first glance.

The original version began as a freely distributed game with simple graphics; the reworked PC release brought a hand-drawn look, smooth animation, local multiplayer co-op, and an arena mode. Technically it's an undemanding title that runs on anything and loads a new run in an instant. The music is playful and adventurous, creating a sharp contrast with how often you die. Spelunky is often credited as one of the titles that kicked off the modern wave of roguelike games, and its influence is visible in dozens of later projects. Today it still stands as a model of clean, honest design. Anyone who gets past the first caves discovers the game is only just getting started, and the deeper levels offer entirely different environments, enemies, and rules.

pc-modern__hyper-light-drifter.article:
**Hyper Light Drifter** is a top-down action adventure telling the story of an ailing wanderer traveling through a decaying world full of remnants of an ancient catastrophe. The game contains no dialogue or explanatory text whatsoever; the story is conveyed through visual vignettes, wall murals, and the places you pass through, so you fill in much of the narrative yourself. The structure is simple: from a central town you set out in four directions, each with its own environment, enemies, and boss, and along the way you collect modules to upgrade your gear as well as a number of well-hidden secrets.

Combat is fast and unforgiving. You wield an energy sword, a ranged weapon with limited ammunition that you recharge through melee hits, and above all a dash that can be chained into very brisk movement. Enemies die after just a few hits, so you're expected to read their attacks precisely and stay in constant motion. Upgrades noticeably change your playstyle, whether through stronger charged attacks, longer range, or the ability to deflect projectiles back. The game never holds your hand and relies on you exploring the map and its hidden paths yourself.

Audiovisually it's a striking title: pixel art graphics complemented by rich neon colors, strong contrast, and gentle blur, so the result doesn't feel retro so much as a modern illustration. On PC the game runs smoothly and supports a gamepad, which is clearly better suited to its fast combat. Ambient electronic music is a crucial part of the atmosphere, quiet and melancholic in open spaces, oppressive during fights. The project came to life after a highly successful Kickstarter campaign, and after release it earned praise for its style, atmosphere, and combat system. Today it ranks among the titles that influenced an entire wave of later independent top-down action games. Anyone wanting to see everything must explore passages the game never points out in any way, since a significant portion of the gear and story vignettes lies entirely off the main path.

pc-modern__guacamelee.article:
**Guacamelee!** is a colorful platformer inspired by Mexican culture, folk motifs, and above all the world of lucha libre wrestlers. You play the farmer Juan, who after a botched clash with the main villain gains a magic mask along with the abilities of a professional wrestler. The goal is to rescue the mayor's kidnapped daughter, but the main joy comes from the journey itself through an interconnected world full of villages, temples, deserts, and jungles, which opens up gradually as you gain new moves.

Combat here matters just as much as movement, which sets the game apart from most metroidvanias. You slam enemies to the ground, launch them into the air, and chain hits and special moves onto them that are also used to smash colored blocks in the environment. Every new attack thus serves both combat and exploration, and because colored barriers require a specific move, fights are often a puzzle about the right order of strikes. The second main mechanic is switching between the world of the living and the dead, where platforms in one plane appear while vanishing in the other. In more complex passages you switch mid-jump, leading to inventive and demanding platforming sequences.

The visuals rely on flat vector graphics with rich colors and bold outlines, so the game looks sharp at any resolution and runs entirely without demands on PC. The music mixes Latin American motifs with electronic elements and holds a brisk pace well. Humor is ever-present, including plenty of references to other games and internet culture, which will land better with some players than others. The title also supports local multiplayer co-op. Reception was very favorable, especially for the combination of combat with exploration, and the game received both an expanded version and a sequel. Today it ranks among the more brisk and accessible representatives of the genre. Difficulty rises considerably in the later platforming passages, and the closing stretches rank among the most demanding the genre has to offer, so there's certainly no shortage of challenge.

pc-modern__bastion.article:
**Bastion** is a top-down action RPG set in a world shattered by a mysterious calamity. You play as a young man called the Kid, who wakes up amid the ruins and sets out to find fragments that could restore the last remaining refuge. The most striking feature is the narrator, who comments on practically everything you do, including your falls, your weapon choices, and how you decide to deal with defeated enemies. What would be a mere gimmick elsewhere becomes the game's central storytelling device here, one that manages to be both funny and surprisingly moving.

The gameplay is built on combat in small floating levels that literally assemble themselves beneath your feet as you move forward. You always carry two weapons out of a fairly wide selection, from hammers and rifles to bows and more exotic pieces, plus a special attack and a block ability that lets you deflect projectiles back at enemies. Weapons can be upgraded, and the game features a system of shrines where you voluntarily raise the difficulty in exchange for better rewards, an elegant way to fine-tune the experience. Alongside the main story there are also challenge arenas where you can compete with individual weapons.

The audiovisual side is the main reason many people remember this game. The hand-painted art, rich with color, feels like an illustration brought to life, and on PC the game runs smoothly even on older hardware. The music blends acoustic instruments with American and folk motifs, and together with two sung tracks it ranks among the best-reviewed soundtracks of its era. Bastion was its studio's first title, and its success opened the door to further projects that kept the same emphasis on storytelling, style, and music. Today it feels shorter and simpler than the same creators' later games, but its atmosphere and the narrator's voice have aged remarkably well. A playthrough takes roughly eight hours, and the game also offers a New Game Plus mode that keeps your gear, which is fitting, since the narration reveals another layer on a second run.

pc-modern__katana-zero.article:
**Katana ZERO** is a fast-paced action platformer about a katana-wielding hitman who can see the near future and replay it until he finds a path that lets him survive. This ability translates elegantly into gameplay: every room is essentially a puzzle you solve through trial and error, since a single hit means death and an instant restart. Once you manage to clear an entire floor, the game shows you a replay of the whole action in one seamless take, instantly turning a string of embarrassing failures into an impressive action-movie scene.

Combat is simple but highly expressive. You slash with your katana, deflect bullets back at shooters, dodge-roll, throw objects, and slow down time in a pinch. Enemies are just as fragile as you are, so milliseconds and knowledge of the layout decide everything. Alongside the action, the game devotes considerable space to dialogue, where you can interrupt the speaker and choose responses, which affects the tone and even certain scenes. The narrative is fragmentary, dealing with trauma, medication, and memory loss, and leaves plenty of questions open, including the ending itself.

Visually it's pixel art with a bold neon palette, strong lighting, and effects reminiscent of damaged video footage. On PC the game runs with virtually no hardware demands and offers smooth movement along with comfortable control via gamepad or keyboard. The music is synthetic, pulsing, and tuned to an aesthetic associated with the eighties, and together with the visuals it forms a very cohesive whole. The game contains pronounced stylized violence, so it's definitely not for everyone. On release it earned praise for its combat system, pacing, and its willingness to tell a nonlinear story. Today it stands among the best-playing examples of the fast-platformer genre where a single hit means the end. A full playthrough takes only a few hours, but the game invites replaying, since the same room can be solved dozens of ways, and the pursuit of the most elegant solution is its own reward.

pc-modern__max-payne.article:
**Max Payne** brought a cinematic noir detective story to PC in 2001, about a New York cop whose wife and daughter were murdered by unknown assailants. The hero sinks into the underworld surrounding a synthetic drug called Valkyr, loses his badge and his name, and fights his way through a series of shootouts across a frozen, wintry New York against the people pulling the strings. The narration carries a bitterly ironic first-person monologue full of similes and metaphors, and instead of animated cutscenes, the story is advanced through static comic-book panels with voiced narration. The result is a game that feels like an interactive version of a dark crime novel.

Mechanically, everything is built around bullet time, the ability to slow down time while still aiming with the mouse at normal speed. Paired with that is the sideways diving jump with mid-air shooting, which became the game's iconic move. The levels are narrow, precisely designed arenas full of wooden furniture, barrels, and glass surfaces that shatter into pieces during a firefight. The arsenal ranges from pistols and shotguns to submachine guns and a sniper rifle, ammunition is always just tight enough, and the game forces the player to plan which room to storm and in what order to take down opponents. Several feverish dream sequences break up the shooter's rhythm and remain among the genre's most memorable scenes to this day.

Technically, it was a showcase of what PCs of the time could do: a custom engine with dynamic lighting, dense particle effects, and scanned faces, with the studio's own screenwriter lending his likeness to Max. The audio rests on a spare, mournfully sounding main theme and the raw noise of wind and city. Critics received the game very well, and bullet time became a commonly used mechanic in action games and beyond within just a few years. Today Max Payne is shorter, more straightforward, and in places brutally difficult, but thanks to its very austerity and style it has aged far better than most of its contemporaries, and it runs without trouble on modern PCs.

pc-modern__need-for-speed-most-wanted.article:
**Need for Speed: Most Wanted** is a 2005 racing game that combined street-car tuning with police chases in a single open city. The player starts with no car and no reputation, and the goal is to climb the Blacklist of fifteen most-wanted racers all the way to the top. Each duel for a position requires not just won races but also so-called pursuit points, so the game directly pushes the player into conflict with the police. The framing story about a stolen car and betrayal is simple, but the live-action footage with its strong bluish filter gives it exactly the swaggering atmosphere that the tuning scene of the era had.

The driving model is arcade-style but has a surprisingly well-readable sense of weight; cars slide, heavy vehicles throw themselves into corners, and nitro gives a short, powerful kick. The heart of the fun is the police chases, which escalate from a single patrol car all the way up to heavily armored units, roadblocks, and a helicopter. The city is dotted with traps that can be triggered, from collapsing towers to gas stations, and a well-timed activation can take out an entire convoy at once. On top of that there's deeper tuning, visual customization, and racing disciplines ranging from sprints and circuits to drag racing and checkpoint runs.

On PC the game ran smoothly even on then-average machines, and its visuals, with pronounced motion blur and an overexposed sky, became a signature look for the whole series. The engine sounds are loud and aggressive, the soundtrack mixes rock with electronic music, and it contributes a great deal to the sense of speed. Reception was very positive, and Most Wanted long remained a fan-favorite entry that later games in the series consciously referenced. Today it looks visually dated, and the color filter is intense to the point of fatigue, but the driving itself and the tension of the chases still work. For a lot of players it remains the entry against which every other Need for Speed is measured.

pc-modern__dead-space.article:
**Dead Space** sends the player, in the role of engineer Isaac Clarke, aboard the massive mining ship USG Ishimura, which has stopped responding to hails. Instead of a crew, silence awaits, along with blood on the walls and transformed humans the game calls necromorphs. The entire story unfolds within the confines of a single ship, which the player gradually comes to know deck by deck, and that gives the horror a tight, claustrophobic logic. Isaac stays silent for most of the game, and his motivation is personal: he's looking for his partner, who served aboard the ship. The sci-fi setting is meanwhile interwoven with a religious cult and with what truly drives its followers.

Combat rests on an unusual idea. Necromorphs don't die from a headshot; you have to blow off their limbs, so even a basic plasma cutter demands precise aiming as you alternate horizontal and vertical cuts. Alongside that there's stasis to slow down an opponent and kinesis to hurl objects, turning workshop tools into weapons. All the interface is rendered directly in the world: health glows on the suit's spine, ammo count displays above the weapon, and the map and inventory are projected as a hologram in space, all without pausing the game. That does away with the classic HUD, and the player never drops out of the tension.

Technically, the Ishimura is masterfully designed, with dark corridors, flickering lights, and passages in zero gravity and vacuum where all you can hear is Isaac's breathing. Sound is really the game's main weapon; the handling of silence, of metal creaking, and of footsteps somewhere overhead is textbook-perfect, and the music is used sparingly, hitting all the harder for it. Critics received the game excellently, and Dead Space quickly became one of the foundational modern sci-fi horror titles, influencing a number of successors. Today its pace is slower than that of today's action games, but that suits it well; on PC it runs without issues, and the fear of what might crawl out of the vent works exactly the same as it did at release.

pc-modern__amnesia-dark-descent.article:
**Amnesia: The Dark Descent** is a first-person horror game in which the player wakes up in a corridor of the Prussian castle Brennenburg with no memory, and with only one piece of information they wrote for themselves on a note: they must descend and find the castle's owner. The game has no combat whatsoever. The player has no weapon, cannot fight back, and the only response to a monster is to hide in shadow, close a door, or run and hope you know the way. It's precisely this stripping away of all the player's power that makes walking through a dark cellar a far heavier experience than the horror shooters of the time offered.

The main mechanic alongside light is sanity. Staying in darkness, looking at a monster, and witnessing disturbing sights gradually break down the hero's mind; the screen warps, sounds distort, and eventually the character collapses. Light protects sanity, but oil for the lantern and boxes of matches remain scarce, so the player is constantly weighing whether to light up and see, or conserve resources and crawl along blind. Interaction with the world is physics-based: doors open by dragging with the mouse, rubble is cleared by hand, and puzzles rely on actual manipulation of objects rather than choosing from a menu.

Technically, this was the work of a small team, yet thanks to its environments, its handling of shadows, and outstanding sound design it hit harder than many far more expensive titles. Sound is the single most important component here; footsteps somewhere around the corner, breathing in the dark, and a musical undercurrent that swells right when something approaches do most of the work. Amnesia had a major impact on the entire genre, kicked off a wave of weapon-less horror games, and became one of the first great phenomena of internet reaction videos. Today it's visually modest, but its atmosphere and tension have aged minimally, and it can still make a player quit the game before they meant to. For newcomers to the genre it's also a good entry point, since it demands no skill with controls, only the courage to go one more corridor deeper; anyone looking for classic jump scares around every corner, on the other hand, may be disappointed, since Amnesia works more through sustained, slowly mounting pressure.

pc-modern__just-cause-2.article:
**Just Cause 2** sends agent Rico Rodriguez to the fictional Southeast Asian island state of Panau to destabilize its regime, back three rival factions, and find his missing mentor. The story is exaggerated action pulp that never takes itself seriously, and mostly serves as an excuse for a massive open world made up of jungles, deserts, snowy mountains, cities, and military bases. Progress through the game is measured in chaos: the player destroys fuel tanks, satellite dishes, radar installations, and statues of the dictator, unlocking further missions and territory. It's a sandbox in the purest sense, where the main reward is the freedom to cause mayhem.

All of this is held together by a pair of tools that make Rico one of the most mobile characters in any game. An unlimited parachute can be opened at any time, and a grappling hook can pull the player toward anything, latch onto a plane in flight, or tie two objects together, letting you tether a soldier to a passing car or a helicopter to a tower. Combining the hook and the parachute creates fluid movement in which the player barely touches the ground, and on top of that, virtually every vehicle can be commandeered, from scooters and speedboats to airliners and fighter jets.

On PC the game was, at the time, among the best-looking things around, thanks especially to its enormous draw distance, letting you see half the island from a mountaintop, and to surprisingly good-looking water and vegetation. The world is one of the largest to appear in an action game up to that point, and it runs without any loading screens. Critics praised the freedom of movement and the explosive physics, while faulting repetitive tasks and a weak story. Today Just Cause 2 is still excellent as a playground; anyone looking for a story will be disappointed, but anyone looking for an hour of goofing around with a hook and a parachute gets exactly what they came for. The game also still lives on thanks to community mods, the most famous of which added full multiplayer to Panau for large numbers of players at once, turning the island into one giant collective playground full of explosions.

pc-modern__no-man-s-sky.article:
**No Man's Sky** is a space sandbox built on a procedurally generated galaxy, in which the player, after crashing their ship on an unknown planet, repairs its engines, gathers resources, and takes off above the atmosphere for the first time. From there, there's no invisible wall: you can fly to a neighboring planet, to another system, and theoretically all the way to the galaxy's center. Every planet has its own fauna, flora, weather, and mineral composition, with some being paradise-like and others toxic or cold enough that surviving outside for even a few minutes requires constantly recharging your suit's protection. The game is heavily about calm exploration and about naming whatever the player discovers first.

The gameplay loop combines exploration with crafting and trade. The player mines elements, uses them to build upgrades for their suit, multi-tool, and ship, seeks out better vessels at wrecks and stations, and trades between systems with differing prices. Alongside that there's building ground bases, mining resources, managing a freighter with its own fleet, and a multilayered story about the galaxy's origin and the beings watching over it. Combat takes place both on the surface against robots guarding nature and in space against pirates, though action is never the main reason to play.

The 2016 launch was rocky, since the finished game didn't match what players had been promised by the early demos. The studio kept fixing and expanding it over the years through major free updates that added co-op, base building, land vehicles, VR support, and a range of other systems, so today's version is incomparably richer than the original. Visually the game rests on saturated, almost poster-like colors and on music that shifts dynamically with the environment, fitting perfectly with slow gliding over an alien landscape. Today it's one of the best examples of how long-term care can save a game. On PC it runs well even on older hardware, offers ultrawide monitor support, and suits both a few relaxing evenings and hundreds of hours spent building your own space empire equally well.

pc-modern__guild-wars-2.article:
**Guild Wars 2** is an MMORPG set in the world of Tyria that, on release in 2012, deliberately tried to break several genre conventions. There's no monthly subscription, just buy the client, and there's no classic holy trinity of tank, healer, and damage dealer; every profession has its own way to defend, heal, and support others. The story begins with a choice of race and personal questions that shape your own narrative thread, and continues with a shared campaign against ancient dragons. The world is colorful, visually striking, and full of places that invite exploration rather than checklist-ticking.

Instead of classic quest boards, the content in the world is built on dynamic events. When a player arrives at a spot where centaurs are attacking a village, they simply join in, and everyone who contributed gets a reward. Nobody competes over killing the same enemies, and players help each other completely naturally. Event outcomes also change the surroundings, so a lost village defense has consequences. Combat is mobile, with dodging, combo fields, and weapons that directly determine available skills. Alongside this, the game offers extensive PvP, massive three-server battles over fortresses, and a deep layer of cosmetic progression.

Technically, this is a game that has aged well thanks to its stylized art direction, and even today on a modern PC it looks good and runs smoothly, though large battles put a strain mainly on the processor. The soundtrack is unusually rich, orchestral, and carries strong themes for the big moments. Reception was very positive, mainly thanks to its accessibility and subscription-free model. The game has since received several major expansions and is still ongoing, so a new player today gets an enormous amount of content and an MMO that doesn't force them to complete chores every evening. That very relaxedness is the main reason players return to it after years: just log in, join the first event you stumble across on the way, and the evening is filled without any need to plan anything ahead.

pc-modern__outlast.article:
**Outlast** puts the player in the role of journalist Miles Upshur, who breaks into the remote Mount Massive psychiatric hospital to verify an anonymous tip about what's happening there. Inside, he finds a facility in ruins, dead staff, and patients who are after him. The game is entirely first-person, the player cannot fight or defend themselves, and the only piece of equipment is a camera. The narrative is built from what's visible in the corridors, from notes Miles writes himself, and from documents he finds; the game explains little and relies on the player piecing the rest together.

The entire tension rests on the camera's night vision. Most of the hospital is pitch black, and without the camera the player sees nothing at all, yet night vision drains batteries that must be found in cabinets and on desks throughout. This creates a constant dilemma between seeing now and saving a reserve for later, and the green-white image with its own faint grain is the game's signature look. Fleeing a pursuer is physical: tipping a cabinet over behind you, crawling under a bed or into a locker, vaulting over obstacles, and above all knowing the route. A mistake made in panic usually means death and repeating the whole passage.

Technically, this was, for its time, a very good-looking game from a smaller studio that leaned on dense lighting, detailed interiors, and a loud, grimy sound design. Sound is by far the strongest thing Outlast has going for it; footsteps behind a wall, labored breathing, and musical stingers at jump scares are timed precisely. The game was well received and, along with other titles of the era, defined a wave of horror games where the player just runs and films it. It's short, very brutal, and leans heavily on jump scares in places, but as a tight, intense ride for one or two evenings it still works excellently today. On PC it has practically no technical demands, runs smoothly even on weaker rigs, and combined with headphones and a darkened room it can create an atmosphere that pricier horror productions often struggle to find.

pc-modern__alien-isolation.article:
**Alien: Isolation** is a first-person horror game in which Amanda Ripley heads to the remote space station Sevastopol following the trail of her missing mother. Instead of the answers she expected, she finds a crumbling structure, terrified survivors, aggressive androids, and a single alien that cannot be killed. The game deliberately follows the atmosphere of the 1979 original film, meaning a future full of boxy monitors, blinking lights, and analog switches, rather than the action-oriented approach of later sequels. The result is a slow, oppressive horror about hiding and survival.

The core is the behavior of the alien itself, which does not move along a fixed path and reacts to sound as well as to what the player does. The motion tracker shows only an approximate direction, and it also quietly beeps on its own, making its use risky. The player hides under desks and in lockers, distracts the creature by throwing objects, crafts smoke bombs, noisemakers, and a flamethrower from scavenged scrap that can only drive the creature off, never defeat it. On top of that there's hacking terminals, prying doors open with a crowbar, and constantly reading logs that piece together the crew's fate. Saving is only possible at designated points, which makes every stretch of corridor you cross feel dramatic.

Technically, the game is a rare case where the visuals serve the atmosphere above all: grainy image, reflections on glass, smoke in cones of light, and a UI styled after old screens. The sound is masterful, from the roar of ventilation through clanking in overhead shafts to music that directly quotes the style of the source film. Reception was very good, though some reviews criticized its length and difficulty. Today, Alien: Isolation is considered one of the best film adaptations in games and a horror title that can keep the player tense for dozens of hours. On PC it's also very well optimized, so even a common rig runs it smoothly at high resolution, which only helps its carefully constructed atmosphere.

pc-modern__elder-scrolls-online.article:
**The Elder Scrolls Online** transforms the world of Tamriel into a large online RPG set long before the events of Skyrim. The player picks a race and alliance, starts out as a prisoner in the realm of a Daedric prince, and gradually travels through provinces the series has so far only shown individually. The main story is a classic fantasy save-the-world plot, but the game's real strength lies in dozens of smaller zone stories, written and voiced with a care much closer to a single-player RPG than what's typical for an MMO. Exploring, reading books, and finding caves feels exactly as a fan of the series would expect.

System-wise, the game is surprisingly open. Race and class determine only part of your abilities; the rest is built around the weapon and armor you use, so practically any class can be built as offensive, defensive, or healing. Combat is action-oriented, with blocking, spell interruption, and dodging, and the hotbar only holds a few abilities, forcing thoughtful loadout choices. Enemy levels scale to the player, so you can go practically anywhere and play with anyone. Alongside the story, the game offers extensive dungeons, twelve-player trials, massive PvP battles over keeps in Cyrodiil, fishing, thieving, player housing, and deep crafting.

Technically, this is a demanding MMO that looks good on a modern PC, mainly thanks to its city architecture and atmospheric effects, though it requires a decent processor in areas with lots of players. The music follows the series' sound and, in some zones, ranks among the best the genre has to offer. The game's launch was rocky, but the studio reshaped it over several years, dropped the mandatory monthly subscription, and regularly added major chapters. Today it's one of the most extensive MMOs on the market, and for Elder Scrolls fans, the largest available slice of Tamriel there is. What's pleasant for a new player is that they can start practically anywhere and play only the stories that interest them, since individual chapters aren't as tightly linked as you'd expect from such a sprawling game.

pc-modern__assetto-corsa.article:
**Assetto Corsa** is a racing simulator from an Italian studio that quickly became a benchmark among PC players with a wheel after release. The game has no career built around a big story or racing spectacle; its core is the most faithful possible driving model, precisely scanned tracks, and the ability to customize practically anything. The roster includes both road and race cars, from small hatchbacks to formula and GT machines, and tracks that were laser-scanned to match real-world bumps and gradients. The main activity is driving against the clock, chasing the ideal line, and gradually mastering individual circuits.

The driving model is uncompromising. Tires have a noticeable operating temperature window, weight transfer under braking is pronounced, and a car loses grip exactly the way it would in reality; an axle that starts to slide won't wait for you. Steering wheel force feedback is among the cleanest in the genre, and a lot of information about lateral slip reaches the player directly through their hands, so you drive by feel rather than by gauges. On top of that there's detailed gearing, tire pressure, stiffness, and downforce setup, telemetry, and the ability to play with either a wheel or a gamepad, though the former is clearly the game's home turf.

Graphically, the game wasn't cutting-edge at release, but it ran smoothly and offered a stable image even in VR, which extended its lifespan considerably. Engine sound is honest, and driving without music, with only the crackle of the exhaust and the wail of tires, is where the experience is strongest. Its greatest strength, however, is the modding community, which added a massive number of tracks, cars, and visual overhauls to Assetto Corsa, pushing the game far beyond its original form. That's exactly why, years later and despite newer entries, it remains one of the most played simulators on PC. Entry is tough for a beginner, and without a wheel much of its quality is lost, but for anyone willing to put in the setup work and truly learn one track, the experience is closer to reality than any arcade racing game.

pc-modern__dirt-rally.article:
**DiRT Rally** is the series' return to hardcore rally simulation, released in 2015 initially, and surprisingly, in early access without much fanfare. The game abandoned the spectacle, jumps, and arcade tone of previous entries and focused on a single thing: driving down a narrow special stage where everything depends on the player and their co-driver. The stages are long, often over ten kilometers, running through snowy Wales, gravel Greece, or Finnish dirt, and can't be memorized right away, so the player really has to listen to the pace notes. The career progresses from old cars to modern four-wheel-drive machines and championships around the world.

The driving model is demanding and unforgiving. The car carries inertia on gravel that must be anticipated, braking on the edge of a drop-off ends in the guardrails, and one botched corner can wreck the cooling or the dampers, because damage is permanent and repairs are handled within a limited time at the service area. There's no rewinding time, so a mistake means a loss you have to drive out to the finish with. Alongside rally, the game offers rallycross on real arenas and hillclimbs up Pikes Peak. Over time an online mode with daily and weekly challenges was added, keeping the game alive.

Technically, it was an excellently optimized game that, on PC, offered a sharp image, convincing surfaces, and changeable weather. Sound is one of its strongest points; the noise of gravel flying into the wheel arches, the muffled roar of the engine in the cabin, and the co-driver's calm voice create an unusually intense focus. Critics and players received it very well precisely because it finally offered a seriously intended rally game on PC, and its successor expanded the concept further. Today, DiRT Rally remains one of the best ways to experience why rally is considered the toughest motorsport discipline. On a modern PC it runs without issue even at high resolution, and with a wheel, or at least sensitive gamepad triggers, it offers a focused drive after which the player really does take a deep breath at the finish.

pc-modern__devil-may-cry-5.article:
**Devil May Cry 5** is the stylish action series' return after a long break, and probably the purest showcase of what combat built on elegance looks like. A demonic tree has grown out of the city center, draining blood from its inhabitants, and three playable characters stand against it: young Nero with his interchangeable mechanical arms, the mysterious newcomer V, who fights exclusively through summoned demons, and the veteran Dante with his entire arsenal. The story is an over-the-top, confidently ridiculous spectacle full of posturing, but it holds together and, for series fans, closes several long-open threads.

Gameplay-wise, it's a combination of swords, firearms, and abilities that the game grades after every fight based on how inventive it was and whether the player kept repeating the same thing or got hit too much. Chasing a higher rank is exactly what drives the whole game and leads to constantly trying new combinations. Each character plays noticeably differently; Nero handles distance with a grappling hook and one-use Devil Breakers, V merely directs a panther and a bird and finishes off weakened enemies himself, while Dante switches between several combat styles and weapons on the fly, making him the most complex but also the deepest choice.

On PC the game runs exceptionally well, since it's built on the studio's modern in-house engine, delivering a sharp, detailed image at high frame rates even on a mid-range rig. Characters and environments use photogrammetry, so faces look almost unsettlingly real, which contrasts with the utterly over-the-top action. The music blends metal with electronic elements and dynamically ramps up during fights based on your rank, so the reward for a good performance is a louder chorus, too. Critics received the game excellently, and today it's considered one of the genre's high points and an ideal entry point into the series even for newcomers. Anyone content with just clearing the story gets a brisk few evenings of action; but anyone who starts learning the combos and chasing the top rank can return to the same levels for many dozens more hours.

pc-modern__subnautica.article:
**Subnautica** begins with a spaceship crash-landing on an alien planet covered in ocean. The player survives in an escape pod with an empty inventory, an empty stomach, and nothing around but water. The first hours are about gathering resources in the shallows, finding drinking water, and fearing what lies beyond the edge of the lit zone. The game never pushes you anywhere, has no classic quests, and is oriented by radio messages and data logs the player finds on wrecks or in stations. Gradually it becomes clear the planet has its own history, and the reason nobody has ever left is far older than the crash itself.

The entire progression is vertical. To get deeper, the player needs better oxygen tanks, a more resilient suit, and above all vehicles they build themselves: the small one-seat Seamoth, the lumbering walking exosuit, and finally a giant submarine that serves as a mobile base. Building your own bases is a full-fledged system with pressure control, power from solar, thermal, or nuclear sources, and greenhouses. The game deliberately has no firearms, so encounters with large creatures are handled by evasion, distraction, or flight. That's exactly what makes descending into dark trenches one of the most nerve-wracking things survival games have to offer.

Technically, this is a game with a rich, color-layered world where every depth has its own fauna, flora, and light, which is key for orientation. Underwater sound is muffled, breathing inside the suit ticks off time, and a distant roar somewhere in the dark is the most effective horror element the game has, without ever presenting itself as horror. Reception was very good, and Subnautica became one of the few survival titles with a genuine ending and narrative. Today it ranks among the best exploration games on PC, especially for players afraid of the deep. On PC it has no heavy demands, though older versions occasionally suffered from terrain pop-in, and it also offers a relaxed mode without hunger or thirst for those who just want to explore and build without survival pressure.

pc-modern__sekiro-shadows-die-twice.article:
**Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice** takes players to a fantastical version of Japan at the end of the Sengoku period, where a one-armed shinobi serves a young lord whose cursed blood grants immortality. When the boy is kidnapped, the hero sets out to find him, journeying through a mountain temple, a fortified town, a flooded village, and a place that has little left in common with reality. The storytelling is more direct than in the studio's earlier games, the hero speaks and has a clear motivation, but the world is still explained mainly through environment, short conversations, and item descriptions.

Combat is the biggest change. It isn't about dodging or stats, but about holding your ground: every successful parry right before a blow lands chips away at the opponent's posture, and once their gauge fills, a lethal finishing blow follows. Combat therefore feels like a rhythmic exchange of strikes, in which the player must read the types of attacks and respond with a jump, a parry, or a counterattack. Add to that the grappling hook, which completely changes movement through the levels, allowing quick traversal across rooftops and full-fledged stealth with silent kills. Death, moreover, is not final — the hero can rise once, right in the middle of combat, though this has consequences for the surrounding world.

Technically the game runs very well on PC, and its visual side ranks among the best the studio has ever produced; mist over a valley, snow, red autumn foliage, and thunderstorms give every location its own mood. The music builds on Japanese instruments and shifts into fierce drumming during boss fights. Critics received the game superbly, praising above all the courage to abandon a proven formula. Sekiro is demanding and uncompromising, with no difficulty options and no way to sidestep combat through stats, but that is precisely why mastering it is one of the strongest feelings today's action games can offer. Anyone able to unlearn reflexes from other action RPGs and accept that the only way forward is through deflecting the opponent's blow will find one of the best-tuned combat systems of recent years.
